**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS, WHETHER LATIN OR GREEK, WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF THE COUNCIL OF TRENT (1545) FOR LATIN AUTHORS, AND OF THE COUNCIL OF FLORENCE (1439) FOR GREEK AUTHORS: A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL EXTANT MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THROUGH THE FIRST FIFTEEN CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH AND BEYOND, ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COMPARED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES, AND MOST DILIGENTLY CORRECTED; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED WITH ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST COPIOUS EDITIONS COMPLETED IN THE THREE MOST RECENT CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDICES FOLLOWING INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ADORNED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AS ALSO WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF INDIVIDUAL PAGES AND INDICATING THEIR SUBJECT MATTER; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL, PROVIDED THAT THEY POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY WITH RESPECT TO ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH MORE THAN TWO HUNDRED INDICES OF AUTHORS AND WORKS—ALPHABETICAL, CHRONOLOGICAL, STATISTICAL, SYNTHETIC, ANALYTICAL, ANALOGICAL—CONCERNING EVERY DOGMATIC, MORAL, LITURGICAL, CANONICAL, DISCIPLINARY, HISTORICAL, AND EVERY OTHER POINT OF RELIGION WITHOUT EXCEPTION; BUT ABOVE ALL WITH TWO IMMENSE AND GENERAL INDICES, ONE OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH ONE MAY SEE AT A GLANCE WHATEVER not merely this or that Father, but every one of the Fathers, without even one omitted, has written on any theme whatsoever; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented upon each verse of each book of Scripture, from the first of Genesis to the last of the Apocalypse. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS, if one weighs the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient form of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the whole course of Patrology, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but for the first time gathered together in our library from works and manuscripts belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**FIRST LATIN SERIES, IN WHICH APPEAR THE LATIN FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE CHURCH FROM TERTULLIAN TO INNOCENT III: edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical science. Patrology, after the pattern of the Church itself, is divided into two parts: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin part, now entirely printed, comprises, in its first series, two hundred and twenty-five volumes, and will shortly be complete after the indices have been finished; it is sold for 1,125 francs. The Greek part has been published in two editions. The first contains the Greek text together with a facing Latin translation, and extends to one hundred and sixty-one volumes, but without indices; the latter presents this translation alone and is therefore confined within fifty-five volumes. Both had appeared in their entirety by 24 December 1860. Each Greek-Latin volume is purchased for eight francs; each purely Latin volume for only five francs. Yet, in either case, in order that the purchaser may enjoy the benefit of this price, it is necessary to buy the complete collection, whether Greek or Latin: the larger edition consists of 326 volumes and the smaller, without indices, of 272 volumes. Otherwise, the varying size and difficulty of individual volumes will entail different prices. Nevertheless, should anyone purchase entire and separately either the Greek-Latin collection or the same collection translated from Greek into Latin, he will obtain each volume for nine or six francs respectively. These conditions apply to the series of Patrology not yet printed.**

# Special Indices of the Latin Patrology

## Twenty-first Series of Indices

[Col. 0009]

[PREFACE.]

This twenty-first series comprises matters pertaining to the art of preaching or homiletics. First, various statements of the Holy Fathers concerning the ministry of preaching and its necessity, rules, and effects are collected; thereafter a fourfold synopsis lists all sermons on the Scriptures according to canonical order; sermons on the Seasons, that is, according to the course of the year, from the first Sunday of Advent to the last Sunday after Pentecost; sermons on the Saints, in alphabetical order of names; and sermons on Miscellaneous Subjects, according to a series of topics at once logical and analogical. The homilies are arranged in the same manner. In addition, we provide a sermon index to the Epistles and Gospels read in the solemnities of Mass during the course of the year, recording the various explanations, sermons, and homilies appropriate to the elucidation of each Epistle or Gospel. With the aid of these indices, therefore, every reader will be able immediately and at a glance to know whether the Fathers have treated a given subject, which Fathers have done so, how often, and in which volume they have dealt with this or that matter. From these collections, consequently, as from a most abundant and perennial spring, the reader may confidently draw an abundance of material for sermons, whether less or more highly polished.

## CLXXXV. INDEX ON PREACHING

### NOTICE

This index treats successively: I. The necessity of preaching. II. Its nature and effects. III. Its rules. IV. Its subject matter. V. The minister of preaching. VI. His virtues. VII. His learning. VIII. The preacher’s office. IX. Things a preacher must avoid. X. The hearer of preaching.

### [INDEX ON PREACHING]

#### I.—On the necessity of preaching

A bishop of the Church owes the ministry of evangelical preaching, St. Hilary, X, 158.—One must not desist from persistence in preaching, St. Augustine, XLIII, 450.—The priest is bound to preach and to cry out vehemently, id., XXXIX, 1814.—Preaching must not be neglected, even though God gives the increase, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 363.—On the necessity of preaching, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 960.—It is a crime to deny the bread of the word to the hungry and medicine to the sick, id., LXXVII, 96.—Likewise, it is a crime not to heal the wounds of minds by the incision of words, ibid.—Let the priest always possess the voice of preaching, lest through silence he incur the judgment of the heavenly Inspector, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 829.—“Preach out of season, in season,” Alcuin, C, 203.—Let no worldly power or vanity impede their voice, ibid.—One must always apply oneself to preaching, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 394.—Teaching belongs to necessity, delighting to pleasantness, and moving to victory, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 408.—The preacher who does not sow the seed of the divine word incurs the punishment of eternal damnation, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 228.—The Lord wills that one who preaches should not merely cry aloud, but should also not cease from crying aloud, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 977.—The necessity of preaching, Alan of Lille, CCX, 613.

#### II.—On the nature and effects of preaching

[Col. 0012]

Preaching, by which bodily wounds are sewn up and death itself is pierced, St. Hilary, IX, 1027.—When it [preaching] has been received as food, the bonds of the devil are loosed, ibid., 867.—Such food also releases the fetters of avarice, lust, and drunkenness, ibid.—By preaching the word of God, as by arrows, the devil’s kingdom is overthrown, ibid., 850.—For the priest’s preaching among the people is correction for those to be saved and testimony against those to be judged, St. Ambrose, XVII, 689.—Evangelical preaching crushes hostile powers and spiritual wickedness exalting itself against the knowledge of God, St. Jerome, XXIV, 416.—Let the preacher crush the most hardened hearts of unbelievers, ibid., 416.—Let the tears of your hearers be your praises, id., XXII, 534.—From this will arise the power of preaching, id., XXVI, 33.—Preaching is of no avail without grace working inwardly, St. Augustine, XLI, 442.—We speak, but God teaches, id., XXXVIII, 825.—The preacher of the word works in the ears; God works in the heart, ibid., 376.—The word of God is nothing less than the body of Christ, id., XXXIX, 2319.—The preacher builds invincible fortresses in human hearts against the devil, ibid., 1539.—On the power of preaching, ibid., 1118.—The power of priestly preaching for overcoming iniquity, ibid., 2206.—It provides remedies for the sick and devises ornaments for the healthy, ibid., 2321.—By preaching God, we are said to bless him, Cassiodorus, LXX, 514.—The word of preaching is seed in the heart of the hearer, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 808.—When preaching is withdrawn, the heart withers, ibid., 960.—The fruit of evangelical preaching, ibid., 854.—What are the effects of preaching upon the minds of the weak, ibid., 1319.—The watering of preaching, like a torrent, divides the good from the evil, ibid., 63.—They shake, terrify, enlighten, and inflame the hearts of those who behold, ibid., 827.—It belongs to preachers to cut branches from trees and spread them in the way for Christ, ibid., 985.—The preacher who separates the precious from the worthless, ibid., 67.—They strive more to rebuke than to console, ibid., 269.—Inspired by God, preachers water and give light, St. Gregory the Great, ibid., 434.—The preacher’s tongue heals the wounds of our mind, ibid., 1302.—Preachers not only restrain themselves from vices, but also prevent others from sinning, lead them to faith, and so forth, ibid., 977.—It belongs to preachers to catch foxes—that is, heretics—for Christ, id., LXXIX, 500.—Preaching is useless without the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, id., LXXVI, 437.—Preaching becomes useless for two reasons, Cassian, XLIX, 987.—The preacher can give words to the ears, but cannot open the heart, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 503.—Through the word of preaching we must season earthly minds with the savor of wisdom, St. Paulinus, XCIX, 296.—May you, by the love through which you say that you languish, also make me burn through the word of preaching, Blessed Alcuin, C, 655.—Through the preaching of truth and faith, and the font of holy baptism, they beget offspring for the eternal King, ibid., 658.—The flesh, without preaching, breaks out into the forest of vices, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 963.—Preachers open the kingdom of heaven to the new people of the faithful, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 626.—By his preaching the preacher opens heaven’s gates to us, Rupert, CLXVII, 1017.—The evangelical preacher gives light like a lamp and rouses like lightning, id., CLXVII, 559.—He moves the hearer to contrition of heart, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 94.—He kindles toward perfection, ibid., 189.—The preacher heals by the word, ibid., 128.—Three things impede its efficacy: hardness of heart, negligence, and avarice, ibid., 155.—For preaching is manifold: namely, teaching, correction, exhortation, stirring up, consolation, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 36.—Let preaching heal the weak rather than delight the curious, ibid., 42.—What preaching is and what kind it ought to be, Alan of Lille, CCX, III, 613.

**Things to which preaching is compared.** Preaching is compared to a needle, St. Hilary, IX, 1027.—With good reason he compared his preaching to a net, ibid., 996.—The words of preachers are gentle rains to the pious, burning snares to the faithless, Cassiodorus, LXX, 95.—The voice of thunder is the preaching of the saints, ibid., 730.—Preaching is signified by arrows, St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 768.—Likewise by neighing, id., LXXVI, 597.—By the name of rain, id., LXXV, 867.—And by the name of water, ibid., 960.—The word of preaching is seed in the hearer’s heart, id., LXXVI, 808.—The divine word is figured by manna, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 380.—The preaching of faith is compared to agriculture, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 527.—The preaching of the apostles is signified by Samson’s visiting his wife, Rupert, CLXVII, 1044, 1045.—Sweet preaching which converts God’s enemies to faith is signified by Saul’s refreshment when David struck the harp, ibid., 1098.—The voice of preachers is the blast of trumpets, id., CLXV, 862.—The words of preachers are sharp arrows, id., CLXVIII, 640.—The preacher is signified by the voice of the turtledove, id., 1868.—It is called a roar, Rupert, id., 1615.—The word of God is called a sword, Hildebert, CLXXI, 778.—Preaching is the good odor of Christ, Lanfranc, CL, 223.—Preaching to the Jews is signified by the morning rain; preaching to Gentiles and Jews together by the evening and morning rain, Rupert, CLXVIII, 235.—Preaching is like water, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1135.—Like thunder, ibid., 886.—The seventh rung of Jacob’s ladder is preaching, Alan of Lille, CCX, III, 613.—The fourth chariot is preaching, Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 676.

#### III.—On the rules of preaching

What speech concerning God ought to be like, St. Hilary, X, 743.—Christian preaching has no need of verbal pomp and ornament, St. Ambrose, XVII, 188.—Whoever preaches without being sent is presumptuous and reprobate, ibid., 319.—Orators sum up briefly at the end what they had previously discussed more diffusely, St. Jerome, XXVI, 453.—Let a priest’s discourse be seasoned with the reading of the Scriptures, id., XXII, 534.—“I do not want you to be a declaimer, a pettifogger, and an unreasoning chatterer,” ibid., 534.—Let the Gospel not be for sale, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 273.—How true preaching may be distinguished from false, id., XL, 682.

[Col. 0014]

You who wish to be heard, first hear yourself, id., XXXVI, 580.—Let the preacher ask his hearers for their ears for himself, but their heart for God, id., XXXVIII, 1149.—In rebuking women, preachers should have regard for their modesty, ibid., 205.—Prayer after the sermon, id., XXXVIII, 213; XXXIX, 1633.—Certain preachers announce truth neither chastely nor from truth, id., XXXVI, 139.—Those who proclaim falsehood do not proclaim Christ, id., XXXVII, 1491.—No one ought to preach with hesitation about that of which he cannot doubt, ibid., 1123.—Those who speak of God should fear lest they say evil things incautiously or good things badly, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 780.—Teaching set forth without order is barren and disfigures, ibid., 267.—The arguments of preaching must be proportioned to the hearers’ capacity, ibid., 136, 141, 530.—Perversities must first be rooted out, and right things then preached, ibid., 49.—The matter of preaching must be drawn from the sacred pages, ibid., 58.—The word of God must be expounded with discernment and adapted to each person, ibid., 50.—Preachers ought to lower themselves to their hearers’ comprehension, ibid., 136.—Strong things must not be preached to the weak, ibid., 141.—Preaching must cease when those who receive God’s word become worse because of it, ibid., 165.—When holy preachers are about to rebuke others, like skilled physicians they first feel the patient, then strike, ibid., 310.—Preachers cannot spiritually beget unless they do so by weeping, ibid., 549.—For the teacher must consider what he says, to whom he speaks, when he speaks, how he speaks, and how much he speaks, ibid., 910.—Therefore the preacher’s discourse must always be shaped according to the character of the hearers, ibid., 914.—The ministry of holy preaching must be assigned and received with the utmost discernment, id., LXXIX, 276.—According to hearers’ capacity, he should teach things now plain, now lofty, ibid., 258.—The preacher must weigh what, how much, when, and to whom he speaks, ibid., 367.—How great diversity ought to be in the art of preaching, id., LXXVII, 50 and following.—Lofty matters ought not at all to be preached to weak minds, ibid., 24.—On the work and voice of preaching, ibid.—Preachers should give varying admonitions according to the condition of particular persons, id., LXXVI, 530.—Men must be admonished differently from women, young persons differently from old persons, and so forth, ibid.—He should not draw his hearer’s mind beyond its strength, id., LXXVII, 124.—They customarily speak terrifying matters first and sweet matters afterward, id., LXXX, 800.—The discourse of teachers must be shaped according to the quality of the hearers, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 828.—Whoever strives to speak wisely should greatly fear lest the unity of his hearers be confused by his eloquence, ibid.—Therefore the heedless ruler must not rush headlong into speaking, ibid., 829.—Let the preacher admonish each person with different exhortation according to the character of his calling and conduct, Isidore of Seville, LXXXIII, 785.—To carnal minds one ought to preach neither things too lofty concerning heaven nor earthly things, but things of a middle kind, St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1094.—He will apply to each person the appropriate remedy of teaching, and proclaim what is suitable to each, according to age, sex, and calling, ibid., 1094; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 855.—One and the same teaching should not be applied to all, St. Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1094–1095; Amalarius of Metz, CV, 855.—Harsh rebuke corrects some, but gentle exhortation others, ibid.—If a sermon of preaching is to be given, it should be delivered in a suitable place before everyone, Charlemagne, XCVII, 620.—On the best manner of speaking, and what a preacher should observe in speaking, Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 408.—What order of preaching must be observed, Alcuin, C, 193, 204.—For whoever preaches rightly first inclines the ear of the heart to inward speech, so that afterward he may open the bodily mouth in uttering admonition, Rabanus Maurus, CX, 575.—The preaching of the Gospel ought to be free of charge, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 412.—Preachers must be sent and directed by Christ, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXX, 397–398.—Let them adapt themselves to particular persons according to the qualities of each, Haymo, CXVII, 1046.—Or at least let those who will preach prepare themselves, ibid., 1123.—For not all are instructed equally, ibid., 777.—The manner of preaching, Radulphus of Bourges, CXIX, 709.—A mission is necessary for preaching, Lanfranc, CL, 140.—Preaching must not be sold, St. Bruno, CLIII, 464.—In what order a sermon ought to be delivered, Guibert, CLVI, 21.—Let prayer precede the sermon, CLVI, 24.—For a sermon delivered tepidly and languidly, when it does not please even the one who delivers it, would very strangely please anyone else, ibid.—Let the preacher not speak excessively, ibid., 25.—An overly long sermon produces weariness; a short one delights, ibid., 24 and following.—How preaching ought to be dispensed, Rupert, CLXVII, 862.—For lesser things ought to be preached to lesser persons, and greater things to greater persons, Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 616.—The preacher’s preaching and rebuke must be varied according to the variety of hearers and sinners, Hildebert, CLXXI, 595, 819.

[Col. 0015]

Prayer must precede preaching, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1158.—Let them speak with discernment according to the hearers’ capacity, ibid., 1063.—The word of God must be brought forth at an appropriate time according to the condition of the hearers, ibid.—The form for beginning a sermon, Hugh of Saint Victor, CLXXVII, 819.—Christ’s preaching has no need of verbal pomp and ornament, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1541.—You ought not so much to consider what befits you, as an educated man, to say, as what those whom you instruct ought to hear, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 141.—On discernment in preaching, Gratian, CLXXXVII, 223.—The diversity of sermons in holy preachers arises from the different dispositions of mind in hearers, Wolbero, CXCV, 1178.—In preaching, one should attend not to affected arrangement of words, but rather to the instruction of hearts, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 184–185.—Preaching is manifold: vain and proud, curious and foolish, subtle and heretical, dutiful and charitable, and so forth, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 40.—The speech should not be elaborate, neat, or polished, and so forth, ibid., 41.—On humility in preaching, ibid., 43.—Preaching must be clear, Alan of Lille, CCX, III, 613.—Public, ibid., 112.—Preaching must be supported by reasons and strengthened by authorities, ibid.—Preaching ought not to contain buffoonish or childish words, ibid., 112.—In its statements, preaching must have weight, ibid., 113.—The conditions of good preaching, ibid., 113 and following.—Preaching must be accommodated to its hearers, ibid., 114, 184.—What authorities should be used in preaching, ibid.—Preachers must be sent by superiors or by God, ibid., 377.—Let the preacher not create weariness in hearers by a torrent of verbosity, ibid., 213.—The pearls of the divine word must not be cast before dogs, ibid., 213.—If he finds the minds of hearers not barren but fit to receive seed, let him preach, ibid.—Let him remember that a word once sent forth is irrevocable, ibid.—Sermons must be brief, ibid., 114.—Examples must be used in sermons, ibid., 115.—Three kinds of preaching, ibid., 113.

#### IV.—On the subject matter of preaching

What holy preachers ought to preach, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 435.—Preachers ought to preach not earthly but heavenly things, and with moderation, ibid., 28.—First faith must be taught, and then the sacraments of baptism received, Alcuin, C, 205.—Then the evangelical commandments must be handed down, ibid.—Admonition ought to be given not so much concerning the origin or preservation of virtues as concerning the interconnection and avoidance of vices, Guibert, CLVI, 26.—For no preaching seems more salutary to me than that which shows a person to himself, ibid., 27.—From what sources a preacher may sometimes take material for speaking, ibid., 30.—What should be preached by priests, Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 228.—They ought to preach the humility of Christ incarnate, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 10.—Let your discourse breathe the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles, Gilbert, CLXXXIV, 83.—Whence preachers of the Church ought to take their subject matter, Wolbero, CXCV, 1076.—What a preacher ought to teach, Richard of Saint Victor, CXCVI, 677.—Subjects on which preaching ought to be delivered, Alan of Lille, CCX, 114.—On contempt for the world, ibid.—On contempt for oneself, ibid., 116.—Against gluttony, ibid., 119.—Against lust, ibid., 121.—Against avarice, ibid., 123.—Against sloth, ibid., 123.—How useful sermons concerning Christ are, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 702.

#### V.—On the holiness of the preacher

A sinner who remains in sin ought to abstain from the office of preaching, St. Hilary, IX, 545.—God wills that his utterances be handled by the chaste mouth of a chaste body, ibid.—He who acts otherwise causes hearers to distrust him, so that they doubt the promises, St. Ambrose, XVII, 233.—When a man’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is held in contempt, ibid., 868.—Preach by word and deed, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 297.—Fulfil in deed what one preaches, Cassiodorus, LXX, 1083.—If the truth of preaching is to be preserved, the loftiness of life must necessarily be maintained, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 908.—Let the preacher stand on high by his life, ibid., 907.—Those who prepare themselves for preaching must first renew themselves in inward virtues, ibid., 549.—A law is laid down for heralds of God’s word: that they fulfil in deed what they preach, ibid., 103.—Those who preach rightly but do not live rightly become heralds of their own condemnation, ibid., 247.—Those are chosen as preachers who are free from crime, id., LXXIX, 188.—Let life not disagree with speech, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 800.—The preacher’s holiness is required, ibid., 828.—One must preach by deed and speech, John of Rouen, CXLVII, 227.

[Col. 0016]

Let the book from which the text of our discourse proceeds be a pure conscience, lest, while the tongue announces good things to others, the memory of sin bite us inwardly, Guibert, CLVI, 24.—The discourse of one whose life is contemptible is despised, Hildebert, CLXXI, 588.—Three things are commonly required in a preacher: holiness of conduct, and so forth, Hugh of Saint Victor, CLXXXVII, 845.—For a perfect preacher, two things are especially necessary: namely, that he shine with the splendor of a religious life, and so forth, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 462.—Who ought to preach, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 480.—The preacher’s threefold cord: right thought, worthy speech, and confirmation by life, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 849.—Let the preacher begin first to do, and then to teach, Adam the Premonstratensian, CXCVIII, 354.—On preaching which ought to be preceded by holiness of life, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 36.—The tongue preaches a man uselessly and harshly when conscience opposes and contradicts it, ibid., 39.—Life, learning, and eloquence are required in the preacher, ibid., 40.

#### VI.—On the virtues of the preacher
The serpent’s prudence in overcoming the first parents is to be imitated by preachers in dealing with sinners, St. Hilary, IX, 971.---For unless the preaching minister burns, he does not set aflame the one to whom he preaches, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1353.---These men speak what they do not believe, and therefore are condemned, ibid., 1491.---Whoever does not possess charity toward another ought by no means to undertake the office of preaching, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1139.---How great the charity of a preacher of truth ought to be, id., LXXIX, 338.---Let humility accompany purity of life in preachers, ibid., 166.---A preacher ought inwardly to preserve humility and purity, id., LXXIX, 922.---Let none undertake the ministry of preaching unless they are distinguished by chastity, id., LXXIX, 414.---For preaching, the conscience of holy love is more edifying than training in speech, id., LXXVI, 890.---When we speak to people about God, we must first remember what we are, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 829.---If you wish to possess a voice that resounds in preaching or is effective in prayer, strive always to be set aflame by divine fervor, lest the numbness of cold cut off your voice, St. Peter Damian, CXLV, 698.---On the purity of mind necessary for preaching the truth, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII.---The law of Christ, a fiery law, must be preached with fiery tongues, ibid., 323.---Preachers ought to thirst for the salvation of their hearers, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 1063.---And for the glory of God alone, not for human favor, ibid., 1157.---Let them speak discerningly, according to the capacity of their hearers, ibid., 1063.---With humility and freedom, ibid., 996.---With confidence and a good conscience, ibid., 881.---Preachers should be gentle in teaching and severe in rebuking, Rupert, CLXVIII, 495.---He who does not burn does not kindle, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 38.---He preaches the word of God sweetly and most pleasantly with his mouth who loves it most sweetly in his heart, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 39.---A preacher ought to be prudent and faithful in word and deed, Alan of Lille, CCX, 183.---If Jeremiah, who was eloquent for preaching, confesses himself mute before God, how can a priest mute in speaking about God declare himself eloquent? ibid., 281.

VII.---On the Learning of Preachers.

How great their learning ought to be, St. Hilary, IX, 445.---Fishermen and unlettered men are sent to preach: why, St. Jerome, XXVI, 33.---For preaching the Gospel, only those were chosen who were not qualified by themselves, St. Gregory the Great, LXXXVI, 693.---Those who keep watch for the office of preaching should not depart from the study of sacred reading, id., LXXVII, 48, 49.---It is necessary that a priest who performs the office of preacher should both rain down the showers of spiritual teaching and shine with the rays of a religious life, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 462.---Those entrusted to him are to be taught by one qualified both in learning and in the grace of eloquence, St. Bruno, CLIII, 463.---Three things are necessary for an evangelical preacher: learning, boldness, and speech, Hildebert, CLXXI, 593.---Three things are usually required in a preacher: holiness of life, perfection of learning, and eloquence that wins favor, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 845.---A preacher requires life, learning, and eloquence, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 40.---The fourth chariot is preaching: its first wheel is knowledge of the Scriptures, its second the faculty of delivery, its third the example of an honorable life, and its fourth authority imposed by superiors, Thomas the Cistercian, CCVI, 676.---Learning belongs to preachers, so that they may be practiced in both Testaments, Alan of Lille, CCX, 184.

VIII.---On the Office of Preachers and the Things to Which They Are Compared.

The preacher of truth is an instrument of the Holy Spirit, St. Hilary, IX, 295.---Preachers bore Christ in heart and tongue [Col. 0017], St. Ambrose, XVII, 773.---The dignity of preaching, St. Jerome, XXVI, 63.---A discussion is required concerning the office of both groups, the hearers and the preachers of God’s word, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 966.---It is safer to hear God’s word than to preach it, ibid., 966; XLV, 1801.---If preachers are reproved, they are troubled; if praised, they are puffed up, id., XXXV, 1792.---The office of teachers is dangerous, id., XXXVIII, 155.---A preacher is a dispenser of spiritual gems, id., XXXIX, 2319.---Let the preacher seek ears from his hearers for himself, but hearts for God, id., XXXVIII, 1149.---Preachers are clouds and winds: clouds on account of the flesh, winds on account of the spirit, id., XXXVII, 1749.---Nourishers of the Church, id., XXXVI, 241.---The Lord’s feet are preachers of the Gospel, id., XXXVIII, 602.---Preachers are called ambassadors of reconciliation, id., XXXVI, 837.---Ascending or descending angels, id., XXXIX, 1761.---Clouds by which the Lord’s vineyard is made fruitful, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 289.---Great mountains that send forth the waters of truth from valleys of humility, St. Prosper, LI, 291.---The heavens are preachers declaring the glory of God, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 410.---The preacher is compared with the pelican, the night-raven, and the sparrow, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 280.---Preaching is a priestly office, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 260.---To whom the duty of preaching belongs, ibid., 1946.---Oxen signify preachers, who, ploughing human hearts with heavenly commands, caused the harvest of virtues to spring up, Cassiodorus, LXX, 77.---Why true preachers are compared to the everlasting mountains, ibid., 542.---Young men ought not to preach, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 796.---It is a preacher’s office to dig out earthly thoughts in hearers and in writing, ibid., 602.---A preacher is compared to an eagle, ibid., 631.---Holy preachers are called angels, ibid., 725.---Let him first open the ear of his heart to the voice of the Creator, ibid., 909.---It is a preacher’s duty to admonish even the righteous, ibid., 914.---Under the name of a gate, each individual preacher can also be understood, ibid., 959.---How great a danger threatens the preacher from the applause of hearers, ibid., 1052.---Preachers are rightly called clouds because they rain with words and flash with miracles, ibid., 1006.---In holy preachers Christ and his Spirit speak, id., LXXIX, 266.---They announce the heavenly kingdom, ibid., 293.---It is a preacher’s office to rebuke sins committed and to teach how future sins may be avoided, ibid., 384.---A preacher’s task is to declare war against the pleasure of the flesh, the desire of the mind, and the pretense of good works, ibid., 240.---It belongs to preachers to capture for Christ the foxes, that is, heretics, ibid., 500.---Like mothers chewing bread for little children, ibid., 508.---Preachers are the columns of the Church, ibid., 510.---The eyes and lips of Christ, ibid., 522, 523.---Streams which water the soil of our heart, id., LXXVI, 903.---A roof which protects us by interceding and by fortifying us with admonitions, ibid.---Preachers are called farmers, ibid., 247.---They are also called hail and coals of fire, because, etc., ibid., 498.---The pillars of heaven, ibid., 30.---Counselors, because they offer their hearers counsel for life, id., LXXV, 963.---Preachers are called rivers and lightnings, id., 828, 527.---How preachers are compared to locusts, ibid., 600.---Holy preachers are called the mouth of God, ibid., 695; CXV, 997.---The Lord’s feet, which he anoints and cleanses, ibid., 110.---Carved gates, the gates of Zion, ibid., 999, 702.---They are called kings and consuls, id., LXXV, 666.---How holy preachers are drops of dew, id., LXXVI, 507.---They are sometimes gods in Holy Scripture, id., LXXIX, 363.---The breasts and neck of the bride, ibid., 485, 492.---They are a shade for those subject to them, because by exhortations they protect them from the heat of desire, ibid., 362; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 715.---Preachers can be called the teeth of the Church, Gregory the Great, LXXIX, 508.---The lips and cheeks of the Church, ibid., 508; CXV, 610.---They are sometimes called dogs by likeness, id., LXXIX, 508.---Some commendably seek the office of preaching, while others are commendably drawn to it under compulsion, Taio of Saragossa, LXXX, 802.---Preachers are compared to angels, Alcuin, C, 765, 1099.---Preachers are the lights of the world, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1599.---They are compared to the tower of David, Haymo of Halberstadt, CXVII, 317.---Holy preachers are figured by the mouth of the Church, Haymo, CXVII, 1066.---Preachers are signified by oxen, St. Bruno, CLII, 918.---By waters, ibid., 941.---By mountains and hills, ibid., 991.---By heaven, ibid., 1406.---By angels ascending or descending on Jacob’s ladder, Rupert, CLXVII, 467.---They are signified by the cows carrying the ark of the Lord upon themselves, ibid., 1082.---A preacher is signified by the cock, ibid., 1731.---A preacher is a gate of the mystical city, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 585.---The servants of the Lord inviting guests to the wedding, ibid., 612.---Preachers are angels of God, St. Bernard, CLXXXIV, 83.---Stars, St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 53.---Preachers are compared to waters [Col. 0018], Peter Lombard, CXCI, 194.---They are called clouds and heavens, ibid., 192.---They are understood to shine like stars in darkness, Garnerius, CXCIII, 38, 39.---Preachers are fittingly called kings and consuls of the earth, ibid., 47.---The task of preachers is to overcome the Canaanite, that is, the devil, id., CLXVII, 889.---A preacher is the steward of the vineyard, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 135.---The office of a true preacher consists of two things, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 202.---A preacher ought to resemble a hen, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 198.---To reconcile those turned away and to raise up the slack is a preacher’s office, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 880.---The office of preaching should not be sought unbidden, Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 88.---The seven angels are preachers reborn by the grace of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 819.---Preachers are guardians of the Church, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 185.---No one ought to usurp for himself the office of preaching, Alan of Lille, CCX, 379.

IX.---What a Preacher Must Avoid.

A preacher must avoid pride, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 967.---Timid preachers are rebuked by the example of John, XXXIX, 2116.---Let preachers of truth claim nothing as though it were their own, and let there be no discord among them, Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 291.---Those who preach for the sake of praise or reward deprive themselves of eternal recompense, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1142.---Whoever undertakes the office of preaching must be free from greed, ibid., 1140.---The proud do not preach sound doctrine soundly, ibid., 265.---What preachers should consider in order to flee pride, ibid., 266.---A ruler of churches should not envy those cooperating with him in preaching, ibid., 247.---Those who, while preaching rightly, serve vain glory are not reconciled, ibid., 254.---One devoted to avarice cannot be a preacher of truth, Alcuin, C, 425.---Presbyters ought not to preach in order to obtain praise or payment, St. Peter Damian, CXLVII, 225.---Let preachers flee empty glory, St. Bernard, CLXXXIII, 987.---Preachers who seek applause and vain glory are severely censured, Gillebert, CLXXXIV, 140 and following.---When you proclaim the Gospel word, do not be puffed up when received, nor crushed with grief when despised, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 274.---Do not think yourself precious when heard, nor worthless when despised, ibid., 274.---I command you not to be anxious about the composition and elaboration of a sermon, Peter the Chanter, CCV, 41.---Let neither avarice, vain glory, nor careless talkativeness impel him to preach, Alan of Lille, CCX, 213.---Let him not think it a fine thing to be pointed at and called: “There he is,” ibid.---Let him remember that a word once uttered is irrevocable, ibid., 213.

A preacher of righteousness, whether received or despised, even if he suffers whatever temporal adversities, will not be deprived before God of the reward of his office, St. Augustine, XLIII, 350.---There are two rewards for a preacher: one on the way, the other in the homeland, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1142.---Even if the preacher does not achieve the result of conversion, he is nevertheless not without the reward of his preaching, id., LXXVII, 688.---The distinctive splendor of preachers in glory, id., LXXIX, 213.---The supreme reward of the best preachers, ibid., 270.---Those who instruct many unto righteousness shall shine like stars for everlasting eternities, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 463.

X.---On the Hearer of Preaching.

With what great reverence the word of God ought to be handled or heard, St. Hilary, IX, 294, 295.---The preaching of the divine word must be received with fear, St. Augustine, XXXV, 1790, 1791.---He who does not fear or stir when hearing preaching is not worthy to be healed, id., XXXVI, 716.---The pleasure of hearing does not bring puffing-up, id., XXXVIII, 967.---On the office of hearers and preachers of God’s word, ibid., 966.---Some hearers of the word build upon rock, others upon sand, ibid., 970.---Not to hear is evil, as though not to build, ibid., 971.---It is safer to hear God’s word than to preach it, ibid., 966, 155.---Which hearers are carnal and which spiritual, ibid., 156.---The fruit of God’s word is to be demanded even from one who does not hear it, ibid., 204.---A sacred sermon was received only by those standing, St. Germanus of Paris, LXXII, 158.---For some who hear the word do not hear it, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 927.---The ministry of holy preaching must be bestowed and received with the utmost discernment, id., LXXIX, 276.---On hearing God’s word rightly, Hildebert, CLXXI, 705.---On hearing God’s word devoutly, ibid., 908.---He who has heard the word of God negligently is no less guilty than one who by negligence allowed Christ’s body to fall to the ground, Ivo of Chartres, CXLI, 189.---On diligently hearing God’s word [Col. 0019], Hildebert, CLXXI, 890.---We read of three kinds of hearers of the divine word: the sluggish, the active, and the contemplative, ibid., 905.---When you hear the spiritual word, you ought to receive it with a pure heart, ibid., 908.---What ruin and punishment await those who do not receive God’s word, ibid.---What has been heard must be put into practice, Godfrey, CLXXIV, 974, 1052.---One must not cease hearing it, even if it is not to one’s taste, ibid., 893.---Hearers of God’s word pay their preacher by putting what they have heard into practice, ibid., 1064.---Let every person be swift to hear, ibid., 350.---The preaching of God’s word must be obeyed with reverence, ibid., 32.---Three things impede its effectiveness: hardness of heart, negligence, and avarice, ibid., 155.---On the threefold hearer of the heavenly word, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 842.---The sluggish hear and despise what they hear, ibid.---The active hear and obey what they hear, ibid.---The contemplative hear and fall asleep in an embrace, ibid.---The sluggish are numb, the active labor, the contemplative rest, ibid.---There are [Col. 0020] some who, when they hear the word of holy preaching, receive it gladly; and there are some who will neither hear nor receive it, Wolbero, CXCV, 1178.---There are many who do not wish, or cannot, receive and hear it in this place or at this time, but hear and receive it in another place and at another time, ibid.---There are others who gladly hear what is said, but approve absolutely nothing unless something new and unheard is said, Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 184.---Eager reception of God’s word is a prognostic sign of the children of God, ibid., 157.---Some hear from vanity, curiosity, or pride; others for usefulness, ibid., 157.---Hearers must avoid two things: disgust and curiosity, ibid., 183, 181.---The tongue of preachers often accords with the merits of their hearers, ibid., 190.---On the manner of hearing God’s word, St. Stephen, CCIV, 1102.---On hearing divine sermons, ibid., 1134.---When a divine sermon ought to be heard, ibid., 1114.---To whom preaching ought to be addressed, Alan of Lille, CCX, 184, 114.

[Col. 0059]

## CXCV. PREACHER’S INDEX TO THE GOSPELS READ DURING THE SOLEMNITIES OF THE MASS THROUGHOUT THE COURSE OF THE YEAR, ACCORDING TO THE ROMAN RITE, SETTING OUT VARIOUS EXPLANATIONS, SERMONS, HOMILIES, AND COMMENTARIES SUITED TO THE ELUCIDATION OF EACH GOSPEL; FROM WHICH THE READER MAY DRAW MATERIAL BOTH USEFUL AND PLEASANT, AS FROM A MORE ABUNDANT FOUNTAIN.

## Twenty-second Series

[Col. 0069]

### Preface

This series consists of only two indexes. The first, alphabetical, comprises all authors who wrote in verse; the second presents all their works, or even shorter writings, arranged according to an analogous order of subjects and genres.

[Col. 0069]

TWENTY-THIRD SERIES.

[Col. 0091]

[PREFACE.]

The *Patrology* comprises almost innumerable letters of great importance; but lest the reader, undertaking a labor at once burdensome and unproductive, should depart empty-handed amid so many and such great riches scattered through two hundred volumes, we have decided to assist him. To achieve this, we have distributed all the letters into various classes: the first contains dogmatic letters, the second moral letters, the third canonical letters, the fourth disciplinary letters; while the fifth contains all those treating of any subject whatever, arranged according to the affinity of their matters and the chronology of their authors. In addition, alphabetical indexes follow of the authors and of those to whom the letters are addressed, etc. Thus not even the smallest letter will escape the reader in this Series.

[Col. 0113]

CXCIX. INDEX OF DOGMATIC AND POLEMICAL LETTERS, IN WHICH THE ANALOGICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS IS PRESERVED TOGETHER WITH THE CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE AUTHORS.

I.—Dogmatic letters.

**On God.**—On God, that He cannot lie, Ambrose, XVI, 1155.—On the ten names of God, Jerome, XXII, 428.—On the hypostases, ibid., 355, 358, 359.—Letters on God, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 431, 452.—On seeing God, ibid., 378, 596, 622; St. Lupus of Ferrières, CXIX, 493.—On the infinite God: how He could be enclosed in a virgin’s womb and in the tiny body of an infant, Volusianus, XXXIII, 512; Augustine, ibid., 515.—On the worship of God, and how it should be performed, ibid., 1030.—On God’s presence everywhere, and in a special manner in the saints as in His temple, ibid., 832.—On His goodness and justice in distinguishing among human beings, ibid., 815, 857, 874; Ruricius, LVIII, 102.—On seeking the one God, William, abbot of St. Arnulf, CL, 880.—That all things are subject to divine providence, Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 227.—Whether it may be said that paternity and divinity are not God, Hildegard, CXCVII, 351, 352.

**On the mystery of the Holy Trinity.**—Pope Julius I, VIII, 953; Jerome, XXII, 355, 359; Augustine, XXXIII, 75, 77, 449, 452, 742, 748, 1025, 1038, 1049, 1051; Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 476; Fulgentius, LXV, 394; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXVII, 910; Pope Benedict I, LXXII, 685; Pope Hormisdas, LXXXIV, 813; Elipandus, XCVI, 861, 864; Guitmund, bishop of Aversa, CXLIX, 1501; Charlemagne, XCVIII, 914; Hildegard, CXCVII, 167; Augustine, XXXIII, 585, 718, 720.

**On the creation of the world.**—Ambrose, XVI, 1136.—On the creation of man, ibid., 1129; Avitus of Vienne, LIX, 200; Hugh of Ribemont, CLXVI, 833.—On the creation of the angels, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 2.

**On Christ.**—On Christ’s divinity and humanity, St. Pope Felix, V, 152, 155; St. Pope Eutychian, ibid., 167; Pope Caius, ibid., 183; Pope Liberius, VIII, 1395; Athanasius, ibid., 1397; Pope Damasus, XIII, 356; Augustine, XXXIII, 75, 370, 381, 462, 515, 538, 585, 630, 709, 832, 899, 901, 904, 942; Capreolus of Carthage, LIII, 843, 849; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 757, 765, 771, 785, 797, 803, 928, 1065, 1163, 1165, 1173 ff., 1257, 1259; Avitus of Vienne, LIX, 205, 215, 245; Fulgentius, LXV, 377, 405, 415, 493; Pope John II, LXVI, 20, 27; Pope Agapetus I, ibid., 77; Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXVII, 889, 908, 910; Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 512; LXXXIV, 814; Victor of Carthage, LXXXVII, 85; Elipandus, XCVI, 861, 870; Amalarius, CV, 1333; Candidus, monk of Fulda, CVI; Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 855.—How Christ is the foretold Messiah, and how He came at the time appointed by the prophets, Alvarus of Córdoba, CXXI, 482, 485 ff., 495.—On Christ made man, Peter the Venerable, CLXXXIX, 175; Gerhoh, CXCIII, 541, 552; Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 34; Alexander, abbot of Jumièges, CCV, 919.—On meditating upon Christ’s infancy and Passion, Adam, abbot of Perseigne, CCXI, 603.

**On the human soul.**—On the nature of the soul, Ambrose, XVI, 1074.—On the origin of the soul, Jerome and Augustine, XXII, 1085, 1124, 1182; XXXIII, 585, 718, 720, 778, 857, 929.—On the soul released from the body, ibid., 77, 693, 698, 704; Licinianus, LXXII, 691.—On the human soul, Alvarus of Córdoba, CXXI, 453; John of Split, CXXI, 458.—On the care of the soul, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 160.

**On grace and free will.**—Augustine, XXXIII, 585, 741, 968, 971, 974, 978; Pope Celestine I, L, 531.—That no one is good by his own powers, except through participation in Him who alone is good, ibid., 532.—That all the merits of the saints are God’s gifts, Pope Celestine I, ibid., 533.—That grace not only forgives sins but also helps prevent their commission, ibid., 534.—That all the prayers of the Church proclaim Christ’s grace, by which the human race is restored, ibid., 535.—On predestination, St. [Col. 0114] Augustine, XXXIII, 1002, 1007; Pope Adrian, XCVIII, 336, 374; Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1519, 1530, 1553; Lupus of Ferrières, CXIX, 601, 606.—On grace and free will, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 77; St. Salvian of Marseilles, LIII, 159; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 593.—African bishops, LXV, 435, 442, 451.—Pope Celestine, LXXXIV, 682.—That four things are necessary for meriting grace, Adam, abbot of Perseigne, CCXI, 69.

**On the Sacraments.**—On the baptism of heretics: whether it should be repeated, Pope Cornelius, III, 840; IV, 432.—On baptizing heretics, Cyprian, III, 1103, 1109, 1127, 1137; IV, 408; Firmilian, III, 1153; Pope Sixtus II, V, 89.—On Maximinus, a Donatist bishop who was said to have rebaptized a Catholic deacon, Augustine, XXXIII, 94.—How parents’ faith benefits infants in baptism, Augustine, ibid., 359.—It is proved that the holiness of baptism depends upon the grace of the divine gift, not upon the merits of the human minister, Augustine, ibid., 396.—On not repeating baptism, ibid., 405.—That in baptism death intervenes through the killing of sin, and the threefold immersion imitates burial, Pope Leo, LXXXIV, 757.—That at every time those pressed by the necessity of death—that is, by illness, siege, persecution, or shipwreck—ought to be baptized, Pope Leo, ibid., 759.—On the form and minister of baptism, St. Pope Zacharias, LXXXIX, 943.—On baptism, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 369; Fulbert of Chartres, CXLI, 200.—On the validity of baptism and other sacraments conferred by criminal priests, Pope Urban II, CLI, 529.—Children not regenerated by the sacrament of baptism cannot attain eternal blessedness, Theobald of Étampes, CLXIII, 763.—On the form of baptism, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 614.—On baptism, when it is to be repeated, Abbot William, CCIX, 652, 653.—Why a certain person’s baptism was valid, Stephen of Tournai, CCXI, 312, 313, 314.—There is no true baptism unless it is performed through water and by a priest, Pope Innocent III, CCXV, 812.—That persons should not be baptized unless they have been sealed by a bishop, Sulpicius Severus, XX, 554; Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 756.—On the sacrament of the Lord’s chalice, Cyprian, IV, 372.—On manna as a type of the Lord’s body, Ambrose, XVI, 1219.—On the Lord’s body and blood, against Ratpert, Rabanus Maurus, CXII, 1510.—On the Lord’s body and blood, St. Paschasius Radbertus, CXIX, 1351; Ratherius of Verona, CXXXVI, 645.—On the sacrament of the Eucharist, Adelmann, CXLIII, 1289; Fulbert of Chartres, CXLI, 201.—On the sacrifice of the Mass, St. Peter Damian, CXLIV, 369.—Exhortation to frequent communion, St. Pope Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 326.—On the truth of the body and blood of Christ the Lord, St. Anastasius, monk, CXLIX, 433.—On the mystery of the Lord’s body, Guitmund, CXLIX, 1501.—He teaches that reception of the Eucharist before the use of reason is by no means necessary for infants’ salvation, Lanfranc of Canterbury, CL, 532.—On the sacrament of the altar, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 254.—On the Lord’s body and blood, ibid., 255; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 212.—On the Eucharist, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 416; Hugh Metellus, CLXXXVIII, 1273.—Pardon must not be denied at the end of life to penitents, Pope Siricius, XIII, 1136.—The necessity of confession is maintained, Alcuin, C, 337.—On the Epistle of St. James the Apostle, in which prayer for the sick is commanded, XX, 559.—On the dignity of the sacrament of orders, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 358.—On impotence in marriage, Pope Gregory II, LXXXIX, 524; Boniface, ibid., 738, 739.—On the impediment of kinship, ibid., 746.—That a son may not marry the woman whom his father received from the sacred font of baptism, Zacharias, ibid., 955.—That the marriage of Abbo, contracted in the fourth degree of consanguinity, must be dissolved, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 809.—How abominable it is to unite in marriage with blood relatives, [Col. 0115] Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 1131.—A certain marriage contracted without the presence of a priest is confirmed, Pope Adrian II, CXXII, 1318.—That no one may have two lawful wives, Pope Stephen V, CXXIX, 807.—How degrees of consanguinity are to be calculated, Pope Adrian II, CXLVI, 1379, 1402.—What should be thought of those who wish to leave their wives because of fornication and take other women to themselves, Lanfranc, CL, 518.—On the marriage of a Christian man and a baptized Jewish woman who, having returned to Judaism, married a Jew: whether her first marriage is invalidated, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 135.—Whether divorce is to be permitted, ibid., 137, 191.—On consent in marriage, ibid., 144.—Whether it is permissible to marry a prostitute, ibid., 159.—Hildebert of Le Mans denies that a lawful marriage can be contracted between blood relatives and relatives by marriage, CLXXI, 221.—On the disadvantages of marriage, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 243.—On dissolving a marriage unlawfully celebrated between blood relatives, ibid., 255.—On degrees of affinity and when they invalidate marriage, ibid., 343.—On the marriage of a free woman with a slave, and conversely, St. Abbot William, CCIX, 645.—On carnal and spiritual kinship, ibid., 646.—When marriage is dissolved, ibid., 649.—Marriage ought not to be separated when both spouses are adulterers, Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 1418.—On grounds for divorce, the same, CCXV, 1493, 1494.—On revoking incestuous marriages, ibid., 79.—That betrothals contracted between those below puberty are to be consummated if, having reached puberty, they consent, Innocent III, CCXIV, 539.

**On the Church.**—On the power of excommunicating in the Church, St. Cyprian, IV, 364.—Outside the Church there is no salvation, Jerome, XXII, 355.—Different members in the Church, ibid., 535.—On the Church foretold in the Scriptures as destined to exist throughout the whole world, Augustine, XXXIII, 189.—On the duration of the Christian religion, ibid., 373.—That the Catholic Church is recognized in the sacred Scriptures, ibid., 396.—The Church, established by Christ upon Peter’s firmness, from which one must not depart, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 628.—On the Roman Church, Pope Vigilius, LXIX, 19; Adam, abbot of Perseigne, CCXI, 327.—The Church of God, like the moon, has had various phases, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 21.—On the primacy and prerogative of the Roman Church, Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 756.—On his reverence and duty toward the Roman Church, ibid., 765.—On the supreme pontiff, St. Pope Felix I, V, 148; Council of Rome, XIII, 577, 578; Pope Gregory IV, CVI, 853.

**On the Last Judgment,** Sulpicius Severus, XX, 223.
