Peter of Blois, CCVII, 537.—That brute animals in some sense accuse the ungrateful, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 205.—On perjury, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 184, 674; Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 91.—On avoiding idleness, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 24, 373.—Against duels, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 581.—On scandals, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 266, 267, 950.—Against simony, Pope Siricius, XIII, 1190.—Instructions for Constantius, recently elected bishop, concerning the chief duties and virtues of the priesthood, St. Ambrose, XVI, 879.—Ambrose, asked by Vigilius, newly chosen for the episcopate, to give him a pattern of instruction, gives him various precepts, ibid., 982.—That a priest ought to shrink from a common or plebeian mode of life, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1051, 1054, 1061.—He encourages in words certain clerics who, because of labour and difficulty, are losing heart, ibid., 1273.—He discusses the virtues especially required in a bishop, St. Jerome, XXII, 653.—The compassion of Christian bishops who intercede for defendants, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 652, 653.—How honour and praise should be accepted by prelates, St. Augustine, ibid., 92.—That bishops ought not improperly to deal with curious questions, ibid., 431.—Letter of St. Lupus of Troyes to Sidonius on the duties and virtues of a bishop, Ruricius, LVIII, 63.—On the duties of a true shepherd, ibid., 86.—He treats at length of a shepherd’s burden, gifts, and duties, St. Gregory the Great, CXXVII, 468, 479, 626.—On priests’ association with women, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 514.—He exhorts a bishop to discharge the pastoral office with the highest prudence and charity, ibid., 558, 575, 644, 847; Alcuin, C, 152, 221, 451; Bede the Venerable, XCIV, 658; Charlemagne, XCVIII, 917.—How a bishop ought to conduct himself in his church, St. Gregory the Great, LXVII, 658.—He exhorts Bishop Ethelred to manly perseverance, lest he flee from the sheep, Alcuin, C, 226.—He impresses upon Bishop Speratus the duties appropriate to bishops, ibid., 241.—He exhorts a bishop to a life worthy of a bishop, ibid., 244.—He exhorts Simeon, a priest, diligently to perform the episcopal office in dangerous times in Britain, ibid., 245.—Whom a priest should beware of, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 115 ff.; Peter Damian, CXLIV, 344.—What the office of a bishop is, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 90, 121.—He exhorts Hugh of Rouen to strive to be both patient and peaceable toward his people of Rouen, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 129. Letter 42, or treatise to Henry, Archbishop of Sens, on the character and office of bishops, ibid., 148.—On the proper administration of episcopal dignity, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, ibid., 107, 108, 129, 131.—Letters exhorting bishops to humility, ibid., 599, 600. Letters of Hildegard to bishops concerning their virtues and duties, CXCVII, 173, 174, 175, 176, 177, 180, 182, 183.—He exhorts bishops to moderation, humility, and repentance, Henry of Albano, CCIV, 247.—On the virtues of a bishop, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 51.

That it belongs to emperors to protect religion, and that restoration of superstition is not to be demanded of them, St. Ambrose, XVI, 961.—On the emperor’s submission to God, ibid., 1176.—A rule of life is prescribed for a commander distinguished in military service, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 854.—That the worst kings are appointed to punish the people’s sins, and the best for the consolation of subjects, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1281.—What a religious commander ought to be in military actions, Fulgentius, LXVII, 928.—That rulers should possess humility of heart, Pope Gregory, LXXXIV, 838.—That rulers should strive after bodily chastity, Pope Gregory, LXXXIV, 839.—That rulers should be moderate and gentle toward their subjects, ibid., 840.—He exhorts kings and princes to royal virtues, Alcuin, C, 157, 160, 213, 214, 229, 232, 353, 354, 475, 500.—That it is fitting for a king so to order his life that he may be an example to all, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXVI, 17.—What ministers of the palace and commonwealth a king should appoint, ibid., 18.—How judges of royal widows ought to be appointed, ibid., 20.—On priests’ obedience to kings, Atto of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 98, 99 ff.—He advises the king to comply with his father’s admonitions, Pope St. Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 570.—That the King of Sweden should rule the kingdom entrusted to him in justice, ibid., 584.—He exhorts a king to obey the heavenly King, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 116.—To govern a temporal kingdom in such a manner as not to lose the eternal one, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 34.—That a king should govern himself so as to be able to please the King of kings, ibid., 40.—On the virtues of kings, ibid., 133.—To King Louis: to live and reign in Him for whom to serve is to reign, ibid., 246.—To reign in Him whose kingdom is without end, ibid., 268.—To live and reign through Him by whom kings reign, ibid., 269.—On the reverence to be shown by kings to the pope and bishops, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, [Col. 0122] CLXXXII, 149, 345.—On peace with the Church, ibid., 385, 394.—Against persecutions of the Church, ibid., 391.—Against exactions, ibid., 501.—On the blessedness of the eremitic life, St. Jerome, XXII, 347.—On the formation of a monk, ibid., 579, 1038.—How one ought to shape a life worthy of the name of monk, ibid., 1072.—Monks should use leisure for piety, not idleness, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 187.

What kind of household attendants suit monks, St. Paulinus, LXI, 254.—He exhorts monks to virtues worthy of monks, Alcuin, C, 162, 166, 167, 173, 176, 215, 217, 218, 297, 489, 495, 500, 503, 504.—He exhorts monks to continual observance of their rule, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 87.—He praises monks’ unbroken constancy amid adversity, ibid., 93.—He exhorts a monk to virtue, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 46.—An exhortatory letter: that care of the soul should be preferred to solicitude for the body, and that the world should be renounced, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 637. Exhortations for entering religious life, ibid., 238, 249, 619, 620.—For progress, ibid., 459, 549, 587.—For zeal in regular discipline, ibid., 478.—On the practices of the earliest Cistercians, ibid., 694, 706.—Congratulatory letters on choosing the religious life, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 135, 139, 251, 286, 527.—For recalling those who had fallen away into laxer ways, ibid., 67.—For recalling apostates, ibid., 79, 255, 623.—For recalling those in error, ibid., 89, 93, 160, 182, 201, 205, 236, 500, 613, 622, 624, 639, 643.—Against those who draw others away from religious life, ibid., 497.—On love of solitude and silence, ibid., 154, 159.—On monks’ avoiding association with women, ibid., 199, 616; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 193.—On transfer to another religious order, ibid., 226, 518, 638.—On removing an undisciplined abbot, ibid., 713.—On contemplation, Geoffrey, subprior of St. Barbara, CCV, 846.—That monks are more liable to temptations than secular persons, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 171.—On monks’ manual labour, ibid., 304.—Excellent instructions are given to an abbot, ibid., 391, 397.—On virginity, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1124; Sulpicius Severus, XX, 227; St. Jerome, XXII, 394, 424, 951.—On study, fasting, obedience, avoiding jokes, and other matters belonging to a virgin’s rule of life, ibid., 1105.—With what rudiments the young age of a girl destined for virginity should be instructed, St. Jerome, XXII, 1095.—Reproof of nuns, and a rule written for them, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 958.—On the veil of virginity, ibid., 645.—That girls who have undertaken the resolution of virginity not under compulsion but of their own will sin if they marry, even though they have not yet been consecrated, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1208.—To certain nuns, Bishop Boniface, LXXXIX, 721.—On monks, handmaids of God, Pope Zacharias, ibid., 933.—On the excellence of virginity, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 22.—On the prerogative of virginity, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 256.—That the state of virginity is far superior to that of married women or widows, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 193.—Whether the purpose of the desert suits a nun, ibid., 261.—A congratulatory letter to a nun who had withdrawn herself to better fruit, ibid., 259.—Women should not seek adornment; white garments befit virgins, Hildegard, CXCVII, 337.—On widowhood, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1124; St. Jerome, XXII, 550, 724, 951, 982.—On the estate of widows, Fulgentius, LXV, 311.—On a widow who, having received the veil, later marries, Pope Stephen II, LXXXIX, 1025.—On the manner of living in widowhood, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 494.—How a widowed queen should conduct herself, ibid., 556.—A consolation concerning a son’s degenerate life, ibid., 502.

II—Philosophical Letters, and Also Letters on the Liberal Arts.

Against philosophy, Pope St. Damasus, XIII, 366.—On philosophers, St. Jerome, XXII, 640.—On the Academics, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 61.—That philosophical questions should not properly be handled by bishops, nor profitably learned, ibid., 427, 431.—On Christian philosophy, ibid., XXXIII, 432.—On the books of Cicero, ibid., XXXIII, 431. There will always be room for disputation if mysteries are allowed to be weighed by human reasoning and the talkativeness of rhetoricians, St. Leo, LIV, 1149.—He dissuades from reading philosophers, Paulinus, LXI, 227.—He considers philosophy beneficial to those who use it cautiously, Seifrid, abbot, CXLII, 723.—He congratulates him on his conversion from secular to Christian philosophy, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 141.—Certain matters against philosophers, Gerhoh, CXCIII, 490; Peter the Venerable, CLXXXIX, 77.—Sayings of pagan philosophers, [Col. 0123] and also of jurists, may rightly be employed in imparting sacred doctrine, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 21.—Whether the soul, concerning which philosophers think wrongly, is a heavenly substance, Ambrose, XVI, 1074.—On the origin of the soul, St. Jerome, XXII, 1085, 1124, 1182.—Whether there is some body of the soul, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 77.—On the soul released from the body, and on prodigious visions, ibid., 698, 704.—On the ideas of things and sensible differences, ibid., 72, 79.—On understanding, memory, and phantasies, ibid., 67, 68.—On dreams and nocturnal images, ibid., 71, 72.—How movements of our mind are perceived by spirits, and how thoughts and dreams are suggested by them, ibid., 72.—On fate against the astrologers, ibid., 1061.—On the soul’s immortality, Alvarus of Córdoba, CXXI, 452, 458.—On true blessedness, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 63; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 172; Peter the Venerable, CLXXXIX, 77.—On friendship, Ruricius, LVIII, 89; Ennodius, LXIII, 24.—On wisdom and folly, Alvarus of Córdoba, CXXI, 448 ff.—On the permission of good and evil, Othion, monk, CXLVI, 137.—He recounts the benefits of literary study, Alcuin, C, 207.—Literary study should be directed toward the spiritual perfection of the inward person, Philip of Harvengt, CCIII, 32, 157, 165.—He shows that by writings men become immortal, Peter of Blois, CCVII, 237.—He exhorts Simon, canon of Chartres, to pursue literary study after the example of many philosophers, ibid., 249.—That the study of jurisprudence brings ruin to many, ibid., 416.—On dialectic, Abelard, CLXXVIII, 352.—On arithmetic, Theodoric, LXIX, 514; Alcuin, C, 270. On grammatical questions, ibid., C, 181; St. Lupus, Abbot of Ferrières, CXIX, 467, 500.—On astronomy, Alcuin, C, 254, 266, 269, 270, 274, 278, 281.—On music, Theodoric, LXIX, 570.—On an unknown chant, Guido of Arezzo, CXLI, 423.—He sets forth the rules of ecclesiastical chant, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 609.—Description of a countryside among the people of Limoges, Ruricius, LVIII, 76.—He describes the qualities of a horse sent by him to Celsus, ibid., 78.—He describes the origin and method of producing purple dye, Theodoric, LXIX, 505.—He wonderfully depicts elephants and their properties, Theodehad, LXIX, 818.—He describes the craft of a goldsmith, Athalaric, LXIX, 768.

[Col. 0123]

CCI, CCII, CCIII. INDEX OF LETTERS DEALING WITH CANON LAW, LITURGICAL MATTERS, CEREMONIES OR RITES, AND ALSO WITH ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINE.

Whether laymen ought to administer ecclesiastical property, Pope Stephen I, III, 1005; Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 316. On those who take away the Church’s property, Pope Lucius I, III, 976.—On certain matters pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline, Pope Felix II, XIII, 17.—Various prescriptions concerning discipline, Pope Innocent I, XX, 468, 495, 526, 551; Pope Celestine I, L, 429, 436; St. Leo the Great, LIV, 610, 615, 617, 624, 628, 645, 653, 666, 695, 703, 799, 1197, 1209; Pope Hilary, LVIII, 17, 24; Pope Felix III, LVIII, 924; Pope Gelasius I, LIX, 47, 57; Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 423; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 635, 673, 723, 1183; Pope Zacharias, LXXXIX, 917, 930; Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 978.—On dissension and the corrupted discipline of the churches of Spain, Pope Innocent I, XX, 485.—What should be done where the customs of regions or churches differ, and where they agree—for example concerning sacraments, feast days, fasting, and the Eucharist—St. Augustine, XXXIII, 199.—On the rites of the Church: those which may lawfully be neglected, and those which are to be abolished if that can be done without greater inconvenience, ibid., 204.—That church estates are not to be alienated unless the reason for alienation is first set forth before a council, Pope Hilary, LVIII, 26; Symmachus, LXII, 54; Pope Agapetus I, LXVI, 45. That in every church over which a bishop presides, four portions should be made, both from its revenues and from the offerings of the faithful, Pope Gelasius, LIX, 56; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 679, 1185.—What penance should be imposed upon invaders of church property, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 1124.—Whether ecclesiastical offices in East and West differ, Fulbert of Chartres, CXLI, 192.—That tithes should be paid to one’s own church, Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 272, 715, 802.—That exactions and tallages are not to be imposed upon churches by laymen, ibid., 474.—On avoiding plurality of benefices, ibid., 437.—On payment of annates and tithes to the Roman Church, ibid., 189.

Who are not to be admitted to make an accusation, Pope Stephen I, III, 997.—That pagans and heretics cannot accuse Christians, Pope Caius, I, 183.—On accusers, or accusations, which secular laws do not admit, Pope St. Julius I, VIII, 985.—That no one be summoned for judgment outside his province, ibid., 987.—That judges must not pronounce sentence against an absent person, and that a traitor is not to be heard, ibid., 988.—The permission to accuse must not extend beyond the limits of a province, ibid., 991.—Persons of ill repute and sacrilegious persons are not to be admitted as witnesses, Pope St. Felix II, XIII, 20.—Who may not accuse or testify, ibid., 21, 23.—The order of ecclesiastical judgments by which the contumacious may be restrained, Gratian, XIII, 586.—On various ecclesiastical cases, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 123, 124, 132, 166, 451, 468, 491, 520.—Clerics are not to be accused before a civil judge, Pope Pelagius II, LXXII, 746.—On appeals of bishops to the priest of the Roman Church, Pope St. Zosimus, XX, 680.—Graver cases are reserved for the Apostolic See, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 616, 645.—That persons rightly appealing to the Apostolic See are not to be impeded, Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 324; CCXV, 310, 1257.

On councils to be held three times a year, Pope Silvester, VIII, 825.—That all should attend synods, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 619.—That two councils of bishops should be held in every year, ibid., LIV, 673.—On a council to be held annually at Rome, ibid., 702.—That councils should annually be held from whatever provinces can do so, Pope Hilary, LVIII, 26; Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 423.—Councils are to be held twice yearly, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 675.—That synods should be held yearly, ibid., 1028, 1322.

On agreement in celebrating the feast of Easter, and against the Jews, Constantine the Great, VIII, 401, 504.—Constantine praises Eusebius’s oration on Easter, Constantine, VIII, 552.—On the observance of the Lord’s Easter, the Synod of Arles, VIII, 819, 825.—On the difficulty, yet at the same time the necessity, of determining the Easter day; and that the observance of days is lawful for prelates, St. Ambrose, XVI, 1026.—On the calculation of Easter, Pope Innocent I, XX, 517.—On the solemnities of Easter, St. Jerome, XXII, 1220.—On the celebration of Easter, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 603.—On Easter in the year 444, ibid., 606.—On the Easter solemnity of the year 452, ibid., 945.—On Easter, ibid., 1055, 1058, 1072, 1081, 1084, 1100, 1101.—That the Eastern Church agrees with the Roman concerning the Easter day, Germanus, bishop, LXIII, 481.—On the calculation of Easter, Dionysius Exiguus, LXVIII, 19; Pope Vigilius, LXIX, 18; St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1061; St. Columbanus, abbot, LXXX, 259, 264; Pope John IV, LXXX, 601; Pope Innocent, LXXXIV, 657; Pope Vigilius, LXXXIV, 832; Pope Vitalian, LXXXVII, 1004; Pope Adrian, XCVIII, 336, 374; Aldhelm, bishop of Sherborne, LXXXIX, 89; Ceolfrith, [Col. 0125] priest, ibid., 349; Bede the Venerable, XCIV, 675, 682; Pope Adrian, XCVIII, 340.—The times and rites for receiving baptism, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1134.—Outside Easter, priests may confer baptism; deacons are not granted the same permission, Pope Siricius, XIII, 1188.—Whether one baptized by heretics should be baptized again, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1194.—That baptismal regeneration is not to be given at every time, except at Easter and Pentecost, unless dangerous illness presses, ibid., 1209.—A person rebaptized is to be received through penance, Pope Felix III, LVIII, 924.—That no fees are to be exacted for baptizing the faithful, Pope Gelasius I, LIX, 50.—That no one should presume to baptize outside the Easter season and Pentecost, ibid., 52.—On properly administering baptism, Pope Vigilius, LXIX, 17, 19.—He approves the rite, introduced by Spaniards on account of the Arians, of a single immersion in baptism, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 496.—Those who receive their own children from the sacred font must separate from their wives, Pope Deusdedit, LXXX, 362.—On baptism given in the name of the Trinity, Braulio of Saragossa, LXXX, 683.—That those coming from the Novatians or Montanists are not to be rebaptized, Pope Innocent, LXXXIV, 646.—That the celebration of baptism on the day of Epiphany is forbidden, Pope Leo, LXXXIV, 755.—That those who, under force or fear, inclined their minds toward repetition of baptism are to be aided by the remedy of penance, Pope Leo, LXXXIV, 776.—That baptismal regeneration is not to be given at every time, ibid., 785.—On those who impiously submitted themselves to rebaptism, Pope Felix, LXXXIV, 794.—On those baptized or rebaptized by heretics: that they are not to advance to ecclesiastical service, Pope Felix, LXXXIV, 795.—On triple immersion, Pope Vigilius, LXXXIV, 831.—On those baptized without interrogation on the Creed by adulterous and unworthy priests, Pope Gregory II, LXXXIX, 525.—On those baptized by pagans, Pope Gregory III, LXXXIX, 377.—On persons doubtfully baptized, Pope Gregory III, LXXXIX, 577.—That baptism administered with corrupted words by an unlearned priest is not to be repeated, Pope Zacharias, LXXXIX, 929.—On the priest who, when water was lacking, baptized an endangered infant with wine, Pope Stephen II, LXXXIX, 1026.—On the priest who baptized while knowing neither the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, nor the psalms, Pope Stephen II, ibid., 1027.—On baptismal rites, Charlemagne, XCVIII, 938, 939; XCIX, 892.—Whether those baptized by someone who was not a priest ought to be baptized again, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 986.—How many times baptism ought to be celebrated throughout the year, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 1006.—On baptism, Hincmar of Rheims, CXXVI, 104.—That baptism is not true unless performed with water and by a priest, Pope Innocent III, CCXV, 812.—That the baptized ought to be confirmed only by bishops, Pope Innocent, LXXXIV, 642.—On certain priests marking the baptized, Eugenius of Toledo, LXXXVII, 403, 409.—On confirming infants, Innocent I, LVI, 515.—On giving the kiss of peace after the mysteries have been accomplished, Pope Innocent I, XX, 551.—On reception of the Eucharist, St. Jerome, XXII, 669.—On repetition of the sacrifice, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 624.—On the peace before the mysteries have been accomplished, Innocent, LVI, 515.—On names to be recited before the priest makes the prayer, ibid., 515.—That the celebration of Mass ought not to take place anywhere other than places dedicated to God, except where great necessity compels, Pope Felix IV, LXV, 15.

That the sacrifice for the departed is not to be offered for Geminius Victor, who had named his guardian contrary to the decree of the council of bishops, St. Cyprian, II, 399.—On the offices of Mass, Pope John III, LXXII, 18.—That the Roman Church receives nine prefaces to be sung during the solemnities of Mass, Pope Pelagius II, LXXII, 758.—On names not to be recited before the priest’s prayer, Pope Innocent, LXXXIV, 641.—On what is to be observed in Mass, Pope Gregory II, LXXXIX, 525.—On bishops’ saying *Gloria in excelsis* on Maundy Thursday, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 885.—How Communion ought to be received, ibid., 1000.—Whether one not fasting may receive Christ’s Communion, ibid., 1004.—Whether it is lawful to receive Communion from a priest caught in adultery, ibid., 1006.—How many Masses a priest may celebrate in one day, Pope Alexander II, CXLIV, 1410.—On the celebration of three Masses at the Nativity of the Lord, John the monk, CLXVI, 1509. On the custom of offering only dipped Eucharistic bread to communicants, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 222.—On the priest who, for lack of unleavened bread, consecrated ordinary bread, ibid., 228.—What the priest’s position on the right at Mass signifies, and on certain other rites, Geoffrey, subprior of St. Barbara, CCV, 864.

That final penance is to be denied to no one, Pope Celestine [Col. 0126] I, IV, 429.—What the order of reconciliation ought to be, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 1011.—That a penitent who dies before reconciliation cannot be reconciled after death, ibid., 1012.—That reconciliation is not to be denied to anyone at the point of death who asks for it, ibid.—That penance is to be denied to no one who requests it by signs, with canonical rules concerning apostates observed, ibid., 1013.—On the penance of the faithful: that their confession is not to be made public, ibid., 1210.—On penitents, Innocent, LVI, 517.—On those who have by no means observed the penance they received, Pope Siricius, LXXXIV, 632.—On those who, after baptism, have at all times given themselves to the pleasures of incontinence and seek penance at the end, Pope Innocent, ibid., 650.—That penitents are not to be received by other bishops, Pope Felix, ibid., 796.—On penance for a fault committed in Mass, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 179.—On penances to be imposed for crimes, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, ibid., 167, 168.—On the excommunicated, Cyprian, IV, 360, 364; Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 187.—On ecclesiastical vestments, Pope Stephen I, III, 997.—That it is not lawful to perform ordinations in another’s territory, Pope Siricius XIII, ibid., 1193.—Certain ordinations contrary to the canons, Pope Innocent I, XX, 490.

Hasty ordinations “by leap” are forbidden, Pope St. Zosimus, XX, 668.—What periods are prescribed for each rank of clergy, ibid., 670.—That illicit ordinations must be abstained from, Pope Celestine I, L, 429.—He commends observance of the canons, especially in ordinations, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 617.—He censures ordinations performed amid tumult, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 645.—The untrained and neophytes ought not to be ordained, ibid., 649.—No one is to be ordained without the consent of clergy and people, ibid., 633. It is not lawful to marry one’s maternal uncle’s wife, Pope Siricius, XIII, 1191.—It is not lawful to marry one’s wife’s sister, ibid., 1189.—He asks concerning the degrees of consanguinity within which marriage is lawful, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1320, 1322.—No one may take his godmother as wife, Pope Deusdedit, LXXX, 362.—That women who had married others when their husbands had been captured must be reunited with their first husbands when those husbands return from captivity, Pope Leo, LXXXIV, 773.—On women who have married two brothers, or men who have taken two sisters as wives, Pope Zacharias, LXXXIX, 936.—On those who have adulteresses as wives, or are themselves adulterers, ibid., 937.—It is not lawful for a son to marry the woman whom his father received from the sacred font of baptism, ibid., 957.—If one spouse cannot render the marital due, Pope Stephen II, LXXXIX, 1024.—On a woman who married another man when her husband was falsely believed dead in another province, Pope Stephen II, LXXXIX, 1028.—On marriage ceremonies, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 979.—Whether it is lawful to have two wives at once, ibid., 999.—Whether it is lawful for a man to have intercourse with or sleep with his wife at night or in daytime on the Lord’s Day, ibid., 1004.—On those who, having dismissed their wives, entered other marriages, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 1125.—He shows that wives are not to be dismissed, Pope John VIII, CXXVI, 745.—On impediments to marriage, Atto of Vercelli, CXXIV, 706.—Whether it is lawful to marry a concubine, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 28.—Whether six-year-old children can contract betrothal, Ivo of Chartres, 118.—That no marriage can take place, on any pretext whatever, between blood relatives and relatives by marriage, Hildebert, CLXXI, 221.—On the impediment to marriage by consanguinity, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 575.—A girl cannot contract betrothal before her seventh year, Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 290.—That unbelievers joined in a prohibited degree should not be separated after baptism, ibid., 475.—That betrothals contracted between persons below puberty should be consummated if they consent when they become pubescent, ibid., 539.—On witnesses to be admitted in a matrimonial case, ibid., CCXV, 192.—On a certain matrimonial case, ibid., 773; CCXVI, 66.—Whether, after his wife’s death, a man may marry the prostitute with whom he had lived while his wife was alive, ibid., CCXIV, 90.—To marry prostitutes is pious and meritorious, ibid., 102.—That a mute and a deaf person can contract marriage, ibid., 304.—On witnesses to be admitted in a matrimonial case, ibid., CCXV, 192; CCXVI, 45.—The manner of receiving heretics into the Church, Pope St. Siricius, XIII, 1133.—And those coming from the Novatians or Montanists are to be received through laying on of hands, ibid., 1160.—On those who have fallen into heresy through fear: that, if converted, they are to be received, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 391.—That the names of heretics are not to be recited at the sacred altar, ibid., 914.—That those involved in heretics’ errors through fear, not will, are to be received upon satisfaction and an unequivocal profession, ibid., 922.—That even heresiarchs seeking pardon are not to be rejected, though neither are they to be received rashly, ibid., 944.—Those [Col. 0127] baptized in heresy with invocation of the Trinity are not to be baptized if they return to the Church, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 1204.—That heretics can neither be elected to any dignities nor elect anyone, Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 256.—How proceedings should be conducted against persons suspected of heresy, ibid., 988.

## On virgins

What is to be done concerning a girl not yet veiled who should likewise fall away from her profession, Pope Siricius, XIII, 1183.—That veiled handmaids of God, if they are publicly to marry or secretly give themselves over to corruption, are not to be admitted to penance unless the man to whom they had joined themselves has departed from the world, Pope Innocent I, XX, 379.—That handmaids of God not yet consecrated, if they later wish to marry, are to be received to penance, ibid., 379.—What ought to be done concerning the aforementioned virgins violated by barbarian force, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 655.—That virgins be consecrated on appointed days, Pope Gelasius I, LIX, 62.—That abductors of virgins be expelled from the communion of the Church, Pope Symmachus, LXII, 54.—That virgins who have professed continence are not to marry, ibid.—A virgin under sixty years old is not to be made abbess, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 679.—That virgins be veiled without charge, ibid., 697.—That soldiers are not to lodge in a convent of virgins, ibid., 1026.—On consecrated virgins if they have fallen, Pope Innocent, LXXXIV, 648.—On un-veiled virgins if they go astray, ibid.—When sacred virgins are to be veiled, Pope Gelasius, LXXXIV, 801.—On veiled virgins if they go astray, Pope Zacharias, LXXXIX, 936; XCVIII, 88, 89, 91.—On virgins who do not keep their profession, ibid., 937.—On certain nuns, Bishop Boniface, LXXXIX, 721.—That a woman consecrated to God refrain from intercourse with secular persons, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 163.—A virgin is not to leave the monastery for any destination, especially not alone, and above all not on feast days, Hildebert, CLXXI, 269.

to review, Pope Innocent I, ibid., 537.—On measures taken at Antioch for peace, ibid., 540.—On the terms upon which Innocent grants communion to Acacius, ibid., 543, 544.—On peace granted to the Church of Antioch, ibid., 546.—That the first see of blessed Peter is remembered as being at Antioch, ibid., 547.—On the Council of Carthage, by which the impieties of Pelagius and Celestius were condemned, so that the authority of the Apostolic See might be added to its judgment, ibid., 564.—On the heresy of Pelagius, Augustine, Alypius, etc., ibid., 572; Innocent I, ibid., 582, 593; Aurelius of Carthage, ibid., 1009.—On the Council of Milevis, ibid., 588.—On Jerome the presbyter, whom Pope Innocent I consoles concerning what he suffered, ibid., 600.—On Paula and Eustochium, and the evils by which they were afflicted, ibid., 601.—On Arcadius, Eudoxia, Arsacius, and Theophilus, condemned by Pope Innocent I, ibid., 629.—On Emperor Arcadius, who writes to Pope Innocent that he and Eudoxia may be released from excommunication, ibid., 633.—On Emperor Arcadius, whom Pope Innocent releases from excommunication, ibid., 635.—On the privileges of the Church of Arles, Pope Zosimus, ibid., 642, 665.—On the case of Celestius, ibid., 649, 654, 669, 675; Aurelius of Carthage, ibid., 1009.—On Ursus and Tuentius, bishops unlawfully ordained, that they are nowhere to be admitted into the Church’s communion, ibid., 661.—On Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, ibid., 666.—On the condemnation of Proculus and unlawful ordinations, ibid., 673.—On Patroclus the metropolitan, ibid., 668, 674.—On the Jews, Severus of Majorca, ibid., 732.—On the lawful ordination of Pope Boniface I, ibid., 750.—On Maximus, bishop of the city of Valence, accused of various crimes, Pope Boniface I, ibid., 756.—On Peregne [name uncertain], a bishop to be received by the Corinthians, ibid., 760, 761, 779.—On the rescript of Emperor Honorius decreeing that, if two bishops are again ordained at Rome, both be expelled from the city, ibid., 768.—On the rights of the Church of Constantinople in Illyricum, Emperor Theodosius, ibid., 769.—On Emperor Theodosius’s rescript that the privileges of the Roman bishop be preserved inviolate throughout Illyricum, ibid., 770.—On the dignity of vicar of Blessed Peter granted to Rufus, Boniface, ibid., 761, 774, 777, 779.—On a woman falsely accused of adultery, who cannot die despite being struck seven times, St. Jerome, XXII, 326.—On Rufinus of Aquileia, ibid., 332, 335.—He asks Florentius for certain books and offers him others of which he had an abundance, ibid., 336.—On the praise of Bonosus, ibid., 339.—On Niceas, his companion in pilgrimage, now returned to his homeland, ibid., 341.—He asks Paul of Concordia for several books, meanwhile sending him the Life of Paul the Hermit, ibid., 343.—On his maternal aunt Castorina, whom he exhorts to peace, ibid., 346.

On Heliodorus, his companion in travel, to whom he commends the blessedness of the eremitic life, St. Jerome, XXII, 347.---On the three men who divide the Church of Antioch, 358.---On Eustochium, Paula’s daughter, to whom he recounts his temptations in the desert, ibid., 394.---On the death of the most devout woman Lea, ibid., 425.---On the praises of the virgin Asella, who at Rome lived a most holy solitary life as though in a desert, ibid., 427.---On certain small gifts sent to him by Eustochium on the birthday of St. Peter, Jerome, ibid., 445.---On other small gifts sent by Marcella, ibid., 480.---On the illness of Blesilla, Paula’s daughter, who after her husband’s death had wholly turned herself to Christ, ibid., 463.---On Blesilla’s death and her praise, 465.---On a certain Onasus, whom Jerome mocks because he had disparaged his writings, ibid., 473.---On Marcella, whom Jerome urges, after leaving Rome, to withdraw to the country because of the advantages of solitude, ibid., 478.---That Paula should move to Bethlehem, ibid., 483.---Jerome clears himself of the slanders of his detractors, ibid., 480.---On Jerome’s books against Jovinian, ibid., 493, 512.---On Paulinianus, ordained priest by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, without consulting the bishop of Jerusalem, ibid., 517.---On the death of the priest Nepotian, ibid., 589.---On Vigilantius, who, having returned to the West, was defaming Jerome’s [Col. 0134] name and his friends, ibid., 602.---On the friend Tranquillinus, whom Jerome instructs how Origen ought to be read, ibid., 606.---On Fabiola, who had gone to Bethlehem to live there with Paula and Eustochium, but was compelled by the impending Barbarians to return suddenly to Rome, ibid., 607.---On Pammachius, who, after his wife’s death, bestowed his wealth upon the poor, ibid., 639. On the title of the book on ecclesiastical writers published by Jerome, ibid., 647.---On Castrutius of Pannonia, whom he consoles concerning blindness of the eyes, ibid., 651.---On Jerome’s shorter works: why he introduces examples from secular literature into them, ibid., 664.---To Lucinius, a Baetican by birth, he sends certain of his works, together with four small hair-shirts and a copy of Isaiah, ibid., 669.---On Fabiola’s death, ibid., 690.---On Rufinus’s preface to Origen’s books *On First Principles* (*Περὶ ἀρχῶν*), 733.---He recounts Paula’s life, and especially her journey to Bethlehem, ibid., 878.---On John, bishop of Jerusalem, that peace may be restored between him and the monks living with him, ibid., 736.---On Pammachius and Oceanus, who urge Jerome to translate the book *On First Principles* (*Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) precisely into Latin, etc., ibid., 743.---What Jerome thought of Origen, ibid., 743, 752.---On Theophilus, through whose efforts the party of the Origenists was defeated, ibid., 754, 755, 756, 757, 769, 771, 772.---On the education of the little girl Pacatula, ibid., 1095.---He laments that, under the appearance of religion, banqueting and drunkenness are commonly practised throughout Africa in cemeteries and at the memorial shrines of martyrs, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 90, 114.---On Augustine’s five books against the Manichaeans, St. Paulinus, ibid., 101.---On Proculeianus, bishop of the Donatist party at Hippo, whom he invites to settle the schism through a mutual conference, St. Augustine, ibid., 129.---On a young man accustomed to beat his mother, who finally threatened her with death, joined the Donatists, and was rebaptized by them, ibid., 132.---On restraining, through Bishop Proculeianus, the license of Donatist clerics, ibid., 134.---On the title of the book on ecclesiastical writers published by Jerome himself, Augustine to Jerome, ibid., 154.---On the proceedings begun toward concord with Fortunius, bishop of the Donatists, ibid., 173.---He informs Aurelius that Donatus and Donatus’s brother had withdrawn from the monastery against his resistance, ibid., 227.---That Donatist clerics coming to the Catholic Church should be received in their own rank, ibid., 228.---On Timothy, ordained subdeacon in the diocese of Hippo against Augustine’s will, ibid., 230.---On Crispinus of Calama, who had rebaptized the Mappalians after subduing them by fear, ibid., 235.---Why he refused to entrust a church to the disreputable priest Abundantius, ibid., 234.---On Castorius, that he should succeed his brother Maximian, who was gloriously yielding up the episcopate of the Church of Vaga, ibid., 238.---He testifies that he has received Jerome’s apology against Rufinus, ibid., 245.---A monk accused by the priest Boniface shifts the charge onto Boniface himself; they go to the tomb of St. Felix of Nola, that the case may be decided by a miracle, ibid., 267.---On Caecilianus, governor, that by his edict he should restrain the Donatists in the region of Hippo and neighboring places, ibid., 296.---On Donatists in the region of Hippo not yet corrected by Festus’s letters, ibid., 309.---On injuries recently inflicted upon Christians by the people of Calama, ibid., 313, 383.---The Catholic clerics of Hippo complain to Januarius, Donatist bishop, about the violence of the Circumcellions against Catholics, ibid., 302.

On Olympius, master of offices, that he should uphold the laws concerning the destruction of idols and the correction of heretics, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 357.---On Donatus, proconsul of Africa, that he should restrain the Donatists but not kill them, ibid., 366.---To Bishop Memorius, who requests his books on music, he sends the sixth book, ibid., 367.---He asks Cresconius to assist his petition on behalf of Faventius, ibid., 428, 429, 430.---On Pinianus, suddenly demanded for the priesthood by a popular tumult in the city of Hippo, ibid., 473, 476.---On how Donatists ought to be punished, ibid., 396, 509, 510, 535.---How the bishops of the Donatist faction were convicted at the Conference of Carthage, ibid., 577.---On the return of the priests Saturninus and Euphrates to the Church, ibid., 583.---On the people of Cirta converted from the Donatist faction to communion with the Catholic Church, ibid., 590.---On Donatus, Donatist priest of the estate of Mutugenna in the diocese of Hippo, ibid., 753.---On the proceedings against Pelagius and Caelestius, ibid., 758.---On the Pelagian heretics, ibid., 762, 772, 783.---On the plan and arrangement of the books of *The City of God*, ibid., 789.---On Dioscorus, converted to Christianity by miracles, ibid., 1012.---On Pascentius, an Arian count of the royal household, who had challenged Augustine himself to a conference at Carthage, ibid., 1038.---On Peter’s baptism and penance, against a certain Novatian, ibid., 1086.---On a certain Fascius, overwhelmed by debt and taking refuge in a church, whose creditors Augustine satisfies, ibid., [Col. 0135] 1991.---On Anthony, bishop of Fussala, who, having been deprived of the administration of his church because of crimes, had appealed to the Apostolic See, the same author, L, 417.---On Apiarius, how he was compelled to confess his misdeeds, ibid., 422.---On the concern of Pope Celestine I for the province of Illyricum, ibid., 427.---On how Pope Celestine ought to conduct himself toward certain Western bishops who complained that they were suffering injustice, Nestorius, ibid., 438.---On how Pope Celestine ought to conduct himself toward Julian and others of the same sect, ibid., 442.---On Nestorius’s doctrine and what he had done thus far, St. Cyril, ibid., 447.---On Nestorius, condemned by Pope Celestine I and, unless he correct himself, to be removed from communion with the Church, ibid., 459, 465, 469.---On the people of Constantinople, that they should reject Nestorius’s new impieties, Pope Celestine I, ibid., 485.---On the Synod of Ephesus, ibid., 503, 505, 511.---On Prosper and Hilary, who accuse certain priests of Gaul of following Pelagius’s teaching, ibid., 528.---On Nestorius’s appointment in Maximian’s place, approved by Pope Celestine, ibid., 537.---That he should be removed from all communion, ibid., 544, 548, 592.---On the possessions in Asia bequeathed to the Church by Proba, ibid., 544.---On the election of Maximian, bishop of Constantinople, ibid., 547, 549, 592.---On Arcadius, driven into exile by Genseric, king of the Vandals, Honoratus, ibid., 567.---On the ordination of Pope Sixtus III, ibid., 583, 587.---On the remnants of the Pelagian heresy growing up in Gaul, St. Prosper of Aquitaine, LI, 67.---On the death of St. Paulinus, addressed to Pacatus, the priest Uranius, LIII, 859.---On Manichaeans discovered in the city of Rome, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 620.---On Valentinian III’s constitution against the Manichaeans, ibid., 622.---On the case of Hilary, bishop of Arles, ibid., 628.---On the vicariate of Thessalonica and the case of Atticus, bishop of Nicopolis, ibid., 668.---On the proceedings against Eutyches at the synod, ibid., 749.---On the Robber Synod of Ephesus, ibid., 823, 840.---On the ordination of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, ibid., 853.---On the disturbance of the Catholic Church, Empress Eudoxia, ibid., 861.---On the privileges of the Church of Arles, ibid., 879, 884.---On the tyranny and impious acts of Dioscorus of Alexandria, ibid., 852.---On Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, ibid., 991, 997, 1001, 1032, 1073, 1094, 1098.---On the crowds and violence of Palestinian monks, by which they harassed Catholics, ibid., 1014, 1060, 1061, 1069, 1070.---On Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, expelled by those same persons, and on another substituted for him, ibid., 1014.

On Aetius and Andrew, Leo the Great, LIV, 1019, 1023, 1024, 1037, 1096, 1132, 1142.---On Timothy Aelurus, expelled from the Church of Alexandria, and on the election of a Catholic bishop in his place, ibid., 1212, 1214, 1215, 1217.---On the Ephesian pseudo-council, Pope Hilary, LVIII, 11.---On Irenaeus, removed from the Church of Barcelona, that he should return to his own church, ibid., 18.---On the city of Cimiez and the town of Nice, that they should return to the governance of one bishop, ibid., 20.---On the beginnings of Leontius’s episcopate at Arles, ibid., 22.---On the rights of the Church of Arles, ibid.; Pope Symmachus, LXII, 65.---On Hermes, said to have rashly usurped the episcopate of the Church of Narbonne, Pope Hilary, ibid., 24.---On the parishes of the Church of Arles, which Leontius claimed back, ibid., 26.---On Bishop Mamertus, who had ordained a bishop for Die outside his own boundaries, ibid., 27, 28, 31, 32.---On the vicariate over all the churches of Spain entrusted to Zeno in the stead of the See, Pope Simplicius, LVIII, 35.---On Gaudentius, bishop of Aups, deprived, on account of unlawful ordinations, of priestly office and one-third of the revenues of the church, ibid., 37.---On Timothy Aelurus, who was attempting again to seize the see of Alexandria, that he should be restrained by royal authority, ibid., 38.---On Timothy, Catholic bishop of Alexandria, restored to his church, ibid., 47 and following.---On Peter, disturber of the Church of Alexandria, ibid., 48, 50, 55.---On the election of Calendion, bishop of Antioch, ibid., 55.---On the election and life of Bishop Sidonius, St. Lupus of Troyes, ibid., 63; Sidonius, ibid., 452, 461, 462, 489, 494.---On the Church of Alexandria, Pope Felix III, ibid., 899.---He wittily depicts the condition of the city of Ravenna, Sidonius, ibid., 461.---On the deposition and anathematization of Peter the Fuller, Pope Felix III, ibid., 911, 917.---On Arvandus, praetorian prefect of Gaul, Sidonius, ibid., 456.---On Acacius, justly and lawfully condemned, Pope Felix III, ibid., 944; Gelasius, LIX, 26.---On the election and life of Pope Gelasius, ibid., 22, 138.---The superstitious celebration of the Lupercalia, ibid., 110.---On the death of Paulina, wife of Pammachius, a man of proconsular rank, St. Paulinus, LXI, 207.---He appends the history of the discovery of the Cross, ibid., 325.---On abolishing the law of King Odoacer, which conflicted with ecclesiastical freedom in the election of a pontiff, and on preserving Church property, Pope Symmachus, LXII, 72.---On settling dissensions in the regions of Scythia, Anastasius, LXIII, 369, 373.---On the [Col. 0136] conversion of the provinces of Dardania and Illyricum, and he requests to be informed of the result of the embassy sent to Constantinople, Pope Hormisdas, ibid., 394.---On the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch, that they should be restored to communion with the Apostolic See, ibid., 461.---On what was done at Thessalonica by the Eutychians, ibid., 467.---On what Dorotheus did at Thessalonica against Bishop John, ibid., 468.---On the Church of Constantinople returned to communion with the Apostolic See, ibid., 470.---On dissensions stirred up by the Scythian monks, ibid., 471, 475, 477, 478, 490.---On the crimes of the Thessalonians, ibid., 483.---On Epiphanius, appointed in the place of John of Constantinople, ibid., 482, 493, 494, 505.---On the reconciliation of the Church of Carthage, Pope Boniface II, LXV, 43.---On confirmation of the senatorial decree issued against Simoniacs, King Athalaric, LXVI, 11.---On Bishop Contumeliosus, deprived of his episcopate, Pope John II, ibid., 24; Agapetus, ibid., 46.---On what was done against Amator, Pope Silverius, ibid., 86.---On Clothilde, wife of Clovis I, St. Nicetius, LXVIII, 378.---On Emperor Justinian recalled from error, ibid., 378.---On imposing penance upon King Theudebert because he had contracted an incestuous marriage, Pope Vigilius, LXIX, 21.---On Auxanius of Arles, to whom use of the pallium is granted, ibid., 27, 29.---On the investigation of Bishop Praetextatus’s case, ibid., 29.---On Aurelian, bishop of Arles, ibid., 39, 41.---On what was done at Constantinople concerning the Three Chapters, ibid., 51.---On Pope Vigilius’s withdrawal to Saint Euphemia, ibid., 53.---On the Three Chapters, ibid., 64, 66, 113.---On confirmation of the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, ibid., 121.---On the patrician Narses, Pope Pelagius I, ibid., 393, 394, 396, 397.

On Sapaudus, bishop of Arles, to whom he grants use of the pallium, Pelagius, LXIX, 405, 406.---On the method of producing purple dye, King Theodoric, ibid., 505.---On the patrician Cassiodorus, ibid., 507, 508.---On Plutianus’s property, fraudulently taken away, ibid., 512, 513.---On the Gallic expedition, ibid., 524.---On pantomimes, that they should practise their arts in specified places, ibid., 529.---On weapons necessary for the soldiers of Salona before they set out for war, ibid., 535.---On Artemidorus, to whom the prefecture of the city is conferred, ibid., 536, 537, 538.---On Boethius, that he should make water-clocks and a sundial to be sent to the king of the Burgundians, ibid., 539, 541.---On the fifteen hundred solidi sent through Montanarius, to be distributed among provincials who had suffered loss through the army, ibid., 548.---On bacon not to be sent to foreign provinces, but kept in Italy for domestic use, ibid., 550.---On the election of Venantius, a man of illustrious rank, to the office of Count of the Domestics, ibid., 553.---On merchants of Apulia and Calabria, that they should not henceforth be burdened, ibid., 560.---On a bronze statue stolen from the city of Como, that it should be sought out, ibid., 566.---On Clovis’s victory over the Alamanni, ibid., 573.---On a cithara-player sent to the king of the Franks, ibid., 570, 574.---On restoring peace between Alaric and Clovis, ibid., 575 ff. On the dispatch of Gemellus to Gaul, to serve in the office of deputy prefect, ibid., 584, 585.---On Colossaeus, a man of illustrious rank, to whom the government of Sirmian Pannonia is entrusted, ibid., 588, 589, 620.---On repairing Rome’s sewers, ibid., 592.---That he had sent military expenditures from Italy to the soldiers, so that Gaul might not be burdened too severely, ibid., 598.---That, when the army enters Gaul, slaves deserting to others should be restored to their former masters, ibid., 599.---On the sum of money sent for repairing the walls and old towers of Arles, ibid., 599.---That the cattle of the Alamanni, worn out by the length and labor of the journey, should be exchanged for Norican cattle, ibid., 604.---On Herminafrid, king of the Thuringians, to whom Theodoric gives his niece in marriage, ibid., 609.---He decrees that all shippers of Campania, Lucania, and Tuscany should give suitable sureties for transporting provisions to famine-stricken Gaul, ibid., 614.---He warns those carrying grain from Sicily to Gaul that they have suffered a most grievous shipwreck, ibid., 615.---On restoring the possessions of the Church of Narbonne, ibid., 622.---On the immunity of the city of Marseilles, ibid., 626.---On the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, ibid., 641.---On Pompey’s theatre, that it should be strengthened and repaired at the king’s expense, ibid., 642.---On constructing walls for a new city in the region of Trent, ibid., 651.---On the Gepids passing into Gaul, that all necessities should be supplied to them, ibid., 652.---That Abundantius, praetorian prefect, should purchase timber for constructing one thousand dromons, ibid., 656, 657, 658, 659.---That trees growing in the channel of the Signine aqueduct should be cut down at the roots, ibid., 670.---The savagery of spectacles, Titus’s amphitheatre, and the games presented in it are described, ibid., 675.---On Athalaric’s elevation to the throne by the joint votes of Goths [Col. 0137] and Romans, ibid., 735, 737, 738, 739.---A description of the province of Bruttium, ibid., 761.---A description of the Fountain of Arethusa, ibid., 762.---On the murder of Amalafrida by Hilderic, king of the Vandals, King Athalaric, ibid., 765.---Oswin is sent to govern the provinces of Dalmatia and Suevia, ibid., 773.---He remits the taxes imposed upon all provincials contrary to custom, ibid., 774.---On decrees against Simoniacs in accordance with the ancient senatorial resolutions, ibid., 778, 781.---On various decrees of King Athalaric, ibid., 782, 786.---That teachers of grammar, rhetoric, and law should receive their established emoluments without any reduction, ibid., 787.

King Theodoric enumerates the offices Cassiodorus had held, LXIX, 791.---On King Theodebald, admitted by Amalasuntha as co-ruler, ibid., 795, 797.---Edicts on maintaining prices at Ravenna and along the Flaminian Way, ibid., 838.---He writes that he was made king by the army, according to ancestral custom, ibid., 819.---He sets forth the calamities Italy suffered because of wars, ibid., 820.---He describes the city of Como, ibid., 840.---He decrees that seven hundred solidi be given to one who has commendably fulfilled the office of *cornicularius*, ibid., 847.---On the method of making paper and its usefulness, ibid., 848.---He praises Palmatian wine and likewise Sila cheese, ibid., 863.---The praetorian prefect describes the region of Reggio and forbids bacon and wheat to be demanded from it thereafter under the designation of compulsory purchase, ibid., 865.---He describes the city of Squillace, his native place, and the fishponds which he had excavated at the foot of Mount Moscius, ibid., 866.---On repairing the Flaminian Way, ibid., 869.---He describes the office and usefulness of scribes, ibid., 871.---A description of the province of Istria, ibid., 872.---He orders the provincials of Istria to pay their tax in wine, oil, and wheat, ibid., 872 ff.---He announces to the Ligurians victory over the Burgundians and the flight of the Alamanni, ibid., 878.---On Clement I, who governed the Apostolic See after blessed Peter, Peter himself having handed it over to him, Pope St. John III, LXXII, 13.---The dispatch of hairs of St. Paul to Eraldus, bishop of Vienne, ibid., 18.---On Pope Gregory’s much-praised book of Rules, Licinianus of Carthage, ibid., 689.---That the deacon Gregory should obtain from the emperor assistance against the Lombards, Pope Pelagius II, ibid., 703.---That the Frankish kings should not make an alliance with the Lombards, ibid., 705.---On John, bishop of Constantinople, who claimed for himself the title of universal bishop, ibid., 738.---That Abbot Stephen should write the life of St. Amator, Aunarius of Auxerre, ibid., 767, 769.

On abolishing the remnants of idolatry and on observing the feasts of holy days chastely, Childebert, king of the Franks, ibid., 1121.---That King Sigebert should not defend Promotus’s case, Council of Paris, ibid., 1123.---On the subdeacon Peter, to whom he entrusts his authority within Sicily, Pope St. Gregory, LXXVII, 441, 455, 463, 489, 494, 498, 508, 517, 523, 525, 526.---On Justin, praetor of Sicily, ibid., 443, 571.---On the deserted Church of Minturnae, which he unites to that of Formiae, ibid., 454.---On transferring a synagogue of the Jews if it obstructs the services of a church, ibid., 457.---That sons of Lombards baptized in the Arian heresy should be reconciled to the Catholic faith, ibid., 462.---On the dispute of Honoratus, deacon of Salona, against his bishop, ibid., 464, 465, 512, 554, 555, 642.---He sends John, former consul and patrician, a key of Saint Peter and something from his chains, ibid., 483.---On Virgil, bishop of Arles, and Theodore, bishop of Marseilles, that they should gently encourage Jews to embrace the faith, ibid., 509.---On building a monastery in Corsica and correcting monks in Gorgona, ibid., 514.---On solemnly placing the relics of St. Agatha in the monastery of Saint Stephen, ibid., 515.---On electing a bishop of Rimini, ibid., 517.---On Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa, that he should order Theodore, master of soldiers, to cease harassing the poor and the Church, ibid., 519.---That the subdeacon Anthemius should see to the restoration of the sacred furnishings of the Church of Venafro, which clerics had sold to a Jew, ibid., 524.---On restoring the possessions and funds of the Church of Taormina, ibid., 527.---On Gennadius, patrician, that he should suppress heretics’ attacks upon the Church, ibid., 528.---That, once a council has been convened as quickly as possible, an inquiry should be made into Argentius, bishop of Lamego, ibid., 537.---On Paul, bishop of Naples, ibid., 546, 550.---That Bishop Castorius and his successors should not administer the monastery’s affairs after the death of the abbot of Rimini, ibid., 378.---He unites the Churches of Cumae and Misenum and appoints Benenatus bishop of both, ibid., 582.---On compelling the schismatic bishops of Istria to unity, ibid., 583.---He unites the Church of Tres Tabernae, laid waste by enemies, to that of Velletri, ibid., 591.

On the praised book *Pastoral Rule*, Licinianus, bishop, [Col. 0138] LXXVII, 599.---On the sedition stirred up against Bishop Paul, ibid., 603.---On the tunic of St. John, which Pope St. Gregory requests from Abbot John, ibid., 605.---On the excommunication of Bishop John, ibid., 607.---On Agnellus, bishop of Fondi, whom he appoints over the Church of Terracina, ibid., 614, 615.---That the subdeacon Gratiosus should hand over to Abbess Flora a house with gardens and lodgings for building a monastery, ibid., 617.---That Peter, subdeacon of Campania, should send the relics of St. Severinus for the consecration of a church, ibid., 618.---He unites the Church of St. Anthemius to that of Nomentum, ibid., 619.---He informs Dynamius, patrician of Gaul, that he has received four hundred solidi from the revenues of the Roman Church, ibid., 630.---On Libertinus, prefect, that he should punish Nasa, a Jewish seducer, and free Christian slaves purchased by him, ibid., 635.---The ministries, monies, etc., of the Church of Siponto are to be described, and an inventory of them sent to Rome, ibid., 638.---Bishop Boniface of Reggio should restore to Stephania property seized by the agents of his predecessor, ibid., 639.---Bishop Andrew of Taranto should lay down the priesthood if he is conscious of sin with a concubine, ibid., 640, 641.---He sends Bishop Columbanus something enclosed in keys from the chains of blessed Peter, ibid., 642.---On consecrating the monastery of Abbess Gratiosa, ibid., 660.---That Emperor Maurice should moderate or alter the law by which he had forbidden both persons bound to public accounts and soldiers to be admitted into monasteries, ibid., 662.---He congratulates Metropolitan Domitian because he had preached the faith to the emperor of the Persians, ibid., 666.---On Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards, ibid., 669, 671, 712, 713, 1314.---That Deacon Cyprian should investigate the wrongdoing of the convert Petronilla and Agnellus, her seducer, ibid., 672.---That the patrician Gennadius should restrain the internal wars of churches, ibid., 573.---A proven man is to be assigned to every monastery of women servants of God, through whom its business may be managed, ibid., 675.---On scattered vessels brought into Sicily by Italian priests, that they should be collected, ibid., 685.---On the Church of St. Pancras granted to monks in perpetuity, ibid., 687.---Jews must not be permitted to retain a Christian slave, ibid., 690.---On Hospito, leader of the Barbaricini, that he should favor Felix and Cyriacus in converting the Barbaricini from idolatry, ibid., 692, 693.---To Empress Constantina, who had requested the head of St. Paul, he relates various miracles, ibid., 700.---On repressing the audacity of the Donatists, ibid., 708, 709, 726.---On John of Ravenna: he is not to be named during the solemnities of the Masses, ibid., 713.---On curbing the arrogance of Maximus, who had caused Gregory’s writings to be publicly torn up, ibid., 720.---That Deacon Cyprian should prosecute the Manichaeans. Chiemsee, ibid., 868.---Against the bishop of Hildesheim, ibid., 871.---Against the bishop of Halberstadt, ibid., 872.---Concerning the absolution of the king of England, ibid., 876, 878, 881, 926.---Concerning the establishment of a new bishopric in Livonia, ibid., 917.---Concerning the accusation against the archbishop of Sorrento, ibid., 928.---Concerning the citizens of Sens, that they ibid., 283.---Concerning Emperor Baldwin, how he was defeated and captured, ibid., 292, 294.---Concerning the agreement made between King Philip and the citizens of Cologne, ibid., 297.---Concerning the agreement between John, king of England, and Queen Berengaria, former wife of King Richard, ibid., 303.---Frederick II’s promise that the crown of Sicily should be separated from the Empire, ibid., 305.

II.---Letters of Praise.

Saint Cyprian congratulates Pope Cornelius on the return of the confessors to the Church, III, 731.---He congratulates Pope Cornelius because, by his courageous confession, he had shown himself a leader to his people in making confession, ibid., 830.---He congratulates Pope Lucius on his return from exile, ibid., III, 971.---He praises martyrs and confessors and urges them to perseverance, the same author, V, 245, 264, 288, 542, 414.---Helena congratulates Constantine because he had turned away from the vanity of idols, the same author, VIII, 529.---Constantine praises Eusebius’s oration on Easter, ibid., 551.---Saint Ambrose praises Emperor Gratian’s humility, faith, and piety, XVI, 876.---He praises Emperor Theodosius because he had laboured to restore unity between the Eastern and Western Church, ibid., 953.---He praises Acholius, ibid., 955, 959.---He praises Valentinian’s supreme piety toward God and goodwill toward himself, ibid., 1165.---He commends Sisinnius for granting pardon to his son, who had married without consulting him, ibid., 1279.---Symmachus praises his son for his verses, the same author, XVIII, 147, 149.---Symmachus praises Ausonius for his verses on the consulship, XVIII, 153, 155, 156, 158.---He highly praises the rhetor Palladius, ibid., 153.---Ausonius replies to Symmachus, who praises him, ibid., 159.---Symmachus praises the ever-Augusti Theodosius and Arcadius, ibid., 365.---On the praise of Praetextatus, ibid., 368.---Pope Boniface I praises Rufus’s vigilance in discharging the office of vicar of the Apostolic See, XX, 761.---Augustine of Hippo, who offers his encomium of Pope Boniface, ibid., 763.---Saint Jerome praises Florentius because he relieved the needs of many poor persons, [Col. 0156] XXII, 335.---He also praises Ruffinus, ibid.---To Chromatius and Jovinus, concerning Bonosus, whom he praises, ibid., 338.---To Pammachius, whom he congratulates because all considered him worthy of the priesthood, ibid., 511.---On the praises of Asella, who lived a solitary life at Rome, ibid., 427.---To Pammachius, on Paulina, daughter of Paula, whom he praises after her death, ibid., 639.---To the widow Theodora, on the death of her husband Lucinius, whose virtues and especially whose chastity he praises, ibid., 685.---On the praises of Blaesilla, who, after her husband’s death, had wholly devoted herself to Christ, ibid., 463.---To Oceanus, on the death of Fabiola, whom he praises because, after her fall, she had turned to Christ and lived a most holy and truly Christian life, ibid., 690.---To Salvina, on the death of her husband Nebridius, whom he praises, ibid., 724.---He praises the prudence of Theophilus, through whose efforts the party of the Origenists was overcome, ibid., 754, 771, 772.---To the virgin Principia, on the praise of Marcella, a woman of the highest nobility, who, widowed in the seventh month after her marriage, afterwards rejected the consul Cerealis when he sought her hand, ibid., 1087.---Pope Innocent consoles Jerome concerning what he had suffered, XXII, 1163.---He congratulates Augustine on his diligence, through which he had opposed the factions of heretics, ibid., 1179.---He praises Apronius because he remained steadfast in the faith against the Pelagians, ibid., 1165.---He congratulates Alypius and Augustine because through their efforts the heresy of Celestius had been extinguished, ibid., 1181.---Paulinus adorns Augustine with refined praises, the same author, XXXIII, 101.---Augustine embraces Paulinus’s goodwill and declares their mutual love, ibid., 107, 121.---Paulinus congratulates Romanianus and the Church of Hippo because it had deserved to receive Augustine as a colleague in the episcopate, ibid., 125.---To Augustine, he recounts the praises of the elder Melania and of her only son Publicola, recently deceased, ibid., 347.---Severus, bishop of Milevis, extols Augustine in the highest terms, ibid., 418.---Saint Augustine congratulates the presbyters Saturninus and Euphrates, and other clerics, on their return to the Church, ibid., 583.---He congratulates the noble widows Proba and Juliana upon their daughter Demetrias, who had received the veil of virginity, ibid., 645.---Macedonius writes to Augustine, whose books he read through with great delight, ibid., 665.---To the presbyter Sixtus (later Roman pontiff), whom he congratulates because he had undertaken the defence of God’s grace against the Pelagians, whom rumour had said he favoured, ibid., 867.---He congratulates Count Darius, sent to bring about peace, ibid., 1019.---Augustine praises Count Valerius, ibid., 925.---Pope Celestine I praises Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, for his zeal in defending the faith, IV, 459.---To the bishops of Gaul: a remarkable affirmation of praise concerning Saint Augustine, ibid., 528.---Salvian of Marseilles praises Eucherius for his books, LIII, 168.---Concerning a young man whom Salvian of Marseilles praises, ibid., 158.---He congratulates Cattula upon recovering her health, ibid., 165.---On the praise and physical appearance of Theodoric, king of the Goths, Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 445.---On the praise of a certain Paul, outstanding in every branch of learning, ibid., 462.---Praise of Leontius, bishop of Arles, Ruricius, ibid., 78.---Saint Paulinus of Nola adorns Augustine with refined praises for his five books against the Manicheans, LXI, 164.---Paulinus praises Severus and shows that his conversion to God was a still greater miracle, ibid., LXI, 167.---He congratulates the Church of Hippo because it had deserved Augustine as a colleague in the episcopate, ibid., 179.---Paulinus of Nola praises Severus because he wrote the *Life of Saint Martin*, LXI, 190.---On the praise of Paulina, who died while still in the flower of youth, ibid., 207.---He congratulates Delphinus on the recovery of his health, ibid., 223, 225.---He vividly describes the praises of Victricius: how, while still a soldier, he showed himself a true confessor of Christ and martyr amid tortures, ibid., 237.---He congratulates him upon the founding of the church of Alingon, ibid., 246.---At the beginning and end of the letter he sets forth the praises of Cardamatus, ibid., 250.---Severus’s charity is praised, ibid., 256, 306.---He praises Sebastian the hermit and Benedict the deacon, ibid., 304.---He commends Victor to Severus, through whom they sent letters to one another, ibid., 308.---He sets forth Melania’s praises at length, ibid., 312, 391.---He praises a man for the apostolic duty of evangelizing, ibid., 353.---He rejoices that he has gained the friendship of Florentius, bishop of Cahors, ibid., 379.---He commends the remarkable conversion of Aper from the forum and law-court to Christ, ibid., 357.---He most beautifully praises the power and sweetness of divine grace breathing in Aper’s writings, and no less that of the graceful Amanda, formerly Aper’s wife, ibid., 385.---He praises the most distinguished bishops of his age, ibid., 398.---He exalts Eucherius and Galla, living on the island of Lérins, with many praises, ibid., 417.---Ennodius offers exceptional praise of John for his eloquence, LXIII, 25.---Pope Hormisdas praises Emperor Anastasius because he seeks the peace of the Church, ibid., 370.---Ennodius praises Avienus with illustrious [Col. 0157] comparisons and urges him to devote himself to letters, ibid., 30.---He praises Dorotheus, bishop of Thessalonica, because he cares for the Church’s unity, ibid., 371.---He praises his piety and devotion to the Roman See, ibid., 372.---Avitus of Vienne congratulates the provinces of Dardania and Illyricum on their conversion, ibid., 394.---Pope Hormisdas praises in Avitus his eagerness to learn about the state of the Eastern Church, ibid., 394.---He praises the Eastern bishops’ steadfastness in the faith, ibid., 401.---Theodoret of Lychnidus congratulates Pope Hormisdas on the union of the Churches, ibid., 452.---He congratulates the Augustus Justin because through his efforts peace flourishes at Constantinople, ibid., 454.---He praises John, bishop of Constantinople, for having returned to the unity of the Church, ibid., 455.---He praises Pompeius because he has shown himself devoted to peace, ibid., 457 ff.---He praises the concern of the deacon Dioscorus for establishing peace firmly, ibid., 462.---He praises Justinian’s zeal for ecclesiastical peace, ibid., 465.---He congratulates the bishops of Spain on the peace of the Eastern Church, ibid., 471.---He congratulates Epiphanius, elected pontiff, ibid., 505.---He praises Paulinus’s concern, ibid., 507.---He praises Sabina’s devotion and observance toward the Church, ibid., 22.---On the praise of a deceased husband, Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe, LXV, 311.---Pope John II praises the outstanding piety of Emperor Justinian, LXVI, 17.---Pope Agapetus I praises Emperor Justinian’s faith, LXVI, 38.---He congratulates the African bishops because they had escaped unharmed from the hands of heretics, ibid., 43.---Pope Silverius praises Amator’s charity, ibid., 86.---Saint Nicetius praises Queen Chlodoswintha of the Lombards, LXVIII, 375.---Pope Vigilius congratulates Mennas that, the heretics having been condemned, he embraces the four holy universal synods, LXIX, 25.---Theodoric praises Emperor Anastasius and sends envoys to him, ibid., 503.---He extols Cassiodorus in the highest praises and confers upon him the rank of patrician, ibid., 507, 508.---He summons him to his court, ibid., 591.---He adorns Artemidorus, prefect of the city, with the highest praises, ibid., 536, 537.---He extols in many praises Felix, *vir illustris* and ordinary consul, ibid., 543, 545.---He confers on Venantius the office of count of the household, both because of the merits of his father, who is greatly praised, and because of his literary studies, to which Venantius himself had wholly devoted himself, ibid., 553.---Stephen is praised, and the rank of *spectabilis*, or a first-rank comital office, is conferred upon him, ibid., 561.---He congratulates Clovis on the victory won over the Alamanni, ibid., 573.---Importunus is praised along with his father and paternal uncle, and is granted the insignia of the patriciate because of his outstanding merits, ibid., 578, 579.---He adorns Argolicus and his parents with many praises, ibid., 582.---He praises Sunhivadus, a senatorial man, and orders him to proceed to Samnium, ibid., 583.---The rank of count of the patrimony is conferred on Senarius, *vir illustris*, and he is highly praised, ibid., 612, 613.---He confers on Cyprian the countship of the sacred largesses and adorns him with many praises, ibid., 673, 674.

King Theodoric praises his sister, whom he had given in marriage to Transmund, LXIX, 677.---King Athalaric extols King Theodoric in distinguished praises, ibid., 735.---The rank of patrician is conferred on Tulu, and he is adorned with distinguished praises together with Gensemund, ibid., 739, 741.---He greatly praises Arator and his father for their eloquence, ibid., 744.---He extols Ambrosius, a man of quaestorial rank, in many praises because he had wisely administered many offices under Theodoric, ibid., 745, 747.---He extols Opilio and his brother in the highest praises and grants him the countship of the sacred largesses, ibid., 748, 749.---He celebrates Felix with the most ample praises and grants him the quaestorship, ibid., 751.---He warmly commends Albinus, praetorian prefect, ibid., 752.---He praises Cyprian for his outstanding deeds of military valour and for his sons, well educated and presented to the king, ibid., 754, 755.---He extols his father and father-in-law with many praises, ibid., 772.---He adorns Paulinus and his family with distinguished praises, ibid., 789, 790.---Having heaped exceptional praises upon Cassiodorus, he confers the praetorian prefecture upon him, ibid., 791, 793.---Queen Amalasuntha announces that she has called Theodahad—adorned with many virtues and much wisdom—into partnership in the kingdom, ibid., 797.---King Theodahad writes that Amalasuntha, whom he greatly praises, has elevated him to partnership in the Empire, ibid., 799.---He praises Patricius, *vir illustris*, and raises him to the quaestorship, ibid., 801.---He praises Emperor Justinian and requests the preservation of peace, ibid., 810.---Senator, praetorian prefect, greatly praises Amalasuntha, her parents, and her son Athalaric, ibid., 824.---He especially praises Palmatian wine and likewise Silanus cheese, ibid., 863.---Praise of the faith of the Frankish kings, Pope Pelagius II, LXXII, 705.---Saint Gregory the Great praises Emperor Maurice’s zeal for the peace of the Church, LXXVII, 744.---He praises Basil’s zeal for the Church’s [Col. 0158] unity, ibid., 776.---He praises Mastalon’s zeal for the Church’s unity, ibid.---He praises Bishop Secundinus because he had rightly examined and settled Anastasius’s case, ibid., 780.---He congratulates him on Anastasius’s correction, ibid., 792.---He praises Queen Brunhild for the proper education of her son, ibid., 796.---He praises in King Childebert his devotion to the Catholic faith, ibid., 797.---He praises him for the order of the community, which he urges him to observe carefully, ibid., 840.---He gives praise to a bishop because he thinks of himself humbly and modestly, ibid., 858.---Though unwilling, he returns praise to Stephen, who praised him, for his continual preaching, ibid., 862.---He congratulates the patrician Theoctista because amid the tumults of humankind she applies herself to reading and longs for eternal things, ibid., 879.---He praises alms sent to captives and the poor, ibid., 883.---He rejoices that Dominica has returned to the unity of the Church, ibid., 896.---Having praised the bond of mutual charity and recalled his friend’s gifts, he prays that Anastasius may have a long life, ibid., 905.---He praises the care of the bishops Adeodatus and Maurentius for ecclesiastical order and uprightness, ibid., 915.---He congratulates Maurentius on his study of sacred reading, ibid., 920.---He congratulates Sabinianus, bishop of Zadar, because he obeys where obedience is due, ibid., 926.---He congratulates Bishop Eulogius upon the conversion of the heretics of Alexandria and the concord of the faithful, ibid., 931.---He praises Dominic’s modesty, charity, and reverence for the Apostolic See, ibid., 934.---He praises Leontius’s gentleness, humility, and justice, ibid., 937.---He praises Queen Brunhild’s charity toward Augustine, ibid., 951.---He congratulates him on his correct profession of faith, ibid., 980.---He praises the writings of Secundinus, breathing truth, charity, and humility, ibid., 982.---He praises the zeal of Gulfarius, master of soldiers, in bringing schismatics back to the Church, ibid., 1019.---He congratulates him on his undisturbed love of ecclesiastical unity, ibid., 1021.---He praises Theodore, steward at Ravenna, for his devotion to peace, ibid., 1022.---He praises Bishop Syagrius for the assistance he gave Augustine, ibid., 1035.---He praises Reccared, king of the Visigoths, for the Gothic people’s conversion to the faith, ibid., 1052; LXXXIV, 835.---He congratulates Maximus, bishop of Salona, on his full satisfaction, ibid., 1058.---Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule* is praised, ibid., 1061.---He congratulates them on the conversion of the English, ibid., 1141.---He praises Isaac’s faith, which Isaac professes as his own, ibid., 1164.---He congratulates him on recovering from a serious illness, ibid., 1219.---He congratulates Bishop Firminus of Istria on his return to the unity of the Church, ibid., 1243.---He congratulates Empress Leontia on attaining the Empire, ibid., 1288.---He congratulates Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, both on not having lost his eyesight and on the increase of the Lord’s flock, ibid., 1291.---He congratulates Paul the scholastic, both on his reconciliation with Bishop Leo and on his zeal against evildoers, ibid., 1303.---He congratulates him on the son’s being joined to the Catholic faith, ibid., 1314.

He commends Justus, lately bishop of Rochester, because he brought King Æthelwald to the faith, Pope Boniface V, LXXX, 435.---He congratulates Ethelburga, wife of King Edwin, on having received the faith, ibid., 438.---On the praise of Pope Gregory, Tayo of Saragossa, ibid., 724.---He congratulates the Emperor Martian on the preservation of the Catholic faith, Pope Leo, LXXXIV, 715.---He commends George, archimandrite of the monastery of St. Theodosius, for defending a minister of the Apostolic See, Pope St. Martin I, LXXXVII, 167.---A letter composed in praise of the most blessed Egeria, communicated by Valerius to the brethren, monks of Bergida, St. Valerius, abbot, ibid., 421.---He extols the constancy of the nobles of Thuringia in Christ’s faith, Pope St. Gregory II, LXXXIX, 503.---He congratulates Bishop Boniface on the conversion of unbelievers, ibid., 506.---Thanksgiving for the rejoicing of the holy Church of God, Pope St. Paul I, LXXXIX, 1143.---He commends Charles and Carloman, sons of King Pippin, ibid., 1185.---He commends the Frankish nation and its kings, and bestows most abundant blessings, ibid., 1188.---Thanksgiving for the concord of Charles and Carloman, Charlemagne, XCVIII, 249.---A certain city congratulates Rudolph on his prosperous successes, ibid., 798, 799.---He commends Duke Eric for his devotion to sacred reading and his humility, Alcuin, C, 139.---He commends Charlemagne for secular power and for preaching the divine law, ibid., 168.---He commends Theophilus’s writings on the apostolic faith and wishes to be instructed by him, ibid., 172.---He launches into praises of Paulinus, ibid., 200.---He commends the good manner of life of the brethren of Corbie, which he himself had formerly experienced, ibid., 218.---He congratulates Archbishop Eanbald upon attaining his dignity, ibid., 221.---He extols in praise the faith and nobility of the people of Canterbury, ibid., 249.---He commends King Domnus’s zeal for religion, piety, and royal power, ibid., 311.---He commends the piety of his dearest sister and exhorts her to labour for eternity, ibid., 362.---He commends the virtues of Archbishop Theodulf, and congratulates him on receiving the pallium from the Apostolic See, ibid., 391.---He commends Ardbert’s goodness, ibid., 492.---He commends Bishop Ratherius, Eraclius, CXXXV, [Col. 0159] 945.---He congratulates Archbishop Fero of Magdeburg on the peace of the Empire, Berno, abbot of Reichenau, CXLII, 1159.---He celebrates the virtues of Emperor Henry II, ibid., 1161.---He commends the piety of Edward, king of the English, Pope Nicholas II, CXLIII, 1358.---He congratulates Alexander, king of the Scots, on his elevation to his ancestral throne, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 166.---He commends a worthy man for integrity of life, ibid., 182.---Praise of the concern of the Roman pontiffs for the peace of monks, ibid., 126.---He congratulates the army fighting in Palestine, Pope Paschal II, CLXIII, 42.---He congratulates Emperor Henry on returning to the bosom of the Church, ibid., 1260.---He congratulates William of Champeaux on his conversion from secular to Christian philosophy, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 141.---He commends Countess Adela, ibid., 144, 145, 149.---He congratulates an illustrious widow on embracing the monastic life, ibid., 148.---He congratulates Matilda, princess of the English, ibid., 153, 160, 289, 290.---He elegantly delivers an encomium upon Athalise, an anchoress, ibid., 193.---He congratulates Peter of Chartres because he reformed for the better monks who had fallen away from their original ardour of regular observance, ibid., 217.---He congratulates Roger upon his promotion to the bishopric of Salisbury, ibid., 219.---He congratulates Cono, bishop of Palestrina, on his integrity in ecclesiastical affairs, ibid., 224.---He congratulates the bishop of the church of Clermont on the archdeaconry conferred upon an outstanding man, ibid., 248.---How highly St. Bernard esteemed Hildebert, etc., ibid., 265.---On Henry, king of the English, whom he extols in great praise, ibid., 290.---He commends St. Bernard of Clairvaux, ibid., 294, 295.---He commends R., archdeacon of Nantes, ibid., 297.---He congratulates Conrad on his election as emperor, Peter the Deacon, CLXXIII, 1141.
