He extols in praise the virtue of Queen Richiza, Pope Innocent II, CLXXIX, 707.---He commends in Alviso a fatherly gentleness toward Godwin, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 170.---He commends Suger, unexpectedly converted from vain display and external splendour to the pursuit of moderation and religious discipline, ibid., 191.---He commends the charity and beneficence of Archbishop Thurstan of York toward religious persons, ibid., 228.---He commends Richard, abbot of Fontenay, and his companions for renewing religious discipline, ibid., 229.---He commends a certain bishop’s favour and beneficence toward poor religious persons, ibid., 233.---He praises the religious poverty of the monk William, ibid., 237.---He commends the virgin Sophia for despising worldly glory, ibid., 256.---He commends a nun, ibid., 259.---He commends the eagerness of Ermengarde, countess of Brittany, in divine service, ibid., 263.---He praises the charity and solicitude of Beatrice, a noble matron, ibid., 263.---He congratulates the Milanese novices on their conversion, and promises that, after the council has been concluded, he will visit them, ibid., 289.---He commends Pope Innocent for various right actions, and stirs up his zeal against Philip’s ambition, ibid., 306.---He commends Eugene’s zeal, ibid., 432.---He declines praise as unworthy of it, but in return renders praise to his eulogist, ibid., 470.---He commends his brother Odo, Peter the Venerable, ibid., 82.---He commends Sigurd, king of Norway, ibid., 196.---He commends Robert, dean of Stavelot, Rainardus, ibid., 1150.---The monks of Stavelot congratulate Abbot Wibald upon his return, ibid., 1153.---He commends the virtues of the monk H., Abbot Wibald, ibid., 1200.---He commends Wibald’s knowledge of the liberal arts, Manegoldus, ibid., 1248.---He commends Wibald’s fidelity, Emperor Conrad, ibid., 1269.---He commends Abbot Wibald’s zeal for the Roman Church, Cardinal G., ibid., 1335.

He commends Atto, bishop of Troyes, Nicholas of Clairvaux, CXCVI, 1597.---Brocandus of Balerna congratulates Nicholas of Clairvaux on his conversion, ibid., 1605.---Nicholas of Clairvaux commends Amadeus, bishop of Lausanne, ibid., 1625.---He congratulates Garner of Cluny on his conversion, ibid., 1644.---He congratulates Fromond, infirmarian of Clairvaux, on his remarkable conversion, ibid., 1647.---Hildegard commends Hertwig and Richard, CXCVII, 162.---Hildegard repeatedly commends Eberhard, ibid., 165.---Bernard of Clairvaux extols Hildegard’s merits and holiness, ibid., 189.---Hildegard adorns Bernard of Clairvaux with great praises, ibid., 189.---M., abbot of Hirsau, adorns Hildegard with great praises, ibid., 199.---He congratulates the nun G. for embracing the narrow way, ibid., 342.---He commends the manner of life of the monks of St. Eucharius at Trier, ibid., 376.---He praises the piety and merits toward the Apostolic See of the kings of France, especially Louis, Pope Alexander III, CC, 100.---Arnulf of Lisieux congratulates Pope Celestine on his promotion, CCI, 18.---Philip of Harveng commends the University of Paris, CCIII, 26.---Geoffrey of St. Barbara congratulates the monks of Baugé upon at last arriving at the newly founded monastery, [Col. 0160] CCV, 831.---He congratulates Peter Mangot on the permission granted him to build a monastery, ibid., 844.---He congratulates W., abbot of St. Andrew’s, on his promotion, ibid., 870.---He commends Prior Mago’s abstinence from wine, ibid., 875.---He commends Augustine and exhorts him to pursue spiritual things, ibid., 876.---He commends Abbot John for the gracefulness of his speech, ibid., 881.---He commends his friend R.’s ardour for contemplation, ibid., 884.---Peter of Blois describes the virtues of St. Thomas the martyr, CCVII, 92.---He commends a nun because she preserved the chastity consecrated to God in religious life, ibid., 114.---He congratulates Adelitia because she aspires to the monastic life, ibid., 166.---He congratulates the archbishop of Palermo because he was raised from a humble station to so great a dignity, ibid., 195.---He congratulates John of Salisbury on being made a bishop, ibid., 341.---He congratulates the novice M. Alexander upon entering religious life, ibid., 404.---He congratulates Walter, archbishop of Rouen, on his return from exile and the restoration of peace to the church of Rouen, ibid., 408.---He congratulates Reginald, from whom he had received great benefits, on his election as bishop of Bath, ibid., 458.---Congratulations for the bishop-elect of Chartres, ibid., 506.---Stephen of Tournai congratulates the legate John on his fortunate return, CCXI, 328.---He congratulates Peter of St. Chrysogonus on his promotion to the cardinalate, ibid., 345.---He congratulates John on his translation to the church of Narbonne, ibid., 373.---Pope Innocent III congratulates Markward, seneschal of the Empire, on his conversion, CCXIV, 718.---On the praises of Henry, count of Malta, the same author, CCXVI, 12.

### III.—Letters of Consolation

Cyprian consoles Rogatianus and his fellow confessors who were held in prison, IV, 424.---He consoles the presbyter Tarasius over the death of his daughter, ibid., 434.---Pope Anastasius I consoles Verianus, a religious man, over the loss of his parents, XX, 78.---St. Jerome consoles Paula, whose daughter Blaesilla had died shortly after her husband’s death and her own conversion, XXII, 465.---He consoles Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum and uncle of the presbyter Nepotian, over Nepotian’s death, ibid., 589.---He consoles Castrutius concerning blindness of the eyes, teaching that it is at times inflicted by a propitious God, ibid., 651.---He consoles Theodora, widow of Lucinius, over her husband’s death, especially praising his virtues and chastity, ibid., 685.---He consoles the presbyter Abigaus, lest he take bodily blindness grievously, since he sees with his mind, ibid., 689.---He consoles the most noble lady Salvina over the death of her husband Nebridius, ibid., 724.---St. Augustine consoles the presbyter Victorianus, urging him patiently to bear the evils which barbarians, invading Italy and Spain, inflicted upon holy men and consecrated virgins, XXXIII, 422.---He consoles Chrisimus, that he may not fail in adversity, ibid., 1059.---He consoles the virgin Sapida over her brother’s death, ibid., 1082.---He consoles Maxima, a pious woman who was deeply distressed to see her province endangered by harmful errors, ibid., 1084.---A consolatory letter to Arcadius, driven into exile by Genseric, king of the Vandals, Honoratus, L, 567.---St. Leo the Great consoles bishops exiled for the faith, LIV, 1134, 1140.---St. Maximus of Turin consoles a sick friend, LVI, 921, 933.---Ruricius consoles Namatius and Ceraunia over the death of their daughter, LVIII, 83.---He consoles Eudomius and Melantia, ibid., 112.---Paulinus of Nola consoles Pammachius over his wife Paulina, who died in the flower of youth, LXI, 207.---Ennodius consoles Armenius over his son’s death, LXIII, 35.---On consolation over the death of a husband, St. Fulgentius, LXV, 311.---St. Gregory the Great consoles the patrician Clementina over Eutherius’s death, LXXVII, 457.---He consoles Bishop Paul over an injury received, ibid., 604.---He consoles Gregoria, who had confessed her sins and was anxious about their remission, ibid., 877.---He consoles an afflicted person, showing that a Christian ought not to reject adversities, ibid., 885.---To console Andrew in sickness, he shows that sickness itself is a pledge of divine love, ibid., 969.---He consoles Aregius, bishop of Gap, over the death of his loved ones, ibid., 1035.---He devoutly consoles Leander, bishop of Seville, in the pains of gout, ibid., 1050.---With what disposition the scourge of pestilence should be received; what fruit ought to be gathered from it; and how those who are struck by it should be consoled, ibid., 1115.---He consoles one afflicted by illnesses, both through his own sufferings and through the general affliction of the whole world, which indicates that the end of the world is near, ibid., 1056.---He consoles a sick man, ibid., 1057.---He consoles one saddened by the words of detractors, ibid., 1119.---He consoles Barbara and Antonina, deeply distressed by their father’s impending death, ibid., 1147.---He consoles Aurelius over his brother’s death and the tribulations he was suffering, [Col. 0161] ibid., 1214.---He consoles Paschal and Consolantia while they are in adversity, ibid., 1275.---Boniface of Mainz consoles Bugga, LXXXIX, 729.---A consolatory letter which Leodegar, bishop of Autun, after the death of his brother Guirinus, after the loss of his eyes and the cutting of his lips, addressed to his mother in the convent of girls at Soissons, XCVI, 373.---Alcuin consoles a sick person and kindly urges him to prepare himself for eternity, C, 187.---He consoles Bishop Æthelred amid persecution and tribulation, ibid., 226.---He consoles a mother over the death of her son, ibid.---A consolatory letter on the death of Liudgard, ibid., 322.---He consoles an afflicted person and exhorts him to patience, ibid., 345.---He consoles a mother over her son’s death, ibid., 473.---He consoles Bishop Leutfred in tribulation, ibid., 493.---How St. Lupus of Ferrières consoles Einhard over the death of his wife, CXIX, 436, 440.---Pope John VIII consoles Engelberga over her husband’s death, CXXVI, 720.---St. Peter Damian consoles Alberic and his wife over the death of their infant, CXLIV, 468.---St. Peter Damian consoles a sick man, ibid., 473.---Lanfranc of Canterbury consoles an invalid, CL, 541.---St. Anselm of Canterbury consoles persons afflicted by tribulation, CLVIII, 1196.---The same author consoles the monks of Bec over his absence, CLIX, 41.---Theobald of Étampes consoles a friend harassed by injuries, CLXIII, 765.---Hildebert of Le Mans consoles a friend who, having long become exceedingly powerful at the royal court through the king’s favour, was afterward reduced by the king’s displeasure to the greatest straits, CLXXI, 186.---He consoles Adela, wife of Henry I, king of England, concerning barrenness, ibid., 189.---He consoles a nun assailed by slanders from certain thoroughly ill-behaved persons, ibid., 191.---How he consoles William, abbot of St. Vincent’s, ibid., 197.---A consolatory letter on the death of Emperor Lothair and Henry, duke of Bavaria, his son-in-law, Peter the Deacon, CLXXIII, 1137, 1139.---Abelard consoles Heloise, CLXXVIII, 199.---Pope Innocent II consoles Petronilla, abbess of Fontevraud, over losses inflicted by Ulgerius, bishop of Angers, and others, CLXXIX, 635.---Guigo the Carthusian consoles the supreme pontiff against the troubles of schism, ibid., 658.---St. Bernard of Clairvaux consoles Bishop Atto, who, while ill and expecting death, had distributed all his possessions among the poor, upon his restoration to health, CLXXXII, 125.---He consoles the abbot of St. Nicasius at Rheims over the departure and transfer of the monk Drogo to another monastery, ibid., 136.---He consoles Geoffrey, abbot of St. Medard’s, in tribulations, ibid., 173.---He consoles one afflicted by a grave injury, ibid., 201.---He consoles Simon, abbot of St. Nicholas’s, in persecution, ibid., 204.---He commends the Pisans for their zeal and support for Pope Innocent, who, when Rome had been occupied by the antipope Anacletus, had gone into exile at Pisa, ibid., 285.---He commends the cause of a certain church situated near Toul, ibid., 293.---He commends to Lothair the Pisans who were devoted to the pontiff, ibid., 295.---He consoles the Alpine monks over the absence of their Father, who had been raised to a higher rank, ibid., 297.---He consoles the countess of Blois, excusing her son’s offences on account of his age and offering hope of better fruit, ibid., 502.---John, abbot of La Case-Dieu, consoles Bernard over the unhappy outcome of the expedition to the Holy Land, ibid., 590.---Abbot Wibald consoles the monks of Corbie over the death of a brother who died at Caminata, CLXXXIX, 1263.---Odo, canon of St. Geneviève’s, consoles a brother and exhorts him to remain in the monastery, CXCVI, 1403.---Hildegard consoles the patriarch of Jerusalem, CXCVII, 179.---She offers the abbot of St. Martin’s at Cologne great consolation together with a perpetual exhortation, ibid., 208.---She consoles an afflicted person, ibid., 282.---Geoffrey of St. Barbara, subprior, consoles a brother weak in the knees, CCV, 838.---Peter of Blois consoles King Henry the father, who grieved excessively at the death of his son Henry III, CCVII, 3.---He consoles his nephew, who grieved beyond measure over his uncle’s death, the burning of his house, and an injury to his foot, ibid., 36.---He consoles John of Salisbury, who was in exile with St. Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, by hope of future recompense, ibid., 77.---He consoles G., bishop of Ely, shamefully deprived by the treachery of certain persons of the administration of the kingdom of England, ibid., 272.---He consoles monks left desolate through the loss of their harvest, ibid., 328.---He consoles H., abbot of St. Denis, in the affliction he suffered from the king, ibid., 345.---He consoles Walter, archbishop of Rouen, exiled from his church, ibid., 367, 373.---He consoles monks who were grievously afflicted, ibid., 425, 498.---Christians from the Holy Land console Eleanor, queen of England, over the untimely death of her son Henry III, king of the English, ibid., 461.---He consoles a queen mourning the death of her sons, [Col. 0162] ibid., 464.---He consoles a certain man grieving over the death of many persons, ibid., 466.---Consolation concerning death, ibid., 472.---He consoles a queen mourning the death of her husband and son, ibid., 473, 474 ff.---A consolatory letter to his bishop, ibid., 515, 548.---Stephen of Tournai consoles parents afflicted by their son’s death, CCXI, 335.---He consoles the bishop of Cambrai, suffering from illness, ibid., 520.---Adam, abbot of Perseigne, consoles an afflicted person, that he may flee to the true physician, Jesus Christ, ibid., 593.---On the consolation of the countess of Champagne over the death of her son, Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 22.---A consolatory and Catholic letter, the same author, CCXV, 166.

### IV.—Letters of Exhortation

St. Cyprian exhorts Rogatianus and the other confessors to observe discipline, IV, 235.---He exhorts the clergy to continual prayers, ibid., 240.---He exhorts martyrs and confessors to perseverance, ibid., 245.---He recalls the same martyrs to the Lord’s commandments, ibid., 253.---He exhorts his clergy to employ every kindness and care toward the confessors, both those living and those who died in prison, ibid., 329.---He exhorts the Roman confessors, seduced by the faction of Novatian and Novatus, to return to unity, ibid., 342.---He exhorts Cornelius and his people to constancy and mutual prayers for one another, ibid., 358.---On exhortation to martyrdom, addressed to Fortunatus, ibid., 651.---Constantine exhorts the Jews all to assent to the decrees of the Synod of Nicaea, VIII, 505.---He exhorts Catholic bishops to use patience in recalling heretics, ibid., 487.---He exhorts the bishops and people of Africa to tolerate the Donatists, ibid., 491.---He exhorts the people of Antioch not to remove Eusebius from the episcopal see of Caesarea, ibid., 533, 543.---He exhorts Sapor, king of the Persians, to receive Christians living in Persia favourably, ibid., 549.---Hosius of Corduba exhorts the Emperor Constantius not to agree with Arius, ibid., 1328.---Ambrose exhorts Bellicius, who had recovered from illness after believing in Christ, to hold fast to Christ himself and hasten to the other sacraments, XVI, 1269.---Honorius exhorts Arcadius to convene a synod at Thessalonica, XX, 511.---Innocent exhorts John Chrysostom to patience, ibid., 513.---Pope Innocent’s exhortation to the noblewoman Juliana, ibid., 518.

Jerome exhorts Niceas, subdeacon of Aquileia, to write to him sometime, XXII, 341.---He exhorts his maternal aunt Casterina, with whom he had had some disagreement, to peace and concord, ibid., 346.---He exhorts Marcella, having left Rome, to retire to the country, ibid., 478.---Paula and her daughter Eustochium, having arrived at the holy places, exhort Marcella to leave Rome and join them at Bethlehem, where she will enjoy all Christ’s memorials, ibid., 483.---He exhorts Desiderius and his sister Serenilla to visit the holy places, ibid., 492.---He urges Paulinus to the study of sacred literature, ibid., 540, 579.---He exhorts Furia, daughter of Titiana, to persevere in widowhood, ibid., 550.---He exhorts Heliodorus to contempt for life, ibid., 589.---He modestly invites Fabiola, since the region of Bethlehem was now at peace, to return to their former companionship, ibid., 608.---He exhorts Pammachius, who immediately after his wife’s death had undertaken the purpose of a monk and bestowed his wealth in aid of the poor, to continue in that holy purpose, ibid., 639.---He exhorts Lucinius, a native of Baetica, who had intended to sail to Jerusalem, to persevere in his purpose, ibid., 669.---He exhorts Epiphanius to strive by every means that, once a synod has been convened, the heresy of the Origenists may be condemned by public authority, ibid., 756.---He earnestly exhorts Theophilus not to cease persecuting the Origenist heresy to the end, ibid., 771.---He exhorts the bishops of Egypt to celebrate the Lord’s Passover, ibid.---He exhorts heretics to repentance, ibid., 792.---He dissuades Jerome from translating the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew, and instead urges him to restore to its true form the remarkably corrupted and variable translation of the Septuagint, ibid., 832; XXXIII, 241.---He exhorts Laeta to train her daughter in Christian piety from her very cradle, ibid., 867.---He consoles and exhorts to the perfect life a certain very wealthy Julian, who had lost two daughters and his wife within a few days, ibid., 960.

St. Jerome exhorts Rusticus to repentance because he had broken the continence promised together with his wife Artemia, XXII, 341.---He dissuades the young widow Ageruchia from contracting a second marriage, ibid., 1046.---He exhorts the virgin Demetrias, who consecrated herself to Christ, to persevere and immediately resist the devil’s enticements toward shameful things, ibid., 1105.---He exhorts Apronius to seek the holy places of Jerusalem, [Col. 0163] ibid., 1165.---He exhorts Exsuperantius, after leaving military service, to devote himself to the perfect Christian life and migrate to Bethlehem, ibid., 1191.---He exhorts the fallen Sabinianus to do penance in a monastery, ibid., 1195. *---He exhorts the matron Celantia to read Holy Scripture, ibid., 1220.---St. Augustine states that he has written a little work on religion to be sent to Romanianus, whom he exhorts to use well the leisure granted him, XXXIII, 80.---He exhorts Gaius, whom he had perhaps drawn to the Church, to persevere in his good purpose, ibid., 86.---He exhorts Licentius, a noble and learned young man, once his pupil, to contempt of the world, ibid., 103.---St. Paulinus exhorts Licentius in both prose and verse to despise the pomp of the court and dedicate himself to Christ, ibid., 125.---St. Augustine exhorts Jerome to expose the errors of Origen and of individual heretics, ibid., 154.---He exhorts Eudoxius, abbot of the monks on the island of Capraria, to employ leisure for piety, not idleness, ibid., 187.---He exhorts his kinsman Severinus, a Donatist, to abandon the wicked and shameless schism, ibid., 194.---He commands Celer to devote himself to the study of sacred letters, so that he may learn that this life, compared with eternity, is smoke, ibid., 223.---He exhorts Quintianus to patience and desires that he be reconciled with Bishop Aurelius, ibid., 232.---Alypius and Augustine exhort Castorius to succeed his brother Maximianus, who had gloriously fallen, in the bishopric of the church of Vagienne, ibid., 238.---Speaking in the person of the Catholic Church, he exhorts all Donatists to repent and return to Catholic communion, ibid., 263.---To Olympius, master of offices: that he protect the laws sent into Africa during Stilicho’s lifetime for the breaking of idols and correction of heretics, ibid., 357.---He exhorts the Donatists to unity, ibid., 396.---He exhorts Donatus, former proconsul, to cast aside all pomp, follow Christ, and draw his own people to communion with the Catholic Church, ibid., 427.---He exhorts the clergy and people of Hippo, because of temporary afflictions, to be more eager than usual in relieving the poor, ibid., 470.---Augustine exhorts Armentarius and his wife Paulina to despise the world, ibid., 483.---Augustine exhorts Volusianus to devote himself to reading sacred Scripture, ibid., 508.---He exhorts the presbyters Saturninus and Euphratus and the other clergy faithfully to carry out ecclesiastical offices, each according to his rank, ibid., 583.---He exhorts the physician Maximus, converted from the Arian heresy to the Catholic faith, to endeavour to bring others to it also, ibid., 748.---He exhorts Palatinus to advance and persevere in Christian wisdom, ibid., 989.---He exhorts Count Boniface, who had formerly conceived a vow of monasticism, to carry out his former purpose if his wife permits it, ibid., 992.---He exhorts the idolatrous people of Madaura to the true religion, ibid., 1025.---He exhorts the virgin Sapida to seek fuller and truer consolation from faith in the divine Scriptures, ibid., 1082.---St. Leo the Great exhorts Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, to mercy if a heretic repents, LIV, 812.---He exhorts Ravennius, bishop of Arles, to write to him more often, ibid., 815.---He exhorts Julian, bishop of Cos, to hold fast to the faith, ibid., 846.

After the false synod of Ephesus, Leo the Great exhorts the people of Constantinople to adhere to the faith and to Flavian, LIV, 842.---He exhorts Faustus and the other archimandrites of Constantinople to constancy in every good, especially faith and charity, ibid., 843.---He exhorts the presbyters Martin and Faustus to aid the cause of the faith, and pledges them his concern, ibid., 874.---He exhorts the presbyter Faustus to diligence, ibid., 897.---He exhorts the Empress Pulcheria to turn Anatolius from his purpose, ibid., 997.---He exhorts the Palestinian monks to repent and embrace the common faith, ibid., 1061.---He exhorts Basil, bishop of Antioch, to resist the fury of the Eutychians, who, after murdering Bishop Proterius at Alexandria, demanded the convening of a new synod, ibid., 1119.---He exhorts Euxitheus, bishop of Thessalonica, and Juvenal of Jerusalem vigorously to resist the criminal enterprises of the Eutychians, who had killed Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, ibid., 1120.---He exhorts Catholic bishops and clergy from Egypt residing at Constantinople to reject every new discussion of the faith, since the authority of the synod is sufficient, ibid., 1140.---He exhorts the presbyters, deacons, and clergy of the church of Constantinople to remain steadfast in the faith and separate from association with heretics, ibid., 1142.---He exhorts the presbyters and deacons of the church of Alexandria to preserve and increase concord, ibid., 1216.---Pope Simplicius exhorts Emperor Zeno to restore the bishop of Alexandria to his see, LVIII, 44.---He exhorts him to protect Timothy, restored to the Alexandrian church through his efforts, ibid., 50.---Ruricius exhorts Ceraunia to repentance, ibid., 95.---He exhorts Capillutus to conversion, LVIII, 101.---Pope Felix III exhorts Flavita, bishop of Constantinople, likewise to refrain from reciting the names of Acacius and Peter, ibid., 971.---He exhorts Bishop Vetranio to induce Zeno to restore union with Rome, ibid., 975.---Pope Gelasius I exhorts Euphemianus to anathematize Acacius as he did Eutyches and the other heretics, LIX, 13.---He exhorts the bishops of Dardania not to communicate with Eutychians and to be vigilant in their pastoral office, ibid., 23.---He exhorts Emperor Anastasius to obey the Apostolic See, ibid., 41.---Paulinus of Nola exhorts Sulpicius Severus, presbyter of Primuliacum in Aquitaine, not to abandon his pursuit of perfection on account of malicious men’s detraction, LXI, 153.---He exhorts Severus to come to him, ibid., 167.---He exhorts Licentius, son of Romanianus, in prose and verse, to despise courtly pomp and dedicate himself to Christ, ibid., 181.---He exhorts the most illustrious man Jovius to read sacred Scripture, ibid., 227.---He advises a nobleman whose name is unknown to pass from the profane military service of Caesar to the sacred service of Christ, ibid., 300.---He exhorts Victricius to steadfastness in sound doctrine and every virtue, ibid., 353.---Ennodius exhorts John to cultivate eloquence, LXIII, 25.---He exhorts Avienus to the study of letters, ibid., 30.---Pope Hormisdas exhorts the archimandrites of Syria to persevere in the Catholic faith, ibid., 115.---An exhortation to the emperor to restore peace to the Church, ibid., 437.---He exhorts John, bishop of Constantinople, to procure union between the churches of Alexandria and Antioch, ibid., 455.---He exhorts Pompey to exert himself so that complete tranquillity may be restored to the Church, ibid., 457, 458.---Pope Agapetus I exhorts Justinian to defend the Catholic faith, LXVI, 38.---Theodoric exhorts Eugenites to obtain better things, LXIX, 516.---Athalaric exhorts the Goths to swear to the Romans, and the Romans in turn to the Goths, that they will render fidelity to the king, LXIX, 738.---Tholias exhorts the senators to give thanks to the king because he has promoted him to the honour of the patriciate, ibid., 743.

Theodahad exhorts the people to keep faith with the king and cast off vain suspicion, LXIX, 807.---Senator exhorts Ambrose to bring aid as quickly as possible to the Roman people suffering from scarcity, ibid., 830.---He exhorts provincial judges to love justice and ensure that it is observed by their subjects, ibid., 836, 854, 859.---He exhorts the Ligurians to give thanks to the king for the hundred pounds of gold granted to relieve their needs, ibid., 841.---Pope Pelagius II exhorts Aunacharius, bishop of Auxerre, to persuade the Frankish kings not to make an alliance with the Lombards, LXXII, 705.---St. Gregory the Great kindly and earnestly exhorts Justin, praetor of Sicily, to seek peace with priests and equity toward all, LXXVII, 443.---He exhorts the Numidian bishops to peace, the defence of the Church, and care for their neighbours’ souls, ibid., 534.---He exhorts Bishop John to fulfil the pastoral office with the highest prudence and charity, ibid., 558.---He exhorts the people of Terracina to obey their bishop Agnellus in all things, ibid., 615.---He exhorts the presbyter Magnus to minister to his church purely and diligently, ibid., 623.---He exhorts Bishop Andrew to lay aside the priesthood if he is conscious of sin with a concubine, ibid., 640, 641.---After a friendly greeting, he exhorts Bishop Adeodatus to fulfil his office, ibid., 644.---He exhorts Bishop Eutychius to persevere in converting worshippers of idols, ibid., 659.---Having set forth the injustice of an enacted law, he exhorts the physician Theodore, by presenting his letter to the emperor, to urge him to revoke the law, ibid., 665.---He exhorts Bishop Constantius to assist Bishop Venantius of Luni in reforming his clergy and the other religious, ibid., 691.---He exhorts to the reading of Holy Scripture, ibid., 705.---He exhorts the prefect Pantaleo to restrain the audacity of the Donatists and send Bishop Paul to Rome as soon as possible, ibid., 708.---He exhorts Queen Theodelinda not to remain outside communion with Bishop Constantius, ibid., 712.---He exhorts the Empress Constantina to continue opposing John’s ambition, ibid., 748.---He directs the notary Castorius to exhort the people of Ravenna to elect a bishop as quickly as possible, ibid., 751.---He exhorts Emperor Maurice to render priests their due reverence, ibid., 765.---He exhorts Bishops Eulogius and Anastasius, by common counsel and one spirit, to oppose John’s pride—for he claimed for himself the title of universal bishop—ibid., 770.---He exhorts Bishop John to restrain simony in the places subject to him, [Col. 0165] ibid., 790.---He exhorts the bishops of Epirus to imitate Metropolitan Andrew, obey him, and remain united with him, etc., ibid., 799.---He exhorts Bishop Fortunatus to pastoral vigilance, ibid., 802.---He exhorts the clergy and people of Zadar to withdraw themselves from communion with Maximus, ibid., 818.---He exhorts Bishop John to show Venantius his former goodwill, ibid., 831.---He exhorts Augustine’s companions to complete the journey to England which they had begun, ibid., 836.---He exhorts Bishop Cyriacus, once the occasion of scandal has been removed, to preserve the things that belong to peace and charity, ibid., 858.---He exhorts Theoctista diligently to oversee the education of the royal children and inspire in them mutual charity and gentleness toward their subjects, ibid., 879.---He exhorts Dominica to come to Rome to her husband, ibid., 896.---He exhorts Bishop Peter to continue turning the inhabitants away from the worship of idols, ibid., 903.---He exhorts Sabinianus, bishop of Zadar, to pastoral solicitude, ibid., 913.---He exhorts Bishops Adeodatus and Maurentius to persevere, ibid., 915.---He exhorts the patrician Rusticiana to come to Rome, ibid., 924.---He exhorts Queen Brunhild to endeavour to recall schismatics to concord and destroy the remnants of idolatry and other vices in her kingdom, ibid., 951.---Having set forth Felix’s bad faith, he exhorts her to order the controversy raised by him to be ended without delay, ibid., 977.

Encourages Gulfar, master of the soldiery, to persevere and to protect those who are returning, St Gregory the Great, LXXVI, 1019.---Encourages Occilianus, tribune of Otranto, to relieve the city of Otranto, burdened by Victor, former tribune of Otranto, ibid., 1024.---Encourages Aregius, bishop of Gap, to discharge his office diligently, ibid., 1033.---Encourages Claudius to make progress in the light of truth and love of the heavenly homeland, ibid., 1050.---Encourages the patrician Clementina nobly to forgive offences, ibid., 1077.---Encourages Libertinus, former praetor, patiently to endure adversity and willingly to accept garments for the use of his household, ibid., 1088.---Encourages Opportunus to a complete conversion, ibid., 1118.---Encourages Talitanus, administrator of the public patrimony, to defend the patrimony of the Roman Church from the vexations of tax-collectors, ibid., 1125.---Encourages Bertha, queen of the English, not to neglect any longer to kindle the king’s mind toward a perfect love of the Christian faith, ibid., 1141.---Encourages Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, after arranging the affairs of the church, to hasten to Rome, where he may be cured in peace of vomiting blood, ibid., 1145.---Encourages Isaac, bishop of Jerusalem, to restrain simony in his churches and, by suppressing some disputes and tolerating others, to lessen their violence, ibid., 1164.---Encourages the calling of a synod and commends the same monks, ibid., 1179, 1180, 1181.---Encourages Æthelberht, king of the English, to extend the Christian faith among the peoples subject to him, ibid., 1201.---Encourages Suvinella, Columba, and Agnella to acquire heavenly treasures by more generous almsgiving, ibid., 1223.---Passivus, bishop of Fermo, encourages Opportunus to grow in good pursuits, ibid., 1226.---Encourages Azimarchus the Scrivener, rescued from peril at sea, never to forget divine mercy, ibid., 1227.---Friendlily encourages Maurilio, former prefect, to write to him more often, ibid., 1229.---Encourages the emperor Phocas to assist the distressed commonwealth, ibid., 1281.---Encourages the patrician Eusebia to think more upon the things of the soul than upon those of the body, ibid., 1282.---Encourages Smaragdus, exarch, to defend Bishop Firminus, returned to the unity of the Church, from Severus’s vexations, ibid., 1283.---Encourages Eulogius to root out simony, ibid., 1290.---Pope Theodore encourages Paul, patriarch of Constantinople, to priestly virtues, LXXXVII, 76.---Pope St Gregory II encourages the nobles of the Thuringians to be obedient to Boniface, their bishop, LXXXIX, 503.---Encourages Bishop Boniface steadfastly to persist in the ministry of the word which he has begun, ibid., 506.---Pope St Zacharias encourages the bishops of Gaul and Germany, together with Archbishop Boniface, steadfastly to persist in their ministries, ibid., 948.---Pope Stephen II encourages the nobles of the Franks to support his petition before Pippin, ibid., 995; XCVIII, 101.---Earnestly entreats King Pippin to give aid and strive actually to fulfil the donation promised to St Peter, LXXXIX, 996; XCVIII, 107.---Pope Paul I encourages Charles and Carloman to follow in their parents’ footsteps in maintaining the defence of the Church, LXXXIX, 1185.---St Lullus of Mainz encourages Gregory to contempt for the world, XCVI, 822.---Alcuin encourages Arno to diligent care for the souls entrusted to his rule, C, 140.---Encourages the priest Cudradus, after the devastation of the holy places, [Col. 0166] to steadfastness, ibid., 144.---Encourages the brethren of the church of York to guard themselves against vices, ibid., 145.---Encourages the brethren of York to follow their fathers’ footsteps, ibid., 147.---Encourages the Lindisfarne community to amend their conduct and observe regular discipline, ibid., 150.---Encourages Æthelhard, archbishop of the city of Canterbury, to follow the footsteps of his predecessors, etc., ibid., 152.---Encourages King Æthelred, the nobles, and the people of the Northumbrian nation to be grateful to God, not to seek riches through injustice, to flee vices and sins, etc., ibid., 157.---Encourages King Æthelred to kingly virtues, ibid., 160.---Encourages the brethren of the churches of Wearmouth and Jarrow to ordered charity and to observance of the regular or canonical life. Encourages the brethren of the church of Jarrow to virtues worthy of monks and to follow the footsteps of their fathers and teachers, ibid., 166.---Encourages monks to virtues, ibid., 173.---Encourages the people of York to concord with Eanbald, their father, ibid., 174.---Urges his son and companion in pilgrimage to virtues, ibid., 175.---Encourages the brethren of St Martin’s at Tours to virtues suited to monks, ibid., 176.---Encourages Patriarch Paulinus to the labour of preaching, ibid., 202.---Encourages the rendering of justice to each person, ibid., 212.---Encourages Offa, king of the Mercians, to kingly virtues, ibid., 213.---Encourages Ecgfrith, king of the Mercians, to virtue, ibid., 214.---Encourages the monks of Saint-Vaast to religious virtues, ibid., 215.---Encourages the brethren in the church of St Liudger, bishop, to virtues suited to monks, ibid., 217.---Encourages the brethren of Corbie to the pursuit of virtue, ibid., 218.---Encourages the people of York to avoid the stain of simony in the election of a bishop, ibid., 219.---Encourages Bishop Eanbald to pastoral care and to ordering all things well, ibid., 221.---Encourages Bishop Æthelred to manly perseverance, lest he flee from the sheep, ibid., 226.---Encourages King Eardwulf, raised to the throne, to procure both his own salvation and that of his people, ibid., 229.---Encourages Osbald, whom he suspects of regicide and of stirring up the people, to change his life and provide for the salvation of himself and his nation, ibid., 230.---Encourages Cenwulf, king of the Mercians, to kingly virtues, ibid., 232.---Dissuades Bishop Speratus from the vanities of this age, while impressing upon him the duties appropriate to bishops, ibid., 240, 244.---Encourages Simeon, priest, diligently to discharge the episcopal office in dangerous times in Britain, ibid., 245.---Encourages Calvinus, priest, to contempt for riches and honours of the age, ibid.---Encourages nobles and priests, ibid., 249.---Encourages Æthelhard, archbishop of Canterbury, to do penance for fleeing his see and to set his church in order, ibid., 251.---Encourages Arno, setting out for Hungary, to discharge the apostolic work well, ibid., 284, 285.

Encourages the brethren of the church of Salzburg properly to perform the offices of monks, Alcuin, C, 297.---Encourages King Charles to devote the greatest care to the Church, ibid., 301.---Praises and urges the king to render justice to the Apostolic See, ibid., 303.---Encourages the work of preaching and the exercises of virtues, ibid., 306.---Encourages Arno to defend Pope Leo against his opponents, ibid., 324.---Encourages brethren in Gothia to repentance, observance of the regular life, and steadfastness in the tribulation that has arisen, ibid., 334.---Urges Patriarch Paulinus to combat certain errors arising in the Church, ibid., 341.---Encourages King Charles to kingly virtues and imitation of his father’s example, ibid., 354.---Encourages Archbishop Riculf to apostolic labours and virtues, ibid., 356.---Encourages Danneta, residing at Rome, to strive to repair the schism in the Church, ibid., 357.---Exhorts his most dear sister to labour for eternity, ibid., 362.---Encourages efforts to restore peace among ecclesiastical persons, ibid., 366.---Encourages Nathanael to honourable and religious conduct, and advises him to avoid crowned doves flying through the chambers of the palace, ibid., 375.---Encourages Count Chrodgar to faithful service and to offer counsel to the king, ibid., 376.---Encourages the brethren of Fulda to religious virtues, ibid., 382.---Invites Arno to come to St Martin’s, ibid., 385.---Encourages Archbishop Theodulf to earnest preaching, ibid., 391.---Encourages Remedius, bishop of Chur, to discharge the episcopal office well, in hope of eternal reward, ibid., 446.---Encourages another bishop diligently to discharge the same office, ibid., 449.

Encourages a certain bishop to patience, virtues, and care of students, Alcuin, C, 451, 452.---Encourages the priest Monna and his brother to contempt for the world and to humility, ibid., 454.---Encourages [Col. 0167] a certain disciple to repentance and combat against the enemies of the soul, ibid., 456.---Encourages a faithful friend to be an example of life to all, ibid., 457.---Encourages his sick son to confession of sins, ibid., 460.---Encourages a mother and son to good works, ibid., 467.---Encourages his daughter Eugenia amid tribulations, ibid., 468.---Encourages the woman Hundrud to devotion and exemplary life in the king’s palace, ibid., 470.---Encourages Magenharius, count of the city of Sens, to virtues, ibid., 475.---Encourages a disciple toward amendment, ibid., 481; 482.---Encourages one converted to better things to steadfastness, ibid., 485.---Encourages monks to charity and the labours of monastic life, ibid., 489.---Encourages Bishops Alchard and Tifred to fulfil the office of preaching, ibid., 491.---Encourages Ardbert to works of justice and mercy, ibid., 492.---Encourages the brethren of Hilliric to mutual charity and peace, ibid., 495.---Encourages the brethren of the island of Ireland to the regular life, ibid., 500.---Encourages the brethren of the monastery of Mont-Olivet to fight for the Catholic faith and persevere in regular observance, ibid., 503.---Encourages certain monks to charity, humility, obedience, etc., ibid., 504, 506.---Encourages Eanulf, priest, to fraternal conduct, the regular life, care of souls, etc., ibid., 507.---Encourages Onia, priest, to virtues, ibid., 508.---Encourages Gisela to every kind of virtue, ibid., 509.---St Benedict of Aniane encourages the monks of Aniane to mutual charity, CIII, 1379.

St Lupus of Ferrières encourages King Charles to virtue, CXIX, 528, 568.---Encourages Franco, bishop of Tongeren, to endeavour to guide King Lothair by his admonitions, ibid., 885.---Encourages King Charles the Bald to favour the restoration of Rothad and order the return to his church of goods taken from it, ibid., 893.---Encourages King Charles the Bald to preserve peace with Emperor Louis, his nephew, ibid., 911.---Pope Nicholas I encourages Emperor Michael to hear the envoys graciously, ibid., 1016.---Encourages Caesar Bardas to repent and plead Ignatius’s cause before the emperor, ibid., 1053.---Encourages Augusta Theodora, whom he adorns with many praises, to patience and to place her hope in God, ibid., 1061.---Encourages Emperor Louis II to make peace, ibid., 1118.---Pope Adrian II encourages the nobles of Charles the Bald’s kingdom to deter the king from invading Lothair’s kingdom and to receive graciously Paul and Leo, his envoys, ibid., 1291.---Encourages Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, to lend his efforts so that no one may invade Lothair’s kingdom, ibid., 1294.---After the death of King Lothair, encourages the nobles of the kingdom to be faithful to Emperor Louis, his brother, to whom the kingdom is due by hereditary right, ibid., 1295.---Pope John VIII encourages Wigbod, bishop of Parma, to stir up all whom he can to the defence of the holy Roman Church, CXXVI, 721.---Encourages Guaifer, prince of Salerno, to persevere in his integrity, ibid., 750.---Encourages Michael, king of the Bulgarians, to return to the bosom of the Roman Church, ibid., 758.---Encourages Count Peter to bring King Michael back to the bosom of the Roman Church, ibid., 760, 762.---Encourages King Louis the Stammerer to remain at peace with the kings who are his kinsmen and to persecute the enemies of the Church, ibid., 767.---Encourages Louis, son of the king of the Bavarians, to preserve peace with his cousins, ibid., 769.

Pope John VIII encourages King Charles to come as quickly as possible with aid against unbelievers and oppressors of the Church, CXXVI, 831.---Encourages Michael, king of the Bulgarians, to return with his people to obedience to the Roman Church, ibid., 832, 938.---Encourages King Carloman to defend the Roman Church, which was suffering many losses at the hands of the Saracens, ibid., 839.---Encourages Airard, archbishop of Auch, to correct the depraved morals of the people, especially incestuous marriages, ibid., 844.---Encourages Tuventara of Marauna, rejecting every false doctrine, to remain in the faith of the Roman Church, ibid., 849.---Encourages King Louis to come to defend the Roman Church against pagan incursions, ibid., 852.---Encourages Athanasius, bishop of Naples, to break, as he had promised, the pact made with the Saracens, ibid., 900.---Encourages Count Barnimer, priests, etc., to perseverance, ibid., 918.---Encourages Anselm, archbishop of Milan, to be faithful to the Roman Church, ibid., 954.---Pope John IX encourages Charles the Simple, king of the Franks, to favour the restoration of Algrin, bishop of Langres, CXXXI, 31.---Peter Damian encourages Pope Gregory VI to settle the condition of the churches of Città di Castello, Fano, and Pesaro, CXLIV, 205.---Encourages the cardinal bishops to whom he writes, amid so corrupt an age and such universal licence in living, to order their lives so that all others may look upon them as an example of morals and propose them for imitation, ibid., 253.---Encourages Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, always to keep his own faults before his eyes and his virtues behind his back, ibid., 275.---Exhorts the same Desiderius tirelessly to carry out the care of the monastery entrusted to him, etc., ibid., 278.---Encourages Bishop Albert, in administering the souls entrusted to him, to do nothing avariciously or greedily, ibid., 297.---Encourages the bishop of Osimo no longer to delay his conversion, ibid., 299.---Encourages Mainard, bishop of Gubbio, to amend his conduct and undertake the arduous path of life, ibid., 309.---Encourages the citizens of Milan, thinking nothing low or earthly, to raise themselves toward heavenly things with the whole force and ardour of their souls, ibid., 348.---Encourages Agnes wholly to enter into Christ’s friendship and to seek every consolation from him, ibid., 443, 446.---Encourages Duke and Margrave B., despising present things, to direct the whole thought of his mind toward future things, ibid., 454.---Encourages Cinthius, prefect of the City, to protect the poor and the Church’s resources, ibid., 461.---Encourages Peter, a man of senatorial rank who had undertaken to build a church, to complete the work, ibid., 470.---Encourages him, while enjoying prosperity, to weigh continually not the fleeting and perishable goods of this present life, but those which will be eternal after death, ibid., 476.---Encourages Rodelinda and Sufficia, both bereaved of husbands, to preserve purity untouched by every stain, not only of body but also of mind, ibid., 489.---Pope Alexander II encourages the people of Milan to exercises of virtue, CXLVI, 1279.---Encourages Harald, king of Norway, to obey Adalbert, archbishop of Hamburg, ibid., 1281.---Pope St Gregory VII encourages the cleric Ubert and the deacon Albert to ensure that prayers are offered for him, CXLVIII, 290.---Encourages Beatrice and her daughter Matilda to avoid simoniacs, ibid., 293.---Encourages the Carthaginians to lay aside enmities and patiently endure attacks by the Saracens, ibid., 305.---Encourages Herlembald, a Milanese soldier, to act manfully in defence of the Roman Church, ibid., 309.---Encourages Albert, bishop of Aachen, to oppose simoniacs and provide aid to Herlembald, ibid., 310.---Encourages the judges of Sardinia, following their parents’ example, to show themselves obedient toward the Roman Church, ibid., 311.

Pope St Gregory VII encourages Countess Matilda to persevere and come with her mother to visit the thresholds of the blessed apostles, 321.---Encourages Countess Matilda to receive very frequently the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist, etc., ibid., 326.---Encourages Alfonso, king of Castile, to receive the Roman Office, ibid., 339.---Encourages William, king of the English, to defend the churches, ibid., 344.---Encourages Matilda, queen of the English, to humility and charity, ibid., 245.---Encourages all the faithful to defend Christians oppressed by unbelievers in overseas regions, ibid., 390.---Encourages Géza, duke of Hungary, to take care of the churches, ibid., 414.---Encourages the monks of St Denis to concord and peace, ibid., 415.---Encourages the Bohemians to live rightly and chastely, ibid., 422.---Encourages Boleslaus, duke of the Poles, to help them, live well, and conduct himself rightly in his government, ibid., 423.---Encourages Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, faithfully to discharge the pastoral office, ibid., 431.---Setting forth the wrong done to the Apostolic See, encourages the imploring of divine help, that God may either convert the impious to repentance or check their designs, ibid., 434.---Encourages Wifred, a Milanese soldier, to persevere in the Church’s defence and advise others to do the same, ibid., 445.---Encourages the people of Hippo to obey the archbishop and preserve mutual charity, ibid., 449.---Encourages the Germans to persevere in faith and love of justice, ibid., 465.---Encourages Udo of Trier to labour for the establishment of peace in the kingdom of the Germans, ibid., 501.---Encourages Olaf, king of Norway, to good and pious works, ibid., 521.---Encourages the monks of Marseilles to bear their abbot’s absence with equanimity, ibid., 524.---Encourages Alfonso, king of Castile, to persevere in good work, ibid., 549.---Encourages daughter A. to strive to draw the mind of her royal husband toward divine love, ibid., 662.---Encourages all the faithful to bear persecutions patiently, ibid., 622.---Lanfranc of Canterbury [Col. 0169] encourages Gothric, king of Ireland, to correct what is said to be wickedly done concerning marriage, CL, 535.---Pope Urban II encourages the bishop of Salzburg and other bishops to contend manfully for the Church, CLI, 283.---Bernard the Carthusian encourages the nuns of Lyons courageously to undertake the stricter discipline which they had recently accepted, CLIII, 889.---St Anselm of Canterbury encourages Herluin to hatred of the world, CLVIII, 1072.---Encourages the monks of Bec, then residing in the church of Canterbury, always to make progress toward better things, ibid., 1113.---Urges Hernost, oppressed by most acute pains, to patience, ibid., 1115.---Encourages Peter to a purer life, ibid., 1117.---Encourages him to endure patiently the envy and calumnies of ill-wishers, ibid., 1122.---Counsels Henry to obedience and patience, ibid., 1135.---Encourages Helinard to persevere and steadfastly resist the devil’s various temptations, ibid., 1160.---Encourages the monks of Bec, in the absence of their superior, to live most uprightly, ibid., 1176.---Encourages Henry to leave the world as soon as possible, ibid., 1181.---Encourages Lambert, a nobleman, to the monastic life, ibid., 1190.---Encourages Waleran, cantor of the church of Paris, vigorously to pursue the monastic vocation he has undertaken, ibid., CLIX, 37.---Encourages Countess Ida to perseverance in holiness, ibid., 42.---Encourages Robert, count of Flanders, to pursue justice more and more, ibid., 58.---Encourages the monks of Chester to exact observance even in the smallest matters, ibid., 79.---Encourages the monks of St Albans to continuous observance of their rule, ibid., 87.---Encourages William, bishop of Winchester, to persevere with the steadfastness of mind with which he began in observing ecclesiastical ordinances, ibid., 142.---Encourages consecrated women to perfection, ibid., 270.---On the basis of a singular intimacy, exhorts King Philip to renounce his kingdom and embrace monastic life, Hugh of Cluny, CLIX, 930.

Pope Urban II encourages Ivo to keep the faith undefiled, CLXII, 13.---Pope Paschal II encourages the army campaigning in Palestine to advance, CLXIII, 42.---Hildebert of Le Mans encourages Countess Adela to humility, CLXXI, 145.---Encourages Matilda, queen of the English, to render sincere gratitude to God, giver of all good things, ibid., 153.---Raises a widow’s mind to perseverance by the hope of eternal rewards, ibid., 162.---Raises the mind of King Henry to steadfastness, ibid., 172.---Encourages the prior of Chartres diligently to complete what he has commendably begun, ibid., 217.---Encourages C., bishop of Palestrina, to perseverance, ibid., 224.---St Bernard encourages his nephew Robert to return to the Cistercian Order, CLXXXII, 67.---Dissuades the monk Adam from attaching himself to Arnold, abbot of Morimond, ibid., 91.---Encourages Adam to return to the monastery, ibid., 93.---Moves Bruno, recently made archbishop of Cologne, to fear, ibid., 107.---Encourages Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, to strive to be patient and peaceable among his people of Rouen, ibid., 129.---Encourages Ardutio, bishop of Geneva, to adorn with subsequent merits the dignity which he obtained without preceding merits, ibid., 131.---Encourages the monk Drogo to perseverance, ibid., 139.---Encourages Ebalus to ensure that a suitable man is placed over the monastery or church of All Saints, ibid., 165.---Encourages Guilencus, bishop of Langres, to cede to the church of St Stephen at Dijon certain possessions vacant through the death of Garnerius, ibid., 166.---Encourages Philip, setting out for Jerusalem, not to place too much trust in worldly glory, ibid., 169.---Urges abbots vigorously to attend to the business for which they assembled, ibid., 222.---Dissuades Duke Conrad from making war on the count of Geneva, ibid., 229.---Encourages Walter of Chaumont to flee the world, ibid., 238.---Urges Henry Murdach to embrace the state of religious life, ibid., 241.---Encourages Thomas of Saint-Omer, leaving aside his studies, to enter religious life, ibid., 249.---Encourages noble youths to perseverance, ibid., 251.---Encourages parents not to attempt to impede or draw back one who wishes to serve God, ibid., 253.---Encourages Geoffrey of Lisieux to repentance, ibid., 255.---Encourages the virgin Sophia to perseverance, ibid., 256.---Dissuades a consecrated woman from the desert life which she was rashly and imprudently seeking, ibid., 261.---Encourages Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, to recognize Innocent, exiled in Gaul because of the schism of Peter Leo, as the legitimate pontiff, ibid., 268.---Encourages William, supporter of the antipope Anacletus, to receive Innocent as the true pontiff, ibid., 281.---Encourages the same William to restore to the Church the clerics whom he had expelled, ibid., 282.---Encourages the Milanese, reconciled to Innocent, to obedience, ibid., 286.---Urges Emperor Lothair [Col. 0170] to suppress the schismatics, ibid., 293.---Encourages Eustace, usurper of the see of Valence, mindful of his age, approaching death, and divine judgment, to repent, ibid., 346.---Urges the bishops to be summoned at Sens vigorously to conduct the case concerning religion against Abelard, ibid., 349.---Encourages Baldwin, abbot of the monastery of Rieti, vigorously to apply himself to his office, ibid., 369.---Encourages Roger, king of Sicily, to show himself kind and beneficent toward poor religious persons, ibid., 374.---Encourages the bishop of Soissons in the pursuit of peace, ibid., 394.---Encourages Conrad, king of the Romans, to defend pontifical authority against the rebellious Romans, ibid., 440.---Urges Pope Eugenius to bring assistance to the Eastern Church, ibid., 465.---Encourages Suger, abbot of St Denis, fearlessly to meet death, ibid., 470.

Encourages the pursuit and zeal of discipline for promoting religious perfection in the Chapter, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXX, 476.---Encourages Louis the Younger, king of France, not to oppose the bishop-elect of Auxerre, ibid., 488.---Encourages Thurstan, archbishop of York, not to abandon pastoral care, ibid., 524.---Encourages the prior of Fountains to ensure a unanimous election of an abbot, ibid., 525.---Encourages Hugh, a novice, to constancy and perseverance, ibid., 527.---Encourages William, abbot of Rievaulx, to patience and equanimity, ibid., 561.---Encourages the clergy and people of East Francia to take up arms against unbelievers for the defence of the Eastern Church, ibid., 564.---Urges the monks of the church of St Bertin to the pursuit of religious perfection and continual progress, ibid., 587.---Encourages W., patriarch of Jerusalem, to humility, ibid., 600.---Encourages a certain person, having shaken off the yoke of carnal pleasure, to fulfil the vow of religious life which he had promised, ibid., 623.---Encourages a husband and his wife to almsgiving and pious works, ibid., 629.---Encourages a certain abbot to reform his monastery, especially its hospice, ibid., 632.---Encourages a certain person, preferring care of the soul to concern for the body, to renounce the world, ibid., 637.---Encourages the brethren to give alms in a time of famine, ibid., 642.---Invites all to the Jerusalem expedition, ibid., 652.---Encourages certain recent converts to constancy in their religious purpose and not to allow themselves to be deterred by the sins of their former life, ibid., 662.---Peter the Venerable encourages Pope Innocent to constancy, CLXXXIX, 65.---Encourages Master Peter to seek true blessedness, ibid., 77.---Encourages Stephen to virtue, ibid., 206.---King Conrad encourages the brethren of Stavelot to bear their abbot’s absence with equanimity, ibid., 1133.---Encourages a person to undertake the burden of pastoral care to which he had been canonically elected, ibid., 1289.---Abbot Wibald encourages Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, to sincere concord with Emperor Frederick, ibid., 1426.---Gerhoh encourages Henry, duke of Saxony and Bavaria, to defend the Church of God, CXCIII, 604.---Encourages Erbo, abbot of Prüfening, to soften the mind of the bishop of Regensburg, ibid., 606.---Odo, canon of St Geneviève, exhorts a brother to religious exercises, CXCVI, 1415.---Nicholas of Clairvaux encourages Peter, dean of Troyes, to religious order and contempt for the world, ibid., 1613.---Encourages Philip, archdeacon of Liège, to religious life, ibid., 1623.---St Hildegard encourages Pope Anastasius boldly to uproot evils, CXXVII, 151.---Pope Adrian encourages Hildegard to perseverance, ibid., 153.---Hildegard encourages Pope Adrian to fortitude, ibid., 154.---Encourages Christian, archbishop of Mainz, to pastoral care, ibid., 158.---Encourages Gunter, among many others, to amendment of life, ibid., 172.---Adelbert, bishop of Verdun, encourages Hildegard to humility, ibid., 174.---Hildegard encourages Adelbert to pastoral care, ibid., 175.---Encourages Godfrey, bishop of Utrecht, to perseverance in good, ibid., 176.---Encourages H., bishop of Prague, to greater steadfastness in virtue, both in prosperity and adversity, ibid., 177.---After salutary instruction, encourages Arnold, bishop of Trier, to embrace virtues appropriate to his station, ibid., 182.---Sends Count Philip of Flanders an instruction in which he especially encourages him to justice, ibid., 188.

Hildegard encourages Adam, abbot of Ebrach, not to lay aside his office, CXCVII, 191.---Encourages E., abbot of St Anastasius, to adhere to his office, ibid., 196.---Hildegard encourages Conrad, abbot of Kaisheim, to repentance and to leave his office, ibid., 197.---Hildegard strongly exhorts an abbot to care for his flock, ibid., 200.---Hildegard encourages the abbot of Nuenburg to fortitude in pastoral care, [Col. 0171] CXCVII, 201.---Hildegard encourages the abbot of St Mary not to abandon his office, ibid., 202.---Encourages Helenger, abbot of St Disibod, to amendment of life, ibid., 205.---Sends a notable exhortation to the abbot of Kempten, ibid., 206.---Friendlily encourages an abbess to continue labouring for her own community, ibid., 214.---Sends the brethren of Hagen a notable instruction, admonition, and exhortation concerning many vices and virtues, urging the pursuit of virtues, ibid., 272.---Encourages good works and the restraining within oneself of worldly cares, ibid., 283.---Encourages the abbot of Salem not to abandon pastoral care, ibid., 286.---Encourages Abbot B. of St Eucharius to exercise gentleness toward those subject to him, ibid., 287.---Encourages Nicholas, abbot of Halesbrunn, to labour, ibid., 291.---Encourages N., abbot of Eberbach, vigorously to teach his flock and turn his eyes upon himself, ibid., 295.---Encourages Abbot Richard vigorously to bear the burden imposed on him by God, ibid., 296.---Encourages one who is wavering to humility, ibid., 302.---Encourages H., provost at Herde, to remain in his place and avoid wandering, ibid., 303.---Figuratively encourages N., provost, to fear and fortitude, ibid., 305.---Figuratively dissuades Frederick, provost of Valle Dei, from abandoning his own people; rather, he should assist them and do penance, ibid., 306.---Encourages A. S., provost of St Andrew’s in Cologne, to perform good works, ibid., 310.---That Provost H. may yearn for God and flee to him with confidence, ibid., 314.---Encourages N., abbess of the Mount of St Cyriacus, not to be troubled in mind and not to exceed moderation in abstinence, ibid., 327.---Encourages L., abbess at Bamberg, to labour and keep her daughters under discipline, ibid., 331.---Encourages N., abbess of Cologne, firmly to bear her burden and restrain her sheep, ibid., 334.---Encourages N., abbess of Didenkirkim, to cultivate the soil of her heart, so as to be useful to her own people, ibid., 335.---Commends charity, obedience, and the renunciation of self-will to A., abbess of N. Crouchdal, ibid., 339.---Encourages N., dean of St Martin’s at Mainz, to repentance, ibid., 356.---Encourages the nuns of Zwifalten to avoid pride, not to be dancers, and not to go outside the monastery, ibid., 371.---Pope Alexander III encourages the bishop of Beauvais to persevere in love for the Roman Church and Pope Alexander’s person, CC, 96.---Encourages the archbishop of Salzburg to remain steadfastly faithful to the Church and endeavour to bring back the emperor, ibid., 101.---Henry, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, encourages the Savigniac community to frugality, on account of the apparent present poverty of their house, CCIV, 221.---Encourages all prelates of the Church to moderation, humility, and repentance, ibid., 247.---Geoffrey of St Barbara encourages Abbot John manfully to investigate vices in the monastery and punish offences, CCV, 832.---Encourages G., chaplain of the bishop of Worcester, to contempt for the world, ibid., 837.---Encourages Peter, his friend, to continual reading of Holy Scripture, ibid., 840.

Peter of Blois encourages Ralph of Beauvais to spend at least his final old age in meditation upon his last things, CCVII, 16.---Encourages a certain cleric, who had promised God that he would enter religious life, to fulfil his vow, ibid., 33.---Encourages an official of the bishop of Chartres to abandon the office he had undertaken, because of the grave and numerous abuses connected with it, ibid., 88.---

Encourages Anselma, a consecrated woman, after overcoming every temptation of flesh and world, steadfastly to protect the treasure of chastity, ibid., 113.---Encourages a consecrated woman to join charity, humility, and perseverance to virginity, ibid., 114.---Dissuades Walter, an eighty-year-old bishop, from the pursuit of hunting, with many arguments, ibid., 169.---Vigorously contends for ecclesiastical immunity: namely, that the king of France should exact from clerics for the Jerusalem war against the Saracens not money but prayers alone, ibid., 335.---Encourages Savaric, bishop of Bath, to return to his diocese, ibid., 436.---Exhortation to those who neither take up nor preach the cross, ibid., 529.---Admonishes nuns to holiness and chastity, ibid., 535.

Stephen of Tournai encourages John, bishop of Poitiers, to steadfastness in adversity, CCXI, 359.---Encourages Roland of Dinan to complete the work he has begun, ibid., 412.---Encourages Nivelon, bishop of Soissons, to complete what he has begun in the church of St John, ibid., 413.---Adam, abbot of Perseigne, dissuades William, bishop of Ély, from the king’s service, CCXI, 624.---Encourages him always to cleave to Christ in mind, ibid., 627.---Encourages his brethren to bear the Lord’s yoke, ibid., 644.---Encourages a certain friend to contempt for the world, ibid., 648. Innocent III, pope, encourages the illustrious King Aimery of Jerusalem [Col. 0172] to piety and moderation, CCXIV, 454.

V.—Reproving Letters.

Felix is reproved for not having visited him for a long time, St Ambrose, XVI, 888.---Defending the judgment he had himself delivered in the case of Indicia, he censures the decision of Syagrius, ibid., 891.---He reproaches Syagrius for having subjected Indicia to an insulting examination, ibid., 898.---Having expressed his grief over the disturbances of the Church, he complains that, after the death of Meletius, another bishop had been put in his place at Antioch, ibid., 950.---He reproves Faustinus for withdrawing from human society because of his sister’s death, ibid., 1098.---He complains that the virgins of Aemona, living on the borders of Italy, though often invited by letter, had never replied to him, St Jerome, XXII, 344.---He rebukes the monk Antony because, though asked so often, he had never replied, ibid., 345.---He reproves Rheticius, bishop of the Aedui, because in his commentaries on the Song of Songs he had absurdly interpreted *Tharsis* as Tarsus of Cilicia, etc., ibid., 461.---He rebukes Paula for her excessive grief at her daughter’s death, ibid., 463.---He rebukes the ignorance of a certain monk who was tearing apart his books against Jovinian, ibid., 512.---He reproves Vigilantius, who was slandering Jerome’s name and his friends, ibid., 602.---St Augustine laments that discord had arisen between Jerome and Rufinus, XXII, 909; XXXIII, 245.---He rebukes Sabinian the deacon, who, after committing adultery, had fled to Bethlehem, ibid., 1195.---He sharply rebukes the matron Celantia because some years earlier she had resolved in her heart to practice continence without an agreement with, and the consent of, her husband; and he shows what she owes her husband, ibid., 1204.---Having greeted Aurelius, he deals with the removal of revelries from the Church, ibid., 90, 114.---He rebukes a certain bishop Paul, who was gravely offending the Church by his frivolity, urging him to return to seriousness and to a life worthy of a bishop, ibid., 295.---He complains of having been so greatly praised by Bishop Severus, ibid., 419.---He censures Flavian’s silence and asks to be informed, St Leo the Great, LIV, 735.---He abominates the opinion of Eutyches and desires him to return to a sounder mind, ibid., 795.---He complains of the silence of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople; the cause of which—namely the devastation at Ephesus—was then unknown to Leo, ibid., 813.---He complains that Timothy was permitted to come to Constantinople, ibid., 1214.---Simplicius, pope, reproves John, bishop of Ravenna, because he had by force ordained Gregory bishop, LVIII, 35.---He complains that, together with the emperor’s letter, he had received no letter from him, ibid., 55.---Felix III, pope, complains that legates had been violated by Emperor Zeno, ibid., 934.---He complains of Severus because he had not come to L. Felix as he had promised, ibid., 234.---Ennodius reproaches Agapitus for negligence in writing, LXIII, 27.---He reproaches Deuterius for excessive grief, ibid., 31.---He reproaches Euprepia, who was travelling at Arles, for her neglect of Lupicinus her son and Ennodius her brother, ibid., 46.---Pope Hormisdas reproaches Hormisdas for excessive harshness, ibid., 409.---Silverius, pope, reproaches Vigilius with ambition for the apostolic see and with the crime of simony, LXVI, 85.---Cassiodorus reproves Theonius for negligence concerning the purple cloth which he customarily sent each year to the royal court, LXIX, 505.---Theodoric complains to them that armed servile fury had pursued innocent persons during the public games, ibid., 528.---Theodahad reproves the senators because, at the very beginning of his reign, they had not checked the fickleness of the populace and vain suspicions, ibid., 806.---Athalaric complains of the murder of Amalafrida committed by Hilderic, ibid., 765.---St John III, pope, reproves certain rash rural bishops, already condemned long ago, because they had assumed too much authority for themselves in the laying on of hands, LXXII, 13.

Pelagius II, pope, reproves John, bishop of Constantinople, who claimed for himself the title of universal bishop, LXXII, 738.---He disapproves bishops’ transfers from one church to another where the good of the Church did not require it, ibid., 749.---St Gregory the Great reproves Paul the schoolmaster because he congratulates him on his pontificate, LXXVII, 446.---Before John, bishop of Constantinople, he complains that John had procured confirmation of his election from the emperor, ibid., 447.---He grieves that he has been cast down from the delight of contemplation, ibid., 450.---He bears with difficulty being oppressed by many occupations and praised by Anastasius, bishop of Antioch, ibid., 452.---He rebukes Venantius because he has laid aside the monastic habit, ibid., 486.---He reproves Anthemius the subdeacon for neglecting the poor, ibid., 493.---He laments the burden of the episcopate, ibid., 496.---He reproves Eusebius, abbot, for pride, because he rejected the pardon and communion restored by Bishop Maximian, ibid., 574.---He especially rebukes Archbishop Januarius because he excommunicated Isidore for no cause except his own personal injury, ibid., 590.---He reproves a bishop over a sexual offense committed by the bishop’s nephew and enjoins upon him the execution of the sentence pronounced against the offender, ibid., 639.---He grieves that Queen Theodelinda has withdrawn herself from the communion of Constantius, ibid., 671.---He reproves nobles and landholders in Sardinia because they do not turn their peasants away from the worship of idols, ibid., 693.---He censures the patrician Rusticiana’s overly hasty return from Mount Sinai, ibid., 719.---He complains of being called a fool because more credit is given to others than to him concerning Ariulf’s disposition toward peace, ibid., 765.---He complains that Bishop Paul was prevented from coming to Rome, ibid., 846.---He reproves Peter, Domitian, and Elpidius because at Cyriacus’s ordination they cried, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” ibid., 860.---He rebukes Januarius, bishop of Caralis, because on the Lord’s Day, before the solemnities of Mass, he had ploughed up a man’s crop in furrows and, after the sacred rite was completed, had himself dug up the boundary-stones, ibid., 939, 941.---He reproves Maurentius, master of soldiers, because he did not restrain the bishop of Naples when he usurped matters belonging to the city’s patrons, ibid., 1005.---He reproves Duke Godiscalc because in anger he had caused the monastery’s doors to be broken down and its goods plundered, ibid., 1073.---He complains that the grain allowance of the Neapolitan diaconate had been withdrawn, ibid., 1080.---He reproves Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, for negligence toward monasteries, ibid., 1082.---He complains that he lacks interpreters skilled in the Greek language, ibid., 1096.---He rebukes the inconstancy and rashness of Abbot Urbicus, ibid., 1167.---He complains that Julian had concealed his poverty from him out of shame, ibid., 1273.---Boniface of Mainz rebukes Ethelbald for fornication, LXXXIX, 757.---St Zachary, pope, refutes the calumny that accused him of the taint of simony, ibid., 927.---Paul, pope, among other charges accuses King Desiderius because he does not restore the cities promised to the Roman Church, ibid., 1177.---He complains of King Desiderius because he does not render the full restoration promised to the legates, ibid., 1180.---Alcuin laments the devastation of the church of Lindisfarne, ibid., 150.---He reproves avarice and excessive exaction of tithes, ibid., 204.---He grieves at the absence of friends, ibid., 210, 211.---He grieves over his country’s unfaithfulness, ibid., 227.---He complains of the silence surrounding many matters, ibid., 237.---He laments calamities, ibid., 249.---He laments dangerous times, ibid., 294.---He complains of the disturbance of Church and kingdom, ibid., 300.---He laments a heinous deed at Rome, ibid., 305.---He grieves at Arno’s presence being awaited in vain, ibid., 318.---He grieves at the brevity of a visit, ibid., 319.---He grieves that because of illness he cannot see the king’s face and enjoy conversation with Gisila, ibid., 363.---He complains that replies to several letters have been discontinued, ibid., 399.---He complains of the evil of simony, which had even crept into the apostolic see, ibid., 401.

Alcuin reproves the congregation of St Martin for defending a certain cleric who had fled to them, against the sentence of his bishop, LXXXIX, 415.---He complains of certain bishops who wish to forbid priests and deacons the office of preaching, ibid., 422.---He complains of a friend’s absence and the interruption of correspondence, and reproves in him an excessive love of Maro [Virgil], ibid., 440, 442, 443, 463.---He shares grief over bodily illness and urges Joseppus to patience, ibid., 444.---He grieves over a friend’s sickness, ibid., 451.---He grieves that he has been snatched from the rank of poverty into the whirlpool of riches, ibid., 455.---He reproves bodily adornment, ibid., 456.---He complains to Antony of being forgotten by him, ibid., 461.---He reproves a disciple for perversity of life, ibid., 481, 482, 484.---He complains of new exactions by which episcopal officials harassed priests serving in the churches of St Martin, ibid., 487.---Nicholas I, pope, complains that a synod at Constantinople had dared, without the authorization of the apostolic see, to deprive Ignatius of his rank and put Photius in his place, CXIX, 773.---He reproves Louis of Germany and Charles the Bald, kings, because they had not sent bishops to the synod at Rome, ibid., 921.---He reproves Emperor Michael, who, puffed up with pride and arrogance, had written many insolent things, ibid., 926.---He reproves Festinian, bishop of Dol, because he had not written to him with due reverence, ibid., 969.---He reproaches Photius with the many crimes he committed in occupying Ignatius’s see, ibid., 1045.---He grieves that he had been deprived of the hope which, because of much he had heard from the beginning about that man’s piety, he had placed in him, ibid., 1053.---He sharply attacks Hincmar because he had acted craftily and dissemblingly in the case of the deposed clerics, ibid., 1093.---He reproves Queen Theutberga because, overcome by weariness, she writes against herself [Col. 0174], ibid., 1136.---He reproves the bishops established in Louis’s kingdom because they desire Theutgaud and Gunthar to be restored to their ranks, ibid., 1163.---He complains of Lothar because he performs none of the things he promised, ibid., 1174.---He complains that Lothar gives too much credit to his enemies concerning him; and he signifies his grief over the excommunication of Theutgaud and Gunthar, CXXI, 371.---He especially rebukes John of Split for his silence.---Alvarus of Cordoba grieves over the alienation of his property, ibid., 464.---Adrian II, pope, complains that Ignatius, archbishop of Constantinople, had not informed him promptly of his restoration to office, CXXII, 1277.---He rebukes Charles the Bald because he invaded Lothar’s kingdom and despised the legates of the apostolic see, ibid., 1297.---He reproves Hincmar because he had not recalled King Charles from the invasion of Lothar’s kingdom and had not replied to apostolic letters, ibid., 1301.---He complains that Ignatius had presumed to consecrate a bishop among the Bulgarians, maintaining that nothing should be altered concerning the three chapters, ibid., 1309.---Hincmar of Rheims reproves the illustrious Engilgar because he had improperly compelled his dependent to swear an oath, CXXVI, 256.---John VIII, pope, rebukes the faithlessness of bishops who, deserting Charles, had attached themselves to King Louis, ibid., 665.---He reproves the bishops established in the kingdom of Louis, king of Bavaria, because they had not restrained King Louis from invading the kingdom of his absent brother Charles, ibid., 667.---He reproves the counts established in the kingdom of Louis, king of Bavaria, because they had attempted to invade Charles’s kingdom, ibid., 672.---He complains of the duke of the Neapolitans, his brother, who did not obey his admonitions, ibid., 681.---He grieves that Count Boso had not brought him aid against the Saracens when he requested it, ibid., 684.---He grieves that Sergius, master of Naples, though often warned, had refused to dissolve his alliance with the Saracens, ibid., 723.---He grieves at the death of Emperor Charles, ibid., 744.---He reproves the archbishop of Embrun because he had consecrated another bishop in the Church of Vence besides the one elected by clergy and people, ibid., 750.---He sharply reproves Count Lambert because in the letters he wrote he had not shown the honor due to the apostolic see, ibid., 753, 769, 771.---He grieves that the Empress Angelberga was being afflicted with troubles and complains of the injuries Lambert inflicted upon the Roman Church, ibid., 754.---He grieves that Michael, king of the Bulgarians, follows the Greeks, ibid., 758.---He grieves that the Church of Constantinople still suffers from schism, ibid., 765.---He laments the death of Emperor Charles, father of Louis the Stammerer, ibid., 767.---He reproves King Charles because, though summoned, he had not come to him, ibid., 786.---He grieves over the death of the bishop of Ravenna, ibid., 812.---He reproves Bishop Wibert because, though summoned twice, he had neglected to come to him, ibid., 825.---He reproves Bishop Wibbo because he had not forbidden the plundering of Angelberga’s property, CXLIII, 831.---He reproves Anspert, archbishop of Milan, on many matters, ibid., 808, 836, 850, 916.---He grieves that dissensions had been stirred up at Capua, ibid., 877.---He reproves Prefect Pulcar because he had neither broken the alliance made with pagans nor defended St Peter’s dominion as he had promised, ibid., 878.---He grieves over the calamities of the monks of the monastery of Pultaria, ibid., 879.---He reproves Romanus, archbishop, because he does not reside in his church, ibid., 884.---He reproves Helmo, bishop of Penne, because he did not attend the synod, ibid., 890.---He reproves Arpald, bishop of Ascoli, because he did not come to the synod, ibid., 893.---He reproves Bishop Egilbert because he had communicated with persons excommunicated by the apostolic see, ibid., 897.---He rebukes Landulf, bishop of the Surici, because he violated the settlement which he himself had made between him and Landenulf, bishop of Capua, concerning the fruits of that church, ibid., 906.---He reproves Otteram, bishop of Vienne, because he favored Boso’s associates and maintained that this had been commanded him by the pope, ibid., 917.---He reproves Adelchis, bishop of Trent, because he had seized the property of the bishop of Verona, ibid., 923.---He reproves Athanasius, bishop of Naples, because he had not broken the alliance he had made with the Saracens although he had promised to break it, ibid., 927.---He reproves Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna, because he had brought Count Alberic into Ravenna and harassed the nobles of Ravenna contrary to the oath they had sworn to him, ibid., 931.---Because he consented that another man’s lawful wife be handed over to an abductor, ibid., 932.---He complains that a certain Marquis Wido had taken away many goods of the Roman Church, ibid., 948.---He complains that no aid is brought to him against Saracen raids, ibid., 949.---He reproves the archbishop of Vienne because, after Bishop Optandus had been thrown into prison, he installed another in the Church of Geneva, ibid., 952.
