Leo IX, pope, reproves Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, because he attempted to subject the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch to his authority, CXLII, 773.---He complains of the arrogance of Michael of Constantinople, ibid., 777.---He complains of violence inflicted upon him by Italians, ibid., 798.---Gozechin the schoolmaster laments the evils of his time, especially those resulting from Berengar’s most perverse doctrine, ibid., 886.---Peter Damian denounces two evil customs then prevalent in the Church and asks that they be abolished, CXLIV, 214.---He vehemently complains that a book which he had recently composed with much labor and sleeplessness had been fraudulently stolen from him, ibid., 270.---He complains to Hildebrand that he has discovered himself to be little loved by him, ibid., 272.---He reproves Bishop V. for alienating the goods of the Church, ibid., 321.---He fiercely attacks certain malicious and ignorant persons because they tried maliciously to make words taken from his discourse odious, ibid., 335.---He refutes those who ridiculed the custom of voluntarily striking the body with scourges as novel and contrary to the sacred canons, ibid., 349.---He complains of the discords and scandals of the Church of Milan, ibid., 367.---He reproves monks living in the desert of a mountain near him because they wholly neglected and violated certain rules established by him in their monastery, ibid., 422.---He reproves Cinthius, prefect of the City, because perhaps through devotion to prayer he did not discharge the office of administering justice to the people entrusted to him, ibid., 464.

St Gregory VII, pope, grieves over the calamities of Ramald, bishop of Como, CXLVIII, 302.---He reproves Geboard, bishop of Salzburg, because he does not restrain his clergy, ibid., 313.---He reproves Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, because he permits a certain Arfactus, contrary to the decrees of Alexander, Gregory’s predecessor, to harass the abbey of St Edmund, ibid., 314.---He attacks Philip, king of the Franks, as a seller and destroyer of churches, ibid., 317.---He complains that war had broken out between Wozelin of Magdeburg and King Henry, ibid., 320.---He reproves Arnald, abbot of St Severus, because, though summoned to a synod, he had not come, ibid., 330.---He reproves Sigifred, bishop of Mainz, because he had presumed to take to himself a cause pending between Jeromir, bishop of Prague, and John, bishop of Moravia, ibid., 336.---He reproves the people of Ragusa because, after throwing their bishop into prison, they had chosen another for themselves, ibid., 340.---He complains of injuries inflicted upon the monastery of St Giles and its abbot, ibid., 342.---He reproves Duke Godfrey because he had not sent soldiers in aid of St Peter, ibid., 346.---He complains that Anno, bishop of Cologne, had sent him no letters after obtaining the pontificate, ibid., 352.---He reproves the bishop of Poitiers for contempt of the apostolic see and injuries inflicted upon apostolic legates, ibid., 359.---He reproves Geboard, bishop of Prague, for contempt of the authority of the apostolic see, ibid., 305.---He reproves Canipert, bishop of Turin, because, though summoned to a synod, he had not come, ibid., 387.---He reproves William, bishop of Pavia, because, though summoned to him, he had not come, ibid., 389.---He complains that Sweyn, king of the Danes, had not written to him, ibid., 402.---He reproves Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, because he had been negligent in the case of the clergy of Châlons, ibid., 408.---He rebukes the people of Fiesole because, by repeatedly pursuing superfluous complaints against their bishop, they inflict losses upon the Church of Fiesole, ibid., 409.---He reproves Dictwin, bishop of Liège, as a simoniac, ibid., 412.---He reproves Cunibert, bishop of Turin, because he harasses the monks of St Michael, ibid., 419.---He complains of princes’ disobedience toward the Roman Church, ibid., 426.---He complains of King Henry’s inconstancy, ibid., 433.---He reproves Tetald, a Milanese cleric, because, while a canonically elected bishop was still alive, he intruded himself into that bishop’s place, ibid., 436.---He reproves Henry, king of the Romans, because he communicates with excommunicated persons, ibid., 439.---He complains of injuries inflicted upon his Church by the bishop of Orléans, and of that bishop’s disobedience and simony, ibid., 446.---He complains of King Henry’s treachery and of the evils the Church suffered from him, ibid., 451.---He reproves the canons of St Martin of Lucca because, contrary to his admonitions and after promising satisfaction, they bought canonries and prebends, ibid., 487.---He rebukes Rainerius, bishop of Orléans, because, abusing the patience of the Roman Church and adding crime to crime, he had squandered nearly all the ornaments of his church, ibid., 505.---He reproves the clerics of St Martin of Lucca for disobedience, ibid., 519.---He reproves Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, because he had not visited him since his own visit, ibid., 535.---He reproves Jordan, prince of Capua, because he had not kept faith with blessed Peter, ibid., 541.---He complains of the practice of false penitence, which among other vices had then become prevalent in the Church, ibid., 553.---He attacks a certain Transmund, who, having been rebuked by him for abandoning his bishopric and warned not to intrude himself into it again, nevertheless dared to seize that very church, ibid., 588.---He reproves Samuel, bishop of the city of Dublin, because he gives away the property of his church at will to outsiders, and urges him to restore it, ibid., 109.---He grieves over the misery of the English Church and its bishops, ibid., 158.---Emperor Henry complains of his son because he had risen against him, CLIX, 933.---Ivo of Chartres reproves Bernard, abbot of Marmoutier, because he keeps certain brothers detained in his monastery, CLXII, 14 and 15.

Hildebert of Le Mans sharply reproaches a certain rich but wicked courtier for abusing wealth and power, CLXXI, 183.---He sharply reproaches an ecclesiastic for negligence and hardness of heart, ibid., 229.---He reproves a certain priest because he had subjected a man suspected of theft against him to a harsh interrogation in order to secure a revelation, ibid., 277.---A letter full of lamentations and grief, Heloise, CLXXVIII, 191.---Abelard attacks a certain man ignorant of dialectic who nevertheless censured its study and thought all Abelard’s doctrines mere sophistries and deceits, ibid., 351.---Innocent II, pope, complains of the disobedience of John, bishop of Glasgow, CLXXIX, 90.---The Cistercians sharply and frankly reproach King Louis, who was hostile and injurious to the bishop of Paris, St Bernard of Clairvaux, CLXXXII, 149.---He gently censures William, who complained that Bernard did not return to him equal offices of affection, ibid., 206.---He disapproves the abdication of pastoral care, even when done for love of quiet, ibid., 211.---He grieves that Geoffrey of Lisieux, abandoning his religious purpose, had returned to the world, ibid., 255.---He censures Humbert, abbot of Igny, because he had rashly and without consultation relinquished the office of prelate, ibid., 296.---He expresses the distress caused by his long absence from his beloved Clairvaux, and his most tender affection and longing for his sons, ibid., 300.---He expresses profound grief of heart over Philip, the usurper of the Church of Tours, ibid., 310.---Bernard complains that the election of a bishop for the Church of Langres had been attempted deceitfully and contrary to faith pledged, ibid., 322.---He complains of the pastoral charge imposed upon him, ibid., 338.---He complains that certain perverse persons harmful to the Church were being supported by pontifical authority in carrying out their evil designs, ibid., 340.---He sharply censures Henry, archbishop of Sens, as harsh, because he had improperly deposed an archdeacon, ibid., 344.---He rebukes Peter, dean of Besançon, for injuries inflicted upon the abbot of Chari-Locus, ibid., 364.---He complains that Count Ralph, who had repudiated his wife and taken another, found patrons at court, ibid., 379.---He complains that Theobald was being oppressed for the cause of justice and fidelity toward the apostolic see, ibid., 380.---He sharply reproves King Louis because, adhering to evil counsels, he rejects counsels of peace, ibid., 386.---He complains of the king’s unjust machinations against Theobald, contrary to the agreement and peace already made, ibid., 387.---Bernard and Hugh complain of the king’s obstinacy in his evil undertakings, ibid., 394.---He complains that the apostolic sentence, which by the pope’s command he had proclaimed in the case of the election at Auxerre, was being despised, ibid., 485.---He rebukes Bruno for writing in a confused and imprudent manner, ibid., 487.---He grieves over the unhappy outcome of the holy expedition and desires his uncle’s arrival, ibid., 493.---He censures a certain layman because he had tried to draw his kinsman Peter away from the purpose of religious life, ibid., 497.---He complains of a heavy exaction imposed on his people by a count, ibid., 501.---He sharply censures certain enemies who opposed the pious undertakings of others, ibid., 513.---He complains that in the monastery of the Saviour not all things had come about according to the pope’s promises, ibid., 547.---He complains of the office of superior imposed upon him, ibid., 548.---He disapproves an excessive concern to preserve health through medicines, ibid., 550.---He reproves the monk Ralph, who was arming the faithful for the slaughter of Jews, ibid., 570.---He mourns over the office of superior imposed upon him, ibid., 578.---He complains that the monks of Vézelay were being harassed by the countess’s retainers, ibid., 580.---He censures the monk Alard because, after expelling the aforesaid novice, who was already planning to return and amend, he persisted more stubbornly in opposing him, ibid., 622.---Suger rebukes the bishop of Amiens because he had admitted Robert of Bova, a thoroughly wicked man, to communion in sacred things, CLXXXVI, 1421.

Peter the Venerable reproaches the priest Stephen for a prolix letter in which he had not preserved rhetorical propriety, CLXXXIX, 76.---He complains of a friend’s silence, ibid., 80.---The monks of Stavelot complain of Count Godfrey, who had broken the truce agreed with them, ibid., 1154.---Abbot Wibald rebukes the men of Corbie because they repeatedly press him to return, ibid., 1483.---He reproves Walter, a wicked monk, on many charges, ibid., [Col. 0177] 1265.---He reproves H., bishop of Minden, because he harasses the brethren of Corbie, ibid., 1272.---Because he had not reconciled the Church of Kamien, ibid., 1275.---He complains that Henry, bishop of Minden, had refused to accept and grant peace that was offered and requested, ibid., 1325.---Henry, bishop of Liège, complains of Count Henry of Namur, ibid., 1353.---Abbot Wibald complains of the bishop of Liège and of the counts of Namur, La Roche, and Montaigu, ibid., 1354.---Arnold of Selenhofen complains of the Count Palatine of the Rhine, ibid., 1455.---Gerhoh of Reichersberg declares his grief at the death of Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, CXCIII, 495.---Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, fiercely attacks Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, because he had construed and circulated his statements in a worse sense, ibid., 524.---Hugh of Peter Leo grieves over the deed of Ervisius, formerly an abbot, CXCVI, 1392.---Nicholas of Clairvaux complains of the absence of Rualen, abbot of St Anastasius, ibid., 1641.---Hildegard sharply rebukes Arnald, archbishop of Mainz, and predicts his death, CXCVII, 157.---She reproves vain glory in the bishop of Constance, ibid., 174.---She disapproves the various schemes of Emperor Frederick, ibid., 186.---Hildegard freely reproves Cuno for excessive severity toward his subjects and predicts his imminent death, ibid., 203.---Helenger, abbot of St Disibod, accuses himself and complains that monastic discipline has been badly observed in his monastery, ibid., 204.---In most grave words, and in God’s name, he reproves clerics’ negligence in the care of souls and other vices, ibid., 244.---He reproves the negligence of pastors and prelates in many ways, ibid., 234.---He reproves those whom the Cistercians themselves call *conversi* (“lay brothers”), since very many of them do not turn to God in their conduct, ibid., 260.---He reproves H., provost at Bonn, because he loves the world, ibid., 315.---He reproves the negligence of the monks of Zwiefalten and exhorts them to come to their senses, ibid., 370.---Alexander III, pope, complains of the bishop of Orléans unjustly harassing certain canons, CC, 162, 186.---Philip of Harveng complains about a Premonstratensian received by the Cistercians against the will of the Premonstratensians, CCIII, 77.---Peter of Blois sharply rebukes a nobleman who had reproached his chaplain with the low condition of his family, CCVII, 7.---He attacks a certain disciple of his who, after completing the course of liberal arts, intended not to devote himself to theology until he had spent two years in idleness, ibid., 24.---He complains sharply that the youthful king of Sicily had elevated a wholly unsuitable man to the bishopric of the Church of Agrigento, ibid., 27.---He reproves a novice monk who prematurely sought a priorship—that is, the liberty to leave the monastery and the power to preach the word of God—ibid., CCVII, 39.---He most severely censures the character, talents, and thoroughly depraved life of a certain bishop, to whose court a friend had invited him, ibid., 65.---He describes and assails the pride and arrogance of H., a canon and former friend, ibid., 75.---He complains sorrowfully that men everywhere unworthy in learning, virtue, or age rush through sheer ambition into bishoprics and other dignities, ibid., 82.

Peter of Blois complains of the inhospitableness of the prior of Wallingford, CCVII, 98.---He attacks H., a prelate who maligns princes, ibid., 119.---He complains that the king of England wanders through uncertain residences, ibid., 124.---Geoffrey, bishop-elect of Lincoln, reproves one of his clerics for disobedience, because abandoning him the cleric had attached himself to a certain abbot, ibid., 184.---He sharply attacks a former companion and friend who, through envy, had procured that Peter of Blois should not be admitted into the household of the archbishop of Sens, ibid., 221.---He assails court flatterers, ibid., 237.---He sharply attacks Bishop Hugh because he had been the principal cause of William, bishop of Ely, being deprived with the utmost disgrace of the office of administering the kingdom of England, ibid., 278.---He vehemently attacks Ralph, bishop of Lisieux, for avarice and the pursuit of usury, ibid., 285.---He attacks Zoilus, the detractor of his writings, ibid., 289.---He complains to an archdeacon of the insolence of the archdeacon’s nephews, who were soldiers, ibid., 293.---He reproves B., a monk, because he pursues courtly life and its vices—detraction and flattery, ibid., 330.---He reproves G., an abbot, because on account of certain land and pasture he had brought the prior of St Cosmas to judgment, ibid., 346.---He reproves G., archdeacon of York, who boasts of his innocence although there were many things in him deserving reproof, ibid., 348.---He reproves R., a canon, because he had insulted those to whom he was being sent, ibid., 350.---He complains that promises made by the archbishop of Sens are fulfilled too slowly, ibid., 380.---He sharply attacks R., archdeacon of Orléans, because he had introduced the plague of simony into the Church, ibid., 381.---He reproves his nephew, a monk, because, neglecting the study of sacred literature and solitude, he seeks the friendships of princes and of the world, ibid., [Col. 0178] 386.---He complains that the income of his benefice had been withheld for five years by a certain Elias, ibid., 422.---He complains that he, now old and retired, is being deprived of the honor of the archdeaconry by the false accusation of ill-wishers, ibid., 439.---He complains bitterly that certain men in the Roman Curia, corrupted by gifts, attempted contrary to the canons to place an illiterate layman over an abbey, ibid., 452.---He complains bitterly that the man whom he regarded as his greatest friend had become a hostile enemy and detractor, ibid., 456.---A certain person is rebuked for charging the archbishop of Canterbury with excessive gentleness, ibid., 458.---He most bitterly laments the untimely death of Emperor Frederick called Barbarossa, ibid., 467.---He laments the death of Master Walter, professor of grammar, ibid., 468, 469.---He laments the death of a certain distinguished professor of civil law, ibid., 470.---An anxious complaint against a prelate, ibid., 543.---Lament of the Church of Orléans over the murder of John the dean, Stephen of Tournai, CCXI, 309.---He complains of the monks of Longpont, who were troublesome and hostile toward him, ibid., 350.---He complains of the rebellion of the canons of St John of Soissons living in the parishes, ibid., 353.---He complains that the Roman Curia was insufficiently well-disposed toward him, ibid., 398.---The clerics of Grandmont complain of the attacks of their *conversi* (“lay brothers”), ibid., 430.---He complains of the burden he suffered undeservedly because of debts, ibid., 474.---He reproves Berter, archdeacon of Cambrai, because he rashly disparages his reputation, and sets out the course of his own life, ibid., 486.---He complains that, without his permission, sacred orders had been conferred upon the monks of St Amand, ibid., 515.---He reproves the excessive multitude of decretals and the teachers who abused them, ibid., 516.---Adam, abbot of Persigne, reproves Odo, bishop of Paris, because he had imposed tallages upon the priests of his diocese, ibid., 597.---Innocent III, pope, rebukes the bishops established in Sardinia because they resort to a secular tribunal, CCXV, 392.

VI.—Letters of Recommendation.

Recommends himself to the prayers of Eusebius, Dionysius, and Lucifer, who were in exile, Pope Liberius, VIII, 1356.---Promises Felix his prayers, and requests his prayers in return, St. Ambrose, XVI, 888.---Commends Theodora, widow of Lucinius, to the priest Abigaus, St. Jerome, XXII, 689.---Commends Praesidium to Augustine, and orders Alypius to be released, ibid., 831, 154.---Commends to Olympius, Master of the Offices, the case of Boniface, bishop of Cataqua, concerning a certain possession of the Church acquired, not without fraud, by his predecessor, St. Augustine, XXXIII, 356.---Commends the case of Faventius, ibid., 428, 429, 430.---Commends to Quintilianus a widowed mother and her virgin daughter, who were carrying relics of Stephen the martyr, ibid., 965.---Commends Basil and John, priests accused of heresy who had come to Rome to give an account of their faith, to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, ibid., 926.---Commends to the Emperor the envoys whom he sends to the synod, and requests that no debate on the faith be reopened there, ibid., 941.---Commends Terentianus, Pope Felix III, LVIII, 927.---Notably commends works of mercy and the spiritual building of a temple in the soul, Paulinus of Nola, LXI, 330.---Paulinus commends to the prayers of Delphinus the soul of his deceased brother and himself, ibid., 350.---Commends to the prayers of Amandus, priest of Bordeaux, the soul of his brother and himself, ibid., 351.---Commends Bassus, the bearer of the letter, Ennodius, LXIII, 32.---Pope Hormisdas commends John of Naples to the Emperor Anastasius, ibid., 406.---Commends himself to the prayers of many bishops, Senator, LXIX, 827.---Commends Maurentius to Paul the scholar, St. Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 446.---Commends Luminosa, widow of Zemarchus, that her retinue may be preserved for her, ibid., 459.---Commends the affairs of Italy, ibid., 484.---Commends Pompeiana, that she may not be burdened contrary to equity, ibid., 521.---Commends Catella, a devout woman, to Januarius, archbishop of Cagliari, ibid., 522.---Commends Hilary, administrator of the patrimony of the Roman Church, ibid., 529, 530.---Commends Dracolfus, returned from the enemy, to Gennadius, patrician of Africa, ibid., 538.---Commends Valerianus, a priest arriving for the ransom of captives, ibid., 616.---Commends Constantius, his very dear friend, ibid., 628.---Commends Sabinianus and Castus, ibid., 646, 649.---Commends the Church of Saint Agatha in the Subura, ibid., 688.---Commends Narses, ibid., 705.---Commends the visitation of the Church of Ravenna, ibid., 753.---Commends Castorius, the chartulary clerk, ibid., 775.---Commends Candidus, a priest designated administrator of the patrimony that was in [Col. 0179] Gaul, ibid., 796, 797.---Commends three churches deprived of their own bishops, ibid., 812.---Commends Alexandria, left to Vincomalus, ibid., 828.---Commends Augustine, going to England with his companions, and Candidus, administrator of the patrimony, ibid., 836, 837, 838, 841, 842.---Commends a certain cleric unable to read, ibid., 865.---Commends Bishop Paul, ibid., 915, 916.---Earnestly commends Abbot Claudius, returning from Rome, ibid., 920.---Commends the wife of John, who was being summoned into litigation concerning her status, ibid., 922.---Commends John, who was to act in the place of the prefect, ibid., 970.---Commends the privileges of Naples and the affairs of the island of Procida, ibid., 1005.---Commends to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, and to Castorius the judgment concerning Maximus, and prescribes its manner, ibid., 1012.---Commends certain persons restored to the unity of the Church and returning from Rome to Istria, ibid., 1020.---Commends Abbot Cyriacus, going to Syagrius, ibid., 1027.---Commends Hilary, that Queen Brunhild of the Franks may protect him under her care, Gregory the Great, LXXVII, 76, 1048.---Commends Hilary, that they may extend to him their patronage, ibid.---Commends Hilary, that he may receive her patronage, ibid., 1049.---Commends Abbot Cyriacus and his envoy, ibid., 1050.---Commends Gregory, former prefect, ibid., 1110, 1111, 1112.---Commends John, deacon of the Church of Ravenna and administrator of the patrimony in Sicily, ibid., 1124.---Commends the Gallic patrimony of the Roman Church, ibid., 1130.---After a most affectionate greeting, commends Candidus the priest, ibid., 1031.---Commends Theodora, a widow, that, because of the ungrateful disposition of her son, to whom she had given all her possessions upon his marriage, she may not suffer want, ibid., 1032.---Commends the monks sent to Augustine in England, ibid., 1173, 1174, 1179.---Commends Bishop Augustine, if he should come to him, ibid., 1208.---Commends Aurelius, a priest, that an oratory or some place may be entrusted to him, ibid., 1210.---Commends the men of Maurentius, ibid., 1222.---Commends the men and possessions of Romanus, former praetor, ibid., 1246.---Commends those converted from the error of the Monophysites, ibid., 1252.---Commends the Roman Church, 1288.---Affectionately commends Peter and his mother, ibid., 1302.---Commends Boniface, that favour may be shown him in the ministry he has undertaken, Pope St. Gregory II, LXXXIX, 498.---Commends the same Boniface and explains the purposes for which he was sent, ibid., 501.---Commends Boniface, returning to Germany, that bishops and priests may assist him, Pope Gregory III, ibid., 578.---Commends himself to the prayers of certain nuns, Boniface of Mainz, ibid., 721.---Egburga commends herself to Winfrid, ibid., 733.---Commends to Grifo, brother of Pippin, the clerics and monks who are in Thuringia, that he may defend them from the injuries of pagans, Boniface, ibid., 954.---Commends himself to the prayers of Felix, apparently bishop of Urgel, whose piety has been praised to him, Alcuin, C, 144.---Commends himself to the prayers of the brethren of the Church of York, ibid., 145, 147.---Commends peace, ibid., 149.---Commends himself to the friendship of the brethren of the Church of Saint Peter, ibid., 167.---Commends himself to the favour of Pope Adrian I, ibid., 170.---Commends himself to the prayers of monks, ibid., 173.---Commends himself to the care of Pope Leo III, as vicar of the apostles and prince of the Church, ibid., 178.---Commends to the favour of Angilbert, primicerius of the palace of King Pippin, a man making pilgrimage to the holy thresholds of the apostles, ibid., 181.---Commends himself to his constant remembrance, and the bearer of his letter to his protection, ibid., 185.---Commends the soul of Archanbald to the prayers of Arno, ibid., 191.---Humbly commends himself to the prayers of a certain Paulinus, ibid., 200.---Sets forth the benefits of literary study, ibid., 207.---Commends himself to the prayers of the monks of Saint-Vaast, ibid., 215.---Commends himself to the prayers of the brethren of Corbie, ibid., 218.---Commends himself to the prayers of Bishop Eanbald, ibid., 221.---Commends the noblewoman Liudgarda to prayer, ibid., 227.---Commends the study of sacred reading and wisdom, ibid., 234, 378.---Commends a certain son to Arno, bishop of Salzburg, ibid., 238.---Commends his friends who had set out from England for Rome, ibid., 258.---Commends himself, infirm in body and spirit, to Arno’s prayers, and sighs for heaven, ibid., 399.---Commends to Arno the care of canons, monks, and those of the third rank, intermediate between the two, ibid., 401.---Commends himself, as an infirm old man, to the sacred memory of Arno, ibid., 406.---Commends Fredegisus to Arno, ibid., 407.---Commends to Arno a pupil in grammar, whom he calls a calf, ibid., 416.---Commends himself to the fatherly affection and holy prayers of Archbishop Peter, ibid., 438.---Commends Liudgarda to Archbishop Peter, to whom gifts are being sent for her, ibid., 440.---Commends himself to the prayers of [Col. 0180] Joseph, ibid., 444.---Commends to Bishop Remigius a merchant travelling to Italy, ibid., 445.

Commends himself, on account of their old friendship, to the prayers of Remedius, bishop of Chur, Alcuin, C, 446.---Commends himself to the prayers of all and each individually, ibid., 448.---Commends the reading of the Holy Gospel and Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*, ibid., 457, 459.---Commends chastity together with generosity in almsgiving, ibid., 469.---Recommendation to friends on behalf of persons making pilgrimage to the thresholds of the apostles, ibid., 486.---Commends Benedict, who is departing from him, ibid., 488.---Commends a certain brother, whom he calls his son, to charity; and himself, tossed on the waves of the world, to Benedict’s prayers, ibid., 494.---Commends himself to the prayers of the brethren of Hittirium, ibid., 495.---Commends himself to the prayers of Eanulf, priest, ibid., 507.---Commends the envoys sent into Francia concerning the cause of his brother Lothair, Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 799.---Commends Theognostus to Ignatius, archbishop of Constantinople, Pope Adrian II, 1277.---Commends the Church of Laon to King Charles the Bald while Bishop Hincmar goes to Rome, ibid., 1280, 1281.---Commends John, metropolitan of Silaeum, to Ignatius, archbishop of Constantinople, ibid., 1282.---Commends his envoys, ibid., 1303, 1305.---Commends Wigbod, bishop of Parma, Pope John VIII, CXXVI, 699.---Earnestly commends himself and his flock to Empress Adelaide, Wigo, dean of Phyutitwagen [reading uncertain], CXXXVII, 10.---Commends two young monks to F., scholar of Augsburg, ibid., 12.---Earnestly commends to Pope Alexander II the bishop of Orléans, whose church, harassed by wicked men, was being tossed by many storms and whirlwinds of calamity, Peter Damian, CXLIV, 213.---Commends Maurice, afflicted in the head, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 1088, 1089, 1090.---Commends Osbern to Henry, ibid., 1130.---Commends the monks of Bec whom he sends to England, ibid., 1150, 1151, 1152.

Commends the bishop of Beauvais to Pope Urban II, Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 14.---Commends his legate Otto, bishop of Todi, Pope Innocent II, CLXXIX, 700, 701 ff.---Commends himself to the prayers of the religious of the Grande Chartreuse, St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 115.---Commends the cause of the Church of Dijon to Pope Honorius, ibid., 117.---Commends the envoys of Reims, ibid., 122.---Commends the cause of the bishop of Meaux, ibid., 124.---Commends the cause of a certain Humbert, ibid., 141.---Commends various causes to Theobald, ibid., 146.---Commends the poor religious Theobald, ibid., 147.---Commends Abbot Vivianus, and admonishes him that care for the soul must be seriously undertaken, ibid., 160.---Commends Humbert’s cause, ibid., 162.---Commends to a bishop a woman burdened by many sins but now repentant, ibid., 168.---Commends the cause of certain religious persons, ibid., 332.---Commends the Knights Templar, ibid., 336.---Commends to Pope Innocent the affair of the archbishop of Trier, ibid., 343.---Commends the monks of Vaucelles to the protection of Simon, son of the castellan of Cambrai, ibid., 348.---Commends a certain kinsman to the queen of Jerusalem, ibid., 373.---Commends to Pope Innocent the cause of the archbishop of Canterbury and also of the bishop of London, ibid., 376.---Commends the bishop of Cambrai and Abbot Godescalc, ibid., 378.---Commends to Pope Eugenius the bishop of Orléans, who had voluntarily resigned his episcopate, that the pope may wish provision to be made for his honour, ibid., 443.---Commends as worthy the prior of La Chaise-Dieu, elected bishop of Valence, ibid., 449.---Commends Odo, abbot of Saint-Denis, and defends him against the suspicious accusations of others, born of envy and ambition, ibid., 491.---Commends the bishop of Le Mans and others to the Pontiff, ibid., 499.---Commends the cause of the archbishop of Mainz, burdened by his adversaries, ibid., 504.

Commends Robert, the king’s brother, St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLVIII, 506.---Praises Abbot Suger and commends his envoys to the Pontiff, ibid., 513.---Commends himself to the prayers of Malachy, archbishop of Ireland, ibid., 545.---Commends envoys seeking Rome on account of the archbishopric of York, ibid., 552.---Commends certain poor persons, ibid., 554.---Commends Premonstratensians making pilgrimage to Jerusalem, ibid., 557.---Trusting in Theobald’s friendship, commends John to him, ibid., 562.---Commends the bishop of Metz, ibid., 572.---Commends the Church of Mont to Abbot Suger, ibid., 575.---Wittily commends a boy to Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, ibid., 614.---Commends to the abbot of Troyes a refined cleric renouncing the world, ibid., 617.---Commends P. Lombard, ibid., 618.---Commends to a certain bishop the cause of the monastery of Saint [Col. 0181] Martin, ibid., 630.---Commends to a certain abbot L., a fugitive who is returning, and asks that he be kindly received, ibid., 639.---Commends to an unnamed person the abbot of Farfa, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, ibid., 640.---Abbot Suger commends himself to the prayers of St. Bernard, CLXXXII, 675.---The bishop of Auxerre commends to Suger the wife and children of Robert the physician, his deceased friend, CLXXXVI, 1406.---The abbot of Pontigny commends to Suger the cause of the treasurer of Auxerre, ibid., 1413.---John, cardinal of Santa Maria Nuova, commends to Suger the case of Master Peter, entrusted to Suger’s judgment by Pope Eugenius, ibid., 1414.---Henry of Winchester commends to Suger the affairs of the king of England, ibid., 1434.---Suger commends the king and queen to God, and the Church of Saint-Denis to the king, ibid., 1438.---Emperor Conrad commends Wibald, abbot of Corbie, to H., duke of Saxony, CLXXXIX, 1141.---Abbot Wibald commends to Cardinal Guy the cause of the abbot of Fulda, ibid., 1150.---Commends to Cardinal Guy the abbot of Braunweiler, ibid., 1190.---Commends to Cardinal Guy the bishop-elect of Bremen and Provost Hartwig, ibid., 1204.---Commends certain affairs to a man going to Rome, especially in favour of the abbot of Hersfeld, ibid., 1244.---Commends to John of Fritzlar, going to the king, the affairs of his monastery of Corbie, ibid., 1293.---Commends to H., notary of the royal court, before the emperor, the Corbie monks’ case concerning Karninata and Visbick, ibid., 1295, 1297.---Commends to Emperor Manuel of Constantinople the bishop of Regensburg, travelling to Jerusalem, ibid., 1306.---Emelerus, monk, commends to Abbot Wibald A., bearer of the present letter, ibid., 1317.---Emperor Frederick commends to Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg, the cause of the monastery of Corbie, ibid., 1443.---Frederick, bishop of Münster, commends to Wichmann, archbishop, the bishop of Osnabrück, ibid., 1445.---Emperor Frederick commends Gerard, abbot of Solignac, to Henry, king of England, ibid., 1448.---Achard, abbot of Saint Victor, commends his church to Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, CXCVI, 1382.---B., abbot of Saint-Evroult, commends to Ervisius, abbot of Saint Victor, the affairs of his monastery, ibid., 1386.---G. commends himself to the prayers of Abbot Ervisius, ibid., 1387.---Hugh of Campfleur commends his clerics to King Louis, ibid., 1588.---Eberhard of Salzburg commends himself to Hildegard’s prayers, CXCVII, 164.---The bishop of Prague requests that Hildegard assist him with her prayers and offer good counsel, ibid., 177.---The bishop of Jerusalem commends himself to Hildegard’s prayers, ibid., 178.

The bishop of Beauvais requests Hildegard’s prayers, CXCVII, 180.---Philip, count of Flanders, requests the prayers and counsel of St. Hildegard, ibid., 187.---Adam, abbot of Ebra, commends himself to Hildegard’s prayers, ibid., 190.---The abbot of Eberbach asks for Hildegard’s prayers and offers her his services, ibid., 194.---The abbot of Kempten commends himself to Hildegard’s prayers, ibid., 206.---The abbot of Saint Martin in Cologne commends himself to Hildegard’s prayers, ibid., 207.---H., provost of Flonheim, commends himself to Hildegard’s prayers, ibid., 298.---Peter of Blois, being ill, implores the aid of prayers from monks, CCVII, 333.---Implores the prayers of monks, that he may be worthily initiated into the priesthood, ibid., 413.---Recommendation of a certain abbot after his death, ibid., 504.---Commends the Church of Saint Samson of Orléans, Stephen of Tournai, CCXI, 320, 322.---Commends a certain canon of his residing at Naples, ibid., 322.---Commends a certain widow and her son to Arald, abbot of Saint Benedict, ibid., 346.---Commends the cause of a certain Simon, which was being heard in his court, ibid., 353.---Commends his kinsman who was setting out for Palestine, ibid., 355, 356.---Commends the chancellor of France against the objections of canons who alleged against him the defect of illegitimate birth, ibid., 378.---Commends the abbot of Saint-Satyrus, extolling his life and virtues in praise, ibid., 388.---Commends the monks of Compiègne and asks that they be protected against those attacking them, ibid., 389.---Commends the same cause of the archbishop of Tours, ibid., 397, 399.---Commends a certain canon residing with him at Paris, ibid., 411.---Commends his nephew Peter to Nicholas, prior of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon, ibid., 414.---Commends his canon G., whom he sends into Denmark, ibid., 436.---Commends the abbot of Sarne, and asks that he not be compelled to return, ibid., 454.---Commends a certain craftsman whose son was requesting the monastic habit, ibid., 493.---Adam, abbot of Perseigne, commends himself to the prayers of the virgin Margaret, ibid., 623.

VII.—Letters of Excuse and Apology.

[Col. 0182]

Cyprian excuses himself for not having held the ordination of Cornelius to be beyond doubt, etc., IV, 341.---Cyprian excuses himself to the Thibaritans for not having visited them, and warns them of the impending persecution, ibid., 351.---Cyprian clears himself before Florentius Pupianus of various charges brought against him by the latter, ibid., 402.---Ambrose excuses himself for not having come to Caesarea, XVI, 876.---Ambrose excuses himself for not coming to the consistory when summoned, ibid., 1003.---St. Jerome excuses himself to Julian for the silence of his letters, XXII, 1345.---Excuses himself for having written little, ibid., 446.---Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, excuses himself to John, bishop of Jerusalem, for having ordained Paulinianus priest, ibid., 517.---Excuses himself to the priest Abigaus for not having written, ibid., 689.---Excuses himself to Theophilus for having translated his attached Paschal letter late, being hindered partly by the death of Paula and partly by his own illness, ibid., 812.---Returns Augustine’s greeting, excusing himself for having answered too freely, ibid., 933.---Paulinus excuses himself to Bishop Alypius concerning Augustine’s books which he received, for having sent him Eusebius’s *Chronicle* late, XXXIII, 98.---Augustine excuses himself for why he will not come to the council, ibid., 226.---Alypius and Augustine excuse to Severus what was done in the affair of Timothy, ibid., 229.---Jerome excuses himself for having answered his letter too freely, and asks that, contentious questions having been set aside, they may henceforth confer amicably with one another, ibid., 273.---Excuses himself to Bishop Novatus for not sending to him his brother Lucillus, a deacon, whom the churches of the diocese of Hippo could not spare because of his knowledge of Latin, ibid., 294.---Augustine excuses his absence to the clergy and people of Hippo, urging them to be more eager than usual in relieving the poor, ibid., 470.---Augustine excuses himself to Albina, Piniana, and Melania, who had come to Africa in their desire to see him and were staying at Thagaste, for not being able to go there to visit them, not so much because of the severity of winter as because of the unstable condition of the Church of Hippo, ibid., 471.---Jerome excuses himself for not yet having refuted the books of the Pelagian Annianus, ibid., 928.---The Gallic bishops excuse their delay in replying, LIV, 966.

Ruricius excuses himself for not having written to Aeonius until now, LVIII, 87.---Excuses himself for not having come to the synod, ibid., 109.---Pope Gelasius I excuses himself for not having written to Emperor Anastasius, LIX, 41.---Paulinus of Nola excuses himself for having sent Eusebius’s *Chronicle* late, ibid., 161.---Excuses himself for being unable to do something requested of him, ibid., 185.---Excuses himself as insufficiently qualified to treat in letters the passages of sacred Scripture which Delphinus of Bordeaux had requested, ibid., 188.---Excuses Victor for returning late, citing the winter weather and Victor’s adverse health, ibid., 382.---Ennodius excuses himself for delay in replying, ibid., 26.---Justifies himself for having said that he loved silence, ibid., 28.---Defends his reputation, attacked by Florianus, ibid., 29.---Excuses the brevity of his letter because he is oppressed by troubles, ibid., 707.---Excuses himself for not having informed Gregory, bishop of Rome, of his conversion until four years later, ibid., 997.---Excuses himself for not having written when Castorius came to him, ibid., 1009.---Attributes his failure to reply sooner, after two years, to gout, ibid., 1091.---Gregory excuses his late arrival in Sicily as caused not by intention but by bodily illness, ibid., 1113.---Excuses delay in supplying relics which he at last sends, ibid., 1116.

Abbot Godfrey of Vendôme excuses himself for not having come to Pope Paschal, CLVII, 35.---St. Anselm of Canterbury excuses himself concerning the proposed solution of a question, CLVIII, 1145.---Excuses himself for not yet having greeted Pope Paschal by letter, ibid., CLIX, 74.---Hildebert of Le Mans excuses himself for being unable to attend the council summoned at Poitiers, oppressed by excessive hardships inflicted by the consuls of Le Mans, CLXXI, 215.---Excuses himself for being unable to settle the business concerning the marriage of Hugh of Credon, ibid., 264.---Excuses himself for having sent late the history of the miracles of the Church of Exeter, ibid., 284.---Excuses himself before a bishop for delaying, because he was detained by necessity, to send him a small gift, ibid., 286.---Peter Abelard excuses himself for not having written to Heloise for so long a time, saying that this did not arise from neglect of her, CLXXVIII, 187.---St. Bernard of Clairvaux excuses himself for not coming when summoned, CLXXXII, 119.---Elegantly excuses himself for not appearing when summoned to discuss affairs, ibid., 123.---Clears himself of a rash act of which he had been accused, CLXXII, 168.---Excuses himself concerning an admission and asks pardon, ibid., 170.---Clears himself against an unjust accusation, ibid., 202.---Excuses the brevity of his writing on the pretext of the sacred season, to which silence is more fitting, ibid., 220.---Excuses his long absence, more burdensome to himself—indeed, more so—than to his own people, ibid., 298.---Excuses his absence, ibid., 302.---Pleads the cause of the bishop of Salamanca before the pontiff with deep feeling, ibid., 377.---Clears himself against the calumny of Hugh, bishop of Ostia, who indignantly opposed the promotion of Turold to the abbacy of Trois-Fontaines, ibid., 507.---Excuses himself to Riquin, bishop of Toul, for having unknowingly received William, Riquin’s professed monk, ibid., 605.---Excuses the brevity of his letter, ibid., 629.---Excuses himself for being unable to go with a certain friend to the legate, ibid., 630.---Commends to a certain judge the cause of the abbey of Fontenay, ibid., 631.

The Venerable Bede excuses himself for not having come to Bishop Egbert, XCIV, 657.---Apologetic letter, because he was accused by some of holding erroneous views concerning the ages of the world, ibid., 669.---Alcuin excuses his absence to the people of York, ibid., 174.---Excuses himself from undertaking a journey to Rome, ibid., 303.---Summoned to court, excuses himself on account of old age, ibid., 369.---Defends the brethren of Saint Martin and himself against slander arising from accusations in the matter of asylum granted to a cleric of Orléans, and reveals the true cause of the disturbance that arose, ibid., 395.---Adventius of Metz clears himself in the affair of Lothair and accepts the decrees made by Pope Nicholas at the Roman synod, CXXI, 1145.---John of Split excuses himself for replying so late to Alvarus of Córdoba, ibid., 420.---Pope John VIII excuses himself for not having sent Agathus to King Charles, since Lambert had blocked the way, CXXVI, 779.---Excuses the delays of the envoys of Theodosius, through whom he sends him certain gifts, ibid., 829.---Peter Damian shows that he had been falsely accused of certain crimes, CXLIV, 208.---Excuses himself for not yet having complied, being detained by the needs of the monks entrusted to his care, ibid., 289.---Excuses himself for being unable to come to Faenza, weakened exceedingly by the weariness resulting from past illnesses, ibid., 352.---Defends himself against the slander of the chaplains of Duke Godfrey, who charged him with avarice, ibid., 358.---Defends himself against a certain monk John, who had reproached him because he intended to resign his episcopate, ibid., 413.---Excuses himself concerning certain charges made against him, casting the blame upon the envoys, ibid., 547.---Lanfranc of Canterbury excuses his prolonged silence to John, archbishop of the Normans, CL, 523.---Defends St. Hilary against the calumnies of Berengar, ibid., 543.

Excuses himself from accepting the dignity to which he had been elected, CI, 641.---Hugh Metellus excuses himself for sometimes replying rather harshly to the calumnies of his Herbert, CLXXXII, 690.---The count of Vermandois excuses his absence and wishes to know Suger’s good pleasure, CLXXXVI, 1355.---The bishop of Sarab[?] excuses himself for being unable, after crossing into Normandy, to visit him before returning to England, ibid., 1363.---The archbishop of Lyons excuses himself for being unable to attend the conference at Chartres, summoned to aid the Eastern Church, ibid., 1411.---Geoffrey, archbishop of Bordeaux, asks to be excused for being unable, at his summons, to attend the assembly at Chartres, ibid., 1412.---Peter, archbishop of Bourges, asks that he be excused before the king for being unable to come to Suger at Meudon, ibid., 1429.---Baldwin of Noyon excuses himself for not coming when summoned to Suger, ibid., 1235.---Peter the Venerable excuses his absence, CLXXXIX, 65.---Excuses himself for not having written earlier, ibid., 81.---Excuses himself for not immediately informing Adela of the death of her brother Henry I, king of England, ibid., 84.---Excuses himself for not having written to his brother Pons, ibid., 85.---Abbot Wibald excuses himself for being unable to go to Fulda, ibid., 1171.---Excuses himself for not having visited his sister Hadewig for a long time, ibid., 1177.---Excuses himself for being unable to attend the chapter at Liège, ibid., 1187.---Henry, king of the Romans, excuses the archbishop of Mainz for not attending the council at Reims, ibid., 1192.---Abbot Wibald excuses himself for not going to Fulda; meanwhile, he gives the people of Fulda salutary advice concerning the future election of an abbot, ibid., 1194.---Excuses himself for being unable to attend the assembly of the abbots of Saxony, ibid., 1259.---Emperor Conrad excuses himself for being unable, detained by illness, to keep his promises, ibid., 1284.---Excuses himself for being unable, stricken by fever, to fulfil the promises of the emperor of Constantinople, ibid., 1284.---Abbot Wibald excuses himself for not having returned sooner to the monks of Stavelot, ibid., 1331.---Excuses himself from undertaking, at his own expense, an embassy to Rome, ibid., 1336.---The chancellor excuses himself from undertaking an embassy to Rome, ibid., [Col. 0184] 1339.---Henry of Minden vindicates Godebold’s innocence, ibid., 1343.---Abbot Wibald excuses himself for being unable to return so soon to the people of Corbie, ibid., 1373.---Excuses himself from attending the conference at Huy, ibid., 1374.---Excuses himself from emancipating his prior, ibid., 1420.---R., abbot of Saint-Evroult, excuses himself for not coming to Ervisius, abbot of Saint Victor, CXCVI, 1386.---Excuses himself for having visited her neither in person nor by writing, ibid., CXCVII, 344.---Arnulf of Lisieux excuses himself for not yet having come to Pope Celestine, CCI, 19.---Henry, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, excuses himself for not yet having paid honour to Cardinal Hyacinth, CCIV, 227.---Excuses himself for being unable to be present on the appointed day to settle the affair of Vallis Lucentis, ibid., 229.---Peter of Blois clears himself as to why he did not return, at the appointed time, a book which he had promised to restore, CCVII, 116.---Defends the reputation of a certain new archbishop accused of excessive leniency, ibid., 308.---Excuses himself for the length of his preceding letter, ibid., 326.---States that illness prevents him from returning to court, ibid., 332.---Clears himself of the slander of certain persons, ibid., 384.---The bishop of Laon is cleared of charges laid against him, ibid., 460.---Excuse and complaints of the same Peter of Blois concerning the lying and falsification of writings, ibid., 491.---Stephen of Tournai excuses himself from preaching because of illness, CCXI, 342.---Excuses himself for being unable to visit him, ibid., 348.---Excuses himself for being unable to come to him because of various occupations in administering justice, ibid., 351.---Excuses himself for not having handed over money entrusted to him, ibid., 444.---Clears himself from the stain of simony, a crime of which detractors had rashly accused him before the recipient, ibid., 453.---Excuses the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés from the killing of a certain scholar, ibid., 471.---Excuses himself for being unable, because of business, to attend the solemnity of a dedication, ibid., 490.---Excuses himself from the consecration of the bishop-elect of Châlons, ibid., 532.---Adam, abbot of Perseigne, excuses himself for being unable to satisfy a request, CCXI, 626.---Excuses himself from writing against the Jews, ibid., 653.

VIII.—Letters for Giving Thanks.

Nemesianus, Dativus, Felix, and Victor give thanks to Cyprian both for the consolation of his letter and for the assistance sent with it, IV, 422.---The council gives thanks to the Gallic bishops and writes to them concerning the condemnation of Palladius, St. Ambrose, XVI, 939.---Gives thanks to the emperors for the convocation of the synod, ibid., 940.---Thanks are given to the emperors for the restoration of tranquillity to the Church, ibid., 947, 953.---Thanks are given to Theodosius for restoring the orthodox to their basilicas, ibid., 950.---Gives thanks to Siricius for sending him letters through the priest Synus, ibid., 1282.---Symmachus gives thanks to Emperor Valentinian and Theodosius for the prefecture bestowed upon him, XVIII, 362, 363.---St. Jerome gives thanks to Castrucius of Pannonia, who had resolved to sail in order to visit him, XXII, 651.---St. Augustine returns thanks to Antoninus for the good esteem and affection shown him, XXXII, 86.---For a second letter received from Paulinus, he offers the service of a grateful heart, ibid., 121.---Paulinus gives Augustine thanks for a book or letter received from him, ibid., 347.---Gives thanks to Paulina for having been concerned for his welfare, ibid., 507.---St. Leo the Great gives thanks for the suppression of disturbances in Palestine and for the restoration of Juvenal of Jerusalem to his see, LIV, 1069.---Gives thanks for the removal of Carosus and Dorotheus from his monasteries, ibid., 1110.---Having complained of silence, he entrusts to him the care of the Church, ibid., 1116.---Pope Simplicius gives thanks for Timothy’s restoration to the Church of Alexandria, LVIII, 48.---Ruricius gives thanks to Namatius and Ceraunia because their lodging had been honoured by the presence and prayers of Postuminus, ibid., 81.---The bishops of Dardania give thanks because Pope Gelasius I warned them against whom they should be on guard, LIX, 21.---Paulinus of Nola gives thanks concerning the affair of Basil the priest, which had been explained, LXI, 223.---Gives thanks for the benefit bestowed upon Basil the priest, whom he had commended, ibid., 225.---Gives Augustine thanks for a book or letter received from Augustine, ibid., 391.---Ennodius gives thanks to God for health recovered, LXIII, 31.---Pope Agapetus I gives thanks to Justinian for congratulating him on his election to the pontificate, LXVI, 38.---Gives thanks for congratulating him by letter on his election to the pontificate, ibid., 45.---Gudelina gives thanks for his envoy and letters, LXIX, 811.---Gives thanks because Labarda, duke of Sardinia, intends to make peace with the Barbaricini on the condition that they serve Christ, ibid., 693.---Returns thanks for money sent to the poor, ibid., 705.---Gives thanks to the emperors for thirty pounds of gold sent as alms, ibid., 755.---Gives thanks for spoons and rings, ibid., 840.---Gives thanks for gifts of hospitality, ibid., 847.---Gives thanks for alms sent to Rome, ibid., 863.---Gives thanks for presents, ibid., 937.---Gives thanks for peace concluded, ibid., 975.---Returns thanks because he devoted himself more zealously to making peace, ibid., 976.---Gives thanks for the protection of the patrimony of the Roman Church, ibid., 1094.---Returns thanks to the king for peace made, ibid., 1314.---Pope Stephen II gives thanks for promises made through Abbot Droctegangus, LXXXIX, 993; XCVIII, 100.---Gives thanks for the city’s liberation and for the benefit bestowed upon the Roman Church, LXXXIX, 1007; XCVIII, 127.---Pope St. Paul I gives thanks for the safety of Pippin, king of the Franks, who wished to obtain assistance against the Lombards, LXXXIX, 1137; XCVIII, 1137.

Pope Paul I offers abundant thanks to King Pippin for the monastery which he granted him, situated near Mount Serapte, LXXXIX, 1140; XCVIII, 221.---Thanksgivings of praise for the rejoicing and liberation of the holy Church of God, the same author, LXXXIX, 1143, 1153, 1160, 1166, 1170, 1174; XCVIII, 159, 172, 174, 182, 184, 186, 189, 194, 288, 291, 297, 304, 328, 352.---Letter of Pope Paul, containing thanksgivings concerning how his envoys, together with the imperial envoys, were honorably received, ibid., 1148; XCVIII, 205.---Another letter of the same pope, containing thanksgivings for the life and safety of King Pippin, LXXXIX, 1155, 1164, 1172; XCVIII, 156, 175, 201.---He gives thanks for the *sabanus* sent to him, in which Pippin’s daughter had been received after being washed in the sacred waters, the same author, LXXXIX, 1183.---He gives thanks for faithful service rendered to the Roman Church, ibid., 1188.---He gives thanks and asks that Queen Bertrada reward Itherius’s fidelity, ibid., 1218.---Letter of Pope Adrian containing thanksgivings for the cross which had been sent to him, XCVIII, 396.---Alcuin gives thanks for a gift, C, 212.---He gives thanks for benefits received, ibid., 300, 303, 348, 372, 455.---He gives thanks for the booklet against Felix which he had read and sent back, ibid., 313.---He gives thanks for a cross presented, ibid., 362.---He gives thanks for a cloak and other gifts, ibid., 363, 406.---He gives thanks for gifts of charity, ibid., 445.---He returns thanks for medicinal herbs, ibid., 494.---Pope St. Leo III gives thanks for gifts sent by Riculf, bishop of Mainz, CII, 1030.---Einhard gives thanks to Lupus of Ferrières because he had deigned to console him by letter on the death of his wife, CXIX, 440.---He gives thanks to Einhard, who had sent him a booklet on the cross to be adored, ibid., 445.---Pope Nicholas I gives thanks for gifts sent by Queen Ermentrude, CXIX, 880.---Pope Adrian II gives thanks for Ignatius’s restoration to the patriarchal see, CXXII, 1276.---He gives thanks to Emperor Basil for his devotion toward the Apostolic See, ibid., 1285.---He gives thanks because, through the efforts of Count Boso, the envoys reached the emperor and completed the matters entrusted to them, ibid., 679.---Pope John VIII gives thanks because he obeyed the admonitions of the Apostolic See, CXXVI, 701.---He gives thanks for Count Suppo’s fidelity toward the Roman Church, ibid., 784.---He gives thanks for King Charles’s observance toward the Roman Church, ibid., 785.---He gives thanks to God because Michael, king of the Bulgarians, sent envoys to him, ibid., 843.---He gives thanks for King Louis’s favorable disposition toward the Roman Church, ibid., 852.---He gives thanks because, when Conspertus had been ordained bishop of the Church of Vercelli by him, King Charles willingly acquiesced in his ordination, ibid., 894.---He gives thanks for the affection of Kings Louis and Carloman toward the Roman Church, ibid., 895.---He gives thanks for King Charles’s observance toward the Apostolic See, ibid., 911.---Gozpert, abbot of Tegernsee, gives fullest thanks for the skillfully made windows provided for the church of Tegernsee, CXXXIX, 566.---He gives thanks to Count Meginhelm for *busones*, a kind of fish, ibid., 367.---St. Peter Damian silently gives thanks to Archbishop Wido because, while staying with him, he had generously bestowed sacred vestments upon him, CXLIV, 295.---He gives thanks to Bishop B. for alms bestowed upon himself and his monastery, ibid., 298.---He gives thanks to the bishop of Sarsina because he had gladly taken in a young man of outstanding promise, but rendered extremely poor by misfortune, and did not cease to assist him with every service of generosity, ibid., 324.---Pope St. Gregory VII gives thanks because they treated the envoys of the Apostolic See kindly, CXLVIII, 299.---He gives thanks because Empress Agnes has concern for the Church’s concord, ibid., 357.

Pope Gregory VII gives thanks for the observance of Dominic, patriarch of Grado, toward the Roman Church, CXLVIII, 444.---He gives thanks for gifts sent and for Christian captives released, ibid., 450.---St. Anselm of Canterbury gives thanks to Gundulf for benefits conferred by him upon the monks of Bec, [Col. 0186] CLVIII, 1071.---He gives thanks for gifts, ibid., 1076.---He expresses gratitude for the careful treatment of the monk Maurice, ibid., 1104.---He returns thanks for the care of Maurice of Bec and counsels flight from the world, ibid., 1108.---He gives thanks for gold, though he praises the giver’s disposition more than the gift, ibid., 1119.---He gives thanks, in his own name and in those of Hugh and Basilia, for gifts sent by Gundulf, ibid., 1131.---He gives thanks for Lanfranc’s almsgiving to the monks of Bec, ibid., 1147.---Thanks are returned to Lanfranc for his generosity, especially for the gold he had sent to make a chalice, ibid., 1149.---He gives thanks for benefits, ibid., 1152.---He gives Ida abundant thanks for benefits conferred upon himself and others on his account, ibid., 1174.---He gives thanks for generosity shown to his envoys, ibid., 92.---Emperor Henry thanks Hugh for health restored through his prayers, CLIX, 931.---Hildebert of Le Mans thanks St. Anselm for the treatise on the Holy Spirit which he had undertaken, CLXXI, 220.---He gives thanks to a bishop who was his friend for services most humanely and voluntarily rendered to certain members of his household, who had been storm-tossed on a journey, ibid., 500.---St. Bernard of Clairvaux gives thanks for tolls remitted hitherto, CLXXXII, 264.---He gives thanks for benefits offered, ibid., 265.---He gives thanks for letters sent to him, ibid., 517.---He gives thanks for beneficence hitherto shown to his people, promising an abundant recompense from God, ibid., 587.---He gives thanks to God for affairs successfully accomplished, ibid., 632.

Abbot Suger gives thanks for consolation afforded him while he was at the point of death, CLXXXII, 675.---The abbot of St. Pantaleon gives thanks to Suger for humanity shown toward a certain boy, his nephew, CLXXXVI, 1401.---He gives thanks to Roger, king of Sicily, because he had not disdained to communicate news of his prosperity, ibid., 1417.---Geoffrey, count of Anjou, gives thanks because he is working for the restoration of peace between the king and himself, ibid., 1427.---Stephen, king of England, gives thanks for friendship and benefits shown him at the court of the king of France, ibid., 1434.---Abbot Suger gives thanks for consolation afforded him while he was at the point of death, ibid., 1440.---The monks of Corbie give thanks because the monks of Stavelot did not begrudge them Wibald as abbot, CLXXXIX, 1134, 1159.---Henry, king of the Romans, gives thanks to Wibald for service rendered to himself and his father, ibid., 1186.---Arnold of Cologne gives thanks for Thiebald’s obtaining the provostship of Xanten, ibid., 1278.---An Anonymous writer expresses gratitude for things received from Wibald, ibid., 1299.---Wibald, abbot, gives thanks because H., archbishop of Reims, visited his monastery, ibid., 1324.---He gives thanks for benefits conferred, ibid., 1362.---He gives thanks for benefits and asks him to continue protecting him, ibid., 1380.---He gives thanks for benefits shown to his people, ibid., 1399.---He gives thanks because he had charitably received the dispossessed Abbot Sifrid, ibid., 1410.---Walter, abbot, gives thanks because, at the synod of Liège, Abbot Wibald undertook his defense, ibid., 1416.---N., abbot of Eberbach, gives thanks to God for gifts bestowed upon Hildegard, CXCVII, 295.---Geoffrey, subprior of St. Barbara, gives thanks for friendship, CCV, 880.---Peter of Blois gives thanks both to Abbot R., because he had pitied him when grievously afflicted by illness, and especially to God, because He had mercifully chastised him, CCVII, 105.---He gives thanks to the bishop of Arras for a gift sent, ibid., 186.---He gives thanks to his friend E., because almost alone he had shown himself a friend and like a brother, ibid., 457.---Stephen of Tournai gives thanks for benefits conferred upon a certain canon, CCXI, 349.---He returns thanks for an elegant horse sent to him from Denmark, ibid., 415.---The clerics of Grandmont return thanks for benefits conferred upon them, ibid., 419.---He returns thanks for gold and gems bestowed to adorn the tomb or shrine of St. Geneviève, ibid., 450.---He gives thanks for letters written to the chapter of Tournai, ibid., 479.---The abbot and convent of La Sauve-Majeure give thanks to the bishop of Tournai for the Office of St. Gerald, which he had composed at their request, ibid., 536.---Adam, abbot of Perseigne, gives thanks for charity bestowed upon two women during a time of famine, ibid., 600.

IX.—Symbolic Letters.

Hilary to Abra, his daughter, concerning a garment and a precious pearl, whose value and symbolic meaning he explains to her, Hilary, X, 549.---St. Ambrose teaches that Satan is represented by the deceit and lustfulness of the partridge, XVI, 1068.---He applies a mystical interpretation to certain small gifts sent him by Eustochium on the feast day of St. Peter, for the instruction of morals, St. Jerome, XXII, 445.---He playfully interprets allegorically small gifts sent by Marcella to himself, Paula, and Paula’s daughter Eustochium, ibid., 480.---He clears himself of the slanders of detractors, namely that he had drawn Paula and Eustochium, women of the first rank, into the monastic way of life, XXII, 481.---He explains to Fabiola, who had gone to Bethlehem, the mystery contained in the vestments of the priests and Levites, etc., ibid., 608.---He interprets allegorically the dispute of the two harlots as the Church gathered from the Gentiles and the synagogue of the Jews, ibid., 682.---He teaches that the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt and the history of their long journey are to be understood spiritually, ibid., 698.---He teaches that the land of promise is not that which the Jews possessed, but another, heavenly land—namely, the land of the living promised in the Gospel to the meek, ibid., 1097.---Paulinus of Nola sends bread and a little boxwood dish, a reciprocal token of friendship, LXI, 167.---An entirely allegorical letter, in which Theodulf is compared with the Father of the vineyards, ibid., 394.---An enigmatic letter, ibid., 466.---St. Peter Damian interprets the hidden mysteries of the creation of the whole world, and especially the Sabbath, the day on which the Creator of all things rested from every work, CXLIV, 260.---He mystically interprets several passages of Holy Scripture from the Books of Kings, ibid., 282.---He discusses the eight feasts of the Old Testament and, by allegorical interpretation, transfers and adapts them to the rule of evangelical faith, ibid., 331.---He shows what is spiritually signified by the figure of the cross, ibid., 404.---Ivo of Chartres gives a symbolic interpretation to a snow-white instrument for arranging hair, sent to him by Gerard, CLXII, 16.---Hildegard speaks mystically and somewhat obscurely, CXCVII, 164.---Under certain figures she exhorts an abbot to act well, ibid., 297.---Under figures she exhorts H., abbess of Althena, to fight for God, ibid., 321.---Under a parable she teaches that one must labor in this world, ibid., 358.---Under a certain parable she exhorts the monk M. to charity, flight from the world, and love of true wisdom, ibid., 363.---Peter of Blois urges Walter, bishop of Rochester, to imitate the spiritual hunting practiced by the apostles, ibid., 169.

[Col. 0187]

CCV. ALPHABETICAL INDEX OF ALL THOSE TO WHOM LETTERS ARE ADDRESSED.

[Col. 0187] To A., bishop of Laon, Fulbert of Chartres, CXLI, 221. To A., bishop of Tours, ibid., 276. To A., prior of the church of St. Frigdianus, Pope Gelasius II, CLXIII, 487. To A., Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, Stephen of Tournai, CCXI, 417. To A., vice-dominus of Fermo, Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 823. To A., queen of Jerusalem, ibid., 417. To A., bishop of Poitiers, ibid., 128. To A., king of Hungary, the same author, CCXV, 702, 1132. To A., archdeacon of Paris, ibid., 1178. To the abbot and canons of St. Peter of the Mount, Abbot Bernard, CLXXXII, 189. To the abbot of St. Albinus, ibid., 372. To the abbot of St. Benedict, ibid., 670. To the abbot of St. John of Chartres, ibid., 202. To the abbot of St. Nicasius at Reims, ibid., 136. To the abbot of Windberg, Gerhoh of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 521. To the abbot of Arremar, Nicholas of Clairvaux, CXCVI, 1636. To the abbot of Celle, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 60, 62, 67, 69. To the abbot of St. Ouen, Pope Alexander III, CC, 1119, 1277.

[Col. 0188] To the abbot and convent of St. Bertin, ibid., 1207; Pope Innocent III, CCXVI, 40; CCXVII, 94, 167, 264. To the abbot of Clairmarais, the same author, CC, 508. To the abbot of St. Denis, ibid., 1196, 1258; Pope Urban III, CCII, 1491; Pope Celestine III, CCVI, 942; Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, 158; CCXVII, 102, 226, 254, 260, 261. ## SERIES TWENTY-FOUR

[Col. 0429]

### [PREFACE]

The Catholic Fathers and Doctors applied themselves steadily and in every way to matters capable of forming the morals of peoples and refining them through the more humane disciplines; and accordingly they always fostered the sciences, letters, and arts, in which most of them themselves became illustrious. Therefore, in this twenty-fourth and final series, we collect every one of the indexes relating to the sciences, letters, and arts, arranged in a logical order and offered to the reader.

[Col. 0429]

## CCVIII. INDEX OF INVENTIONS MENTIONED IN PATROLOGY, MAKING KNOWN THEIR AUTHORS, DATES, AND THE WRITERS WHO RECORDED THEM

(Year 160.) Tertullian.—Divination: those who divine by the tricks of demons (*tables tournantes*, “turning tables”), I, 411.—The fallen angels disclosed the working of metals, made known the properties of herbs, publicized the powers of incantations, and set forth every sort of occult inquiry, even to the interpretation of the stars, ibid., 459 and 1306.—Aesculapius, discoverer of medicines, ibid., 413; II, 87, 88.—He was the first to investigate remedies, ibid., 87.—Anatomy was known to the ancients, ibid., 662, 692.—The Seres were believed to spin trees, ibid., 1305.—The Tyrians dyed wool, ibid.—The Phrygians sewed garments, ibid.—The Babylonians wove them, ibid.—Arachne’s workshop, II, 1309.—The battering ram, a military engine, was invented by the Carthaginians, ibid., 1032.—Archimedes’ hydraulic organ, ibid., 669.—Images were invented by the Etruscans, ibid., 430.—They were made from earthly and cheap material, and from vessels intended for ordinary and most lowly use, I, 399.—Formerly the Romans had no images of gods, ibid., 430, 608.—That is, before Numa Pompilius, ibid.—Before they were fashioned in the likeness of human beings, how ridiculous they were, ibid., 339, 366 ff., 578.

(Year 300.) Minucius Felix.—Saturn taught men to imprint letters and to stamp coins, III, 308, 309.

[Col. 0442] (Year 300.) Arnobius, rhetorician of Carthage.—Aesculapius, discoverer of medicinal preparations, V, 770.

(Year 317.) Lactantius.—Aesculapius invented medicine, VI, 213.—Vulcan invented metalworking, ibid.—Minerva discovered the arts, ibid., 213, 214.—Venus instituted prostitution, so that women might make a profit by publicly selling their bodies, ibid., 207.—Ceres and Liber transmitted grain and wine, ibid., 213.—Stercutus was the first to introduce the method of manuring fields, ibid., 227.—Numa Pompilius established among the Romans the worship of the gods, ibid., 242.—Noah planted a vine with his own hand, ibid., 327.—The Egyptians were the first to possess the knowledge of the stars, ibid., 328.—Astrology, divination from entrails, and similar arts are inventions of demons, ibid., 336.—Lactantius mockingly dismisses as fables the antipodes and the principle that weights tend toward the centre, which ancient philosophers held as certain; but Christopher Columbus and Isaac Newton have now remarkably confirmed the testimony of those ancient philosophers, ibid., 427.

(Year 430.) St Augustine.—*On Music*, XXXII, 1081.

(Year 482.) Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of the Arverni.—Coloured windows, LVIII, 487.

[Col. 0443] (Year 525.) Boethius, consul.—*On Music*, LXIII, 1167.

(Year 560.) Cassiodorus.—*On Music*, LXX, 1208.

(Year 636.) St Isidore of Seville.—*On Music*, LXXXII, 163.—Jubal invented music, ibid.—Pythagoras discovered the science of numbers, ibid.—The Greeks say that the same Pythagoras discovered the first principles of music, ibid.—The Egyptians discovered geometry, ibid., 161.—The Egyptians invented astronomy, ibid., 167.—Apollo was the discoverer of medicine, ibid., 183.—His son Aesculapius enlarged it, ibid.—After Aesculapius was killed by a stroke of lightning, the art of healing perished with its author, ibid.—Hippocrates of Cos restored it to light, ibid.—A certain Chiron invented the medicine of beasts of burden, ibid., 194.—Moses first gave laws to the Hebrew people, ibid., 197.—Phoroneus gave laws to the Greeks, ibid.—Mercurius Trismegistus was legislator of the Egyptians, ibid.—Solon gave laws to the Athenians, ibid.—Lycurgus established laws for the Lacedaemonians, ibid.—Numa Pompilius established Roman institutions, ibid.—Ninus, king of the Assyrians, was the first to bring in wars, ibid., 639.—Tyrian pirates were the first to invent the trumpet, ibid., 645.—The Cretans invented arrows, ibid., 647.—The Lydians, immigrants from Asia into Etruria, instituted spectacles, ibid., 651.—According to the Greeks, Circe instituted the circus, ibid., 654.—Mespres, king of Egypt, is said to have been the first to make an obelisk, ibid.—Erichthonius is said to have first yoked four horses together, ibid., 655.—The Egyptians first devised painting by tracing the outline of a man’s shadow, ibid., 676.—Minerva showed the use of wool-working, and likewise of the olive, ibid., 683.—Embroidered clothing was invented by the Phrygians, ibid., 687.—Prometheus is said to have been the first to set an iron circle containing a stone around a finger, ibid., 701.—Daedalus first made a table and a chair, ibid., 705.—Apicius was the first to compound culinary seasonings, ibid., 706.—Pottery was invented on the island of Samos, ibid., 714.—Perdix, a youth and pupil of Daedalus, invented the saw and compasses, ibid., 682.—Daedalus first made a table and a chair, ibid., 705, 706.

(Year 730.) Venerable Bede.—Square or measured music, XC, 919.—Theoretical music, ibid., 909.

(Year 856.) Blessed Rabanus Maurus.—Minerva invented the use of wool-working, CXI, 568.—Daedalus first made a table and a chair, ibid., 587.—Pottery was invented on the island of Samos, ibid., 597.—*On Music*, ibid., 495.

(Year 908.) Remigius of Auxerre.—*On Music*, CXXXI, 931.

(Year 911.) Notker Balbulus.—Ibid., 1171.

(Year 930.) Hucbald, monk of Saint-Amand.—*On Harmonic Instruction*, CXXXII, 905 and 957.—*Scholia Enchiriadis*, ibid., 981.

[Col. 0444] (Year 942.) St Ado, abbot of Cluny.—*On Music*, ibid., CXXXIII, 773.—Rules of *rhythmomachia*, ibid., 795.—Rules concerning the abacus, ibid., 807.—On the *organistrum*, ibid., 815.

(Year 1001.) Pope Sylvester II.—*Short Treatise on the Division of Numbers*, CXXXIX, 85.—*On Geometry*, ibid., col. 91.—Letter to Adelbold, ibid., 129.—*On the Construction of the Sphere*, ibid., 155.—*Short Treatise on the Rational and on the Use of Reason*, ibid., 157.

(Year 1017.) Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht.—*On the Method of Finding the Thickness of a Sphere*, CXL, 1103, 1104.—*On Music*, ibid., 1109, 1110.

(Year 1304.) Guido of Arezzo, abbot of Santa Croce at Avellana.—*Micrologus*, CXLI, 379.—Verses on music, ibid., 405.—Rules for unknown chant, ibid., 413.—Letter on unknown chant, ibid., 423.—On errors widespread in many places in Gregorian chant, ibid., 431.—How music proceeds from arithmetic, ibid., 435.

(Year 1048.) Odorannus, monk of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens.—Letter to Robert on music, CXLII, 807.—Letter to Walcher and Robert, ibid., 809.

(Year 1048.) Berno, abbot of Reichenau.—Prologue to the *Tonary*, ibid., 1097.—Berno’s *Tonary*, ibid., 1115.—On the various modulation of psalms and canticles, ibid., 1131.—On the harmonious variety of tones, ibid., 1155.

(Year 1054.) Hermannus Contractus.—Hermann’s *Music*, CXLIII, 413.—On the measurement of the astrolabe, ibid., 379.—On the uses of the astrolabe, ibid., 389.

(Year 1065.) Franco, scholar of Liège.—A specimen of his work on the squaring of the circle, ibid., 1373, 1374.

(Year 1090.) Aribo Scholasticus.—*On Music*, CL, 1307.

(Same year.) William, abbot of Hirsau.—*On Music*, ibid., 1147.

(Year 1093.) John Cotto.—*On Music*, ibid., 1391.

(Date uncertain.) Bernelinus, musician.—A ready and true division of the monochord in the diatonic mode, CLI, 653.

(Date uncertain.) *On Music*, Anonymous I, ibid., 674.—Anonymous II, ibid., 682.—Anonymous III, ibid., 685.

(Date uncertain.) Anonymous IV.—Boethius’ measurement of the monochord, ibid., 687.

(Date uncertain.) Otker, monk of Regensburg.—Measurement of the four-part figure, ibid., 691.—The monochord of *Enchiriadis*, ibid., 693.

(Year 1119.) Theoger, bishop of Metz.—*On Music*, CLXIII, 777, 778.
