## CCIX. INDEX OF OCCULT SCIENCES, ALPHABETICALLY ARRANGED BY SUBJECT, REPORTING WHATEVER THE FATHERS WROTE CONCERNING SCIENCES PROHIBITED BY THE CATHOLIC RELIGION

### FIRST SECTION. Magic, ventriloquism, engastrimism, theurgy, *bascania*, *utesetura*, vampirism

The great power of demons, however great it may be, is subject to the greater power of Christ, Tertullian, I, 410.—Magicians, aided by the power of demons, have customarily divined through goats and tables, ibid., 411.—Those whom demons could not bring by force to worship the gods, they strove to suborn by tricks and evil arts, ibid., 874.—How demons attempted to steal away divination, ibid., 877.—Turning tables through which magicians divine, and likewise through goats, ibid., 879.—Vampirism in some fashion: a kind of appearance of the dead accompanied by a bloody bite, which had currency in the eighteenth century; magical tricks by which the souls of the dead are maligned, ibid.—Tertullian demonstrates most plainly that the oracles and other things which pagans claimed were accomplished by their gods beyond human powers were performed by the demons themselves, ibid., 882.—Those whom Tertullian calls “those who breathe upon altars” (*aris inhalantes*) are undoubtedly the *arioli* of whom Donatus speaks in his observations on Terence, etc., ibid., 854.—By magical art Aesculapius, under the name Asclepion, promises remedies for every disease, ibid., 886.—Tertullian speaks of those who vainly attempted by magical art to cure persons possessed by a demon, ibid., 887.—The demons themselves could not, even before the very pagans who heard them, refute, conceal, erase, or deny the mark of their own disgrace and condemnation, ibid.—On the impious and fraudulent arts of demons and deceitful spirits (Augustine, from Porphyry’s letter to Anebo, *City of God*, book X, chapter II, p. 247 ff.), ibid., 888.—He shows how perversely the pagans set up Simon Magus as a holy god by a statue, as they did their other gods, ibid., 1435.—Simon Magus, heretic, same author, II, 61.—Souls do not return here from the underworld at the command of demons by magic (of which Tertullian lists several kinds), nor by their own choice, ibid., 748.—Refutation of Marcion, who taught that human beings can follow vain idols, invent a multitude of gods, see omens, lots, and the false names of the stars by inspection of entrails, await future events, and marvel at magical art, ibid., 1055.—Magic is nothing but deception, ibid., 749.—Magic, a second idolatry, is a many-formed plague of the human mind, the artificer of every error, and the destroyer of salvation and of the soul, ibid., 648.—Magic is twofold, same author, I, 672.—Astrology is a species of magic, ibid., 673.—Egyptian magic, rivaling Moses, prolonged God’s patience until the Gospel, ibid., 672.—Magicians knew that demons existed, ibid., 405.—They violently strike children in order to produce oracular utterance, ibid., 411.—They produce phantasms, ibid., 410.—They send dreams, ibid., 411.—They defame the souls of the dead, ibid.—They appear to do certain things beyond the order of nature by the tricks of demons, ibid., 407–412.—Their consultations were invented by the fallen angels, ibid., 459.—Magicians consulted concerning the emperor’s life, ibid.—Persian magicians, same author, II, 260.—The East commonly had magicians as kings, ibid., 339, 619.—Magicians and astrologers were the first to announce and offer gifts to the newborn Christ, same author, I, 672.

Demons invented the tricks of magical art in order to deceive the eyes, Lactantius, VI, 1036.—Magical art was invented by demons, ibid., 336.—The magical arts of Maxentius, same author, VIII, 25.—The magical arts of Licinius, ibid., 39.—Magicians were princes, St Hilary, X, 124.—Those devoted to magical art, ibid.—Professions far removed from the divine science of knowledge, ibid., 672.

The magicians traced their descent from Balaam and were devoted to magical arts, St Ambrose, XV, 1550.

Magic was formerly astrology, C. V. Aquilinus Juvencus, XIX, 95.

The deeds of magicians, Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 763.

Saint Augustine’s utter abhorrence of magic, *Life of the Same*, book I, XXXII, 82.---Against those who imagine that Christ converted peoples to himself by magical art, id., XXXV, 1050.---Why Pharaoh’s magicians performed certain miracles like Moses, the servant of God, id., XL, 90.---He shows that the demons themselves—being subject to vices, and bringing in and wholly favoring and delighting in the things which upright and prudent men shun and condemn, namely the sacrilegious fictions of poets, theatrical spectacles, and the harmful practices and crimes of magical arts—cannot by any means reconcile men to good gods, id., XLI, 223–224.---How the deceit of demons, while promising through its own mediation a way to God, strives to turn men away from the way of truth, ibid., 272.---On unlawful arts connected with the worship of demons, in which Porphyry the Platonist occupies himself, approving some things and, as it were, disapproving others, ibid., 286.---On theurgy, which promises a false purification of souls through the invocation of demons, ibid., 288.---What is to be believed about transformations which, through the art of demons, seem to happen to human beings, ibid., 574.---Great miracles through magical arts, ibid.; id., XLII, 875.---God alone also creates those things which are transformed by magical arts, ibid.

Ham, author of magical art, Cassian, XLIX, 755 ff.---Ham, author and promulgator of magic, ibid.---Magicians and sorcerers sacrificed to demons, ibid., 751 ff.---What they can do in relation to demons, ibid., 991.

The devil’s cunning and arts, St. Leo the Great, LIV, 218, 269, 296, 299, 331, 383, 438, 445.---Instruments of the devil, ibid., 258.---He uses men to deceive others, ibid., 218.---By superstitions the devil subjects to himself the greater part of humankind, ibid., 160.---The devil has as many forms as there are images of falsehood, ibid., 370.---Clerics who are magicians or enchanters are to be expelled from the Church, id., LVI, 718.---Canonical punishment for sorcery, ibid., 442.

“By magical murmuring to summon up thin apparitions and to charm sepulchral ashes, and likewise to rob others of life: harmful art knows this,” Aurelius Prudentius, LX, 126.---Magic, id., LIX, 703 ff., 1205.---The second syllable lengthened, ibid., 177–180.---Magic imputed to Christians, ibid., 1137.---*Magicus* frequently altered into *Magnus*, ibid., 770.

Magic, Dracontius, LX, 247 ff.---*Magus*, with the first syllable lengthened, 317.

The facility of demons in performing deceptions, Abbot Eugyppius, LXII, 869.---The shrewdness of demons in deceiving, ibid., 865.---In what Pharaoh’s magicians were inferior to Moses, ibid., 863.---When magicians can accomplish something through magical art, ibid.---The rods of the Egyptian magicians, ibid., 998 ff.---Magic is not to be investigated at all, ibid., 865.---The Egyptian magicians acknowledged both magical deceit and the power of God, ibid., 865.---Magical deceptions, ibid., 867 ff.---Magical art is superstition, ibid., 947, 948.---Why magical observances have efficacy with some persons, ibid., 949.---Whether Simon Magus was truly baptized, ibid., 872.---What kind of miracles magicians perform, ibid., 1064.---The pest of magical observances, ibid., 949.---On miracles performed by magical arts, ibid., 585.---On the ease with which unclean spirits deceive human beings by tricks, ibid., 591.---On false and deceptive purifications, ibid., 592.---On the serpent’s speech to Eve, and the incantations of the Marsi, ibid., 607.---How Aaron’s rod swallowed the rods of the magicians, ibid., 717.---How enchanters could turn water into blood when it had already certainly been done, ibid., 718.---On Pharaoh’s magicians, ibid., 1064.

The Apostle calls Pharaoh’s magicians Jannes and Mambres, St. Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, LXV, 597.

The magicians of Persia: their priestly office and identity, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 944.---Punishment is inflicted upon persons accused of magical arts, ibid., 624.---In Christian times one may not practice magical arts, ibid., 623.---King Theodoric relates that he had learned that Basilius and Praetextatus had been accused of magical arts; he decreed that, taking five senators with him and also summoning Count Arigern, they should examine the case with due legal procedure, and, should they find them guilty, punish them by the severity of the laws, ibid., 624.---King Theodoric orders Count Arigern to seek Basilius and Praetextatus, accused of magical art and escaped by flight, and, once found, bring them before the court of five, so that he may ensure the case is examined and concluded, ibid., 625.---What magical practices were discovered after Julian’s death, ibid., 1062.

Magical art, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 164.---The demon’s tricks exposed, ibid., 1053.---Female sorcerers punished at Paris, ibid., 402.---Sorceries uncovered, ibid., 485.

The devil’s various arts for overthrowing men, *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIII, 841 ff.---The devil’s trick of illuminating a cell, ibid., 895.---The devil’s various arts for drawing a monk out of his cell, ibid., 897.---The steadfastness of believers makes a mockery of the devil, ibid., 230.---The devil’s devices and deceptions, ibid., 137.---How sorceries are to be cured, ibid., 177–199.---A servant of Proterius consults a sorcerer, ibid., 302.---A sorcerer’s letter to the devil, ibid.---Sorcery removed from spouses, ibid., LXXIV, 54.---The cross dispels the devil’s tricks, ibid., LXXIII, 328 ff.---The devil’s trick of illuminating a cell, ibid., 842.---The demon’s horrible tricks, ibid.---Prayer defeats the demon’s tricks, ibid., LXXIV, 89.

Magicians attacking Gregory’s horse with their sorceries are struck with blindness and delivered over to demons, *Life of St. Gregory the Great*, by Paul the Deacon, LXXV, 56–104.---A demon deceives through dreams, ibid., 827.---On the arts and snares of Satan, id., LXXVI, 477.---The demon’s various arts exposed, ibid., 667.---On diviners by lots, id., LXXVII, 1450.---*Canterma*, a type of sorcery, ibid., 757–758.---What phylacteries are forbidden by councils, ibid., 1316.---Gregory congratulates Paul the schoolman on his zeal against sorcerers, ibid., 1203.---He urges the pursuit of enchanters and sacrilegious persons, ibid., 1771.---Theodore the Jewish sorcerer, ibid., 902.---He orders that the cleric Paul, if caught practicing sorcery, be assigned to penance, ibid., 697.---He orders care to be taken that Theodore the sorcerer not oppose Paula, ibid., 902.---Phylacteries, that is, amulets and bindings worn on the arms, legs, and neck, ibid., 461.

On magicians, St. Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 310.

Peter’s contest with Simon Magus, Mozarabic Liturgy, LXXXV, 578.

Notice concerning harmful herbs, Marculf, LXXXVII, 770.---Another notice concerning harmful herbs, ibid., 836.

On sorceries and poisonings, St. Cummianus, LXXXVII, 990.---That a cleric must not be a magician or enchanter, nor make phylacteries, id., LXXXVIII, 876.

That a deacon or cleric must not be a magician or enchanter, nor make phylacteries, Fulgentius Ferrarius, ibid., 824.

Let no deacon be a magician, Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 224.---Let there be no magicians, ibid., 825.---Let magicians perform penance, ibid., 826.---Let no cleric make phylacteries, ibid., 824.---Let anyone who practices divination or admits diviners into his home perform penance, ibid., 826.

On Saul’s seizure by an evil spirit, the Venerable Bede, XCIII, 434.

## SECTION TWO. Superstition, Alchemy, Palmistry

## SECTION THREE. Astrology

Astrologers mentioned in the appendix to the apologetic books, Tertullian, I, 697.---Tertullian shows that those who consulted astrologers, haruspices, augurs, and magicians regarding the life of emperors were the emperors’ greatest enemies, ibid., 1060.---Tertullian shows that no Roman or other Gentile gods can at all be proved to exist by divinations or oracles, ibid., 1126.---Astrology permitted until the Gospel, ibid., 672.---Why astrology was permitted until the Gospel, ibid.---The partnership of astrology and magic, id., II, 1050.---The arts of astrologers, like those of haruspices, augurs, and magicians, disclosed by the apostate angels and forbidden by God, id., I, 459.---Astrologers censured, ibid., 268.---They consulted demons concerning the future death of the Caesars, ibid., 459.---Why ancient astrologers calculated a person’s nativity from the beginning of conception, id., II, 693.---The astronomer observes flying things, ibid., 1050.---Diviners, or soothsayers, mentioned, id., I, 495.

## SECTION FOUR. Metempsychosis

Tertullian attacks Plato’s rash falsehood, after Pythagoras, of **μετεμψύχωσις** (*metempsychōsis*), that is, the recurrence of souls, revolving through the alternating replacement of the dead and living, II, 697.---Even if this were so, he shows that individual souls must return into individual bodies with the same age, habits, talents, arts, and from every nation, sex, and rank, ibid., 901.---He demonstrates that Empedocles is still more delirious in introducing **μετενσωμάτωσις** (*metensōmatōsis*), turning beasts back out of humans and humans out of beasts, ibid., 702.---Nor can this doctrine be vindicated even under the name of judgment, for judgment is nullified if crimes are punished in no other way, or if the good receive no other reward, than restoration into animals, ibid., 705 ff.---By the same refutation he attacks the similar opinion of Simon the Samaritan heretic concerning his Helena, whom he said had passed through one female form after another, even claiming that she was that Helena most ruinous to Priam, ibid., 709.---Likewise on Carpocrates’ reincorporation of souls, by which he wished a soul to be recalled into bodies as often as it had made insufficient satisfaction for its sins, ibid., 710.

SECTION SIX. Auspices and auguries; palmistry.

Roman auspices and auguries, penitently abandoned, were observed with success, Tertullian, Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, III, 253.—By auguries and omens from birds, Octavius turns back against Caecilius himself a weapon lightly hurled by Caecilius, using the examples of Regulus of Mancinus, Paul, and Caesar, ibid., 320.—Demons lurking beneath statues and images animate the fibres of entrails, direct the flights of birds, govern lots, and issue oracles wrapped in deceptive replies, ibid., 323.—Auspices, auguries, dreams, and other such things could never prove that gods exist, as Caecilius maintained, ibid., 604.—The false argument of Caecilius, by which he attempts to prove that the Romans, because auspices and auguries had been disregarded by Sulpicius, Claudius, [Col. 0453] Junius, Flaminius, and Crassus, were slaughtered and defeated through the vengeance of the gods, ibid., 610.—Minucius refutes Caecilius by the examples of Regulus of Mancinus, Paul, and Julius Caesar, concerning the sun’s standing still and the sacred chickens’ dance, ibid., 612.—Auspices, auguries, dreams, and other practices among the heathen arose from the deceits and tricks of demons, ibid., 615.—How deeds seemingly accomplished among the heathen by demonic arts and tricks beyond the customary powers of nature were performed; with further material there on dreams, various lots, and prophetic frenzy, ibid., 618.—Demons declared themselves the authors of extraordinary effects among the heathen; and those are refuted who chatter that these things were produced solely by the artifices and frauds of priests, ibid., 622.

Auguries forbidden, St. Cyprian, IX, 325.—The power of the Roman Empire is not to be attributed to auspices or auguries; it is clear that all these things are demonic tricks, ibid., 572.

The heathen had altered their ancestral and inherited rites by observing signs from heaven, auguries from the citadel, the ritual declaration of war, and omens drawn from sharpened weapons, Arnobius, V, 420.—On white bulls sacrificed on the Alban Mount among the heathen; on entrails, thoroughly cooked or half raw, being cast away, etc., ibid., 427.—Haruspicy began after Tages, ibid., 431.—Avarice drove heathen haruspices, diviners, and seers to absurd accusations against Christians, ibid., 735–736.

Haruspices were alarmed, Lactantius, VII, 672.—Haruspices differed entirely from augurs, ibid., 673.

The silence of the haruspices, St. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, IX, 789.

On birds foretelling rain or winds, and on the faithful watch kept by geese, St. Ambrose, XIV, 224.

On Diodorus the haruspex, Ausonius, XIX, 832.

The diviners of Samaria observed certain institutions of the Law, Rufinus the priest, XXI, 984.

Through diviners the future is often foretold, St. Jerome, XXIV, 57.—It belongs to the Gentiles to listen to diviners, haruspices, etc., ibid., 814.

Whatever wonderful thing St. Augustine recalls concerning Albicerius the diviner in his *Life*, XXXII, 82.—Augustine scorns a haruspex who promises victory, ibid., 694.—Whether a diviner is wise, and what a wise person is, ibid., 916.—On the falsity of the omen by which the strength and stability of the Roman state seemed to be signified, id., XLI, 135.

The Roman emperors Trajan, Nerva, Severus, Titus, and also the mighty Neros waged war under auspices, Aurelius Prudentius, LX, 143.—Auspices of the consulship, id., LIX, 1076.—They fed chickens in order to draw auguries from them, ibid.—The water-auguring crow, ibid., 430.

On the auspices of the emperor Jovian and how he departed from the borders of Persia, Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1063.—On a demon’s answer concerning who would rule after Valens, and on Valens’s killing many persons for this reason, ibid., 1095.—On the death of the elder Valentinian and the auspices of the younger Valentinian, ibid., 1117.—On the auspices of the emperor Arcadius, ibid., 1136.—On the frauds which pagans practised through their temples, ibid., 1143.

On deceivers and diviners, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 484 ff.—On a boy led to diviners, ibid., 825.

The sin of divination is called disobedience, Gregory the Great, LXXV, 765. Haruspices and sacrilegious persons who do not repent: how they are to be dealt with if free, and how if slaves, id., LXXVII, 1002.—One who observes haruspices and diviners is excommunicated, ibid., 1340.—Why the disobedient are like diviners, id., LXXIX, 430 ff.—Whence diviners are so called, ibid., 462.—What sort of sin divination is, ibid.

Whoever admits diviners into his house, or practises divination himself, is to do penance, Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 826.

Blessed Alcuin wishes auguries, birdsong, and sneezings to be abolished, C, 449.—Who the haruspices are, id., CI, 1192.—Diviners, or properly haruspices, are those who utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols, ibid.—Who augurs are, ibid.—Auspices come unsolicited, ibid., 196.—Sneezings, id., C, 450.

On vengeance against the Midianites and Balaam the diviner, Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 794.—On sorcerers and augurs, id., CX, 491.

Who haruspices are, Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, CXXV, 718.—Who augurs are, ibid.—Diviners are those who utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols, offer baneful sacrifices, and receive the responses of demons through these observances, ibid.—Enchanters are those who practise the art of sorcery with words, ibid.—What Pythonesses and ventriloquists are, ibid.—Augurs are those who attend to the flight and cries of birds, ibid.—Sorcerers are to be investigated and punished, ibid., 726.—Various kinds and examples of magical harm between spouses, ibid., 716.—A girl delivered from sorcery through St. Basil, ibid., 721.—There are also others who divine from the bones of the dead, ashes and extinguished coals, hair, [Col. 0454] hair from the genitals of men and women, threads of many colours, diverse herbs, little shells, and portions of serpents, ibid., 717.

Augurs and pantomimes who renounce their arts may be received into the faith, Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 419.—Auguries and all other delusions of that kind are to be wholly avoided, ibid., 1176.—One devoted to auguries and divinations is excommunicated, ibid., 405.

On enchanters, sorcerers, and lot-casters, Regino, abbot of Prüm, CXXXII, 349–350.—Auguries forbidden, ibid., 350.

That clerics are not to believe auguries or seek divinations, Atto, bishop of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 37.

On enchanters and augurs, Burchard, bishop of Worms, CXL, 831.—On those who submit to auguries and incantations, ibid., 834.

Haruspicy or lots are not to be practised, Blessed Lanfranc, CL, 52.

Diviner and haruspex, or diviner, St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 745–746.—Those who observe diviners and persons of that kind are excommunicated, ibid.—What the Pythian spirit is, ibid., 747.—Days, Kalends, and auguries are by no means to be observed, ibid., 747, 750, 751, 756.—Diviners are not to be believed, ibid., 748.—Sorcerers are to be condemned, ibid., 147.—The courses of the stars or flights of birds are not to be observed; nor are Egyptian days to be observed, ibid., 748, 755.—Planet-readers, astrologers, soothsayers, etc., are to be condemned, ibid., 751, 757.—No trust is to be placed in lots, ibid.—Who lot-casters are, ibid., 751.—On the correction of one who has accused a woman by magical art, ibid.—Lot-casters and sorcerers are to be expelled, ibid., 752, 757.—Trees are not to be worshipped; but if any exist to which the populace gives honour, they are to be burned, ibid., 753, 755.—Penance for clerics who have consulted augurs, ibid., 747.—If anyone observes diviners, haruspices, or enchanters, or uses amulets, let that person be anathema, ibid., 1317.—Diviners were so called because they utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols, ibid.—Augurs are so named because they attend to the flights and cries of birds, ibid.—Haruspices are called, as it were, “observers of the hours,” ibid.—Haruspices inspect the entrails of cattle and foretell from them, ibid.—Auspices are observations made by travellers; they are called *auspicia*, as if “inspection of birds,” and auguries, as if “the chatter of birds,” ibid.—One who submits to auguries or incantations is to be separated from the Church, ibid., 1323.—On those who pursue auguries and divinations, ibid., 1321.

Diviners are horses’ tails, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXIX, 1003.

By sinning Adam became a diviner and idolater, Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 847.

What kind of auguring is permissible, Godfrey, abbot of Admont, CLXXIV, 876.

Haruspices are so called as *horuspices*, that is, observers of hours: they observe times in undertaking affairs; or they are called haruspices as those observing hours, who consider the future in the entrails and fibres of sacrifices, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 811.—An augury or an auspice sometimes concerns the eye and is called an *auspicium*, as if “bird-inspection”; sometimes it concerns the ears, and then is called an augury, as if “the chatter of birds,” because it is perceived by the ear, ibid.—Horoscopy is when the destinies of human beings are sought in the stars, ibid.—Genethliacs are so named because they observe births; they are the same persons who were formerly called magi in particular, ibid., 812.—The Phrygians invented auguries, ibid.—Tages, the first Etruscan, handed down haruspicy and lot-casting, ibid.

On Joseph’s saying to his brothers: “Do you not know that no one is like me in the knowledge of augury?” Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 538.

Astrologers are called those who attempt to foretell the outcomes of actions, Peter Lombard, CXCI, 1526.

What diviners, magi, Chaldeans, and haruspices signify, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1304.

“There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel,” Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1238.—On the Pythian spirit cast out from the girl, ibid., 1699.

Who enchanters, diviners, haruspices, natural philosophers, bird-diviners, image-makers, conjecturers, palm-readers, mirror-diviners, astrologers, dancers, lot-casters, and augurs are, John of Salisbury, CXCIX, 407.—Horoscope-casters are the same as astrologers, ibid., 408.—That astrologers are rash in presuming indiscriminately to subject future things to their judgment, ibid., 455.—On haruspices, palm-readers, and Pythian practitioners, and Saul’s rejection, ibid., 461.—On mirror-diviners; that malignant spirits sometimes know future things beforehand; that they often deceive, whether themselves deceiving or deceived; and that undoubted evils follow mirror-diviners, ibid., 472.

SECTION SEVEN. Necromancy, sciomancy, phycomancy.

[Col. 0455]

Pagans desire to see the departed in images and delight to preserve their memories in statues, Tertullian, Minucius Felix, III, 299.

The absurd heathen story by which Numa Pompilius was said to have learned from Jupiter, summoned by the arts of Faunus and Picus, how to avert lightning, Arnobius, V, 590.

Demons themselves invented necromancies, lots, and oracles, so that they might deceive human minds by a lying divination with ambiguous outcomes, Lactantius, VI, 1036.

Whether Samuel was truly summoned from the underworld by the Pythoness; perhaps a phantom of Samuel, not his spirit, appeared; and how demons know future things, St. Augustine, XL, 162.—Appearances of the dead: they do not know what happens here, and how they learn it, ibid., 799.

On Samuel and the Pythoness, St. Eugyppius, LXII, 1017.—That the dead are often thought to appear to the living in dreams, ibid., 1022.

The error of necromantic ingenuity, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 484.

On the Pythoness who, at Saul’s request, raised Samuel, who informed him of his approaching death, Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda and archbishop of Mainz, CIX, 1257.

Necromancers are those by whose incantations the dead seem to be raised up, to prophesy, and to answer questions, Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, CXXV, 718.

Inventors of necromancy, Blessed Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 760.—Necromancers are those by whose incantations the dead seem to be raised up, to prophesy, and to answer questions, ibid., 1318.—When necromancy is performed, blood is mixed with water, so that demons, said to love blood, may be more readily summoned by its bloody colour, ibid.

Necromancy is called divination by means of the dead, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 810.—A Jewish necromancer displays the power of his art, William, monk of Malmesbury, CLXXIX, 1144.

SECTION EIGHT. The false learning of heathen seers.

The learning of pagans—or rather fables—handed down by unlearned people: pleasant inventions and lies by which the minds of boys are corrupted, and in which they therefore grow old, Tertullian, Minucius Felix, III, 306.—How many ridiculous, obscene, and cruel rites were observed among the heathen in celebrating the mysteries of their gods, ibid., 312.

Divination is not understood in a favourable sense, St. Jerome, XXV, 1183.

On the vanity of Egyptian priests, Paulus Orosius, XXII, 709.

One book on the divination of demons, St. Augustine, XXX, 643.—He rejects the divinations of astrologers, id., XXXII, 637.—The divinations of Albicerius, ibid., 914.—One book on the divination of demons. The divinations of demons and practices belonging to their worship are not thereby rightly done because they do not occur unless God permits them; whence those demonic divinations arise, and why they are sometimes true although generally false, id., XL, 581–582.—Demonic divination excels through three causes: keenness of sense, swiftness of movement, and long experience of things, ibid., 584.—How far demonic divination is removed from the height of true prophecy, ibid., 586.—The arts and experience of demons in deceiving, ibid., 799.—On the most lying vanity of the Egyptians, who ascribe one hundred thousand years to the antiquity of their learning, id., XLI, 599.

On the woman possessed by a Pythian spirit, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 445.

On those who seek divinations, Cresconius Africanus, LXXXVIII, 876.

On divination concerning death and life, the Venerable Bede, XC, 963.

On those who seek divinations, Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, [Col. 0456] CV, 685. (See above, Cresconius Africanus, LXXXVIII, 876.)—That Christians may not observe diverse observances, ibid., 685.

On those who seek divinations, Burchard, CXL, 834.—On the nature of demons, ibid., 834.—On the divination of demons, ibid., 845.

The knowledge of demons is folly, St. Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, CXLII, 351.—The Devil is supremely wicked and deceitful, ibid., 180.—The Devil is called an asp, basilisk, lion, and dragon, ibid., 340.

The nature of demons, St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, CLXI, 765.—On the divination of demons, ibid.—On those who sacrifice to demons or invoke demons, ibid., 755, 757, 758.—Nothing from the threshing-floor or winepress is to be sacrificed to demons, ibid., 777.—Various kinds of divinations, ibid., 761.—Causes of divinations, ibid., 762.—What penance applies to those who seek divinations, ibid., 746.—On the manifold kinds of divination, ibid., 1318.—In how many ways demons foreknow future things, ibid., 1322.—A lot is nothing other than divination and is called sorcery, ibid., 1323.—Punishments of soothsayers, ibid.—The examples of Jonah and Matthias do not warrant indiscriminate belief in lots, ibid.—Those who profess, consult, or teach the science of divination, auguries, or lots are to be held outside the Church, ibid., 1394.—Soothsayers who proclaim that they know future things are to be beaten and cast out of the city, ibid., 1323.

Divination is never understood in a favourable sense, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXVIII, 469.—Vision differs from divination, ibid.

To catch men, the demon spreads hook, dragnet, and net, Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 722.

*Mantic* means divination, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 810.

Divination on land is called geomancy, ibid.—Divination in water is called hydromancy, ibid.—Divination in air is called aeromancy, ibid.—Divination in fire is called pyromancy, ibid., 811.—Mathematics is divided into three kinds: haruspicy, augury, and horoscopy, ibid.

What the noonday demon is, Richard of St. Victor, CXCVI, 395.—How demons deceive, ibid., 456.—Why demons are likened to birds, ibid., 840.—On the difference between doctrinal mathematics and condemned *mathesis*, on the tradition of astrologers, and on their errors, id., CXCIX, 440.—That *mathesis* is a path of damnation, ibid., 459.

The demon’s cunning in three respects, Thomas of Cîteaux and John Algrin, CCVI, 215.

SECTION NINE. Fatalism; fate.

Why Christians do not believe in fate, Zacchaeus the Christian and Apollonius the philosopher, XX, 1097.

Macarius asks Rufinus to explain to him Origen’s teaching against fate, Rufinus, XXI, 115.

Fate is excluded, St. Jerome, XXVI, 135.

Augustine instructs Lampadius, who was perplexed by the question of astral fate, St. Augustine, XL, 725–726.—He treats of removing belief in fate at the outset, lest those should eventually arise who, after he had shown in the preceding book that the strength and growth of the Roman Empire could not be ascribed to false gods, might wish to attribute them to fate, id., XLI, 140.—On those who call “fate” not the position of the stars but the connection of causes dependent upon God’s will, ibid., 148.—What Catholics think concerning fate, id., XLV, 577.

What fate is; its influence and necessity are refuted, St. Maximus of Turin, LVII, 932.—How many philosophical opinions concerning fate there are, ibid.—“You say that all things occur by fate; but what you say occurs by fate, according to some uncertain opinion, I say occurs by God’s will or permission,” ibid., 782.

Fate defined, Anicius Manlius Boethius, LXIII, 815.—What fate is, ibid., 1146.—According to the Stoics, all things occur by fate, ibid., 493.

## CCXII. INDEX OF GEOLOGY AND PALAEONTOLOGY, ALPHABETICALLY ARRANGED BY SUBJECT, RECORDING EVERYTHING WRITTEN BY THE FATHERS CONCERNING THE TERRESTRIAL GLOBE AND ITS VARIOUS CHANGES, THE UNIVERSAL FLOOD AND ITS CONSEQUENCES, EARTHQUAKES, ETC.

[Col. 0473] **Abyss.** — On the abyss, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 314.

**Acheruntia, burned by itself.** — Lupus Protospatarius, CLV, 141.

**Etna.** — On Mount Etna, St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 1016. — Fire erupted from Mount Etna, St. Jerome, XXVII, 456. — Mount Etna spewed out rivers of flame. It is recorded that the sea so boiled from the fires of Etna that rocks were burned and the pitch of ships melted. The roofs of the city of Catania were destroyed by the force of ash erupting from Etna, St. Augustine, XLI, 111. — The conflagration of Etna, the Venerable Bede, XC, 276; Freculph, CVI, 1060. — On the fires of Etna and Lipara, Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 938, 945. — On Etna’s eruption, ibid., 930. — On the earthquake in Sicily and the severe fiery heat of Etna, Freculph, CVI, 1005. — At what time Etna spewed forth unprecedented fires beyond measure, ibid., 1057. — Empedocles hurled himself headlong into Etna, Tertullian, II, 702.

St. Ado, Archbishop of Vienne, CXXIII, 27; St. Nicephorus, CXXIX, 514; Ekkehard, CLIV, 503; Claudius of Turin, CIV, 919; Freculph, CVI, 932; Annals of Lambert, CXLI, 452; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 624; Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 697. — The universal Flood in Noah’s time, St. Augustine, XLI, 566. — In what year from Adam it occurred, ibid., 463. — Duration, increase, and decrease of the Flood, ibid., XXXIV, 350. — The Flood was not confined to the plains, as Plato thought, but destroyed the whole world, Tertullian, I, 483; II, 1033. — Shells and trumpets [conch shells] found in the mountains prove this, ibid. — The world changed in form during the Flood, ibid. — But even now its aspect changes locally when its situation is damaged, ibid. — During the Flood even high places floated, ibid. — All cities are later than the Flood, ibid., 482. — Why, after Noah entered the ark, the Flood occurred seven days later, St. Ambrose, XIV, 379. — The Flood occurred in spring, so that human beings might suffer more from it; **Gallaecia.** — Continual earthquakes in Gallaecia, Idalius, LI, 883, 884.

**Gaul.** — Earthquakes in Gaul, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 216, 564, 582. — In Gothic Gaul a mountain roared for many days, Maximus of Saragossa, LXXX, 646. — In the year 800 an earthquake occurred which shook many places in Gaul and Germany, St. Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 130. — In the year 801 certain places around the River Rhine, both in Gaul and in Germany, trembled, Einhard, CIV, 461. — In the year 950, numerous and great earthquakes occurred in places in Gaul and Germany, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 186. — In the year 1178, an inundation of rivers broke forth throughout all Gaul of such a kind as to overthrow houses and kill many people, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 313. — On the inundation of waters in Gaul, Aimoin, CXXXIX, 716.

**Gomorrah.** — The cities of Sodom and Gomorrah consumed by fire, Tertullian, I, 382. — There is great desolation there, a bereft region, everything ashes, ibid., II, 1034. — The soil of Gomorrah and Sodom still smells of fire, Tertullian, I, 482. — Its fruits turn to ashes, ibid., I, 453. — The region of Pentapolis was struck from heaven and burned because of the unspeakable crimes of lust, Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 701, 702.

**Whirlpools.** — On whirlpools, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 325.

**Chasm.** — On a chasm, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 373. — A mountain falls through a chasm, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 293. — A vast chasm in the earth appeared in the middle of Rome, Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 800. — From a chasm in the earth at Rome, a flame burst forth which was seen to extend as far as heaven, St. Ado, Archbishop of Vienne, CXXIII, 67. — In the middle of the forum of the City, the earth split apart and the gaping depths below lay open, Ekkehard, CLIV, 559, 560.

**Fire kindled by God.** — Rufinus, XXI, 506.

**The conflagration of Phaethon.** — See Phaethon.

Island.---On islands, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 512; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 353.---Islands swallowed up by the waves of the sea or by earthquakes, Tertullian, I, 480, 571; II, 1034.---Islands set on fire by divine agency, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 464.---Islands consumed by fire, Anastasius, CXXVII, 513.---A new island, thirty stadia in extent, appeared in the sea, Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 58; Ekkehard, CLIV, 462; *Monumenta Gregoriana*, CXLVIII, 1305.---Under Emperor Claudius an island arose between Thera and Therasia, thirty stadia in extent, St. Jerome, XXVII, 580; Cassiodorus, LXXIX, 1229; Ekkehard, CLIV, 671.

Great flood.---Godefridus of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 908.

Italy.---Flooding in Italy, Anastasius, CXXVIII, 637.---Frequent earthquakes in Italy, Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 775.---Countless and very great earthquakes occurred in Italy, CXLVIII, 1362.---In the year 800, an earthquake occurred on the day before the Kalends of May, at the second hour of the night, and shook almost all Italy, St. Ado, Archbishop of Vienne, CXXIII, 130; Eginhard, CIV, 461.

Jerusalem.---By an earthquake at Jerusalem and by a fire kindled by divine agency, the Jews were driven from their unlawful undertakings, Rufinus, XXI, 506.---On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord (1105), an earthquake occurred at Jerusalem, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLV, 406.

Judaea, thirty-two years before Christ, was shaken by a violent earthquake, Prolegomena to Anastasius, CXXVII, 422.

Lake.---On lakes, St. Ambrose, XIV, 151; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 316.---Certain lakes which Julius Caesar was said to have permanently dammed by a square-built work burst through because of an excessive inundation of waters, causing the river Nar and the Tiber to overflow beyond measure, Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 261.

Lipara.---On the fires of Aetna and Lipara, Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 938, 945.

Shore.---On the shore, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 372.

Places.---On summer places, Rabanus, CXI, 372.---Pleasant places, ibid., 371.---Sunny places, ibid., 372.---Rugged places, ibid., 370.---Deserted places, ibid., 371.---Out-of-the-way places, ibid.---Slippery places, ibid., 372.

Lombardy.---Earthquake in Lombardy, Ekkehard, CLIV, 1035.---A very great earthquake also occurred in [Col. 0477] Lombardy (A.D. 1118), Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 425.

Lucania, formerly joined to Italy, Tertullian, I, 481.---The force of the waves severed Lucania from Italy and assigned it the name of Sicily, Tertullian, II, 1034.

Sacred grove.---On sacred groves, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 367, 371.

A plague seized many provinces, and Rome was afflicted in part (A.D. 170), St. Jerome, XVII, 629.

Wild-beasts’ lairs, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 370.

Island of Maillezais.---On the antiquity of the island of Maillezais and its alteration for the better, Peter of Maillezais, CXLVI, [reference incomplete].

What the sea is.---St. Augustine, XXXII, 853.---On the sea, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 311.---On the Mediterranean Sea, ibid., 512.---Why the sea is bitter, Venerable Bede, XC, 240; St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 1013.---Why the sea does not increase, ibid., 1012.---On the names of the sea, ibid.---Living old men are adduced as witnesses that seas have increased beyond their ancient boundaries, St. Augustine, XXXV, 2158.---The sea, having overstepped its bounds, unexpectedly submerged part of Flanders together with its inhabitants, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 371.

Marble dug from a cemetery in the Veranus field, Anastasius, CXXVII, 550.

Mesopotamia.---In Mesopotamia the earth was split for as much as two miles; another earth, less white and sandy, rose from its depths, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 143.

Mainz.---At Mainz the earth is said to have shaken twenty times, Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 183.---A great earthquake on the third day before the Nones of December destroyed Mainz, ibid., 191.---An earthquake occurred at Mainz on the third day before the Kalends of January, ibid., 193.---Mainz experienced a great earthquake on the Kalends of December (A.D. 1080), Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 220.

Mountain.---On mountains, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 359.---On mountains and the other names of the earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 521.---Mountains burn and endure, Tertullian, I, 528.---Mount Tauretunensis, in the territory of Veelles, suddenly collapsed, Marius, Bishop of Avenches, LXXII, 799.

The river Meuse, as though hanging in the air, was seen to have abandoned its bed, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 241, 242.

Naval stations.---On naval stations, Rabanus Maurus, CXL, 372.

Ship.---Near Balabriga, in the Ocean Sea, the ships of the Northmen, which had settled there, were sunk through the prayers of St. Gundisalvus (A.D. 846), Liutprand, Bishop of Cremona, CXXVI, 1145.

Angered Neptune, as the sea-waves surged, ravaged the lands of the Athenians, Ekkehard, CLIV, 513, 514.

Nicaea.---On the earthquake that occurred at Nicaea in Bithynia, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1010.---Nicaea fell in an earthquake, St. Jerome, XXVII, 572.---It was utterly overthrown by another earthquake, ibid., 695.---Nicaea, which had often previously fallen through earthquake, was utterly overthrown, Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 710.---When an earthquake occurred, Nicomedia fell, and very much of the city of Nicaea was destroyed, St. Jerome, XXVII, 614; St. Prosper, LI, 559; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 663.---Under Emperor Hadrian, earthquakes at Nicomedia and Nicaea, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1232.

Nicomedia, utterly overthrown by earthquake, while neighboring cities were partly afflicted, St. Jerome, XXVII, 690; Anastasius, CXXVII, 498; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 707.

Nicopolis and Caesarea fell in an earthquake, St. Jerome, XXVII, 617 (A.D. 130); Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 303, 304; Anastasius, CXXVII, 502; Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 63; *Monumenta Gregoriana*, CXLVIII, 1308; Ekkehard, CLIV, 466, 683.

Nile.---On the Nile, Venerable Bede, XC, 261; St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 1013.---On the recession of the river Nile and its subsequent return, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1158.

Ocean.---On the Ocean, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 312; St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 1011.---On the origin of the Ocean, Venerable Bede, XC, 258.---Why the sea does not increase, ibid., 260.

World.---The world changed in form in the Flood, Tertullian, II, 1033.---But even now it changes its configuration locally when its position is disturbed, ibid.

East.---Many cities of the East fell in a terrible earthquake, St. Jerome, XXVII, 681; Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 485, 486.---Great earthquakes in the East and Africa, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 136.

Palestine.---Many cities and villages of Palestine were destroyed by an earthquake, Marcellinus Comes, LI, 924.---A great earthquake in Palestine and Syria, Anastasius, CXXVII, 867.---A great earthquake in Palestine, ibid.

The Pantheon at Rome was burned by lightning (A.D. 112), St. Jerome, XXVII, 609.

So great a pestilence occurred throughout the world that the Roman army was almost destroyed to the point of annihilation (A.D. 175), St. Jerome, XXVII, 629.---A pestilential [Col. 0478] disease seized many provinces of the whole world, especially Alexandria and Egypt (A.D. 255), ibid., 649.

Phaethon.---The conflagration which occurred under Phaethon, St. Jerome, XXVII, 176; Freculph, CVI, 955; Ekkehard, CLIV, 513, 514.---At this time (A.D. 2649), so vast and severe a heat flared up that the sun, passing beyond its course, is said not merely to have affected the whole world with heat but to have terrified it with fire; hence the absurd fable of Phaethon was woven, St. Ado of Vienne, CXXIII, 35.

Poitiers.---The burning of the city of Poitiers, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 1003.

Pompeii.---Fire from its mountain flooded the Campanian city of the Pompeians and Tarpeians, Tertullian, I, 485, 571; II, 1034.

Deep.---On the deep, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 373.

Promontory.---On promontories, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 540; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 358.

Well.---On wells, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 324.

Flooding of the Rhine.---Eginhard, CIV, 442.

Rhodes.---Caria and Rhodes were so shaken by an earthquake that the great Colossus fell, St. Jerome, XXVII, 494.---The island of Rhodes was shaken by earthquake, Anastasius, CXXVII, 496.

Rome.---An earthquake and solar eclipse at Rome, St. Jerome, XXVII, 585; Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 185, 186; Ekkehard, CLIV, 674.---Many signs and portents occurred at Rome and throughout the world, St. Jerome, XXVII, 603.---With a great part of the Roman world shaken by earthquake, the sea went beyond its shore, and many cities in Sicily were overwhelmed, Anastasius, CXXVII, 638.---A great earthquake at Rome, in Libya, and Asia, ibid., 569.---An earthquake at Rome, Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 647.---At this time an unusual fire and flood of waters almost destroyed the city of Rome, Freculph, CVI, 1036.---The earth opened at Rome, ibid., 1009.

Red Sea, Venerable Bede, XC, 261; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 312.

Woodland pasture.---On woodland pastures, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 367.

The city of the Santones in Aquitaine is said to have shaken in September, Eginhard, CIV, 842.

Sicily.---After an earthquake throughout the world, the sea went beyond its shore and overwhelmed the cities and innumerable peoples of Sicily and many islands (A.D. 369), St. Jerome, XXVII, 693; Anastasius, CXXVII, 638; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 709.---On the earthquake in Sicily and the formation of the island Atalante, Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 790.

Sidon.---In a terrible earthquake near Tyre and Sidon many structures fell, and an innumerable population was overwhelmed (A.D. 306), St. Jerome, XXVII, 604, 663.

A sign in heaven, like a spreading and burning column, appeared for thirty days (A.D. 393), St. Jerome, XXVII, 708.

Smyrna, a city of Asia, fell in an earthquake, St. Jerome, XXVII, 632; Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 349, 350; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 669.

Sodom and Gomorrah set aflame, St. Jerome, XXVII, 122.---On the overthrow of Sodom, Godefridus of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 1100.---See Gomorrah.

Sun.---Three suns appeared simultaneously and immediately united into the same disk, St. Jerome, XXVII, 583.

Cave.---On a cave, Rabanus Maurus, CXL, 373.

Pool.---On pools, St. Ambrose, XIV, 161; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 316.

The river Sucro rises in Spain, Liutprand, *On Spain*, CXXXVI, 1143.

Earthquake at Soissons, St. Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 390, 391.

Syria is shaken by a great earthquake, Anastasius, CXXVII, 895, 911.

Earth.---On the earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 495.---When the earth was created, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 256.---Whether the earth was that which was made is a great question, Tertullian, II, 222, 1034.---The earth was virgin, not yet pressed by work, from which we understand that man was made by God into a living soul, ibid., 782.---When the earth is called “dry,” its principal quality is indicated, St. Ambrose, XIV, 163.---The earth, previously invisible because waters covered it, appeared when those waters flowed together into one place, ibid., 158.---The earth is higher than the water, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 383, 750.---Whether the earth is founded upon water, ibid., 264.---How it is founded upon water, idem, XXXVII, 1759.---The earth is like a globe, Venerable Bede, XC, 264.---On the position of the earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 1014; Venerable Bede, XC, 263.---Division of the earth, ibid., 276.---On the parts of the earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 1016.---On the circles of the earth, Venerable Bede, XC, 266.---On the lower regions of the earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 525.

Earthquake.---St. Isidore, LXXXIII, 1015; Venerable Bede, XC, 275; Anastasius, CXXVIII, 685, 1307; Hermannus Contractus, [Col. 0479] CXLIII, 57, 63, 134, 182; *Monumenta Gregoriana*, CXLVIII, 1307, 1308; Ekkehard, CLIV, 466, 471, 774, 932, 957; Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 360; Helinandus the monk, CCXII, 1019, 1023; Sicard, CCXIII, 504.---An earthquake overthrew many cities, Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 62, 79, 80; *Monumenta Gregoriana*, CXLVIII, 1308, 1312; Ekkehard, CLIV, 471.---An earthquake destroyed many cities, and the Golden House perished in fire, Ekkehard, CLIV, 465.---An earthquake lasted for many days, and the sky seemed to burn, St. Prosper, II, 588.---The imperial city was shaken by earthquake for forty continuous days, Marcellinus Comes, LI, 932; Anastasius, CXXVII, 724.---There was an earthquake, followed by mortality, Ekkehard, CLIV, 483.---An earthquake occurred, and a comet was seen, ibid., 485.---When a huge earthquake threatened in various places, many walls of the imperial city, with fifty-seven towers, collapsed; very great stones in the Forum of Taurus and many statues likewise fell, while many cities also collapsed, Marcellinus Comes, LI, 927.---In the year of Christ’s Passion, an earthquake occurred throughout the world, Ekkehard, CLIV, 23, 472.---On the earthquake and darkness that occurred at the Passion of the Lord: what pagan writers, or Josephus the historian, thought, Freculph, CVI, 1121.---The earthquake in Achaia compared with that at Constantinople, Lucius Dexter, XXXI, 806.---In Asia three cities fell in an earthquake: Laodicea, Hierapolis, and Colossae, St. Jerome, XXVII, 588.---Four cities of Asia were overthrown by earthquake—Elaea, Myrrhina, Pitanae, Cyme—and two of Greece, those of the Opuntians and Oritans, St. Jerome, XXVII, 606; St. Prosper, LI, 557; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 661; Ekkehard, CLIV, 681.---Thirteen cities fell in an earthquake: Ephesus, Magnesia, Sardis, Morthene, Aegaea, Hierocaerea, Philadelphia, Tmolus, Temnus, Cyme, Myrrhina, Apollonia, and Hyrcania, St. Jerome, XXVII, 566, 567; Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 56; Ekkehard, CLIV, 461.---Dyrrachium fell in an earthquake; Rome swayed for three days and nights, and many cities of Campania were afflicted, St. Jerome, XXVII, 683; Marianus Scotus, CXLVII, 705.---In the year 399, an earthquake lasted for many days and the sky seemed to burn, St. Jerome, XXVII, 708.---In the year 502, a great earthquake occurred with great flashes of lightning and hail, and a disturbance of the whole heaven and earth, Victor of Vita, LXVIII, 949.---In the year 618, a greater earthquake occurred in August, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 117.---In the year 632, an earthquake occurred, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 119.---In the year 801, an earthquake, Gregory of Catino, CXXVII, 337.---In the year 823, an earthquake, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 157.---In the year 1000, a very great earthquake occurred; a comet appeared, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 198.---In the year 1013, a very great earthquake occurred about noon, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 201.---In the year 1020, the church of the Holy Resurrection before the basilica of blessed Eparchius was overthrown by earthquake, Ademar the monk, CXLI, 64.---In the year 1081, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, a great earthquake occurred with a grave rumbling of the earth, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 220.---In the year 1117, on the octave of St. John the Evangelist, the earth was shaken far and wide throughout the world by a terrible and hitherto unheard-of [Col. 0480] earthquake. In Italy, through the collision and overthrow of mountains, the course of the river Adige was blocked; Verona fell; and in Parma, Venice, and other cities, no few thousands of people perished, Ademar the monk, CXLI, 599.---In the year 1117, an earthquake occurred, at one time milder and at another stronger, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 241, 242.---In the year 1117, a great earthquake occurred, Cosmas of Prague, CLXVI, 226.---In the year 1139, a great earthquake occurred, Falco of Benevento, LXXXIII, 1256.---In the year **, an earthquake occurred in Advent, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in one night, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 399.---A great earthquake on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 168.---An earthquake occurred in the evening on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, ibid., 178.---A great earthquake occurred on the Kalends of January, ibid., 185.---A great earthquake occurred on the seventh day before the Ides of October, ibid., 188.---An earthquake occurred on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, ibid., 215.---A great earthquake on the fourth day before the Ides of May, ibid., 231; Ekkehard, CLIX, 489.---A great earthquake occurred at night, on the third day before the Ides of October, Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 251.---On the sixth day before the Ides of February there were an earthquake, lightning flashes, and thunderclaps, ibid., 269.

A pot made of clay is no longer clay, Tertullian, II, 776.

Thizaha.---Earthquake near the river Thizaha, *Monumenta Gregoriana*, CXLVIII, 1410.

Thrace.---Earthquake in Africa and Thrace, St. Augustine, XXXV, 2174.

Tiber.---Under the reign of Emperor Augustus, for eight days the Tiber, in its pitiful violence, brought destruction upon persons and homes, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 1227.---On the flooding of the Tiber, Paul the Deacon, XCV, 648.---A huge inundation of the Tiber for seven days, Anastasius, CXXVII, 896.

Pavia is said to have shaken eight times by night on the third day before the Kalends of January, Hermannus Contractus, CXLIII, 178.

Torrent.---On torrents, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 322.

Tralles fell in an earthquake, St. Jerome, XXVII, 551 [the source misprints the citation].

Tripoli.---On the feast day of the apostles Peter and Paul (A.D. 1170), the city of Tripoli fell in a terrible earthquake, together with part of Damascus and very much of Antioch, Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 510.

Tyre.---In a terrible earthquake near Tyre and Sidon many structures fell, and an innumerable population was overwhelmed (A.D. 306), St. Jerome, XXVII, 604, 663.

Valley.---On valleys, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 365.

Vesuvius.---A fire on Mount Vesuvius (A.D. 82), St. Jerome, XXVII, 598.---Mount Vesuvius in Campania vomited forth its burned-out entrails and, as night-time darkness came on in daytime, covered the whole face of Europe with fine dust, Marcellinus Comes, LI, 931.---On the eruption of Vesuvius, Paul the Deacon, XCV, 630.---Mount Vesuvius spews ashes, Anastasius, CXXVIII, 867.---Ashes spewed from Mount Vesuvius were carried as far as Byzantium, ibid., 719.---Pliny the Second died while observing the fire of Vesuvius, St. Jerome, XXII, 609 (note).

Vienne.---On the earthquake at Vienne, a city of Gaul, Aimoinus the monk, CXXXIX, 661.

## CCXIII. INDEX OF MINERALOGY, ALPHABETICALLY ARRANGED BY SUBJECT, SETTING FORTH EVERYTHING CONCERNING MINERALS CONTAINED IN THE *PATROLOGIAE CURSUS*

Abeston, Asbeston.---St. Eugenius, Bishop of Toledo, LXXXVII, 392; Marbod, CLXXI, 1778.

Absictum.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1778.

*Achates lapsis*.---St. Isidore, LXXXII, 298; Marbod, CLXXI, 1775, 1777.

Diamond (*adamas*).---St. Eugenius, Bishop of Toledo, LXXXVII, 392; Marbod, CLXXI, 1771.

Bronze.---All the necessities of life depend upon bronze and iron, Tertullian, I, 1310.---Iron and bronze are in greater use among human beings than gold and silver, ibid.---Bronze was discovered before iron, St. Augustine, XLI, 214.---On bronze, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 476.

Alabandine gems.---Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVIII, 1515, 1281.

[Col. 0480] Almandine.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1777.

Androdragma.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1778.

Silver.---Whence gold and silver come, Tertullian, I, 1309; II, 803.---Whence the value of gold and silver arises, idem, I, 1310.---They are good not in reality but by rarity, ibid., 1328.---Native and abundant gold and silver among certain barbarians, ibid., 1309, 1311.---Gold and silver, the principal materials of worldly adornment, ibid.---Iron and bronze are in greater use among human beings [Col. 0481] than gold and silver, ibid., 1310.---Silver, the earth’s pallor, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 136.---On silver, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 585; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 476; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1347.

Asbeston.---St. Eugenius, Bishop of Toledo, LXXXVII, 392. See Abeston.

Gold.---Tertullian, I, 1309, 1310, 1311, 1328; II, 803. (See Silver.)---Gold, the earth’s pallor, St. Augustine, XXXVIII, 136.---Shining earth, idem, XXXIX, 1655.---On gold, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 583; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 475; Adam of Bremen, canon, CXLVI, 619; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1347.

Beryl stone.---St. Hildephonsus, XCVI, 316; Marbod, CLXXI, 1774, 1777.

Buticulated gems.---Anastasius, CXXVIII, 1285.

Chalcedony stone.---St. Hildephonsus, XCVI, 293; Marbod, CLXXI, 1773, 1777.

Calchophanum.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1778.

Calibe.---St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1350.

White gems.---St. Isidore, LXXXII, 575.

Ceraunia.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1777.

Chelonis.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1778.

Chryselectrum.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1778.

Chrysoclava gems.---Anastasius, CXXVIII, 867, 1353.

Chrysolite stone.---Hildephonsus, XCVI, 311; Marbod, CLXXI, 1774, 1777.

Chrysopastus stone.---Hildephonsus, XCVI, 313.

Chrysoprase.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1777, 1778.

Coral.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1777.

Carnelian.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1776, 1777.

Cuidrum.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1778.

Cyprinum.---Anastasius, CXXVIII, 1219.

Digitiae gems.---Anastasius, CXXVIII, 1285.

Dionysia.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1778.

Electrum.---St. Isidore, LXXXII, 590; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 478.

Heliotrope.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1777.

Emathis.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1778.

Epistis.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1777.

Ethis.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1777.

Exacontalitum.---Marbod, CLXXI, 1778.

Iron.---All the necessities of life depend upon bronze and iron, Tertullian, I, 1310.---Iron and bronze are in greater use among human beings than gold and silver, ibid., 1310.---Bronze was discovered before iron, St. Augustine, XLI, 214.---On iron, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 586; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 479; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1349.

## CCXV. INDEX OF ETHNOGRAPHY

Arranged alphabetically by subject, presenting everything the Fathers have said concerning the origin and races of nations or peoples, their various migrations, dress, customs, practices, and so forth.

### TERTULLIAN

The Egyptian kingdom is older than the Roman, I, 432.

Egypt had the Chaldaean race among its inhabitants, II, 1035.

Egypt and Ethiopia: every people is so called by transfer from species to genus, I, 635.

Phoenicians occupied Africa, II, 700, 1035.

Amazons, I, 308.—Their kingdom is older than the Roman, 432.

Anthropophagi: who they are, I, 321, 323, 370.

Arabian women cover not merely their heads but also their whole faces so completely that, with one eye left free, they are content to enjoy half the light rather than expose their entire face, II, 912.

Athenians occupied Asia, II, 700.—Foreign refinements were brought from Asia into Libya and Europe, [Col. 0510] 1040. The churches of Asia Minor were established by John, 366.

Ninus was the first king of the Assyrians, II, 1034. Herod was another king, 339. This kingdom is older than the Roman, I, 432.—Profane histories begin with the Assyrians, II, 1035.

Athens, the eloquent city, II, 651.—The keenest in wisdom and speech are born at Athens, 683.—The Athenians occupied Asia, ibid., 700.

Whether the Libyan people ever dream, II, 733.

The Babylonian kingdom is older than the Roman, I, 432.

Barbarian infants rush into battle, first being united to the sun, armed with rags, and paid with butter, II, 338, 618.—Among barbarians, reputation is sometimes slanderous, 733.—Barbarian head-tufts, 903.

The Britons are enclosed within the circuit of Ocean, II, 661.

Carthage, a city most zealous for warfare, II, 1032.—The Punic city, Rome’s rival, I, 427.—The Carthaginians, distinguished by antiquity and fortunate in novelty, II, 1030.—Their former style of clothing: what it was, ibid.—Carthaginian contests, 133.

Who the people of Casinum are, I, 420.

Celts seek oracles by passing the night beside the tombs of brave men, II, 740.

A Chaldaean stock is led into Egypt, II, 1035.

All cities are later than the Flood, I, 482.—The human race once existed without cities, 432.—To obliterate a city by assuming the garb of an inn, 452.

Cretans are liars, II, 683.

The bloodstained faces of the Cyclopes, I, 308.

The fierce Dalmatians, II, 683.

The errors of the Gentiles concerning gods and morals, I, 485, 486, 699, 445, 472, 473.

The Gauls sacrificed to Mercury, I, 316.—Gallic faces, or mules, 1281.—Gallic and German women with saffron-colored hair, 1322.—African women envied their beauty, ibid.

The Galato-Greeks, descended from the Gauls, I, 316.

Each people has its own speech, but the material of speech is common, I, 618.—All nations have one soul, but diverse voice; one spirit, but diverse sound, ibid.

The sources, in a manner of speaking, of the human race: Cain, Abel, Seth, II, 583.---The abundance of the human race, 699.---It is diminished by public calamities, 700.

The Germans are not permitted to cross their boundaries, II, 611.---They were already subject to Christ, ibid.---German locks of hair, 903.---German porters, I, 1281.

The Getulian people do not leave their own borders, II, 611.

The most ancient corpses of giants have not been devoured; their skeletons still remain, II, 854.

Etruria was occupied by the Lydians, I, 636.---It was the first to establish the names and rites of superstitious religion, ibid.

Men were uncultivated in Saturn’s time, I, 331.---Who ate human flesh, 313.---Some swallowed human substance in a dreadful crime, 323.---Africans, Gauls, and Romans sacrificed human beings to their gods, 314, 316.---Where and for how long, ibid.

Italy was occupied by the Phrygians, II, 700.

From its beginning the Jewish nation was divided by tribes, families, and households, II, 450.

The Jews now wander homelessly throughout the world, I, 393.

The Lacedaemonians first devised the *penula* for games, I, 302.---The flogging of Lacedaemonian boys, 626.---What benefit the lashes of the Laconians conferred, 533.

The Libyan people called the Atlantes are said to pass through death in a sleep without dreams, II, 733.

The inhuman Massagetae, II, 247.---They ate the flesh of parents worn out by old age, I, 321.

Countless peoples inhabit the entire earth, II, 700.

## CCXVI. INDEX OF ANTHROPOLOGY, IN WHICH, FROM THE HOLY FATHERS, THERE IS DISCUSSION OF MAN AS A RATIONAL ANIMAL, COMPOSED AT ONCE OF SOUL AND BODY, OR OF MAN PHYSICALLY AND MORALLY.

## Tertullian

[Col. 0517]

A.D. 162–252.

Adam was established by God free, possessing both free choice and authority over himself, II, 290.---He was not made from a man’s seed, ibid., 723.---He was innocent, very close to God as a friend, and a dweller in Paradise, I, 1257.---Adam, that source of the human race, drank sleep before he thirsted for rest; slept before he labored, before he ate—indeed before he was even tested—II, 723.---Adam, certainly naked and unclothed, stood before his Potter; only afterward did he obtain wisdom, stealthily snatched before it was yet permitted, ibid., 1038.---Adam, the one husband of Eve, and Eve his one wife: one woman, one rib, I, 1277.---Adam was called “man” before the union of marriage, II, 900.---Adam and Eve went naked as long as they lacked understanding, ibid., 904.---What befell Adam after the Fall, II, 297.---The grace of Paradise and intimacy with God were taken from him, ibid., 286.---From fig leaves he retained an itching, ibid., 990, 1038.---Adam and Eve fell from immortality by acting against the Lord’s command, ibid., 599.---Because of the condition imposed by the law, he was given over to death, but hope was preserved for him, ibid., 315.---He is condemned to death for tasting a single little tree; and from that point sins arise together with their punishments, and now all perish who know no turf of Paradise, ibid., 272.---Banished into the prison-house of cultivating the earth, in labor itself bent and sloping down toward the ground, he transmitted to his whole race the world’s spirit, taken from that earth, ibid., 286.

The ages act through bodies, II, 746.---The five ages of a human being: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, old age, ibid., 746.---Duties suited to each age, ibid.

[Col. 0518] Food.---In the beginning God assigned human beings only grassy and herbaceous fodder, II, 958.

“Female” is a natural designation, II, 894.---The general natural designation is “woman,” ibid.---Only one woman was formed from Adam’s ribs, to show the unity of marriage, ibid., 920.

Man, a rational animal, II, 160.---“Man” is one name among all nations, I, 618.---He is the work of the Creator, I, 514.---Created by God from nothing, I, 524.---How he was fashioned by God, II, 82.---The work of fashioning man, with waters joining in, was completed from earthly material, I, 1202.---He is composed of a twofold substance, II, 452, 850.---Man is both body and soul, II, 841.---Man was built by God for this purpose: that, being made by the Lord, he might be a lord, II, 801.---All things are servants to man, I, 1256.---A beautiful description of humanity’s creation, II, 802.---The creation of man according to the Demiurge, ibid., 578.---Man was made in God’s image not in bodily outlines, but in freedom and power of choice, II, 290.---Man was not created by God for death, II, 294.---He was worthy to know God, II, 291.---Why he was given to the earth and driven from God’s sight, I, 1257.---He is not disposed toward good by nature, but by instruction, II, 291.---Nothing is more necessary for man than concern for the true God, II, 285.

The impediments of a newborn child, II, 758.---Why they weep upon entering life, II, 682.---The movements of the soul of an infant immediately upon leaving the mother’s womb are described, ibid.---Whether infants dream, II, 733.---Infancy is naturally spirited and emotional, II, 682.

Labor is necessary, II, 487.

[Col. 0519] Marriage exists when God joins two persons into one flesh, or, finding them joined, seals their union in that same flesh, II, 941.---Through the bond of marriage, two are made one flesh, I, 1302; II, 896.---The necessity and causes of marriage, I, 1280.

Eve, the mother of the female sex, II, 896.

“Woman” is not by nature the name of a wife; “wife” is the name of a woman by condition, II, 896.---The term “woman” pertains to sex, not to a rank within the sex, ibid., 895.

It has been reported that dull and brutish persons are born at Thebes, II, 683.

The craftsman God has apportioned vital functions appropriate to every animal according to the constitution of each kind, II, 662.

## St. Augustine

(We indicate the volumes of the Works of St. Augustine, which comprise sixteen volumes, from volume XXXII to volume XLVI.)

Adam means “human being,” a word common to both sexes, VII, 460.---In Hebrew, Adam signifies a human being, X, 1583, 1585.---By his own name Adam signifies the world, IV, 1236.---In the name Adam the four regions of the world are indicated, III, 1465, 1473; and the number forty-six is found there, ibid., 1474.---Adam, the first human being, VIII, 211.---At what age or stature Adam was created, III, 348.---Various difficulties if Adam’s soul was not created before it was breathed into the body, ibid., 370.---For what purpose woman was given to Adam, VI, 331.---What Adam was like when created, VII, 790.---How he was created in God’s image, VI, 331.---Whether he was created wise, I, 607, 1305.---Adam was created just, V, 1426.---Adam was in a nature without fault or vice, ibid., 172.---Adam’s blessedness, VII, 434.---Adam was made by God with a good will, X, 1496.---Adam was created free for good work, ibid., 271, 1144.---What Adam’s body was like, VII, 393, 395.---Adam, according to the body, was earth, X, 110.---Adam did not suffer discord between flesh and spirit, ibid., 172, 173, 1536.---Adam was created immortal, ibid., 1598.---Though spiritual in mind, Adam nevertheless had an animal body, even when established in Paradise, III, 355.

Eve, the first parent, V, 1439.---What Eve signifies, III, 207, 215.---Why she was called Life, ibid., 212.---The pains of Eve in childbirth arose from the condemnation for sin, not from the condition of nature, X, 1564, 1566.

William, Abbot of St Theodore near Rheims. Physics of the human body, CLXXX, 695.

We provide an analysis of this part of the work, so that by the help of this table the state of the science of human physiology at that time may be clearly seen.

Human body.—Every living body is formed from earth, that is, composed of four [elements] . . . There are four elements of which it consists; each element is possessed of one quality only: fire, of heat; air, of moisture; water, of coldness; earth, of dryness . . . According to Hippocrates, if a living body consisted of one element, it would never suffer pain, because, being one thing, there would be nothing from which it could suffer; but the elements are corrupted, and in this way corruption comes about . . . It remains to be seen whence the four humors arise or are nourished in the body. Every food taken consists of four elements; but the book on degrees shows how variously and differently the nature of the elements is found in edible things, according to heat and cold, dryness and moisture. When food is taken, the mouth first divides it with teeth and tongue into fine, small parts . . . Food prepared in this manner is sent to the stomach through the throat and gullet . . . The gullet is a long, round, hollow, and hairy member, having inside it long hairs: some transverse, others directed upward toward the mouth. The hairs directed upward naturally draw food in, while those crossing it constrict it. The stomach has two mouths, one upper and one lower.---When the upper mouth of the stomach has received food, it closes until the food is digested. Then, retaining what it finds suitable for its nourishment, it expels the rest downward after opening the lower gate. The stomach performs these operations through four powers natural to it: appetitive, retentive, digestive, and expulsive. These powers are not absent especially from the brain, on account of the animal or sensory power; from the heart, on account of the spiritual power; from the liver, on account of the natural power; and from the genitals, on account of the generative power . . . Nor are the intestines below the stomach without them. The duodenum receives what is expelled through the lower gate; it is so called because its measure is twelve fingers. As soon as digestion and, through digestion, alteration of the digested thing have occurred, the evacuation of feculent matters follows. Other intestines receive what is expelled: three fine ones above, around the mouth of the stomach, and three coarse ones below. There is also one lower intestine called fine; after the expelled matter has descended into it, it remains there for a time, until by a second digestion the fluid is better purified and refined. Through the veins called mesaraic veins, it sends what is fine and pure back to the liver. The liver receives the aforesaid fluid through the aforesaid veins and through what is called the portal vein, transforms it into its own nature, and digests it again. For whatever in it is fiery is taken up by red bile for its nourishment; whatever is airy, by blood; whatever is watery or moist, by phlegm; whatever is coarse and earthy, by black bile. Thus the four humors, created in the liver and distributed from the liver throughout the whole body, if they proceed according to the right rule of nature, although they are of different quality, nevertheless produce one condition of health, cooperating with and helping one another . . . From this digestion also a mild and sweet vapor rises, gently touches the brain, and oppresses its ventricles so greatly that it puts all its activities to sleep: this is sleep. During it, when all the soul’s faculties have ceased, the natural faculty alone remains active . . . At first foods become white, that is, phlegmatic, in the middle of the stomach; around the lower regions near the liver, like watery blood; when cooked in the liver, blood; more thoroughly cooked, red bile; excessively cooked, black bile. (Other similar matters relating to human physiology follow.)

Puberty begins approximately in the fourteenth year for males and in the twelfth for females, II, 716 and 905.

ARNOBIUS.

Corrupted air, a cause of diseases, V, 731.

Aesculapius, discoverer of medicaments, V, 770.

LACTANTIUS.

Aesculapius, discoverer of medicine, VI, 213.

[Col. 0529] On the Workmanship of God.—On the generation of beasts and humankind, VII, 14.—On the constitution of livestock and humankind, 16.—On human frailty, 20.—On the forms and limbs of animals, 24.—On Epicurus’ error concerning the limbs and their use, 27.—On all the parts of the body, 30.—On the human parts, the eyes and ears, 33.—On the senses and their power, 39.—On the external limbs of humankind and their use, 40.—On the intestines in humankind and their use, 48.—On the womb, conception, and the sexes, 53.—On the lower limbs, 58.—On the unknown function of certain intestines, 60.—On the voice, 62.—On the mind and its seat, 64.—On the soul, and philosophers’ opinions concerning it, 68.—On soul and mind, and their affections, 70.—On the soul, given by God, 72.—Physicians cut the skullcap, 246.

ST. DAMASUS, POPE.

Leprosy of the Emperor Constantine, VIII, 799.

CASSIODORUS, ROMAN SENATOR.

The waters of Barmia cure gout, LXIX, 817.—Gout is graphically described, ibid.

ST. ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE.

On medicine, LXXXII, 183.—Etymology of the name, ibid.—On the inventors of medicine, ibid.—On the three schools of physicians, ibid.—The Methodic school, 184.—The Empiric school, ibid.—The Rational school, ibid.

On the four humours of the body, LXXXII, 184.—The humour of blood, ibid.—Cholera, 185.—Melancholy, ibid.—Phlegm, ibid.

On acute diseases, LXXXII, 185.—Fever, ibid.—Phrenitis, ibid.—Cardiac disease, ibid.—Lethargy, ibid.—Synanche, 186.—Phlegmon, ibid.—Pleurisy, ibid.—Peripneumonia, ibid.—Apoplexy, ibid.—Spasm, ibid.—Tetanus, ibid.—Telum [“dart”], ibid.—Ileus, ibid.—Hydrophobia, ibid.—Carbuncle, 187.—Pestilence, ibid.—Inguinal disease, ibid.

On chronic diseases, LXXXII, 187.—Headache, ibid.—Scotoma, ibid.—Vertigo, 188.—Epilepsy, ibid.—The comitial, or divine, disease, ibid.—Mania, ibid.—Melancholy, ibid.—Types [of fever], ibid.—Rheum, ibid.—Catarrh, 189.—Coryza, ibid.—Bronchial disease, ibid.—Hoarseness, ibid.—Peripneumonia, ibid.—Haemoptysis, ibid.—Consumption, ibid.—Cough, ibid.—Abscess, ibid.—Empyema, [Col. 0530] ibid.—Hepatic disease, ibid.—Disease of the spleen, ibid.—Dropsy, ibid.—Nephritis, ibid.—Paralysis, ibid.—Cachexia, 190.—Atrophy, ibid.—Obesity, ibid.—Sciatica, ibid.—Gout, ibid.—Arthritic disease, ibid.—Stone, ibid.—Strangury, ibid.—Satyriasis, ibid.—Diarrhoea, ibid.—Dysentery, ibid.—Lientery, ibid.—Colic, ibid.—Anal fissures, ibid.

On diseases visible on the surface of the body, LXXXII, 191.—Alopecia, ibid.—Parotid swellings, ibid.—Freckles, ibid.—Erysipelas, ibid.—Sarpedo is a redness of the skin, ibid.—Impetigo, ibid.—Itching, ibid.—Night-blindness, ibid.—Warts, ibid.—Elephantiasis, 192.—Jaundice, ibid.—Cancer, ibid.—Boil, ibid.—Stye, ibid.—Yawning, ibid.—Ulcer, ibid.—Pustule, ibid.—Papule, ibid.—Ichor, ibid.—Scar, ibid.

On remedies and medicaments, LXXXII, 193.—Regimen, ibid.—Pharmacy, ibid.—Surgery, ibid.—Antidote, ibid.—Arterial remedies, ibid.—Theriac, ibid.—Purgatives, ibid.—Catapotia [pills], ibid.—Diameron, ibid.—Diacodion, ibid.—Diaspermaton, ibid.—Electuary, ibid.—Trochisk, ibid.—Eye-salves, ibid.—Epithem, ibid.—Poultice, ibid.—Plaster, ibid.—Emollient, ibid.—Enema, ibid.—Pessary, ibid.—Medicine for beasts of burden, invented by Chiron, ibid.—Critical days, ibid.

On medical books, LXXXII, 194.

On physicians’ instruments, LXXXII, 194.—Phlebotome, ibid.—A similar instrument, ibid.—Hook, ibid.—Spatomele, ibid.—Guva, 195.—Ball, ibid.—Pestle, ibid.—Mortar, ibid.—Whetstone, ibid.

On perfumes and ointments, LXXXII, 195.—Scent, ibid.—Thymiama [incense], ibid.—Thyme, ibid.—Incense, ibid.—Tetraidos, ibid.—Stacte, ibid.—Myrobalan, 196.—Telinian ointment, 195.—Amaracine ointment, 196.—Anethine ointment, ibid.

On the origin of medicine, LXXXII, 196. It is called the second philosophy because it contains all the arts, ibid., 198.

RABANUS MAURUS.

On medicine, CXI, 500.
