[Col. 0529]

CCXX. INDEX OF BOTANY. ALPHABETICALLY RECORDING EVERYTHING THE FATHERS WROTE CONCERNING VARIOUS PLANTS AND THEIR PROPERTIES.

[Col. 0529] *Aaron maculatum* (Herb of Aaron), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1148.

Fir: why it is so called, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 114, 135.—The fir is called so because it rises far above other trees, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 614; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 516.—Some call it Gallic because of its whiteness, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 615.

Abratanum (*olus odoratum*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 639.

Wormwood, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1124.—Wormwood grows in the region of Pontus, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630; Werner, abbot, CLVII, 1151.

Acanthus, an Egyptian herb, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 626.

Maple, unequal in its colours, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 616.—Sycamore maple (*Acer pseudoplatanus*; *Ahorn*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1237.

Yarrow (*Achillea millefolium*; *Garwa*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1175.

Grape-berries (*acina*), St. Isidore, CLXXXII, 604.

Aconites. Acone is a harbour in Bithynia so celebrated for the production of harmful herbs that we call poisonous plants *aconita* from that place, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 626; Werner, abbot, CLVII, 1151.

Acorus, resembling iris in its leaves, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 625.

The fat of wheat, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1046, 1930.

*Adoreum*, a kind of wheat, also commonly called seed. [Col. 0530] *Ador* was formerly so named from eating, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599.

Holm oak (*aesculus*), from food: an acorn-bearing tree, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 614; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 515; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 113.

Agaric, the root of white vine, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

*Agenbaum*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1243.

Agrimony, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1128; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1176.

Alga grows in standing waters, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635.

*Alica*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600.

*Alicastrum*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600.

Garlic is so called because it has a smell, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 531.—Shallot (*Allium ascalonicum*; *alslauch*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1162.—Onion (*Allium cepa*; *Unlauch*), ibid., 1163.—Welsh onion (*Allium fistulosum*; *lauch*), ibid.—Leek (*Allium porrum*; *borrum*), ibid., 1162.—Garlic (*Allium sativum*), ibid.

Alder is called so because it is nourished by a stream, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 616; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 519; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 115.—Black alder (*Alnus glutinosa*; *Arla*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1237.

Aloes, a tree of very sweet scent, is produced in India and Arabia, [Col. 0531] St. Isidore, LXXXII, 622; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 525.

Aloe, an herb of most bitter juice, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 627; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1196, 1209.

Medicinal chickweed (*Alsine medica*; *Hunsdarm*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1189.

Marsh mallow (*Althaea*), because it rises high; wild mallow, or mallow-mist, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632.—Marsh mallow (*Althaea officinalis*; *ybischa*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1187.

Ambrosia, which the Latins call wild celery, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632.—*Ambros*, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1128.

Amomum is so called because, when old, it gives off the scent of cinnamon. It grows in Syria and Armenia, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 622.—Zedoary (*Amomum zedoaria*; *Zituar*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1135.—Ginger (*Amomum zingiber*; *Ingeber*), ibid., 1135.

*Ampelos leuce*, without bryony, which the Latins call white vine, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 634.—*Ampelos melaina*, that is, black vine, likewise the wild vine, ibid.

Amurca, the watery part of oil, so called from rising up, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 613; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 523; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXII, 113.

Almond tree. *Amygdala* is a Greek name; in Latin it is called the long nut, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 613; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 514, 523.—Common almond (*Amygdalus communis*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1226.—Peach tree (*Amygdalus persica*; *Persichbaum*), ibid., 1220.—On almonds and their properties, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 113.

Anchusa, whose crushed root stains the fingers, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 631.

Anise, very hot and promoting urination, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 639.

Dill, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 639.—Fennel (*Anethum feniculum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1156.—Dill (*Anethum graveolens*; *Dille*), ibid., 1158.

*Anthenis pyrethrum* (*Bertram*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1138.

*Apiago*, so called because bees are especially attracted to its flowers, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632.

Celery is so called because the boar (*aper*), that is, the head of ancient triumphants, was crowned with it, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 531, 532.—Its kinds are *petroselinon*, *hipposelinon*, and *oleaselinon*, ibid.—On celery, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1127.—Celery (*Apium graveolens*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1159.—Parsley (*Apium petroselinum*), ibid., 1158.

*Apapores*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

Common columbine (*Aquilegia vulgaris*; *Agleija*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1184.

Tree. The name *arbor* (“tree”), unlike that of herbs, is believed to be derived from fields (*arva*), because trees adhere to the earth by roots fixed in it. An *arbor* may be fruit-bearing or sterile; *arbos*, however, only fruit-bearing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 508.—On the origin of trees, St. Ambrose, XIV, 175.—On the utility and variety of trees; on the method of yoking and treating them; finally, on the properties of tree juices, ibid., 176 ff.—On evergreen trees and their distinctions, ibid., 185.—How and when trees were created, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 275.—Created on the third day according to causal reasons, ibid., 259.—Herbs and trees are spoken of not only according to kind but also according to likeness, ibid., 287.—Grafting of trees, ibid., 405.—How a tree comes from seed and seed from a tree, ibid., 358.—Everything belonging to a tree was originally in its seed by causal force and potential, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 357.—The Manichaeans think that trees live in such a way that they feel and suffer when injured, id., XLII, 37.—On trees, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 137.—Aromatic trees, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 620.—On the proper names of trees, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 511.

Young tree (*arbustum*): a young and tender tree into which grafting can be made, and so called as though “the spear of a tree.” Others understand *arbustum* as a place in which trees stand, as *salictum* means a willow grove, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 508.

An awn (*arista*) is so called because it is itself the first to dry up, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

Long and round birthwort (*aristolochia*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630.

Horseradish, that is, *lapsana*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638.

Mountain arnica (*Arnica montana*; *Wolfesgelegena*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1190.

*Arnoglossos*, that is, “lamb’s tongue,” called *plantago* by the Romans, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629, 630.

Aromatics are all fragrant substances sent from India, Arabia, or other regions, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 620; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 523.

[Col. 0532] Aromatic trees, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 620; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506, 511, 523; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111, 137.

*Arrotonum*, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1129.

Artemisia (Greek *artemis*, ἄρτεμις), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629.—Southernwood (*Artemisia abrotanum*; *Stagwurtz*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1161.—Wormwood (*Artemisia absinthium*; *Wermuda*), CXCVII, 1172.—Mugwort (*Artemisia vulgaris*; *Riboz*), ibid., 1171.

Reed is so called because it dries quickly, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 521.

Asarum grows in shady mountains and has leaves like cassia, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 624.—European asarabacca (*Asarum europaeum*; *Haselwurlz*), St. Hildegard, CXCXII, 1146, 1206.

Ascalonion, so called from Ascalon, whence it was brought, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

Asparagus is so called because it is thorny and its shrub is rough, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 628.

Asphodel, called *Albutium* by the Latins from its colour, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

Shield fern (*Aspidium filix*; *Farn*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1147.

Spleenwort, *asplenos scolopendrium*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633; St. Hildegard (*Hirtzunge*), CXCVII, 1142.—Wall-rue (*Asplenium ruta muraria*; *Stembreka*), ibid., 1185.

*Astrantia ostruthium* (*Astrcncia*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1192.

*Athamanta meum* (*Berurtz*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1184.

Orache and garden orache (*Atriplex* and *Atriplex hortensis*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637; (*Melda*) St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1170.

Hazelnuts (*avellanae nuces*) are named from Avellano, where they abound, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 613; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 514.

Oats, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 529; cultivated oats (*Avena sativa*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1130.

Bird-haunted woodland is called *aviaria*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.

*Babela*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1067.

*Balsamita*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1202.

Balsam, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 622, 623; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 523, 526; St. Hildegard, DVII [probably CXCVII], 1197.

Burdock (*Bardana lappa*; *cletta*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1167.

*Basilisca*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1210.

*Bathenia*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1182.

Bdellium, a tree of India and Arabia, whose Arabian “tear” is better, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 621; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 525.

*Bencala*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

Beet: a kind of vegetable, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

Betony, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1127.

White birch (*Betula alba*; *Bircka*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1238.

*Birckwurtz*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1192.

*Blitum*, a kind of vegetable, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

*Boberella*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1152.

*Borith*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1204.

Cluster of grapes (*botrus*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 604.

*Batryo*, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 507.

*Brachwurtz*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1150.

Cabbage, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.—Cabbage (*Brassica oleracea*; *Kale*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1163.—Turnip (*Brassica rapa*; *Ruba*), ibid., 1164.

Bryony, St. Hildegard, CXCXII, 1204.

Bugloss is so called by the Greeks because it has very rough leaves like an ox’s tongue; it is also taken for a vegetable, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629.

Bulbs are so called because they are rounded and globular, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638.

Ox-eye has a flower resembling a saffron-coloured eye; it grows beside the walls of cities, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 634.

Box tree (Greek *pyxos*, πύξος), an evergreen tree, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 617; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 521; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 115, 139.—Common box (*Buxus sempervirens*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 232.

*Byverwurtz*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1188.

Chervil, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1125.

*Calamites*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

Aromatic reed is so called from its likeness to the ordinary reed, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 622; Rabanus Maurus, CCI, 526.

Pot marigold (*Calcudula officinalis*; *Ringula*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1179.

Hemp (*Cannabis sativa*; *Hanf*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1133.

Maidenhair grows in watery places, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 731.

The caper seems to have taken its name from Greek, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638.

Tendrils are so called because they seize trees, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 683.

The caprifig is so called because it tears at the walls on which it grows, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 612; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 513.

Cardamom, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 625.

[Col. 0533] *Cardus*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1210.

Thistle, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638.—Blessed thistle (*Carduus benedictus*; *Distel*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1168.

Sedge, a sharp and very hard herb, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635.

Wood-rot is the decay of timber, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608.

Cassia, a bough with strong bark and purple leaves like those of pepper, grows in Arabia, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 622; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 524, 525, 526.—Cassia, an herb also called *fistula*, grows in water, is hollow, and grows to an immense height, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 140.

Chestnut (Greek *kastanon*, κάστανον), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 613; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 514, 515; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 113.—Sweet chestnut (*Castanea sativa*; *Kistenbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1126.

A stalk (*caulis*) is generally the central stem of herbs or vegetables, commonly called a *thyrsus*; it is also a kind of vegetable, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 636.

Cedar (Greek *kedron*, κέδρον), wood of pleasant scent and long duration, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 615; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 517.—On cedar and its properties, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXVII, 114, 140.—Cedar and palm do not bend even in storms, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1180.

Centaury is so called because it is said to have been discovered by Chiron the centaur, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 628.—Cornflower (*Centaurea cyanus*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1180.

*Centenum* is so called because a cast of its seed produces a hundredfold increase of grain, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600.

The onion is so called because it is nothing other than a head, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 531.

The cherry tree is named from Cerasus, a city of Pontus, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 612; Rabanus Maurus, CXL, 523.

Tufts (*cespites*) are shrubs, as if *cuspites* [“points”] or as if “around the feet,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.

Chamomile is so called in Greek because it has the scent of the “Martian apple,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629.

*Chamaedrys*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629.

Chamaeleon, called *viscarago* in Latin because it produces mistletoe, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 631.

Ground pine is so called by the Greeks because it clings to the earth and has the scent of pine, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

Celandine is so called because it seems to burst forth at the coming of swallows, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 628.

Chickpea, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 602; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.—Chickpea (*Cicer arietinum*; *Kikher*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1201.

Chicory (*Cichoreum intybus*; *Sunnewirbel*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1153.

Hemlock is so called because it lies hidden, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618.—Because it has nodes in its jointed stalk, ibid., 631.—Poison hemlock (*Cicuta virosa*; *Scherling*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1144.

*Cimicia* is so called from its resemblance to a bedbug, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630.

Cinnamon is so called because its bark is rounded and slender in the manner of a reed, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 622; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 525, 526; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1139.

*Citocatia* is so called because it quickly purges the belly, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 631.

Citron tree (*Citrus medica*; *Boneziderbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1138.

*Coccimela*, which the Latins call *prunum* from its colour; others call it *nixa* from the multitude of fruit it bears, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 611.

A codex is so called, as it were, from a little trunk, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 603.

Colocasia, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

Colocynths are wild and very bitter gourds, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 628.

*Colymbades*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619.

Foliage (*comae*; see *cymae*), Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 112.

Hemlock (*conium*), Werner, abbot, CLXVII, 1151.—Poison hemlock (*Conium maculatum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1144.

Bindweed, of fields and hedges (*Convolvulus arvensis et sepium*; *Winda*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1152.

Bark is so called because it covers decayed wood, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.—On the bark of trees and on the inner bark (*liber*), Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 1225.

Hazel (*Corylus avellana*; *Haselbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1225.

Corymbs, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 604; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

Costus is the root of an herb growing in India, Arabia, and Syria, but Arabian costus is better, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 624; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 528.

*Croco magna*: after aromatic ingredients have been pressed out, saffron ointment is made into little cloth packets, and is thus called, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 624.

Saffron is named from a Cilician town called Corycium; it is the best and sweet-smelling, etc., St. Isidore, LXXXII, 624; Rabanus Maurus, BXI [probably CXI], 527.

The *crustumium*, also called *volemis*, is so named because it fills the hollow of the hand in size, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619.

Cucumbers are so called because they are sometimes bitter, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

Gourd, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 532; Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1123.—Bottle gourd (*Cucurbita lagenaria*; *Kurbesa*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1164.

The culm is the stalk of an ear of grain itself, which grows from the roots, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600; Rabanus Maurus, CXL, 506.

Cumin, *cyminum*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 639; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1138.

Cypress, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 517; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1231.

Cyclamen (Greek *kyklon*, κύκλον), so called because it has a round root, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 933.

A shoot (*cyma*) is called, as it were, a “head of hair” (*coma*). It is the topmost part of vegetables or trees, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608, 635.

Cypress is so called in Greek because its head rises from roundness to a point. Its wood has a virtue almost equal to cedar, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 615; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 517.

Cyperus is called so by the Greeks because it has a heating power. Another kind of cyperus grows in India and is called *gingiber* in their language, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 624.

Cypress. On the cypress and its solid wood, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 114, 143.

Cypros tree, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 527.

*Daneus*, with leaves like fennel and a two-palm-long stalk, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 631.

*Dauwurtz*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1150.

White dittany (*Dictamnus albus*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1177.

*Dolone*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1149.

*Dorth*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1210.

Dracontium is so called because its stalk is variegated in the manner of a serpent, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 628.

*Dryobalanops camphora*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1145.

Dittany (from Mount Dicte in Crete) is an herb of such power that it expels iron from the body and ejects arrows, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 627.—Dittany, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1177.

Ebony grows in India and Ethiopia; when cut, it hardens into stone, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 615; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 518.

*Ebulo*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1210.

Elaeomeli grows in the Syrian city of Palmyra, so called because oil flows from its trunk with the thickness of honey, St. Isidore, LVXXII [probably LXXXII], 611.

Hellebore is named from the Greek river Helleborus; it has two kinds, white and black, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 626.

*Epimelis*, a medium-sized tree resembling the service tree, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 611.

*Epithymum* (“thyme-flower”) is a flower like thyme, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 625.

*Erlizbaum*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1240.

Erigeron is named from Greek because it grows old early in spring, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630.

Stork’s-bill (*Erodium cicutarium*; *cramchnabel*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1188.

Rocket is so called, as it were, from *urnea*, because it has a fiery quality; it has two kinds, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638.

Vetch, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 602.—Bitter vetch (*Ervum ervilia*; *Wisela*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1201.—Lentil (*Ervum lens*; *lente*), ibid., 1132.

Clove (*Eugenia caryophyllata*; *Gariofiles*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1141.

Leafy spurge (*Euphorbia esula*; *wulffesmilch*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1149.

Caper spurge (*Euphorbia lathyris*; *Springwurtz*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1184.

Euphorbium is so called, and its juice sharpens the sight of the eyes, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 627.

Spindle tree (*Euonymus europaea*; *Kynelbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1238.

Bean, as if from Greek *phagein* (φαγεῖν, “to eat”), because human beings first used this legume. It has two kinds: the common bean and the Egyptian bean, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 601; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1132.

Beech (Greek *phagein*, φαγεῖν, “to eat”) and holm oak (*aesculus*, “food”) are acorn-bearing trees, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 614; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 515; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 113.—Wild beech, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1235.

Spelt is so called because at first it was broken, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599.

[Col. 0535] *Farrago* (from *far*, “spelt”) is barley grass still green, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600.

*Frasetas*, a cheap kind of legume, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 602; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 596.

*Felbaum*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1240.

The Latins call fennel so because the juice of its stem or root sharpens the sight, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 688; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 632.—On fennel, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1123.

Hay is so called because flame is fed by it, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 335; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 529.—On hay, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 147.

Fertility.—On the fertility of the earth, St. Ambrose, XIV, 169, 173.

Giant fennel is named from its pith (Greek *apoderon*, ἀπόδερον). Some derive *ferula* from striking, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 634; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 528.

Lesser celandine (*Ficaria verna*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1205.

The fig is so called from fecundity, for it is more fruitful than other trees, St. Isidore, CLXXXII, 612; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 513; Hugh of St. Victor, CXXXVII, 113, 146.—On its properties, the same authors, ibid.—On the fig leaf, St. Ambrose, XIV, 182.—Egyptian fig wood does not float on water, St. Augustine, XLI, 715.—Common fig (*Ficus carica*; *Fuckbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1227.

Fern is so called from the singularity of its leaf, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635.

Branches are called *flagella*, the uppermost parts of trees, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 1120.

*Flomos*. See *Phlomos*.

Flowers are named as though *fluentes* (“flowing”), because they quickly perish, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 528.—On flowers, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 112, 146.

What hay and hay-flower are, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1333.—By the name “hay” crops of grain are also meant, ibid., 1400.—Roof-hay: an herb that grows on roofs, ibid., 1694.—See *Fenum*.

*Folbaum*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1240.

Leaves are called *phylla* (φύλλα) in Greek, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 527.—A leaf is thin, broad, and light; it makes shade, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 147.—On the diversity of leaves, St. Ambrose, XIV, 182.

*Folium* is so called because it is collected floating without any root upon the shores of India, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 623.

The husk (*folliculus*) is the sheath of grain in which the kernel is kept inside, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 596.

*Fornhaff*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1238.

Wild strawberry (*Fragaria vesca*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1194.

Ash is so called because it grows chiefly in rough and mountainous places, among crags (*fragae*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 616; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 519; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 115.—Common ash (*Fraxinus excelsior*; *asch*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1236.

Foliage (*frondes*) is so called because shrubs bear it, or because it bears shade, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.

The manner of fruit-bearing, St. Ambrose, XIV, 169.—How fitting is the order maintained in the earth’s fruit-bearing, ibid., 171.

What fruits are, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 112, 147.—The name *fructus* derives from *frumen*, that is, the projecting part of the throat by which we eat, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608.—The difference among fruits nourished in water, St. Ambrose, XIV, 182.

Grains, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599, 608; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 505.

Properly, cereal grains (*frumenta*) are so called from chewing (*frumendo*) and are those which have awns, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 505.—The fat of wheat, St. Augustine, XXXVII, 1046, 1930.

*Frusus*, a kind of bramble, grows naturally; it is thorny and impassable, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 147.

A shrub (*frutex*) is called short because it covers the ground with foliage, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.

*Fuous* is a kind of herb from which cloth is dyed, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 634.

Fungi are so called because, when dry, they take up fire, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1194.

Galangal (*Alpinia galanga*; *galgan*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1134.

Galbanum is the juice of giant fennel, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 627; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 528.

Gallnut, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 518.

*Genicularis*, an herb spread beneath one to repel the power of scorpions, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

Gentian takes its name from its discoverer; its roots resemble those of birthwort, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629.—Yellow gentian (*Gentiana lutea*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1142.

Meadow cranesbill (*Geranium pratense*; *storcksnabel*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1191.

Buds.—A *germen* is a fruit-bearing shoot, so called from bearing, [Col. 0536] whence also “germination,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 112.

Germination, St. Ambrose, XIV, 166, 169; St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 112.

Wood avens (*Geum urbanum*; *benedicta*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1192.

Gladiolus is so called because it has leaves like a sword, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.—*Gladiola*, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1125.—Common gladiolus (*Gladiolus communis*; *swertula*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1177.

Acorn, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 614; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 514, 515.—The acorn comes from the oak and is food for pigs, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 148.

Ground ivy (*Glechoma hederacea*; *gunderebe*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1171.

Liquorice is so called because it has a sweet root, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 628.

Grass is named from its situation because it belongs to very many fields, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635.

Grain is sown, dies, sprouts into grass, then into an ear and afterward into cereal grain; it is harvested and threshed, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 148.

*Grensing*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1189.

*Grintwartz*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1185.

*Gumen* is a Greek name: this is what they call *kori* (κόρι), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 523.

*Harbeum*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1242.

*Hartenauwe*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1208.

*Hartrogelbaum*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1241.

*Hartz*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1201.

Ivy is so called because it clings by creeping to trees, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 626; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 528.—Ivy creeps, remains ever green, is sterile, does not shed its foliage, has an attractive nature, and crowns victors, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 148.—Ivy (*Hedera helix*; *ebich*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1186.

Heliotrope takes its name because its leaves turn in accordance with the motions of the sun; hence it is also called *salsequia* by the Latins, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 628.

Hellebore, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 626; Werner, abbot, CLVII, 1151, 1152.—Black hellebore (*Helleborus niger*; *cristiana*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1141; (*nyosewurtz*), ibid., 1189.

Herb, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 508, 527.—On herbs, Werner, abbot, CLVII, 1151.—On the healthfulness and remedies of herbs, St. Ambrose, XIV, 167, 169.—On the herb upon which *Bifilbere* grow, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1151, 1152, 1208.

Shepherds called it *herbitum* because it is supplied to livestock in place of grass, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618.

*Herpyllus*, called *serpillum* among us because its roots creep far; it is also *matrisaminula*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630.

*Heylbeubt*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1147.

*Hierabotane* (*sagmen*, *sancimen*, *verbena*) is so called because, among the pagans, it was judged suitable for the purifications of priests, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630.

Mouse-ear hawkweed (*Hieracium pilosella*; *musor*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1177.

*Hiffa*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1243.

Horse celery is so called because it is hard and astringent, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 532.

Mare’s-tail (*Hippuris vulgaris*; *catzenzagel*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 1208.

*Hirceswurtz*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1207.

*Hirtzwam*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1143.

Barley is so called because its ear has an order, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 505; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1131.

*Humela*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1149.

Hops (*Humulus lupulus*; *hoppho*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1153.

Hyacinth is an herb having a purple flower, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 625.—The hyacinth changes with the air: clear in fair weather, dark in cloudy weather, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 149.

Henbane is called so by the Greeks; by the Latins, *herba calicularis*, because its little cups grow in the form of goblets, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629.—Black henbane (*Hyoscyamus niger*; *bilsa*), Hildegard, CXCVII, 1173.

Hyssop, an herb suitable for cleansing the lungs, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 628; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 527; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 149; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1156.

*Iffa*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1242.

Holm oak is called from “chosen.” For human beings first chose the fruit of this tree for their food, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 613, 614; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 515; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 113.

Elecampane (*Inula helenicum*; *alant*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1167.

[Col. 0537] Grafting is when a shoot of a fertile tree is inserted into the cleft trunk of a sterile one, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.

Endive is so called because there is *tophus* [a porous stone] within it, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

Elecampane, called *alano* by country people, with an aromatic root, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 639.

Illyrian iris received its name from its likeness to the heavenly rainbow, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 624.

Walnut (*Juglans regia*; *Nuszbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1219.

Juncus (“rush”) is so called because it clings with joined roots, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 634; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 521.---The rush grows in water; it is flexible, pointed at the top, slender, green, etc., Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 150.---On the rush, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1191.

Juniper is said to have a Greek name, either because it tapers from broad to narrow, or because it retains the fire conceived for a long time, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 615; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 518.---On juniper, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXVIII, 114, 150.---Common juniper (*Wacholderbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1241.---Phoenician juniper and *Oxycedrus* (“cedar”), ibid., CXCVII, 1230.---*Juniperus sanbia* (*Sybenbaum*), ibid., 1233.

The *labrusca* is the wild vine that grows at the borders of fields; *labrusca* derives from *labra* (“edges”), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 602–603; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

Tears.---The difference among tears dripping from trees, St. Ambrose, XIV, 182.

Lettuce is so called because it overflows with an abundance of milk, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 531–532.---Garden lettuce (*Latich*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1165.---Wild lettuce is that which we call *Sarratia*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1165.

White dead-nettle (*Binsuga*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1155.

*Lapago*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

*Lapathum*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638.

*Lapella*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

*Lapistus*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638.

Burdock is so called because it has a stalk in a lineage [reading uncertain: *in gentem*], St. Isidore, LXXXII, 631.---Burdock, ibid., 633.

The larch is named from the fortress of Laricinum, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 616.

Laserwort is a herb that grows on Mount Oscobagi, where the river Ganges also rises, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 627.

The laurel is named from the word for praise.---The Greeks call this tree δάφνη, *daphnē* (“laurel”), because of its perpetual greenness, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 609; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 512.---On the laurel and its properties, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 112. Cinnamon laurel, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1139.---Noble laurel, ibid., 1228.

Lavender spike, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1140.---True lavender, ibid., 1143.

Legumes derive their name from gathering, as though “chosen things”; there are very many kinds of legumes, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 601; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

*Lemnae* (*Merlinsen*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1208.

The lentil is so called because it is moist and pliant, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 601.

*Lenticula*, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

The mastic tree is so called because it is pliant and soft, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 617; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 520, 523, 325.

Garden cress, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, [reference omitted in source].

Lebanon is a tree in Arabia, with broad bark and leaf, resembling frankincense; it emits a juice like that of the almond tree, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 150.

The inner bark (*liber*) is the interior part of the bark, so called from the bark having been freed, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.---On the inner bark, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXVII, 111.

Lovage, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1125.

Firewood is so called because, when burned, it is changed into light. Hence—

Lovage takes its name from a region; it has an aromatic smell and a sharp taste, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 532.

Lilies are, as it were, *liclia*, a plant with a milky-white flower, whence their name, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 626; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 528.---On the lily, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1126; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1151; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1153.---The lily grows from uncultivated ground, springs up in valleys, is fragrant, white, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 151.---White lily, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1140.

Flax is sown first, is quickly injured, and is slender and sparse, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 151.---Common flax (*linsamo*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1189.---On flaxseed, ibid., 1202.

Darnel, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 529; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1151.---Darnel by no means grows from the seed of wheat, St. Ambrose, XIV, 173.

*Lubestuckel*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1186.

A grove (*lucus*, “from light”) is a density of trees that takes away the sunlight, [Col. 0538] St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606–607; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.

Lupine is a Greek name, because its bitterness makes the face sad, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 602.---White lupine (*Vigbona*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1201.

*Lyciniae* derives from λύχνος, *lychnos* (“lamp”), because they give the best light, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619.

A lamp (*lychnum*) is so called because it gives light, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608; St. Isidore [probably Hugh of St. Victor], CLXXVII, 112.

*Mal­leolus*, St. Isidore, 603.---A *malleolus* is a young vine-shoot growing from the previous year’s tendril, ibid.

The apple is said by the Greeks to be so called because its fruit is the roundest of all fruits. The Matian apple, quinces, pomegranate, Persian apple, clingstone peach, and Armenian apple received their names from the places from which they were first brought, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 609–610; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 512–514.---Pomegranate, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 512; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 113.---Pomegranate, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 112–113.

Why the apple tree is so called, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 112.

Mallow (ἀπὸ τοῦ μαλάσσειν, “from softening”), because it has the nature of softening and loosening the belly, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 636.

Mandrake is so called because it has sweet-smelling apples as large as a Matian apple. There are two kinds, female and male, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 627; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 528–529; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1152.---*Mandragora atropa*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1151.

Sheaf.---By a sheaf we mean a bundle of hay, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635.

Horehound is so called because of its bitterness; it grows in fields, St. Isidore, LXXVII, 630.---On horehound, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1125.---Common horehound (*Andron*), St. Hildegard, CXVII, 1142.

*Masal*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1240.

Mastic is a drop from the mastic tree. It is called *granomastix* because it is shaped like grains, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 621; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 525.

The citron tree takes its name from the Medes. The Greeks call it κεδρόμηλον, *kedromēlon*, “citron”; it is nearly always full of fruit, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 610–611.

Honey, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1197.

The *melimelum* is so called because its fruit has the taste of honey, or because it is preserved in honey, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 610; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 512.

*Melipepo*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

The *mella* tree, commonly called the Syrian bean, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 611.

The *melopos* is a tree in Africa from which a viscous juice flows, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 611.

*Menna*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1170.

Mint.---It has six kinds, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 639.

Mint, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1126.---Wild mint, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.---Water mint (*Bachmyntza*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1161.---Field mint (*Myntza*), ibid., 1161.---Curly mint (*Rossemyntza*), ibid., 1161.---Wood mint (*myntza minor*), ibid., 1161. Pennyroyal mint (*polega*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1181.

*Meranda*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1200.

*Merrich*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1177.

The medlar is a thorny tree, with fruit resembling apples, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 611.---German medlar (*Nespelbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1227.

*Metra*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1177.

*Metzbaum*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1241.

*Men*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 625.

*Meygilana*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1191.

Myrobalan, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

The mulberry is so called by the Greeks; the Latins call it *rubus* (“bramble”), because its fruits redden like those of a shrub, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 612–613.---On the mulberry and its properties, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 113.---Black mulberry (*mulbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1225.

*Musetha*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1192.

Forget-me-not (*Myosotis scorpioides*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1184.

*Myricæ*, called tamarisk by the Latins, are named from bitterness, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 617; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 519.---On tamarisks, St. Ambrose, XIV, 184.

Nutmeg (*Myristica moschata*; “concerning the musk-nut”), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1139.

Myrrh is an Arabian tree five cubits high. Its spontaneously flowing drop is more precious; when extracted by a wound in the bark, it is judged less valuable, St. Isidore, LXXX, 621; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 523, 525–526; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 153.---On myrrh, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1197.

The myrtle is named from the sea, because it is chiefly a coastal tree, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 617; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 519–520.---Common myrtle (*mirtelbaum*), [Col. 0539] St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1240.

*Napocaulis* has a compound name from two vegetables, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 636.

Turnip, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 636.

Narcissus is a herb with a fabulously given name, from a certain boy whose limbs were transformed into this flower, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 626.

Nard is a spike-bearing herb; hence it is called by the Greeks ναρδοστάχυς, *nardostachys* (“nard-spike”). One kind is called Indian, another Syrian, another Celtic, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 623; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 527.---On nard, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 153.

The name nasturtium comes from its taste, because its sharpness twists the nose, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.---Watercress (*bions crasse*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1161.

A sacred grove (*nemus*) is named from divine powers, because pagans set up idols there, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111, 160.

Catmint, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1128.---Catnip (*Nepeta cataria*, *Nebetta*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1187.

Black cumin, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1133.

*Nimphia*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1208.

*Nucicla*, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 514.

Kernels, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 515.

The walnut is so called because its shade or the dripping of its leaves harms neighbouring trees. The Latins call it *juglans*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 613; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 514.---On the different kinds of walnut, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXII, 113, 154.

Eyes are the nodes from which leaves emerge, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.

Basil, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

Olive tree (*Oleybaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1229.---On the virtue of olive twigs, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1150.

The wild olive is so called because it resembles the olive in its leaves, though they are broader, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 522, 532.

*Oleoselinon*, because it is softer and tender in leaf and stalk, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638.

Oil is named from the olive tree, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 522.

*Olisatrum*, St. Isidore, CXXXII, 637.

The olive is the fruit of the olive tree, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 518; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 522.---The olive tree is a sign of peace, yields oil, and is beautiful, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 154.

Vegetable (*olus*) is named from smelling, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 530–531.---*Olus malle*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

Opium, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 627; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1152.

The *orchades* are olives, so called in Greek from their resemblance to testicles, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619.

*Orcibeta*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

Oregano, which in Latin is interpreted “colouring,” because when infused it colours wine, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632.---Common oregano (*dost*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1175.

Fodder was created for cattle before food for humankind: why, St. Ambrose, XIV, 167.

*Palea* is named from *pala* or from *pale*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 601.

*Paliurus* is a very rough and thorny herb, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 521.

The palm is so called because it is the ornament of a victorious hand, or because its branches are spread out. It is a tree distinguished by victory, with a tall and graceful growth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 609; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 511.---On the palm and its fruits, called dates, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 122, 155.---On the palm, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1247.

The vine-shoot bears fruit on the vine; apart from the vine it withers, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 155.---A vine-shoot is soft material of the vine which, sent out through young arms, bears fruit. *Palmes* derives from *palma*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 603; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

The vine-leaf is a leaf by whose protection the vine is defended from cold or heat, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 603; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVI, 155.---On the *campinus* [probably *pampinus*, vine-leaf], St. Ambrose, XIV, 182.

Panacea is a herb of fragrant smell, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 627.

Millet is so called because in many regions people are sustained by it in place of bread, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600.

Italian millet (*venich*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1133.---Common millet (*hers, milic*), ibid., 1133, 1202.

Poppy is a sleep-inducing herb, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 627.---On the poppy, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1126; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1167.

[Col. 0540] *Paphiae*, named from Paphos, whence they were first brought, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619.

Papyrus is so called because it is suitable for fire and wax candles, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 634.

Grass-of-Parnassus (*morkrut*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1189.

Parsnip is so called because its root is a chief nourishment for humankind, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 636.---Cultivated parsnip, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1204.

The *pausia*, which country people corruptly call *pusiana*, is suited to yielding green and sweet oil, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619.

*Pefferkrut*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1144.

Burnet saxifrage (*bibenzella*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1184.

Five-leafed plant, so called from the number of its leaves, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 628.

Melon, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 532; Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1124.

Parsley is so called because it resembles celery and grows among rocks and steep mountains, which we may call “rock-celery,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 532.

The bean is said to be named from Phaselis, an island of Greece, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

Date palm (*Datilbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1230.

*Phlomos*, which the Latins call *verbascum* (“mullein”), has one kind male and another female, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632, 634.

*Phu* grows in Pontus, with leaves like those of the wild olive, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 624.

Spruce, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1247.

Spices, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 523.

Stone pine, St. Ambrose, XIV, 184; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 514.

The pine is a pitch-tree, so called from the point of its leaves, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 614; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 516.---The pine is a pitch-tree because it sweats out pitch, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 114.---Fir pine, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1232.

The pepper tree grows in India and on the side of Mount Caucasus. The nature of pepper is white, though its fruit is varied, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 621; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 525.---Cubeb pepper (*cubebo*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1141.---Long and black pepper, ibid., CXCVII, 1137.

The pear tree (*pirus/pyrus*) seems to be so called because it is shaped like fire. *Pyrus* is the tree; its fruit is the pear, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 611–612.---Common pear (*birbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1217.---Quince pear (*Quittenbaum*), ibid., 1220.---Apple pear (*affaldra*), St. Hildegard, 1215.

Peas (*pisa*, “gold-weight”), because a small quantity of gold was weighed by them, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 602.

Pistachio is so called because the rind of its fruit has the scent of genuine nard, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 614; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 516.---On the pistachio tree, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 114.

Ground grain (*pistum*) derives from feeding, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600.

Pea, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

Pitch is a Greek name; the Greeks call it πύσσαν, *pyssan*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 620; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 516.

Plants are derived from trees, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.---How all plants contain either seed or something that performs the function of seed, St. Ambrose, XIV, 184.

Seedlings are those that have grown from seeds together with roots, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.

Greater, middle, and lanceolate plantain, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1169.---Flea plantain, ibid., 1140.

The plane tree (πλάτος, *platos*, “breadth”) is named from the breadth of its leaves, or because the tree itself is spreading and broad, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 616; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 514, 518; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 114, 147.

Peony is named after Paeon, its discoverer; it is a herb of sweet taste. It grows in woods, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629.---Common peony (*beonia*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1181.

*Plionia*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1210.

*Polion* is called by the Greeks; the Latins call it *omnimorbia* (“remedy for every disease”), because it relieves many illnesses, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 631.

*Knotweed*, which the Latins call the blood-herb, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 631.---Water-pepper (*Ertpeffer*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1193.

*Polypodium* is a herb whose root is shaggy and hairy like a polypus, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630.---St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1205.

Fruits, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606.---Fruit derives from *opimus*, that is, the abundance of plenty, ibid., 608; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 514; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 152, 157.---On the difference among simple fruits, [Col. 0541] St. Ambrose, XIV, 182.

The poplar is so called because a multitude grows from its stump. It has two kinds: one white and the other black, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 616–617; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 519; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 115.---Aspen (*aspa*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1266.

Leek has two kinds, headed and cut, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

Purslane, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632.---Garden purslane (*burtel*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1161.

Silverweed (*gensekraut*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1189.---Tormentil (*dornella*), ibid., CXCVII, 1191.---Species of cinquefoil (*fünffblat*), ibid., 1150.

Cowslip (*hymels schlussel*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1205.

*Pruma*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1242.

Sweet and bird cherries, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1222. Domestic and damson plums, ibid., CXCVII, 1223. Blackthorn, ibid., 1243.

*Psaffus*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1208.

Psyllium is so called because its seed resembles a flea, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630.

Pennyroyal among the Indians is more precious than pepper. It has warming power, cleanses, and digests, St. Isidore, CLXXXII, 630.

*Prileium*, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1127.

Lungwort (*Lungen wurcz*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1141.

Pyrethrum is said in Greek to have an incendiary root, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632.

The oak, or *quernus*, is so called because the gods of the gentiles were accustomed to give commands through it to those who sought them. It is a very long-lived tree, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 616; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 518.---The oak is a very long-lived tree, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 114, 158.---Pedunculate oak, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1234.

Sweepings are straw mixed with twigs and dry leaves, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608.

A grape-cluster is part of a bunch, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 604; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 507.---The grape-cluster is spherical, full within, and contains berries; it is first bitter and hard, and becomes sweet when ripe, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 158.

*Radiolae* are so called because they are oblong in the manner of rays, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619.

The root, as though fixed in the earth by certain rays, plunges into the depths, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.---The root is fixed in the earth; it is rough, hidden, supports the tree, and sends moisture to the branches, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111, 158.

Branches are what flow out from the trunk, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.---A branch grows together with the tree while on it; cut off, it withers, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 158.

The turnip derives from snatching; it is larger in root than the napus and sweeter in taste, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 636.

Radish, which the Latins call *radix* (“root”), because it puts forth a broad back, whereas the other vegetables project more at the top, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638.---On radish, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1128.---Cultivated radish (*retich*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1164.

*Rasela*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1210.

Regrowths of trees are those which sprout again after others have been cut, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.

Resin (ῥητίνη, *rhētinē*, “flowing”) is the tear exuded as sweat from wood. The first resin is turpentine; the second, mastic resin; the third, pine resin, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619–620; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 523.

Rhubarb, or Pontic rhubarb, as though “foreign root,” “Pontic root,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 628.

*Rhamnus* is a kind of bramble, commonly called the bear-bramble, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 521.

Rhododendron, which common speech corruptly calls *horandrum*, has leaves like those of the laurel and a flower like a rose, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618.

*Risza*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1192.

Oak timber, because it is the strongest of all wood, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 616; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 518.

Rosemary, whose leaves resemble those of fennel, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632.

The rose is so called because it is red with a glowing colour, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 626; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 528.---On the rose, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1128.---The rose is ruddy, fragrant, beautiful, and grows from thorns, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 159.---On the rose which at first grew without thorns, afterward bristled with them, and became an image of our life, [Col. 0542] St. Ambrose, XIV, 175.---Hundred-leaved rose, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1139.

Madder is so called because its root is red, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 636.

Bramble, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 513; Abbot Werner, CXIV, 1152.---Dewberry and bush bramble (*brema*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1193.---Bramble leaves kill a serpent, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1151.

*Rumer acetasus* (*amphora*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1145.

Sharp dock (*Sichterwurtz*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1183.

Rue is so called because it is very hot, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 639; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 532.---On rue, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1122.---Strong-smelling rue, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1155.

Country people call the outermost part of a shoot an arrow, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 603.

The willow is so called because it leaps quickly, that is, grows rapidly; it is a flexible tree, suitable for binding vines, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 617; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 519.---Goat willow (*Salewida*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1240.

A woodland pasture (*saltus*) is a dense stand of tall trees, so named because it springs up high, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.

Sage, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 639; Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1122.---Common sage (*Selba*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1154.---Clary sage (*scharlega*), ibid., 1191.

The elder is a soft, porous tree, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618.---Dwarf elder (*hatich*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1179.---Black elder (*Hulderbaum*), ibid., 1241.

*Sampsuchus* is what the Latins call *amaracum*; it is a herb suitable for ointments, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 625.

European sanicle, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1146.

A vine-branch (*sarmentum*) derives from sowing, as though *serimentum*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 603.---Worthless vine-branches are thrown away; they are fit for no use except fire, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 159.

Savory is hot and nearly fiery, because it makes people prone to Venus, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629.---Garden savory, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1190.

Satyrion is named from satyrs, because it inflames lust, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629.

Saxifrage is so called because its seed breaks stones in the bladder, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629.

*Scrininonia*, which the Latins call *acridium*, is a herb full of juice, gathered beneath a hollowed root, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 631.

*Scampina*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1207.

Chervil (*Kirbele*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1160.

A shingle is named from division, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600.

*Mastic tree*, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 520.

*Schulbaum*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1242.

Sedge, from which mats are woven without a knot, St. Isidore, 634.

Clary sage, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1126.

Rye, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1130.

Seed, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 159.---Seeds never properly degenerate when not their kind, but their perfection, is changed, St. Ambrose, XIV, 173.---On seminal power, ibid., 169.

Houseleek, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1204.

Common houseleek (*huswartz*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1145.

A thorn-bush is so called from a site, that is, uncultivated ground, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618.

Sesame is a Greek name, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600.

*Sichtewurtz* (“white”), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1183.

Spelt is a kind of wheat, named from selection, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 505; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1130.

A forest is a thick and short woodland, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606.

Mustard is so called because its leaf resembles a turnip leaf, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 636.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 531.---White and black mustard, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1166.---Field mustard (*senff*), ibid.

Skirret (*Gerba*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1204.

Black nightshade (*nachtschade*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1179.

Service tree (*spirbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1225.

Sterile shoots are called *spadones*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 603.

Spanish broom is a twiggy shrub without leaves, named from its roughness, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

[Col. 0543] Ear of grain, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1204.

Thorn, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 518.---The thorn clings firmly, is low, rough, prickly, and hard, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 161.

*Spleenwort* is so called because it removes the spleen, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630.

Chickweed (*syme*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1191.

*Stickwurtz*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1146.

Stipa is so called because beds are stuffed with it, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618.

Straws are leaves, or sheaths, by which the stalk is enclosed and supported; *stipula* derives from burning, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 601; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

The *squinum* that grows on the Euphrates is better than that of Arabia; it is tawny, many-flowered, and strongly burns the tongue in taste, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 625.

Stavesacre grows in pleasant places, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

*Staechas* grows in the Stoechades Islands, St. Isidore, LXXII, 633.

Storax is an Arabian tree resembling the quince tree. Its distillation is pure when it falls to the ground, but is preserved in a hollow of its own bark, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 621; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 524–525; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 161.

*Struthios*, which some call moon-herb, grows in cultivated places, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630.

*Strychnos* is a healing herb, so called because it relieves headache and burning of the stomach, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632.

*Stur*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1203.

*Stutgras*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1164, 1203.

The cork oak is so called because pigs eat its fruit, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 614.

Shoots are named from the cutting of the saw, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.

The sycamore (*sycomorus*, “like a mulberry”) is so called because its leaves resemble those of the mulberry. The Latins call it *celsa*, “tall,” from its height, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 613; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 513.---On the sycamore, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 113.

*Symphyton* is a Greek name because its root has such virtue that, when pieces of flesh are sprinkled with it in a pot, it coagulates them, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 630.---Comfrey (*consolida*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1188.

*Syrian* is so called because it was brought from Syria, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 619.

*Sysemera*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1143.

Tamarisk, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 519.

Costmary, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1202.---Common tansy (*Reynfann*), ibid., 1173.

The yew is poisonous, a tree from which toxic poisons are extracted, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 616; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 519.---English yew (*ybenbaum*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1237.

The terebinth is a tree with a Greek name, producing the finest of all resins, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 617.---On the terebinth, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 162.

Wall germander (*gamandrea*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1180.

Frankincense is an Arabian tree yielding a white aromatic sap. *Thus* is said to derive from pounding, because when drops of gum fall from the tree they are mixed with clods of earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 620–621; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 523.---On frankincense, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1196.

Thyme is so called because its flower gives off a scent, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 625.---Common thyme, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1208.---Wild thyme (*quenula*), ibid., 1142.

The lime tree is so called because, by its brightness and lightness, it is useful for the use of missile weapons, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 617; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 519.---On the lime tree, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1234.

*Tithymallum* (Τιτᾶνα μᾶλλον, “more [than] Titan” [the etymology is uncertain]), because it turns the foliage of its leaves toward the sun’s ray, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632.

A firebrand is a burnt piece of wood, which common people call a *tision*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608.

Caltrop, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 522; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1248.

Clover (τρίφυλλον, *triphyllon*, “three-leaved”), because it has three leaves at each attachment, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 632.---Red clover (*cle*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1172.

Fenugreek, “Greek hay” (*foenu Graeco*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1143.

Three-month wheat, so called because it is gathered three months after sowing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599.

Wheat is named either from threshing, because the purest part is stored in the granary, or because its grain is ground and rubbed, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 505.---Spelt wheat, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1131.---Common wheat, ibid., 1129.---On wheat, CLVII, 1151.

The trunk is the standing form of the tree resting upon the root, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.

[Col. 0544] Truffles are swellings that the earth produces; this cause gave them their name, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 638.

The *turbiscus* is, as it were, a crowd, because many shoots spring from a single rootstock, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618.

Great coltsfoot (*hufflata major*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1206.---Common coltsfoot (*hufflata minor*), ibid.

*Typhe* swells itself from water, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635.---Kinds of cattail (*dudelkolbe*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1208.

*Typus* herb, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635.

*Ugera*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1185.

The elm received its name because it thrives better in boggy and moist places, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 616; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 519.---On the elm, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 115.---Field elm (*hagenbucha*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1239.

*Ulpicum* is so called because it has the smell of garlic, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 637.

*Ulva* is an herb growing around springs and marshes, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635.

Nettle is so called because its touch burns the body, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 629; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 522.---On nettle, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1168.

Grapes are so called because they are full of moisture within, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 604–605; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

Bilberry (*walt beris*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1194.

Valerian (*denemarcha*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1187.

*Vehedistel*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1205.

Bramble-bushes are so called because they seize by force, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 618; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 522.

Mullein, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.---Great mullein (*wullena*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1180.

Vervain (*ysena*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1190.

Brooklime (*pungo*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1160.

The vetch is so called because it scarcely reaches a threefold yield, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 602.---Broad bean, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1132.---Cultivated vetch (*vichim*), ibid., 1201.

A twig is so called because it has much force of greenness, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 617.---On the twig, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 115.

Vineyard, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 507; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 163.

The violet is named from the power of its scent; it has three kinds: purple, white, and yellow, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 626; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 528.---The purple violet is low-growing, fragrant, cool, and soft, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 164.---On the violet, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1170.

Rod.---What a rod is, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 112.---A rod which is from branches, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607–608.---The rod is straight and slender, has a flower at its top, and scourges and instructs, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 164.

A thicket is named from a rod because it grows at the root of a tree, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.---How, at the Lord’s word, every kind of thicket suddenly blossomed and supplied food, delights, and medicine, St. Ambrose, XIV, 184.

A little shoot is that which sprouts from a root, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.

Greenness, St. Ambrose, XIV, 166; St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608.

Seminal power, St. Ambrose, XIV, 169.

*Viticella* is a herb so called by the Latins because, like a vine, it catches with its tendrils whatever is near it, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 634.

The vine is so called because it has the power of taking root quickly. Others think vines are so called because they entwine one another with bands, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 602 ff.; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.---On the vine, St. Ambrose, XIV, 175, 185; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1244.

*Vulvus* is so called because its root is winding and round, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 633.

*Weyt*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1205.

*Wida*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1239.

*Wichwurtz*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1196.

Wild lettuce (*Wildelatich*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1165.

*Wiszgras*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1164.

*Wuntwurtz*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1146.

*Xylicon*, or in Latin *siliqua* (“pod”), Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 113.

*Xyliglycon* (ξύλον γλυκύ, *xylon glyky*, “sweet wood”) is a tree from whose fruit a pressed juice, called *acatia* by the Greeks, is obtained, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 614; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 515.

[Col. 0545] *Xylobalsamum*, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 526.

Darnel (*zizania*)—which poets call “ever-unlucky darnel”—is so called because it is unfruitful and useless, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 529.---Darnel and tares [Col. 0546] never grow from wheat seed, St. Ambrose, XIV, 173.

Sugar, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1197.

*Zugelnich*, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1208.
