## CCXXI. INDEX OF AGRICULTURE, ALPHABETICALLY GATHERING EVERYTHING THE FATHERS HAVE SAID CONCERNING THE CULTIVATION AND PRODUCE OF THE SOIL, RURAL IMPLEMENTS, THE MORE SUITABLE SEASONS, ETC., ETC.

### Notice

Agriculture may be broadly defined as the industry whose object is the cultivation of the soil and the production of substances serving for the sustenance of human beings and also domestic animals. Agriculture is a science insofar as it includes principles, and an art with respect to the application of methods. Botany and zoology are highly useful for the practice of agriculture.

The Index of Agriculture is, as it were, a supplement to the INDEXES OF BOTANY and ZOOLOGY.

[INDEX OF AGRICULTURE.]

[Col. 0545] A vinegar-vessel (*acetabulum*) is, as it were, a bearer of vinegar, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715.

Vinegar is so called either because it is sharp or because it is watery, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 712; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 596.

Rustic buildings: *casa* (cottage), *tugurium* (hut), *tesqua* (wilderness places), *magalia* (huts), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 552; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 409.

*Afractum*, called *spumeum* (“foamy”) in Latin, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 710.

A field is said to be called *ager* in Latin because something is done (*agatur*) in it, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 553; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 410.—Every field is divided in four ways: it is either arable, planted, pasture, or flowering land, ibid.—A field is cleared of harmful things, manured, ploughed in several ways, sown, and fenced, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 135.—On fields, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 553; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 410.—On the boundaries and measurements of fields, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 554, 555; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 412.

Homer, Osiris, Triptolemus, and Ceres taught the rural arts, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 597.

The farmer rises in the morning, yokes the oxen, observes the proper times for ploughing and sowing, and patiently awaits the seed that he has cast, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 135.

Very many delight in agriculture, St. Augustine, XXXIV, 1304.—Its praise, ibid., 1304, 1305.—Agriculture is the most harmless of all arts, idem, XLII, 37.—It began to be practiced among the Greeks in the reign of Argus, ibid., 564.

An *alabastrum* is a vessel for ointment, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718.

Nourishment (*alimonia*) derives its name from nourishing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 706, 707; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 587.

Starch (*amolum*) is the very finest flower of flour, thrown out from the mill because of its lightness, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 591.

An *ampulla* is, as it were, a large bubble, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 716; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600.

*Amystis* is a kind of drinking-vessel, St. Isidore, 617; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600.

An *antella* is that which is before a seat, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728.

Apicius was the first to arrange the equipment of a kitchen, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 705; CXI, 587.

*Apophoreta* (parting gifts), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715.

Spring and autumn ploughing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 598.

The plough (*aratrum*) is named from ploughing the earth, as though *araterrium*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 610.—It is uncertain whether Ceres first instituted turning the earth specifically with a ploughshare or with a plough, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 597.—A plough is made of iron and wood; it cleaves the earth, is held by the farmer, improves the soil, and is left in the field, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXII, 137.

Trees, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606–623; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 508, 511.—See the Index of Botany.

[Col. 0546] A chest (*arca*) is so called because it shuts off sight, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 719; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 604.

A threshing-floor (*area*) is named from its flatness and evenness, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 554.

Garden channels are made from hollowed stone and carry water to the garden, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 137.

Arettine vessels are named from Arezzo, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715.

Roasted food (*assum*) is so called because it burns, as though *arsum*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 592.

Authors who wrote on such matters according to St. Isidore: namely Hesiod of Boeotia, Democritus, Cato, Marcus Tarentinus, Vergil, Cornelius Celsus, Julius Atticus, Aemilianus, and Columella, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 597.

Axle-grease (*axungia*) is named from anointing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709.

A berry (*baccea*) derives first from Bacchus, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 716; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600.

A small staff (*bacillus*) derives from a staff (*baculus*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 609.

A staff (*baculus*) derives from Bacchus, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 609.

A *basterna* is a travelling vehicle, as though “road-spreader,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724.

Beasts, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 433; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 217.—See the Index of Zoology.

The *buris* (Greek: **βοὸς οὐρή**, “the ox’s tail”) is the curved part of a plough, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725.

A kettle (*cacabus*) and a cooking-pot (*cucuma*) receive their names from the sound of boiling, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 602.

*Coelia* is a drink made by art from the juice of wheat, named from heating, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713, 714.

A curling-iron (*calamistrum*) is a needle for twisting the hair, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725.

Foot-straps (*calcaria*) are so called because they are fastened at a person’s heel, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

A candle (*candela*) is named from shining, because it is consumed by shining, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 721; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 605.

A *canicula* is an iron grappling-hook, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 727.

A basket (*canistrum*) is woven from reed canes, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 719; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 604.

A *cantharus* (cup), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717.

A halter (*capistrum*) is named from the head of beasts of burden, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

A *capsus* is an enclosed carriage, covered on every side, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724.

A handle (*capulum*) derives from taking hold, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

A *caracutium* is a vehicle with extremely high wheels, as though a “sharp cart,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724.

Meat (*carnes*) is so called either because it is dear (*chara*) or from creating, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 591.

[Col. 0547] A *carpentum* is, as it were, a ceremonial cart, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 608.

A cart (*carrum*) is named from the pivot of its wheels, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 723; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 608.

Cheese (*caseus*) is so called because it lacks whey, as though *careum*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 710; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 593.

A chain (*catenatum*) is so called because it holds by grasping, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 610.

A *catinum* is an earthenware vessel, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.

A cautery (*cauterium*) is named as though *cauturium*, “that which burns,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 613.

Beer (*cervisia*) is named from Ceres, that is, from grain, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

A *chamus* (bit), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 727.

A brand (*character*) is a heated iron by which marks are burned into livestock, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 613.

Food (*cibus*) is so called because it is taken by the mouth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 706; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 587.

*Cibutum* is a Greek name for what we call an *area*, a threshing-floor, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 719.

Ash is a burning by which the sick person sweats out useless moisture, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 598.

A small basket (*cistella*) is named from the ribs of reed or wood by which it is woven, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 720.

A key (*clavis*) is so called because it closes, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 610.

A spoon (*cochlear*) was first named from its use with snails (*cochleae*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715.

Cooked food (*coctum*) is, as it were, “compacted” (*coactum*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 592.

Supper (*caena*; Greek **κοινόν**, “common”) is the evening meal, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 708; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 589.

Colostrum is new milk and is a neuter noun, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 710.

Seasoned food (*conditum*) is made by a mixture of spices, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 712, 713.

A *cophinus* is a vessel woven from twigs, suitable for clearing dung and carrying earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 720; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 604.

Apicius was the first to arrange the equipment of a kitchen, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 705; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 587.

Large baskets (*corbes*) are so called because they are woven from bent twigs, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 720.

A mixing-bowl (*cratera*; Greek **ἀπὸ τοῦ κρατεῖν**, “from ruling”) is a cup having two handles, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 716; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 599.

A sieve (*cribrum*) is, as it were, a “grain-runner,” because grain runs through it, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 719; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 603.—A sieve separates the clean from the unclean, retains the coarse, and expels the fine, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 143.

Raw (*crudum*) means bloody, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 592.

Crust is the surface of bread, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 708; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 591.

Knives (*cultelli*) are named from cultivation, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 611.—A knife is held by its handle, cuts with iron, and is protected by a sheath, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 143.

The cultivation of fields, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 597, 598; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 503.—The cultivation of plants, Walahfrid Strabo, CXIV, 1122.

Cups (*cupi*) and tubs (*cupae*) derive their names from containing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.

A wagon rolls on four wheels; the more heavily it is loaded, the more it creaks, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 143.

*Cyathi* and *scyphi* are likewise kinds of drinking-cups, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 716; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 608.

A cylinder is a smooth stone in the form of a column, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726.

*Cymbia* are a kind of drinking-vessel, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600.

The *dentale* is the first part of a plough, as it were its tooth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725.

The finger is the smallest unit of rural measurements, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 555.

A dish (*discus*) was formerly called *iscus*, from its resemblance to a shield, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 598.

A cask (*dolium*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.—A cask is round, bound with hoops, woven, deep, and broad-mouthed, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXII, 143.

How a house is built, St. Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 144.

Sweet cakes are kinds of baked work, named from their taste, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 708; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 591.

Boiled food (*elixum*) is cooked in water alone, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 592.

[Col. 0548] Food (*esca*) is so called because the mouth takes it, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 706; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 587.—On foods, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 705–711; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 587–594.

*Faecula* is a rich grape, cooked down until thick, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

Lees (*faex*) are so called because, rising up, they cling to the vessel, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 711.

A billhook (*falcastrum*) is named from its likeness to a sickle, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 611.

A sickle (*falx*) is used to prune trees and vines, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 411.—A sickle is sharp and curved and cuts more closely, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 146.

Sausage (*farcimen*) is chopped and minced meat, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 710.

Flour and bran are named from *far* (spelt), of which they are the purgings, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 591.—Flour is fine and clean, obtained with labor; it is bound together by water, leavened, and takes on sourness, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 146.

A honeycomb (*favus*), from Greek **φαγεῖν**, “to eat,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 711; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 594.

Leaven (*fermentum*) is named from boiling or fermenting, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 597.—A small amount of leaven is put into the kneaded flour, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 146.

Earthenware (*fictilia*) is so called because it is made and fashioned from earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 714; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 594.—Earthenware vessels are said to have been first invented on the island of Samos, ibid.

Scattered manure makes the earth fertile, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 146.

Boundaries are so called because fields are divided by cords, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 554; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 411.

A *fisclum*, as though *fisculum*, is named from straining oil, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726.

The hearth (*focus*; Greek **φῶς**, “light”) is fire, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 720; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 605.

A *fomes* is a kind of splinter, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608.

Shears, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 610.

Digging, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 597.

A digging-tool (*fossorium*) is so called because it digs pits, as though *fovessorium*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726.

Bridles are so called because they make horses champ or neigh, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 727; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

Fried food (*frixum*) is named from the sound it makes while burning in oil, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 592.

Grain, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600, 601; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 505.—See the Index of Botany.

A morsel (*frustum*) is so called because it is taken in the mouth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 710; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 591.

Forks are so called because grain is tossed with them, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726.

Stakes are so called because, driven into the earth, they stand there, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724.

A sprout, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 112.

A *girgillus* is so called because it turns in a circle, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 727.

An acorn is food for pigs, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 148.

The grain is sown and dies, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 148.

Reins (*habenae*) are named from holding, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728.

A splinter (*hastula*) is named from lifting, as though *abstula*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 608.

Water-wheels (*haustra*), that is, wheels, are named from drawing water, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 726.

A half-measure (*hemicadium*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

Aromatic herbs, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 527.—See the Index of Botany.

Barley, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 505.

A garden (*hortus*) is so named because something always springs up there, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 530.—A garden is dug around and fenced around, adorned by the arrangement of trees and delightful with flowers, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 154.

A clock (*horologium*) is so called because there we read the hours, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 610.

A hydria, from Greek **ὕδωρ**, “water,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600.

Hydromel is made from water and Matian apples, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

Budding by insertion: when the bark of a tree is cut, a bud from another tree is inserted, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.

Grafting is so called when, after the trunk has been split, a shoot from a fruitful tree is inserted into a barren one, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.

[Col. 0549] Fallowing is the practice by which a field, left empty in alternate years, recovers its strength, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 598.

Equipment for horses, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 727; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

Garden tools, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

Rustic implements, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 705–725; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 610.

Roads, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 412.

Breakfast (*jentaculum*) is the first meal by which a fast is broken, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 707.

A yoke joins two, presses upon the earth, and is fastened to the head, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 149.

Beasts of burden, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 199.—A beast of burden wallows and rests in its dung, feeds on cheap fare, has bony substance, and does not distinguish its riders, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 149.

A basin (*labrum*) or small basin (*labellum*) is so called because infants are usually washed in it, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.

Milk (*lac*) derives from the Greek word **λευκόν**, “white,” because of its whiteness, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 710.—Milk is white, nourishes little children, dries when curdled, and rises when boiled, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 150.

*Lactatum* is a drink made from milk, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

A reservoir (*lacus*) is that through which liquid flows, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

A *laganum* is a broad, thin cake which is first cooked in water and afterwards fried in oil, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 708.

A flask (*lagena*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600.

A small cask (*laguncula*) is woven from several staves, bound with iron hoops, has a bung-hole, and preserves wine, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 150.

Lard is so called because it is stored and preserved in the house; for the ancients called houses *lares*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709.

A lantern (*laterna*) is so named because it has light inside, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 721; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 606.

*Lebetes* are bronze vessels, so called by a Greek name, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 602.

Beds, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 722; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 606.

Litters (*lecticae*) are named from gathered herbs, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 722; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 606.

Legumes, from *legendo*, “gathering,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 600; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

A *lenticula* is a small vessel for dice, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 602.

Hoes (*ligones*) are so called because they lift the earth, as though *levones*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 610.

Boundary-lines, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 555.—There are two principal boundary-lines in fields, the *cardo* and the *decumanus*, ibid.

Flax is gathered into bundles, put into water, dried in the sun, whitened by many beatings, rubbed, separated from the tow, spun, knotted, unwound, and warped into cloth, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 151, 152.

*Lorea*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728.

*Lora*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

Lucanian sausages are named from Lucania, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 710.

A lamp (*lucerna*) derives its name from *lychnus*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 720; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 605.

A night-light (*lucubrum*) is so called because it shines in darkness, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 721.

*Lupata* are very harsh bridles, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 727.

A *lupus* is an iron grappling-hook, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 727.

A sheaf (*manipulus*) is made from many things gathered by hand; it is collected with labor but possessed with joy, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 152.

*Martisia* is made in a mortar from fish, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 710.

*Medus* is as though *melus*, because it is made from honey, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

Honey (*mel*; Greek **μέλισσα**, “bee”), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 711; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 594.

*Melicratum* is wine mixed with honey, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

Tables, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 705; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 587.

Measurements of fields, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 587.

An afternoon meal (*merenda*, “to be eaten after midday”) is food taken as the day declines, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 707, 708.

To take an afternoon meal (*merendare*) is, as it were, to eat at midday, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 708.

We say *merum* when we mean pure wine, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 711; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 595.

*Minutal* is so called because it is made from fish, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 710.

Apples (*mala*) are named from their roundness, as are the apples of fruit trees, St. Isidore, [Col. 0550] LXXXII, 718; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 603.

A milking-pail (*mulgarium*) is a vessel in which livestock is milked, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.

*Mulsum* is made from honey mixed in, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

Must is wine taken immediately from the vat (*lacus*)—“mouse, earth” (*mus, humus*)—St. Isidore, LXXXII, 712.—New wine is sweet, inflates the stomach, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 153.

A razor (*novacula*) is so called because it renews the face, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 610.

Fallow land, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 554.

Digging around trees or vines, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 597.

*Oenomelum* is must mixed with honey, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

An *oenophorus* (Greek **οἶνος φέρω**, “wine-bearer”), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 716; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600.

An *offa* is properly a morsel for the teeth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709.

Vegetables, from *olendo*, “smelling,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 635; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 530.

A pot (*olla*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 602.—An earthen pot is hardened by fire; it is fragile, and once broken is useless, Hugh of St. Victor, CCXXVII, 154.

An *orca* is a kind of amphora; its smaller name is *urceus*, and its diminutive *urceolus*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.

Oxymel is made from a mixture of vinegar and honey, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

A shovel (*pala*) is named from chaff (*paleae*), which is commonly called a winnowing-fan, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726.

Chaff is dry, light, barren, and clinging; it is cast out by the winnowing-fan and divided from the grain, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 155.

Marshes (*paludes*) are named from Pales, the pastoral goddess, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 554.

A stake is long, sharp, and rigid; a hole is dug for it beforehand so that it may enter more easily. It is suitable for a fence, is sharpened, hardened by fire, and set in a row, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 155.

Bread (*panis*; Greek **πᾶν**, “all”) is so called because it is served with food, or because every animal desires it. Bread is common bread, leavened bread, unleavened bread, lightly leavened bread, wheat bread, reddish bread, bread baked under ashes, hearth bread, and oven bread, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 708; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 590; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 155.

A linen cloth is spread out, moistened, put into hot lye, heated, scrubbed, beaten, wrung, and dried, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 155.

A *paropsis* (dish), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 598.

Farmers call *pastinum* a forked iron tool with which seeds are planted, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726.

A pan (*patella*) is, as it were, something open or broad, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 602.

Paterae, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 716; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 599.

A *patina* (dish), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 598.

A comb is so called because it makes the hair combed, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724.—A comb is toothed with close and wider-set teeth; it arranges and orders the hair, cleans the head, and is made of bone, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 156.

A basin (*pelvis*) is so called because feet are washed there, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.

A *portica*, a measure of ten feet, is named from carrying, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 556.

A bolt fastens a door; it is movable, drawn out and drawn back, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 157.

*Phalascae*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600.

*Phalerae*, ornaments for horses, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 727; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

Bowls (*phyalae*; Greek **ὕαλον**, “glass”) are so called because they are made of glass, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 716; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 599.

A *pilentum* or *petoritum* is a woven vehicle with four wheels, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724.

A fisherman has a boat with its equipment, wears cheap clothing, keeps the nets he has cast, and knows what bait suits each fish, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXII, 157.

*Cakes* (*placentae*) are made of spelt; others call them *liba*, because they please and are pleasing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 708; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 591.

Nurseries, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.

Planting, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 607.

A *plaustrum* is a two-wheeled vehicle, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 724.

A drinking-cup (*poculum*) derives from drinking, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 716; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 599.

[Col. 0551] Fine flour (*pollis*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709.

A *postella* is behind a seat, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728.

Drink, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 711; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 594.

Dinner (*prandium*) is named from the preparation for eating, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 707; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 589.

A meadow is that by whose abundance of hay herds are sustained.—Meadows are lands which can be mown, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 554.

A press is a beam by which trodden grapes are pressed, and by which oil is pressed, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

Propagation, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 597.

First ploughing (*proscissio*) is the first tillage, while the field is still hard, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599.

Pottage (*pulmentum*) derives from porridge (*puls*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 707; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 588.

Pulp (*pulpa*) is so called because formerly it was eaten mixed with porridge; hence also *pulmentum* and *pulmentarium*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 710.

To prune means to cut away the superfluous shoot from a vine, by whose tendrils it grows luxuriantly, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 606; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 597.

A *pyxis* is a small ointment-vessel made from boxwood (Greek **πύξον**), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718.

*Quactum* is, as it were, “compacted” and “curdled,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 711; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 593.

A *qualus* is named from straining, because must flows through it, St. Isidore, CXXXII, 726.

Rakes (*rastra*) are named from scraping the earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725.

Straps (*retinacula*) derive from holding back, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728.

A *rheda* is a kind of four-wheeled vehicle, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 608.

*Rhodomel* is so called because honey is mixed into rose-juice, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

A wheel (*rota*) is so named because it rolls or rushes along, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 723; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 608.

A wheel is a machine by which water is drawn from a river, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

A *rotabulum* is named from removing manure, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 719.

Weeding (*runcatio*) is pulling herbs out of the ground, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 598.

Pruning-hooks (*runcones*), with which brambles are cut, are named from weeding, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 611.

Rural matters.—Authors who wrote on rural matters, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 597.

*Saccatum* is a liquid made by mixing water with wine-lees and pressing it through a bag, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

A sack (*saccus*) derives from a *sagum*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 719; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 604.—A sack is rough, hard, and heavy; it conceals grain and is quadrangular, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 159.

A pack-saddle (*sagma*) derives from a layer of blankets, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728.

Salt dries meat, keeps decay away, and kills worms, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXII, 159.

A salt-cellar, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715.

Salted food (*salsum*) is, as it were, sprinkled with salt, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 592.

A woodland pasture (*saltus*) is a dense growth of tall trees, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.

A frying-pan (*sartago*) is named from the noise it makes, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 603.

Sowing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599.

A leather oil-vessel, made from hide, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718.

A *scudicia* is so called because it opens the earth around a tree-trunk, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725.

A small dish (*scutella*) derives from a shield, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 715.

A *scyphus* (cup), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.

Tallow (*sebum*) derives from pig (*sus*), as though *suebum*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709.

An axe has a handle by which it is held and an iron blade by which it cuts, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 159.

Crops, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599.

A seat (*sella*) derives from sitting, as though *sedda*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 612.

Stars, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 722; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 606.

Seed is entrusted to the earth and multiplied: first grass arises, second the ear, third the grain from which flour is made, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 160.

A hedge is woven from stakes and twigs, made beside a road, and protects fruits, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 160.

What sowing is, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 599.

[Col. 0552] A *seriola*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.

A small saw, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725.

*Sicera* is every drink, other than wine, that can intoxicate, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 713.

A *sicula*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600.

Fine wheat flour (*simila*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709.

A siphon is a vessel that pours water by blowing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.

A bucket (*situla*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600.

A sponge-cake is bread long kneaded with water, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 708.

A basket (*sporta*) is so called either because it is commonly made from broom (*spartum*) or because it carries something out, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 720; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 605.

The method of manuring, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 597.

Manuring, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 598.

Stercutius first introduced into Italy the method of manuring fields, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 597.

A dung-heap (*sterquilinium*) is a foul receptacle for filth, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 161.

A couch (*stibadium*) is named from logs, as though *stipadium*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 705; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 587.

Goads (*stimuli*) derive from *stigo*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 613.

A mat (*storia*) is so called because it is spread upon the ground, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 722; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 722.

Bedding (*stratus*) derives from spreading, as though *storiatus*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 722; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 606.

Strigils are named from rubbing or scraping, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 728; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 613.

*Subsecivi* are fields, divided by the surveyor’s rod, which are rejected as barren or marshy, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 554.

*Succidia* is meat laid aside for use, so called from cutting it up, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709.

A furrow, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 598.

Shoots, simple or forked, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 111.

*Tacea* is the Gallic name for lard, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 709.

A *telo* is a long piece of wood by which water is drawn, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 727.

Boundary-markers are so called because they distinguish and define measurements of land, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 555.

Tallies are used to mark the number of grains, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726.

A mattress (*torus*) is named from twisted herbs laid beneath the shoulders of reclining persons, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 705; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 587.

A *trapetum* is an olive-grinding mill, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726.

A threshing-sledge (*tribula*) is a kind of vehicle by which grain is threshed, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726.

A *trifinium* is so called because it joins the boundaries of three properties, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 555.

Tripods are so called because they stand on three feet, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718.

Wineskins (*utres*) derive from the womb (*uterus*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 717; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 601.—A wineskin is made from the hide of a dead animal; it holds and preserves wine, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 164.

Grapes are so called because they are full of moisture within. The grape varieties are suburban, early-ripening, hard-skinned, purple, date-like, Rhodian, Libyan, Ceraunian, Stephanite, three-footed, ounce-sized, and Cydonian, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 604, 605; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 507.

A vessel (*vas*) derives from eating, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 714; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 597.

Vessels for food, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 714; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 567. Drinking-vessels, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 716; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 599. Vessels for wine and water, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 716; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 600. Oil-vessels, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 718; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 602.—Cooking-vessels, St. Isidore, 718; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 502.—Storage-vessels, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 719; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 603. Lighting-vessels, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 720; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 605.

Levers are so called because they are carried by hand, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 724; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 609.

Vehicles, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 723; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 608.

*Verennes* derives from carrying, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 726.

A spring woodland (*vernaetum*), St. Isidore, 598.

Wine is so called because drinking it quickly fills the veins with blood, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 711; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 595.—Rosé wine, *animeum*, amber-colored wine, clear wine, cloudy wine, Falernian wine, strained wine, *gazetum*, *infertum* wine, foul wine, honorary wine, and *crucium*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 712; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 595.

[Col. 0553] Vines, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 602, 603, 604; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 506.

A ploughshare (*vomer*) is so called because it forcibly tears up the soil, or from vomiting forth the earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 725; Rabanus Maurus, [Col. 0554] CXI, 610.—It is uncertain whether Ceres first instituted turning the earth specifically with a ploughshare or with a plough, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 597.
