## CCXXII. INDEX OF ZOOLOGY, ALPHABETICALLY RECORDING WHATEVER THE FATHERS SAID ABOUT BEASTS OR LIVING CREATURES

### PREFACE

The ancients distinguished mammals, birds, reptiles, fishes, insects, and zoophytes.

Eustathius discusses (LIII) fishes, 935; birds, 948; quadrupeds; reptiles; and insects.

St. Isidore (LXXXII) discusses animals, 423; beasts, 433; small animals, 440; serpents, 442; worms, 448; fishes, 450; birds, 459; and small flying creatures, 469. He enumerates 38 animals, 28 beasts, 11 small animals, 35 serpents, 23 worms, 55 fishes, 65 birds, and 19 small flying creatures.

Rabanus Maurus (CXI) discusses cattle, beasts of burden, and animals, 199–215; beasts, 217–226; small animals, 226–228; serpents, 228–235; worms, 235–236; fishes, 237–239; birds, 241–255; and bees and flies, 255–258. He enumerates 27 cattle, beasts of burden, and animals; 28 beasts; 10 small animals; 21 serpents; 20 worms; 25 fishes; 40 birds; and about 13 bees and flies.

St. Hildegard discusses (CXCVII) 34 fishes, 1265–1284; 71 birds and flying creatures, 1285–1311; 45 animals, 1311–1338; and 17 serpents, 1339–1344.

Before undertaking the alphabetical order of subjects, it is worthwhile to identify the authors who discussed these matters:

1. St. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in the fifth and sixth books of the *Hexaemeron*, XIV, 205 ff., year 397.
2. Eustathius, LIII, 935 ff., year 450.
3. St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, LXXXII, 423 ff., year 686.
4. Rabanus Maurus, bishop of Mainz, CXI, 199 ff., year 856.
5. Adam, canon of Bremen, in the *Description of the Islands of the North*, CXLVI, 649, years 1073–1076.
6. Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 244 ff., year 1135.
7. The Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1215 ff., year 1135.
8. Honorius of Autun, in the three books *On the Image of the World*, CLXXII, year 1136.
9. In the appendices to Hugh of St. Victor, in the work entitled *On Beasts and Other Things*, CLXXVII, 15 ff., year 1142.
10. St. Hildegard, in the work entitled *Physica*, CXCVII, 1265 ff., year 1178.

### ALPHABETICAL INDEX

[Col. 0553]

**Hawk.**—On the hawk, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 466; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 135.—The hawk is a bird armed more by courage than by talons, bearing greater strength in a smaller body; it is a bird eager to seize other birds, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 252.—How a hawk puts forth feathers, spreading its wings toward the south, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 20.—On two species of hawks, ibid., 21.—On the care of domestic hawks, ibid., 22.—On carrying a hawk on the left hand, ibid.—On the perch upon which a hawk stands or sits, ibid.—On the hawks’ jesses or fetters, ibid., 22.—On the hawk’s strap and tether, ibid., 23.—Hawks are by no means to be accused of cruelty, St. Ambrose, XIV, 231.—On hawks, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1147.

**Admoditae** (a kind of serpent), Rabanus Maurus, XI, 234.

**Lamb.**—On the lamb, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 426; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 89, 135.

**Agredula**, or **Acredula** (French *chouette*, “owl”), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 458.

**Lark**, Venerable Hildebert, CLXXI, 38, 1237; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1304.

**Elks in Sweden**, Adam, canon of Bremen, CXLVI, 649.

**Birds.**—On birds, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 459, 469; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 241.

[Col. 0554] **Alkreya** (a bird), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1299.

**Alroppa** (*gadus lota*, burbot), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1284.

**Amera** (a bird), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1306.

**Ammodites**, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 446.

**Amphibians.**—On amphibians, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 450; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 105.—What *anfivia* or amphibians are, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 237.

**Amphibaena** (a kind of serpent), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 444; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 101.

**Amsla** (*turdus merula*, blackbird), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1303.

**Duck.**—On the duck, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 466.

**Domestic duck**, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1294.—**Wild duck**, ibid.

**Eels.**—On eels, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 455; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 108.—On the eel (*muraena anguilla*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1283.—Eels catch their young, Eustathius, LIII, 987.—Their resemblance to a snake gave eels their name, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.—They report that the eastern river Ganges produces eels thirty feet long, ibid., 238; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 124, 125.

**Snake.**—On the snake, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 442.—The term *anguis* is a class of serpents which can be folded and twisted; and it is called *anguis* because it is angular and never straight, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 228.—The slow-worm (*anguis fragilis*; *Blintsleich*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1341.

Living creatures.---On animals, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 423.---Why animals are so called [Col. 0555], LXXXII, 425.---Animals are so called because they are endowed with life and moved by spirit, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 199.---Why beasts of burden, or animals of the earth, are assigned to the work of the sixth day together with man, Abbot Rupert, CLXVII, 244.---By God’s word animals were given the law of generation, so that they might endure in the succession of their species, St. Ambrose, XIV, 245.---On the remarkable instinct of certain animals in avoiding what harms them and pursuing what benefits them, ibid., 247.---On the names, species, and properties of animals in general, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXII, 88.---To the strongest beasts, the tiniest animals are a terror and a cause of destruction, St. Ambrose, XIV, 253.

Goose.---On the goose, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 466; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1293.---On the moral nature of the goose, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 46.---On wild geese, ibid., 136.---The goose took its suitable name from its continual swimming, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 218.---The name *anser* (“goose”) was derived from *aner* (“man”), ibid.---On the faithful watch kept by geese, St. Ambrose, XIV, 224.---Watchful geese, Eustathius, LIII, 953.---(The Capitoline geese), Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 248.

Antula.---On the *antula*, or *anto*, or antelope animal, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 57.

Wild boar.---On the wild boar, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 428; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 89.---The wild boar is so called because it dwells in rough places, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 207.

Aphorus (fish).---On the aphorus, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 455.

Bee.---On the bee, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 136; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1309.---On bees, St. Ambrose, XIV, 233; Eustathius, LIII, 949, 954; St. Isidore, LXXXII, 469; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 255; Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1237; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 97.---Ground bee, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1380.

Eagle.---On the eagle, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 466; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1217; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 137; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1292.---On the nature of the eagle, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 53.---The eagle is named from the sharpness of its eyes; for its sight is said to be so powerful that, while it is borne over the seas on motionless wing and lies beyond human vision, it sees little fish swimming from such a height. It is said not to turn its gaze away from the rays of the sun. Hence it exposes its young, suspended by a claw, to the sun’s rays; those which it sees hold their gaze steady it preserves as worthy of their stock, but those which turn their eyes aside it rejects as degenerate, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 243.---The eagle’s harshness is by no means to be blamed, St. Ambrose, XIV, 231.---But the coot, which rears the eagle’s rejected young, is to be commended, ibid.

Spider.---On the spider, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 441, 448; Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1221; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 104, 137; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1342.---On the sea-spider, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 452.---The spider is a worm of the air, surnamed from an instrument of the air, because with its tiny body it draws out long threads; always intent upon its web, it never ceases to work, enduring continual loss in its craft, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 235.

Heron.---On the heron, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 461.---On the nature of the heron, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 47.---The heron is called, as it were, *ardua* (“lofty”), that is, because of its high flights; it fears rain and flies above the clouds so that it cannot feel the storms of the clouds, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 246.---On the heron (*reyger*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1290.

Ram.---On the ram, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 435; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 137.

What herds signify, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 425.

Ascarids, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 449.---Ascarids, or *costi*, are lice of the feet, worms of the skin so called from the feet, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236.

Ascha (*salmothymallus*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1279.

Ass.---On the ass, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 429; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1320.---On the Arcadian ass, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 430.---On the wild ass, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 137.---On the ass and the colt, ibid., 91.---The ass and colt are named from sitting, as though *aseddus*; for it is a slow animal and offers no resistance, and as soon as a man wishes, submits its back to him, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 212.---Dull-witted asses, Eustathius, LIII, 958.

Asp.---On the asp, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 443; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 66, 77, 137.---The asp is so called because it introduces and spreads poisons by its bite; it has diverse kinds and species, with differing effects in doing harm, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 230.

Aspidochelo, an aquatic monster having one part in the form of an asp and another of a tortoise [Col. 0556], Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 82.

Sea crayfish, Eustathius, LIII, 937.

Augurs.---On augurs, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 469.

Southern fish, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 454.

Bird.---What the terms *avis* (“bird”) and *volucris* (“flying creature”) signify; what wings, feathers, and plumage are, and why they are so called, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 241.---Why birds, winged creatures, fliers, chicks, wings, feathers, and plumage are so called, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 459.---On birds, St. Ambrose, XIV, 222.---On birds in general, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 94.---On the various kinds and differences among the various birds, St. Ambrose, XIV, 225.---Birds differ in form, size, color, habits, activities, and variety of food, Eustathius, LIII, 948.---One name of birds, but a diverse kind, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 459.---As innumerable in habits as in kind, ibid., 459.---Birds of prey, Eustathius, LIII, 948.---Some birds are gregarious; some live in communities, ibid.---Migratory and native birds, ibid.---On birds organized under a kind of commonwealth, St. Ambrose, XIV, 233.---On nocturnal birds, ibid., 239.---Some birds have feet useless for them, others feet useful for obtaining nourishment, Eustathius, LIII, 948.---The characteristics of those which eat flesh, ibid.---The characteristics of those nourished on seeds, ibid.---Of those which take for food whatever chance offers, ibid.---On birds that foretell rain or winds, St. Ambrose, XIV, 224.---Comparison of fish and birds, ibid., 225; Eustathius, LIII, 947.---Yet no birds lack the use of feet, St. Ambrose, XIV, 225.---The diverse habits of birds, Eustathius, LIII, 949.---On birds’ eggs, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 469.---On water-birds, Eustathius, LIII, 954.---On the diversity of body observable in birds, St. Ambrose, XIV, 237.---On the nature and habits of birds, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 253–255; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1146.

Badium (bird), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 431.

Whales.---On whales, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 451; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 105.---Whales are beasts of immense size, named from their expelling and pouring forth water, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 237.

Barbus (*silurus*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1276.

Basilisk.---On the basilisk, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 443; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1343.---On the basilisk, king of serpents, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 138.---On the basilisk and its hiss, ibid., 100.---The Greek *basiliskos* is translated in Latin as *regulus* (“little king”), because it is king of serpents, so that those seeing it flee: for it kills them by its smell. Indeed, if it so much as looks at a man, it kills him. No bird passes its gaze unharmed. Yet it is overcome and killed by weasels. It is half a foot long and marked with white spots, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 231.

Batracha, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 101.

Bersich (a species of perch), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1279.

Beasts.---To which creatures the term “beast” applies, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 433; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 217.---Why beasts are called wild beasts, ibid.---On the threefold kind of beasts of burden, reptiles, and beasts, Abbot Rupert, CLXVI, 245.---God created some beasts with shorter necks and others with longer ones, St. Ambrose, XIV, 253.

Beynstereza (yellow wagtail), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1307.

Bibiones, which arise in wine, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 472.

Bisons are captured in Slavonia and Russia, Adam of Bremen, canon, CXLVI, 649.

Cockroaches, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 470.

Blicka (fish), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1281.

Boa.---On the boa serpent, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 445; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 101.

Bocae.---They say that *bocae* are sea-cows, as though *boacae*, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 237.

Silkworm. On the silkworm, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 104.---Silkworms are worms of leaves, from whose weaving silk cloth is made. It is called by this name because, when it is emptied out, it produces threads and only air remains within it, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 235.

Bonascus (wild bull), Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 84.

Ox.---On the ox, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 428; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 90, 139; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1325.---On the Lucan ox, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 436.---Heavy oxen, Eustathius, LIII, 958.---Three-horned oxen with horses’ feet, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 124, 125.

Botrax.---On the botrax, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 446.

Bradypus (bird), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 466.

[Col. 0557] Bresma (*sparus paegyrus*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1278.

Bruchus, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 258.

Buffalo.---On the buffalo, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 428.---Buffaloes are so called by derivation because they resemble oxen, and are so untamed that, owing to their wildness, they do not accept the yoke upon their necks; Africa produces them, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 210.---Buffaloes are captured in Sweden, Adam of Bremen, canon, CXLVI, 649.

Owl.---On the owl, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 464; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 139.---On the moral nature of the owl, ibid., 45.---The *bubo* is larger than the *noctua*, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 247.---A funereal bird, indeed laden with feathers, but always weighed down by sluggishness; it haunts tombs night and day, always dwelling in caverns, ibid., 247.

Buprestis, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 470.

Horse.---On the horse, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 430.---The horse was formerly called from *cavo* (“I hollow”), because, walking, it hollows the earth with the impress of its hoof, which other animals do not do; hence also *sonipes* (“sounding-footed”), because it makes a sound with its feet, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 213.

Caecula (serpent), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 446.

Callitriches.---On callitriches, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 459.

Camedracontes (serpents), Rabanus Maurus, LXXXII, 234.

Chameleon.---On the chameleon, St. Ambrose, XIV, 237; St. Isidore, LXXXII, 436.---The chameleon has no single color, but is sprinkled with diverse variation, like a leopard; it is so called because its little body is changed with the greatest ease into the colors which it sees, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 222.

Camelopard.---On the camelopard, an animal of Ethiopia, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 437.---It is so called because, although it is spotted with white marks like a leopard, has a neck like a horse, and feet like an ox, it nevertheless resembles a camel; Ethiopia produces it, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 222.

Camel.---On the camel, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 429; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 139; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1313.---On the nature of the camel, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 90.---Why the camel has a long neck, Eustathius, LIII, 237.---The camel received its name from lying down while it is loaded; although other regions also send them, Arabia sends the greatest number. They differ among themselves: Arabian camels have two humps on their backs, those of other regions one each, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 211.

Crab.---On the crab, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 108; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1282.---On crabs, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 457.---Crabs are counted among fishes because swimming is their principal mode of movement, Eustathius, LIII, 936.---On the cunning of the crab, St. Ambrose, XIV, 215.---Crabs are shellfish with legs, creatures hostile to oysters. They live on the oysters’ flesh by remarkable ingenuity. When a crab cannot open the oyster’s strong shell, it watches for the time when the oyster opens the enclosure of its shells; then the crab secretly throws in a stone, and, by preventing it from closing, gnaws away the oyster’s flesh. There are two kinds of crabs: river crabs and sea crabs, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 239.---On the crab, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 893.

Dog.---On the dog, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 437, 438; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXVII, 140; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1327.---On the dog and its nature, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 65, 86.---An obliging dog, Eustathius, III, 958.---Nothing is more sagacious than dogs, Rabanus Maurus, XIV, 224.---They possess more sense than other animals, ibid.

Spanish fly.---An earthworm which, as soon as it is applied to the human body, by its burning produces blisters full of fluid, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 235.

He-goat, she-goat, roe-deer: so called from cropping shrubs, or from the cracking sound of their legs, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 426.---Wild roe-deer, because they see exceedingly sharply, were called *dorcades* from the Greek *ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀξῦ δερκέσθαι*, “from seeing keenly,” ibid., 426; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 204.---On the she-goat, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 140.---On the nature of the he-goat, ibid., 63.

Capus (perhaps a heron-hawk), a bird of prey, so called from catching, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 252; St. Isidore, LXXXII, 467.

The goldfinch is so called because it feeds on thorns and thistles, ibid., 469.

Carp (*Cyprinus carpo*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1277.

Beaver.---On the nature of the beaver, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 61.---Beavers are so called from castration; for their testicles are suitable for medicines, and therefore, when they sense a hunter approaching, they castrate themselves and cut off their powers with their teeth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 437; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 222.---Beaver, *fiber* (*Biber*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1329.

[Col. 0558] Celidros serpent, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 233.

Cenchris, a winding serpent, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 445.

Centipede, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 446.

Cerastes, a serpent so called because it has horns (*κέρατα*) on its head, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 444; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 228.---On the cerastes, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 100.

Cercini. Eustathius, LIII, 937, 939.

Deer.---Deer are named from their horns (*κέρατα*), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 427; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 284.---On the deer, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1220; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1320.---On the nature of deer, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 64.---A timid deer, Eustathius, LIII, 958.---To restore their strength, they eat serpents, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 204. Deer revealed the herb dittany, ibid.---Roe deer (*rech*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1321.---A sick deer chews olive twigs and becomes well, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1151.

Sea monsters (whales), Eustathius, LIII, 940; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1269.---*Cetus*, Greek *τὸ κῆτος*, plural *τὰ κήτη* (“sea monster,” “sea monsters”), is so called because of its enormity, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 451.---On the sea monster, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 892; Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1221.

Cencocroca beast, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 124.

Charadrius, or Charadrus, or Caladrius, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 77, 139.---A sea-bird which Theodore Gaza calls *charadrius*; Suidas, *charadrus*, and says that it is a large, voracious sea-bird, by looking upon which persons with jaundice are cured, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 77.

Chelydros (*χέρσον ὕδωρ*, “land-water”), a serpent also called *chersidros*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 445.

Cicada.---On the cicada, St. Ambrose, XIV, 237; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1310.---Cicadas are recognized from the spittle of cuckoos, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 471.

Cicendela, a kind of beetle, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 470.

Stork.---On the stork, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXXIII, 141.---On storks, Eustathius, LIII, 950.---On the nature of the stork, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 43.---Storks are so named from the sound which they make by clattering, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 461; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 245.---They are heralds of spring, companions in association, enemies of serpents; they fly across seas and go in a gathered flock to Asia, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 461; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 245.---Crows go before them as leaders, and the storks themselves follow as though an army, St. Ambrose, XIV, 228; St. Isidore, LXXXII, 461.---The storks’ filial devotion toward their parents, St. Ambrose, XIV, 228.---Their devotion toward their young, over which they brood continually, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 345.---On the stork (*odebero*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1292.

Bedbug, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 105.---The bedbug is named from its resemblance to a certain plant, whose stench it possesses, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 450; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236.

Cinnamologus, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 95.---An Arabian bird so called because it weaves nests in lofty groves from the fruits of cinnamon, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 462; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 246.

Sea snails, Eustathius, LIII, 937; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.---See Shellfish.

Blue fish, named from their color, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 451; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 237.

The *coluber* is so called because it inhabits shadows, or because it glides in slippery tracks with sinuous bends, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 442; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 228.---On the coluber, Eustathius, LIII, 963.---Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1218.

Doves are so called because their necks change color at every turn, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 467.---Gentle birds; called amorous, ibid.---The dove loves human dwellings, a pleasant inhabitant of houses, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 248.---Gregarious doves, Eustathius, LIII, 948.---A lustful dove, ibid., 949.---On doves, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 15–20; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1299.---On the dove (*mewa*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, ibid.

Shellfish, Eustathius, LIII, 937.---Shellfish and snails are so called for this reason: when the moon wanes, they become hollow, that is, emptied, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 456; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.---There are many kinds of shellfish, including pearl-bearing ones, called *celae*, in whose flesh a precious stone hardens, ibid.---On shellfish, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 110.---On a fish having a shell, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1279.

Congelin (bird), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1307.

Conger eel, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 455.

Copprea (fish), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1275.

[Col. 0559] Coredulus, a kind of bird, as though “heart-eating,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 463; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 246.

Crow, a long-lived bird, is called among the Latins by a Greek name, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 466.---On the crow, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 252; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 96.---St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1298.---The hospitality of crows is praised, St. Ambrose, XIV, 228.---Human beings are taught love for their children by crows, ibid., XIV, 230.---How storks are raised and protected by crows, St. Ambrose, XIV, 228.---On the crow, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1147.

The raven, or *corax*, takes its name from the sound of its throat, because it croaks *coracinet*, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 465; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 252.---It first seeks out the eye in corpses, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 465.---On the raven, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 31, 32, 33, 96, 143; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1298.---The raven *caryocatacles* (*hera*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1299.

Costi (worms), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 449.

Costros (among small flying creatures), St. Isidore, LXXXII, 470.

Quail, or the *squalea* bird.---Quails are named from the sound of their voice; the Greeks call them *ὄρτυγας* (“quails”), because they were first seen on the island of Ortygia, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 468; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 249.---On the quail, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 143.---On the quail and the *squalea* bird, ibid., 49.

Crabones are named from *cabo*, that is, “horse,” because they are produced from horses, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 470.

Crassus (fish), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1280.

The crocodile is named from its saffron color; it is produced in the Nile, a four-footed animal living on land and in water, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 452; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.---At night it rests in the water, by day on land, ibid. It warms its eggs on land, ibid.---On the crocodile, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 60, 105.---Crocodiles are counted among fishes because swimming is their principal mode of movement, Eustathius, LIII, 936.

Cuckoo, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1302.

The gnat is named from its sting, because it sucks blood, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 471; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 258.---Gnats, Eustathius, LIII, 935.---Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1151.

Rabbits are a kind of wild animal, called as it were little dogs, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 427.

The swan is so called from singing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 461.---On the swan, St. Ambrose, XIV, 23; Eustathius, LIII, 954; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 51, 143; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1289.

Cyniphes, very tiny flies but exceedingly troublesome in their stings, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 472; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 258.

Cynocephali, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 439.

*Cynomyia*, so called in Greek, that is, “dog-fly,” St. Isidore, LXXXII, 471; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 257.

Fallow deer.---Fallow deer are more fertile, Eustathius, LIII, 961.

The little fallow deer is so called because it escapes from the hand, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 427; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 205.---A timid and unwarlike animal, the same authors, ibid.---On the little fallow deer, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 143.

Darant (serpent), St. Hildegard, 1344.

Dolphins have a certain name because they follow human voices, etc., St. Isidore, LXXXII, 451; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 237, 238.---Nothing in the sea is swifter than they, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 451.---They are properly called *simones*, ibid., 452.---There is also a kind of dolphin in the Nile that kills crocodiles, St. Isidore, 452; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 237, 238.---Dolphins give birth to young, Eustathius, LIII, 938.---On dolphins, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 105.

Dentix, so named because of the number and great size of its teeth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 453.

Diomedean birds (Greek *ἡρῴδιοι*, “herons”), so called from the voices of Diomedes, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 463.

Dipsas, a kind of asp, called in Latin *situla* (“water-bucket”), because one bitten by it dies of thirst, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 444; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 231.---A serpent so tiny that when it is trodden upon it cannot be seen, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 446.---On the dipsas serpent, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 101.

Distelwincke (goldfinch, *Fringilla carduelis*), St. Hildegard, CXCVIII, 1306.

Dragon (*δράκων*), the greatest of all serpents or living creatures upon the earth, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 442; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 229, 230.---It has its strength in its tail, ibid.---It is free from poison, ibid.---It is produced in Ethiopia and India, ibid.---On the dragon, greatest of living creatures, Eustathius, LIII, 937; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 71.---On the dragon, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1339.

The sea-dragon has spines in its gills pointing toward its tail, [Col. 0560] St. Isidore, LXXXII, 455; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.

Dromeda, or dromedary (*dromedarius*; Greek *δρόμος*, “running”), is a kind of camel, indeed of smaller stature but greater speed, whence it has its name . . . This animal chews the cud, St. Isidore, LXXII, 429; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 211.---On the dromedary, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1338.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 91.

Drosela (bird), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1304.

Eale, a beast whose body is that of a horse, its jaw that of a boar, its tail that of an elephant; it has cubit-long horns, one of which it bends back over its spine while fighting with the other. It is equally strong in water and on land, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 124.---On the eale, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXII, 86.

Echineis, a small fish, half a foot long, took its name from its ability to hold a ship fast by attaching itself to it, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 454.---On the small echeneis, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 108.

Sea urchin, which took its name from the land hedgehog; its shell is double and armed with spines, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 457–458.---On the sea urchin, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 109.---On the foreknowledge of the sea urchin, which foretells a coming storm, St. Ambrose, XIV, 216.---On the sea urchin, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 894.

Elaces are caught in Sweden, Adam, canon of Bremen, CXLVII, 649.

Elephantiae, a kind of serpent, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 234.

Elephant, *elephas* (*λόφος*, “mountain”), so called from the size of its body, because it presents the form of a mountain, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 436; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 221, 222.---Elephants possess great intelligence and memory; they carry their young for two years; now India alone produces them, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 221, 222.---The elephant’s limbs, properties, and military use, St. Ambrose, XIV, 253.---On the elephant, Eustathius, LXII, 962; Venerable Hildebert, CLXXX, 1222, 1237, 1238; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1313.---On elephants, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 145.---On the nature of the elephant, ibid., 72, 73.

Enhydris, a snake living in water, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 445; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 232.

Enhydras, a small animal so named because it lives in water, especially in the Nile, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 439; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 225.---How it kills the crocodile, ibid.

Horse.---Horses are so called because, when they were yoked to four-horse chariots, they were matched and joined as equals in form and alike in speed, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 430; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 213.---Clever horses desire females, Eustathius, LIII, 958.---On the horse, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1319.---On the horse and its nature, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 91.---On the untamed horse, ibid., 145.---Sea-horses, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 451; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 237.

Ericius (*Erinacius*), an animal altogether timid, always armed by provident nature, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 205, 206.---On the hedgehog, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 145; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1331.

Caterpillar, a leaf-worm so called from gnawing, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 235.---On the caterpillar, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 104.---The caterpillar, the itching of lust, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 258.

Falcon. On the falcon, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1296.

Lynx-cat (*Lulis*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1330.---See CAT.

Wild beasts.---On wild beasts, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 146.---They are called wild beasts because they exercise natural freedom and range according to their own desire, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 434.

Fig-eating birds are so called because they eat figs more especially, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 469.

The ant is so called because it carries crumbs of grain, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 441; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 227.---The industrious ant, Eustathius, LIII, 958.---On the nature of the ant, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 75.---On the ant, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1219; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1336.

Ant-lion, so called because it is either the lion of ants or at once ant and lion, an animal hostile to ants, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 441–443; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 228.

Fornha (*salmo trutta*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1278.

Drone, larger than a bee but smaller than a hornet; it is called a drone because it eats the labor of others, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 470; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 256.

Coot, so called because its flesh tastes like hare, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 466.---A gentle, black bird, smaller than a duck but similar in bodily composition, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 248.---A pond-bird, St. Isidore, [Col. 0561] LXXXII, 466; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 248.---The coot which rears the eagle’s rejected young is to be commended, St. Ambrose, XIV, 231.---On the coot, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 56.---Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1148.

Furfurio (*farfario*).---A bird so called because it formerly fed on grain reduced to flour, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 469.

The ferret is named from its dark color; hence also *fur* (“thief”), because it digs out hidden rabbit-burrows, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 440.

Hen.---On the hen, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 147.---Domestic hen, Eustathius, LIII, 949.---On the hen, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1295.---Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 248.

Cock, so called from castration, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 466.---A lustful cock, Eustathius, LIII, 949.---On the cock, St. Ambrose, XIV, 239; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 248; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1150; St. Hildegard, the pheasant-cock, CXCVII, 1295.---On the moral nature of the domestic cock, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 33, 34, 35, 148.

Gerundula (fish), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1281.

Swordfish, so called because its beak is pointed like a sword, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 452.---On the swordfish, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 105.

Glaeuus (fish), so named from its color, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 453.

Glimus, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1311 (the glowworm, *Lampyris noctiluca*).

Dormice, named from *gliscere* (“to grow fat”), because sleep makes them fat, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 441; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 227.---They sleep throughout the winter, ibid.

Jackdaw, so called from its chattering; for it is a most talkative kind of bird, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 465; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 247.---Gregarious jackdaws, Eustathius, LIII, 948; St. Isidore, LXXXII, 247.---On the moral nature of the jackdaw, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 45.

Grasemucka (a kind of wagtail), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1306.

Griffo, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1287.

The cricket takes its name from the sound of its voice; it walks backward, bores into the ground, chirps at night, and hunts with the ant, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 441; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 227.

Cranes took their name from their own call, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 460.---On cranes and their vigilance, St. Ambrose, XIV, 227.---On the letter-shaped formation they maintain in flight, St. Ambrose, XIV, 227; St. Isidore, LXXXII, 460; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 40.---Gregarious cranes, Eustathius, LIII, 948.---On cranes, ibid., 950; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 244; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 148; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1289.

Griffins are so called because they are winged and four-footed animals, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 436; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 222.---On the griffin, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 84.

Gurgulio is so called from the throat, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 472.

Kid, so called from eating, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 426.---On the kid, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 89.

Haemorrhois is an asp so called because one bitten by it sweats blood, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 444; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 231.

Halcyon, a sea-bird, is called as though *alea cyanea* (“blue sea-bird”), because in winter it builds its nest and rears its young in the pools of Ocean, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 462; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 226.---On the halcyon, St. Ambrose, XIV, 224; Eustathius, LIII, 950; Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 95.---On the halcyon (*isenbrado*, *Alcedo hispida*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1304.

Herring, a small fish suitable for the liquid of salted provisions, and hence so named, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 455; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1280.

Halegans (*grandula*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1294.

Hamio, a rock-fish; called *hamio* because it is caught only by a hook.

Harumna, St. Hildegard, XCVIII, 1342.

Hasela (fish), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1280.

Pike (*Esox lucius*), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1276.

Helim, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1338.

Henneramus, a worm of the head, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236.

Hercynian birds are named from the Hercynian forest of Germany where they are born, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 463.---On Hercynian birds, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 95.

Hedgehog, an animal covered with spines, so called because it raises itself up when it closes itself within its spines, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 441; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 227.---On the hedgehog, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 58.

Hippopotamus, so called because it resembles a horse; by day it remains in water and by night grazes upon crops, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 453; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.---The Nile produces it, ibid.

[Col. 0562] The he-goat is so called because the corners of its eyes are *hirqui*; it is a lascivious and wanton animal. Its blood alone has power to dissolve the adamant stone, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 426; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 203.---On the he-goat, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 89, 149; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1325.

The swallow is so called because it does not take food while sitting, but catches its nourishment in the air; it is a chattering bird; it is never prey; it crosses seas and spends the winter there, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 468; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 251.---On the swallow’s usefulness, industry, and devotion to its young, St. Ambrose, XIV, 230.---On the swallow, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 42, 149; St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1307; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1146.

Hamocentaur, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1222.

Huso, St. Hildegard, CLXXVII, 1272.

Huwo (bird), St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1301.

Hyena, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 61.

Hydra, from water, Greek *ὕδωρ*, a dragon with many heads, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 445; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 233.---Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 60.

Hydras, an aquatic serpent, whose victims swell up, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 445.

Hypnalis, a kind of asp so called because it kills by sleep, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 444; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 231.

Porcupine, an African animal resembling the hedgehog, so called from the rattling of its spines, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 439.

Ibex.---Ibexes dwell on the highest rocks, and if they perceive the approach of men or wild beasts, they throw themselves down from mountain summits and are received unharmed upon their horns, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 204.---On the nature of the ibex, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 64.---St. Isidore, LXXXII, 426.---Ibex-goat, St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 1322.

Ibis, a bird of the Nile River, eats serpents’ eggs, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 427, 463.---On the ibis, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 55.

The ichneumon is so called in Greek because by its smell both wholesome and poisonous foods are revealed, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 439–440; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 225.

Icini, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 239.

Fawns are the offspring of deer, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 427; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 205.

Jaculus, “the thrower,” a flying serpent, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 446.---On the jaculus, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 191.

Beasts of burden derived their name from helping our labor, St. Isidore, LXXXII, 425; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 200.---On the beast of burden, Hugh of St. Victor, CLXXVII, 149.---On the threefold kind of beasts of burden, reptiles, and beasts, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 244, 245.---On the adulterous interbreeding of beasts of burden, ibid., 246.

Juvencus (“young bullock”) is so called because it begins to assist human labour in tilling the land, St Isidore, LXXXII, 428; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 207, 209.---On the young bullock, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 89.

Kraha and Krewa (birds), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1298.

Lizard, St Isidore, LXXXII, 446.---On the lizard, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 74, 101; Hildegard, CXCVII, 1342.

Lampreys (fish), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1284.

Lasz (pike, *Esox*), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1275.

Lice, St Isidore, LXXXII, 450; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 104.

Lendix is the same as *tarmus*, from *lende* (“louse”), Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236.

The lion, moreover, is Greek **λέων** (*leōn*), and in Latin is interpreted “king,” because it is the prince of all beasts. Its kind is threefold. Of these, those that are short and have a curled mane are cowardly; those that are long and have a plain mane are fierce, St Isidore, LXXXII, 434; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 217.---On the generation of the lion, Eustathius, LIII, 962.---On the lion’s short neck, ibid., 962.---On the lion, Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1217; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 56; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1314.---On the lion, king of beasts, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 150.

Leontophonos: a small beast whose roasted flesh kills lions, St Isidore, LXXXII, 439.

The leopard is born from the adulterous union of a lioness and a pard, St Isidore, LXXXII, 435; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 226.

Hare, as though *levipes* (“light-footed”), because it is swift, St Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 205.---More fertile hares, Eustathius, LIII, 961.---Black hares in Normandy, Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 649.---On the hare, St Ambrose, XIV, 237; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 150; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1326.

Hare (fish), so named from the likeness of its head, St Isidore, LXXXII, 453.

Leuerocuta, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 85.

[Col. 0563] Lunax, a worm of mud, is so called because it is born in mud, or from mud, St Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 235.

Lira, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1336.

The locust, because it has long legs, St Isidore, LXXXII, 471; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 256.---On the locust’s service in carrying out the final divine [act; text incomplete], St Ambrose, XIV, 237.---On the locust, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 151; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1310.---The land-locust and the sea-locust, St Isidore, LXXXII, 471; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 256.

Cuttlefish, St Isidore, LXXXII, 456.

Earthworm, a worm of the intestines, so called as though *lubricus* (“slippery”), because it slips, or because it is in the loins, St Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236.---On the earthworm, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 104.

The wolf (**λύκος**, *lykos*), a rapacious beast desirous of blood; Ethiopia produces wolves with maned necks, St Isidore, LXXXII, 437; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 223.---The untamed wolf, Eustathius, LIII, 958.---On the wolf, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 106, 151.---On the wolf, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1326.

The sea-wolf, a fish ingenious in catching fish, St Isidore, LXXXII, 453; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 106.

The nightingale, a bird which takes its name from its custom of signalling by its song the rising of the day, as though *lucinia* (“light-singer”), St Isidore, LXXXII, 464; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 247.---On the song of the brooding nightingale, St Ambrose, XIV, 239.---The nightingale keeps watch while brooding over its eggs, Eustathius, LIII, 953.---On the nightingale, Abbot Werner, CLXII, 1149; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 96.---Hildebert, CLXXI, 1237.

Lyciscus.---Lycisci, according to Pliny, are dogs born from wolves and dogs when they happen to mate with one another, St Isidore, LXXXII, 438; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 224.

The lynx is so called because it is counted among the kind of wolves; Pliny says that lynxes do not admit a second male in addition to one, St Isidore, LXXXII, 437; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 222.---On the lynx, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 84.

Mantichora, a beast, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 85; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 124, 125.

Pearl-bearing shellfish, St Isidore, LXXXII, 456; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 80.

Marmot, hamster (*cricetus*; Hamstra), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1332.

White martens in Normandy, Adam of Bremen, CXLVI, 649.

Melanurus, a fish, so called because it has a black tail, St Isidore, LXXXII, 453.

Melo, either because it has a very rounded limb, or because it continually seeks honey, St Isidore, LXXXII, 440; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 248.

Memnonides: Egyptian birds named from the place where Memnon perished, St Isidore, LXXXII, 463.

The merganser takes its name from its continual diving, St Isidore, LXXXII, 466; Rabanus Maurus, CXL, 248.---On the merganser, Eustathius, LIII, 954.

Merla (bird), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1307.

Meropes: birds said to bury and feed their parents, St Isidore, LXXXII, 463.

Merswin (a species of seal), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1273.

The blackbird was formerly called *medula*, because it sings melodies, St Isidore, LXXXIII, 468.---On the blackbird, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 152.---On the nature of the blackbird in a moral sense, ibid., 44.

Meygelana, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1310.

Meysisch (fish), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1279.

Milvago, a fish, so called because it flies up above the water, St Isidore, LXXXII, 454.

The kite, as though *mollis avis* (“a weak bird”), weak in strength and flight, yet very rapacious, St Isidore, LXXXII, 467; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 252.---On the kite, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 152; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1297.---On the nature of the kite, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 41.

The jackdaw (*choucas*), as though *monotula*, which, when it finds gold, carries it away and conceals it, St Isidore, LXXXII, 463.

Monoceros (a one-horned animal), St Isidore, LXXXII, 435; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 220; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 124; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 59.

Monuwa (fish), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1279.

The mullet takes its name from being very agile, St Isidore, LXXXII, 453; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.---On the mule, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 106.

Mugya (bird), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1310.

The red mullet (*surmulet*) is so called because it is soft and very tender; a red mullet killed in wine brings nausea to those who drink from it, St Isidore, LXXXII, 453; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.---On the red mullet, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 106.

The centipede, a terrestrial worm, is named from its multitude of feet, St Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 235.---On the centipede, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 104.

The mule is so called from Greek because, in grinding, it draws slow millstones in a circle, St Isidore, LXXXII, 432, 433; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 215.

The moray (**μύραινα**, *myraina*), because it coils itself into circles, St Isidore, LXXXII, 455; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.---Morays bear young, Eustathius, LIII, 937.---On the moray, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 108; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 893.

The murex is a sea-snail, so called from its pointedness and roughness; it is also called *conchilium*, because when cut open with iron it emits tears of purple colour, from which purple dye is made, St Isidore, LXXXII, 456; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.---On the murex, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 110.

Murilegus, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 153.

The mouse, a very small animal: its liver grows at the full moon, St Isidore, LXXXII, 440; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 226.---On the mouse, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 93, 153; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1335.

Shrew-mouse, St Isidore, LXXXII, 441.

Musar (gull), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1299.

The fly comes from Greek, as does *mus* (“mouse”), St Isidore, LXXXII, 471; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 257.---Flies, Eustathius, LIII, 235.---The housefly, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1309.

Mussels are shellfish by whose milk oysters conceive; and they are called *musculi* as though *masculi* (“males”), St Isidore, LXXXII, 457; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 239.---On mussels, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 110.

The cat is so called because it is hostile to mice; *catus* is derived from catching, or from **καίεσθαι** (*kaiesthai*, “to burn”), St Isidore, LXXXII, 440; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 226.---On the cat, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 93; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1330.

The weasel, as though *mus longus* (“long mouse”), St Isidore, LXXXII, 440; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 226.---On the weasel, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 66.---Polecat weasel (*Mustela putorius*, Illediso), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1331.---Marten (*Mustela martes*, Marth), ibid., 1332.---Sable (*M. zibellina*, Zobel), ibid., 1333.---Ermine (*M. herminea*, hermini), ibid., 1333.---Common weasel (*Mustela vulgaris*, Wisela), ibid., 1334.

Nachtgalla (wagtail-nightingale, *motacilla luscinia*), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1305.

The water-snake, a serpent infecting water with venom, St Isidore, LXXXVII, 445.

Nebelkraha (bird), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1298.

The owl is so called because it flies about at night and cannot see by day; the owl is smaller than the horned owl, St Isidore, LXXXII, 464; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 247.---Light-shunning owls, St Ambrose, XIV, 239; Eustathius, LIII, 953.---On the owl, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1150.

The nycticorax is itself the owl, because it loves the night, St Isidore, LXXXII, 464–465.---Nycticorax, by its Greek name, means “night-raven”; some have called it a horned owl, others an owl, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 251.---On the nycticorax, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 30, 163.

The oestrus (gadfly; in Latin *asilus*, *tabanus*), an animal exceedingly troublesome to herds with its sting, St Isidore, LXXXII, 472.

The swan is the bird called **κύκνον** (*kyknon*).---The swan is so called because it is wholly white in its feathers, St Isidore, LXXXII, 461; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 245.---On the swan, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1237.

Onager is interpreted “wild ass” (**ὄνος ἄγριος**, *onos agrios*).---Africa has these, large and untamed. Individual males preside over herds of females. They bite off the testicles of male offspring at birth, St Isidore, LXXXII, 429–430; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 212, 213.---On the onager, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 62.

Onycha (fish), Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 154.

Onocentaur, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 58–78.

The onocrotalus (bittern): the Greeks call by this name a long-beaked bird, one kind aquatic and another of the wilderness, St Isidore, LXXXII, 463; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 246.

Ordumel (bird), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1299.

Ormella, Venerable Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1237–1238.

The ortygometra (crake), which is said to lead the flock, feeds upon poisonous seeds, St Isidore, LXXXII, 468; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 250.

Songbirds, St Isidore, LXXXII, 469.

The bone-breaker (*orfraie*) is commonly called the bird which drops bones from on high and breaks them, St Isidore, LXXXII, 467.

The oyster (*huîtres*) is named from its shell (**ὄστραξ**, *ostrāx*), by which the softness of its inner flesh is protected, St Isidore, LXXXII, 457; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 239.---Oyster, Eustathius, LIII, 937, 939.---Mussels are male oysters, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 239.

Otther (a species of otter), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1329.

Ovifici (“egg-making fish”), Eustathius, LIII, 937.

The sheep, a soft, wool-bearing flock-animal, defenceless in body, is so called from being carried away, St Isidore, LXXXII, 425.---On the sheep, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 88; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1326.---Wild sheep are more fertile, Eustathius, LIII, 961.

Pafendunus (fish), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1281.

The pagrus (**φάγρον**, *phagron*; pagre) is so called because it has hard teeth, St Isidore, LXXXII, 453.

Wood-pigeons are so called because they are fattened by fodder; the common people call them *titos*, St Isidore, LXXXII, 467.

The panther is so called either because it is the friend of all animals, or because it delights in the companionship of its own kind; it bears offspring only once in all its life; wherefore, St Isidore, LXXXII, 435; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 219, 220.---On the nature of panthers, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 69.---On the panther, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1223; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 155; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1313.

Butterflies, St Isidore, LXXXIII, 471.

The pard is second after the panther, a variegated kind, headlong in its thirst for blood, St Isidore, LXXXII, 435; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 217, 220.---On the pard, Eustathius, LIII, 958; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 83, 156.

Parias, a serpent which always moves upon its tail, St Isidore, LXXXII, 445.

Parix, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1311.

Parus (Meysa), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1303.

Sparrow.---Sparrows are small flying creatures named from their smallness, St Isidore, LXXXII, 468; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 230.---There are many kinds of sparrow: some delight in openings in walls; others seek dewy valleys, ibid.---On the sparrow, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXXII, 23, 156; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1303.---On sparrows nesting in the branches of the cedar, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 26.---On the house which the sparrow finds, and on the habits of the tamed sparrow, ibid., 27, 28, 29.

The peacock takes its name from the sound of its voice; its flesh is so hard that it scarcely undergoes decay and is not easily cooked, St Isidore, LXXXII, 466; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 247.---The attentive peacock, Eustathius, LIII, 949.---On the nature of the peacock, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 52.---On the peacock, ibid., 156; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1288.

Cattle, *pecus*, derives from grazing: we call everything lacking human speech and appearance by this name.---Strictly speaking, however, the name *pecora* is usually applied to animals fit either for food or for use advantageous to human beings; and there is a distinction between *pecora* and *pecudes*, St Isidore, LXXXII, 425; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 200.

Scallops (*petoneles*), Eustathius, LIII, 937.

Lice are skin-worms, named from their feet, St Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 104.

The pelican is an Egyptian bird living in the solitude of the Nile River, from which it also takes its name, St Isidore, LXXXII, 462.---Similar to storks in size of body, it consoles itself by its delight in solitude, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 250, 251.---On the nature of the pelican, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 29, 74, 156.

Pelonides (*palourdes*, clams) are named from Cape Pelorus in Sicily, St Isidore, LXXXII, 457.

The partridge takes its name from its cry; it is a deceitful and unclean bird, St Isidore, LXXXII, 467; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 249.---The deceitful and jealous partridge, Eustathius, LXII, 949.---On the partridge, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 49, 156.

The pheasant is named from the island of Phasinde in Greece, St Isidore, LXXXII, 466.

Philomela.---See Nightingale.

Seals.---Seals are said to be sea-cattle, St Isidore, LXXXII, 451.---Seals bear young, Eustathius, LIII, 938.

The phoenix, a bird of Arabia, is so called because it has a Phoenician-red colour; the resurrection of the phoenix is fabulously related, St Isidore, LXXXII, 462; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 246.---On the phoenix, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 48.

Magpies are so called as though *poetricae* (“poetical”), because, like human beings, they articulate words with distinction of voice, St Isidore, LXXXII, 465.---Magpies hanging among the branches of trees and sounding with troublesome chattering, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 247.---On the magpie, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 95; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1300.

The woodpecker takes its name from Picus, son of Saturn, because they employed it in auguries, St Isidore, LXXXII, 465.---On the woodpecker, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 247; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 95.---On the woodpecker (*specht*), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1302.

[Col. 0566] Why fish are so called, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 237.---Fish, from feeding, St Isidore, LXXXII, 450.---Why certain fish are called creeping things, Ambrose, XIV, 203; St Isidore, LXXXII, 450; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 237.---On the generation of fish, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 239.---The manifold manner of fish generation and their singular instinct of affection toward their offspring, St Ambrose, XIV, 208.---Why fish are so well supplied with teeth; they yield themselves to one another as food, ibid., 210.---To each kind of fish its own habitats have been assigned.---Some fish change places for the sake of their young, ibid., 217.---On fish of the Atlantic Sea, ibid., 220.---There are open-sea fish, shore fish, high-swimming fish, rock fish, shoaling fish, monstrous fish, huge fish, and small fish, Eustathius, LIII, 937.---Fish have their own allotted condition, their own nature, differing food, and a fixed mode of life, ibid., 937.---Of one kind are those called shell-bearing, and of another those called many-shelled, ibid., 937.---Those who fish in the Indian Sea know some fish, and those who explore the Egyptian deep know others, ibid., 938.---Great is the diversity in the way fish live, and excessive too the distinction in the succession of each kind, ibid., 938.---Many fish do not brood over their own eggs, but the water, receiving the egg, makes an animal, ibid., 938.---No fish is armed with teeth only in one half, as sheep and cattle are; rather, all fish are furnished with the sharpest edge of teeth, ibid., 938.---Migrations of fish, ibid., 940, 941.---On wandering fish, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 239.---Comparison of fish and birds, St Ambrose, XIV, 225; Eustathius, LIII, 947.---On the natures of different fish, ibid., 935; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 105, 106, 107, 157; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1365, 1266–1269.

The polypus, that is, “many-footed,” St Isidore, LXXXII, 455.---On the cunning of the polypus, St Ambrose, XIV, 215; St Isidore, LXXXII, 455.---On the polypus, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 108; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 893.

Many-footed creatures (*polypodes*), Eustathius, LIII, 937.

Pig, as though *spurcus* (“filthy”), for it stuffs itself with mud, St Isidore, LXXXII, 428; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 206.---On the pig, CLXXVII, 137; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1325.

Sea-pigs dig the earth under water in the manner of swine, St Isidore, LXXXII, 452; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 238.---On sea-pigs, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 105.

Praester, an asp, always runs with its mouth open and steaming, St Isidore, LXXXII, 444.

The parrot is born on the shores of India, green in colour, with a scarlet collar and a large tongue. It articulates speech, St Isidore, LXXXII, 462; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 246.---On the parrot, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 94; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1300.

Fleas are so called because they are nourished chiefly from dust, St Isidore, LXXXII, 450; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236.---On fleas, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 104; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1336.

Newly born young are called *pulli* because they are defiled, St Isidore, LXXXII, 459–460.

Punbelen (fish), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1284.

Quadrupeds are so called because they walk upon four feet, St Isidore, LXXXII, 425; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 200.---Quadrupeds are distinguished by diverse properties, Eustathius, LIII, 958.---The weaker are more fertile, so that the species may not easily be destroyed, ibid., 961.---Beasts that devour others are regarded as more sterile, ibid., 961. Characteristics of different wild animals suited to nourishment and preservation, ibid., 962, 963.

Frogs, Eustathius, LIII, 985.---Frogs are named from their chattering: some are called aquatic, some marsh frogs, some toads, others *calamitae*, St Isidore, LXXXII, 458; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 228.---On the frog, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 158.---Toad frog (*Rana bufo*, credda), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1341.---Edible frog (*Rana esculenta*, frosch), ibid., 1341.---Tree frog (*Rana arborea*, lambfrosch), ibid., 1342.

Reguli, also called *sibili* (“hissers”; serpents), St Isidore, LXXXII, 443; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 231.

Creeping things, from creeping, St Isidore, LXXXII, 450.---Not only serpents but fish too are called creeping things, St Ambrose, XIV, 105; St Isidore, LXXXII, 450.---On creeping things, Eustathius, LIII, 963; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 105.---On the threefold kind of beasts of burden, creeping things, and beasts, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 245.

Rhinoceros, so called by the Greeks, is interpreted in Latin as “horn in the nose.” It is also monoceros, that is, unicorn, because it has one horn in the middle of its forehead, St Isidore, LXXXII, 425; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 220.

Ricinus, a dog-worm, so called because it clings to dogs’ ears, St Isidore, LXXXII, 450; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236.---On the *ricinus*, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 105.

[Col. 0567] Rotega (fish), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1279.

Rulheulet (fish), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1282.

Sagena, Hugh of St Victor; St Isidore, CLXXVII, 159.

The salamander is so called because it has power against fires; among all poisons its force is greatest, St Isidore, LXXXII, 446; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 233.---On the salamander, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 65.

Salmon (fish), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1274.

The leech, an aquatic worm, is so called because it sucks blood, St Isidore, LXXXII, 448; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 235.---On the leech, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 104, 159.

Satyrs (fabulous beings), St Isidore, LXXXII, 439; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 225.

Saura, a lizard whose eyes are blinded when it grows old, St Isidore, LXXXII, 447.---On the saura, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 102.

Hornets are named from *cabo*, that is, *caballo* (“horse”), because they are produced from horses. For just as hornets are born from the putrefied flesh of horses, so beetles are often in turn born from them, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 256.

The scarus (*sarget*) is so called because it alone among fish is reported to chew the cud, St Isidore, LXXXII, 454.---On the scarus, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 892.---Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 108.

Scherz bedrae, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1344.

Squirrel (Eschorn), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1332.

The scorpion, a terrestrial worm: an animal armed with a sting and called by this Greek name because it strikes with its tail and diffuses venom through its curved wound, St Isidore, LXXXII, 448–449; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 232.---On the scorpion, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 104, 105; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1344.---The sea-scorpion, St Isidore, LXXXII, 452.

Scytale, a serpent so called because it shines with such diversity upon its back that it delays onlookers by the beauty of its markings; in winter it casts off the slough of its heated body, St Isidore, LXXXII, 444.---On the scytale, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 101.

Seleucis, a bird that devours the locust, St Ambrose, XIV, 237.

The cuttlefish is so called because it is more easily caught when enclosed by hedges; it is an obscene kind in mating, St Isidore, LXXXII, 456.---On cuttlefish, Eustathius, LIII, 937.

Seps, a wasting asp which, when it has bitten a person, immediately consumes body and bones with its venom, St Isidore, LXXXII, 444, 446; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 231.---On the seps, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 101.

The serpent takes its name because it creeps by hidden approaches; serpents are creeping things because they crawl upon belly and breast, St Isidore, LXXXII, 442; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 229.---Not only serpents but fish too are called creeping things, St Ambrose, XIV, 205.---Serpents have as many poisons as kinds, as many destructive powers as species, and as many pains as colours, St Isidore, LXXXII, 442; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 229.---On the usefulness of serpents, St Ambrose, IV, 253.---Every kind of serpent, whether venomous or not, has been corrupted because the devil used it for human death, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 245.---There are serpents so huge that they devour stags and even swim across the Ocean itself, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 124.---On kinds of serpent, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 100.---On the diverse nature of serpents, ibid., 102.---On siren-serpents, ibid., 104.---On the serpent, ibid., 160.---On a certain serpent, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1339.---On serpents, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 234, 235.---Bramble leaves kill a serpent, Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1151.

The sawfish is so called because it has a serrated crest, St Isidore, LXXXII, 452.---On the sawfish, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 69, 105.

The sponge (*éponge*) is so called from *fingere*, that is, “to polish and wipe clean”; it is taught to be an animal, with blood, adhering to rocks, St Isidore, LXXXII, 458; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 239.

Sibitus.---See Reguli.

“Monkey” is a Greek name, meaning “with compressed nostrils”; monkeys are clever at flattery, rejoice at the new moon, and are saddened at its half and waning. They carry before them the young which they love; the neglected young cling about their mother. There are five kinds of them, among which the cercopitheci have tails, St Isidore, LXXXII, 439; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 225.---On monkeys, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 62.---On the monkey, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1329.

Sirens.---On sirens, Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1222.---On siren-serpents, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 101.

Sisegonino (bird), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1301.

Slya (fish), St Hildegard, ibid., 1281.

Snepha (bird), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1302.

[Col. 0568] Solpunga is a serpent which cannot be seen, St Isidore, LXXXII, 446.

Sorex is Latin, because it gnaws and cuts in the manner of a saw, St Isidore, LXXXII, 440; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 226.---On the shrew, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 93.---The spider-shrew (*Sorex araneus*, spiezmo), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1336.

The sparus, a fish, derives its name from scattering (*a spargendo*) and from a thrown spear, because it has the same shape, St Isidore, LXXXII, 454.

Sperwere (bird), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1297.

Sphinxes are shaggy with hair, have projecting breasts, and are teachable to forget their wildness, St Isidore, LXXXII, 439.

Squatus, a fish, so called because it has sharp scales, St Isidore, LXXXII, 455.

Stechela (fish), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1282.

Stellio, a serpent, takes its name from its colour; for it is painted with shining spots in the manner of stars, St Isidore, LXXXII, 447.---On the stellio, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 65, 74, 102.

Steinbisza (fish), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1282.

Storus (*Acipenser stario*), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1273.

The screech-owl, a nocturnal bird, takes its name from the sound of its voice: when it cries, it screeches; it is commonly called *amma*, from loving, St Isidore, LXXXII, 465.

The ostrich is called by a Greek name because, though it appears an animal resembling a bird and has feathers, it does not rise high from the ground; it leaves its eggs in the dust to be warmed, St Isidore, LXXXII, 461; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 245.---On the ostrich and its feathers, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 35, 161.---St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1287.

Flocking starlings, Eustathius, LIII, 948.---Common starling (*stara*), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1305.

The Stymphalian birds are named from the Stymphalian islands, St Isidore, LXXXII, 462.

The hedgehog is named from its bristles; it also pursues serpents. How it fights the asp, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 225; St Isidore, LXXXII, 452.

The sow is so called because it roots up pastureland, that is, seeks food in soil which it has dug up, St Isidore, LXXXII, 428; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 206.

The mole is so called because it is condemned to perpetual blindness. It digs the earth and casts out soil, St Isidore, LXXXII, 441; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 226.---On the mole, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 94, 161; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1333.

*Tarmus* is a lard-worm, St Isidore, LXXXII, 450; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236.---On the *tarmus*, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 104.

“Bull” is a Greek name, as is “ox,” St Isidore, LXXXII, 428; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 207, 208.---The bull of India is swift and tawny, with the rapidity of a bird, St Isidore, LXXXII, 428; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 124.---On the bull, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 89, 161.

“Bulls” are terrestrial beetles resembling ticks, St Isidore, LXXXII, 470.---“Bulls” are terrestrial or woodland beetles resembling ticks, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 256.

Teredona.---The Greeks call wood-worms *teredones*, because they eat by boring; we call them termites, St Isidore, LXXXII, 449.---Teredones, or termites, which felled trees produce in their unseasonable time, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 235.---On the teredo, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 104.

The tortoise is so called because it is covered with a shell-like covering in the form of a vault; there are land, sea, river, and mud tortoises, St Isidore, LXXXII, 457.---The Indian Sea produces tortoises from whose shells people make spacious dwellings for themselves, Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 125.---On the tortoise, Eustathius, LIII, 963.

Tetrao (capercaillie, partridge grouse, black grouse), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1296.

Tharandus, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 86.

Thymallus, a fish, takes its name from a flower, St Isidore, LXXXII, 454.

Tunnies have a Greek name, St Isidore, LXXXII, 452.

The tiger is so called because of its swift flight; for the Persians and Medes give this name to an arrow. It is a beast marked with diverse spots, remarkable for strength and swiftness, St Isidore, LXXXII, 434; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 219.---On the tiger’s short neck, Eustathius, LIII, 962.---On the tiger, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 83; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1318.

The clothes-moth is a worm of garments, so called because it clings to them and remains there until it gnaws them away, St Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 235.---On the moth, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 104, 162.

[Col. 0569] The torpedo is so called because it makes the body numb if anyone touches it alive, St Isidore, LXXXII, 455, 456.---On the torpedo, Eustathius, LIII, 937; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 108.

Tragelaphi are so called by the Greeks; though they have the same appearance as stags, they have shaggy shoulders like goats, and are found nowhere but about the Phasis, St Isidore, LXXXII, 427; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 204.

Tuci, which the Spaniards call cuckoos, are named from their own cry; their saliva produces cicadas, St Isidore, LXXXII, 468.---On the *tuco* (cuckoo), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1302.

Thrushes are named from slowness, for they return at the boundary of winter, St Isidore, LXXXII, 468.

The mistle-thrush, as though a larger thrush, from whose droppings mistletoe is thought to be produced, St Isidore, LXXXII, 468.

The turtledove is named from its cry, a modest bird always dwelling on mountain ridges and in deserted wildernesses, St Isidore, LXXXII, 467; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 248.---The turtledove is praised for widowhood, St Ambrose, XIV, 232.---On the cry and nest of the turtledove, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 23, 24, 25.---On the turtledove, Eustathius, LIII, 951; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1148; Hildebert, CLXXI, 1223; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 23, 163; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1300.

Tyriaca, a worm, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1344.

The ulula (**ὀλολύζειν**, *ololyzein*, “to wail”), a bird named from lamentation and mourning; for when it cries, it imitates either weeping or groaning, St Isidore, LXXXII, 464; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 247; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1301.

Ulwurm, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1344.

Ungues (“nails”; fish), so called from their resemblance to human nails, St Isidore, LXXXII, 457.

Unicorn, St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1517.

The hoopoe is so called by the Greeks because it settles upon human excrement and feeds upon foul dung; it is a most filthy bird, always dwelling among tombs and human excrement, St Isidore, LXXXII, 468; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 252; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 50.---On the hoopoe (*vedehoppo*), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1305.

The uranoscopus, a fish, is named from the eye which it has in its head and with which it always looks upward, St Isidore, LXXXII, 454.

The bear is said to be so called because it forms its young with its mouth, as though *orsus* (“formed”). The bear’s head is weak; its greatest strength is in its forelegs and loins; hence it sometimes stands upright, St Isidore, LXXXII, 437; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 223.---On the bear’s short neck, Eustathius, LIII, 958, 962.---Normandy has white bears, Adam, canon of Bremen, CXLVI, 649.---On the bear, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 85, 164; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1316.---Badger (*Ursus meles*, dasch), ibid., 1330.

Urus.---Aurochs are wild cattle in Germany, having horns so extended that capacious drinking vessels of remarkable size are made from them for royal tables. They are called *uri* **ἀπὸ τῶν ὀρῶν** (“from the mountains”), St Isidore, LXXXII, 429; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 210.---Aurochs are captured in Sweden, Adam, canon of Bremen, CXLVI, 649.---On the aurochs, Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 90.

Usia is a pig-worm, so called because it burns; for where it has bitten, the spot burns so greatly that blisters form, St Isidore, LXXXII, 450; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 105.

The cow is so called as though *boacca*; for it belongs to the category of movable nouns, St Isidore, LXXXII, 429.---On the cow, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 208; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 163.

A worm is an animal usually generated from flesh or wood, and without any sexual union; there are worms of earth, water, air, flesh, plants, etc., St Isidore, LXXXII, 448.---A worm does not walk, as a serpent does, with visible steps; rather, by successively extending the contracted parts of its little body straight forward and contracting those extended, it executes motion, St Isidore, LXXXII, 449.---What a worm is, Hugh of St Victor, LXXVII, 103.---On worms, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 235; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 105, 163.---On flesh-worms, ibid., 104.---Worms of flesh: *hemicraneus*, earthworm, *ascaridae*, *costi*, lice, fleas, *leudes*, *tarinus*, tick, *usia*, bedbug, St Isidore, LXXXII, 449; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 236.

Indian worm, St Ambrose, XIV, 237.

The boar is so called because it has great strength, St Isidore, LXXXII, 428; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 206.

The wether (*mouton*) is named either from strength, because it is stronger than other sheep; or because it is male; or because it has a worm in its head, St Isidore, LXXXII, 425, 426; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 89.

Wasps or hornets signify pursuing enemies or fear of enemies, Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 256.---Wasps, St Isidore, LXXXII, 470.

The bat takes its name from the time, because, fleeing the light, it flies about in evening twilight; it has the form at once of a flying creature and a quadruped, which is not usually found in other birds, St Isidore, LXXXII, 464; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 246.---Light-shunning bats, Eustathius, LIII, 953.---On the bat, St Ambrose, XIV, 239; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 96; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1308.---Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1150.

Vyneo (chaffinch, *fringilla caelebs*), St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1306.

The viper is so called because it gives birth by force, St Isidore, LXXXII, 443; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 232.---On the viper, Eustathius, LIII, 963; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 66; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1342; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 893.

Sea-calves, Eustathius, LIII, 936, 937.

Flying creatures, from flying, St Isidore, LXXXII, 459; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 241; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 164.

The fox (*vulpes*) is so called as though *volupes* (“swift-footed”), for it is nimble on its feet; it is a crafty animal and deceives by ambushes: St Isidore, LXXXII, 438; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 225.---The wily fox: Eustathius, LIII, 958.---Normandy has black foxes: Adam of Reims, CXLVI, 649.---On the fox: Hildebert of Le Mans, CLXXI, 1220; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 59, 164; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1328.

The vulture is thought to take its name from its slow flight: St Isidore, LXXXII, 460; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 243.---Vultures are said to breed without coupling with a male: St Ambrose, XIV, 233; St Isidore, LXXXII, 460; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 243.---On the foresight of vultures: St Ambrose, XIV, 237.---Vultures announce the death of human beings: Eustathius, LIII, 953.---On vultures: Hugh of St Victor, CLXXVII, 39, 164; St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1290; Abbot Werner, CLVII, 1148.

*Wachtela* (quail, *Tetrao coturnix*): St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1305.

*Walca* (wels catfish, *Silurus glanis*): St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1275.

*Wargkrengel* (a bird): St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1307.

*Wasser Marth.* (water marten): St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1333.

*Waszerceltza* (white wagtail, *Motacilla alba*): St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1307.

*Weho* (a bird): St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1298.

*Wespa* (wasp): St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1311.

*Widderwalo*: St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1308.

*Wisant* (bison): St Hildegard, CXCVII, 1322.

## CCXXIII. INDEX OF ARITHMETIC, SETTING FORTH THE VARIOUS TREATISES ON THE SCIENCE OF NUMBERS INCLUDED IN THE PATROLOGY, AND PROVIDING A BRIEF ANALYSIS OF EACH

**BOETHIUS.**---Two books on arithmetic, LXIII, 1079.

Here we set forth an analysis of the first book only, since the second book will be more suitably placed in the Index of Geometry.

according to Pythagoras, ibid.---Another, according to the older method, definition of even and odd, 1084.---Definition of even and odd by mutual alternation, 1085.---On [Col. 0571] the primacy of CCXXV. INDEX OF MEASURES, WEIGHTS, AND COINS MENTIONED IN THE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, ARRANGED IN LOGICAL ORDER.

I.—Measures in general.

Various definitions of measure: Boethius, LXIII, 1307, 1337; St Isidore, LXXXII, 593; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 485. — The threefold class of measures: Boethius, LXIII, 1337; St Isidore, LXXXII, 593. — Measures expressed by letters: Boethius, LXIII, 1352; St Isidore, LXXXII, 596, 597. — Reform of measures under King Theodoric: Boethius, LXIV, 1430, 1431. — The usefulness of measures reduced to a uniform standard: Cassiodorus, LXIX, 515. — Origin and etymology of measures: St Isidore, LXXXII, 590, 593. — Equity in measures: Charlemagne, XCVIII, 178; XCVII, 729; Smaragdus, CII, 967; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 675; CX, 1026, 1027; CXI, 485; Regino of Prüm, CXXXII, 365 ff.; Peter the Chanter, CCV, 85.

II.—Measures of length.

1. **Actus.** — The different divisions of the *actus*: Boethius, LXIII, 1335, 1336. — Antiquity of the *actus*: Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 96.

2. **Cubit.** — What the geometrical cubit is: St Augustine, XLI, 474; XXXIV, 349, 549; Walafrid, CXIII, 108. — The cubit listed among ancient measures: Boethius, LXIII, 1335. — The length of a cubit: Boethius, LXIII, 1336; Venerable Bede, XCI, 401; Charlemagne, [Col. 0578] XCVII, 384; Rabanus Maurus, CIX, 177; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 97, 98; Rupert, CLXVII, 704; Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 46. — On the square cubit: Gerhoh, CXCIV, 1447.

3. **Ten-foot rod (*decempeda*).** — Antiquity of the *decempeda*: Boethius, LXIII, 1335; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 96. — Its length: Boethius, LXIII, 1336; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 97.

4. **Finger (*digitus*).** — The finger, one of the twelve measures of length: Boethius, LXIII, 1335; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 98. — Prescribed length of the finger: St Isidore, LXXXIII, 555; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 90, 98.

5. **Cord (*funiculus*).** — The cord, an Egyptian measure: St Jerome, XXV, 986. — Who measures the earth with a cord: Rupert, CLXVII, 1133.

6. **Pace (*gradus*).** — The pace, one of the twelve measures of length: Boethius, LXIII, 1335; CXXXIX, 96. — Prescribed length of the pace: Boethius, LXIII, 1336; St Isidore, LXXXII, 555, 556; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 97, 98. — Etymology of *gradus*: Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 97.

7. **League (*leuca*).** — Length of the league: Lactantius, VII, 825; Boethius, LXIII, 1358; St Isidore, LXXXII, 557; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 98. — The league as a road measure: Constantine the Great, VIII, 783; St Jerome, XXV, 986; [Col. 0579] St Isidore, LXXXII, 557; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 98. — Etymology of *leuca*: Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 91.

8. **Mile (*milliarium*).** — Miles used as a road measure: Lactantius, VII, 826; Constantine the Great, VIII, 784 ff.; St Augustine, XXXVIII, 609, 1027; XXXIX, 1547, 1665; Boethius, LXIII, 1335; St Isidore, LXXXII, 555; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 412; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 98. — The stated length of the mile: Boethius, LXIII, 1335; St Benedict, LXVI, 389; St Isidore, LXXXII, 555, 557; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 412; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 91, 98; Hildebert, CLXXI, 419.

9. **Palm (*palmus*).** — The palm as a measure of length: Boethius, LXIII, 1335; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 96. — The accepted length of the palm: Boethius, LXIII, 1336; St Isidore, LXXXII, 555; Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 90, 96, 98. — Etymology of *palmus*: Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 96.

10. **Parasang.** — The parasang, a Persian road measure: St Jerome, XXV, 986; St Isidore, LXXXII, 557.
