VII.—Measures of time.

Various methods of reckoning time: St Jerome, XXIV, 392; Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 484 note; St Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 477; Venerable Bede, XC, 953, 954; Claudius of Turin, CIV, 797; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 676, 678; Wandalbert, CXXI, 631, 633; Herman, CXLIII, 405 ff., 409, 410. — Definitions of time: St Isidore, LXXXIII, 974; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 676. — Etymology of time: Venerable Bede, XC, 579; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 678. — Various divisions of time: Venerable Bede, XC, 579; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 677. — What *aevum* is: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 145. — Various measures of time follow.

1. **Year.** — Reckonings of the year among the Egyptians: Lactantius, VI, 325 note. — Definitions of the year: St Isidore, LXXXII, 222; LXXXIII, 971; CXXIX, 1295, 1296. — Etymology of the year: St Isidore, LXXXII, 222; Venerable Bede, XC, 589. — Various kinds of year: St Isidore, LXXXII, 249; Venerable Bede, XC, 284; Helperic, CXXXVII, 21. — Discussions of the year: St Isidore, LXXXIII, 971 ff.

2. **Atom.** — Duration of the atom: Venerable Bede, XC, 302 note; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 677; CXXIX, 1316. — The minuteness of the atom: Venerable Bede, XC, 305, 580; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 147.

3. **Day.** — Discussion of the three days of Christ’s burial: Lactantius, VII, 194 note. — Names of the days: D. Ausonius, XIX, 910; St Isidore, LXXXII, 217; LXXXIII, 967; Venerable Bede, XC, 583; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 150; Peter the Chanter, CCV, 419. — Various considerations concerning days: St Augustine, XXXIX, 193; Venerable Bede, XC, 309 ff.; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 679, 680. — Kinds of day: St Benedict, LXVI, 411, 413; St Isidore, [Col. 0584] LXXXII, 215. — Different beginnings of the day among different peoples: St Isidore, LXXXII, 215; Venerable Bede, XC, 279, 280. — Etymology of day: Venerable Bede, XC, 307 note. — Duration of the day: the same author, XC, 309 ff.

4. **Hour.** — Various hours of the day: St Jerome, XXVI, 141. — Hours formerly unequal: Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 485. — Etymology of hour: St Isidore, LXXXII, 215; Venerable Bede, XC, 580; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 147. — Duration of the hour: Venerable Bede, XC, 302; CXXIX, 1316; Honorius of Autun, CLXVI, 147.

6. **Lustrum.** — The *lustrum* among various divisions of time: St Isidore, LXXXII, 208.

8. **Minute.** — Duration of the minute: Venerable Bede, XC, 302 note, 580; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 678; CXXIX, 1293; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 147. — Etymology of minute: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 678; CXXIX, 1293.

12. **Part.** — Etymology of *pars*: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 678. — Duration represented by a part: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 678; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 147.

13. **Point.** — Duration of the point: Venerable Bede, XC, 302 note, 303; CXXIX, 1292, 1317. — Etymology of *punctum*: ibid., XC, 580; CXXIX, 1293.

14. **Quarter.** — Duration of the quarter variously estimated: Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 678; CXXIX, 1293, 1319. — Etymology of *quadrans*: CXXIX, 1319.

15. **Age (*saeculum*).** — Ages constructed out of periods of time: Tertullian, II, 483. — Various interpretations of *saeculum*: St Hilary, IX, 577; Venerable Bede, XC, 278, 279; Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 306; Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 157. — Etymology of *saeculum*: St Isidore, LXXXII, 233.

16. **Ounce.** — The ounce, an ancient measure of time: Venerable Bede, XC, 307.

17. **Seasonal cycle (*vicissitudo*).** — Four seasonal changes in the year: D. Ausonius, XIX, 911; Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 687; CXI, 307. — The seasonal cycles consist of three months: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 153, 154.

### Idols

All arts formerly had reference to the making or worship of idols, Tertullian, I, 668 ff.---The Romans summoned craftsmen from Etruria, idem, II, 1050.---The pagans worshipped asses along with Epona and Isis, idem, I, 557.---Christians were falsely accused of worshipping an ass’s head and image, ibid., 364.---Tacitus gave occasion for this calumny, ibid., 364.---With what effrontery a rogue of a Jew circulated a ridiculous painting of it bearing the inscription: “THE GOD OF THE CHRISTIANS, ONOCHOETES [ass-bedfellow],” ibid., 372 ff., 579.---Phidias sculpted Olympian Jupiter, idem, II, 803.---Images were invented by the Etruscans, idem, I, 430.---They were made from earthly and cheap material, and from vessels intended for common and most contemptible use, ibid., 399 ff.---They are valued according to their metals, ibid., 341.---There were no images of gods among the Romans, ibid., 430 and 608.---That is, before Numa Pompilius, ibid.---Before they were fashioned in human form, how ridiculous they were, ibid., 339, 366, 578.---The pagans thought such things to be gods, ibid., 488, 579.---And that gods were made by a ridiculous consecration, ibid., 339 ff.---They are sometimes headless, ibid.---They are built upon a cross or a stake, ibid., 340, 579.---They are hewn with axes and polished with planes and scrapers, ibid., 579.---Defiled, violated, broken, shattered, destroyed, consumed, ibid., 344.---Defiled by kites, mice, and spiders, ibid., 343.---Whether they came into existence depended upon the emperors’ decision, ibid., 439.---Craftsmen changed their fate, ibid., 339 ff.---They converted them into another shape, pledged them, and sold them, ibid., 344.---The holier the god, the more dearly it was sold, idem, II, 346, 576.---Anyone could choose or reject them, idem, 344.---On the vanity of idols, St. Cyprian, V, 563–564.---The manufacture of gods portrayed, Minucius Felix, III, 311, 312.---The manufacture of images, Arnobius, V, 767.---Ridiculous forms of gods, ibid., 1213, 1214.---Ridiculous statues of gods and goddesses, Lactantius, VI, 226 ff.---Statue of Venus, St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, XI, 195, 296–305.---On the error of profane religions, Julius Firmicus Maternus, XII, 981, 982.---Aurelius Prudentius, LX, 117, 118.---Description of the images of Serapis, Saturn, and Canopus, Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, XXI, 529, 540, 534 ff.; St. Augustine, XLI, 184.---On the bronze statue at Como, Cassiodorus, LXIX, 566.

## CCXXVII. INDEX OF PRIESTLY, MONASTIC, AND LAY GARMENTS MENTIONED IN THE *PATROLOGIA*, EXPOUNDING THEIR MYSTICAL SIGNIFICATION

### PART ONE

On the garments of the High Priest and of priests in the Old Testament.

1. Linen drawers, or breeches, extending to the knees and hams in order to cover the priest’s private parts; they are also called trousers.  
2. A full-length tunic of fine linen, clinging to the body, with tight sleeves and descending to the legs; it must have no wrinkle. Among soldiers the same garment is called a shirt.  
3. The belt, girdle, or sash, woven under a covering of scarlet, purple, hyacinth-blue, and linen thread, and diversified by embroidered workmanship. The belt binds the linen tunic between the navel and the breast.  
4. A round cap; called *tiara* by the Greeks and *galerus* by us. It has no point at the top and is of fine linen.

These are garments common to priests and the High Priest; the following, however, belong specifically to the High Priest.

1. The full-length tunic, called *mail* among the Hebrews, entirely hyacinth-blue, with sleeves of the same colour and an opening at the upper part through which it is put on over the neck. At its lower edge hang seventy-two bells, intermingled with an equal number of pomegranates, so that when the High Priest enters the Holy of Holies he proceeds wholly resounding; otherwise he is at once to die.  
2. The *ephod*, that is, the shoulder-garment, woven from four colours—hyacinth-blue, fine linen, scarlet, purple—and gold. Nothing is woven opposite the breast, so that room may be left for the Rational. On each shoulder it has a stone fastened with gold, upon each of which are six names of the patriarchs, so that, when entering the Holy of Holies, the High Priest may bear upon his shoulders the names of the people for whom he is to pray.  
3. The *theraphim*, or *logion*, which we call the Rational, is a short cloth woven of gold and four colours, one palm in length and breadth. Twelve most precious stones are woven into it in four rows. On the individual stones are engraved, according to their generations, the names of the twelve tribes. At the four corners of the Rational are four golden rings, by which it is attached to the shoulder-garment with hyacinth-blue bands and golden chains.  
4. A golden plate upon which is written the ineffable Name of God in four Hebrew letters: *yod, he, waw, he*, that is, Jehovah. This is added to the linen cap, common to all priests, in the case of the High Priest; it is bound upon the forehead by a hyacinth-blue band, and the Name of God crowns and protects the whole beauty of the High Priest. St Jerome, XXII, 613.

There are eight priestly garments in the Old Testament.

1. *Podaris*: a linen garment fastened to the body and descending to the feet, also called a shirt.  
2. *Abameth*, that is, a girdle, woven with embroidered workmanship from scarlet, purple, and hyacinth-blue, so that flowers and gems appeared distinguished upon it.  
3. A round cap of fine linen, covering the priest’s head and fastened at the back of the head with a band; Greeks and Latins call this a tiara or *galeria*.  
4. *Mahil*, that is, the full-length tunic, wholly hyacinth-blue, having at the feet seventy-two bells and as many interspersed pomegranates.  
5. *Ephod*: a shoulder-cloak woven from four colours and gold, with two emeralds mounted in gold upon each shoulder, upon which the names of the patriarchs were engraved.  
6. *Logion*, that is, the Rational: a double cloth woven from gold and four colours, a palm square, into which twelve most precious stones were woven in four rows; upon each were engraved the names of the twelve patriarchs.  
7. *Petalum*, or golden plate, set upon the High Priest’s forehead, bearing the Name of God, the Tetragrammaton, written in Hebrew letters.  
8. *Badim*, or drawers: that is, Greek linen garments extending to the knees, by which the priest’s private parts were covered. St Isidore, LXXXII, 684 ff.

[Col. 0596] In the Venerable Bede there is an outstanding description and mystical interpretation of the sacred garments of the ancient Law. These are: the Rational, worn upon the breast; the shoulder-garment, covering the shoulders; the inner tunic, of linen or fine linen; the linen tiara, or *cidaris*; the golden plate placed upon the forehead; the belt or girdle; and the drawers. Of these eight garments, four were allowed to priests of lower rank: namely drawers, the close-fitting linen garment, the belt, and the *cidaris*. All, moreover, were made of gold, precious stones, and splendid colours, because nothing cheap or unclean ought to appear in a priest’s speech or action; rather, all that he does, everything that he says, all that he thinks, ought to be glorious before human beings and in the sight of the inward Judge. Venerable Bede, XCI, 464.

There were eight kinds of priestly garments in the Old Testament: the linen tunic, the hyacinth-blue tunic, the shoulder-garment, the Rational, the *cidaris*, the belt or girdle, the golden plate on the High Priest’s forehead, and drawers. Priests of lower rank, however, were permitted to use only four: the close-fitting linen tunic, the *cidaris*, the belt, and the drawers. (See the author himself for a fuller account.) Alcuin, CI, 1238 ff.

Rabanus Maurus enumerates the garments of the High Priest and priests of the Old Law, already explained by us above several times, CXI, 568. He also explains the names and origins of various other garments, of which we shall speak below under Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 693.

Description and mystical signification of sacred garments in the Old and New Testaments: Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 524 ff.

Among the Hebrews there are eight garments of the High Priest: the fine-linen tunic, the girdle, the hyacinth-blue tunic, from which seventy-two golden bells hung, intermingled with an equal number of pomegranates; the shoulder-garment or *ephod*; the Rational or *logion*; the mitre, tiara, or *cidaris*; the golden plate; and the drawers. Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 434.

The same matters as above are explained by this author, who should be consulted: Thomas, Cistercian monk, CCVI, 663 ff.

Four legal garments were common both to lower priests and to the chief of priests:

1. Drawers woven from twisted fine linen.  
2. A shirt, or linen under-tunic of fine linen, double.  
3. A belt four fingers wide, woven from fine linen, scarlet, purple, and hyacinth-blue.  
4. A tiara, or infula, or *cidaris*, representing the form, as it were, of a round helmet.

The High Priest’s own ornaments were:

1. The hyacinth-blue tunic, that is, the *poderis*, or full-length garment, from which pomegranates hung in place of fringes, with seventy-two bells set among them, so that a sound might be heard when the High Priest entered the sanctuary, lest perhaps he die.  
2. The *ephod*, that is, the shoulder-garment, woven from four colours and gold, sleeveless like a *calobium*, with a square opening in the breast into which the *logion*, or Rational, was inserted. Two onyx stones were fastened with gold upon the shoulders; the twelve names of the sons of Israel were engraved upon them.  
3. The *logion*, or Rational, which the High Priest wore on his breast, containing twelve stones in four rows, on each of which were written the names of the twelve sons of Israel. These two words were also engraved on the Rational: “Doctrine and truth.”  
4. The head-ornament was the *cidaris*, having a golden circlet with pomegranates and flowers.  
5. A golden plate laid above the forehead, on which was written the holy Name of God, the Tetragrammaton. Innocent III, Pope, CCXIV–CCXVII.

### PART TWO

Typical signification of the legal garments.

The linen drawers signified the earth, because fine linen grows from the earth. The belt or girdle with its bands represented the encircling Ocean. The hyacinth-blue tunic, by its very colour, represented the air; the bells signified the sound of thunder; the pomegranates, flashes and lightning. The four colours foreshadowed the four elements.

The *ephod*, through its variety, showed the starry heaven; the two onyx stones denoted the sun and moon, or the two hemispheres; the twelve gems represented the Apostles and the twelve signs of the Zodiac. The Rational represented divine reason, with which all things are filled and by which earthly things adhere to heavenly ones. The chains, hooks, rings, and fastenings signify the bonds of the elements and the times. The *cidaris*, the empyrean heaven; the plate set above it, God presiding over all. Hence Wisdom xviii says: “Upon the long robe was the whole world, and the glories of the fathers were engraved in four rows; and thy majesty was written upon his diadem.”

Moral signification of the same garments.

The drawers signified chastity; the linen garment, innocence; the girdle, the cutting off of concupiscence; the full-length garment, perseverance in good works; the bells, preaching of the truth; the pomegranates, good works; the *ephod*, patience and obedience; the two borders of the *ephod*, the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left; the two onyx stones, truth and sincerity; the twelve names, the union of good desires with good works; the two little chains, the twofold affection of charity toward God and neighbour; the Rational, discernment between light and darkness; its square form, discernment of true and false, good and evil; the four rows of stones, the four virtues—justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance; the twelve stones, the various virtues which the High Priest ought to possess; the *cidaris* or tiara, the pre-eminent dignity of the High Priest; the golden plate, wisdom; the divine Name, the Tetragrammaton, God himself, the beginning and end of all things; the variety of workmanship, various virtues; and the four colours: purple, power; twice-dyed scarlet, pontifical teaching, which ought to shine and burn like fire; fine linen, excellence of reputation; hyacinth-blue, serenity of conscience. St Innocent III, Pope, CCXVII, 786 ff.

### PART THREE

What were the garments of High Priests and priests of the New Law, and what is their mystical signification?

The *lacerna* and *byrrus*, linen garments common to all bishops; some call these the *ephod*, while among Italians it is called the rochet. The *byrrus* was red in colour. The dalmatic was another priestly garment. St Cyprian, III, 1504.

Note.—When St Cyprian had been led out to the field of Sextus, where he was about to suffer martyrdom, he there removed his *lacerna* and *byrrus*. Kneeling upon the ground, he prostrated himself in prayer to the Lord; then, having removed his dalmatic and handed it to the deacons, he stood in linen and began to await the executioner.

The dalmatic, or purple *colobium*, was a priestly garment with which martyrs were also adorned for burial. Victorinus, Bishop of Poitiers, V, 158. The full-length garment was a priestly vestment, ibid., 318.

The *planeta*, or *planica*, called in sacred vesture a chasuble, as though a little house, because in former times it covered the whole person like a house, was made for ceremonial display: it was ample and splendid. Cassian, XLIX, 60 ff. The *birrus* or *byrrus* is considered to have been a sort of shorter cloak, formerly used by ecclesiastics and monks. Sometimes it was linen; at other times silk and costly. The ancient dress of bishops was as follows: first, over the ordinary garment they put a linen vestment called a rochet; then a loose sleeved tunic called a dalmatic; and finally a short cloak covering only the shoulders and arms, ibid., 73.

Priests and Levites used white garments in sacred rites. “There was,” says Gregory of Tours, “a considerable choir of priests and Levites in white garments.”

The sacred garments mentioned by this author are:

1. The alb, or linen garment in which a bishop or priest was clothed when about to celebrate.  
2. The tunic, or chasuble.  
3. The orarium, placed before the breast in the form of a cross.  
4. The *capsa*, now called a cope, the back portion of which hung down from the shoulders; St Cyprian calls it likewise a processional garment. St Germanus, Bishop of Paris, LXXII, 146.

The ancients collectively called sacred vessels the “ministry of the Church”:

1. The chalice: a vessel of gold, silver, glass, or crystal for consecrating the sacrament.  
2. The paten.  
3. Towers, or receptacles in which the chalice was placed.  
4. A ewer, or small ewers, for serving wine and water.  
5. A linen corporal cloth.  
6. A silk or wholly silk covering.  
7. A veil.  
8. A censer.  
9. A fan with which the deacon drove flies away from the sacred things and the priest.

A travelling priest customarily took with him a chalice and paten, so as always to be prepared to celebrate the sacred rites whenever necessity required, ibid.

The *lacerna* was a clerical garment flowing to the ankles. The *camelanchium* was a kind of hood, though at times a cap resembling a tiara. A shirt was a linen night-garment. The *poderis* was a close-fitting priestly linen tunic descending to the feet. The *caracalla* was a priestly garment worn over the ordinary dress and without a hood. A certain Roman emperor was surnamed Caracalla from this garment because he gave it to the people. The *colobium*, or *libiton*, was a linen garment without hood or sleeves; it was transformed into the dalmatic, which was woven with gold and purple. *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIV, 413–424.

Various ornaments of the Roman Pontiffs and the clergy of the same Church, taken from the Roman Order published by command of Gregory X:

1. A cope or chlamys of crimson velvet, lined with ermine.  
2. The Roman alb.  
3. A shirt, a long linen garment.  
4. The orarium, or priestly stole.  
5. The *planeta*, or chasuble.  
6. The mantle.  
7. The ring.  
8. Red papal footwear.  
9. The rain-cloak or cope.  
10. The mitre, infula, *cidaris*, or tiara; and the diadem or crown, also called the kingdom.  
11. A red mantle.  
12. A red infula of scarlet, that is, purple or scarlet-red.  
13. Tunics and garments of scarlet.  
14. A girdle of red silk over the shirt.  
15. The maniple.  
16. The *fanon*, a small priestly mantle.  
17. The amice, or *anabulagium*.  
18. The subgirdle.  
19. The pectoral.  
20. The tunicella.  
21. The dalmatic.  
22. Gloves.  
23. The *capiturgium*, a thin veil placed upon the head.  
24. A staff, or crozier.  
25. A pallium fitted with three golden pins.  
26. A surplice.  
27. The Pope uses a mitre embroidered in gold in a circle on feast days.  
28. The rochet.  
29. Keys and ferula.  
30. Stockings.  
31. Sandals.  
32. A golden rose with balsam and musk, blessed by the Pope on Laetare Sunday.  
33. A pectoral cross.  
34. The *gremiale*, placed over the Pontiff’s breast when he sits.

Garments of deacons and subdeacons.

A deacon was required to have:

1. An amice.  
2. An alb.  
3. A girdle.  
4. A stole.  
5. A dalmatic.  
6. A maniple.

A subdeacon, however, was required to have:

1. An amice.  
2. An alb.  
3. A girdle.  
4. A tunicella.  
5. A maniple.

All acolytes must be dressed in cottas, or surplices.

When the Lord Pope was to celebrate in a place where there was no church, he was required to take with the chapel: a portable altar; a silk cloth called a dorsal; gold embroidery to adorn the front of the altar; a cross to be set upon the altar; a pall, corporal, chalice, paten, and cruets for wine and water for the sacrifice; a little vessel containing the hosts; a basin, or vessel for water needed in the ministry; a censer and incense-boat with incense and spoon; books, namely a Missal and a book of Gospels and Epistles; towels for wiping the mouth and nose. The one who attends him must also have the mitre, towels for holding it, and another towel to spread over the Pontiff’s lap when he sits. He should also have other towels and silk cloths which may be used if necessary. They should also carry a comb, carpets, and other ornaments in the colour of the day; in summertime, a fly-whisk to drive flies away from the ministry. The Holy Roman Church uses five colours in sacred vestments: white, red, green, violet, and black.

Order in which garments are presented to and put upon the High Pontiff when he is to celebrate:

1. The subdeacon shall put stockings and sandals upon him.  
2. Once shod, the Pontiff removes the cope and remains in the linen shirt which he must always wear over woollen garments when going to celebrate.  
3. The amice.  
4. The alb.  
5. The girdle with subgirdle.  
6. The pectoral cross.  
7. The stole.  
8. The tunicella.  
9. The dalmatic.  
10. The glove.  
11. The *planeta*.  
12. The pallium.  
13. The maniple.  
14. The mitre.  
15. [Col. 0599] The ring. St Gregory, Pope, LXXVIII, 958, 1156.

Note.—This entire order should be consulted with great profit by those wishing to learn more fully the older liturgical rites of the Holy Roman Church.

The sacred vestments sent by St Gregory to England were these: one wholly silk cloth of sapphire-blue or azure colour, decorated on the front with golden borders and stones; two wholly silk copes of purple colour, adorned with golden borders; three wholly silk copes of purple colour, woven all over in variegated work of golden and milky-white colour; and one wholly silk chasuble of purple colour, adorned with gold embroidery and stones. Venerable Bede, XCV, 314 ff.

Enumeration of sacred ornaments in use during the time of Blessed Alcuin:

1. Sandals, or soles.  
2. The shoulder-garment, made from the purest linen.  
3. The alb, or *poderis*, descending to the ankles.  
4. The girdle.  
5. The orarium, or stole; it is called an orarium because it is granted to preachers.  
6. The dalmatic, instituted by Blessed Pope Sylvester.  
7. The *mappula*, with which the nose and sweat are wiped.  
8. The chasuble, placed over all the garments.  
9. The pallium of archbishops. Alcuin, CI, 1242 ff.

Note.—See in the same author the typical signification of these garments, drawn from various Fathers, which we shall set forth at the end of that question.

What are the sacred garments of priests, and what is their mystical signification: Amalarius, Bishop of Metz, CV, 1094 ff.

Priestly ornaments, so named by Rabanus Maurus:

1. The shoulder-garment, or amice.  
2. The alb, or *poderis*, a full-length linen tunic.  
3. The girdle, or belt.  
4. The *phanon*, or *mappula*.  
5. The stole, or orarium.  
6. The dalmatic.  
7. The chasuble, which the Greeks call the *planeta*.  
8. Sandals.  
9. The pallium. Rabanus Maurus, CVIII, 306.

Note.—That author also recounts the names and origins of various other garments, which we shall explain under Isidore of Seville, LXXXII, 693.

John, Bishop of Rouen, makes mention of pontifical vestments and their signification. According to him, these are:

1. The amice.  
2. The linen shirt, which he calls the alb, the breast-garment, or the full-length garment.  
3. The girdle.  
4. The stole or orarium.  
5. The dalmatic.  
6. The chasuble.  
7. Sandals.  
8. The pallium.  
9. The staff.  
10. The shoulder-garment.  
11. The *culubium*, or sleeveless garment.  
12. The towel for wiping sweat. John, Bishop of Rouen, CXLVII, 208.

An excellent description and typical explanation of sacred garments in the Old and New Testaments is found in Ivo of Chartres, LXII, 524 ff.

The stole derives from the Greek word *στολή* (*stolē*), that is, “a full-length garment.” It is also called an *orarium*, from praying or preaching, because no public prayer is offered without the stole. Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, 57.

Note.—He also explains the names of other sacred garments and their mystical signification; he should usefully be consulted.

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, describes these same sacred garments by name and in their mystical sense. According to him, the tongues, or tongues/wings, of the surplice signify generosity in charity and teaching, CLXXVIII, passim.

Description of priestly and monastic garments and their moral interpretation: Sicardus, Bishop of Cremona, CCXIII, 57 ff.

There are six garments common to bishops and presbyters: the amice, alb, girdle, stole, maniple, and *planeta*. There are nine special ornaments of pontiffs: stockings, sandals, subgirdle, tunic, dalmatic, mitre, gloves, ring, and staff. The pallium, however, belongs properly to metropolitans, primates, and patriarchs, so that they may be distinguished from other bishops by it and possess a privilege. Innocent III, Pope, CCXVII, 780 ff.

Mystical and moral interpretation of the sacred garments of the New Law.

The mystical and moral interpretation of the sacred garments of pontiffs and priests of the New Law according to the holy Fathers, and especially St Bruno, Bishop of Segni, vol. CLXIV, 406 and 1104 ff.; Honorius of Autun, vol. CLXXII, 604 ff.; Hugh of St Victor, vol. CLXXVI, 434 ff.; and Innocent III, vol. CCXVII, 786 ff.

1. The amice signifies righteousness, chastity, humility, and hope of heavenly things; the concealment of Christ’s divinity; and strength in good works.  
2. The alb signifies innocence, purity, angelic life, the brightness and newness of life which Christ possessed and granted us in baptism, and the righteous deeds of the saints.  
3. The stole, or orarium, signifies the Lord’s yoke which the priest lays upon himself, patience, and obedience.  
4. The girdle signifies custody of the mind, chastity, restraint of carnal desires, righteousness, and faith, according to the Prophet: “Righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins.”  
5. The maniple signifies good works, the wiping away and cleansing of every stain of the soul, caution, the prize, and the reward.  
6. The chasuble, or *planeta*, signifies perfect charity and the beauty of all virtues, and also the twofold Church, or the Old and New Testaments.  
7. The dalmatic signifies abundant mercy, the exercise of good works, readiness to perform every office of charity, care for one’s neighbour and especially for the poor, and the concerns of active life.  
8. The cope signifies holy conduct and the splendour of all virtues in which the Pontiff ought to shine.  
9. The pallium signifies the burden of pontifical dignity, the Pontiff’s wisdom and teaching, the perfection of charity, and the discipline by which he must govern himself and his subjects.  
10. Sandals signify readiness to proclaim the Gospel of peace.  
11. The mitre signifies the glory and honour with which Christ was crowned, and the summit and pre-eminence of episcopal dignity.  
12. Gloves signify purity of hands and heart, good works, caution in doing good works, and likeness to sinful flesh without sin.  
13. The staff signifies the authority to govern and feed Christ’s flock.  
14. The ring signifies the sacrament of faith, by which Christ betrothed to himself his holy bride, the Church; it is the sign, bond, and pledge of the Pontiff’s union with Christ and the Church.  
15. The bishop’s bands signify his cares.  
16. The pectoral cross is worn in place of the golden plate of the Old Law.  
17. The surplice signifies purity of conduct.  
18. The tiara, or kingdom of the Supreme Pontiff, signifies his twofold authority.  
19. The cantor’s staff summons singers to hasten in the way of God’s commandments and to labour to exhort others cheerfully to render the praises of God.  
20. The chalice represents the tomb; the paten, the stone of the tomb; the corporal cloth and pall, the winding-sheet in which Christ was wrapped; and the altar, the cross.  
21. The Roman Pontiff does not use a pastoral staff because Blessed Peter sent his own staff to Eucherius, the first Bishop of Trier, whom he sent with Maternus and Valerius to preach the Gospel to the German people. Maternus succeeded him in the episcopate and had been raised from death by St Peter’s staff. The Church of Trier preserves that staff to the present day with great veneration.  
22. The four principal colours used by the Church according to the character of the days are white, red, black, and green, just as the legal vestments had four colours: fine linen, purple, hyacinth-blue, and scarlet. Innocent III, Pope, CCXVII, 786 ff.

### PART FOUR

What were the garments of monks and nuns?

1. The girdle: for the monk, as a good soldier of Christ, must always go with his loins girded.  

2. The hood, *cucullio*, or cowl, surrounding and protecting the head and shoulders, was a symbol of simplicity and innocence. It ended in a point; it was shaggy in winter and thin in summer. Some Transalpine peoples call the cowl *flocus* or *frocus*: a long and broad sleeveless habit. Egyptian monks continually used the cowl, by day and night, and it was very often marked with a purple cross.

3. The *colobium*, also called *libitonarium*, *levitonarium*, *lebeton*, or *lebiton*, was without sleeves and had some resemblance to tunicellas. At times it was white; at others dark-grey, brown, or black. It signified mortification and a disposition ready for every good work.

4. *Rebrachiatoria*, also called subgirdles, *redimicula*, and *analabus*, were a kind of scapular hanging from the shoulders like the yoke of the cross.

5. The *mafors* or *mavors*, otherwise *maforte* or *moverte*, and in the plural *mafortes*, was a narrow cloak covering neck and shoulders. It was inexpensive and signified humility. The Greeks called it a stole; the Latins, a *ricinium*; others also called it a shoulder-garment.

6. The *planeta* or *planica*, in sacred vestments called by another name a chasuble, as though a little house, because in antiquity it covered the whole person like a house. In some monasteries there still exist *planetae* entirely round and enclosing the whole person.

7. The *birrus* or *byrrus* is considered to have been a kind of short cloak, formerly used by ecclesiastics and monks. It was sometimes linen, sometimes silk and costly.

Such was the ancient dress of bishops: first they put over their ordinary garments a linen garment called a rochet; next, a loose sleeved tunic, otherwise called a dalmatic; and finally a short cloak covering only the shoulders and arms.

8. The final garment of monks is the *melos*: a goatskin or sheepskin called *melotes* or *pera*. It was a garment made from sheep- or goatskin, worn by monks in imitation of those who led an eremitic life in the Old Testament. Some called it a *penula* or *ependytes*. It hung from the neck to the loins.

9. They also carried a staff in imitation of the prophets, so that they might walk steadfastly in the way of God’s commandments.

10. Footwear: considering themselves forbidden this, as it were, by the evangelical precept, they protected their feet only with stockings, when bodily weakness, the early-morning severity of winter, or the burning heat of noon required it.

11. Haircloth: a harsh garment furnished with stiff hair, nails, and points, suited to mortifying the flesh. It was distinguished from the sackcloth. Cassian the monk, XLIX, 60–65.

Let everything necessary be given by the abbot: namely, cowl, tunic, foot-coverings, stockings, *bracile*, knife, stylus, needle, towel, and writing-tablets, so that every excuse of necessity may be removed.

The cowl must be shaggy in winter and thin and worn in summer. The scapular, for work, was open on either side; the part which hung before and behind extended to the ankles. Footwear consisted of foot-coverings and stockings. For bed-clothing, a mat, blanket, woollen covering, and pillow should suffice.

The cowl was also worn by nuns, and monks approached Holy Communion clothed in it; whence one may conclude that it later covered the whole body. It was also called a cope. Travellers may, instead of cowls, use a round cope with a shorter hood, open on either side, to which a capuchon is sewn above. Beneath the cope they are to wear a scapular and a black felt hat, not shaggy but smooth. According to others, as years passed the cowl became a broad, full-length, sleeved garment, having the appearance of a cross extended in four directions. *Flocus* or *frocus* was also the name of a larger cowl, sometimes without a capuchon, sometimes with one. The *colobium* was a linen tunic with very small sleeves, indicating a life without hypocrisy; some called it a *cotardia*. Cooks wore tunics of sackcloth and cowls of sedge.

Benedictine monks did not use shirts or under-tunics, but only hairshirts, as did Carthusians and Cluniacs, except in case of illness, when they used garments of woollen thread. Aelred, however, granted his nuns two hempen or woollen-thread shirts.

The foot-coverings allowed by St Benedict were shoes covering the foot, and ankle-stockings or socks which did not cover the foot and were tied. The *tibiacum* covered the shin. Greaves were high shoes, called *botae* in the German language. Sandals were a kind of stocking. They were sometimes studded for journeys; in winter, however, wooden and leather. Drawers clothed the thighs; trousers bound the lower part of the body. The *fasciola* was a part of monastic dress. *Mannariola* and *facitergia* were linen cloths for monks’ use.

These various garments differed in colour among different orders: among some they were black, among others white, and among others brown.

The Camaldolese, Carthusians, Celestines, and Olivetans wear white along with the Cistercians; many nuns used broad and milky-white garments.

Monks’ garments were neither excessively short nor long, but measured. That was considered excessively short which did not reach the ankle; excessively long, that which trailed upon the ground and stirred dust.

Certain other monastic garments were called [Col. 0602] *sotularis*, *pellicia gemella*, and *nocturnalis*. Some were given yearly, others every second year, and others once every three years.

A monk’s head-covering was sometimes called a *biretum*.

According to some, monks’ shoes were called *crepidae*, and in other regions *viltronae*. They wore *wantos*, or gloves, on journeys. Benedict the monk, LXVI, 72 ff.

Monastic bedding.

1. A mat: a mat woven from rushes. Monks spread it upon the ground; it was their daily bench, mattress, feather-bed, coverlet, and every comfort of the bed. They slept on the mat—or rather, lying upon one part of it, covered their bodies with the other. They sat beside the mat, using it as a seat. They knelt upon it to pray; they were laid upon it when dying. Hence it may be inferred that the mat was a hard bed suitable for mortification.

2. A blanket: bedding made either of coarse linen or hemp, generally shaped like a sack and laid over the mat, which monks used as bedclothes. In a more recent sense, however, *sagum* is that which contains either straw or hay. It was also called a *sagellum*. It may likewise be understood in the French sense: “a thick shaggy serge to put upon the mattress” (*une grosse serge velue à mettre sur le matteras*).

3. A woollen covering: a double cloak, a kind of shaggy garment which we call a *toxa*, while others call it *galnape* or *galbane*; a shaggy cover suitable for repelling cold.

4. A pillow: a head-rest filled with wool, straw, or feathers, which we call a feather-bed. St Benedict granted these bed-clothes to the brethren.

St Pachomius, warned from heaven, commanded his monks to sleep sitting upright in high-backed chairs, with coverings thrown over them.

Under the Rule of Isidore, monks’ bedding consisted of a *storca*, or mat; a covering; two woolly skins; also *galnabis*; a double *fecis tergium*; and a pillow for the head.

Some consider the *brachile* to be a covering for the arms; Juvenal renders it in his French translation as *manche, manchon* (“sleeve, muff”). More probably, however, it may be taken as a belt or girdle by which trousers are fastened. A *graphium* was a stylus with which monks wrote on wax.

A *mappola* is a handkerchief suited for wiping the nose.

*Mensurae* are small tablets on which writing was done. Benedict the monk, LXVI, 792 ff.

Let monks wear garments of no other colour than broad grey, milky-white, or natural black. St Aurelian, Bishop of Arles, LXVIII, 391.

According to sixth-century authors, certain garments belonged to monks.

Ancient Christians in Egypt wore white garments; monks, however, dark-grey or black. The *epydentes* was the monks’ scapular. The *camelanchium* was a kind of capuchon. The *eriaciestes* was a woollen tunic sewn with a needle. The *esophorium* was an inner garment or shirt. The *lebiton*, *lebeton*, *lebitonarium*, or *levitio* was a linen garment resembling a *colobium*, used by monks throughout the Thebaid and Egypt; it was very often sleeveless. The *psiathus*, *psiathius*, or *psiathium* was a mat or rush covering made from rushes or papyrus. *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIV, 413–488.

Monastic garments, drawn from the *Concordia Regularum* of St Benedict, Abbot of Aniane:

1. Cowl (*cuculla*).
2. Tunic, shaggy in winter, plain and worn in summer.
3. Scapular, also called *analabus* and *epomodium* or *epomodion*, covering head and shoulders and marked with a cross.
4. Foot-coverings (*pedales*), socks (*pedules*), and boots (*caligae*). The *pedales* cover the whole foot; the boots are fastened with straps.
5. Socks, or footwear beneath the ankle; the *cuspus* was a wooden shoe.
6. Thigh-coverings (*femoralia*), *feminalia*, or breeches, which generally extended tightly from the navel to the knees and were fastened closely around these parts of the body.
7. *Levitonaria* or *lebitonaria*, also called a *colobium*: a sleeveless, ankle-length garment.
8. *Sabanum*, or *mavorte*, *maforte*, *mafortes*, *mafortium*: a narrow linen mantle.
9. *Orarium*: originally an elongated woven linen cloth for wiping away sweat; later made of silk and called a stole.
10. *Birrus*: a short reddish, or sometimes yellow, garment, like a cloak or travelling cape (*paenula*); later it was made from costly fabric.
11. *Planeta*: a kind of mantle which in time became a priestly vestment.
12. Shirt (*camisia*), or woollen or linen under-tunic for sleeping.
13. *Mannariora*, *mannariola*: a small cloth or handkerchief for wiping. St Benedict of Aniane, CIII, 1230.

Garments of the monks of Font-Evrard:

[Col. 0603]

1. Linen veils.
2. White *gimpae*.
3. Tunics and mantles of coarser undressed cloth, in its natural colour.
4. Sleeves two feet wide and reaching to the knees.
5. Lambskin coverings for beds.
6. *Balamia*, a fringed kind of garment.
7. White surplices.
8. Woollen belts.
9. They must shave their hair three times a year.
10. The sleeves of fur garments must be close-fitting, reach to the tips of the fingers, and be half a foot wide.

Regular monks ought not to possess black mantles or shirts; they ought, however, to have woollen belts and loin-cloths, and lambskins. Their cowls, tunics, and boots should be undressed, of one colour, and inexpensive. Robert of Arbrissel, CLXXII, 1079 ff.

Each brother shall have one lambskin, one hooded cloak, one double cloak, two mantles, two under-tunics, two pairs of breeches, two pairs of boots, two pairs of foot-coverings, and one shoe. They shall also have in their beds a mattress, pillow, sheet, quilt, and woollen or sheepskin coverlet; two linen tunics and one sheepskin or lambskin fur garment each. Peter of Honestis, CLXXIII, 726.

Garments of the Templars.

Their garments are to be of one colour: white, black, or russet. John of Michel, CLXXVI, 864.

Note.—The following may usefully be consulted on this subject: Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 604; St Hildegard, abbess, CXCVII, 1061; Adam the Scot, CXCVIII, 461 ff. (According to him, Premonstratensian monks wore white garments); Thomas of Cîteaux, CCVI, 663; Sicard, Bishop of Cremona, CCXIII, 57.

## PART FIVE

What were formerly the garments of various secular or lay persons, of both sexes.

Note.—We judge that this fifth part of the Index should begin with St Isidore of Seville, although he is not first in chronological order, because he describes nearly all ancient garments; thus the matters which we have excerpted on this subject from earlier Fathers will be more readily understood.

Description of various civil, or lay, garments among the ancients. The most ancient garment was the *perisoma*, that is, a loincloth by which only the private parts were covered. A tunic was so called because, while its wearer walked, it made a sound. It was known by various names:

1. *Talaris*, reaching to the ankles; *pectoralis*, over the breast.
2. *Manicleata*, that is, sleeved.
3. Dalmatian tunic, first used in Dalmatia and later adopted by the clergy at Pope Sylvester’s urging.
4. Red tunic (*russata*), invented by the Lacedaemonians because its colour resembled blood and concealed it.
5. *Laculata*, having certain square compartments with woven-in or needle-added pictures.
6. Hyacinth-coloured, shining with a vivid colour.
7. *Malochina*, *malocina*, or *malvella*, either made from mallow yarn or resembling the colour of mallow.
8. Silken, from the silk-worm.
9. Silk, from silk.
10. Entirely silk (*holoserica*).
11. Silk weft with linen warp.
12. *Byssina*, woven from flax.
13. *Febrina*, with a weft of beaver wool.
14. *Mena*, that is, black-coloured.
15. *Masticina*, the colour of mastic.
16. Linen, made of flax alone.
17. *Linostema*, woven of wool and flax.
18. Upright-woven (*recta*), woven by persons standing upright.
19. Segmented, decorated with bands and, as it were, cut-out ornaments.
20. *Levidensis*, lightly ornamented.
21. *Pavitensis*, the opposite of *levidensis*, heavily worked.
22. Citron-coloured.
23. *Velensis*, imported from islands.
24. Exotic, that is, foreign.
25. Many-coloured (*polymina*).
26. Needle-painted or needle-woven, invented by the Phrygians.
27. Three-threaded, from three warp-threads.
28. *Ralla*, commonly *rasilis*.
29. *Interpula*, an old garment restored to a new appearance.
30. *Pannutia*, sewn from diverse pieces of cloth. St Isidore, LXXXII, 684 ff.

Garments of various peoples:

1. *Colobium*, a long sleeveless garment, also called *lebitonarium*.
2. Loincloth, bound around the loins.
3. *Limus*, flowing from the navel to the feet.
4. *Licinum*, whose weaving is bound together throughout.
5. *Armetausa*, also *armiclausa*, open and divided in front and behind.
6. Shirt (*camisa* or *camea*), in which we sleep in bed.
7. Thigh-coverings, covering the thighs; also called breeches (*braccae* or *bracchae*).
8. *Tubruci*, *tubrici*, or *tubraci*, covering the legs.
9. *Tubraci*, because they flow from the arms to the legs.
10. *Sarabara* or *saraballa*, the loose and flowing dress of the Parthians.
11. *Lenae*, a Gallic garment: a kind of square, soft cloak.
12. *Rhenones*, named from the Rhine: a German garment descending from the shoulders to the navel, rough with twisted shag.
13. *Mastruca*, a Sardinian garment made from wild-animal skins.
14. *Stringes*, a kind of Spanish garment.

[Col. 0604] Nations differ in dress as in language. Persians cover arms and legs with linen wrappings and the head with a tiara. The Alans stand out by their lofty, peaked headgear; the Alemanni wear cloaks; Indians linen garments; Persians jewels; the Seres silk; Armenians quivers. Certain peoples claim distinctive marks for themselves not only in dress but even in body: thus we see the long hair of the Germans, the greyish or cinnabar-red [reading uncertain] hair of the Goths, and the tattooing of the Britons. Jews circumcise the foreskin; Arabs pierce their ears; the Getae are yellow-haired with uncovered heads; the Albani gleam with white hair; dark night gives the Moors their dusky bodies, while the Gauls have fair skin. The Alans are unarmed without horses; the Picts paint their bodies with a needle. St Isidore, LXXXII, 689 ff.

Mantles of men:

1. *Pallium*, named from the skins of which it was first made and from its covering of the shoulders.
2. *Chlamys*, worn from one side and not sewn, but fastened with a clasp.
3. Toga, so called because it covers the body. The *pallium*, however, is rounder in shape, with a fuller, almost overflowing fold; it comes beneath the right arm and is placed over the left shoulder. The palm-decorated toga was worn by triumphators; in peace they used it at Rome, but in wartime they used the military cloak. The toga measured six ells. The white toga, likewise called the chalked toga, was worn by candidates.
4. *Trabea*, a kind of toga made from scarlet and purple, the distinctive ornament of kings, magistrates, and augurs. It was so called because it seemed to make those wearing it blessed.
5. *Paludamentum*, the distinguished military mantle of generals, marked with purple and gold.
6. *Diplois*, a double mantle.
7. *Sagum*, a Gallic name and a garment peculiar to the Gauls.
8. *Paenula*, a mantle with long fringes.
9. *Lacerna*, a fringed mantle once worn only by soldiers, so called because its fringes were shorter.
10. *Mantum*: the Spaniards call it so because it covers only the hands; it is a short wrap.
11. *Praetexta*, the boy’s mantle worn by noble Roman boys until their sixteenth year, so called because a broader purple band was woven into it.
12. *Casula*, a hooded garment, so called because, like a little house, it covers the whole person.
13. *Planeta*, a kind of mantle, so called because it spreads about in wandering edges.
14. *Birrus*, a kind of head-covering.
15. *Melotes*, a monastic garment made of goat- or sheepskin.
16. Fringes, borders, or edging: the ends or boundaries of garments. St Isidore, LXXXII, 689 ff.

Mantles of women:

1. *Regillum*, the splendid wrap of queens.
2. *Peplum*, a matron’s purple-marked mantle with golden fringes.
3. *Palla*, a square woman’s mantle extending to the feet, with gems set in order.
4. *Stola*, a matron’s covering, cast from the right side over the left shoulder, with head and shoulder covered; it is also called *ricinium*.
5. *Amiculum*, a linen mantle of prostitutes.
6. *Theristrum*, a light mantle worn in summer.
7. *Anabolodium*, a linen shoulder-wrap; Greeks and Latins call it a *sindon*. St Isidore, LXXXII, 689 ff.

Various ornaments of emperors, bishops, magistrates, men, and women follow. Ornaments are so called because they adorn the edges and the face.

1. Crown, the emblem of kings and of victory. Roman kings and emperors wore crowns; Persians wore the tiara, invented by Semiramis; Athenians wore golden cicadas, partly on the crown of the head and partly on the forehead. Pagan priests were adorned with the *infula*, *apex*, cap, *galerus*, *galerium*, or *galearium*.
2. *Infula*: a white priestly band in the form of a diadem, from which ribbons hang on either side and bind the *infula*. It is twisted from white and scarlet.
3. *Apex*: a light cap used by pagan priests, named from *apiendo*, “binding.” The small rod in the cap was bound with a thread made from the wool of a sacrificial victim.
4. *Pileus*, named from the skin from which it was made.
5. Diadem, a head ornament woven from gold and gems.
6. *Galerus*, a kind of cap.
7. *Nimbus*, a transverse band of gold sewn onto linen and placed on women’s foreheads. The light painted around angels’ heads is called a nimbus.
8. *Capitulum*, also called *capitulare*, a head ornament.
9. Mitre: a Phrygian cap adorning the head; it is called a cap in men, but a mitre in women.
10. *Redimicula*: bands by which the mitre is tied.
11. *Ricula*: a maiden’s mitre.
12. Ribbons bind flowing hair; they are named from binding.
13. *Tenia*: the hanging end of a ribbon.
14. Hairnet, gathering the hair.
15. *Discriminalia*, dividing the hair with gold; the same as *discerniculum*.
16. *Antiae*: curls hanging beside the ears.
17. Hairpins, holding the arrangement of hair together.
18. Earrings, named from the ears. In Greece girls wore these in both ears, but boys only in the right.
19. Torcs are golden circles hanging from the neck to the breast; torcs [Col. 0605] and bullae are worn by men, necklaces and chains by women. They are so called because they are twisted.
20. Necklace, an ornament of gems, named from a gift; “necklace” commonly signifies all a woman’s ornaments.
21. *Murena* and *munerula*: a flexible gold ornament for the neck in the form of a serpent.
22. Chains or little chains: likewise ornaments for the neck.
23. *Dextra*, *dextralia*, *dextracheria*: arm ornaments common to men and women.
24. Armlets, awarded especially to men for martial courage; also called *viriolae* and *viriae*.
25. Clasps adorn women’s breasts or fasten men’s mantle or belt at shoulders or loins.
26. Little moons: ornaments in the shape of the moon, small hanging gold bullae.
27. Mirrors, in which women look at their faces.
28. *Periscelides*, ornaments for women’s legs.
29. *Olfactoria*, small vessels in which perfumes are carried. St Isidore, LXXXII, 689 ff.

People first began to wear rings on the fourth finger from the thumb, because a certain vein in it reaches to the heart; the ancients thought it should be marked and adorned with some emblem. Among Romans only freeborn persons wore a gold ring, freedmen a silver ring, and slaves an iron one.

Rings were called by various names:

1. *Ungulus*: a gemmed ring, because, as a nail is set upon flesh, so the gem is set in the ring’s gold.
2. Samothracian: golden indeed, but with an iron setting, so named from the place.
3. Thynnian: plain, first manufactured in Bithynia. St Isidore, LXXXII, 702.

On belts:

1. Half-belt, or girdle, and a belt smaller than either.
2. *Balteus*, military belt.
3. *Zona*, so called by the Greeks.
4. *Strophium*, a golden belt with gems.
5. *Limus*, worn by public slaves, so called because it had transverse purple stripes or borders.
6. *Catulus*, a kind of fastening, sometimes called a dog.
7. *Filbula*, a Greek word, so called because it binds.
8. *Suffibulum*, also called *subligaculum*.
9. *Redimiculum*, a girdle, *brachile*, or arm-band, because it is fastened beneath the arms.
10. Band covering the breast and compressing the nipples.
11. [Number omitted in the source.]
12. Ribbon, because it binds the breast.
13. Border, the same as ornamentation.
14. Narrow band surrounding the outer parts of garments, whether woven with gold or thread. St Isidore, LXXXII, 704.

The same author also treats footwear. Shoemakers are so called because they sew with bristles from pigs inserted into thread, as though they were “bristle-sewers.” A bootmaker (*caligarius*) is named either from the callus of the feet or from the Greek word κάλον, meaning “wood”; for shoes were first made from willow. The Greeks called them *calopodia*.

These are the different sorts of footwear:

1. *Crepidae*, so called because they make a rattling sound when walking.
2. Shoes worn by kings and Caesars.
3. Romulus devised patrician shoes; they were tied with four straps.
4. Greaves, footwear for the legs.
5. Buskins worn by tragedians; heroes too wore buskins.
6. *Baxeae*, footwear of comic actors, also called *calones*.
7. Ankle-shoes, shoes below the ankle, and a kind of socks touching the ankle.
8. *Obstrigilli* or *obstragula*, tied back with straps from above.
9. *Ossae*, first made from bone.
10. *Mullei*, so named from their red colour.
11. Sandals, covering only the soles of the feet.
12. Socks, also *socelli*, into which part of the foot is put.
13. Small boots, little shoes, and boots, named from the callus of the feet.
14. *Cernui*: socks without a sole.
15. *Singulati*, also *foliati* and *folleati*, distinguished by diverse segments.
16. *Elavati*, furnished with small nails.
17. *Perones* and *sculponeae*, rustic footwear.
18. Straps, named from hides or fastening together. St Isidore, LXXXII, 704.

Bed coverings and certain other articles in use:

1. Coverlet, so called because it is suited both for a bedspread and for a wrap.
2. Theatre-cloths, named from plays and theatres, because young men leaving the theatre covered their faces with them when going to a brothel.
3. *Galnapes*, a kind of coverlet.
4. *Fulcra*, ornaments of beds.
5. *Cercivalia*, placed beneath the neck.
6. Small pillow, the same as *pulvinar*, a rich person’s mattress.
7. Mattress, stuffed with feathers and wool.
8. Carpet, spread beneath the feet.
9. *Sipla*, carpets shaggy on one side.
10. *Amphitepa*, carpets shaggy on both sides.
11. Tablecloths: linens for covering tables and wiping hands.
12. *Mappae*, *mampa*, *mapellae*: a table covering.
13. *Toralia*: a long tablecloth.
14. *Sabanum*: a kind of cloth.
15. Face-cloth or hand-cloth, for wiping the face or hands.
16. *Aulaxa*: long painted curtains.
17. *Cortinae*: curtains made of skins.
18. *Cilicia*: fabrics woven from goat hair.
19. Wool stuffing, by which thread or cloth becomes thick.
20. *Byssus*: a kind of very white [Col. 0606] and very soft flax.
21. Beaver wool: wool of the animals called *fibres*, such as beavers.
22. Silk, because the Seres first sent it.
23. *Placium*: a kind of tow, or coarse silk.

The various colours of garments are enumerated as follows:

1. Scarlet: among Greeks it is called *cocceus*, among Latins red or vermilion; for the kermes insect is found on woodland leaves.
2. Shell-purple (*conchylium*), extracted from shells; it is also called *ostrum*. Cut shellfish emit a purple colour.
3. *Ostrum*, used for purple colouring.
4. Purple, a red colour named from the purity of light.
5. *Ferrugo*, a darkish-purple colour.
6. Glaucous, a darkish or sea-blue colour.
7. Whitish, named from white.
8. Yellow, a reddish colour, namely saffron.
9. *Menum* or *melon*, black.
10. *Masticinum*, the colour of mastic.
11. *Blateum*, blue, mastic-coloured.
12. *Osticium*, so called because it is burnt: it is made from soot produced by continual fires; it is flame-coloured. St Isidore, LXXXII, 693.

Tertullian enumerates various adornments of women and men.

“Come now: suppose that from the beginning of things Milesian sheep had been shorn, the Seres had spun trees, Tyrians had dyed, Phrygians had embroidered, Babylonians had woven, pearls had gleamed, and thunderstones (*ceraunia*) had flashed; suppose that gold itself had already emerged from the earth accompanied by covetousness, and that it had already been permissible for a mirror to lie so greatly.” Tertullian, I, 1305.

“The lustres of little stones with which necklaces are varied; the circle of gold constricting the arms; cosmetics of rouge by which wool is dyed; and that black powder with which the outlines of the eyes are extended.” Ibid., 1306.

“By ‘dress’ we mean what they call women’s adornment; by ‘adornment’ what it is fitting to call women’s defilement. The former consists in gold, silver, gems, and clothes; the latter in care of the hair and skin and of those parts of the body which attract eyes.” Ibid.

“And whatever ambition fishes from the British and Indian Ocean is a kind of shell; it also extracts gems from dragons’ foreheads, and there is stoniness in fishes’ brains. Emeralds lie hidden in rings, and pearls desire to emerge in shoe-clasps.” Ibid., 1312.

“Ten million sesterces are strung upon one thread; a tender neck bears estates and islands, and a great fortune is brought forth from the tiniest caskets. Women sin against God who anoint their skin with cosmetics, stain their cheeks with rouge, and daub their eyes with soot.” Ibid., 1321.

“Why are your hairs not allowed to remain at rest—now drawn tight, now loosened, now raised, now smoothed? Some delight to confine them in elaborate arrangements; others let them escape loose and flying. Moreover, you attach I know not what monstrous additions of sewn and woven hairpieces, now in the form of a cap, now raised behind onto the neck. Indeed, you add weight by building certain rolls, or bosses like those of shields, upon your necks.” Ibid., 1323.

Hairdressers ought to be employed by men. “Man appropriates to himself the peculiar artifices of feminine appearance and sex: closely cutting, plucking, or shaving the beard; arranging the hair, even dyeing grey hair; removing the first down from the whole body; distinguishing himself too with feminine cosmetic paint; smoothing all else with the roughness of some powder; then consulting a mirror on every occasion and looking into it anxiously.” Tertullian, I, 1224.

“I do not know whether the hand, accustomed to be enclosed in a bracelet, can endure to be benumbed by the hardness of a chain. I do not know whether the leg, through its *periscelides*, allows itself to be constricted down to the sinew. I fear that a neck occupied by snares of pearls and emeralds will not leave room for a sword-belt.” Ibid., 1332.

“Doubtless God showed how to dye wool with the juices of herbs and the spittle of shellfish; he introduced painful wounds into the ears, so that, upon the scars of infancy, then suffering for the first time, grains might hang—such as the Parthians attach everywhere upon their persons in place of bullae.” Ibid., 1328.

Various garments and ornaments of men and women mentioned by Tertullian follow:

1. *Paenula*, a kind of mantle: “And, having laid aside their *paenulae*, they prayed,” I, 1172.
2. *Sarabra*, a covering for the thighs: “God heard the three saints praying in the furnace with their *sarabrae* and tiaras,” ibid., 1171.
3. Cap and wooden sword: “He grants the gladiator the wooden sword and cap as a sign of freedom,” ibid., 653.
4. Buskin: “Thus he exalted tragedians with buskins,” ibid., 655.
5. *Flammeum*, a kind of veil.
6. *Apex*, a sewn cap with which the flamines covered their heads, id., II, 1259.
7. *Baxa*, a kind of gilded shoe worn by women, ibid.
8. Beryl, a bright green gem produced in India, ibid., 1263.
9. *Birculum*, an implement of iron for trimming nails, ibid.
10. *Botronates*, a clustered mass of hair, ibid.
11. *Byssum*, Indian flax, ibid.
12. “The delicate skins of the ears spend their calendar,” ibid. [Col. 0607] 1266.
13. Boot, military footwear, I, 1266.
14. *Calliblepharium*, a cosmetic rouge sharpening women’s beauty, ibid.
15. *Catactistis*, a more costly garment, ibid., 1268.
16. *Cerannia*, a gleaming gem, ibid., 1270.
17. *Crobylus* was a kind of male curl; among women it was called a *corymbus*, among boys a *scorpius*, and among Athenians a *cicada*, ibid.
18. *Cinerarius*, hairdresser, ibid.
19. *Ciria*, an untanned and bristling lion skin, ibid.
20. *Cirrus*, a twisted lock of hair, ibid.
21. *Crepitulum*, a head ornament that rattles when the head moves, ibid., 1282.
22. *Dracontium*, a crown of the herb dracontia: “Why do you condemn the head with a little band and a *dracontarium*?” 1293.
23. *Endromis*, a shaggy and rather long garment worn after running and athletic contest, ibid., 1296.
24. *Infula*, a priestly ornament, ibid., 1318.
25. *Interula*, a tunic worn beneath a mantle, ibid., 1321.
26. Mitre, a woman’s head ornament, a fine ribbon, ibid., 1332.
27. *Perones*, rustic shoes of raw hide and very high, ibid., 1316.
28. *Scrobulum*, *stropus*, *stroppus*, *stroppius*, *strophilus*, *strophiola*, *stropuli*: a head ornament resembling a crown, II, 1368.
29. *Sipara*, a maiden’s veil and a theatrical and mime’s veil, 1366.
30. *Spathalium*, a woman’s ornament fashioned from various flexible materials, ibid., 1368.
31. *Synthesis*, a more elegant woman’s garment, soft and transparent, ibid., 1374.
32. *Syrma*, the loose, flowing garment of tragedians, ibid.
33. Purple and gold were, among most peoples, emblems of rank, as among the Romans were the bordered and palm-decorated garments and the golden crowns of provincial priests. Kings were called “purple-clad” from purple, just as candidates were named from the white toga. Magistrates and priests were called broad-striped (*laticlavi*) because golden studs were fixed upon their togas, ibid.
34. Stola, a girl’s garment, id., II, 188.
35. Among the Carthaginians tunics were distinguished by an exceptional harmony of colours and fitting size, so that they were neither too long nor too short, ibid.
36. Their mantle was square and rested upon the shoulders in the bite of a clasp, ibid.
37. *Patagium*, a woman’s garment adorned with golden studs, ibid., 1030 ff.
38. *Multiciae*, women’s garments, delicate and transparent, ibid., 1042.
39. *Cataphractis*, a kind of triumphal garment, ibid., 1040.
40. *Caliendrum*, a head-covering, ibid.
41. *Supparum*, a linen veil, ibid., 1044.
42. *Mullei*, shoes of magistrates; soldiers wore nailed footwear, while others wore *perones* and shoes, ibid.
43. *Crepida*, a kind of Greek shoe, ibid.
44. *Peplum*, a kind of mantle, ibid.
45. *Suggestus*, a priestly ornament, ibid.
46. Philosophers and, for the most part, the earliest Christians wore the *pallium*. Hence Tertullian says: “A great benefit of the *pallium* is that, at the thought of it, immoral conduct blushes,” ibid., 1050.

Hair ornaments and little moons; partings of the hair, armlets, a clustered hair arrangement, bracelets, rings, earrings, silks woven with gold: you gird the straight hyacinth-blue garment with a belt. St Cyprian, IV, 451.

A striped garment was invented in Asia and used by the luxurious. A mitre was a band binding the hair, more commonly used by barbarians than Greeks. Among Romans it was an ornament of old women, prostitutes, and sometimes effeminate men. A *strophium* was a band with which women restrained their breasts and girded the chest. Bands or narrow bands were ornaments for feet and arms; their first use was for the sick. Hence the poet Honoratus: “You will display the insignia of illness: narrow bands, elbow-bindings, neck-wraps.” A *muccinium* was a handkerchief. A *loena* was a thicker toga placed over other clothing. A *subucula* was an under-tunic fitting close to the body; a *suppara* was a girl’s linen garment placed above the under-tunic and fastened at the shoulders by a clasp. A *sacernula* was a military garment like a *paenula*. A *trabea* was the garment of senators, knights, and consuls, interwoven with purple. A *calantica* was a woman’s head-covering; a *mastruca*, a garment woven of skins. Three-threaded tunics were made with three warp-threads. A sock, sandal, and shoe: shoes covered the whole foot; sandals only the sole; the sock, looser and lower, was worn by women and by softer men. A *mantile*, *mantele*, or *mantilia* was a shaggy linen cloth for wiping. Arnobius, V, 838–965.

Perhaps it will not be irrelevant here to set out the garments of blessed Gregory the Great, and of Gordian and Sylvia, his parents, from portraits painted at Gregory’s own command.

These are the garments of blessed Gregory: a chestnut-coloured *planeta* over a dalmatic; the Gospel-book in his left hand, a cross in his right; a moderate pallium, drawn from the right shoulder below the breast, around the stomach, then raised over the left shoulder and laid down the back, one part coming over that same shoulder and hanging straight down in its proper line. Around his head he bears something resembling a square tablet, the mark of a living person, not a crown. Gregory himself composed the following distich beneath this image:

> Mighty Christ, Lord, giver of our honour,  
> Govern with your accustomed mercy the office granted us.

The clothing of Gordian, father of Blessed Gregory, is a chestnut-coloured *planeta*, with a dalmatic beneath it and boots on his feet; he is tall, with a modest beard and a grave countenance.

Sylvia, mother of Blessed Gregory, is portrayed covered with a white veil folded from the right shoulder towards the left, and with a tunic about the breast of a colour described as *pseudofactus* [uncertain term], falling over the feet in ample folds. It is marked with two bands, like those of dalmatics but much broader. On her head she wears a mitre, clouded by the sparse texture of gleaming white threads [reading uncertain]; with two fingers she appears to make the sign of the cross for protection. In her left hand she holds an open Psalter, in which is written: “My soul lives and shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.” From the right elbow to the left, around the shoulders, runs an inscription reading: “Gregory made [this] for his mother Sylvia.” St Gregory, Pope, LXXV, 462.

The following may usefully be consulted on this subject: Rabanus Maurus, LXXXII, 693; Liutprand, CXXXVI, 1123.

[Col. 0607]

## CCXXVIII. EPIGRAPHIC INDEX, MENTIONING ALL INSCRIPTIONS, WHETHER LAPIDARY OR NUMISMATIC, DISCUSSED IN THE COURSE OF THE *PATROLOGIA*.

[Col. 0607] TERTULLIAN, presbyter.—The first coin stamped by Saturn, I, 330.—What the memorials of martyrs mentioned there are, 386.—Likewise, what those images are, the records and guardians of events, ibid.—The Greek *censuales* were so called because they compiled daily records, annals, and public acts, 388.—One must travel through histories and the writings of the world, ibid.

CYPRIAN, bishop.—Memorials of martyrs are noted, IV, 328.

MINUCIUS FELIX.—An ancient inscription of Minucius Felix, Rome, III, 231 note.—A Roman inscription on a stone of the ancient Pantheon: “To the resident, present, and sojourning divinities,” 256 note.—An inscription on the Quirinal in which an altar is said to have been dedicated to Germanicus by Emperor Domitian, 369 note.

[Col. 0608] ARNOBIUS.—Two inscriptions at Rome, one to Fortune, the other to the Household Gods, V, 998.—An ancient inscription “To perpetual Health,” 1005 note.—A Roman inscription: “To the eternal Peace of the house of Vespasian,” and another to Fortune, 1007 note.—A collective burial, that is, sepulchral inscription, 1176 note. When the ancients consecrated anything, they spoke cautiously and precisely and always added laws and express conditions, lest they bind themselves by some unspoken religious obligation; this appears from several inscriptions, 1261 note.—A lapidary inscription to a spouse, 1267 note.—On certain stones and coins is inscribed “To Fortune the Strong,” 1285.—An ancient Roman inscription to a Tutelary God, 1346.—An inscription to a certain Silvanus, by Diadumenus, Augustus’ food-taster, 1351.—An inscription to Jupiter Sabazius, 1357.

[Col. 0609] LACTANTIUS.—Ancient coins on which the image of two-faced Janus appears on one side and a ship on the other, VI, 188.—On coins of Constantine the Great, VII, 559, 560 notes.—Christ’s monogram, ordered by Constantine to be stamped upon standards, coins, and shields, by means of the letter X intersected with a curved upper stroke, 261, 369, 370, 559, 560.—Inscription: “May you live in God, F[eliciter],” that is, “happily,” 559, 560.—*Moneta* is the name of the building in which coins are struck, 205, 400, and 483 note.

ST HILARY, Bishop of Poitiers.—An ancient epigram of St Hilary, IX, 212, Prolegomena.

ST ZENO, Bishop of Verona.—Inscription of St Zeno and certain martyrs in the church of St Helena at Verona, XI, 160.—Another inscription of the same in the church of Monte Aureo in the diocese of Verona, dedicated in 1060, 166.—Inscription of Pacificus, archdeacon of Verona Cathedral, consecrated in 846, 172.—Various coins of the ancients are discussed, 429 note.—*Moneta*, a surname of Juno among the Romans, is derived from *monendo*, “warning,” 433 note.—Epigram beneath the image of Bishop St Eusebius on the cover of the manuscript of his works, 74, 76, Prolegomena.

JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS.—Inscriptions to Jupiter Sabazius, XII, 1005 note.—Ancient inscription concerning the priestesses of Vesta, at Rome, 1019.—Inscriptions mentioning the *taurobolium* and *criobolium*, 1043 note.

ST DAMASUS, Pope.—Inscription dedicated for the victory of Gratian, under the consulship of Anicius and Bassus, XIII, 249.—Inscription of the name of Damasus at Rome on marble found by Cardinal Farnese, 279.—Epitaph of Heracius, a Roman knight, at Rome, in the year 338, 385 note.—A Christian stone bearing two inscriptions and the names of many martyrs, 390 note.—Inscription of Pope St Zephyrinus, 393.—Verses on the tomb of St Saturninus, martyr, 394.—Roman inscriptions, one on the gate of the Aelian castle at the city entrance, another on the gate of the suburb of St Paul, 396 note.—Verses in the apse of the Basilica of St Agnes, 402 note. Epitaphs and various inscriptions, 405, 406.

LUCIFER, Bishop of Cagliari.—Cagliaritan inscriptions concerning Lucifer, XIII, 737 note.

PUBLIUS VICTOR.—An ancient inscription concerning the division of the city of Rome into fourteen regions by Augustus, XIX, 22.

ST CHROMATIUS, Bishop of Aquileia.—An ancient lead seal or coin bearing the name of Chromatius and a year, XX, 420.—Found at Venice by Dom Mauro Boni, XX, 295.—The lettering of this coin is examined, 296 ff.—A small tomb or sepulchral stone found between Aquileia and Romatium, with an inscription to Caesar Augustus, 301.—Another stone from Aquileia, in the form of a column, whose inscription is referred to Caesar Augustus, with the reason why, 303.

ST GAUDENTIUS, Bishop of Brescia.—Inscription to Gaudentius, corrector of Venetia, XX, 800.—Inscription to his wife, ibid.—A stone found at Tusculum, with almost the same inscription to the wife of Gaudentius but with the additional name of Lorenia, 800 note.—An inscription to a certain Benivolus, prefect of military service, 327 note.—An inscription written upon the manuscript of Petronius’ commentaries, 908 note.—Inscriptions in which, as often happens, K is read for C, 997 note.

RUFINUS TYRANNIUS, presbyter of Aquileia.—An inscription in the pavement of the church of St Paul on the Via Ostiensis, in which Paul the Elder and his brother dedicated something to their sister Heraclia, identifies Concordia as their native city, XXI, 77.—As regards the name *Tyrannius*, another inscription upon a fragment of stone from Concordia establishes it, 79.

ST JEROME.—A fragment of an inscription is cited showing that the letter *m* was sometimes added to the ablative case through faulty pronunciation, XXII, 771 note.—Mention is made of an ancient inscription to a certain Claudianus Postumus Dardanus, to whom Jerome wrote, 1099.—Memorials, that is, the tombs of saints, in the Ephesian church, which some think to be those of John the Evangelist, XXIII, 625 note.—Mention is made of an inscription in marble beneath an image of St Hippolytus displayed in the vestibule of the Vatican Library, 671 note.—The Arundelian marble is cited among the notes to Jerome’s *Chronicle*, XXVII, 213, 266, 340, 386.—An ancient clay lamp, remarkable for rarity and workmanship, representing Triptolemus riding in a wheeled chariot drawn by two winged serpents, ibid.—The inscription on an ancient coin published by Palatinus under the name of Asclepiades of Ephesus, 309.—On coins, *Gonates* and *Gonaton* signify the same person, 485 note.—Coin of Ptolemy Euergetes, 517 note.—A marble inscription bearing the second year of Trajan’s reign, under the consulship of Appius A. Gallus and Lucius Verullanus Severus, 605.—On coins, the inscription “To the best prince, consul for the fifth time” on the obverse, and on the reverse: “Dacia Captured,” beneath a seated woman, ibid.—On a coin cited by Mediobarbus, bearing the title “The eternal city Rome, by decree of the Senate,” 617.—Inscription on a coin: “Priest of the Sun-god Elagabalus,” 640 note.—Various coin inscriptions, 646 note.—An inscription to a certain prince of the Baquates, 658 note.

FLAVIUS LUCIUS DEXTER, *Chronicle.*—Epitaph [Col. 0610] of L. Seneca on a very ancient stone, XXVI, 166 note.—Inscription composed by Alderete and affixed to the church of Mount St. Granata, 178, 179 note.—Inscription on a marble column to Nero Caesar, 180.—Statue of Lucan at Corduba, with inscription, 201.—Stone at Rome bearing an inscription to Atterius Paulinus, a man of military service, 269.—Column at Marguissa in Spain with an inscription to Caesar Nerva, 273.—Marble inscription at Alcántara in Spain to Vespasian Caesar, 283.—Consecration of the church of Assidonia in Spain, inscribed on marble by Pimenio in the year 618, 302 note.—Marble inscription at Como to Pliny the Younger, dated 1498, 364 note.

PAULUS OROSIUS.—Coins spell Carrhae, or Charrae, the city of Armenia, without an aspirate, 682 note.—Coin bearing a vulture holding a laurel branch in its beak and commemorating the name of Marathon, 765 note.—Coins of the city of Olynthus and their devices, 711.—Epitaph of a woman who, through excessive piety, had become impious, 776.—Coin bearing the double head of Janus and, on the other side, a ship, inscribed with the names of Eppius and Rome, 843 note.—Several coins of Greek kings, 939 note.—Ancient coins of Bituitus, king of the Arverni, 966.—Roman coins of Fabius and Sulla with inscriptions, 970.—Other Roman coins bearing Pompey’s inscription, 999.—Silver coin of King Mithridates, 1002 note.—Coins of Aretas, king of the Arabs, 1004.—Coin of Orgetorix, king of the Germans, 1006.—Various coins depicted, 1007, 1008.—Coin of Ambiorix, 1015, 1016.—Various coins of Litavius the Aeduan, 1019 ff.—Gallic silver denarius of the prince Vergasillaunus, with his likeness and a horse on the reverse, 1020.—Another denarius of Viridomarus, whose head is encircled with a diadem, 1021.—Other Gallic coins with Greek letters, 1022.—Notable bronze coin of Julius Caesar, 1039.—Two coins of Augustus Caesar, 1045.—Coins with likenesses of Antony and Cleopatra, 1050.—Coin of Licinius, triumvir in charge of the mint, preserved at Rome, 1052.—Two similar coins of the emperor Tiberius and Sejanus, consul, struck at Bibilis in Spain; their likenesses and inscription are depicted, 1067 note.—Coin of Caesar Augustus and Drusilla, his sister and wife, 1070.—Small coins bearing likenesses of Claudius and Nero, 1076.—Various coins of various persons, 1078, 1079, 1081, 1085.—Notable medallion in the Pisan museum, with Trajan’s likeness on one side and, on the other, several figures prepared for sacrifice before the doors of a temple, bearing the inscription: “The eternal city of Rome,” 1090.—Other Roman coins, ibid.—Coin of the emperor Hadrian, 1091.—Coin of the Augusta Sabina, with her likeness and, on the reverse, a woman seated upon a running lion, 1094.—Coins of Antoninus, 1094, 1095, 1097.—Coins of Commodus, Julian, and others, 1099 and 1102.—Very rare coin of Pescennius Niger, with a figure of Ceres, 1103.—Coin of Albinus, with Minerva, 1105.—Another coin of Bassianus and Geta, ibid.—Coin of Gallienus, 1119.—Various coins bearing the names of Claudius, Aurelian, Numerian, Carausius, Allectus, and Diocletian, 1122, 1123, 1126, 1128.—Silver coin of Constantine the Great, 1137.—Likewise of the emperor Constans, 1139.—[Coin] of Julian, with a figure of Isis in a ship, 1141.—Coin of the emperor Theodosius, 1154.—Likewise of Arcadius and Honorius, 1155.—Nearly all the aforesaid coins are in the museum of D. Havercamp and are cited by him in his annotations on Dexter.

ST. AUGUSTINE.—A monument is so called because it reminds one of the mind, XL, 596.—The tombs of martyrs were called *memoriae* (“memorials”), XXXII, 719; XXXIII, 269; XXXVII, 1782; XXXVIII, 1441.—A martyr’s *memoria* is still said of relics or of the receptacle in which they were kept, XLI, 768.—Marble memorials of wealthy dead persons, XXXV, 322, 554.—Inscriptions containing the name Glycera, reported by John Phereponus in his observations on the book *On the Deeds of Pelagius*, XLVII, 542, 543.—Another inscription in which the same woman is called Ramus Ursula; whence it is evident that women’s names sometimes claimed the form of masculine names among the Latins, 544 note.—Inscription of the Ceionian family in Gruter’s collection, 556.—Another inscription concerning the same family in Panvinius, cited by Phereponus, ibid.—That the Ceionii were formerly pagans is established by another inscription in Gruter, 557.

JOHN CASSIAN.—What the signet-rings or sealing-rings used by the ancients were, XLIX, 171 note.—*Paracharagma* or *paracharaxima* are called counterfeit and false seals or coins, 516 note.—Diptychs were tablets in which all Christian faithful were entered; in every church two kinds were distinguished, one for the living and one for the dead. The diptychs of the dead were publicly read before the people during the solemnities of Mass, 531 note.—“It is the skill and training of money-changers or bankers to determine what gold is most pure and, as it is commonly called, *obrizum* [refined gold], and what has been less thoroughly purified by the fire; not to be deceived, by the most prudent discernment, if a base bronze coin imitates a valuable coin beneath the appearance of shining gold; and wisely to recognize not only coins expressing the faces of tyrants, but also those which indeed bear the image of the true king, yet are not lawfully struck. Then they must carefully investigate, by the judgment of the balance, whether anything has been taken from their lawful weight,” 511, 512.—Defects in coins may be of four kinds, 512 note.—Nearly the same passage occurs below in Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 37.

ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE.—It is established both from coins and from ancient inscriptions that Antoninus held the tribunician power for the fifteenth time under Marcus Aurelius, when victory over the Quadi and Sarmatians was won through the prayers of Christians, in the very year in which Antoninus assumed imperial power, LI, 564.—The first silver coin was struck at Rome in the thirteenth year of Ptolemy’s reign, 154.—Prosper composed an epitaph on the Nestorian heresy and its mother, the Pelagian heresy, ibid.

ST. NICETAS, bishop of Aquileia.—Inscription on the tombstone of the virgin St. Columba, LII, 943.—That the final abbreviation of this inscription indicates the second indiction, 944.
