SALVIAN, priest of Marseilles.—Inscription on a stone extant at Narbonne, to the emperor Nerva Trajan and to the urn of authority or magistracy, LIII, 35.

ST. LEO THE GREAT.—In the apse of the Liberian basilica at Rome, Nicholas IV placed an image of St. Peter with these words beneath it: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” LIV, 56 note.—In the Pauline basilica on the Ostian Way, in the arch of the apse, an inscription: “To the Augusta Placidia and to Pope Leo,” 57 note.—In a Lateran mosaic, beneath the statue of St. Paul, the inscription: “We await the Savior,” etc., ibid.—In another mosaic at the titular church of St. Sabina, the inscription: “Of the Church from the circumcision and from the Gentiles,” etc., ibid.—An ancient inscription exists at Narbonne in the archiepiscopal palace, on a marble altar collected by Gruter; its image may be seen among Quesnel’s annotations, 1479.—Inscription, in the year 1607, when the second translation of the holy pontiffs named Leo took place, fixed to the sarcophagus itself on a lead plate, LV, 334, Dissertation.—Inscriptions and subscriptions of formal letters, LVI, 129, 130.

ST. MAXIMUS, bishop of Turin.—From volume III of Mamachi’s *Antiquities* is cited a notable bronze lamp in the museum of the Archduke of Florence, bearing the image of a ship: Peter sits at the stern and guides the rudder, while Paul is represented standing at the prow and preaching, LVII, 107, Preface.—What is established from a silver vessel and from sarcophagi found in cemeteries of ancient Christians, in which the Savior is seen handing keys and a book to the prince of the apostles, ibid.

SIMPLICIUS, pope.—An inscription of this pontiff, composed in verse, survives in the ancient church on the Esquiline Hill, now in ruins, LVIII, 33, 34 note.

VICTOR OF VITA.—An epitaph in verse, in the church of St. Augustine in the city of Hipporegium, LVIII, 186 note.—Discussion of the authenticity of an inscription, reported by Papebroch, concerning African bishops who died as exiles in Sardinia, 426 note.—Inscriptions of better authority found among the ruins of the church of Turris by Gavinus, bishop of that place, ibid.

SIDONIUS APOLLINARIS.—In an old Cluniac manuscript is found the epitaph of Sollius Apollinaris Modestus Sidonius, dated the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, in the reign of the emperor Zeno, LVIII, 438, 443.—Inscription of Eugenius Asellus, prefect in Gaul, 457 note.—Likewise, inscription recording the burial of Celerinus the clerk, 463 note.—Inscription on an ancient base of Diocletian, under the name of Campanianus, 463 note.—Ancient formulas of inscriptions, 482.—*Gestatio* used in the style of inscriptions for “the exercised,” 483.—Epitaph of Sabinus, a young man, 490.—Inscription of Petronius’s statue in the basilica of St. Mary Major, Rome, 492.—Inscription on an ancient marble altar at Ricomagus, to the Genius of the Arverni, 525.—Inscription at Alba Julia in which *flammii* is read for *flaminis*, 537.—Ancient inscription at Sisteron, in the province of Narbonensis Secunda, on a stone commonly called the “split rock,” bearing the names of Postumius Dardanus and others, 540.—Epitaph of Gabinia, a most chaste woman, inscribed in the old basilica of St. Peter at Rome, 553.—Ancient inscription in Narbonensis establishing that the Reii were surnamed Apollinares, 561 note.—Epitaph of a certain Augustus, priest, in the basilica of St. Agnes at Rome, 587.—Inscription at the monastery of Compiègne under the name of Philoxenus Theodorus, 595.—Marble inscription at Rome to Audax, prefect of the City, 598, and another bearing the same name, 599 note.—Inscription preserved at Vesunna, establishing that the name Vesunna must be restored on a coin of Postumius Augustus, on which “Hercules Deusonniensis” is read, from Deusone, an ancient city of the Franks beyond the Rhine, 603.—Inscription of an ancient stone at Arles, [concerning] Valli’s grandson, 622.—Ancient inscription at Narbonne containing the name Biterrense, 626.—What is to be inferred from the name of the Chalcedonians on ancient coins, 642.—The fact that ancient coins often read: “the deified Julius,” “the deified Augustus,” “the deified Trajan,” 647.—Stones with inscriptions in the Lateran basilica and in the church of St. Agnes on the Nomentan Way, 676.—Ancient inscription, bearing the name of Hoenius Severus, on an old marble altar at Rome, 704.—A most elegant unpublished inscription in the Montaltini gardens, 703.—Unpublished inscription at Narbonne in which the initial letters denote the colony Julia Paterna, 724.—Inscription on the base of the statue of Antonius Epitynchanus, lictor, inscribed at Aix-en-Provence, 731.—Inscription of the statue of Maximus Petronius, 735.—Two stone inscriptions at Rome enumerating the racing victories of Polynices and Tatianus, sons of charioteers, 739.—Milestone stone or column with inscription, found on the road from Augustonemetum to Lyons of the Arverni, 745.—Another inscription of the same kind, ibid.

AURELIUS PRUDENTIUS.—Inscription in Onuphrius Panvinius mentioning a certain Solea, consul, LIX, 582.—The same person is mentioned in another inscription to his deceased wife in the monastery of St. Paul Outside the Walls, 771.—Inscription to Jupiter Quirinus for the welfare of C. Nerva Trajan, 780.—Ancient painting from the Cemetery of St. Priscilla on the Salarian Way, 783.—Ancient coin from the museum of Victorius, bearing an image of the Savior on one side and Christ’s baptism by John in the Jordan on the other, with the inscription: “Redeemer, Son of Man,” 791.—Very ancient painting representing Christ’s Nativity with an ox and an ass, 807.—Ancient prototype of the Seven Holy Sleepers, in the frontispiece of this volume LIX. Drawing of an ancient earthenware lamp for Christian use, ibid.—Series of plates depicting various kinds of instruments by which martyrs were tortured, in the preliminary pages of the same volume LIX.—Ancient coin with a Greek inscription, depicting the Savior on one side and his Resurrection on the other; made of bronze at Velletri and extant in the Roman museum, 109 note.—Christian inscription in which “To the divine Manes” is read, written covertly, as sometimes occurred, 153 note.—Inscription of Constantine’s triumphal arch, 150 note.—Another inscription, “Constantine, founder of tranquility,” on the same arch, ibid.—Inscription found at Praeneste about 1779, to Anicius Bassus, 235.—Inscription extant at Rome to Flavius Stilicho, master of the cavalry, ibid.—Two stones in the gardens on the Caelian Hill, one bearing an inscription to Symmachus and the other to Nicomachus, 252.—Lead plate depicting the offering of a candle at the altar of St. Lawrence, 321.—Various bronzes and gems of St. Lawrence, 335.—Inscription in Spain in which Diocletian boasts that he destroyed the Christian name, 346.—Inscription at Clunia on the same matter, 347.—Ancient inscription to the procurator of the province of Vettonia, 353.—Inscription establishing the boundary between the Eboracenses and the Pacenses, 381.

DRACONTIUS.—Inscription of the statue of Simon Magus, erected by decree of the Roman senate on the Tiber Island, LX, 859.—Stone excavated on the bank of the Tiber in the sixteenth century, with the inscription: “To Simon, the holy god,” etc., 880.

VIGILIUS OF TAPSO.—Inscription of Constantine’s victory over the tyrant Maxentius, extant at Rome on his triumphal arch, LXII, 526.—To the same subject belongs the inscription which Constantine himself affixed to his own statue, 526.—Small gold coin attributed to a certain Arian king of the Goths, with a triple likeness arranged triangularly, whereby a triple divinity was assigned, 535.—Bronze coins attributed to Clovis, inscribed with the name of Reims, ibid.

MAGNUS FELIX ENNODIUS, bishop of Pavia.—Inscription in the Parma codex concerning Ennodius Felix and Deuterius, his disciple, LXIII, 30.—A Greek and Latin epitaph of a certain Benenatus, dedicated by his wife, survives at Rome, 63, 64 note.—Acrostic epigram on King Thrasamund, affixed to the baths founded by him, 76 note.—Greek and Latin inscription at Rome of Claudius Eugenites, set up by his father, 82.—Double inscription of Boethius in the suburban church of St. Agnes at Rome, 104 note.—Another inscription of the same Boethius in the church of St. Pancras, 132.—Epitaph on a marble tomb of a certain Petilius, a man wearing the toga, at Rome in the basilica of St. Paul, 320.—Epitaph of Remus and his sister Argontia, who died on the same day, 349.—Inscription of Eusebius in the church of St. Thecla which he had restored, 350.

MANLIUS SEVERUS BOETHIUS.—Boethius’s tomb in the church of St. Augustine at Pavia, distinguished by several eulogies, LXIII, 562.

DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS.—Ancient inscription in the foundations of St. Remigius at Reims, LXVII, 472.

[Col. 0613] ARATOR, subdeacon and poet.—Stone with an inscription by a mother for her daughter, LXVIII, 66.

PELAGIUS I, pope.—Epitaph of Pope Pelagius, at Rome in the Vatican church, LXIX, 393.

CASSIODORUS.—Mention of a painting wrought with marvelous art, representing Solomon’s Temple, LXIX, 473.—Cassiodorus devised mechanical lamps for the use of his monks, 476.—During the demolition of the walls of the city of Chalcedon, ordered by the emperor Valens, a stone was found upon which an answer was inscribed—formerly concealed but then revealed—1085.—*Moneta* (“coinage”) is so called from *monendo*, “admonishing,” 688.—It is stamped with the image of a king’s face, ibid.—Servius, king of the Romans, is said to have been the first to stamp coinage in bronze, 725.—Formula of a recommendation for coinage, ibid.—What coinage ought to be, ibid.

ST. GREGORY, bishop of Tours.—Inscription on white marble of a certain Palenopis, in the reign of Theudere (Theodoric), at Narbonne in the convent of the Minims, LXXI, 199–200.—Another inscription at Narbonne of Rusticus, a bishop of the fifth century, 200.—Various brief inscriptions upon reliquary caskets, identifying the names of saints, 213, 314 note.—Tombstone inscription reporting the true name and the date of the reign of Leovigild, 300–301.—Inscriptions establishing that the worship of Diana was formerly celebrated in the Ardennes region, 458 note.—Tomb of King Childeric in the church of St. Germain-des-Prés, with the brief inscription: “King Child[eric],” 667 note.—Inscription of the fifth year of Childebert’s reign, indicating an era from the creation of the world, 5900, and that Easter in that year was celebrated on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, 671.—An inscription carved on stone survives in which King Pippin declares that he granted this exarchate to the Holy Pontiff, 688 note.—At the summit of the spire of the basilica of Reims is inscribed the name of Atolus, an eminent man, perhaps the founder of this church, 819.—At Clermont, in the church of St. Cassius, on the Gospel side, is a stone chest that formerly contained the body of St. Georgia, with an inscription, 864.—In the church of St. Venerandus, an inscription whose half-worn letters can scarcely be read, ibid.—An inscription on white marble, carved within a cross, states that it contained the bodies of unnamed saints; it survives in the oratory of St. Mary among the Saints, ibid.—At Clermont, in a chapel of the church of St. Illidius, now dedicated to St. Benedict, marble tablets bear inscriptions, one of which gives the name of St. Justus, bishop of Clermont, ibid.—In the same church at Clermont, a bronze inscription is read on the tomb of the son of the emperor of Germany, 1018.—Tomb inscriptions of St. Germanus, bishop, 1188.—Tomb of Queen Fredegund in the abbey basilica of St. Denis, 1192.—Inscriptions of Chilperic’s tomb, 1195.

ST. GERMANUS, bishop of Paris.—Epitaph of St. Germanus composed by King Chilperic and polished by Alcuin, LXXII, 56.—Specimen of Merovingian characters engraved in bronze, 106.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—Gregory’s tomb with its inscribed epitaph in the basilica of St. Peter at Rome, LXXV, 221.—In the church of St. Martina in the Forum Boarium, at the foot of the Capitol, survives a very ancient apse distinguished by mosaic work, containing images of two pontiffs, with an inscription almost wholly obliterated, though Gregory’s name can still be read there, 473.—In the basilica of St. Peter there is an oratory in which these words are read: “John was an unworthy bishop,” understood of Pope John VII, 473.—Marble tablet of donors, fixed to the wall of St. Peter’s portico under Gregory himself, 479.—Another tablet, similar to the preceding one, on the wall of the basilica of St. Paul, 481. Notes on the aforesaid donor tablets, 483 ff.—How money-changers proceed in testing any coin, LXXVI, 711, 712.—Title of the book on sacraments, set out in the form of an inscription in a manuscript sent to Charlemagne, LXXVIII, 23.—Verses in the sacristy of the apse of the basilica at Nola, built by Blessed Paulinus, 265.—Inscriptions on a lead cross at Périgueux, found among the graves of the monastery of St. Front, 446, 447 note.—Image of St. Gregory and his name inscribed in Greek letters, 545, 546.

ST. AUGUSTINE, bishop and apostle of the English.—Epitaph of St. Augustine and his companions in the church at Canterbury, for which they substituted another inscription found to be more fortunate, LXXX, 92, 93.

ST. BONIFACE IV, pope, A.D. 607.—Epitaph of Boniface, LXXX, 99.—Inscriptions on the façade of the Pantheon, the construction of which temple is attributed to Agrippa, 100 note. Another inscription attributing the restoration of the Pantheon to Severus and Marcus Aurelius, 103.—The city Emerita and the name Emeritensis are read in inscriptions, 166.—Vettonia and the Vettones are read in inscriptions, 167.—Inscriptions of Emerita, 167, 168.

ST. COLUMBANUS.—Roman inscription in which Christians attribute the designation of Jupiter to God, LXXX, 302.—Inscription [Col. 0614] mentioning the coin which pagans placed in the mouth or hands of the dead, 303 note.

HONORIUS I, pope.—The epitaph of this pope, composed in verse, is read in the apse of the church which he himself founded, LXXX, 494.

MAXIMUS, bishop of Caesaraugusta.—Epitaph of this bishop, LXXX, 614.

ST. ISIDORE, bishop of Seville.—Various epitaphs of St. Isidore, LXXXI, 36 ff.; LXXXII, 50.—The use of bronze extended to statues, vessels, and building structures, especially to ensure the permanence of monuments; public enactments were written on bronze, LXXXII, 586.—Coins were named from Numa, king of the Romans, who first among the Latins marked them with images and prefixed the title of his own name, 585.—*Moneta* is so called because it warns that no fraud should occur in the metal or the weight, ibid.—A *nomisma* or *numisma* is a gold, silver, or bronze solidus, and derives its name from being marked with the names and likeness of princes, ibid.—Three things are sought in a coin: metal, image, and weight; if any of these is lacking, it will not be a coin, ibid.—The bronze coin was invented by Saturn, 584.—Bronze money was first in use, then silver, and afterward gold, 584.—Marginal inscriptions and Gothic lettering in a manuscript of the works of St. Isidore, LXXXIV, 857, 858.

AUTHOR OF THE MOZARABIC LITURGY.—Inscription establishing that the inner part of the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian at Rome was built by Pope Felix IV, LXXXV, 866.—An ancient Neapolitan marble calendar inscription shows that the conception of Blessed Mary by St. Anne was already celebrated in the church, 934.

ST. EUGENIUS, bishop of Toledo, A.D. 657.—He wrote for himself an excellent acrostic epitaph, LXXXVII, 356.—In a poem of the same kind he composed an epitaph for Evantius, his predecessor, 365.

VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS, bishop of Poitiers.—Epitaph of Fortunatus copied by Alcuin in a certain monastery, LXXXVIII, 54.—Poems concerning the Holy Cross written in acrostic and lapidary style, 91, 93, 95.—Another acrostic poem mourning the fall of the first parents, 195.

SERGIUS I, pope.—Epitaph of King Cædwalla, who died in the second year of Sergius’s pontificate, LXXXIX, 9, 376 note.—Very ancient epitaph of Pope St. Leo, found in the church of St. Peter, 27.

ST. GREGORY II, pope.—Tomb inscription of a certain Theatimus, subdeacon and rector, at Naples in the church of St. Andrew, LXXXIX, 467 note.—Inscription beneath the statue of St. Peter in the Vatican church, placed by Cardinal Annibale of St. Clement for his health miraculously restored in 1727, 486 note.

ST. BONIFACE, bishop of Mainz.—Epitaphs of St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 670.

STEPHEN II, pope.—Inscriptions from Gruter’s collection bearing the names of certain Roman patricians, LXXXIX, 976, 978.

Inscription at Ravenna on an ancient tablet, recording that King Pippin enlarged the church, 991.

ST. CHRODEGANG, bishop of Metz.—Epitaph composed in verse, LXXXIX, 1054.

BEDE.—A quite brief epitaph of the venerable Bede, CX, 23.—Inscription in the church of St. Paul at Jarrow, 122.—Other epitaphs celebrating the memory of the venerable Bede, ibid.

PAULUS WINFRIDUS, deacon.—Epitaph of Paul the Deacon, carved as an acrostic poem by Abbot Hilderic, his disciple, XCV, 430.—Inscription in which *stator* (“one who causes to stand”) is said for *prostrator* (“one who casts down”), 485.—Epitaph over the tomb of Blessed Doctrulf, 520.—Ancient inscription of Memmia Tertulla, dedicated to her foster-child and mother, ibid.—On the façade of the church of the monastery called Novo is read an inscription establishing that this church was built by Pertharit, king of the Lombards, 613 note.—Inscription at the tomb of Cuniberga, queen of the Lombards, 613 note.—Tomb inscription of a certain Theodota in the church of St. Mary, 615.—Epitaph of Romoald by Abbot Hilderic, 625 note.—Epitaph of Cedoald, king of the English, 633. His epitaph composed in prose by Bede, ibid. note.—Stone bearing an inscription in honor of Queen Ragintruda, set up in the church of St. Mary ad Persicas at Pavia, 636.—Inscriptions on the tomb of King Anprand, 647 note.—Fragment of an epitaph on the tombstone of King Liutprand, 660 note.—Inscriptions of King Liutprand’s tomb, 670 note.—Inscription on the tomb of Blessed Cumianus, bishop, in which King Liutprand is praised, 671 note.—Epitaph of Rothais, daughter of King Pippin, 707; and of Adelaide, daughter of King Charles, by Paul the Deacon himself, 908.—Above the likeness of the empress Placidia these words were read: “Vows [for] thirty years; multiplied [by] forty,” 549 note; and on the other side: “Victory of the Augusti, threefold; R. V.,” 551.—In the monastery of St. Andrew, on the wall beneath the image of Bishop St. Peter Chrysologus, is read an inscription of that saint, 557.—On the façade [Col. 0615] of the church of St. Vitalis at Rome is read an inscription in memory of Blessed Ecclesius, 588.—Greek and Latin inscription of Isaac, commander of the army, 592.—Verses inscribed on the tablet of the bath built by St. Victor, in praise of its founder, 601.—Epitaph on the tomb of St. Agnellus, 621.—In Rubeus is read an ancient inscription which existed in the church of Blessed Severus, 625.—Inscription on the doors of the monastery of St. Mark, 643.—Epitaph on the tomb of St. Marinianus outside the walls of Classe, 648.—Epitaph of the tomb of St. Maurus, bishop, on porphyry marble, 673.—Epitaph of St. Damian beneath the church of St. Apollinaris at Ravenna, 698.—Another brief inscription of the same man in the basilica of St. Apollinaris in Classe, 702.—In the same church is read the epitaph of St. Felix, bishop, 711.—And another inscription of St. Felix survives in the cathedral of Comacchio, 715.

CHARLEMAGNE, emperor.—Epitaph of Charlemagne in the church of Seligenstadt, attributed to Rabanus Maurus, XCVII, 13.—Seal of Charlemagne, 676.—Inscription of a very ancient parchment manuscript of Charlemagne’s letters, XCVIII, 51.

PAULINUS, bishop and patriarch of Aquileia.—In the hall of the palace at Udine, beneath an image of the prelate and upon the wall, an inscription under the name of Paul, XCIX, 19. But the inscription which was in the same place before restoration of the hall bore the name of Paulinus, 20.—Inscription in the same patriarchal palace at Udine under the name of Bishop Sigualdus and concerning an official act of King Desiderius, 49.—Inscriptions on the reliquary of St. Paulinus, 126.—Old and recent inscription in the hall at Udine concerning St. Paulinus, 128, 129.—Very ancient inscription on a silver-gilt tablet on which appeared various images of saints of the city of Aquileia, 130.—Inscription of a legal hearing concerning advocacy, in the portico of the church of Aquileia, 646.

ALCUIN, OR ALBINUS, abbot and Charlemagne’s teacher, A.D. 804.—Epitaph of Alcuin himself, in the church at Tours, C, 106.—Very rare silver coin of Offa, king of the English, to whom Alcuin wrote, 214.—Various inscriptions of churches, altars, tombs, and so forth, composed in verse by Alcuin, CI, 738.—Inscriptions of the church of St. Vedast, 741.—Inscriptions of the monastery at Tours, 744.—Likewise, perhaps of the monastery of Nobiliacum, 747.—Likewise of the monastery of Fleury, 752.—Likewise of the monastery of St. Nabor, 753.—Likewise of the monastery of Cormaricus and others, 754.—Of the monasteries of St. Peter at Salzburg and St. Amand at Elnone, 757.—Other inscriptions of sacred places, 759 ff.—Inscriptions of various places, 777.—Epitaphs, 799 ff.

SEDULIUS SCOTTUS.—Among this author’s works see the following inscriptions: at Rome, in the right-hand atrium of St. Peter’s, CIII, 331 note.—On the shrine above the body of St. Peter, 332.—Outside, on the façade of the church of St. Peter, where four animals are depicted, ibid.

BENEDICT, abbot of Aniane.—Inscription carved in marble on the tomb of the learned Holstenius, at Rome in the church of Blessed Mary of the Soul, in 1661, CIII, 396.

LOUIS I, surnamed the Pious, A.D. 840.—Epitaph of Louis in the monastery of St. Arnulf at Metz, CIII, 979.—Another epitaph of the same man from an old parchment of St. Arnulf, ibid.

AUTHOR OF THE *LIBER DIURNUS* OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS.—Epitaph which Honorius placed for his predecessor Boniface V, CV, 29, 30.

THEODULF, bishop of Orléans.—Epitaph on the tomb of St. Nazarius, CV, 313.—Epitaph of Queen Fastrada, 314.—Inscription on the front of a house, ibid.—Inscription on the door of a library, 376.—Another on a second tablet, ibid.—Inscription at the bishop’s door, ibid.—Another in the drinking-room, 376.—Inscription in the hospice, 380.

BERNOWIN, bishop of Clermont.—Epitaph of Bernowin, CV, 445.

DUNGAL, recluse and poet.—This author composed very many inscriptions for a church, fountains, a window, and so forth, CV, 529.—Epitaph of Folrad, abbot of St. Denis, 530.—Likewise, of Fardulf, abbot of the same monastery, ibid.—Likewise, of King Pippin, 531.—Likewise, of a certain person named Motharius, ibid.—Epitaph of Dungal, 531.—Likewise, of the monk Anthelm, 532.

ADALHARD (ST.), abbot of Corbie.—Epitaph of Adalhard, CV, 550.

AGNELLUS, OR ANDREAS, abbot.—Inscription in honor of Saints Stephen, Gervasius, Protasius, etc., under Theodosius and Valentinian, CVI, 509.—Stone inscription at Ravenna in the Ursian church, in mosaic, in honor of St. Neonus, 317.

RABANUS MAURUS.—Epitaph of Tutin, brother of Rabanus Maurus, CVII, 11.—Epitaph of Rabanus Maurus himself, buried at St. Alban’s, 30.—Inscription above the bones of Saints Januarius and Magnus, 61.—Likewise, various inscriptions [Col. 0616] on the relics of certain saints, 63 ff.—Titles and inscriptions of altars and churches, composed in verse by Rabanus, CXII, 1022 ff.—Epitaphs of various persons, CXII, 1669 ff.—WALAFRID STRABO, monk of Fulda.—Fragments of an epitaph mentioning the Brabantine town of Lier, CXIII, 19.—Epitaph of a certain Abbot Verdo, CXIV, 1103.—Various inscriptions, CXIV, 1104 ff.—Epitaph of Count Gerold, 1129.

ST. EULOGIUS, archbishop of Toledo.—Epitaph of St. Eulogius, CXV, 722.—Epitaph of Abbot Samson, in Ambrosius Morales’s work on St. Eulogius, 875.—Epitaph on the tomb of Ramiro, king of Spain, 922.—Marble inscription at the town of Linares, brought from the ruins of Cástulo, bearing the name of Valeria of Corduba, priestess, 927.—Marble inscription at Corduba dedicated to Cornelia, wife of Augustus, 928.—Another inscription there to Lucretius Verna, ibid.—Likewise, inscription at Lora to Lucretius Severus, patrician, ibid.—In a village near Seville, a cippus bearing an epitaph with the name of Fabius, 929.—Stones in the form of columns with inscriptions to Augustus Caesar, 933, 934.—Inscription on the stone base of Fabia Prisca, 937.—Inscription on a jasper cippus with the name of Domitius, teacher of grammar, 957.

EBBO, bishop of Reims.—Inscription which Ebbo himself prefixed to the Church of St. Peter, CXVI, 21.

FLORUS, deacon and monk.—Title in the apse concerning the most holy pledges [relics], CXIX, 259.—Title in the apse of the memorial of St. Justus, 278.

SERVATUS LUPUS, priest and abbot of Ferrières.—Epitaph of the priest Ratlaicus, composed by Rabanus, CXIX, 524 note.—Ancient epitaph found in the cemetery of Callixtus, bearing the name Alexander, who died under Antoninus, 599 note.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS, abbot of Corbie.—In the life of St. Adalhard, he appended the latter’s epitaph, CXX, 1552.

CYPRIAN, archpriest of Corduba, in the appendix to Alvarus, A.D. 928.—Epitaph on the tomb of Lord Samson, CXXI, 568; and CXXXII, 787.—Epitaph in honor of Hermildis, a noblewoman, ibid.—Epitaph on the tomb of St. John the Confessor.

JOHN SCOTUS ERIGENA.—Inscription on the statue dedicated to John Scotus in the church of Malmesbury Abbey, CXXII, 100.

HINCMAR, archbishop of Reims.—His epitaph, CXXV, 17.

HARMOTUS, abbot of St. Gall.—He fixed inscriptions upon the walls of the church of St. Othmar, CXXVI, 989.

ANASTASIUS, abbot and librarian of the Vatican.—Inscription on a stone, from the foundation of the city, from the collection of Alexander Albani, CXXVII, 82.—The dignities of Caesar are recorded in a calendar engraved on stone, 53.—Fragment of an inscription from the Alban Museum, 54.—Another inscription, dedicated to certain emperors and carved in stone, ibid.—Stone inscription in the Barberini Palace, 55.—Tablet with a statue and inscription of St. Hippolytus, 56.—Certain inscriptions mentioning the names of St. Paulinus and Felix, etc., 58, 59.—The Grimaldi codex reports very many inscriptions, 63 and following.—Inscription mentioning a taurobolium, 66, 67.—Inscription concerning Pope Damasus, 71.—Likewise concerning St. Crescentinus and his relics, 75, ibid.—Another, to Valentinian Augustus, ibid.—Inscription to St. Lawrence the martyr, 77.—Another concerning certain priests, and another concerning Pope Gregory III, ibid.—Epitaph of Eusebia, a most devout woman, 80.—Inscriptions to St. John the Baptist and to a certain Ursus, a goldsmith, 87.—And to Pope John, 82.—Marble inscription dedicated to the blessed Peter and Paul by Pope Gregory, 85.—Other inscriptions likewise, 86.—Ancient marble engraved by Gregory IV, 87.—Titles inscribed on marble under Gregory the Great, 90.—Another title engraved on marble, 91.—Inscription for the church of St. Erasmus, expressed in Greek letters and language, ibid.—Marble inscription in the sacristy of St. Angelo in Borgo, ibid.—In Anagni Cathedral, Bishop Grimaldus caused an inscription to be engraved, of which a fragment is given, 93.—Marble inscription of the year 731, under Emperor Leo, concerning the Jews, ibid.—Inscription on a marble tablet, carved under Pope Nicholas in the lettering of that period, 111.—Other inscriptions of Pope Nicholas and Benedict XIII, discovered in 1727, ibid.—Inscription of Pope Innocent XI, in the year 1689, 114.—On a bronze tablet of ancient catalogues, an inscription of Pope Alexander VIII, 115.—Inscription of Clement XI; likewise very brief inscriptions of Clement X and Innocent XIII, 116.—Easter of the year 222 appears to be engraved in the Cycle of St. Hippolytus, 125.—Inscription on an ancient stone in Blanchini, signifying that a boy was born to Jovian in 245, [materially uncertain], ibid.—In the basilica of St. Paul a series of the holy pontiffs is inscribed on the wall, and St. Innocent is cited, 251.—Titles of paintings inscribed in the basilica of St. Paul on the Ostian Way, 282, [Col. 0617] and following.—Inscription on the arch of Emperor Gratian, 350.—Likewise on the Porta Papia, 354.—Inscription dedicated to Germanicus on an arch erected at Spoleto, 354.—Various Caesarian inscriptions, 355.—Inscription making mention of the districts of the regions of the city, 369.—At Rome an inscription is read in the house of the Caesian family; likewise at Tivoli on the wall of the church of St. Paul, 378.—Ancient coins elucidating, from the Fathers, the year of Christ’s birth, 439.—Epitaph from Candia for the year 585, cited from Baronius, 801.—Ancient marble inscription belonging to the year 731 under Emperor Leo, 803.—Ancient coins published by Cangius, dedicated to the prosperity of Ravenna, 803.—Remarkable fragment of an inscription on a marble tablet found among the ruins of ancient Antium, adorned with chronological notes, 927.—Greek tablet containing a letter of the Tyrians dwelling at Puteoli, in the consulship of Gallus and Flaccus, to the senate and people of their native city, 929 and following.—Inscribed tablets praised by Blanchini, 933, 934, 935.—Seal and coins of Emperor Constantine, 989.—Images of the blessed Peter and Paul engraved by Pietro Rotari in 1728, with inscriptions, 999, 1001.—Remarkable fragment of a marble tablet containing inscribed consular fasti, 1090.—At the Lucan Bridge stands a monument with an inscription to Plautius, 1154, 1155.—Image of Pope Sixtus, 1164.—Inscribed stone from the museum of Alexander Albani, for Emperor Pertinax, 1287.—Tablet of St. Hippolytus with its inscribed cycle and his image, 1293, 1294.—Inscription of a most devout woman who gloried in having been confirmed by Pope Liberius, 1490.—Fragments of the consular fasti, 1573.—Ancient inscription in which a reader from Pallacine is mentioned, in Aringhius, CXXVIII, 16.—Coin of Crispus Caesar from the museum of Prince Borghese, 69.—Inscription of Benedict, titular of the chapel of St. Peter under Gregory VII, 71.—Marble tablet with the inscription of the basilica’s consecration by St. Damasus, 78.—Inscription on the relics of St. Crescentinus, 79.—Inscription on a marble tablet commemorating Ursus Togatus, inventor of the ball game, 141.—Ancient inscription showing Sixtus as dedicating a church to the Virgin Mother of God, 232.—Engraved architrave from the museum of Alexander Albani, by which Hilary, archdeacon, dedicates that monument to St. Lawrence, 358.—Inscription read by Plutina and Ciampini in the ancient basilica of St. Andrew, 374.—Inscription engraved through the care of Gregory, cardinal priest, 421.—A rather shapeless fragment of an inscription on a marble tablet, 424.—Inscription engraved beneath images of Saints Cosmas and Damian, 530.—Ancient inscription in the title of St. Peter in Chains stating that John succeeded Boniface in 532, 538.—Marble inscription surviving in the church of the Crucifers at the Acqua Vergine, concerning its foundation, 574.—Carved marble concerning the grant of a place for the burial of Marcellus the subdeacon, 627.—Inscription on a lead pipe concerning the cemetery of martyrs repaired by Stephen, 628.—Near Rome, an inscription engraved by Narses under Justinian, 631.—Epitaph engraved upon the tomb of certain Roman pontiffs, 653.—Coin of Honorius Augustus, 667.—Inscription taken from the first Vitonian codex concerning the burial of Boniface III, 674.—Epitaph of the younger Boniface, 683; likewise 684.—Lead seal of Pope Honorius, 703.—Ancient epitaph found in the basilica of St. Peter, concerning the translation of the body of St. Leo, 911.—Funerary inscription on a marble tablet at Naples, in the church of St. Andrew, 1015.—Inscription beneath an image of St. Peter in the Vatican church, 1022.—Lead bull of King Chilperic, greatly corroded, 1084.—Inscription of a certain master of the soldiers, 1132.—Inscription of Asterius, patrician of the City, 1133.

FULCO, Archbishop of Rheims.—Epitaph of Fulco, CXXXI, 11.

NOTKER THE STAMMERER, monk of St. Gall.—Epitaph of Notker in the Bollandists, CXXXI, 989.

ANASTASIUS III, pope.—Epitaph of Anastasius, CXXXI, 1195.

REGINO, abbot of Prüm.—Fragment of that abbot’s epitaph, CXXXII, 9.

CYPRIAN, archpriest of Córdoba.—See above at vol. CXXI; here, however, CXXXII, 787.

HUCBALD, monk of St. Amand.—Epitaph of Milo, Hucbald’s master, CXXXII, 1050.—Double epitaph of Hucbald, 1050.

FLODOARD, canon of Rheims.—Ancient epitaph of Flodoard rendered in French rhythms, CXXXV, 11, 421 note.—Another epitaph which Flodoard appears to have composed for himself, 15.—Inscription prefixed to the church of St. Nicaise at Rheims by Jovinus, a most devout man, 40.—Inscription on a vessel preserved at Rheims, mentioning St. Remigius the priest, 44.—Inscription on the tomb of St. Remigius which stood in the church of St. Christopher, 59–60.—Inscription affixed to his tomb at the translation of his body into the church of the Virgin Mary by Archbishop Hincmar, 76.—Epitaph of Attolus, a most distinguished man and most zealous devotee of St. Remigius, 84.—Epitaph of Tilpin, bishop of Rheims, beside the feet of the body of St. Remigius, 123.—Inscription of a title on the pinnacle of the church of St. Peter and the Apostles, distinguished by images of Pope Stephen and Emperor Louis, 123.—Epitaph of Bishop Ebbo, ibid.—Hincmar provided an inscription for the repaired altar of the Blessed Mother of God, 144.—Hincmar distinguished with verses a book of the Gospels written in gold and silver letters, given to the same church, 145.—Hincmar prefixed an inscription to the little window through which the new place into which he had transferred the body of St. Remigius could be seen, 150.—Epitaph of Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, 261.—Inscription on a column standing in the quarter of St. Denis at Rheims, testifying to the benefits of St. Remigius, 357.—Epitaph of Adalbero, Archbishop of Rheims, 416.

RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona.—Epitaph of Ratherius himself upon his tomb, CXXXVI, 142.

LIUTPRAND, bishop of Cremona.—In the Appendix, inscription concerning the Cornelian family, found upon a stone in a certain ancient temple in the city of Aquaria, CXXXVI, 964, note.—Inscription on a remarkable stone found in the district of Oriola, 980, note.—Ancient inscription found among the ruins of the city of Assota, 979, note.—Funerary poem in honour of St. Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, 992.—Bronze coin in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Antiqua, 1003.—Epitaph of St. Eugenius, bishop, 1007, note.—Epitaph of St. Honoratus, bishop of Zaragoza, dedicated by Taio, his successor, 1011.—An inscription is engraved on the sarcophagus of the counts of Carrión, 1042.—Christ’s monogram was engraved on lamps intended for sacred use, ibid.—A bee appears engraved on an ancient Ephesian coin, 1067.—Inscriptions in Bernardo José de Aldrete’s *Antiquities of Spain*, 1069.—Inscriptions on a stone dedicated to Furia Sabina and Cornelius, a citizen of Florence, 1076, note.—Bronze coin bearing an inscription to Nero Claudius, 1082; and another to Emperor Marcus Aurelius, ibid.—Inscription on a bronze cymbal given by Abbot Samson, 1110.—In an ancient inscription, a maker of felt goods is called a *coactor*, 1124.—Likewise on a very ancient stone, one who makes felted goods is called a *lanarius coactilarius*, “a worker in woollen felt,” ibid.—Ancient inscription in which the cities Aeminium and Oscel in Lusitania are mentioned, 1138.

THEODERIC, bishop of Metz.—Epitaph of Theoderic himself, CXXXVII, 362.—Epitaph of Count Evrard composed by Theoderic, 363.

ADALBERO, Archbishop of Rheims.—Epitaph of Adalbero, CXXXVII, 506.

FOLCUIN, abbot of Lobbes.—Epitaph of Folcuin, CXXXVII, 541.—Another epitaph of the same in the church of St. Ursmar, beside that of Bishop Ratherius, 546.—Epitaph of Fulrad, abbot of this monastery, 555.

ADSO, abbot of Montier-en-Der.—Acrostic verses on St. Mansuetus within his Life, CXXXVII, 621.

GREGORY V, pope.—Epitaph of Gregory V on his tomb at St. Peter’s in the Vatican, 902.—Verses inscribed on the walls of the church of St. Prosper by Gregory V, 909.

ANONYMOUS.—On the foundation of the monastery of St. Arnulf at Metz in the tenth century.—Epitaph of King Louis and Emperor, son of Charlemagne, buried in this monastery, CXXXVIII, 196.—Epitaph, in the same place, of Drogo, Archbishop of Metz and son of Charlemagne, ibid.

Little book on the successors of St. Hidulf in the Vosges.—Inscription on a small cross fastened to the breast of Bishop Gerard, composed by Abbot Sicco, 214.

On the Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre.—Epitaph and lament for Bishop Robert, 286.—Epitaph of Archbishop Fulco, who was struck down on the road by wicked men, 290.—Epitaph of Bishop Peter of Belleperche, 368.—Epitaph of Bishop John Baillet, dedicated in 1518 by his nephew Francis of Dinteville, 583.

SILVESTER II, pope.—His successor Sergius IV composed an epitaph for Silvester, CXXXIX, 59.—Epigram of Gerbert, bishop of Ravenna and later Pope Silvester II, inscribed beside an image of Boethius, 287.—Epitaph of Lothair, king of the Franks, 287.—Epitaph of Duke Frederick, 288.—Epitaph of Adalbert the Scholastic, ibid.—Epitaph of Emperor Otto, ibid.

ST. ABBO, abbot of Fleury.—Acrostic poem to Emperor Otto by St. Abbo, CXXXIX, 519.

CONSTANTINE, abbot of St. Symphorian.—In the Life of Adalbero II, bishop of Metz, epitaph of the same Adalbero, CXXXIX, 1575.

ST. HENRY, emperor of Germany.—Inscriptions on his tomb, which stands at Bamberg in the church of St. George, CXL, 31.—Carved bust of the same emperor, 37.—Seal of Emperor Henry, 140, 141.—Mantle of St. Henry adorned with diverse figures and written inscriptions, 159, 161.—On the celebrated cross and other treasures of St. Henry at Bamberg, 167, 169.

[Col. 0619] THANGMAR, priest of Hildesheim.—In the Life of St. Bernward he supplied an epitaph of that saint, CXL, 434.—Another inscription is read on the right side of St. Bernward’s tomb, 435.

ST. FULBERT, bishop of Chartres.—Epitaph of St. Fulbert, in prose and again in verse, CXLI, 471.

ST. WILLIAM, abbot of St. Benignus at Dijon.—Epitaph of this holy abbot, CXLI, 838.

ROBERT, king of the Franks.—Epitaph of Hugh the Great, son of King Robert, CXLI, 935.

ELTINGER, abbot of Tegernsee.—Epitaph upon his tomb, CXLI, 1322.

ANGELRANN, abbot of Centula.—Epitaph of Angelrann, CXII, 1417; CXLVI, 1510.—Another epitaph of the same, affixed to his tomb by Guy of Amiens, 1420.—There also, funerary verses in praise of Angelrann, ibid.

ST. ODILO, abbot of Cluny.—Inscription on his tomb, CXLII, 840.

ST. MAIOLUS, abbot of Cluny.—Coin struck by St. Maiolus, 958.—Epitaph of Emperor Otto the Great by Odilo, 967.

GUY OF CHÂTILLON, Archbishop of Rheims.—His epitaph, CXLII, 1410.

HERMANN THE CRIPPLED.—Inscription of the monument which Bishop Gebehard of Salzburg erected to St. Gregory, CXLIII, 310.—Epitaph on the tomb of Blessed Gebehard, 322.—Epitaphs of Eppo of the Holy Mountain and Hermann in the church of the monastery of Petershausen, 330.

ODO, monk of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés.—In the Life of Burchard, whose epitaph is found there, CXLIII, 860.—Epitaph of the venerable Countess Elizabeth, 860.

BLESSED MAURILIUS, Archbishop of Rouen.—Epitaphs of Rollo and William Longsword, CXLIII, 1389, 1390.

STEPHEN, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—His epitaph dedicated by Bishop Alfanus, 1410.

ST. ANNO, bishop of Cologne.—Epitaph of this bishop, 1579.

PETER DAMIAN, cardinal of the Roman Church.—Epitaph of Blessed Peter Damian, buried at Faenza, CXLIV, 114.—Verses inscribed on the arch of the tomb, ibid.—Inscription on a column of the church at Faenza concerning St. Damian, ibid.—Epitaph in the new tomb in the church of St. Mary of the Angels, to which the body of Blessed Peter Damian was transferred in 1353, CXLV, 14, 18.

ST. JOHN GUALBERT.—Inscription in the metropolitan church of Siena concerning a council held under Gregory VII, CXLVI, 708.—Inscription on the cross from which the Lord greeted the body of St. Gualbert, 966.—Inscriptions on tablets depicting Blessed Gualbert, 967.—Autograph subscription of St. John Gualbert, 979.

ANONYMOUS, on the bishops of Eichstätt.—Epitaph of Blessed Leodegar, CXLVI, 1020.

JOHN, bishop of Rouen.—Epitaph of this bishop, CXLVII, 27.

LANDULF, cleric of Milan.—Device of a coin engraved on stone, with alpha and omega inscribed, CXLVII, 835, note.

ST. GREGORY VII, pope, in the Appendix.—Inscription concerning the year 1207, etc., during the expedition to Jerusalem, CXLVIII, 1281.

DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS OF CAMBRAI.—Marble inscription in memory of Bishop John, CXLIX, 58.—Inscription of a bell of the church of Cambrai which, having been broken, was recast and blessed under the name Aldegundis by Bishop Wibald, 95, note.

OSBERN, monk and precentor of the church of Canterbury.—In the Life of St. Ælfheah, whose epitaph he gives, CXLIX, 394.

WILLIAM CALCULUS, monk of Jumièges.—Double epitaph of Abbot Herluin in the history of the Normans, CXLIX, 842.—Triple epitaph of Henry, king of the English, 902.

VICTOR III, pope, formerly abbot of Monte Cassino.—The church is dedicated to St. Martin, with a golden inscription on its façade, 947.

WILLIAM THE CONQUEROR.—Double epitaph of William, CXLIX, 1271.

DURAND, abbot of Troarn.—Epitaph of Durand himself, CXLIX, 1375.—Epitaph of Ainard, abbot of Saint-Martin of Dives, inscribed by Durand, 1423.—Epitaph of Countess Mabel, by the same Durand, ibid.

ST. LANFRANC, Archbishop of Canterbury.—Epitaph of St. Lanfranc, CL, 98.—Epitaph of Robert of Neubourg, viscount of Normandy, 654.—Epitaph of William of Bénneville, called Poppeline, abbot of Bec, 672.—Epitaph of Abbot William on the tomb which John of Chambrai raised for him, ibid.—Epitaph of another Abbot Robert, 682.—Epitaph of Thomas, abbot of the same monastery of Bec, 683.—Epitaph of Blessed Herluin, first abbot and founder of Bec, 711.—Double epitaph of Abbot William, 723.—Epitaph of Boso, abbot of Bec, 731; another of the same, 734.—Epitaph of William Crispin the Elder, abbot of Bec, 741.—Epitaph of William, twenty-sixth abbot of the same monastery, 767.—Epitaph of Geoffrey the Spaniard, abbot of Bec, 770.

WILLIAM, abbot of St. Arnulf at Metz.—His epitaph, CL, 873.

GILLEBERT, monk of Elnone.—His epitaph, CL, 1434.

WILLIAM, monk of Chiusa.—In the Life of St. Benedict, verses inscribed upon his tomb, 1486.

DURAND, bishop of Clermont.—His epitaph, CL, 1187.

## CCXXIX. INDEX OF MUSIC, SETTING FORTH THE VARIOUS TREATISES ON THIS SCIENCE PROVIDED FOR US BY THE *PATROLOGIA*, AND OFFERING A CONCISE ANALYSIS OF EACH

[Col. 0625] ST. AUGUSTINE. — Six books *On Music*, XXXII, 1081.

The observation of fixed measurements of sounds belongs not to grammar but to music, ibid. — What is music? What is modulation? 1083 ff. — Why knowledge is included in the definition of music, 1085. — Whether the sense of music is innate, 1089. — Theatrical singers do not know music, ibid.

BOETHIUS. — Five books *On Music*, LXIII, 1167.

music, 1172. — On the species of inequalities, 1173. — Which ratios are suited to which musical consonances, 1175. — What sound, interval, and consonance are, 1176. — How Pythagoras discovered the ## CCXXX. INDEX ON PEDAGOGY, ARRANGED IN THE CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE FATHERS, WHICH TREATS IN TURN OF INSTRUCTION AND THE FORMATION OF CHARACTER, OF THE METHODS BY WHICH CHILDREN OUGHT TO BE EDUCATED AND TAUGHT, AND OF VARIOUS SCHOOLS AND MORE CELEBRATED TEACHERS

I. — On the two elements of which education consists: instruction and the formation of character, taken in a general sense. — The nature, necessity, excellence, and effects of each are examined.

[Col. 0631]

TERTULLIAN. — Literacy for the whole of life, I, 675. — Letters are necessary for commerce, practical affairs, and our pursuits toward God, II, 87. — Secular studies are not to be rejected, I, 675. — How natural abilities are developed, II, 682, 683. — In developing them, place matters greatly, ibid. — More ready intellects occur among eastern and southern peoples, 692. — Thus it has been reported that dull and brutish people are born at Thebes, while at Athens they are exceptionally keen in thinking and learning, 682, 683. — The seeds of all arts and ages are implanted in us, and God, the teacher from hiddenness, develops natural abilities, ibid. — Empedocles located the cause of sharp and dull dispositions in the quality of the blood, II, 683. — Nature is the first of all instruction, 82. — The teacher of the soul, I, 616. — Divine literature is more fruitful for the capacity of every subject matter, II, 53. — The method of teaching differs from that of learning, I, 675.

ST. ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—That knowledge is true which is joined to virtue, LII, 636.—What human knowledge has accomplished, 198.—What its hunger has accomplished, ibid.—How great is the knowledge of the saints, 525.—He deserves to know who fears to know, 583.—God, author of knowledge, 549.

EUGYPPIUS, African abbot.—What studies devout and diligent young people ought to reject, LXII, 955, 956.—That among the disciplines found among the Gentiles nothing is useful except the history of matters pertaining to bodily perception, and the method of argument and number, 956.—Young people should not neglect to learn those human institutions that serve the fellowship of people living together, ibid.—The discipline of numbers was not established by human beings but discovered, 955.—Which liberal disciplines and teachings a Christian teacher may take from pagan philosophers, 956.—Why letters were instituted, 944.

CASSIODORUS SENATOR.—The glorious knowledge of letters, LXIX, 595.—It purifies character in a person and supplies grace of speech, ibid.—It adorns those who are silent and those who speak, ibid.—Literary education renders a praiseworthy nature exceptionally well adorned, 798.—There the prudent person finds the means to become wiser; there the warrior finds the means to be strengthened by courage of soul, ibid.—From letters the ruler learns how to order peoples in equity, 798.—To judge rightly, discern the good, venerate divine things, and contemplate future judgments: these are benefits of learning, 798.—Knowledge of languages is praiseworthy, 825.—An eloquent tongue gathers together every good, 746.—The highest praises of grammar, LXIX, 787.—Grammar, mistress of words and ornamenter of the human race, ibid.—The first school of grammarians is the most beautiful foundation of letters, ibid.—A eulogy of arithmetic, LXIX, 514; LXX, 1204.—The usefulness of cosmography, LXX, 1139.—Astronomy, music, and the other liberal arts are praised throughout the whole work.—See the index under grammar, etc.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—The gift of understanding is insufficient without wisdom, LXXVI, 1017.—Understanding is given as though it were money borrowed, to be repaid with interest, 217, 1106.—The distinction between wisdom and knowledge, 998.—Wisdom belongs to life; knowledge belongs to teaching, ibid.—Knowledge without piety is harmful, LXXV, 547.—The devil often permits knowledge in order to corrupt life, 735.—Why a diligent student is given a slow intellect, while a negligent person receives a keen one, 736.—Human knowledge is useful, 865.—Some become more liable to punishment through their knowledge, LXXVI, 48.—Moderation in knowledge must be maintained, 147.—The effects of true knowledge, 269, 270.—What perfect knowledge is, 435.—Secular learning sharpens the blunted edge of the mind, LXXIX, 356.

The humanities do not supply us with weapons, but divine learning does, LXXIX, 355, 356.—Yet they are useful for understanding sacred Scripture, ibid.—The devil is the author of our not knowing secular letters, ibid.—Their usefulness is demonstrated by the examples of Moses, Isaiah, and Paul, 356.—They are useful not only to preachers but also to those living a private life, 356.

ST. ISIDORE OF SEVILLE.—The first pursuit of knowledge is to seek God, LXXXIII, 682.—Most people use knowledge not for God’s glory but for their own praise, 682.—Nothing is sweeter than knowledge, 860.—Ignorance is the mother of errors and the nurse of vices, ibid.—Knowledge keeps one from evils, ibid.—It is better to pursue the study of living well than that of knowing much, 601.—A judgment arising from knowledge is better than one arising from opinion, 600.

BLESSED ALCUIN.—The effectiveness of education, and how necessary it is in every rank, C, 209.—The old age of those who trained their youth in honorable arts reaps the sweetest fruits of studies, 210.—The light of knowledge is natural to human minds, CI, 850.—Why young people ought to love wisdom, ibid.—Wisdom: an ornament and an inward good, 851.—Wisdom is supported by the seven pillars of liberal learning, 853.—Training in the liberal arts is the foundation of tender age, C, 501.—The benefits of philosophy, CI, 854.

RABANUS MAURUS.—To what end all knowledge ought to be directed, CVII, 379.—The order and nature of the liberal arts, 395 ff.—The degrees of knowledge, 380.—A person must first seek what true knowledge and true wisdom are, CX, 88.—The benefits of dialectic, 397.—Likewise those of grammar, 395.—Knowledge of arithmetic is not to be despised, 399.—The Scriptures praise it, ibid.—The excellence and benefits of rhetoric, [Col. 0634] 396.—Other sciences whose knowledge should be acquired, 400 ff.—Wherein eloquence consists, 409.

ST. IVO OF CHARTRES.—Secular letters ought to be read, CLXI, 1115.—They are necessary for understanding sacred Scripture, 1116.—Secular letters contain truth in their learning, but that learning is not the knowledge of piety, ibid.—The teaching of grammarians can benefit life when it is adopted for better uses, ibid.

RUPERT, abbot of Deutz.—Nothing is more useful than the invention of letters for the knowledge of God the Creator, CLXIX, 1288.—Both human and divine knowledge among the Fathers before Abraham, 85.—Of the three principal languages, Latin is the youngest, 1273.—Hebrew letters discovered through Moses, ibid.

HONORIUS OF AUTUN.—Ignorance is a human being’s exile; wisdom is his homeland, reached through the liberal arts as though through an equal number of cities, CLXXII, 1243.

HUGH OF ST. VICTOR.—The functions of eloquence, CLXXVI, 880.—It comprises three things, ibid.—On the three sciences, CLXXVII, 195.

ST. BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux.—Knowledge of letters is not to be condemned, CLXXXIII, 967, 971.—How much letters benefit the Church, 967.—The usefulness of knowledge consists in the manner of knowing, 968.—That manner of knowing, ibid.—Knowledge of letters adorns and instructs the soul, and enables it to instruct others also, 971.—Without knowledge zeal collapses, 352.—Dignity without knowledge is useless; without virtue it is harmful, CLXXXII, 976, 977.—Knowledge is not to be sought except through the Word, 1113.—Different kinds of knowledge, 968.—One kind puffs up, another saddens, ibid.—Some wish to know in order merely to know; others in order to be known; others in order to sell knowledge; others in order to build up; others in order to be built up, 968.—The manner of knowing has three elements: order, affection, and end, ibid.—Secular knowledge intoxicates with curiosity, not charity, 817.—Excessive curiosity in knowing must be avoided, CLXXXIV, 1280.—What true knowledge is, 1115.—The fullness of knowledge is to know God, 552.—God teaches a person knowledge, CLXXXII, 621.

PETER THE VENERABLE, abbot of Cluny.—He teaches a certain master that secular sciences should be despised and that wisdom should instead be sought in Christian teaching, CLXXXIX, 77, 78.—Without Platonic meditations and without Academic disputations, the way of blessedness has been discovered, 77.

PETER LOMBARD.—The marvelous order of Christian teaching, CXCI, 1179.—Where the highest knowledge consists, 855.—There is one knowledge that approaches God, 321.—Knowledge useless in itself becomes useful when joined with charity, CXCII, 1601.

ADAM THE SCOT.—The benefits and praise of human speech, CXCVIII, 91.—Knowledge is blameworthy when love does not accompany it, 165.

PHILIP OF HARVENG.—Praise of the liberal arts, CCIII, 712.—A eulogy of the Latin language, 154.—Why letters are called liberal, 152.—Philip elegantly recounts the origin of literary knowledge and human speech among all peoples, 1015 ff.—First among the Hebrews, ibid.—Among the Egyptians, 1017, 1018.—Among the Phoenicians and Greeks, 1019.—Among the Latins, 1021, 1022.—Natural ability is not situated within the choice of the human will, 17.—What young people’s natural abilities are like, 212.—The great persons in whom literary knowledge has shone, 32.—Yet no knowledge deserves commendation unless it is directed to spiritual perfection, 33.—Literary sciences are to be preferred to riches and other such things, ibid.—Literary studies are necessary for ecclesiastical persons, 157 ff.—Holiness without knowledge usually goes astray through error, 158.—Knowledge without holiness becomes foul, 158.

II.—The ways in which children ought to be brought up and educated.—The principles necessary for acquiring knowledge are set forth.—And various precepts for the formation of character.—The gifts with which both teachers and pupils ought to shine.—The vices to be avoided in both.

TERTULLIAN.—Discipline is the index of teaching, II, 58.—The vices of the flesh and of the world draw people greatly away from divine disciplines, I, 1283.—A faithful pupil will not attend schools because of their defilements, II, 675.—Memory, the treasury of all studies, from Cicero, ibid., 688.—It is the salvation of the senses and understandings, ibid.—Its glory is as great as the injury caused by forgetfulness, 668.—God requires children to honor older age, 417.

CYPRIAN.—We quickly become accustomed to what we hear and see, IV, 785.—When the human mind is itself led toward vices, what will it do if it has examples from the nature of the slippery body, which falls of its own accord? [Col. 0635] ibid.—Fear is the guardian of innocence, 202.—Discipline is the guardian of hope, the restraint of faith, the guide of the saving way, the kindling and nourishment of a good disposition, the teacher of virtue, 440.—It makes one remain always in Christ and live continually for God, 441.—The severity of discipline among the Romans, 309.—Children’s virtue surpassing their age, 419.—A teacher who destroys children, 362.

LACTANTIUS.—Youth, unless restrained by fear, will produce in license a boldness that will issue in every disgrace and crime, VI, 704.—The emotion of anger for restraining the sins of those in our power, VI, 704.—Nothing is so hostile to the mind, this divine gift and endowment, as pleasures, 706.—Young people are inflamed with lust by theatrical spectacles, 711.—Spectacles must therefore be avoided, 712.—Examples are more effective than words, 520.—How young people were formerly trained in eloquence, 348.—Who are called masters, VII, 400.—Masters of correspondence in the courts of princes, ibid.

ST. HILARY, bishop of Poitiers.—A child must be habituated from tender years to God’s teaching and to the precepts of fear, IX, 511.—The true and perfect foundations of the fear of God are contained under these rudiments of letters, ibid.—Philosophy is weak of itself for ordering human morals, 502.—A person cannot attain knowledge of the devout life and its true practice without God’s grace, 502.—It is necessary to pray to God for the gift of understanding, IX, 456, 567.—Understanding must be sought from God, lest a false one be introduced by the devil, 611.—Understanding is hindered by carnal pleasures, 327.—For one lacking understanding, it is prudence to ask wisely, 535.—It is best to teach by example rather than words, 951.—It is not enough to teach what is right unless what is impious is also refuted, X, 238.—For knowledge of God, neither worldly instruction nor innocence of life suffices, 143.

ST. AMBROSE, bishop of Milan.—The first task of formative discipline is to turn away fault; the second, to instill virtue, XVI, 238.—The teacher ought to excel the person taught, 207.—Not all are fit to teach—would that all were capable of learning, 1293.—Before speaking, a wise person considers what to say, to whom, in what place, and at what time, XVI, 33.—Utter no word from your mouth that you may wish to recall, 228.—The beginning of human error is a person’s speech, 25.—The nobility of a teacher is the first ardor for learning, 209.—Who teachers are, XVII, 387.—Teachers are those accustomed to instruct children who are to be imbued with letters and readings, ibid.—Suitable authority is conferred on teaching when it rests upon one’s own example, 981.—A capable teacher fulfills in deeds what he teaches in words, 459.—The teaching of a command would be empty if the teacher’s action did not first provide authority, 998.—One advances more through examples, and why, XVI, 207.—It is the part of a good teacher to prevent the occasion of sin, 238.—The pedagogue is feared; the teacher shows the way of salvation, 1558.—The ignorant must be educated gently, XVI, 172.—The perfection of pupils is the teacher’s joy and crown, XVII, 446.—The pupils’ crown is the teacher’s glory, 456.—The authority of a teacher lies in the confidence of pupils, ibid.—Whoever despises a teacher seeks to be corrected, 335.—Whatever faults pupils commit reflect upon teachers, 919.—Young people are recalled from vice more by fear than by reason, XIV, 665.—Adolescence is weak in strength, feeble in judgment, hot with vice, impatient of advisers, and alluring through pleasures, 866.—The fullness of perfect discipline does not allow the mind to be consumed by the devouring heat of desires, 346.—Under bad leaders one quickly goes astray, 595.—Physical strength is increased by exercise, 352.—Avoid seeking what it is not permitted to know, XV, 1704.

ST. JEROME.—No art is learned without a teacher, XXII, 1080.—Even dumb animals and herds of beasts follow their leaders, ibid.—There is no one, however gifted, who can comprehend everything, XXIII, 514.—A teacher of proven age, life, and learning should be chosen, XXII, 871.—Those who, in a moment of time, are not yet pupils but already teachers fall into arrogance, 664.—Do not be a teacher before you have been a pupil, XXII, 1077; XXIII, 166.—Some are teachers of the unlearned before they are pupils of the learned, XXII, 1121.—What the worst teacher is, XXIII, 603.—Pupils are punished through teachers’ fault, XXV, 1491.—What teachers’ concern for the salvation of their pupils ought to be, XXVI, 385.—Perfect concern is scarcely found, ibid.—Teachers ought to share their counsels with pupils, XXVI, 3.—The best pedagogue is one who advises and terrifies by severity of countenance, XXII, 959.—What a pedagogue is, XXVI, 368.—Why he is assigned to little children, ibid.—So that a playful age may be restrained while tender childhood is educated in studies, ibid.—The salvation of pupils is the reward of teachers, XXV, 447.—A pupil [Col. 0636] who imitates the faults of a teacher, XXIII, 477.—Teachers’ faults are not to be imitated, but their virtues, ibid.—Pupils should provide teachers with the necessities of life, XXVI, 429.—How children’s upbringing and instruction ought to be provided, XXII, 870, 871.—How Christian childhood ought to be trained, 871.—By what ingenious means it should be educated, ibid.—Let boxwood or ivory letters be made for the child to play with, so that he may gradually become accustomed to joining words, ibid.—Let him join syllables for a reward, and let him be invited by little gifts with which that age can delight, 870, 871.—Above all, care must be taken that he does not come to hate study, ibid.—The child should have companions in learning whom he may envy and whose praise may sting him, ibid.—He should not be scolded if he is slower, but his ability should be stimulated by praise, ibid.—Precepts concerning the dress and food of young girls, 872 ff.—Their occupations in spinning wool, 875.—On the education of children, XXII, 1095, 1096.—An infant should associate with peers of the same sex, 1098.—Let the child love its mother as a parent, submit to her as a mistress, and fear her as a teacher, ibid.—Let the child learn sacred Scripture by heart, ibid.—Let the child not go out in public too freely, ibid.—Other precepts, ibid.—On educating one’s own children, XXVI, 565, 579 ff.—To bring up children well is no small merit before God, XXII, 729.

ST. AUGUSTINE.—How excellent the office of teaching is, XXXIV, 18.—The sweetness of truth ought to invite us to learn, XL, 161.—We are led to learn by authority and reason, XXXII, 957, 1007.—Understanding occurs in us in two ways: either through the mind itself, by itself, or through an admonition from the senses, XXXIIII [sic], 78; XLII, 93.—The disciplines, sciences, and arts to which one should devote oneself, and how, XXXIV, 62, 63.—Those who ought to devote themselves to their own salvation and the Church’s benefit should have no time for treating curious questions, 271, 277.—In studying every science, one must observe moderation, 62.—For what end persons devoted to letters may seek human praise, XXXIII, 436.—Prayer should precede study, XXXII, 919.—How learners’ studies are kindled, XLII, 972, 973.—Tranquility of mind is necessary for study, XXXII, 1075.—Childhood is suited to moral formation, XXXIII, 1108.—In nearly all matters, whatever is tender is more quickly habituated, ibid.—The studies of letters themselves are more effectively implanted in tender minds, ibid.—Corruption of ability and disposition reveals itself by many signs in children, XXXII, 674.—Very few adolescents commit no blameworthy sins from the beginning of adolescence, XLI, 730.—What vices usually abound in adolescence, 756.—Among adolescents devoted to letters, impulses of rivalry and empty boasting must be restrained, ibid., 991.—Moral precepts are given to adolescents, 1006.—What children often learn in vain matters can be learned more safely in matters that are not vain, 671, 672.—Life must especially be corrected in youth, XXXVII, 1512.—A bad method of educating youth, XXXII, 672.—Augustine strongly condemns it, ibid.—How harmful to a student are poets’ fictions, incentives to lust, 672.—Another method of training youth in literary matters ought to be proposed, and the reading of pagan authors avoided, 673.—No one can be educated without labor and pain, XXXVII, 1145; XLI, 728.—Free curiosity has greater force in learning languages than fearful compulsion, XXXII, 671.—How customary and vain it is to learn letters in hope of temporal advantage, XL, 675.—Every praiseworthy ability, without true piety and religion, evaporates in pride, XL, 51.—The most outstanding talents have fallen into greater errors in proportion as they ran with greater self-confidence, XXXIII, 669.—Augustine asks Jerome whence diversity of talents arises, 728.

CASSIAN.—No one should easily judge himself fit to teach others, XLIX, 367, 986.—In teaching, vain glory must be cast aside, 986.—What reward is deserved by one who dispenses God’s words from love of human praise, 987.—Unlearned persons who presume to teach others rebuked, 81, 1307.—The office of a teacher, 851.—The authority of one who instructs will never be effective unless he has fixed it in the listener’s heart through the result of his own work, 851.—Do not presume to teach anyone by words what you have not first done in deed, 968.—It is impossible for an impure mind to obtain the gift of spiritual knowledge, 970.—With every care avoid producing, through study of reading, not the light of knowledge but instruments of perdition from the vanity of arrogance, ibid.—What is necessary to attain spiritual knowledge, 965 ff.—Above all, the mind must be purified from every vice, 966.—It is one thing to possess ease of speech and polish of expression, another to enter the veins and marrow of heavenly sayings, 969.—Neither human learning nor secular education can achieve this at all; only purity of mind can, ibid.—Paul prepared himself for spiritual knowledge by diligent study and exertion, 288.—Understanding of the Scriptures is acquired more by prayer than study, [Col. 0637] 195.—Reasons why spiritual teaching may be unfruitful, 987, 988.

ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE.—The first vice of the soul is the will to do what the supreme and innermost Truth forbids, LI, 494.—The distinctive mark of good talents is to love truth, not words, in the utterances of speakers, 465.

ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS.—The vices to which younger age is subject, LII, 522.—A child’s mind is led toward prudence by gentle inducements, 499.—A father draws his son to the rigor of discipline not by power but by love, ibid.—Chrysologus taught the Creed to little children in the faith, 355, 356.—He forbids the mysteries of faith to be given in books, but commands that they be entrusted to memory, 354 ff.—In teaching children, he wholly reduced himself to a child, 371.—He expounded the Gospel soberly, 544 ff.—He prayed to God to pour knowledge into the minds of his hearers, 549.—He acknowledged himself fit for understanding the Scriptures only through God, 197.—How great are pupils’ labor and punishment in learning letters, 882.—A pupil wrongs his teacher if he does not follow that teacher’s instruction, 405.—Just as a pupil’s uprightness is a teacher’s praise, so a pupil ignorant of discipline is a teacher’s reproach, 405.—A pupil does not attain knowledge if he strives to be taught according to his own will, 651.—A skilled teacher, when listening to the untrained and understanding the slow, strikes pupils’ minds in different ways of instruction and kindles their talent, 495.—Childhood holds the whole person, more through tears than through the force of reason, 554.—Public correction should be applied to one whom private correction has been unable to amend, 550.—A mind oppressed by drunken excess judges badly, 653.—For learning human matters, the whole of human life is short, 508.—How much more so for learning divine things, ibid.

ST. VALERIAN.—What discipline is and how great a good it is, LII, 691.—Harsh to the perverse, but sweet to the upright, ibid.—There is nothing that labor does not overcome, 700.

ST. LEO THE GREAT.—Correction should be applied in such a way that love is always preserved, LIV, 669.

ST. PAULINUS OF NOLA.—The ways in which children ought to be educated, LXI, 390.

EUGYPPIUS, African abbot.—The method of teaching to be observed by schoolmasters, LXXII, 605.—How diligent students ought to be educated, 606.—They are to be educated by authority and reason, ibid.—Authority appears more salutary for the unlearned, but reason more fitting, ibid.—Letters must be taught before syllables, 605.—Other things that the adolescent should later learn, 606.—For the good fruit of studies, discipline is especially necessary, 605.—And observance of the divine commandments, ibid.—Young people should endeavor to restrain vices, as enemies of study, ibid.—At every time they should either have worthy friends or strive to acquire them, ibid.—How studious adolescents ought to live, 605.

BOETHIUS.—On the formation of students, LXIV, 1229.—The matters arranged for students’ education are examined, 1234.—The discipline of students, 1223.—On teachers, 1235.—On their qualities and characteristics, ibid.—A teacher must be learned, gentle, and strict, 1235.—Let him be devout in affection, distinguished by virtues, and praiseworthy in goodness, ibid.—A teacher must shape a pupil’s character, 1043.—For excellence in public office, three kinds of status must be carefully understood, 1233.—What must be done for a pupil to strive toward perfection, 1228, 1230.—He is not worthy of knowledge who rises against the teacher of knowledge, 1227.—The pupil’s three duties, 1226.—The criterion of truth, LXIII, 851.—We know by understanding, reasoning, imagination, and sense, 848, 849.—The thing precedes understanding, understanding precedes voice, and voice precedes letters, but not conversely, LXIV, 402.—Wine taken moderately appears to give keenness to the intellect, 1228.—Taken immoderately, it dulls the intellect, ibid.—Knowledge of truth is impeded by disturbances, which therefore must be expelled, LXIII, 655.

ST. FULGENTIUS.—On the education of children, LXV, 310.—Those who truly love their children should provide for them more by acting well than by gathering riches, ibid.—Let reading not be absent from good works, 352.

ST. BENEDICT.—How children or youths are to be restrained when they offend, LXVI, 534.—Let them be afflicted with fasts or beatings, ibid.

CASSIODORUS SENATOR.—The happier praise of parents is to be praised for their children’s uprightness, LXIX, 755.—What is not learned in youth is unknown in mature age, 524.—The most difficult kind of rule is for a young person to exercise mastery over his own impulses, 824, 825.—Young people’s virtue is encouraged by undertaking labor, 663.—One whom a constant admonisher attends does not easily become vicious, 825.—One who sins after being warned has no place for pardon, 628.—The mind languishes unless renewed by continual reading, 824.—Frequent meditation is the mother of understanding, LXX, 1108.

ST. GREGORY THE GREAT.—He knows how to speak rightly who knows how to speak in order, [Col. 0638] LXXVI, 538.—Through pupils’ eager hunger for truth, the gift of understanding increases in the teacher, 543.—The righteous ought to fear more than rejoice over the gift of understanding entrusted to them, 218.—One who loses the order of living well loses the correctness of speaking, LXXV, 964.—How long teachers ought to devote care to educated pupils, LXXIX, 198.—How spiritual matters ought to be examined, 232.—When we wish to examine spiritual matters, it is necessary that we remove them from our intention [reading uncertain], ibid.—A teacher’s study is idle if through it the heavenly building is not increased, 218.—With what splendors of virtue a teacher ought to be adorned, 456.—Adolescence is suited to good deeds, LXXV, 981.—Adolescence is the womb of perverse thought, LXXVI, 474.—Not to know is ignorance; to have refused to know is pride, 340.—Humility opens the light of understanding, 341.—Obedience is the ornament of innocence, 768.—Those who make good progress should strive above all to hold fast the good of obedience, LXXIX, 297.—It is easier to obey than to command, 312.—Royal children should especially be instructed in morals, LXXVII, 881.—May their minds be touched by charity toward one another and by gentleness toward those subject to them, ibid.—The words of those who nourish them will be milk if good, poison if bad, ibid.—Young people must be admonished differently from old people, 52.—A child of five accustomed to blaspheme is handed over to the devil, 349.

ST. ISIDORE OF SEVILLE.—Learn what you do not know, lest you be found a useless teacher, LXXXIII, 860.—The pursuit of learning and teaching is not to be despised, ibid.—Show by examples what you teach in words, 861.—When you teach, do not use obscurity of language; speak so that you are understood, 861.—A teacher’s speech should be proportioned to the hearer’s understanding, ibid.—Take care lest, while raising others by teaching, you yourself be sunk by the desire for praise, ibid.—Everyone must be taught according to his profession, ibid.—Who a pedagogue is, LXXXII, 389.—Children must be formed not only by literary studies but also by the lessons and instruction of virtues, LXXXIII, 891.—On correcting little children who lack knowledge, 1209.—Whoever neglects the capacity for understanding granted him by God becomes guilty of condemnation, 681.—On those who possess the ability of understanding but neglect the study of reading, ibid.—Reading increases understanding, ibid.—Many are lively in keenness of understanding but are hampered by poverty of expression, 682.—Slower abilities are sharpened by studies, 860.—Torpor overcomes understanding; dullness extinguishes the light of knowledge, ibid.—Diligence makes understanding better; negligence makes it worse, ibid.—Idleness blunts understanding, ibid.—On books of the Gentiles, 685.—A Christian ought not to read poets’ fictions, ibid.—Why this is so, ibid.—The sayings of the Gentiles shine outwardly with eloquence of words, but inwardly remain empty of the wisdom of virtue, 686.—Why the sayings of the Gentiles are loved, ibid.—The reading of books that lure a person into their errors and sprinkle sweet snares through ornaments of language must be avoided, 687.—In reading, one must love not words but truth, ibid.—All progress arises from reading and meditation, 679.—Things above human understanding are not to be investigated, 600.

ST. CHRODEGANG, bishop of Metz.—On nurturing and guarding children, LXXXIX, 1078.—Children should be entrusted to a most approved elder, whom they may have both as teacher of doctrine and witness of life, ibid.

BLESSED ALCUIN.—The moral principles and precepts by which adolescents ought to be formed, CI, 851 ff.—Without God’s help, no human ability can make progress, C, 501.—Young people should strive with their whole attention to grasp the grounds of the Catholic faith, ibid.—Let them learn the traditions of Catholic teachers, ibid.—The order of faith to be observed in teaching a man mature in age, 190, 204, 205.—Natural ability is not preserved without chastity, 501.

RABANUS MAURUS.—Poems and books of the Gentiles must be read cautiously, CVII, 396.—They are compared to a captive woman, ibid.—Care must be taken lest their license become a stumbling block to the weak, ibid.

HINCMAR, archbishop of Rheims.—The necessity of an upright pedagogue, CXXV, 990.—Demonstrated by the example of Alexander the Great, ibid.—The virtues with which instructors of royal children ought to shine, 991.—King Charles commands that prudent and sober instructors, who also hate avarice and teach justice, be chosen, ibid.—Pedagogues should teach royal children by word and example to honor the Church and its ministers, ibid.—And to preserve due law and justice for the nobles of the kingdom and all the other faithful of the kingdom, ibid.—Other outstanding duties of those who educate princes, 991, 992.—The moral precepts they ought to impress upon them, ibid.

RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona.—Admonitions for young people, CXXXVI, 204 ff.—Let the teacher strive to impart discipline to his pupils with affection [Col. 0639], 176.—To correct their faults both by words and by blows, ibid.—Excessive severity in a teacher is reprehensible, ibid.—On unequal capacity among pupils, 177.—On the manner of teaching the capable and the incapable, ibid.—The precepts of the disciplines ought to be adapted to each individual’s capacity and to the diversity of minds, ibid.—On the various faults a teacher must avoid, 177–178.

PETER DAMIAN (St.).—The method of teaching boys in schools, CXLV, 620–621.—The human mind is as absorbed by small things when needy as by many things when rich, 257.—The studies of philosophers serve the understanding of the Scriptures, 560.

OTLOH.—Monk of St Emmeram.—Prudence and moderation in punishing boys’ faults, shown to Otloh in a vision, CXLVI, 347.—Otloh himself relates how he undertook to learn, without a master’s help, to paint letters elegantly, 56–57.

JOHN, archbishop of Rouen.—Youth must be formed for the true faith, piety, and learning, CXLVII, 257.—A schoolmaster must not allow vices to grow up in children, 250.

LANFRANC, archbishop of Canterbury.—The honourable life of pupils is a teacher’s ornament, CL, 370.—Teachers ought to be venerable to their pupils, 255.—Mature and discerning, 506.—On the discipline of boys in monasteries, 506–507.—How boys should conduct themselves in church, in the refectory, and in school, 506.—In the dormitory, 507.—Young people must not go anywhere outside their assigned place of custody without a guardian, ibid.

GUIBERT, abbot of Nogent.—Guibert was imbued with the very best instruction and morals, CLVI, 845.—He was kept under a rather strict discipline, ibid.—In nothing, whether speech, gaze, or action, did he act without moderation, ibid.—He studied even on Sundays and saints’ feast days, ibid.—He was restrained by beatings, ibid.—Through his master’s zeal he made much progress in upright conduct, ibid.—But little in letters because of that master’s ignorance, ibid.—A mind oppressed by excessively harsh study is dulled, ibid.—Alternations of exercises must be employed in order to make the intellect keener, ibid.

ANSELM (St.), archbishop of Canterbury.—The first part of prudence is to assess the person whom one is about to instruct, CLVIII, 465.—Teachers who instil more terror than love and piety into boys are reproved, 696.—Boys compared to plants, ibid.—The more earnestly a young man applies himself to learning, the more effectively he ascends to knowledge of the supreme nature, 213.—Meditation produces knowledge, 741.—One ought to exercise oneself more in prose than in verse, 217.—Errors of the dialecticians, 265.

IVO (St.) of Chartres.—Why Christians are forbidden to read poetic fictions, CLXI, 1116.—Jerome is rebuked by an angel because he had read a book of Cicero, 1114.—Actors corrupt boys, 774.

PETER DE HONESTIS.—How boys and adolescents who are being reared ought to conduct themselves, CLXIII, 729.

MARBOD, bishop of Rennes.—The instruction of a boy who is a pupil, CLXXI, 1724.

HUGH OF ST VICTOR.—Three things necessary for a student: nature, practice, and discipline, CLXXVI, 877.—There are two things that exercise the intellect: reading and meditation, ibid.—The beginning of learning lies in reading; its completion, in meditation, 878.—The greatest delight lies in meditation, ibid.—Various intellectual exercises in schools, 709.—The method of acquiring sciences, 741.—What hinders study, 793.
