[Col. 0643]

CCXXXI. INDEX OF LINGUISTICS, IN WHICH ARE NOTED WHATEVER THE FATHERS HAVE HANDED DOWN CONCERNING THE ORIGIN, CHARACTER, USE, ETC. OF VARIOUS LANGUAGES AND IDIOMS. AT THE SAME TIME ARE GIVEN INNOVATIONS OR CORRUPTIONS OF WORDS THAT HAVE CREPT IN WITH THE PASSING OF YEARS, ETC.

NOTICE.

In this index there are presented not only those things which sound less than correct to educated ears, whether through negligence of syntax and obscurity of meaning, or through an unusual use of certain expressions and their very, as they say, barbarism; but also those things which each writer’s talent has felicitously discovered. For surely absurd, although commonly accepted, is the opinion of those who reject all writings of the Middle Ages as distasteful and repugnant to the stomach. As we note in the case of Coelius Sedulius, this has been the act only of impious men, by which they have succeeded in causing the study of antiquity to be neglected; and, sad to say, their perversity has prevailed far too long. Latin, precisely because it is called low or lowest, is not therefore to be despised; rather, it becomes a reason for more careful study.

The fate of the idiom and empire of the ancient Romans was bound to be the same: namely, the spoil of conquerors. Here began that age-long labour of childbirth from which the languages of more recent peoples arose, not suddenly but gradually, newly imbued by the baptism of the Scriptures; and who would dare call into doubt that each language has wonderfully claimed such great riches for itself? That God of Moses, that Christ of the Apostles, with his angels and his most beloved Church, thrusts down the gods and goddesses of the whole Olympus; and, preached everywhere throughout the world, substitutes one language for another according to the custom and genius of each people. Whatever the trumpeters of ancient fables may mutter, great and most beautiful things have arisen from the labour of the Middle Ages, most highly to be commended to beginners in languages. Among thousands upon thousands of examples of neologisms, what could sound sweeter to the ears of the most refined poet than these expressions, now so familiar: “Our Lady,” “your Guardian Angel,” “my bell-tower,” “sweet Providence,” “a lovely Sunday,” “the holy altars,” “Peter’s cross,” etc., etc. And I say this not only in French, but also in German, English, Spanish, and Italian. Moreover, how many less decent words are not even tolerated by Christian ears and are banished from the language. Therefore let the reader carefully remember that every author, even of the lowest Latin, had his own archaisms and his own distinctive charm; but if he has sometimes employed barbarous words because new things very often required proper terms, he did so in order that he might more easily be understood by readers to whom the Latin writer himself appeared barbarous.

The rationale of the arrangement we have followed is this. We judged it necessary first to leave to every author what is his own, lest confusion should arise more readily from the contrary course. Thus, as it were, a light mirror is set before the eyes, whose image and form preserve the character of their own homogeneity and unity. At the end of the index it contains a list of all authors, by whose aid every inquiry is easy, account being taken both of the chronology of times, which we have noted accurately, and of the order of volumes in the *New Course of Patrology*. Moreover, we arrange all authors in the same chronological order in which they occur in the *New Course*; but what belongs to each author we distinguish into two parts: namely, the dialectical and grammatical part, which discusses languages in general or a particular language specifically, and the diacritical part, which deals with a word or words. The former includes matters concerning the origin and use of sound, voice, words, speech, and writing, as well as the uses and laws of grammar, likewise the studies and labours of human intelligence by which writings have passed from one language into another. In the latter part, words and expressions worthy of notice are arranged alphabetically, in as many categories as there are languages. Three are commonly distinguished: Hebrew words, Greek words, and Latin words.

N.B. The Roman numeral gives the volume of the *New Course of Patrology*, and the Arabic numeral the column; whenever the Roman numeral is omitted, refer back to the last one cited.

II, 72, 460, 486, 630, 973.—Pharaoh, 301.—Pharisees: whence they are called, 61.—The Phoenicians pour forth into Africa, 700, 1035.—Rebecca, 598, 904.—What the Sabbath is; who the Sadducees are, 46, 61, 846, 937.—Solomon, king, 14, 311, 350, 382, 611.—Samaria, 339, 619.—Samuel, 740.—Sardanapalus, 1042.—Satan, prince of demons, I, 405, 613, 1258; II, 104, 297, 710, 877, 928.—Saul, II, 14, 311.—Serapis, Egyptian god, I, 305.—*Serapeum*, for the temple of Serapis, I, 380, 574.—What Serapic banquets are, I, 474.—Simon Magus, I, 346, 672; II, 62, 708.—*Vae* (“woe”), a Hebrew interjection, II, 392, 462, 952.—Zechariah, 137.

Greek Terms in Tertullian.---Athens, the city “tongued” or eloquent, II, 651. Those most acute in wisdom and speech are born at Athens, 683. Greek and Latin are regarded as languages akin to one another, I, 618. How the Greek alphabet supplied an occasion to the New Heresy, II, 70. The Lord assumed for himself the two letters of Greece, the first and the last, 935. Why Christ is called Α and Ω, 70. The testimony of Aristeas concerning the Greek translation of the Old Testament, I, 380. Menedemus the philosopher approved the Greek version of the Old Testament, 380. The apostle Paul wrote his epistles in Greek, 1186. The Academics were so called from the place of their meetings, 282. The Aeons of the Valentinians, II, 47, 68. Agape, or love: what it is, I, 474, 623. Who the Anthropophagi are, 321, 323. The Antipodes, 370, 570. Writings of the Apocrypha, II, 649. What apotheosis is, I, 451. The term Ἀρχή (*Archē*) is not only ordinal but also authoritative: it denotes primacy or rule, II, 215. Ἄρχοντες (*Archontes*): thus princes and magistrates are called, 215, 339, 620. Atom; the atoms of Epicurus, 703. What Βέκκος (*Bekkos*) is, I, 570. A library, 610. The Alexandrian Library, 379. Who is called Catholic, II, 23, 931. Charis, an aeon of Valentinus, 551. Christ is called from *chrism* (*chrisma*), which means anointing, I, 1207. Who the Cynocephali peoples are, 312. Διαμαστίγωσις (*diamastigōsis*), that is, the flogging customarily practised among the Lacedaemonians, 626. Diespiter, a god, 600. The origin of the name Church, used frequently by Tertullian and all the Fathers, II, 32, 922. Whence εἴδωλον (*eidōlon*, “image, idol”) is derived, [Col. 0647] I, 665. What the Embryosphactae, Embryoncetae, Embryorectae, Embryopactae, and Embryosectae are, II, 692. What the Enthymesis of the Valentinians is, 564. The Ἐπερχόμενος (*Eperchomenos*, “the Coming One”) of Marcion, 416, 422. *Exomologesis* in the sense of confession, I, 1243, 1245, 1247. The Gallo-Greeks are descended from the Gauls, 316. Grammarians so named from Aristarchus, 282. Who the Gymnosophists of India are, II, 260. Ἵππιος (*Hippios*), an epithet of Neptune, I, 641. Homer, 575; II, 707, 726, 796. What Homerocentones are, 53. Horon, an aeon of Valentinus, 565, 577. What the Hipsoma of the sun is, I, 701. Ἰχθύς (*Ichthys*): Christ, that is, “fish,” an acrostic word each letter of which in Greek contains names of Christ, thus: Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour, 1198. Astrology was permitted until the Gospel, and why, 672. What the monarchy of God is, II, 158. Who the Ophites are, 63. What Pancarpon is, 563. A pantomime, I, 576, 649. The Montanist Paraclete, II, 886. Mercury Trismegistus, master of natural philosophers, 567. What Valentinus’s Pleroma is, 68. Plato the philosopher, I, 510, 511, 517; II, 20, 260, 651, 671, 678, 686, 702, 1033. Pythagoras, I, 511, 521; II, 697, 701, 732. Who the Sciapodes are, 312. Sige, the Mother, or Silence, 551. Sophia, an aeon of Valentinus, 212. Whence the Stoics were so called, I, 282. What xerophagy is, II, 955, 960, 964.

Latin.---On Tertullian’s Latinity, I, 48, 251; II, 1249. For expressions and words peculiar to Tertullian, consult the exceedingly full *Index of Tertullianic Latinity* by Gottfried Schulz, 1251.

MINUCIUS Felix, Roman jurist or advocate.---His manner of speaking and writing followed that of the Africans: Tertullian, Cyprian, and Arnobius, III, 201. His style is ingenious, sharp, forceful, compressed, dense, and sinewy, 204. He imitated the earlier authors called classics, 223. Logical analysis of the Dialogue of Minucius Felix by Johann Gottlieb Linder, 225 ff.

Latin expressions.---*Autumnitas* (“maturity”), III, 286. “He flatters them with terror,” 259 note. “The banquet grew warm,” 263 note. What *Cantabra* means, 332 note. “With crisp and swelling waves,” 239. What it means “to have accommodating gods,” 250 note. Who municipal gods are, 251 note. What “edible cattle” are, 355 note. “Fashioned into images”; Savaro has much to say on the verb *effigiare*, 238 note. Hellenisms in Minucius: “thus, not to desire willing adherents to your sect,” 269; “we are found among one another,” 287. *Hennei* Mountain and *Lesui* for Mount Etna and Vesuvius, 305, 349. Holstenius’s letters on the spits of Ephesian Diana, 366. “It has been rendered impious,” 317 note. “A speech sweeter.” Meursius thinks it should be restored as: “sweeter in speech than the very broken utterance of an offended tongue,” 235 note. *Natura* for genitals, 201. “The greater part of you,” 325. *Strepitus* for *crepitus* (“noise” for “crackling”), 330. Ephesian Diana constructed of spits, 305. A woman married once; a woman married many times, 315.

ST. CYPRIAN, bishop of Carthage.---This holy doctor especially loved Tertullian among writers, and habitually said of him, “Bring me the Master,” IV, 81. Cyprian’s writings contain the highest gravity of thought and brilliance of expression, ibid. The letter to Donatus, adorned with so many elegant descriptions, bears no trace whatever of the age in which it was written, ibid.

Hebrew.---Cyprian, like Tertullian, mentions proper names drawn from the sacred Bible; since these are the same and are almost never accompanied by an interpretation, we omit them altogether.

African terms, Greek and Latin.---In Cyprian one finds many proper names of African places whose Greek or Latin form indicates an Arabic origin, as follows.---Abbir Germaniciana, III, 1061, 1089. Adrumetum, 710, 1087. Aggyva, 1197. Amedera, 1091. Assuras, 1070. Asturica, 1021. Ausafa, 1097. Ausvaga, 1095. Badi, 1061. Bagai, ibid. Baruch, 1063. Bitta, 1054. Bulla, 1069. Bussacena, 1069. Cappadocia, 1153. Capso, 1070. Carpi, 1063. Carthage, 728; IV, 232, 257, 299, 301, 325, 334, 430, 468, 470. Castra-Galbae, III, 1058. Cedias, 1060. Chullabi, 1099. Cibaliana, 1095. Cirta, 1058. Cuiculi, 1097. Dionysiana, 1095. Emerita, 1021. The Three Fates, IV, 278. Galatia, 1161. Gazofala, 1071. Gemelli, 1072. Germaniciana, 1061. Girba, 1061. Gor, 1066. Gurgites, 1097. The Hadrumetine colony, 709. Hippo of Diarrhytus, 1070. Hippo Regius, 1061. The Granaries of Caelia, 1070. Iconium, 1161, 1170. Lamasba, 1071. Lambaesis, 1058. Lares, 1062. Whence Latium was named, IV, 567. Legio, III, 1021. Greater Leptis, 1073. Luperciana, 1067. Macomades, 1062. Mactaris, 1066. Marazana, 1067. Marcelliana, 1070. Mascula, 1071. Mauretania, 1048. Membresa, 1069. Merrha, IV, 650. Midila, III, 1067. Mileum, 1061. Misgerpa, 1053. Neapolis, 1074. Nova, 1069. Numidia, 711, 1052, 359. Obba, III, 1067. Octavum, 1071. Oea, 1072. Oetei, IV, 567. Rucuma, III, 1067. Rutili, IV, 332. Sabrata, III, 1073. Samaria, 1114, 1143. Sicer, 1064. Sicilibba, 1066. Siguenses, IV, 424. Sufes, III, 1062. Sufetula, ibid. Telepte, 1069. Thabracca, 1063. Thambei, 1072. Thamugade, [Col. 0648] 1056. Tharassa, 1069. Thasvalte, 1065. Theveste, 1064. Theni, 1061. Thibari, 1066. Thubuni, 1056. Thucca, 1068. Timisa, ibid. The Three Fates, IV, 278. Tuburbu, III, 1062. Tuchabori, 1061. Ululae, 1068. Uthina, 1063. Utica, 1066. Vago, 1064. Victoriana, 1068. Caesar’s Village, 1062. Zama, 1068.

Cyprianic Latinity.---“An abortion hastening toward parricide,” III, 720. *Abstentus*, and *abstinere aliquem*: their meaning in Cyprian’s mind, 808, 810, 993; IV, 330, 531. What “the Lord’s summons” means, 280, 596. Criminal aggravations, III, 701. An adulterous chair, 994. What “adulteries of colours” are, IV, 455. *Agon* (“contest”) for battle, from Greek, 261, 247, 429; III, 765. “Hearers,” otherwise catechumens, IV, 259, 287. “To inaugurate peace,” 320. What forensic calumny is, 616. The new name of Christians, 693. “Do you not consider Corban?”: a Hebrew expression from the Gospel, 612. “To belch up a carousal with indigestion,” 391. “To speak with one’s fingers,” 785. “He purchases with filth,” 216. A tale of Greek lust, 782. Eternal famine, 363. Foliage-roofed dwellings, 196. “To drink a jewel,” an expression of Virgil, 218 note. The winter of persecution, III, 1163. The blow of the contest, IV, 429. Delicate ostentation, 590. Whence the Janiculum was named, 568. “Those who labour,” that is, the poor, 327, 363. What lay communion is, III, 1049. Who the *lapsi* (“fallen”) are in Cyprian, IV, 258, 278, 312, 333, 345; III, 767, 794, 1158. Whence Latium was named, IV, 567. What certificates (*libelli*) are, 259, 260, 265, 310, 671. Who the *libellatici* are, III, 763, 767, 792; IV, 310, 487, 671. Native features, 454. Contentions about colours, 783. Saturn taught the stamping of letters, 367. “A male being broken into a female,” 211. *Nabla*, a musical instrument, 782. “The breeding-ground of error,” III, 1060. To be choked, 779. Wandering sheep, 707. Cyprian called pope, IV, 224, 268, 303, 307.---Parricidal words, III, 799. “God’s plastic work,” for God’s creature, IV, 454. Cut-off rotten shoots, 477. Sanctity, 278. Whence the name serpent comes, 495. The devil’s antimony, 612. Roofs for enclosures, 799. The course of salvation, 392. What the course of life is, 442. The course of discipline, 288. “The unhappy rich man keeps watch upon his feather-bed,” 218.

COMMODIANUS OF GAZA, African poet, of uncertain date.---“Commodian wrote in a plain style, as though in verse,” says Gennadius, V, 195. In composing verse he observes neither rules nor metres, 196. He employs throughout unusual words in Latin, ibid. “His style,” says Dupin, “is harsh, his words barbarous,” 197.

Commodian’s Latinity.---“Amen blazes,” that is, “the Word of God blazes,” V, 234 note. Made *biothanati* (“self-slain”), 212 note. Isaiah, speaker of heavenly things, 246. *Cottidie* (“daily”), 241. To blame, 207. “May he live on,” 212 note. A belly made wild by luxury, 247. *Ficulna* for *ficulnea* (“fig-tree”), 243. “Your ignorance deceives you,” 206. “Before,” 236. *Inararem* for *enarrem* (“I should recount”), 254. Poor in spirit, 204. “Look upon,” 224, 230. A monster-devouring nature, 211. *Oblivitos* for *oblitos* (“having forgotten”), 222. Abel, offerer, 230. *Periculones* for *periculosi* (“dangerous”), 210. Present stars, 207. What *saraballum* is, 207 note. *Satellem* for *satellitem* (“attendant”), 242. What the neuter *solox* is, 236. To thunder, 205. A hymn-making choir, 247.

ARNOBIUS, African rhetorician.---His most flourishing diction triumphs everywhere, V, 252. Arnobius’s eloquence is outstanding, ibid. His answers to those who accused Christians of speaking a barbarous language, 797 ff.

Words and expressions peculiar to Arnobius.---To squander in gluttony, V, 1221. “From himself,” 850. To take pleasure, 1163. To neigh toward, 1029, 1127. *Adorare* for “to address,” 759. To grow sick, 1138. Flattering humility, 744, 871. An ethereal covering, 1169. “To perform its own nature”: what this means, 1247. Amorous wantonnesses, 1207. In a twofold manner, 1152. The cackling of geese, 1204. To burn with artists’ devices, 1191. The height of perfection, 889. The crux of a question, 938. Untamed silver, 1195. An arched little chair, 847. What it means “to close one’s hearing,” 1144. Maturity, 742, 931. Who the *babecali* youths are, 1044 note. What pomegranate blossoms are, 1106. *Betacei*, beet-stalks, 1021. *Busticeta*, a kind of country tomb, 620, 770. *Calamistrum*, the heated iron by which hair is curled, 877. What a *calantica* is, 846. What Canacheni are, 1210 note. Who the Cilunculi gods are, 956. To gape around, 1140. Enmeshed around, 1249. What *catillamina* are, ibid. *Calumeum*, 1250. A stripping of spoils, ibid. *Conditio*, that is, creation, 880. Little chambers, ibid. “To speak with peace and pardon,” 827. To impose a condition, 734. *Defanata*, that is, profaned, 1077. A delight, 1058. “Scoured from files.” Hence a file is called *scobina*, because by rubbing it produces filings (*scobs*), 1194 note. The fastenings of heaven, 923. Days for notebooks, 1075. Diversity, 834, 1152. What *dolare* (“to hew”) means, 1142. *Durus* (“rough”) for hairy, 1134 note. Who is speechless, 1155. Eminence of designation, 1281. To deprive of office, 1260. Various kinds of sausage, 1248. *Fellitare* for *fallere* (“to deceive”), 871. What a millet wick is, 842. Fading pleasure, 1044. Feminine softness, 1264. Fiery little fragments, for stars, 901. *Furfuracula* or *perforacula* (“gimlet”), a borer, 1194. What *furunculus* and *fervunculus* are, 826. Prolific mothers, 968. What astrological calculation is, 923. *Genitur* for *gignitur* (“is begotten”), 1042. The cackling of geese, 1204. Who a *grollator* is, 868. *Gratilla*, 1250. *Grosfus*, [Col. 0649] or *Grosphus*, that is, a spear-point, 1194. *Hirae*, 1250. *Hirciae*, 1248. The Hyperborean regions, 1171. Little livers, 1024. *Imitus* and *intusque*, 1102 note. Bands of supplication, 1128. Little contrivances of fictions, 1088. To rave, for to prophesy, 718. *Insensilia* for *insensibilia* (“insensible things”), 1196. To invite with incense, 770, 781. The proper rites of marriage, 723. Who the Labeones gods are, 956. What a little cloak is, 838. *Laura*: thus Greeks call lanes or districts, 998. To be smooth, for beardless, 1181. What *lienosus* (“spleenish”) is, 1270. *Longavi* appears to mean the rectum, 1248 note. A conspicuous body, 1124. *Mactatis* for *aptatis* (“prepared”), 770. *Mactatas*, 856. “Be thou made greater by this wine which I offer,” the formula whereby a libation of wine was made to Jupiter, 1035 note, 1260. The moisture of the earth, 1155. What a *mastruca* is, 846 note. *Miracula* for shameful monstrosities, 1134. The badges of miseries, 1138. What a *mitra* is, 846. *Momen* for *momentum* (“moment”), 853. Bursting nostrils, 956, 1181. What *offae* are, 1249. To heap up, 1133, 1225. Caul, 1249. What *pellacia* is, 1225. Pendulous objects, 1167. Little cloths, 1104. Smeared with dung, 1128. A broad-brimmed hat, 1188. A little ham, 1189. What “to make plain” means, 902. What *polimina* are, 1249. Who the *praetextati* are, 1144. What is meant by *proles* (“offspring”), 1128. A shameful crime, 1135. What it means “to add fish-sauce to fish-sauce,” 1139. A puncture or stitch, 1106. A pretty little boy, 1146. *Querqueras*, 780. Those called *ravi*, whose colour lies midway between yellow and blue-grey, 958. Reciprocal things, 754. A hangnail, 786. To uncover, 1135. To plane, 1143. Rustic, 1059. Clotted blood, 1106. *Saccati*, extremely obscene serious plays, 967. What a female sambuca-player is, 882 note. Pretty, 1146. A small weight, 1210. What a little axe is, 838. *Secus* for *sexus* (“sex”), 1108, 1134. Little seals, 1187. The festival of little images, ibid. note. Significance, 1009. A funeral feast, 1248. *Sympuvium*, 1065. Solifugae, 844, 1237. A solecism, 797. To presume hope, 916. What a spiritual tract is, 954. To stand on elevated places, 1233. Stentorian cries, 932. To be received with dung, 1239. What *stribiligo* is, 798. A slender little boy, 1134. Oral prostitution, 883. Supplemental praises, 1145. To enter secretly, 1190. What an undershirt is, 838. To provide offspring, 947. Torches, 1249. The regular course of duties, 836. A little weaving-girl, 1110. What *tinnire* means, 1033. A *tippula*, a kind of tiny creature walking upon water, 904. Three-threaded tunics, woven with triple thread, 965. What *tuceta* are, 881 note. Wet, 962. Moisture, 732. Urban subtlety, 1145. Use, 1263. Water-skins and skins, 799. A winnowing-fan, 847. A vaporous garment, 1205. A shape-shifter, 1146. A small one-hilled eminence, 890. A covering garment, 845. Substitution by a deputy, 1181. A rod-bearing virgin, 1240. Vitiligo, 776. LACTANTIUS, Christian rhetorician.---How great his eloquence was in expression, VI, 58. He held the foremost rank in letters, ibid. Lactantius loves ancient formulae and the elegances of speech, 393. He frequently employs customary verbal formulae, 416. He often uses compound words for simple ones, and simple ones for compounds, VII, 26. Those who devoted themselves to interpreting the languages of brute animals, 917. The Gallic language has very many expressions borrowed from Latin, 618, 639. The name of the Franks is older than the time of either Valentinian, VI, 767. Hermes Trismegistus is said to have invented letters and delivered them to the Egyptians, 138. What the definition of the human voice is, VII, 62, 63.

Hebrew and languages related to it.---Abraham is first called *Heber*, that is, “across” or “beyond,” VI, 328. Ammon is said to be named from Ham, who first possessed Egypt, 327. Apis, with the head of a bull, is worshipped in Egypt as a god, the same as Serapis, 235, 472. Belus: how ancient his altars at Edessa are, 229. Canaan, the ancient name of Arabia, 327 note. Chemia, Egypt’s old name according to Plutarch; in the prophets it is called the land of Ham, because the sons of Ham inhabited that region, ibid. Cirta, an African city later called Constantina, VII, 555, 556. Daniel the prophet, VI, 480. David, king and prophet, 468. Hebrews are so called from Heber, meaning “across” or “beyond,” Greek πέρα (*pera*), 328, 473 note. According to others, Hebrews were so named because they descended from Heber, Noah’s great-grandson, 473 note; but other peoples descended from the same Heber are nowhere called Hebrews, because, having abandoned the Hebrew tongue, they imitated the speech of the peoples among whom they lived, 328 note. When the Hebrews lost their name, 967. Emmanuel: what is signified by this name, 479. Ibis, the name of a bird which the Egyptians regard as a goddess, 786. Jacob, VII, 494. Japheth, VI, 312. Jesus is called in Latin *salutaris*, “saving” or “Saviour,” 479. John the apostle, 440; John the Baptist, VII, 628. Whether Josephus is the same as Serapis, VI, 235. Joshua, 459, 956. Jews, so called from Judah, from whom they were born, 473. Mnevis, a bull worshipped by the Egyptians, 621. Moses, leader of the Hebrews, 472. Whether Moloch is the same as [Col. 0650] Saturn, 232 note. Whence the Sabaeans originated, 971. Whence Sabbath was named, 782, 1006 note. Whence the Egyptian Saites were named. Solomon, king, 468, 486, 487, 974, 976. Saint Susanna, a Hebrew name, VII, 320. Whether Tubal-cain is the same as Vulcan, VI, 213 note. Zechariah, last of the prophets, 460.

Greek etymologies.---Greek terms are often written in Latin letters among the Fathers, VII, 687. Lactantius often uses Hellenisms, VI, 142. Αἰγίοχος (*Aigiochos*), an epithet of Jupiter, 240. The Aeolians change Δ into Ζ, VII, 408. The oesophagus is called the gullet, 40. Ἀγάλματα (*agalmata*) and ἀνδριάντες (*andriantes*); how ἀγαλματοποιὸν (“maker of cult-images”) differs from ἀνδριαντοποιὸν (“maker of statues”), 550, 551. Who are called Ἀγρονόμοι (*Agronomoi*) among the Greeks, 400. Why Jupiter was called Ἀκραῖος (*Akraios*), VI, 501. Amalthea: the goat, 240; the Sibyl, 143; the nymph, 240. What Ἀναβολεύς (*Anaboleus*) is among the Greeks, VII, 478. Why man is called Ἄνθρωπος (*anthrōpos*), VI, 257. Ἀγυιεύς (*Agyieus*) and Ἀγυιάτης (*Agyiatēs*), epithets of Apollo, 498. *Anastasis*, that is, resurrection, 806. Whence the name Areopagites derives, VII, 162. The Argo, ship of the Argonauts, VI, 130. Whence the name Athens derives, 195. What atoms are, 401, 949. Whence Bacchae or Bacchants are so called, 163 note. What a canon is, VII, 399, 771. *Cataclysmus*, that is, flood, VI, 313. Who Catamites are, 169. Who Chiliasts are and whence they are named, 781, 1018. What chlamydes are, VII, 362. *Chrestus*, a Roman name commonly used for Christ, VI, 961. Who the Corybantes were, 187. What *daemon* meant among the ancients, 151, 534. Whence Δαιμονιάρχης (*daimoniarchēs*, ruler of demons) derives, 331. Δεοσάρης or Δευσάρης (*Deosarēs* or *Deusarēs*), the name by which Bacchus was called among the Arabs, VII, 494. Why the Devil is so called, VI, 924; why he is called the adversary, VII, 191, 471, 600. Deacons simply called ministers, 503, 695. Who Dicaearchus was, VI, 404. Diespiter, an epithet of Jupiter, 190. The Eleusinian mysteries, 237. Ἑρμόπολις (*Hermopolis*), a city of Egypt, 139. What office the Galatarchs held, VII, 537. Who Gnostics are, VI, 542. Helicon, a mountain dedicated to the Muses, 132. Hermaphroditus: his origin, 207. Who Hermes Trismegistus was, 138. What idolothyta are, 253, 363. Who Καλωκρέτης (*Kalōkretēs*) is, VII, 541. Κέλευσις (*keleusis*) for command, 646, 703. Κέλευσμα (*keleusma*) is not of the same kind as κελεύσματα (*keleusmata*), 637. Κλιμακίδαι (*Klimakidai*), the name of certain women, 482. Why the Greeks call the world Κόσμος (*kosmos*), VI, 122. Κρίσσων or Κρίττων (*Krissōn* or *Krittōn*), for a despiser, VII, 458. Why Saturn is called Κρόνος (*Kronos*), VI, 186. Κυνίαι (*kyniai*), helmets of dogskin, VII, 823. What Κωρίον (*kōrion*) is, 513, 525. Whence the name lethargy comes, VI, 774. Whence the river Lethe is so called, 804, 806. Λόγος (*Logos*), the name of the divine Word, 469. Λυκείαι (*lykeiai*), helmets of wolfskin, 823. What Μετανοία (*metanoia*) is, 723. Who the Peripatetics are, 364, 367, 370, 688. What Περιτόναιος (*peritonaeos*) is, VII, 59. The ambiguous meaning of Φῶς (*phōs*), VI, 639. What Phrygian speeches are, 120. Plato called Moses speaking Attic Greek, 955. Πλούτων (*Ploutōn*) is the same as Dis, 900. Σκαιὸς (*skaios*), foolish or stupid, 829; τὰ σκαιά (*ta skaia*), trifles and nonsense, ibid. What a σχοῖνος (*schoinos*) is, 969. Στήλη (*stēlē*) for column or statue, VII, 511. Whence the Stoics are so named, VI, 807. What *synthema* is, 414, 415. Whence the word Θεωρία (*theōria*) derives, 1004. Why the letter Υ is called Pythagorean, 641. *Zabulus* for devil, 218. That expression frequently found in ancient books, VI, 323. *Zacones* for deacons, 323, 702. *Zeta* for *diaeta* (“residence”), 408, 702. Why Ζεύς (*Zeus*) is the name of Jupiter, 169.

NAZARIUS, Roman rhetorician. In the Panegyric of Constantine the Great: “the covered things of minds” was used substantivally, like “the bitter things of cares,” “the hidden things of lands,” and, below, “the desired things of vows,” VIII, 583. *Disseparata* for *disparata*, 584. “To aspire to praises,” a very unusual mode of speech, 585. *Solitario modo* for *solummodo* (“only”), a word of the later age, 605.

ANONYMOUS, in the Panegyric of Maximian and Constantine: *velis nolis* (“whether you will or not”), used flatteringly, VIII, 610. *Ut res est* (“as the matter stands”), a formula current in this age, 616.

EUMENIUS, superintendent of the schools of Autun, in the Panegyric to Constantine, A.D. 310. “Concerning the memory of his father”: among writers of this period the preposition *de* is almost used in place of *propter* (“because of”), as in Tertullian, Cyprian, etc., VIII, 635 note. “Forgive the expression”: a remarkable passage, if any is full of artistry, 937. “When he conquers,” used flatteringly, ibid. *Nimium quantum*, a Ciceronian expression, 645. *Caluit*, that is, the mind exulted with joy, 649. *Remisisti*, a frequent mode of speech among writers of that age, ibid. *Confinis forte* for *confiniis* or *confinium*, 652.

MARIUS VICTORINUS, African rhetorician, A.D. 362.---His books against Arius are written in dialectical fashion and, according to Jerome, are very obscure, VIII, 997. The Greek terms λόγος (*logos*), ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*, “of the same substance”), and νοῦς (*nous*, “mind”) are used very frequently, 1056 ff.; as likewise the following terms, scarcely understood by ordinary people: substance, form, image, cause, accident, generation, passion, motion, etc., as will be apparent throughout to the reader.

HILARY (Saint), bishop of Poitiers.---The obscurity of Hilary’s style, IX, 26. Jerome, in Letter 4 to Rusticus, says of Hilary that he is at times involved in long periods and far removed from the reading of simpler persons; this the same doctor seems to attribute to the Gallic temperament, ibid.; nevertheless he calls Hilary “the trumpet of Latin speech against the Arians,” ibid. In Hilary, though rarely, grammatical rules are sometimes neglected, ibid. Latin words were not yet sufficiently suited to the matters he treated, ibid. The Latin language is narrower and less copious than Greek, 26, 27. Gregory Nazianzen’s opinion on this subject, 27. Hilary himself confesses that he lacks not thought but words, and elsewhere that in divine matters the signification of words is narrower than understanding, ibid. Men very often contend with one another because they do not know the force of each word, ibid. How Auxentius the Arian, Hilary’s adversary, played with words by which he might deceive even the elect, X, 614, 615. The Roman language is placed between Hebrew and Greek, IX, 241. The Gospel is proclaimed chiefly in these three languages, ibid. Speech touches certain meanings which it does not explain, 1001. Speech is merely a sound when it is heard, neither before nor after, X, 61. It is the utterance of matters and the expression of thoughts, ibid. According to Hilary, *imago*, *forma*, *vultus*, and *facies* do not differ in a certain sense, IX, 486. He was the first to write Latin hymns, 26. The proper meanings of words must be known, 282.

Hebrew language.---The Hebrew language is ambiguous, IX, 263. Hebrew speech consists of twenty-two letters, 262. Blessed Paul used the Hebrew text of Scripture among the Hebrews, 264. How the Hebrew text was compared with the version of the Seventy interpreters after Christ’s resurrection, 263 note. Abimelech, that is, “the rule of my brother,” X, 79. Amorite, that is, “embittered,” 534. Babylon, “confusion,” 779. Barabbas, a Syriac word interpreted “son of the father,” 1073. Bethsaida, that is, “house of hunters,” 742. Canaan, “movement,” 763. What Cherubim and Seraphim are, 718. What Edom means, 783 note. What Gilead signifies, 388. Mount Hermon: “anathema,” 748. Hosanna: “redemption of the house of David,” 1036. Jacob, that is, “supplanter,” 336. Jerusalem, “city of peace,” 875. Jesus, “saving,” 439, 572, 638. Israel, “seeing God,” 298. How the Jews are now submerged and divided in languages, 352. Latin does not always express the precise force of either a Hebrew or Greek word, 352. What Manasseh means, 388. Moses, X, 27; he composed the Old Testament in writing, 56. Og, “a wall” or “rampart,” IX, 762. Selmon, “peace,” 452. Sehon, “fruitless tree,” 762. Zion, in Latin, “observation,” 489, 681.

Greek terms and expressions.---*Allegoroumena* (“allegorical matters”), IX, 506, 761, 877. What *anomoeousion* and *homoiousion* are, X, 591. *Anquira* for Ancyra: in Hilary *ci* is changed to *qui*, X, 677; *Quimatius* for *cimatius*, 674. *Homoousios*, a term invented by Greeks and adopted by Latins, 535, 600, 711. Λίαν (*lian*), that is, exceedingly, very much, IX, 812. Solomon’s *Paroemiae*, not *Prooemia*, for Proverbs, 704 note. Greek usage always employs pronouns in an honourable and necessary manner, X, 411. The book of Psalms among the Greeks corrected from the Hebrew, IX, 552. The version of the Seventy interpreters is preferred to the Latin, 532, 615; concerning that version, 262; Saint John Chrysostom esteems it most highly, 264 note. Σχοινίον (*schoinion*) for a certain distance of a journey, IX, 798. *Theoteta*, that is, divinity, IX, 1058. A word-for-word translation of Greek speech is obscure, 532. Τρίβος (*tribos*), that is, a path, 586, 798. What *usia* (*ousia*, “substance”) is, X, 98, 100, 567, 703, 711.

### Hilary’s Latin

Hilary, as is his custom, uses an abstract noun in place of a concrete one; for example, *authority* for *author*, X, 506; *dwelling* for *dweller*, IX, 935; *the nativity of God* for *the Son of God*, X, 312. He likewise uses the case of a substantive noun in place of an adjective: “the Lord is of eternity,” for “eternal,” IX, 460; “life of eternity,” 486; “nativity of divinity,” X, 404; “humility of will,” 67. At times he reverses the natural order of nouns, as “will of creation,” for “creation of will,” X, 170; “the origin of his nature,” for “the nature of origin,” 210. *Absolvere* for *solvere* (“to loose”), IX, 236, 266. *In absoluto*, adverbially, for “not obscurely,” IX, 995; X, 74, 78, 125. *Adoptatur* (“is adopted”), in place of *assumitur* (“is assumed”), X, 68. “To worship cattle,” IX, 992 note. *Aenigmatum* for *aenigma*, 363. *Anima corporis* (“soul of the body”), X, 383, 387. “Assumptive appellations,” 206. *Calumnia* for that which affords an occasion for quarrelling and contradiction, X, 66, 395. *Coexcitatus* (“roused together”), IX, 637, 386, 398. *Coinnascibilis* (“born together with”), X, 327. *Concaptus est* (“was conceived together”), IX, 690. *Concorporalis* (“of one body”), IX, 366, 393, 499. “Incorporated with Christ,” X, 589. “The configured appearance of truth,” IX, 629. “Innate power,” X, 305. *Corruptivus* (“corruptible”), 145. *Cum* for *quando* (“when”), IX, 245, 475; X, 121. *Curiosus*, that is, “one who has care,” X, 326. *Dehonestas* (“dishonourableness”), 403. *Desum esse* for *desino esse* (“I cease to be”), 401. “Diabolical ingenuity,” 594. *Dominicum* for a basilica, 564. *Donec* with *cum*, IX, 731. “Bodily efficacies,” X, 169. “Mary was evangelized by an angel,” IX, 849. The preposition *ex* signifies a prior state, from which a transition to another has occurred (in Hilary); for example, “man from God,” IX, 282, 669; “dying from immortality,” that is, although he was immortal, 35; “he spoke from being a persecutor of the Church,” 125. *Fastigium* for pride, IX, 593. *Floriet* for *florebit* (“will flourish”), 744. *Forma* (“form”) is used in contrast with nature and substance [Col. 0653], X, 273. What *frequentare* means, 306. *Genus* for nature, 44. “General [soul]” for universal, IX, 321. *Habebat gigni*, that is, “he was to be begotten,” X, 123. The “heresy of weakness”: thus Arianism is called, and why, 376. *Immoderata* for immense, 29. *Inconsummatum* (“uncompleted”), 267. “Incontinent in the formation of a body,” X, 82. “To accomplish the strength of a journey,” IX, 1006. *Lucificat* (“makes luminous”), 590. *Magis non* for *magis quam* (“rather than”), 489. *Magis promptior* (“more ready”), X, 283. Which sea is called internal and external, IX, 417 note. “Mighty in the world,” IX, 710, 711 note. “The nature of being born is nativity,” X, 168. “The nature of nativity,” that is, the nature of that from which the nature is born, 281. “The nativity of the human race” for human nature, IX, 421. “The nature of God subsists into the nature of God,” that is, the Son was born from the Father, IX, 213. A doubled negation nevertheless retaining negative force, X, 238, 341. Nests are places of rest, 957. What a “natural name” is, X, 207. *Notescitur* (“becomes known”), IX, 467. *Obtunsio*, the dullness of an unbelieving heart, X, 146. *Occupare intelligentiae opinione*, for “to comprehend,” 338. *Oporteant* (“they ought”), IX, 247, 793. *Oportuissent* (“they ought to have”), X, 51. “Opinion of efficacies,” that is, concerning created things, 468. *Partitudo* for *partus* (“birth”), 494. *Paupertavit se* (“he made himself poor”), IX, 487. *Per hoc*, *per id*, in the sense of “consequently,” X, 400, 401. A “perishable treasure,” that is, one that can perish, IX, 943. *Poeniterent* (“they might repent”), 276, 285. *Poenituissent* (“they had repented”), 525. *Potius non*, 390, 854. *Praeceptum* for *praeconceptum*, X, 417. “There is battle to the devil,” that is, the devil is sent, IX, 682. *Religiones* for religious acts, 614, 734. What “God rises again” means, X, 382. *Rheuma*, 581. “Roman language,” that is, Latin, IX, 282. *Sacramentum* for nature, X, 394; for property, 399; for figure, IX, 1042. “Forensic disputes of scholastic matter,” X, 47. *Secundum* in the sense of “in the manner of,” IX, 465, 663, 820. *Sententiare* (“to pronounce judgment”), X, 666. What “to follow one’s own nature” means, 155. The force of the words “solitary” and “alone,” X, 111. *Spania* for *Hispania*, 642. “Suppurating impiety,” 562. “The common *theoteta* of Father and Son,” that is, deity, IX, 1058. “To pass by one in need,” that is, to deny him help, 674. *Unimores*, 447, 449. *Vinculati* (“bound”), 617. *Vincere esse*, X, 238.

### St Zeno, Bishop of Verona, about 384

Panvinio, in his *Antiquities of Verona*, says that the phraseology of St Zeno’s sermons has a certain Greek and foreign flavour, XI, 146. On the other hand, a Greek author, just as Zeno, cannot speak and write pure Latin, ibid. He falls short of purity in Latin expression in no respect, whether one considers individual words or their arrangement and syntax, ibid. Casaubon and others pronounce Zeno most elegant, 147. Basil Faber, a learned man and highly skilled in Latin, did not hesitate frequently to cite Zeno in his *Treasury of Learning*. In St Zeno’s treatises are found many expressions and numerous words of the African Apuleius, as also of Tertullian and Cyprian, ibid. He is conjectured himself to have been of African origin, ibid.

With respect to Hebrew, Zeno is utterly deficient.

#### Greek terms

*Agapes*: what they are, 566 note. *Autochthones* (“native-born”) and antipodes, XI, 416 note 6. *Apophoreta*: gifts distributed at banquets; what they are, 485 note. *Bromosus*, from βρόμος, “a roar,” 364. *Cata Joannem*, *cata Lucam*: a Greek expression for “according to John,” “according to Luke,” 405, 436. *Cataclysmus*, that is, “flood,” 315. *Hemithei*, that is, demigods, 436 note. *Neophyti*: who they are, 370 note 26. A stater, or shekel, consists of four sixes, 429. *Symbolum*: what it is, 475 note.

What *desiderata* means among the Fathers, 478 note. *Elogium* is used in a bad as well as a good sense, 459 note; “a eulogy of condemnation,” ibid. What it is “to make an *exagium*,” 498. *Fabula* for history, 516 note. “A battle famed in report,” 440 note. *Flagitat* for “defames,” 277 note. *Furtum* for adultery, 297. *Impiata* for polluted, 314. What “the law’s right” and “divine right” mean in Zeno, 420 note. *Nundinari* for *diffarcari*, 465. “Publican faith,” 265. “Publican women,” 368. “The Father wholly reciprocated himself into the Son,” 392. *Symbolum* is a consecrated word designating the formula of Catholic faith, 475 note. *Teneritudo*, 515. *Tristifudo*, 456. *Turbulentare*, 312. *Vel* for *et* (“and”), 318. *Vians*, 322.

### Optatus, Bishop of Milevis

Optatus uses words and expressions most suited for conveying what he wishes to express, XI, 766. He is magnificent, forceful, and compact, but less polished and refined, ibid.

#### Hebrew

*Aelamites*: that is, “choirs of camps,” 998 note. *Asmodaeus*, the name of a demon, 991. How *Israel* should be interpreted, 985 note. *Mitra*, a Syrian word, means “diadem” in Greek and “fillet” in Latin, 1072 note. *Tharsis* means “sea,” 1001 note.

#### Greek

Ἀτέλεστα, Wisdom III.16: what it means, [Col. 0654] 1040 note. *Cataclysmus* for flood, 1046. *Catholicum*: the etymology and meaning of this word, 942 note. ΙΧΘΥΣ: what it means, 991 note. Ecclesiastical metropolises, 827. Presbyters: who they are, 765. *Schisma*: what it is, 904 note.

#### Latin

Water for baptism, 990, 993; “to move” or “make water,” for baptize, ibid. *Cai sci, caia scia*: “you are still a pagan,” masculine or feminine; in Africa *caio scio* was said for “this man” or “that man,” 1024 note. Why the Circumcellions were so called, 1007 note. Collations in a religious case: what they are, 1456. What it means “to gather the people,” 954. “Thanks be to God,” a customary formula of peace among Christians, 915. *Concilium*, a word consecrated to designate assemblies of bishops and Christians for the sake of faith, 1036. What *dispungere* means, 1006 note 66. What an *erraticus* is, 953. *Formatae*, a substantive used for letters, 849. “Living homicide”: what it is, 976, 977. *Inventum* for *invectum*, 939. “You have cut the throats of names,” meaning, “you have stripped away dignity,” 979. Memorials of saints: what they are, 851. *Metatores*: who they are, 1011. *Mitella* or *mitra*: what it is, 973 note. What *pallae* were among the ancients, 1077 note. *Quanto quod*, 1000. “His whole self,” 1038.

### Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli

The twelfth volume of the *Patrology Course* deals extensively with the various manuscripts of the Gospels. Although collating these manuscripts does not properly belong to this index, we shall nevertheless indicate the principal labours upon which so many and such distinguished men expended themselves in publishing, correcting, and annotating manuscripts of the four Gospels. Philippus Garbelli’s letter to Blanchini concerning the Brescian manuscript, XII, 11. The corrector of this manuscript is shown to have been scantily furnished with Latin, 20. The Latin versions of this prologue of St John are discussed: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος, “In the beginning was the Word,” where λόγος is rendered now *sermo* (“discourse”), now *ratio* (“reason”), now *verbum* (“word”), 46 ff. Dissertation of Jean Martianay on the Italian version of the Gospel according to Matthew, and on the Corbie and Saint-Germain manuscripts, 59 ff. Letter of Ruggieri, canon of the Eusebian cathedral of Novara, to Blanchini of Verona, 69. Blanchini of Verona’s judgment concerning the Vercelli manuscript, 73 ff. Blanchini’s letter to Musellus, canon of the Church of Verona, 123. The Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia manuscripts are given in four columns, with Blanchini’s notes and variants of the Saint-Germain manuscript, 142. Blanchini’s variant readings in the appendix, 838. The more notable readings of the Brescia manuscript are elucidated in Blanchini’s second letter, 851 ff. Elsewhere Blanchini describes the Graeco-Latin manuscript of the Gospels and Acts preserved in the Cambridge library, 865. Readings in which the fourfold Gospel-book agrees with ten Greek manuscripts preserved at Rome, 865. Readings in which the Gospel-book manuscript of Verona agrees with the Syriac, Arabic, Persian, and Ethiopic versions, 902. Old-Testament testimonies cited in the four Gospels, 918.

### Julius Firmicus Maternus

Two writings are attributed to him; but the reprehensible Latin of the former does not prove it to be by the same author, whereas the latter shines in a much purer style, XII, 975. Hence it is necessary to admit two Firmici, ibid. How his Latin differs from that of Apuleius and Tertullian, 976.

#### Hebrew and related languages

Anubis the dog is worshipped as a god by the Egyptians, XII, 985. Isis, goddess of the Egyptians, 984. Isiac mysteries, 1031. *[Uncertain word]* means “to plough,” from which Schelling derives the name of Ceres, 1021 note. Mithra, the Persian name of the sun, is worshipped, 1025. Mithraic mysteries, 1025, 1026, 1038. Nephtho, goddess of Egypt, 984. Osiris is worshipped as a god among the Egyptians, 984. Sabazius, an epithet of Jupiter, according to Bochart derives from the Pehlevi Persian language, from the word *Zabzeba*, interpreted “sun,” 1006 note. According to others, it derives from the Hebrew *Saba*, meaning “to become drunk.” Others finally wish it to arise from the Greek σαβάζειν, “to cry ‘Sabazius.’” Whether the name Serapis derives from Sarah according to Firmicus—for Serapis is identical with Joseph, who was Sarah’s great-grandson, as though from Σάρας ἀπό—or rather from an Egyptian origin, 1012 note. Typhon, an Egyptian god, 984, 985.

#### Greek

According to Firmicus, Apollo is named from ἀπόλλειν, “to destroy,” 1020, 1021. What an *aenobolium* is, 1043 note. *Apothecae Dominicae* (“the Lord’s storehouses”) for granaries, 1018. What a *criobolium* is, 1043 note. What Ἐλιλίκερες δίμορφοι (“curved-horned, two-formed”) denotes, 1030. How Γέγονα μυστικός (“I have become an initiate”) is translated rather badly into Latin by Firmicus, 1022 note. What the Isiac verses Θαῤῥεῖτε, μύσται, etc. (“Take courage, initiates, etc.”) mean, 1032. *Taurobolium*: what it is, 1043 note. Ταῦρος δράκοντος καὶ δράκων ταύρου πατήρ, “the bull, father of the serpent, and the serpent, father of the bull”: the final symbol of Mithraic initiations, and its source, 1038 note. Χαῖρε νύμφιε, χαῖρε νέον φῶς, “Hail, bridegroom; hail, new light”: uttered in Mithraic mysteries, and how these words are to be understood, 1025.

#### Latin

*Carnifex* for the devil, 1040. According to Firmicus, Ceres is called from *serere* (“to sow”), 1020. Diana from *dies* (“day”), because she turns night into day by light, according to the same author, ibid. *Dis, ditis*, from enriching, ibid. *Fabricatio*, *fabricator*, for creation and creator, 981, 983. *Incandidat* for “makes white,” 1043. Luna is named from *lumen* (“light”), 1020. Mavors from *magna vertere* (“to turn great things”) and *mala vertere* (“to turn evils”), [Col. 0655] XII, 1022 note. Minerva from *minuere* (“to diminish”) and *minari* (“to threaten”), ibid. note. Neptune from swimming, with Cicero, ibid. The Penates are named from *penus*, 1016. What *penus* is, ibid. Sol is derived from *solus*, “alone, one,” 1020. Venus is named from loveliness, 1020 note.

### St Philastrius, Bishop of Brescia

There is a heresy that disputes concerning language and languages, because Scripture says, Genesis XI.1, “And one language and languages,” XII, 1217. To investigate this is by no means useless, 1218. The confusion of languages occurred in the year 2700 after the creation of the world, ibid. Before the Babel confusion, men possessed knowledge of many languages, ibid. Through forgetfulness sent by the Lord, they could scarcely learn—not all, nor many, but scarcely a few—languages, ibid. Under the apostles, the Lord restored this knowledge of languages through the Holy Spirit to those believing in him, 1219. One heresy says that the first name of a language proceeded from the Jews; another, from pagans; both are certainly false, 1219. From Adam to Heber—namely, for 2700 years—the name of the language of all human beings was one, and the language was one, ibid. The builders of Babel’s tower and the Aloidae, who piled mountains upon mountains and dared to assault heaven by force, are compared, 1220.

#### Hebrew and related languages

Accaron, a Syrian city situated in the region of the Philistines, from which came the Muscaccaronites, who worshipped the fly-god, 1125 note. *Ochamoth*, a name invented by Basilides or Valentinus to designate the heavenly power from which Jaldabaioth, the maker of the world, arose, 1145 note. How the Hebrew words *Almoni* and *Ploni* are interpreted, 1215 note. The Astarites are called from Astar or Astaroth; the etymology of these names, 1128, 1137 note. Baal, an idol, is not derived from Baal, king of Tyre—for his worship is much older—but from Bel, king of the Assyrians, 1127, 1134 note. Hence its worshippers were called Baalites or Belites, ibid. Balaam, the false prophet, is the same as Baalam according to Fabricius, 1134 note. Barbelo is the same as Achamot, 1145 note. Barchaban, a name invented by Basilides, is a power born from Cavlacav, 1150 note. Beelphegor: see below under Chamos. Beelzebub, “fly-god,” an idol worshipped in Accaron, 1125 note. Belites or Baalites are so named from King Bel, 1134. See below under Greek Βέλος and Latin *bellum*. The Cainians are named after Cain, Adam’s son and a fratricide, 1115. *Cathath* means “to crush,” 1131 note. Cavlacav, the name of a certain power borrowed by Basilides from Isaiah XXVII.10. According to some, it is the same as Jaldabaoth, 1149 note. Chabediel, a barbarous name for an angel invented by Basilides, 1145 note. Chamos, the idol of the Moabites, is called by another name Beelphegor, 1128 note. Dositheus, the name of a Jewish heretic, 1118. Ennon, the name of a man given to the valley in which he lived, whence the Hebrew *Ghi ben Ennon*, “Valley of the son of Ennon.” From this derives the word *Gehenna*, signifying punishment; for in this place criminal men were subjected to punishments. Ennon derives from the verb *nham*, meaning “to groan,” 1130 note. *Haldebargadol* means “on account of a matter of great importance.” *Jao*, according to Basilides, is the word uttered by the Limit when he dared resist the will of his father or mother, Achamoth, 1146 note. *Jaldabaoth* can be interpreted “God of strength”; it is a name invented by Basilides and denotes the maker of the world, 1145 note. See Cavlacav. Japheth derives from *phatuh*, meaning “to enlarge,” 1246 note. Manes, after whom the Manichaeans are named, means “contentious man” in Persian, 1173 note. Mithra is the same as Achamoth, 1145, 1148. Moloch, meaning “king,” is an idol of the Ammonites. Some maintain that it is Saturn, others the sun; but Moloch, like Baal, seems to have been a name common to several gods, 1129 note. Muscaccaronites: see above under Accaron. Nazaraeans were so called because of the hair they grew, 1122. *Panav* means “his face,” namely God’s, 1294 note. The Pharisees, a Jewish sect, derive their name from *paras*, “to divide,” 1119. Ploni and Almoni: how the Hebrew words are interpreted, 1215 note. Prosorael, a barbarous angel-name invented by Basilides, 1145 note. Prunnico is the same as the Achamoth of Valentinus or Basilides, 1145 note. Raglav means “his feet,” namely God’s, 1294 note. Remphan, an Egyptian idol (Amos V.27): how it should be written; it seems to derive from King Remphi, 1129 note. Sabuoth is the same as Jaldabaoth, 1145. Saddoc, a Jewish heretic and disciple of Antigonus of Socho, is called Σάδδουκ by the Greeks and Zendic among the Arabs; from him come the Sadducees, who do not admit the resurrection, 1118 note. Samaritans are so named from King Samarius, 1120. Samson is said to derive from the two words *sames hon*, “sun of strength,” 1122 note. See Greek Ἡρακλῆς. Sethians, Sethites, and Sethoites are heretics who take their name from Seth, Adam’s son, 1116. Thamus, a god mourned and bewailed by Jewish women, is perhaps the same as Thammous, king of the Egyptians, or Adonis, as Diodorus Siculus holds, 1133 note. Tophet: whether it is the name of a place or person, or identical with the Egyptian Photus; in Hebrew it derives from *Toph* and means “drum,” 1120 note. Zendik is the Arabic name for Saddoc, author of the Sadducees, 1118 note.

[Col. 0656]

#### Greek

Ἀβράξας, an occult name invented by Basilides, whose letters produce the number 365, 1144 note. Augustine defines *Aeon* and *Aeons* as fabulous emanations of ages, 1164 note. *Ana*, meaning “according to” or “beside”: this little word is used by Philastrius, 1258. The Apocryphites, a class of heretics who neglected canonical Scriptures and followed Apocrypha, that is, secret writings, 1199. The Artotyrites were called from ἄρτος, “bread,” and τυρός, “cheese,” because they offer bread and cheese, 1186. The Ascodrogytes are named from ἀσκός, “wineskin,” and δρουγγός, “company”; for, in madness, they carry an inflated wineskin about in groups in their churches, 1187 note. Βέλος is called “a missile” from Bel, king of the Assyrians, who first used it, 1134 note. See Latin *bellum*. Biothanati, heretics named from βία, “force, violence,” and θάνατος, “death”: why they are so called, 1198 note. Borborians are named from βόρβορος, “filth,” 1186. Why the Cataphrygians are so named, 1165. Chaos: see below under Σιγή. Encratites, that is, abstainers, 1186. *Gigas* (“giant”) is said to derive from γῆ, “earth,” and γυῖα, “limbs,” properly “feet,” 1224 note. *Haereseon*: Latin writers not infrequently use the Greek plural genitive inflection, 1111 note. Heliognosti: whence they are named, 1123. Ἡρακλῆς, Hercules: said to be named from ἥρας κλέος, “keen glory,” 1122 note. See above under Hebrew, Samson. Chillionites or Chiliasts, in Latin “millenarians”: why they are so called, 1174 note. Ναΐσκος and πάσιον, meaning “tabernacle,” 1120 note. The difference between ὁμοιούσιος and ὁμοούσιος, 1180 note. Ophites, in Latin “serpent-people,” because they worship the serpent, 1113. Passalorynchites, from πάσσαλος, “peg,” and ῥύγχος, “snout”: followers of silence, 1188 note. Patripassian heretics, 1168. Pogonians, a class of stars, from πώγων, “beard,” 1216 note. Proclinians are named from a certain Proclinus, 1170. Valentinus’s Σιγή, “Silence”: what it is and how it differs from the poet’s chaos, 1156 note. Troglodytes are so called from τρώγη or τρώγλη, “hiding-place,” and δύω, “I enter,” 1126 note. Tropites, from τρέπω, “to turn,” 1184.

#### Philastrian Latin

*Alligaturae*: what they are, 1132. Gaudentius used *Suballigaturae*, Sermon 4. *Bellum* is said to derive from Greek βέλος, “missile,” and also from Bel, who first used a weapon, 1134 note. *Beluinus*, 1250; in Gellius and Ambrose. *Capaciter*, that is, “with one perceiving him in mind and sight,” 1185. *Carra* or *carrus*, a kind of Gallic wagon, 1125. *Christianitas*, 1228, 1249. *Circuitores*, Circumcellions who wander through lands and compel those whom they find on the road to be killed by them, 1197. *Clima*, 1248. *Condescensio*, 1208. *Continentia* for the act of restraining oneself, 1167. *Fructuositas*, 1265. *Historiographi*, 1244, 1247, 1259, 1278. *Immensibilis* for immense, 1205. *Incapabilis*, 1296. *Incapacitas*, 1185. *Inconvertibilis*, 1185. *Incorporatio*, 1183. *Indocilitas*, 1231; likewise in Apuleius. *Intellectum* for *intellectu*, 1144. *Intendere* for “to understand,” 1296. *Numeralis*, 1174. *Numerositas*, 1155. *Paganitas*, 1247, 1249, 1278. *Passibilis*, 1204. *Pecudialis*, 1176. *Poenitudo*, 1201, 1251, 1263. *Positio*, 1269. *Putative*, 1139, 1147, 1160. The Puteorites, heretics who worshipped wells, 1130. *Repensatio*, 1216. *Repensio*, 1252. *Scintilla*, a biblical word for soul, 1143. *Sempiternitas*, 1254. *Suggestio*, that is, deceitful insinuation, 1226, 1264. *Sustinentia* for endurance, 1255. *Temporalitas*, 1247, 1259. *Titulatio* for inscription, 1260. *Transgressio* for “prevarication,” 1243. *Umbratiliter*, 1143, 1161, 1267.

### Pope St Damasus

#### Greek

Acrostic verses on the name of Jesus, XIII, 377, 378. *Anathema* and *anathematize*: already the ancient Fathers of the Church used these terms to condemn someone as a heretic, 301, 306, 353, 358. *Archibis* for archive, 110 note. Catacombs, from κατά, “down/against,” and κύμβος, “a hollow recess”: underground places in which Christians buried their dead at Rome, 260, 268, 269, 382 note. *Homoousion* and *Homoeusion*: what they are, 301, 304. *Hypostasis*: what it is, 134, 180. Οὐσία, *usia*: what it is, 135, 293, 351, 333, 358 ff. The *Syclaeum* of Mithras: in what part of Rome it was situated, 188. *Synodus*, Latin *concilium*: even Latin Fathers frequently used this Greek word to denote a council, 120, 134, 135 and passim. *Tropaeum* is written without aspiration, as it apparently is also in Cicero, who said *pulcros*, *triumpos*, and *Cartaginem*, 392 note, 408. XPM and XPI: “Christ” and “of Christ.” *Zabulus* for *diabolus*, 416.

#### Latin

*Acqua* for *aqua*, 418. *Auriscalpium*, French *cure-oreille*, “ear-cleaner,” 209. Acrostic verses on the name of Jesus, 377, 378. A poem whose individual words contain a designation of Christ, 378. *Confessio [fidei]*, “confession [of faith],” for a public declaration: a word consecrated in the Church, 357, 358. *Dejecti* for *delicti*, 395. *Discolor corpus* for *discolor corporis*, 352. An ecclesiastical shorthand writer: who he was, 409 note. What *flagella currere* means, 405. What “the Word of God has been made human” means, 258. *Pasqua*, perhaps for *pascua*, “pastures,” 417. *Quaestiunculae*, 372. *Retentare* for “to detain,” 395. A *silentiarius* was one who stood watch by the curtains when the emperor administered justice or heard envoys, 369 note. “May you be in peace”; “peace be with you”: ancient formulae on the titles or inscriptions of Christian tombs [Col. 0657], 272. The suburban churches: which they were, 142.

### Latinus Pacatus Drepanius, a Gaul of Bordeaux, contemporary and friend of the poet Ausonius

#### Latin

*Atratus*: a black garment was proper to men in mourning, XIII, 501. A *cavea* properly is an enclosure in the middle of a theatre, though it is often used for the whole theatre, 493. *Comens*, perhaps *conans* (“attempting”), 486. *Crotatum*, a wooden or bronze rattle, from Greek κρούειν, “to strike,” 512. A *culeus* was a bag or sack made of wood, hemp, or leather, named from concealing; criminals were shut into it and cast into a river or sea, and this was the punishment of parricides, 516. “Servile eloquence,” that is, flattering in the manner of a slave, 479. *Fluentes* for those overflowing in luxury, 491. The Janiculum is a hill overlooking the Trans-Tiberine district, 487. *Lecticis*: litters were used in the countryside, not in the city, before Cicero’s time, 497 note. *Tensis*: *tensae* or *thensae* were sacred carriages in which images of the gods were conveyed to the Circus games, 497. *Palmatae vestes*, namely triumphal garments, 486 note. “Placated populace”; in other manuscripts, better, “a soothed ulcer,” 480.

### Lucifer, Bishop of Cagliari, about 371

Most errors found in his writings should be attributed to an uncultivated and almost barbarous style rather than to the fault of scribes and copyists, XIII, 697–658. He used Latin translations of Scripture which he did not always cite faithfully, 701. Among Latin versions, that which Augustine called the Italian, Jerome the Vulgate, and Gregory the Great the Old, was pre-eminent, ibid. A theological observation on certain expressions of Lucifer, 710. Pope Silvester entrusted to Lucifer himself, most accomplished in Greek and Latin, the task of translating the sacred Scriptures, 737.

#### Hebrew

*Bariesubam* for *Barjhesus*. Lucifer interprets this word as “prepared,” as though he had read *Bar shuman*, as it occurs in the Syriac version. But Barjhesus is called Elymas in Greek, that is, “seeking,” 978, 979 note. *Jabadias* for Zabadias, 847. *Jambri* for Zambri, 941. *Odias* for King Ozias, 946. *Scariothem* for Iscariothem, with the iota removed. Thus he very frequently corrupts proper names, just as the common people spoke, delighting in cutting them in half. See Arnobius: *striculus* for *histriculus*, *strionem* for *histrionem*, 847 note. *Zmabel* for Ishmael, 847.

#### Greek

*Adoxius*, by antiphrasis, for Eudoxius, the Arian bishop of the province of Germanicia, 830, 1028. Crypts: hollow and hidden places in mountains, 795. Elymas, that is, “seeking,” 979 note. *Heremias difficiles*, “difficult wildernesses,” that is, desert and rugged places, using a Greek expression, 862. Cagliari, over which Lucifer presided, was variously called Καραλις and καρακαλεος in Greek, 737 note. Κατὰ πάντα ὅμοιον, “similar in every respect”: the Semi-Arians used this of the likeness of the Word to his Father, 863 note. The book of Paralipomenon is called the book of things left over by Lucifer, 774. *Schisa*, from Greek σχίζα, “a split piece of wood,” 842. Σοφία Σειράχ, “Wisdom of Sirach,” is the title of Ecclesiasticus in the Septuagint, 866 note.

#### Luciferian Latin

*Adhoc* for *adhuc*, 866. *Apostata factum* for *apostatam*, 782. *Arma induti* for *armis*, after Greek usage, 855. Imperial *comites*: what they were, 990. *Constipare schizas*, for “collect split pieces,” that is, cut wood, 842. *Custodire* for *custodi*: infinitive for imperative, 825. *Deleam* for *delebo*, 810. *Demorare* for *demorari*, 790. Dictators: what they were, 1028. *Dignus anathema* for *anathemate*, 773. *Dura multa* for *multum dura*, after Greek usage, which very frequently employs such adjectives as adverbs, 824 note. *Frendoribus*, that is, furious cries, 854. *Illos* for *illuc*: “do not lead [us] there,” 940. *Inspecta opera tua* is an ablative absolute which Lucifer, following Greek usage, employs for the plural, “your works having been seen.” He often uses this number, both in nominative and accusative cases, 819. *Judicium* for *judicio*, 874. *Justitiae* for *justae*, 823. The Luciferian heretics are named not after our Lucifer but after a certain Lucifer, bishop of Sirmium, 738. *Non est nihil*, in Greek fashion, for “there is not something,” “there is nothing,” 842. *Non* for *nonne*, 833. *Non sumus vertentes*, a Hellenism, for “we do not translate,” 841. *Palam* for *palum*, 769. *Perfrui inanem pulchritudinem*, for “to enjoy empty beauty,” 777. *Quia* for “why,” 871. *Quod* for “what,” 947. *Quosdam noceret* for *quibusdam*, 902. *Speculantes unusquisque*, 769. “The book of things left over,” that is, Paralipomenon, 774. *Tenebra*, singular, for *tenebrae*, 901. *Tinnibunt* for *tinnient*, 810. *Translet* for *transibit*, 832. The curtain by which the emperor’s inner chamber was shut off, 1009, 1014.

### St Ambrose

The brain is the origin of the nerves and of all voluntary motions of the senses; from it flows every cause of the things we have mentioned, XIV, 267. Therefore the human brain is softer than that of other creatures, because it receives all sensations; hence all the nerves carry back everything which the eye has seen, the ear heard, the smell inhaled, the tongue uttered, or the mouth received as flavour [Col. 0658], 268. The faculty of hearing is most excellent, ibid. The ears project outwardly . . . so that, reflected in their cavities without obstruction, sound may enter their inner windings, 268. The enclosure of the teeth makes full vocal expression possible, 269. The tongue is, as it were, the plectrum of the speaker . . . The voice is borne by a kind of rowing of the air and carried through emptiness; and that same force which strikes the air now moves, now gently touches, the hearer’s ear, 269. What is the human mouth but a kind of sanctuary of speech, a fountain of discourse, a hall of words, a storehouse of the will, 270? Arms follow, with the strong muscles of the upper arms; hands powerful for work; and longer fingers fit for grasping. Hence comes a more capable use in working, hence elegance in writing, and that swiftly-writing pen by which the oracles of the divine voice are expressed, ibid. The word first works within; the office of the voice follows, XV, 1577. “For me, nothing differs in the word which does not differ in meaning,” 1568. The manner of speaking is the first function, XVI, 33. Nature itself teaches us in little children that they first practise the sounds of speech in order to learn to speak, ibid. Sound is a kind of exercise and training-ground for the voice, ibid. Bind up your speech lest it run riot or become wanton; let it be more restrained and checked within its banks, 27. Often a person is not unfolded by his own words but entangled, 882. Under the apostles, God bestowed on very many the gift of speaking in different languages, XVII, 254. Why Paul rebukes such persons, ibid.

Hebrew and Related Terms.—Both the Hebrew name and language derive from Abraham, XVII, 415. The Hebrews were so called after Abraham, with a letter altered for euphony, so that they were not called Abraeans but Hebrews, 415. The first language, which had been without a name, when restored to him received its name from him, ibid. There is no reason why it should derive its name from Heber: for Abraham was a Chaldean, yet the Hebrews do not possess the Chaldean language, ibid. Abba, that is, “father,” XVII, 123. Abdemeleck, that is, “taken up by the Lord,” XVI, 767. Abram, after his name was changed, is called Abraham, XIV, 432. Ethiopia, “cast down and lowly,” XV, 281. Agar, that is, “dwelling,” 491. Aggaeus, that is, “feasting,” XVI, 1063. Ain, a letter: “eye” or “spring,” XV, 1424. Aleph, the first letter, that is, “teaching,” 1199. Alleluia denotes praise of God, ibid.; XVI, 223. Amen, that is, “faithfully,” occurs frequently in John, XIV, 1084; XVI, 625. Aminadab, or “father of good pleasure,” XV, 1222. Aseroth, that is, “blessednesses,” XVII, 24. Aser, “riches,” XIV, 685. Asia is said to mean “exalted,” XVII, 24. Asiongaber, “counsels of a man,” 32. Babylon, “confusion,” XIV, 416. Bancjachan, “cultivation,” XVII, 31. Barabbas, that is, “son of the father,” XV, 1820. Bathuel, “wisdom,” or “daughter of God,” XIV, 580. Among the Hebrews, *to bless* is sometimes used for *to curse*, 745. Bersabe, “well of the seventh,” or “of the oath,” XVI, 1210. Beth, a letter, signifies “confession,” XV, 1208. Bethania, that is, “place of obedience,” XVI, 1242. Bethel, that is, “house of God,” XV, 422. Bethleem, that is, “house of bread,” LXVI, 1237. Bethsaba, “daughter of the Sabbath,” “full daughter,” XIV, 908. Caph, a letter: “bent,” XV, 1348. Calatha, that is, “rod,” “dominion,” XVI, 26. Cethura, that is, “fragrant,” XIV, 328. Cham, that is, “heat,” 408, 414. Chanaan, “their disturbance,” 408, 614. Choratah signifies “understanding,” XVI, 1210. Choreb, “the whole heart,” or, as it were, “heart,” ibid. Daleth, a letter: “fear,” or “birth,” XV, 1240. Dan, “judgment,” XIV, 684, 1079. David: the Hebrews call it “exalted”; the Latins interpret it “humbled,” 902. Depheha, “health,” XVII, 20. Dothain, “defection,” XIV, 645. Esom, that is, “earthly and hot,” XV, 1485. Elim, “rams,” XVII, 18. Elmon Deblathaim, “contempt of figs,” 37. Engaddi, “temptation,” XV, 1225. Ennon, “eye of punishments,” 1424. Enoch, “grace of God,” XIV, 282. Enos, that is, “man,” 503. Ephrata, “house of one possessed by fury,” XVI, 1236. Esmona, “haste,” XVII, 29. Ethan, that is, “strength,” 15. Gad is interpreted “temptation,” XIV, 685. Gadgad, “testing,” XVII, 31. Ghimel, a letter: “retribution,” XV, 1223. Gog, “roof”; Magog, “from the roof,” XVII, 952. Gog is a Goth, XVI, 588. Gomorrha, “blindness,” XIV, 394. Halus, that is, “labour,” XVII, 20. He, a letter, signifies “is” or “living,” XV, 1250. Whether Heber gave his own name to the Hebrews, XVII, 415. How the Hebrews were named after Abraham, 415. Some Hebrews used the Syrian language in treatises or offerings, others Hebrew, for greater distinction, 256. How, among the Hebrews, proper names were formed according to a rationale: Isaac from laughter, Jacob from the heel, and likewise Saul from restlessness, 47. Heth, a letter, signifies “terror,” XV, 1294. Hierusalem, “vision of peace,” 790. Icabarim signifies “heap of stones of those passing over,” XVII, 36. Jod, a letter: “confession,” “desolation,” XV, 1329. Isaac: in Latin, “laughter,” XIV, 501. Issachar is called “reward,” 683. Jacob, that is, “heel,” XVII, 47. Japhet, “breadth,” XIV, 414. Jericho: what it signifies, XV, 1717. Jesababel, “outpouring of vanity,” XIV, 585. “Vain and empty redundancy,” XVI, 564. Jethebatha, that is, “goodness,” XVII, 304. Jethro, that is, “superfluous,” [Col. 0659] XIV, 329. Jordan, that is, “descent,” 471. Koph, that is, “conclusion,” or “look,” XV, 1469. Laban, that is, “white,” XIV, 582, 623. Lamed, a letter: “heart,” or “to a servant,” XV, 1360. Lebna, “whitening,” XVII, 26. Levite, “taken in place of me,” or “light to me,” XIV, 345.
