Satan, “adversary,” XVI, 1069; XVII, 878. Scin, a letter, signifies “upon a wound,” XV, 1502. By the name *sicera* the Hebrews meant every intoxicating drink, XIV, 717. Sichima, that is, “shoulder,” 677. Sin, “bush,” XVII, 19. Socoth, “tabernacles,” XV, 1252; XVII, 14. Tau, a letter: “he erred,” or “he completed,” XV, 1511. Thaat, “long-suffering,” or “endurance,” XVII, 28. Thare, “stupor,” Greek *ecstasis* (ἔκστασις), XVII, 28. Theth, a letter, signifies “exclusion,” XV, 1320. Urias is called “my light,” XIV, 907. Vau, a letter: “he is, and no other,” or “and he is,” XV, 1267. Zabulon, “deliverance from nocturnal [things?],” XIV, 582. Zain, a letter, signifies “lead yourself,” or “hither,” XV, 1280. Zara, that is, “rising,” 1601.

Ambrosian Greek.—*Aēr* (Ἀήρ), in Greek name [slightly altered], is called *ver* (“spring”) in Latin, from *ear* (ἔαρ), “the spring season,” XIV, 400, note. What *adoleschēsai* (Ἀδολεσχῆσαι) signifies, XVI, 1159. Who the *Amphiskioi* (Ἀμφίσκιοι) are, XIV, 199. What it is to drink *amystide*, 720. What an *anaboladium* is, 681. Who *anaglypharii* are, 775. Why man is called *anthrōpos* (Ἄνθρωπος), 260. The Anthropomorphite heretics are identical with the Vadians, XVI, 757, note. When the title “antipope” was first heard, 462. What *apophoreta* were, and their various kinds, 336. What Arcturus is, 689, note. Who the *Askioi* (Ἄσκιοι) are, XIX, 199. What the name *basilica* signifies, XVI, 877, note. What the *catadupa* are, XIV, 147. Clindiae, or Clindia, 719, note. What *chromata* signifies, 157. What the *diaconicon* (Διακονικόν) and *skeuophylakion* (σκευοφυλάκιον) are, and what custodians each had, XVI, 101, note. *Dia pantos* (Διὰ παντός) means “at all times” and “through all things,” XV, 1258. What *dioraticon* (Διορατικόν) is, XIV, 480. Some thought that *doxan* (Δόξαν) meant rather “opinion” than “glory,” XVI, 643. The origin of the name *Empirikoi* (Ἐμπειρικοί), XIV, 164. What *entelecheia* (Ἐντελέχεια) signifies, XVI, 1074. What *epithymeticon* (Ἐπιθυμητικόν) is, XIV, 480. Why Epiphany was so named by the Greeks, XVII, 619. What “daily” (*epiousios*, Ἐπιούσιος) bread is, XVI, 452. *Hepou Theō* (Ἕπου Θεῷ), that is, “follow God,” XIV, 421. What *euschēmonos* (Εὐσχήμονος) signifies, XVI, 89. *Idolothytum* was the name of what had been consecrated to idols, XVII, 783. What *kollyra* (Κολλύρα) and *kollyris* (κολλυρίς) are, XVI, 1197, note. A *kosmopolitēs* (Κοσμοπολίτης) is a man, that is, a citizen of the world, 1144, note. What *thymeticon* (Θυμητικόν) signifies, XIV, 480. What the Heptateuch is, XV, 1506. What the *logisticon* (Λογιστικόν) in man is, XVI, 480. Who was the author of the doctrine of metempsychosis, 1331, note. *Monotēs* (Μονότης), that is, singleness, which pertains to person, 658. *Nous* (Νοῦς), that is, mind, 987, 1133. How *homoousion* (Ὁμοούσιον) is understood in various ways, XIV, 552, 562; XVI, 614. What *hormē* (Ὁρμή) is, XVI, 91. What *oros* (Ὄρος) signifies, 915. Why heaven is called *ouranos* (Οὐρανός) by the Greeks, XIV, 236. The etymology of *ousia* (Οὐσία), 614. Greek *palē* (Πάλη) is Latin wrestling, XIV, 994. *Paradisus* in Greek, in Latin “garden,” XVII, 1142. *Parthenikos Logos* (Παρθενικὸς Λόγος), “the Virginal Word,” is said of Christ, XVI, 1066. What *rheuma* is, 218. What *scamma* signifies, 714. What a *skeuophylakion* (Σκευοφυλάκιον) is, XVI, 101, note. Why *stoicheia* (Στοιχεῖα) are so called, as the elements of the world, XIV, 164. The Greek letter T has the numerical value of three hundred; νηʹ, eighteen, 427. *Tautotēs* (Ταυτότης) signifies identity, XVI, 776. Who the Troglodytes are, 845, note. *Hylē* (Ὕλη) means what the Latins call matter, XVI, 912.

Ambrosian Latinity.—*Absolvo*, “I conclude,” XIV, 1019. *Acerbo*, “I exaggerate,” 405. *Acta, -ae*: what it is, 221. *Adipsal*: what it signifies; perhaps a scribal error, 842, note. Who the *agentes in rebus* were, XVI, 996, note. *Ancylae suffragines*, for the joints of elbow or knee, XIV, 253. *Apparitores* were those who attended various magistrates, XVI, 996, note. *Attactu nullo*, “gradually and imperceptibly,” XV, 1273. *Austrigo*, *ustrigo*, for scorching heat, XIV, 173. *Castimonium*, for continence, 424. *Cerva*, “hind,” for “virgin”: the origin of the proverbial expression, XVI, 215, note. *Cognitor*: the various senses of this word, 1015, note. What the *comites consistoriani* were, 994, note. *Conscientia*, for knowledge, XIV, 1131. What *cremium* is, XVI, 1139, note. *Defendi*: “A cause which is not defended and proved is better,” XV, 1828; “Let those seek to be defended who fear being defeated,” ibid. *Defensor*: “Such defenders I seek,” XVI, 1022. To *deflare* something is to pour out, in a sudden rush, what comes into one’s mouth, 1150. Etymologies of the name God, 530, note. What a didrachm was worth, 905. Whether the drachma and the denarius were equal in value, 911, note. *Effingere*, that is, to represent by imitation, 208, note. “Prison-house of the body”: an *ergastulum* is a place where slaves were confined for labour, 1320, note. Whether the prepositions *ex* and *de* differ from one another, 751, note. *Exspectatum*: “Before the expected time Sarah was to give birth,” XIV, 591. “Little skins of letters”: a *folliculus* is the skin enclosing the grains of seeds, XVI, 491, note. *Generatio*, for childbirth, 1124. *Gignentia*, for things begotten, XIV, 475. *Glarea* is sandy ground full of small pebbles and stones, XVI, 109, note. What woodland *grumae* are, 1197. Formerly those were called *honorati* who, though enjoying palatine rank, abstained from administration, 996, note. *Hypogaea*: underground places where tavern-keepers and prostitutes were accustomed to lodge, 1061, note. The occasion on which the *labarum* was instituted, and by whom it was carried, 1105, note. *Lentandum*, for “to be gently moderated,” XV, 1841. The trees of Paradise, living and rational, 1142. *Lacernarium*: formerly the term for vigils performed in church during the first hour of the night, 1054, note. *Maforte*: a sort of veil with which virgins covered their heads at their consecration, after the manner of the flaming veil with which brides covered themselves, XVI, 206–207, note. *Mandare occulta*, “to entrust secrets,” XIV, 1134. *Memoriales* were those placed in charge of the archive of records, XVI, 996, note. *Missam facere*: the Eucharistic sacrifice already bore the name of the Mass, 995. In Ambrose, *neptis* means a son’s daughter; only among later writers is it used for a brother’s daughter, 1184, note. What *occatio cohibere* means, XIV, 170. The etymology of the word *officium*, XVI, 31, note. *Orarium*, that is, the cloth in which the sacred mysteries were sometimes wrapped when carried outside, 1021, note, 1306. The etymology of *perdix*, 1069. The term *personaliter* is to be used cautiously in divine matters, 796, note. *Plumarium*: a feather-stuffed mattress upon which the limbs lie more softly, 1039, note. *Pone*, that is, “suppose,” “grant,” 108. *Pulcium*, or *pulegium*, a kind of herb, 889, note. “Someone is pumiced by words”: a metaphor drawn from the pumice stone used by certain craftsmen for polishing, 1132, note. The etymology of *religio*, 203, note. “The billow of this life,” that is, “the sea of life,” from Greek *zalos* (ζάλος), “heaving water,” XVI, 1316, note. *Scrupus*, “rock,” whence *scrupulus*, XIV, 1144. A bilge-filled vessel, into whose bilge water enters through cracks, 1298. *Seria*, an oblong earthenware wine-vessel, 197, note. The duty of the *silentiarii* was to stand guard at the doors of the emperor’s chamber, XVI, 1367, note. What *substantia* and *consubstantialis* signify, 611. *Togati* were those who pleaded cases, such as advocates, 1276, note. What the distortion of sin is, XIV, 1062. *Tractatus*, that is, a sermon or exposition of a reading, XVI, 995. *Vadimonium* was a promise to appear before judges on an appointed day, 215, note. *Veneretur* is used in a passive sense, 961. Discussion of certain words in the annotation upon newly discovered Ambrosian sermons, XVIII, 93. The goddess Venus was called *Caelestis* by the Africans, Mithra by the Persians, 980. *Veri fide comperti*, “ascertained by trust in the truth,” XIV, 736. *Viriae*, that is, rings, 452.

## Aurelius Symmachus

The letters of Symmachus are strongly recommended to lovers of antiquity and, as it were, of more cultivated literature, XVIII, 442. Macrobius declares that Symmachus was inferior to none of the ancients in elegance of writing, 143. Prudentius calls him a tongue flowing from a wondrous fountain of words, ibid. St Prosper says that Symmachus was endowed with remarkable eloquence and learning, ibid. Cassiodorus calls him most eloquent and marvellous in his mastery of Roman speech, 114. Johannes Cuspinianus presents Symmachus’s letters as most elegant, of remarkable brevity and rounded finish, [Col. 0661] 145. Caspar Barth likewise highly praises these letters, 146.

Greek Expressions.—Greek words are rare in Symmachus; the following occur. *Archaismos* (Ἀρχαϊσμός), for Hellenic elegance, XVIII, 211. *En metra* (“in metres,” words), that is, poems, 146. *Epica* (discipline), 148. *Palingenesiam*, that is, regeneration, 142. *Panēgyrikōteron* (Πανηγυρικώτερον), that is, “in the most laudatory fashion,” 212. *Parergon*, that is, a work, 141. *Pegmata*, theatrical machinery, 174. *Pelorio*, a larger kind of oyster; Greek *pelōrios* (πελώριος), “monstrous, wonderful,” 147. *Phalerae loquendi*, for an ornate and polished style, from *phalara* (φάλαρα), 173.

Symmachian Latinity.—*Adorea*: properly the reward awarded to a victor, a certain measure of grain, from *ador*, “grain”; it is used for military glory, 175. *Amicitior*, for “more friendly,” 224. *Antistare*, that is, “to conquer, surpass,” 147, 158. *Cavea* is used in various senses: sometimes for a small enclosure, constructed from rods or poles, suitable for holding birds or beasts—iron cages, 197; sometimes for the part of a theatre in which spectators assemble, and by extension for the theatre, as at 174. “Genuine colour”: Symmachus said, “to overlay things with German colours,” 174. *Conrugare frontem*, “to wrinkle the brow,” 266. *Creperum noctis*, that is, “the duskiness of night,” with *tempus*, “time,” understood, 152. *Crepera res*, that is, an uncertain, doubtful matter, a word of very late Latin, 147. Curule horses, 256. *Habeo*: “That opinion held me in vain,” that is, “I entertained this opinion in vain,” 156. *Fuat*, for *sit*, “may be,” 149. *Homullus*, a rustic and uncultivated man, is a Ciceronian word, 233. *Honestamentum*, 150, 169. *Impraesentiarum*, “at present,” “now,” 175. “To forge the coinage of Latin speech upon a Tullian anvil,” 148. *Insubidae litterae*, letters conceived with too little care or rashly, 148. *Labor*: “The heat of labours enters into minds,” 233. *Laudaciani*, *Laudiciani*, for Laodiceans, 241. *Libo*: “to sip words,” 146. “Ornaments of speech,” for polished and ornate style, 173. “More rancid Minerva,” that is, learning grown old and of less value, 174; “the sow [teaches] Minerva,” a proverb, that is, “to teach a master,” 148. “I am of no value,” with *pretii*, “in worth,” understood, 148. *Pagina*, for a writing or letter, from *pango, pangere*, “to fasten, write,” 173, 253, 254, 366. “By God,” a common form of oath, 147. *Pernox* and *perdius*, that is, “through the entire night” and “through the entire day,” 166. The Quadragesima customs-duty or tax, 258. *Potiebatur* used with the genitive case, 175. *Quid quod*, interrogative, 250. *Quis* for *quibus*, 156. “A priesthood of virtues and letters,” 298. “The persuasive cups of Circe”: *suada* is a Symmachian word, 164. *Subolis* for *sobolis*, “offspring,” 233. *Subpalpandi*, that is, “of gently flattering,” 174. *Summas*, which denotes pre-eminence, as likewise *primas*, a word very frequently used by Symmachus, 153, 154, 155, and passim.

## Ulfilius, Bishop of the Moesian Goths

How he translated the sacred books into Gothic, XVII, 362. He does not appear to have translated the Books of Kings, 463. It is established that the Goths possessed the whole body of Scripture, 463–464. The Goths spoke their own language in conquered regions, especially where the seat of their kingdom lay, 464. The Gothic translation flourished in Italy and in other lands held by the Goths, 465. Testimony of Walafrid Strabo, ninth century, ibid. Only the Gospels, the letters of St Paul, and certain fragments survive in the Gothic language, ibid. On leaving the banks of the Ister, the Goths brought with them into Italy their Bibles translated by Ulfilas, 474.

A Gothic grammar translated from German by Tempestini, XVIII, 879. The Gothic language is the common speech of the East Germanic peoples designated collectively by the name Goths, 881. The Greeks called them *Gotthoi* (Γότθοι), with an aspirated dental, while the Romans called them *Gothi*, without doubling, ibid. Some wrote the glosses *Goti, Gotica*; Germans have *Guti* and *Gudi*, ibid. This language belongs to the Indo-Germanic stock and is one of the Germanic family of languages, 883. Gothic speech stands midway between Sanskrit and German, 884. How it is the foundation of the German language, ibid. The Gothic, High German, and Icelandic languages have a common origin; Gothic, however, is the most ancient, ibid. There is the closest affinity between the northern languages and Gothic, ibid. Nothing certain can be determined concerning the dialects of Gothic, 885. The treasury of the Gothic language contains not a few foreign riches, 885. It is established that the Goths possessed poems and songs, 887. Whether the Goths had written laws, 888. The Gothic language flourished only for a short time, 890. Ulfilas appears to have first devised writing in Moesia, ibid. The Goths did not impose their language upon the conquered, 891. At Constantinople, through Chrysostom’s efforts, a school was opened in which Goths were taught, 892. If travellers are to be believed, Gothic survived for a very long time in the Tauric Chersonese (in French, *la Crimée*), 893. This language is exceedingly rich in synonyms, 895. Whether it is easy to learn, ibid.

Syllabus of the Chapters of the Gothic Grammar.—The Gothic alphabet consists of twenty-five letters, 897. Names of the letters, 905. Pronunciation, 910. Vowels, 911. Consonants, 930. Declension, 946. Adjectives, 966. Numerals, [Col. 0662] 971. Pronouns, 975. Conjugation, 979. Formation of words, 1002. Nominal formation, 1006. Pronominal formation, 1014. Verbal formation, 1015. Adverbial formation, 1019. Formation by compounding, 1025.

Syntax, 1031. Syntax of the verb, 1034. Proper nouns, 1069. Adjectives, 1074. Numerals, 1087. Pronouns, 1090. Personal pronouns, ibid. Demonstrative pronouns, 1101. Relative pronouns, 1105. Interrogative pronouns, 1107. Indefinite pronouns, 1109. The simple sentence: subject, predicate, and copula, 1115. Negation, 1123. Attribute, 1127. Object, 1134. Determination of place, 1160; likewise of time, 1166; of measure, 1171. The compound sentence, 1183. Appendix on pleonasm, 1223.

Gothic-Latin Glossary, translated from German by Tempestini, 1238.—Greek-Gothic Glossary, 1511.

## Aquilinus Juvencus, Spanish Presbyter

Juvencus, the most ancient of Christian poets, XIX, 11. Distinguished by brilliance of language, elegance of style, and ancient simplicity, ibid. St Jerome’s exceptional praise of Juvencus, 12.

Hebrew Expressions.—Abelus, XIX, 350. Abia, 56. Abimelus for Abimelec, 363. Abram, 356. Adamus, 347, 350. Anchialum, that is, Anchialon, or “the Most High does not live,” 128, note. Benjamin, 377. Cain, 350. Cana of Galilee, 158. What *Corban* is, 226, note. Daniel the prophet, 290. *Davida* for *Davidem*, 83, 86. Emmanuel, 82, note. Enoch the Righteous, 351. Esau, 366. Esdras, 62, note 38. The formation of Eva, 347. Gessen, 378, note; 1364. Golgotha, 334. Gomorrha, 361. Hebron, 74, note; 115. Hosanna, an acclamation of the Jews, 268. Isaac, 362. Ismaelus, 359. Israelites, 92. Jacobus, 366. Jeremias, 100. Jesus, 88, 110, 111, 116, 217. Joannes, 66, 110, 118, 176, 217, 272, 274. Jonas, 204. Jordan, 117. Etymology of Jordan, 61, note. Joseph, 85, 94, 99, 101, etc. Josephus, 372, 373. Juda, Judaea, Jews, 120, 290, 312, 378, 386. Judas Maccabaeus, 386. Judas Iscarioth, 316, 330. Lod, Lodus for Loth, 355, 361. Maccabaeus, 386. Magedarus, 233. Maria, 83, 88, 89, 101, 312. Moses, 89, 203, 241. Nathanael, 156. Nazara for Nazareth, 156. Pascha, 102, 160, 312, 314. Pharisees, 175, 193, 225, 312. Sabbath, 193, 194, 195, 291. Sadducees, 233, 234. Salomon, 137, 205. Samaritans, 168, 170. Sarra, 355 and following. Sichem, 168, 356. Sidon, 229. Simeon, 89, 93; the patriarch, 368, 377. Solymae for Jerusalem, 128, 171, 239, 263. Syria, Syrians, 83, 119, 120, 229. Tyre, 229. Zabulon, 117, 368. Zacharias, 73, 105. Zebedaeus, 119.

Greek Expressions.—*Aethera* and *Aethra* for accusative *aether*, 59, 259, 285. *Alabastrum*, a type of small vessel without handles, 313. *Anchora*, 224. *Barathron*, that is, “pit,” properly a deep place at Athens into which criminals were thrown, 285, note; 303, note. What a *chlamys* is, 332, note. *Chorea*, from *choros* (χόρος), 176. *Chorus*, 298. *Cophinus*, a wicker basket, 235, note. *Daemon*, 153, 181, 183. *Didrachma*, 247, note. Bishop: formerly bishops strove to remove their shoes, 108. *Glaucicomans* [olive], from *glaukos* (γλαυκός), “bluish-grey in colour,” and *komē* (κόμη), “hair,” 267. *Gumphus*, or *Gomphus*, that is, “nail,” 334. *Haemorrhoissa*, a woman suffering from an issue of blood and healed by Christ, 179. Hymn, 317. *Hydria*, a stone vessel suitable for holding water, 159, note. Description of bridal lamps, 297. *Lethum*, that is, death, 93. *Machaera*, a type of sword, from *machē* (μάχη), “battle,” 93, note. Magic; magician. The *Magoi* (Μάγοι) were formerly called astrologers because of astrology, 96, note. *Nomisma* and *numisma*, 280. *Orama, oroma,* and *horama*, that is, “vision,” 243, note. *Peplum*, a loose sleeveless garment, 179. *Rhomphaea*, a type of sword, 93, note. *Sinapi* and *sinepi*, 216. *Spongus*, Greek *spongos* (Σπόγγος), “sponge,” 337. *Synedrion*, a Jewish tribunal, called *sanedrin* by the Hebrews, 124, note. *Tartarus*, hell, from *tarassō* (ταράσσω), “to frighten,” 217, note. *Thronus*, throne, from *thraō*, “to sit,” 76, 122. *Tricliniarcha*, the slave set over banquets, 160, note. Description of the triclinium, 266, note.

Juvencian Latinity.—Absolute ablative: *se judice quaerit*, “he asks with himself as judge,” for *ipse judex quaerit*, “he himself, as judge, asks,” XIX, 200. The ablative with the particles *quam* and *pro*, 250. “To kindle renown,” 152. “To drive on a weary labour,” 304. “A column of water,” 253. What an apex in writing is, 123. *Causare*: *natam causata jacentem*, “having alleged that her daughter lay [there],” 229. “To bark around,” 323. “The vaulted heaven,” 233. “Kindred bodies,” 281. *Correptare*, for “to attack” or “to enter,” considered a barbarous word by some, 164, note. “Elbow-length additions,” 137. What “the feeble multitude of legs” means, 231. “A hand devoted to madness,” 342. “To grant error,” 154. *Duellum*, single combat, 198. *Famoso*, for “infamous,” 328. “With exhausted fortunes,” 304. *Flammicomans*, “flame-haired,” 297. *Flammipes*, “flame-footed,” 191. *Flammivomus*, “vomiting flame,” 60. *Fretum* is said to derive from *fervere*, “to boil,” 234, note. “To rejoice joys,” a pleonasm, 98. Two genitives of the same substantive, 85, 173, 216. *Genitor* and *genitrix* are words more proper to poets than orators, 257. Hiatus, as in *accipite ergo*, an expression familiar to Virgil in his leisure, 166. *Iteris* for *itineris*, 98. [Col. 0663] *Itiner* for *iter*, 149. What marriage festivals are, 277. *Lustratis* for *illustratis*, 92; likewise *lustrata* for *illustrata*, 98. *Marita*, that is, wife, 282. *Miro* for *miror*, 219, note 58. “With thick barriers,” 210. *Pactus*: “A wife joined by no crime,” 81. “Words that tremble,” 75. *Parvi*, for children, 249. *Pleramque* used in the singular, 65. Juvencus delights in compounds formed with the prefix *prae-*, 259, note. A preposition is often omitted by poets, as *Aegyptum* for *in Aegyptum*, “into Egypt,” etc., 99, note; 291. *Pupare*, a barbarous word for “to grow,” 374. *Scrupus*, “rock”; *scrupeus*, “rocky,” 140, note. *Sinuamen* [of a dancing girl], 219. *Sinuamen uteri*, “the curve of the womb,” 74. *Super* with the genitive, 150. *Terniqua*, that is, “of a threefold race,” 357. *Terrificare*, “to terrify,” 224. What a *triclinium* is; description of it, 266, note. Whether *tueor* may be taken passively, 383. *Tutus* for *totus*, 358. The sound of waves, 247. *Urgeo* with an infinitive, 101, 334, note. *Vacuum fuit*, that is, “was vacant,” 235. “The sail-flying sea,” 148. *Venit* for *est*, “is,” 238. *Viare*, “to travel,” 80. “The binding of companionship,” 281. “Virgin dwellings,” 70. *Voco* with an infinitive, 145. “The rolling day,” 77. *Vulnus*, for injury and for crime, 251.

## Caelius Sedulius, Lay Poet and Christian

How certain impious men held nothing more important than declaring war upon approved writers and therefore upon the Latin language itself, XIX, 435. How they succeeded in causing the study of antiquity to be neglected, ibid. The French language is fertile in impious books, ibid. Many do not dare approach the Fathers and Christian poets unless some exposition is supplied, as though they had spoken in a language of another kind, 436. It is not Jerome but Gennadius who mentions Sedulius, 437. He probably held the episcopate, 445–446. Testimony of Isidore concerning Sedulius, 504. Likewise Fortunatus, Arator, Bede, Gerson, Barthius, Borrichius, and Valchius discuss him, 510.

Greek Expressions and Hellenisms.—Achaemenian [wrath], 573, note. What acrostic and anacrostic are, 782, note. The rule of an acrostic poem, ibid. *Aethra, Aethram* for *aethera*, 708, note. “Nile papyrus leaves,” 554. *Bibliotheca*, for the sacred books, 542. *Canistrum*, from *kanēs* (κάνης), which comes from *kanna* (κάννα), “reed,” 551. *Carbasa*, from *karpasos* (κάρπασος), a kind of very fine linen, 638. *Charaxat*, from *echaraxen* (ἐχάραξεν), that is, “he pierces the body with darts,” 589. *Colymbum*, that is, basin, ibid. *Daedalius*, 557, note. *Hyalum*, “glass,” from *hyalos* (ὕαλος), 513. Alphabetic hymns, 763, note. Labyrinth, 537. *Malum*, that is, apple; in the Middle Ages it was often called *melum*, from Greek *mēlon* (μῆλον), 552, note 13. Monogram of Christ, 768. *Myron*, for ointment, 768. *Numisma* and *nomisma*, 708. Ancient orthography, 466. *Lethum*, death, properly oblivion, 593. Ancient orthography, 466. *Paraclitus*, 512. What *paracteria* poems are, 752, note; 438. Paradise, 952. A paralytic is healed, 643. Paraphrase of the decree of Pope Gelasius, 794, title. What an alphabetic rhythm is, 770. What *syncletice* is, 542, note. *Syncrasis*, 704, note. *Tartarum*, for the lower world, from *tarassō* (ταράσσω), “I frighten,” 699. What tautology is, and its familiarity to poets, 567, note. A telestich is a poem in which the final letters of the verses form a name, 782. *Thesidae*, or Athenians, 557. *Xeromyrrha*, 768; *Xerolibya*, ibid.; *Hylobalsamum*, ibid. Formerly Χρο was written for Christ, ibid. *Ymnus* for *hymnus*, 769.

Latinity of Caelius Sedulius.—What *accepta vox* is, 696. *Agens* for *aiens*, “saying,” 591. *Agit* for *ait*, “he says,” 587, note; 321. “Winged cock,” 712. *Attitilas*, 672, note 11. “The blacknesses of the tomb,” 731, note. *Audere* said of fire, 573. What “Nile papyrus leaves” are, 554. “Blind power,” 666. “The pious camp of Christ,” for the cross, 589. Rules of a cento poem, 780, note. “The barriers of the cheeks,” 696. *Cohaerent*, for “they attach,” 512. “To ripple laughter,” 588. “Stripped of hair,” 514. “Learned cook,” 550. Whether *dubitatis Christum* can be used, 698. *Extremescere*, 699. “He made there be an end,” 680. “Fiery sword,” 570. “Thunderbolt-like heaven,” 571. *Fusus*, for “born,” 709. *Gentes* said of fishes, 683. *Germen* and *gramen*, 660, note. What hiatus is, 565, note; hiatus in verse, 583, note; 664, note. What alphabetic hymns are, 763, note. “The depths of the deep,” 576, note. “Imaginal punishment,” 573. “To fill a friend with tears,” 698. “With fasting bites,” 670. *Jugulus*, for killing, 719. K is read for C in manuscripts: *Katerva, Karus, Kastra*, 765. *Lambere*, “to kiss repeatedly,” 678. *Lancinari*, “to tear to pieces,” 513. *Lumen* and *limen*, 572, 597, note. “Sea of Tears,” 610. “Sea of the sea,” 567. *Marmora*, for sea, ibid. *Metallum*, for rock, 569. “Mute silence,” 537, note. “Birth-mud,” 696. *Ninguem* for *nivem*, “snow,” and *ninguidus* for *niveus*, “snowy,” 512. *Numen* and *nomen*, 599, note. Pagans were so called from the districts of Athens where Cecrops first established the ceremonial procession of the gods, 511, 553. *Populatio*, 697. “Polar death for the wretched,” 593. “Childish thousands,” that is, innumerable trifles, 608, 609. Sedulius was the first to use *relambere*, 695, note. Rufius, a gentile name, 489. *Salii, salivi, salvi*, 569, note. Sedulius’s words are often used in liturgical offices, 506. *Spiritu* and *spritu*, 762, note. *Sudum*, for serenity, 513, note. *Destra*, [Col. 0664] for “your,” characteristic of very late Latin, 538. What *virginal* is, 513. When the letter X was invented, 768, note. *Xristo* for Christ, ibid.

Valeria Faltonia Proba: Virgilian centos, XIX, 803.—What kind of poem a cento is, and its rules, 780, note.

## Decius Ausonius, Rhetorician and Poet of Bordeaux

Ausonius was a most learned grammarian and rhetorician, and a charming and ingenious poet, XIX, 817. Teacher of Gratian and Valentinian, ibid. He was also the teacher of St Paulinus, 818, note. He was a Christian, but wanton and licentious, ibid. Paulinus disliked his writings because they had something of a more pagan flavour (*ethnikōteron*, ἐθνικώτερον), ibid. Among his poems Ausonius often mixed Greek verses, 829, 830, 833, 873. Ausonius played with verses intertwined by a multiple knot, 898 and following.

Greek Expressions of Ausonius.—*Abacus*, tablet or table, 826. *Bibliotheca*, 830. *Eclogarium*, 907. *Ephemeris*, or the business of an entire day, 834. *Epigrammata*, 826. *Metanoia*, that is, repentance, 827. *Myobarbum*: a word with a half-Greek and half-Latin etymology, denoting a bearded mouse; its sense in Ausonius is not readily understood, 829. Nemesis, the name of the avenging goddess, is said to derive from *nemesizō* (νεμεσίζω), “I am indignant,” 828. *Parecbasis*, that is, digression, 839. *Periochae*, title of a poem, 947. *Rhabdouchos* (Ῥαβδοῦχος), that is, lictor or attendant, from *rhabdos* (Ῥάβδος), “staff, rod,” 829. Rhetor, 824. What rophallic verses are, 820, note. *Stemma*, that is, crown, 824. A *technopaegnion* poem, 898. *Toxicon*, that is, poison, 826. Tetrastich poems, 866. *Tribon* (τρίβων), a worn cloak, 831. The Trinacrian shore, that is, Sicily, because of its three promontories, 827. *Zelotypus*, for envious.

Ausonian Latinity.—“A winged right hand,” for the hand of a notary writing with the greatest speed, 838. *Amnigena, amnicola*, 888, 889. *Anteperire*, 829. “Foremost of the world,” that is, earlier, 840. “Arcadian beast,” that is, ass, 833. “Rich, rich in wealth,” 837. *Dodra*, a drink pressed from nine herbs; it is said to derive from *dodrans*, a weight denoting nine ounces, 833. *Fictilibus*, for earthenware vessels, 826. “A Roman Homer also falls to your lot,” 825. “Moist little locks,” 834. *Humificare*, 886. “It is not fitting to count the uncertainty of life,” 828. “Slippery path,” for the posterior part of the body, 827. “The mockeries of death,” 840. “Samian clay,” for earthenware made at Samos, 826.

The letter M, initial and marked with an apex, is the beginning of several names, 830. *Ollis* for *illis*, 909. *Oti* for *otii*, 830. *Parentalia*, the title of a poem by Ausonius, 842. Various kinds of fish: *alaura, balaena, barbus, capito, delphina, gobio, mustela, perca, redo, saler, salmo, saravi, tinca*, 888, 889. *Puer*, for servant, 839. *Quotiens* for *quoties*, 842. *Reminisco*, a barbarous word condemned by Ausonius himself, 831. “Resounding echo,” 834. “Health-bringing Jupiter,” 886. *Secta*, for religion, 824. *Semivir*, for an unskilled man, 830. “A torrent tongue,” in words, 837. “Two three-hour intervals of the month,” 888. “Flying verses,” 826. “Serpentine crime,” 840. “To live as we live,” with *quod* for *ut iam*, “as now,” 828.

## Sulpicius Severus

Severus left many writings composed in brilliant language, chiefly in imitation of Sallust, XX, 80. Paulinus of Nola says that he flourished in the vigour of life, abounded in praise, and held the prize of an eloquent reputation in the theatre of the forum, 81. Paulinus of Périgueux says of him: “Severus is present as a witness, marvellous in learned speech,” 86. Guibert Martin wrote in 1208 that Severus had obtained the bishopric of Bourges, 93.

**Hebrew.**—Sulpicius Severus followed the Septuagint translators in writing Hebrew names: thus he wrote *Sampson* instead of *Samson*, 112; *Melchor* for *Michol*, Saul’s daughter, 116, 117; *Chebron* for *Hebron*, 118; *Gotholia* for *Athalia*, 123. In the Assyrian language, Samaritans are called “guards,” 125.

**Greek.**—Plato’s Academy, 222. *Allophylus*, that is, “foreigner,” from ἄλλον φῦλον, “another race,” 111, 112, 114, 115, 116, and frequently.

*Anachorete*, 193. Ἀνομοιουσία, that is, “dissimilar substance,” 151. *Archdeacon*, 201. *Catechumen*, 162. *Catholicly; catholic*, 188. *Chlamys*, 162. *Demon*, 207, 221. *Devil*, 163, 172, 174. The office of the diaconate, 163. *Deacon*, 201. *Diocese*, an episcopal province, 208. *Desert*, 190, 197. *Modern [books]*, 188. The meaning and difference of ὁμοούσιον and ὁμοιούσιον, 151. *Paralysis*, a disease, 169. *Presbyter*, 175, 201, 208, 211, 213. *Scholar*, 217.

**Sulpician Latin.**—*Adorandus* (“to be adored”) for *honoratus* (“honoured”), 99. “To abound in riches,” 125. *Afficitor* for *afficiatur*, 105. “To brood over gold,” 109, 227. *Barbarian* for “foreigner,” 136, 138. *Calumnia* for examination or disputation, 95. *Continens* for *solo solido* (literally, “on solid ground alone”), 104. “The banquet grows warm with cups,” 136. “From the field of harvest,” with *tempore* (“at the time”) understood, 110. “Fierce through victories,” 138. The preposition *in* is very often understood: “to descend [into] Egypt,” 103. “To seek tears and hiding-places”: perhaps an error here, [Col. 0665] 115. *Macti episcopi*, perhaps *acti* (“the bishops were driven”), 152. A womanly caress, 136. *Occoepit* for *occepit*, a typographical error, 110, 112, 116. *Pestis* (“plague”) for ruin, 136. *Quaestio*, a form of punishment, 145. *Salum*, that is, a mass of waters or the sea, 97. *Summa rerum*, that is, sovereignty, 145, 146. *Tangentur*, that is, “they shall be affected with joy,” 224. A comma should be inserted in *consequentibus inopiam*, so that the sense is: “in the seven following years, there will be scarcity,” in accordance with the preceding part of the sentence, 101. *Virtutes* for miracles, 110.

**CHROMATIUS (St.), bishop of Aquileia.**—Chromatius was among the most distinguished Western bishops of his age. St Ambrose admired his holy mind in the study of the divine sayings; St Jerome called him the holiest and most learned of bishops; Rufinus called him a second Bezalel of his own time; and John Chrysostom praised his sincere tongue, filled with great freedom and confidence, XX, 250. The few writings of his which survive have always been highly valued by the most learned, both for their elegance of expression and for the weight of their subject matter and excellence of doctrine, 250. The Church’s use of doxologies—that is, formulas by which the Saviour of humankind or the Holy Trinity is glorified—is derived chiefly from Chromatius, 269. These doxologies are called in Latin *clausulae* (“conclusions”), because a discourse is customarily concluded through them, 270. Adulterous marriages, and how and why they are discussed in the preface to Chromatius’s works and in the Code Napoléon, 285 ff.

Chromatius’s lead seal or medal, 295. Ancient forms of Roman letters are visible on this seal, 296. They are found to be almost like our own, ibid. In this leaden and fragile material there has been preserved an ancient and precious monument of the ordinary alphabet, 298. For the sake, perhaps, of a certain elegance, letters were drawn angularly; for example, O assumed a square shape, 298. What should be thought of the authenticity of the aforesaid seal, 219, 300.

**Hebrew.**—*Abbas*, that is, “father,” 359. Who Bezalel was, and why Chromatius is so called, 288, 289, 290. Jerusalem: why one must not swear by it, 352, 353. *Mammon*, that is, money; it is the devil because he himself is the author of mammon, Chromatius, 368. Who a Pharisee is, 358. What *raca* means in the Gospel, 345.

**Greek terms.**—Βλέφαρα, “eyelids.” Μηδὲ συναρπασθῇς ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῆς βλεφάρων: “nor be carried away by her eyelids” (LXX, Proverbs 6:25); Chromatius reads: “nor be snatched away by your eyelids,” 349. *Doxology*, Latin *clausula*: a form of speech by which praise and glory are attributed to God, from δόξα, “glory,” and λόγος, “speech,” 269. Gentiles, 358. What the Eucharist is, 277, 278. Ἐξεταζόμενος, “examined”; Chromatius has *flagellatus*, “scourged,” 352. *Exomologesis* for sacramental confession, to be made before communion, 279. *Hypocrisis; hypocrite*, 358. *Liturgy; liturgical matters*, that is, matters belonging to Church discipline, from λειτουργία, “public service,” 275, 290. Chromatius’s medal, 295. Ὀνομάζων, “naming”; Chromatius interprets it as *negotians*, “trading,” 352.

**Latin expressions.**—*Beatitudes*: a term which among Christians commonly denotes Christ’s words blessing those who attain the eight headings of perfection or evangelical life (Matthew 5:1–10), 323 and frequently. *Clausula*: see below. What daily or frequent communion is, 276. What sacramental confession is, 278 ff. What are called adulterous marriages, and following. The Flaminian or Postumian Way, 293. *Hujus modi* for *hujus mundi* (“of this world”), 354. *Multiloquax* and *multiloquentia*, “talkative” and “verbosity,” 358. “Sweat” is used for the odour of food sacrificed to idols, 279. *Passivam*, wrongly, for *pessimam* (“most evil”), 351. What prayers said silently are, 278. Where Portus Grecarius was situated, 293. What place Portus Romatius or Romatinus was, and where it was situated, 292, 293, 294. “Barbarian storm” for the Gothic incursion, 285, 286. “What indeed [are] servants,” etc.: this passage appears defective, 329. “The Lord’s holy thing,” that is, the sacred Eucharist, 279. *Tractatus*, that is, a discourse to the people, 323, 327, 330, and frequently. Whether *vide* (“see”) or *unde* (“whence”) should be read, 330, note.

The principal concluding formulas, or doxologies, with which Chromatius customarily ends his homilies are indicated:

“[The] Lord, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen,” 328.

“The Son of God, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen,” 330.

“[The] Holy Spirit, through whom be praise and glory to the Father and the Son for ages of ages. Amen,” 331.

“May we deserve to be made sharers in glory, through Christ our Lord, who is blessed for the ages,” 337.

“[The] Lord: to whom be honour, praise, and glory together with the Holy Spirit, before all ages, and now and always and for ages of ages. Amen,” 363.

The forms of speech we have supplied already belong to Christian Latin and adorn it like so many jewels. For an abundance of material, consult *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, elucidated by B. de Rubeis, 407.

[Col. 0666] **INNOCENT I, pope.**—That pontiff is rightly called by Theodoret “a man adorned with shrewdness and understanding” (ἀνὴρ ἀγχινοίᾳ καὶ συνέσει κοσμούμενος), XX, 461. Speaking of Innocent’s deeds, Pagius says, in Pliny’s words, that God so claimed him for heaven that, after that divine and immortal act, nothing mortal could make him mortal, 462. He wrote several letters to Greek bishops in Greek, 494, 502.

**Greek terms found both in the Prolegomena and in this pope’s writings.**—*Ama*, or better *hama*, Greek ἄμη: a vessel for water, the same as what the French call a *bénitier* (“holy-water stoup”), XX, 458. An embossed cup (*anaglyphus scyphus*), that is, a cup ornamented with carvings, ibid. *Canon; canons of the Church*: thus the laws and rules concerning faith or ecclesiastical discipline were already called, from κανών, “rule,” 486. *Cantharus*: see *Pharus* below. *Cerostrota*, κερόστρωτος: work made with fragments of differently coloured horn, such as the French call *marqueterie* or *mosaïque*, ibid. *Cleric* is derived from κλῆρος, “lot” or “allotment”; these are persons initiated, or to be initiated, into the priesthood; by contrast the rest are called *laity*, from λαός, “people,” 473, 474. *Diaco*, or deacon, 359. *Didascalic* or doctrinal book, 470. Metropolitan bishop, 471. *Pharus cantharus*, a kind of elongated and large vessel, 458.

**Latin terms.**—Apostolic see or chair, for the seat of the Roman bishop as successor of the apostle Peter, 461, 486. *Aquamaniles*, vessels suitable for washing the hands, 458. *Cleric* and *layperson*: who these are, see above under Greek terms.

*Curiales* or *decuriones* were those who performed municipal magistracies and offices, 466. Who the *coronati* are, 492. “Divine discipline” for “the Lord’s [discipline],” 471.

“Your love,” “your piety”: customary honorific formulas in the second person in this period, 489. *Discederunt* for *discesserunt*, 486. *Orbis*: “to make an eternal circle of evil,” that is, by speaking to engage in a vicious circular argument, 486. *Ordinare*, *ordinator*, and *ordinatio* are said from the sacred order by which clerics and priests are made, 492. “Obstinacy in obtaining” is said of litigants who strive to obtain what they ask, whether it is just or unjust, 491. *Sacrosancta*, a word of eminent ecclesiastical use, 509. *Saeculum* for this life, 379. *Sedere*, “to sit,” for discharging an episcopal office, 469. See “Apostolic see.” A *siliqua*, the sixth part of a given number, 459. A *solidus* is the same as an *aureus*, 158. A *tremissis*, one third of a solidus, 458, 459. An *uncia*, one twelfth of a pound or of another number, 459.

**ZOZIMUS, pope.**—His Latin, which has no slight Greek flavour: “a ram of deceit,” XX, 658. Paschal candle, 639. “I remind your charity,” for “I remind you”: thus the holy men of the Church spoke, 653. *Circulatores*, those who carry their wicked persona from place to place, 664. *Clerus*, that is, clerics or the body of clerics, 651. *Comperendinatio*, or adjournment of a judicial proceeding, 659. *Diacones* for *diaconi*, 139. “Divine archives” for the Holy Scriptures, 658. “Wandering footsteps amid deceptive darkness,” 658. *Formatae*, that is, letters of communion, without which travelling clerics were not even admitted to communion, 642, 643 note. “Your fraternity” or “your paternity,” used as an honorific title, 650. What *linostimae pallae* or *palleae* are, 638. “The great weight of examination” for a lengthy examination, 649. *Parochia* and *paroecia*, from παροικία: this was the name for ecclesiastical districts entrusted to priests and was sometimes used for the diocese itself, 644. “Your holiness,” a phrase of honour, 652, 653. *Telonarii* or *temonarii*, those who collect taxes, 683. “Snares of questions,” that is, vain questions, 653. “Transmarine documents,” that is, African documents, 660. “The wind of truth,” 658; “to arrive at the bedchamber of truth,” that is, to uncover the truth, 652.

**GAUDENTIUS (St), bishop of Brescia.**—How greatly Gaudentius flourished in the praise of learning and eloquence, XX, 798. He so excelled that whatever he said was swiftly taken down in writing by notaries, 798. “To you, Gaudentius,” says Rufinus, “the eminent glory of our teachers: so great is your vigour of intellect—indeed, so great the grace of the Spirit—that whatever you say even in the manner of everyday speech, whatever is declaimed in church, ought to be preserved in books and handed down for the instruction of posterity,” 823. Nevertheless, Gaudentius’s style was criticized by the very distinguished Du Pin, of the Protestant party; we have not transcribed his judgment, but see his words and their refutation, 812, 813, 814. An account of Du Pin’s criticism is given, 802.

**Hebrew.**—Babylon means “confusion,” 833. *Cana* is called “possession,” 892. Galilee is interpreted either “rolling” or “wheel,” ibid. The family name of the Maccabees, 949. Maimonides, the rabbi, testifies that the Hebrews first dipped unleavened bread in the dish *Charoseth*, likewise bitter herbs, and then ate them, 885 note. *Mammona*, in Syriac, means money, [Col. 0667] 973–974. In what sense Moses, of the tribe of Levi, is called the *architriclinus*, 909. *Pascha* or *phascha*, according to the language of the Hebrews, means “passage,” 845 note.

**Hellenic terms.**—*Anicii*, or “unconquered,” from ἀνίκητος, XX, 952. *Architriclinus*, master of the banquet: what his office was, 908 note. *Ascitae*, heretics so called from ἀσκός, “wineskin,” with which they revelled, 897 note. *Azyma*, from the privative α and ζύμη, “leaven,” 882. Βρῶμος, rye, a kind of herb growing among crops; perhaps *brodium* should be supplied, 860 note. *Chiliasts*, that is, in Latin *Millenarians*, a kind of heretics, 861 note. *Chrysopolis*, the ancient name of the city of Besançon, 971 note. The devil, called prince of the world, 930. Doxologies used by Gaudentius and the Fathers at the end of a homily, 867 note. *Almsgiving*, 835, 938, 941. The Erythraean Sea, called the Red Sea by Latin writers, 913. *Exodus* is the same as “departure,” 848. *Hydria*, a vessel, 903. Hyperbole in the Gospel text, 921 note. *Idolatry*: in manuscripts it is almost always written *idolatria*, and the source from which it took its beginning, 833 note, 870. *Idolothyta*, sacrificial offerings to idols: what they are, 902 note. *Metreta*, an Attic measure of ten congii, an amphora larger than twelve sextarii, 904 note. Μύρον, Latin *unguentum*, “ointment,” 934. *Myrothecium*, a vessel or repository for ointment, 935 note. *Neophytes*: who they are, 871. *Oenoplae* at banquets: who they were, 908 note. Ὁμοούσιον, 830 note. Οὐσία, ibid. Whether *Paracletus* or *Paraclitus* should be said, 944 note. *Problema*: among philosophers, an investigation of a hidden matter, 840 note. Προσήλυτοι: what they are, 919. An *idiographic psalm* is one in which the Psalmist speaks about himself, from ἴδιος, “proper” or “one’s own,” and γράφω, “to make a description,” 927 note. *Schedula*, *scheda*, and *schedium*, from σχεδή, “a tablet on which a notary writes,” 831. *Strategi*, those responsible for military affairs; *strategia*, the command of military affairs, 929 note. Whether there were στρατηγοὶ τοῦ ἱεροῦ (“commanders of the Temple”) or rather στρατηγοὶ τῆς Ἀντωνίας (“commanders of the Antonia”), 930 note. *Tricliniarchs*: see *Architriclinus* above. *Zona*, from ζώνη, “girdle,” 858.

**Latin usage.**—*Ad*, as a prefix: whether *adfligo*, *adgravo*, *adquiesco*, etc. should be written, is investigated, XX, 868 note. “Wings of faith”: what they are, 945. Apostolic men, that is, successors of the apostles, acting in their place, 960. The discipline of the secret, that is, of sacred mysteries, 852, 853 note. “To seize upon works of piety,” 942. Staff: Gaudentius says, “I need a staff, while still celebrating Passover in Egypt,” 876. On the very ancient use of the staff in the Church, ibid. note. For *balbutire* in “they stammer in thirst for the Spirit,” it seems that *Spiritum siti rebalbutiunt* should be read, “in thirst for the Spirit they stammer again,” 871 note. *Brodium*, a new word which, according to some, belongs to the Italian language then beginning to emerge, from which perhaps derives the French word *brouet*; see, however, what we said above under the Greek Βρῶμος, 959 note. What visible and hidden reeds are, 832 note. The Kalends, Ides, and Nones, as also the months and days, received their names from the pagans, 846. “Forgetting the mire of vices,” 950. Serpentine gestures, 890. *Defectis* for *deficientibus*, 887 note. *Deus*: this word is very often deleted in manuscripts and *Dominus* substituted for it, 919 note. *Et caetera*, a conclusion sometimes used by Gaudentius, 927 note. “It is ploughed by worms,” 838. G placed for C at the beginning of a word, as seems to occur in *Gallica* or *Gallicula*, from which *Caligula* was called. A *gallicula* was a kind of shoe used especially by travellers, 875. The letter K was often formerly used for C: thus *Karissime* for *carissime*, 997. The Magi, ambassadors of all nations, 983. What the *magister memoriae* was, 830 note. What “sending” and “being sent” signify in the Trinity, 948. Hidden notaries assigned [to record], 831 note. What it means to perform *parentalia*, 870. One must command money, not serve it, 975. Pomp of eloquence, 831. *Scrinia*, repositories for documents and various writings, rightly called *portefeuille* in French, 830 note. *Spiritualis* and *spiritalis*, 839 note. *Suballigaturae*, amulets superstitiously used as protections, whether by pagans or by uneducated Christians weaker through excessive credulity, 870 note. “The heat of temptations” and “the burden of tribulations,” 843. *Tractatus* and *tractare*, or discourse and discoursing, 843 note. *Tunc temporis*, “at that time,” 922, 950. The shod word of God and its venerable footprints, 874. The interchange of Y and U in Greek words, very common among ancient writers: thus *murum* for *myrum*, *Aeguptus* for *Aegyptus*, *Suria* and *Suracusa* for *Syria* and *Syracusa*, 996.

**RUFINUS, presbyter of Aquileia.**—He is called one who argues most eloquently concerning divine matters, Preface, XXI, 47. His works possess such learning and doctrine that they yield to scarcely any writings of the other Fathers then flourishing in the Church, ibid. Why they have remained almost neglected in obscurity, ibid. His *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed* is worthy of the highest praise, Preface, 57. In matters which he borrowed from the Greek of Cyril of Jerusalem, the deeper meaning and the proper force of the words are evident, ibid. He is defended against an ignorant error concerning the words *fumosum genium* (“a smoky genius”), which he applies to the idol Serapis (*Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 23), 60 ff. A list of the various works which Rufinus translated from Greek may be found at 15. In the heat of controversy Jerome says of Rufinus: “I pass over the Greeks, whose learning you boast of, and while you pursue foreign things you have almost forgotten your own language,” etc. “I am astonished that you, the Aristarchus of our age, have despised the precepts of grammarians and orators, considering it of little account to render hyperbata after their windings, to avoid harshness of consonants, [and] to flee gaping diction,” 162.

**Hebrew.**—*Aser* means “blessed,” XXI, 325. *Benjamin* means “son of sorrow,” 333. *Dan*, “judgment” or “judge,” 322. *Gad*, Greek πειρατήριον, means in Latin “temptation,” 323 note. *Jarim* is explained as “wooded,” 359. *Jesus*, a Hebrew name, means “Saviour,” 307, 318. India is inhabited by many and diverse languages and peoples, 478. *Joseph* means “increased,” 327. *Issachar*, “wages,” 319. *Judas* means “confession,” 307, 318. *Naphtali*, “a spreading tree” or “vine,” 327. *Reuben*, according to earlier authorities such as Origen, means “a son seeing,” 315 note. Serapis, whose temple in Alexandria is described, 529. *Zebulun*, “nightly flow,” 318. *Sidon* means “senator” or “huntress,” 717.

**Hellenic terms.**—*Angel*, ἄγγελος, that is, “messenger,” from ἀγγέλλω, “I announce,” 331, 429. *Antichrist*, Christ’s adversary, to be born from the tribe of Dan, 321. What books the Fathers call apocryphal, 230. Ἀθηνογέρος, “a scholar of an old man,” 162. *Crocodile*, a kind of beast: Κροκόδειλος, from κρόκος, “saffron,” and δειλία, “fear,” or “fearful,” 430. A demon designated by the name Satan, 323. Deacon, 475. Ἔλιξ, “a tendril,” and figuratively a wooden support planted beside a young tree in order to strengthen it, 305. *Heresy*, αἵρεσις, “choice” or “sect,” from αἱρέω, “to choose, to take away,” 375, 477. How Γένειον is to be understood, 61, 62 Preface. Καταβολὴ κόσμου, “the establishment of the world,” 563. Κατήγητης, “teacher” or “instructor,” 93. Λεβητον or λεβετον: a sleeveless tunic, 411 note. *Martyrium*: a church or temple of God, 107. What the Greek *menologia* are, 436 note, 455 note. Ὄλβιος, “blessed,” has the same meaning as *macarius*, 116. Ὀξύρυγχος, a certain city of Egypt, 408. Παντοκράτωρ, “almighty,” 344. Περὶ ἀρχῶν, the title of one of Origen’s works, “On First Principles,” 71, 127; the same work is written in Latin as *Periarchon*, 127; Rufinus translated these books of Origen partly into Latin, 124. Ποά: the herb used by fullers, 369 note. *Presbyter*, that is, priest, from πρεσβύτης, “elder.” *Symbolum*, that is, a sign and a contribution, 337. Σχῆμα, “habit.” Among Greeks a twofold habit is distinguished: τὸ μικρόν (“the lesser”), belonging to novices, and τὸ μέγαλον καὶ ἀγγελικόν (“the greater and angelic”), belonging to men of proved character, 466 note. *Typus tertianus*, that is, a tertian fever, 393 note.

**Latin usage.**—Ablatives used for accusatives in the articles of the Creed, 339 note. Who is “the tiller of his own land,” 322. *Amictus*: garments covering the exterior are so called, 306. The apostles are called farmers, 322; likewise hunters, 317. “The plough of God’s word,” 322. Who is said “to bite the heel,” 323. “The field of the soul,” “in the soul’s countryside,” 322. What “the everlasting hills” signify mystically, 332. “Delights amid things of little worth,” 399. “Teeth whiter than milk,” 306, 307. Who the dispersed are, 317. “A spring—not a river; nor a river, a spring,” 345. A twofold cold, of weather and of faith, 362. What Christ’s hook is, 354. *Huic* for *nunc*, “now,” 349. How long people are called enemies, 302. *Iniquus* for *inimicus*, in accordance with the Greek, 370. What an insubstantial generation is, 346. *Invitentur* for *irritentur*, 316. Various meanings of the word “lion,” 321, 322. What is called a lion’s whelp, 308, 309. Who is the hand of Christ, 306. *Medium*: what it means “to be in the midst,” 320. Death is called wages, 360. The eye alone capable of light, 352. Blessed bread, 434. Why the Patripassians are so called, 344. Who the chief man of a village, or *protocomes*, is, 437. The pyramids of Memphis: what their use was, 440. Religious people mock the world, and the world mocks secular people, 455. What things are called *reposita*, 304. Various meanings of the word “serpent,” 322. What a lot is, 320. *Spirante* for *inspirante*, 350. Various meanings of *stola*, 305, 310. What it means “to turn one’s back upon God,” 301. Tertian fever, 393 note. What the narrow way is, and what the broad way, 398. What is called viaticum, 437. What the power of the Most High is, 349.

**JEROME (St).**—Words bursting forth from the inner person are signs, XXV, 80. The meanings of words must be considered, XXIII, 556. Ambiguities of words are condemned, ibid. The names of commentators are sometimes introduced without reserve, 417. Obscurity of expression arises from three things: the greatness of the subject, the teacher’s incompetence, or the hearer’s dullness, XXV, 406. Great force belongs to the living voice, which, sounding from its author’s mouth, is uttered and articulated with the pronunciation in which it was conceived in a person’s heart, XXVI, 386. Etymologies of false names must not be fabricated, [Col. 0669] XXIII, 259. Egyptian monks wrote to one another and conversed together in a certain mystical language expressed by a special alphabet, 64–65. “I, Jerome, philosopher, rhetorician, grammarian, dialectician, Hebrew, Greek, Latin, am trilingual.” Likewise Pope Epiphanius: “You will be bilingual, because you have such knowledge of Greek and Latin speech that the Greeks think you Latin and the Latins Greek,” 1462. The words themselves, not merely the things, are seen, XXV, 1100.

**Figures of speech.**—Every metaphor, if transferred word for word from one language to another, chokes the sense and shoots of discourse, as it were, with certain thorns, XXVI, 503–504. Allegory properly belongs to grammatical art; and when we are little children in school we learn how it differs from metaphor or the other tropes. Allegory presents one thing in its words and signifies another in its meaning, 389. What metonymy is, XXV, 1088.

**On the Holy Scriptures.**—On obscure passages of Scripture Jerome says: “Not because individual matters cannot be explained in their proper places and senses, but because, when separated from the higher subject, they form one difficult body; and, if they are understood as they sound, they appear inconsistently and abruptly to conflict with one another and to teem,” XXVI, 406. Difficulty of interpretation, XXII, 512, 754. What ecclesiastical interpretation ought to avoid, 512. What kind of interpretation is to be followed in Scripture, 829. Cause of different interpretations, 705. An interpreter should follow the sense, not the letter, 842. Rule of a good interpreter, 839. The duty of a true interpreter, 570. Rules prescribed for interpreters, 571. On the dangers and difficulties in interpreting the Scriptures, 322, 323. Meaning is clearly disclosed by comparing statements, 456. Editions explain one another, XXIV, 464. How the versions of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion express the scriptural text, XXIII, 452. Theodotion agrees in many places with the Septuagint, 937. The Septuagint translators altered Hebrew names as they wished, XXV, 380. The Septuagint edition was rejected in some respects by teachers of the Church, 514. The whole school of the Jews maintains that only the five books of Moses were translated by the Septuagint, 55. Their translation differs in some respects from the Hebrew truth and the other editions, XXIV, 125. Some things occur in Hebrew books which the Septuagint do not have, XXIII, 454. Scripture’s custom of speaking of the future as though it were past, XXVI, 468. The Septuagint coined new words, 323. They represented Hebrew letters by other letters, 595.

**Hebrew.**—The truth of the Hebrew language, XXIII, 413. The truth of the Hebrew Scripture, 456. In Jerome’s time the Egyptian language was called the language of Ham, 950. The Punic language is related to Hebrew, 994. The Canaanite language lies between Egyptian and Hebrew, but is largely akin to Hebrew, XXIV, 256. The Canaanite language is also called Syriac and was in use at Rhinocolura and Casium, 185. Why we ought to devote ourselves to Hebrew books, XXV, 379. Jerome devoted much time to the study of Hebrew, 1416. Jerome’s teacher was a certain Hebrew, 1019. Baranina, Jerome’s teacher, XXIII, 407. What happens to those who endeavour to render particular Hebrew difficulties, XXVI, 323. In expounding history we should follow the Hebrew truth, that is, the Hebrew text of Scripture, XXV, 1114, 1115. The Jews imagine that all will speak Hebrew, 1378. How Jews mock if their names are not rendered as they themselves pronounce them correctly, XXVI, 595. How easily they attain the true understanding of their own language, 595. Hebrew codices have variant readings, XXV, 1321. The Hebrews have the custom of naming books from their opening words, XXIII, 938. The Hebrew method of calculating numbers, XXV, 552. How the alphabet was read among Greeks and Hebrews, XXIV, 838. The Hebrews express in the feminine gender what we customarily call absolute and neuter, XXIII, 1072. Hebrew names and words are very often corrupted in translations, XXV, 376. Why Hebrew words and names are variously interpreted, 258. The dual number among the Hebrews, 534. They have diphthongs, XXIII, 817. They often use *dabar*, which literally means “word,” in the sense of a thing or matter, XXIV, 398; likewise *cup* in the sense of an instrument or object, XXV, 649; and *horn* for strength and kingship, 1313, 1314. Among the Hebrews there is a forest of ambiguous nouns and verbs, XXIII, 413. Thus, if *daleth*, *beth*, and *resh* are written without a vowel, it must be read either *dabar*, “word,” or *deber*, “pestilence,” XXV, 1314.

**Interpretations of Hebrew, Chaldaic, Syriac, Persian, Egyptian, and Punic names and words.**—Aaron: “strong mountain,” XXII, 786. Aaz (*Achaz*): “seize,” 839. Arazia (*Ozias*): “seizing the Lord,” “the Lord’s strength,” or “his strength,” ibid. Habakkuk: Greek περίληψις, Latin *amplexatio*, “embrace,” XXV, [Col. 0670] 1273. Abba: “father,” in Hebrew and Syriac, XXIII, 843; XXVI, 374. Obadiah: “servant of the Lord,” 557. Abed: “servant,” XXIII, 809. Abel: “mourning,” “vanity,” “vapour,” “wretched”; 773; likewise “committing,” 809. Aber: “he committed,” 791. Abiasaph: “the gathering of my father,” 786. Abimelech: “my father is king,” 775. Abisa: “the burning of the father,” 815. Abiu: “the burning of the father,” 786. Abiud: “the father’s strength,” ibid. Abram: “exalted father,” 775. Abraham: “father seeing the people,” ibid.; “chosen father,” XXVI, 390. Absalom: “father of peace,” XXIII, 827. Achan: “necessity” or “labour,” 775. Achaz: “seizing” or “holding,” ibid., 831. Achibor: “mine,” 823, 832. Accaron: “instruction of sorrow,” “sterility,” 801. Accumarim: temple-servants or fanatics; this was the name of the priests of Baal, Greek τεμενῖται, XXV, 1343. Accem (*Accam*): “nest,” 801. Acheldama: “field of blood”; it is Syriac, not Hebrew, 839. Acheri: “turning aside,” 775. Achi: “my brother” (XX), ibid. Ada: “testimony,” 773. Adad, 775. Adam: “human being,” “earthly,” “native,” or “red earth,” 773. Adama: “soil,” “earth,” or “earthly,” 775. Adar: “sublime” or “cloak,” 791. Adollam: “bearing witness” or “testimony of water,” ibid. Agar: Greek παροικία, Latin *advena*, “sojourner” or “sojourning,” XXIII, 775; XXV, 390. The Septuagint read the letter Ain as G, XXIII, 780. Allel: “praise,” XXIII, 809. Alleluia: “Praise the Lord,” 857. Alluoth: tablets upon which one writes with a boxwood stylus, XXVI, 1289. *Alma* means not “virgin,” but “young woman,” 254. How the alphabet was read among Hebrews and Greeks, XXIV, 838. The names of each letter of the alphabet are interpreted, XXIII, 827; XXV, 787 ff. Amasia: “the work of God,” 832. Amen: “truly,” “faithfully,” XXIII, 839; XXIV, 643; XXVI, 45, 317, 438. Amma: “his people,” XXIII, 801. Amon: “faithful,” “nourishing,” or “burden,” 832. Ana: “answer” or “answering,” 775. Anathot: “obedient,” “answering,” or “sign,” 801; XXV, 644. Anna: “I beseech,” Greek δέομαι, XXVI, 615. Ar: “he raised,” “watch,” XXIII, 791. Arasthem, *arastis*, XXV, 911. Arbe: “locust,” 932. Arnon: “their light” or “their curse,” XXIII, 800. Aroer: “lifting up,” “emptiness of the watchman,” “tamarisk,” 791. Asa: “lifting” or “raising up,” 819. Asael: Greek ποίημα, “work of God,” 815. Asan: “smoking,” 812. Aser: “blessed,” 801. Asida: “heron” or “kite,” XXV, 1450. Assar: “blessedness” or “step,” XXIII, 791. Astaroth: “sheepfolds” or “a work,” that is, ποίησις, “of spies,” 809. Ataroth: “crowns,” 791. Avith: “ruin,” 775. Aun: “useless” or “idol,” 835. Axa: “limping” or “angry,” 807. Azara: “edge” or “border,” 736. Azel: “going away,” “proceeding,” 812.

Baal: “possessing,” “man,” XXIII, 792; XXV, 838. Baala: “possessing her,” ibid., XXIII, 802. Baalgad: “he possessed one girded,” “a girded man,” “a pirate man,” or “fortunate,” XXIII, 802. Baal: “my man” or “possessing me,” XXIII, 792. Baalberith: “possessing birth,” 809. Baalosth: “in ascent,” “ascents,” in the plural number, 802. Babylon: “confusion,” XXIII, 775, 802, 495. Bala: “aged,” XXIII, 776. Balaam: “without a people,” or “in them,” ibid. Badam: “alone” or “in judgment,” 813. Balac: “precipitating,” “devouring,” 809. Bar: in Syriac and Hebrew, “son,” 407, 413, 839. Bara: “he created,” 809. Barabban: “son of our master”; a Syriac, not a Hebrew, name, 840. Barec: “bless,” 41. Barachia: “God is blessed” or “blessed of the Lord,” 839. Barjona: “son of a dove,” 413. Baruch: “blessed,” 833. Basan: “fattened oxen,” XXV, 1023. Basecath: “fat,” 824. Bathel: “virgin of God,” 775. Bazeotha: “his contempt,” 802. Bel: “ancient,” 833. Beelzebub: “possessing” or “devouring flies,” 845. Beelsephon: “ascent of the watchtower.” Benjamin: “son of the right hand,” 776. Benur: “son of air” or “son of fire,” 820. Beor: “in a skin,” 776. Bera: “well,” 809. Beri: “my well,” 775. Benennam: “in them,” “in their midst,” 803. Berith: “covenant,” “pact,” 809. Beselchel: “in the shadow of God,” 803. Beten: “belly,” 803. Beth: “house,” 827. Bethagia: “house of his festival,” ibid. Bethania: “house of his affliction” or “house of obedience,” 839. Bethanoth: “house of those singing before,” ibid. Betharraba: “great house,” 803. Bethaun, Bethaven: “house of uselessness and of an idol”; formerly called Bethel, “house of God,” XXV, 854. Bethlabaoth: “house of those coming,” XXIII, 803. Beth macha: “low house,” “market,” or “tribute,” 816. Bethoron: “house of wrath,” ibid. Bethroob: “house of streets,” ibid. Bethphrage: “house of the mouth of the valleys,” 839. Bethsabec (*bath*, with a short first syllable): “daughter of the oath,” 820. Bethsabee (*bath*, with the first syllable shortened): “daughter of satiety,” 810. Bethsaida: “house of hunters,” XXV, 275. Bethsames, Bethsemes: “house of the sun,” XXIII, 803, 820. Bethula: “virgin,” 803. Booz: “in strength,” 811, 820. Borith: Greek ποά, a certain herb used by fullers, XXV, 685. Bosor: “flesh” or “in tribulation,” XXIII, 385. Bosra: “flesh,” or “in tribulation,” 563, 829. Buz: “despised” or “despising,” 833. Buzites: “contemptible,” 839.

Caath, molar teeth, or patience, XXIII, 776, 786. Cabasam, their assembly, 803. Cades, holy, or changed, [Col. 0671] 786, 792. Cademoth, from the beginning, or the beginning of death, 798. Cades-barne, holy of the chosen, or changed of the chosen, 803. Cain, possession, or lamentation, 776. Cainam, as Cain, ibid. Camon, useless resurrection, 809. Cana, reed. Jerome notes that the Latin word *carma* is derived from the Hebrew *Cana*, 803. Canath, walking, or jealous, 793. Capharnaum, field or village of consolation, 843. Carcar, investigation, 809. Cariathaim, their village or town, 793. Cariatham, their city, or perfect calling, 803. Carmelus, tender, soft, or knowledge of circumcision, 803, 820. Carnaim, horns, 776. Cave (*coa*), patience, or the shouting of a crowd, 820. Cedar, darkness, or grief, 776. Cedma, eastern, or preceding, ibid. Cedmonaei, ancient grief, or easterners, ibid. Cedron, sad grief, or pain, 833. Cenez, contemptible possession, 809. Ceni, my craftsman, or my nest, or possession, 792. Cephas, Peter, a Syriac name, 845. Cetrum (*cetron*), their darkness, or incense-offerings, 809. Cison, they struck, or their hardness, or joy, ibid. Cis, hard, or “vomit of a man,” or “a vomiting man,” 813. Ciscion, whether it signifies a gourd, ivy, or something else, XXV, 1147, 1148. Chabonim, hands, or a heap of thorns, but better, preparations, 833. Chabratha, election; there is much discussion of this word, 824. Chabon, as though understanding, 803. Chaldaic language, XXV, 490. Chaldaeans, who are so called, 703. Chaleb, as it were heart, or whole heart, or dog, XXIII, 793, 813. Chamos, assembled, or as though touching, 793, 820. Cham, hot; it is written with *heth*, 777. Chanaan, σάλος, that is, “their motion,” or merchant, or humble, ibid. “He returned,” or “as though answering,” or “as though moving,” 793; “as though surging,” XXV, 146. Chananaei, merchants, XXIII, 840. Chanani, merchant, changeable, himself poor, ibid. Chaphthorim, hands of explorers, or of turtledoves; better, Cappadocians, 777, 779. Charith, division, or knowledge, 820. Charmi, my vineyard, or my knowledge, 777, 786. Charran, holes, or wrath, or digging them out, 777. Chaseluim, their covered region, ibid. Chaslon, wicked grief, or protection, 793. Chazbi, a cup in me, or sacrifice to me, ibid. How it is used in various senses among the Hebrews, XXV, 649. Chebron, union, or enchanter, or everlasting vision, XXIII, 777. Chelion, completion, or all pain, or from the beginning, 809. Chenneroth, sign of lyres, or as it were lamps, 793. Chennor, recognition of light, or lyre, 836. Cherchoro, recognized removal, ibid. Cherethim, those disposing, Greek διατιθέμενοι, ibid. Chereloth, “you saw a sign,” 803. Chermel, as Carmelus above. Cherubim, multiplied knowledge, or as though “many”; knowledge and understanding, 776, 787, 813. Chesil, strong, 803. Chesiloth, sign of fools, ibid. Cheslon, their revelation, 803. Cheth, striking, 777. Chettim, that is, broken, ibid. Chettura, offering incense, or joined, or united, 777. Chidon, shield, buckler, 803. Chiphara (*caphora*), his whelp, or scattered hand, scattering, ibid. Chladoca, as though demons, XXV, 146. Choadad, chief, XXIII, 777. Chobal, condemnation, 777. Chobar, the name of a river; it is interpreted “heavy,” XXV, 18. Chodchod: Jerome does not know what it truly signifies, 255. Chodorlabomer, as though “generation of a sheaf,” or “as though the god of their sheaf,” XXIII, 777. Chomarim, temple-servants, fanatics; see above, Accumarim. Chorazain, “this mystery of mine,” 840. Chorrethi, scattering or dispersing, 816. Chorri or Chorraeus, flour or floury, or “after me,” or “my hole,” 777. Chorraeus, wrathful, or “from a hole,” whom the Greeks call τρωγλήτης, “cave-dweller,” 798. Chusam, their Ethiopia, 809. Chusi and Chus, Ethiopia, 319, 777, 816.

Dabar, word, matter, XXIV, 398; XXV, 1314. Dabbath (*dabereth*), buttock, XXIII, 804. Dabir, oracle, 820. Dabira, speaking, eloquence, or fearing a bear, 804. Dabrath, speech, ibid. Dachar, those pricking, 820. Dadan, judging, 777. Dafica, “he clung,” or remission, 793. Dagon, fish of grief, 809. Dalaia, “the Lord drawing out,” or “poor one of the Lord,” 833. Dalani, needy, poor, 804. Dalcam, their poverty, ibid. Damaim (*Dommim*), of bloods, 813. Damascus, drink of blood, or kiss of blood, or blood of a sack, 777, 820. Dan, judgment or judging, 777. Daniel, judgment of God, or “God judges me,” 840. Dardahe (*darda*), generation of knowledge, 820. Dasem (*Desem*), bridle, 777. Dathan, their gift, or sufficient gift, 793. David, strong of hand or beloved, XXIII, 813, 840; XXV, 845. Debbora, bee or eloquence, XXIII, 777, 809. Debelatham, of a side, or of the cake customarily made from fresh figs, 793. Deber, plague, XXV, 1314. Debon, abundantly, XXIII, 804. Debongad, sufficiently understanding temptation, 793. Decla, slender, or palm-bearing, 777. Dedan, solitary, or their kinsman, 777. Dedura, his generation, 804. Dennaba, bringing judgment, 777, 839. Desan and Deson, strong nipple, or “he will tread it down,” 777. Deseth, treading, anointing, 829. Deuel, [Col. 0672] “let them acknowledge God,” 793. Dibon, sufficient for understanding, or abundantly understanding, 793, 833. Dimaon (*dibon*), grief is sufficient for them, 820. Dimonia, numbering sufficiently, or height, 804. Dina, this judgment, 777. Dodanim, paternal cousins, 829. Doec (*doeg*), moved, anxious, 813. Domna (*dimona*), silence, 804. Dor, generation, ibid. Dothain, their green pasture, or sufficient failure, 777. Dui, beauty, 820. Duma, silent, 777. Duma, silence, or joy, 804.

Ebal, old valley, 779. Eber, passer-over, 778. Ebraei, those passing over, 787. Ebrioth, crossings, ibid. Ebron, participation in grief or strength, or everlasting increase, ibid. Ebruna, passage over, or transgression, 793. Eceb, afterwards, Greek ὕστερον, XXV, 1033. Ectheta, eminence, XXV, 400. Eden, pleasure or delights, or adornment, XXIII, 778. Edom, red, earthly, 787. Edrai, “the flood will feed me,” 794. Edraim, descent of shepherds, 793. Ecbor, “I shall pass over,” XXV, 1050. Eennathan, “to one giving,” or “God giving,” XXIII, 825. Ela, terebinth, 779. Elam, people of God, or “before the doors,” 825. Elcana, possession of God, 787. Elchiam, portion of the Lord, 824. Eleazar, God my helper, 787. *Eli, Eli, lama azabthaui*, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” 841. Elia, God the Lord, 825, 840. Eliab, God my father, 787. Eliacim, resurrection of God, 825. Eliezer, God my helper, 787. Elim, ram, ibid. Elisa, God my salvation, or salvation of my God, or “to an island,” 778. Elisabeth, fullness of my God, or oath, or seventh, ibid. Elisac, salvation of my God, 821. Elisama, God hearing me, 794. Elisame, God has heard me, 794. Elisaphan, watchtower of my God, or “my God hiding,” 787. Eliu, “this is my God,” 813. Eloecha, your God, XXV, 1030. Eloi, God, XXIII, 809. Elon, army, strength, 794. Elon, oak, ibid. Emath, wrath, XXV, 477. Emim, terrible ones, XXIII, 779. Emmam, their mother, 804. Emmanuel, God with us, 829. Emmer, saying or word, 837. Emor, ass, 778. Emori, mother, my light, 787. Enac, humble, rising, 809. Enaim, eyes or springs, 779. Enam, cloud, 794. Endor, spring of generation, 805. Engaddi, spring of the kid, XXV, 473. Eniel, “my grace, God,” XXIII, 794. Enoch, “he dedicated,” 787. Enon, spring of grief, 794. Epha, loosened, measure, 787; XXV, 449. Ephod, shoulder-garment, XXIII, 793. Ephraim, increasing, fruitful, 793. Ephratha, fruitful, or coming from ashes, or dusty, 809. Er, wakeful, rising, a furrier, 794. Eram, lofty life, 805. Eran, “he emptied,” 794. Erma, his anathema, 793. Ermon, anathema, condemnation, 804. Esaan, “I lean upon” or “I strengthen,” 804. Esaia, salvation of the Lord, 825. Esaion, will or counsel of grief, 821. Esau, making or robust, or heap of stones, or empty, or in vain, 779, 799. Esban, fire in them, 778. Esbel, old fire, or vain, 778, 793. Eschol, cluster, or all fire, 778. Esebon, thought or girdle of grief, 793. Eser, formation or fashioned thing, 778. Esrom, seeing an arrow, or strong, 778, 787. Estmoe, woman of the womb, 805. Etham, completed, or undertaking navigation, 787. Etthan, strong, 794. Etthi, “they feared,” or “they were astonished,” 787. Eva, life, or calamity, or woe, 778. Evi, deadly or fierce, 787. Evi, “I desired,” 793. Evila, suffering, or in labour, 778. Evilath, from the beginning, 813. Evim, wicked, 799. Eud (*Aod*), receiving glory, 809. Ezaion, vision, 821. Ezri, my help, ibid. Ezraeli, seed of God, 820.

Words initially written among the Hebrews with P or Ph are rendered by the Latins with F, but improperly, XXIII, 844, 847. Faarai, “these before me,” 817. Facee, opening, 829. Faceia, “the Lord opening,” or lifting up of the mouth, 825. Pacud, visited or visiting, 837. Fadai, redemption of the Lord, 825. Fadaia, redemption of the Lord, as Fadaid, 721. Fagiel, “meet me, God,” or meeting of God, 794. Fagur, skin of the mouth, or “he gaped,” 794. Falasar, falling prince, 825. Faldas, ruin of poverty, or falling shoot, 779. Falec, dividing, “he divided,” 843. Faleg, as Falec, 779. Falleti (*Phalti*), my saviour, 794, 805, 813. Fallu, wonderful, 779. Fanuel, face of God, 779, 809. Faran, their fierceness, increase, growing up, 779, 794, 799. Faran, mouth of the seer, XXV, 1311. Farao, scattering, uncovering him, XXIII, 779, 787. Faraothoni, “of my flying-away grief,” 817. Fares, dividing, division, 779, 795, 810; XXV, 521. Farisaei, dividers or divided, 841. Farnach, fattened calf, or my departure, 795. Farerrim, torn apart, 825. Fasee, having crossed, crossing, 787. Fathures, deceived, trodden down, or strengthened morsel, 833. Fau, nothing, or suddenly, 779. Felistim, falling ones, or ruin of a cup, or those falling through drink, 779. Felistim, “two fell,” 787. Feleth, ruin or overthrow, 794. Felethia, salvation of the Lord, 837. Fenenna, turning, 813. Fennador, turning of generation, 799. Fennag, nod, 837. Feresaei, separating, or scattered, or fruitful, 779. Fesga, cut off, hewn, or “much mouth,” from *mouth* [*os*] and not *bone* [*os*], 794, 805. Fesor, mouth of blackness, 833. Fetrusim, loosening a measure, 779. Fethuel, breadth of God, or “God opening,” 831. Fichol, mouth of all, from *mouth* and not *bone*, 779. Faennon, “to their mouth,” or “to a bound mouth,” 779. Filisthiim, double ruin, ibid. Finees, sparing the mouth, or “the mouth rested,” was silent, or omen of the mouth, 787, 794, 813. Finoni, my mouth, or mouth of grandchildren, 795. Fison, mouth of the pupil, or change of the mouth, 779. Fithon, mouth of the abyss, or suddenly, 787. Foa (*Phua*), worker, or sound, or manifest, 810. Foa, see Fua. Fodassur, redemption of the strong one, or fortified, 794. Forthommim, perfect division of the glorious people, 835. Fotiel, “this one declining, God,” decline of God’s mouth, 787. Fua, “here,” an adverb of place, or red, 779. Fud, “put on,” 829. Ful, ruin, or falling, 825. Fura, flask, or fruitful, 809. Fut, Libya, or decline of the mouth, 779, 837. Gaam (*Gadim*), valley of heat, 779. Gaas, gaasar, motion, 24, 810. Gabaa, height, 788. Gabaad, hill of a kinsman, 805. Gabaon, hill of grief, 805. Gabaoth, hills, ibid. Gabatha, hill, or lofty, 810. Jaan, answering, 817. Jaare, woodland, ibid. Jaasael (*Jesiel*), “God divided in half,” 795, 829. Jaaxaer, “he will help,” 817. Jabes, dried-up dryness, 810, 814. Jabin, understanding, intelligence, 805, 810. Jaboch, sand or struggle, 781. Jachalia, strength of God, 825. Jachin, preparing, 781, 787. Jacob, supplanter, struggle, or dust, 781, 795. Jacomam, “he avenges the people,” 821. Jactet, assembly of God or help of God, 825. Jael, hind, union of a hind, 810. Jagael, near, 817. Jugur., cultivator or stranger, 805. Jalel, rest of God, 806. Jair, giving light, 795. Jalel, “he awaited God,” 795. Jamin, right hand, 788. Jamna, sea, or his right hand, 795. Jamuel, “his day is God,” 781, 788. Janua (*yanoc*), rest, 805. Janum, sleepy, ibid. Japheth, breadth, 780. Juphie, “it is a mouth,” 805. Japhie, opening, showing, or surface, ibid. Jarden, their descent or—see judgment, 795. Jarec, moon, 780. Jared, descending, or strengthening, ibid. Jarib, judging, avenging, 829. Jarim, of woods or forests, 805. Jasan (*Jassen*), old, 817. Jassa, half, or “the command was made,” 795. Jedala, hand, curse, 806. Jecba, winepress, 810. Jepheel, “God will open,” 806. Jephone, naked, ibid. Jephte, opening, or opened, 805. Jeracon, rust, 806. Jeremia, high of the Lord, 825, 833. Jerico, his fragrance, or moon, 841. Jerimoth, fearing death, or heights of death, 805. Jero-baal, “let Baal judge,” or having judges, 810. Jeroboam, merciful, or judging the people, 814, 821. Jesu, Jesus, Jesua, Saviour, 781, 789, 795, 851. Jetta, inclination, 806. Jetheth, giving, 781. Jeze, he himself, or “is,” 821. Jezecia, holding the Lord, or strength of the Lord, 825. Jezechiel, strength of the Lord, 837. Jezer, strength, help, 806. Jezonia, his ear, 837. Jezrael, seed of God, 805. Joaaz, “where is holding back?” or restraint of the Lord, 825. Joab, enemy, or father, 814. Joach, “whose brother is he?” and better, confessing or glorifying, 829. Joachal, robust and strong, 835. Joadahe, he himself knowing, 817. Joadina (*Joadan*), delicate or tender one of the Lord, 825. Joahe, “where is a brother?” or brother of the Lord, 825. Joalel, life of God, or beginning of God, or awaiting God, 781. Joanan, “he was giving,” or gift of the Lord, 835. Joanna, “the Lord is her grace,” or “the Lord is merciful,” 844. Joannan, “to whom is grace,” or grace of the Lord, 841. Jobel, letting go, changed, or flowing down, 780. Jochabed, “where is glory?” or “is weighty,” or glory of the Lord, 789. Jod, beginning or knowledge, or ruler, 827. Jodane, knowing or recognizing, 817. Joel, beginning, or “he was of God,” 814. Joiachim, “where is preparation?” or preparation of the Lord, 841. Joiacim, resurrection of the Lord, or “he who is rising,” 825. Joradahe, knowledge of the Lord, or “he himself knowing,” 817. Jona, dove, 841. Jonadab, willing one of the Lord, 817. Laabim, burned, or flaming, 781. Laamas (*Leheman*), to iniquity, 806. Laban, white, 781. Labec, acceptable, 806. Labeni, “to my son,” or “heart, I,” or whiteness, 789. Latusim, hammerers, 781. Lazarus, helped, 844. Leben, building, or white, 821. Lesem, “to a name,” 806. Lesendan, judgment of a name, ibid. Levi, added, taken up, 781, 789. Lia, laborious, 781. Maabeel, assembly of God, 807. Maacha, breaking, or broken, 781, 818, 821. Maachathi, “they were broken for me,” or struck womb, 799, 807. Maalaph, from a thousand, or from teaching, 807. Mamad, desirable, XXV, 893. Mamre, “from vision,” or clear, XXIII, 781. Man, manna, “what?” 789. Manaim, camps, 807, 987. Manasse, forgetful, or necessity, 782, 795. Meddin, judgment, 807. Medon, their waters, or measuring, 825, 834. Megia, contempt, 837. Melcha, his king or his queen, 781, 795. Melcham, their king, 834. Melchia, 833. Melchiel, “my king [is] God,” 782. Melchisedech, righteous king, 702. Meleth, choir, or from the beginning, 781. Mello, full, 810. Melloth, fullness, 821. Memphin, from their mouth, 782.
