Samson: their sun, or strength of the sun, 811. Samuel: God is his name, 796, 815, 849. Sanir: remove birth, or giving to a lamp, 837. Saphan: hedgehog, or hare, or his lip, 837. Saphane: his lip, 837. Saphania: the Lord hid, or protection of the Lord, 827. Sapharvaim: books or letters, ibid. Saphat: judging, 822. Saphatia: the Lord judges, 835. Saphau: his lip, 827. Saphir: beautiful, XXV, 1160. Saphon: watchman, XXIII, 785. Sar: see Sor below. Sara: princess; in Greek, Ἄρχουσα, “Ruling Woman,” XXIII, 785; XXVI, 391. Saraa: coals, or distress of evils, 807. Sarad: “that he might descend,” 785. Sarahe: prince of my brother, 797. Sarai: my princess, 784. Saraia: “he was prince,” 835. Sarasar: prince of tribulation, 827, 835. Sarathan: their tribulation, 807. Sare: malicious, or hissing, 785. Sargan: prince of the garden, 830. Sarid: remnants, 808. Saron: prince of sorrow, 807. “His bonds,” or “his distress,” 807. Sarthan: their tribulation, of those demolished, or of those compressing, 822. Sarua: leprosy, ibid. Sasai: long-lived, sixfold, 811. Satan or Sathan: opponent, adversary, 797, 822. Sau or save: worthily, or elevation, 785. Saul: desired, ibid., 790. Sava: eloquence, or cry, 785. Sebacha: little net, 800. Sebean: “with iniquity standing,” 785. Seboim: of goats or does, 784, 800. Sechchothbanoth: tents or shades of daughters, 827. Sechoth: tents, 790. Sechrona: drunkards, or tent, 808. Sechui: variety, 840. Sedada: from his side, 797. Sedecia: “the Lord is righteous,” 822. Sedrach: my splendour, 832. Seffor: bird, 797. Segon: useless speech, 835. Segor: little, 784. Selon: going forth, 838. Seir: hairy or shaggy, 785, 797. Sela (with *sade*): shelter, or his shadow, [Col. 0678] 783. Sela (with *sin*): “as for him,” or his dismissal, or petition, 785. Sela (with *samech*): always, 827. Selam: side (from “side”), 808. Selemia: “the Lord rendering back,” 835. Selom: plucking away, dismissal, or “where is he himself?” 800. Sem: name, or named, 783. Semanoth: humble name, 811. Seme: hearing, 807. Semebad: name of destruction, or “there is destruction,” 781. Semdae and samidae: “my name is knowledge,” 797, 808. Samexi: hear, or my hearing, 790. Semeia: hearing the Lord, 822. Semegar: name of a stranger, or “there a settler,” 811. Semel: idol, 837. Semer: sun, 808. Semoth: names, 839. Semro: his guardian, or “he saw a name,” 807. Sena: lifting up, distress, tooth, 815. Senna: will, 797. Sennaab: father of a tooth, or stench of a father, 784. Sennaar: shaking of teeth, or their stench, 784. Seon: useless sprout, or speech, 796. Sephamoth: lip of death, 815. Sephela: low or level country, 834. Sephion: “it went forth, and of sorrows,” 785, 797. Sephora: his bird or his beauty, or pleasing, 789. Sephra: “she adhered,” or pleasing, ibid. Seraphim: burning ones, or those setting ablaze, 830. Serug: thong, or perfect, 784. Sesac: fine linen of haircloth, or joy of haircloth, 822, 834. Seth: position or placed; or cup; or grass or seed; or resurrection, 783, 797. Setta: thorns, 811. Settim: a kind of incorruptible wood, interpreted “thorns,” 790, 797, 800; XXV, 986. Sia: needy persons, or sleepers, 819. Siba: went forth, came, ibid. Siceleg: sediment of a brought voice, or “he poured out a sextarius,” 807. Sichem: shoulder, 785, 822. Sicher: drunkenness, 797. Sidon: hunting of sorrow, or uselessness, 799. Sigub: lifting up exceedingly, 822. Sihor: little one, or turbulent, 808. Siloa: sent, 830. Simeon: “he heard sorrow,” or name of a dwelling, 789. Simon: “place sorrow,” or “hear sorrow,” 845. Sin: amphora, or temptation, or bush, or thirsty, 790, 797. Sina (with *samech*): temptation, bush, 800. Sinai: my amphora, or my measure, or commandment, 790. Sion: watchtower or watchman, or rock, 819, 822, 830. Scor: firmament, new, or troubled, 834. Sir (with *samech*): cauldron or pot, 826. Sisa: temptation, or floury, 822. Sisai: my long-lived one, 796, 887. Sisaim: going forth, 830. Sisara: exclusion of joy, or “taking away one who departs,” or vision of a horse, 811. Soar: very small, 796. Soba: division, from cutting, 819. Sobab: turning back, ibid. Sobach: turning thee back, ibid. Sobnam and Sobnas: sitting, returning, 827. Soca: branch, 822. Socha: tent, shelter, 807. Sochoth: tents, 797. Sodada: his side, 838. Sodi: my secret, or “he excluded me,” 796. Sodoma: cattle, silent, blindness, 784. Somer: guardian, 822. Somtonphanech: corruptly said from the Hebrew *Saphneth phanee*, “discoverer of hidden things,” 785, 998. Sonam: their cattle, 838. Soni: scarlet, or my pupil, 787, 797. Soon: Tanis, a city of Egypt, 796. Soor: small or southern, 784. Sor: southern, or strong, or rock, or Tyre, 790, 834. Sophan: lip, 797. Sophar: trumpet, to scatter, to divide, 787, 797, 822. Sorec: chosen, excellent, 811. Sua: Saviour, 838. Suba: burnt, turning back, 822. Subochai: dense growth, or thicket, 819. Sue: speaking, or song, 785. Suhalim: foxes, 807. Sui: speaking, 840. Sunamith: whoever shall die, or mortified. Sumen: teeth, scarlet, variety, 826. Sur: wall, strong, distress, straight, or containing, 785, 790. Suriel: God constricting, or strong God, 690. Surisadai: containing, “my breasts,” “the Lord most strong,” 796. Susanna: lily, or his grace, 835. Susi: my horse, 796. Susis: riding, turning away, 835. Suthale: mixed cup, green or moist thorn, 797. Syria is named from Sur, and means lofty or moist, 785.

Tabath: good things, 811. Tabee: slaying, killing, 785. Tabeel: good God, 830. Tabitha: damages or roe-deer, 850. Tabremmon: good to behold, or good height, or good vision of them, 822. Tachor: silent, 785. Talam: dew, or their dew, 822. Tachor: silent, 785. Talam: dew, or their dew, or bedewed, 785, 808. Taphat: a little one comes, 822. Tapnas: mad mouth of a serpent, or covered sign, 835. Tyre: see Sor above. Thaamath: “he gave indignation,” or bile, 835. Thaanac: answering, or humility, 808. Thabor: light coming, or “let light come,” 828. Thaffee: evil, apple, open drum, 838. Thafisa: lameness, remission of life, 823. Thalasar: suspended prince, 827. Thalmai: suspension, or furrow, 811. Thalme: furrow or hanging down, 808, 819. Thamar: palm tree, or bitterness, or changing, 785. Thamath: perfect portion, or consummation given, ibid. Thammuz: consummating, or contempt, 838. Thamna: preventing, or failing, 785. Thamna thares: enumeration of the sun, 811. Thanac: humility, or “he will answer thee,” 811, 823. Thaphnes: covered sign, 823. Thaphse: indignant, or a seat of stumbling, 827. Thara: explorers of scent, or exploration of ascent, or division, 785. Thare: exploration, pasture, wickedness, 797. Tharsis: explorers of [Col. 0679] joy, or joy, 785, 823. Thargel: knowing a yoke, or explorer, 785. Thurtan: “he gave a turtledove,” superfluous, or lengthening, 827. Tharthach: overthrow, ibid. Thau: sign or beneath, 828. Thebes: conversion, or “to make eggs,” or “they were in her,” or “my works made,” 811, 819. Thebni: my straw, 823. Thecue: sounding, trumpet, striking, 819, 831. Thecum: patience, 827. Thedor: peg, 823. Theeth: beneath, 790, 797. Theethim: lower, beneath, 819. Thelabun: scattered, 838. Thelame: streams of water, or bank of waters, 790. Theman: the south wind or the African wind, 785, 831. Themana: south wind, 790. Thena: against, or given, 797. Therac: distant, as though it were called *Proculus*, 827. Theraphim: burning, images, figures, 827, 838. Thersa: pleasing to herself, 797, 823. Thesbites: taking captive, 832. Thesbon: swift to understand, 785. Thicon: the middle, 838. Thiras: fearing, or returning, or superfluous, 785. Thobel: led to mourning; all things; vanity; or to offer, 785, 828, 838. Tholae: little worm, or scarlet, 785, 790. Thomas: abyss, or twin, 843. Thoph: protection of the mouth, or Gehenna, 827, 835. Thophel: tastelessness, 800. Thou: mad or wandering, 815. Thubal: bearing, borne, 838. Totihioc: an Egyptian word, interpreted “overseer,” XXIII, 65. Ulai: marsh, from marsh; or pain of the thigh, or shelter, 835. Ul: suffering, or bringing forth, 785. Ur: fire or light, or airy; or provoking to anger, 790, 808. Urchi: my length, 819. Uria: my light is God, ibid. Us: counsellor, 785. Uram: their swift one, ibid. Urathi: “with me hastening,” 819. Usi: hastening, ibid.

Vaphsi: “and my end,” 797. Vau: “and he himself,” 827.

Zabadia: gift of the Lord, 823. Zabdi: violent flow, or abundant, 809. Zabud: a flowing torrent, which the common people call a firebrand, 823. Zabulon: their dwelling, or his oath; or dwelling of strength; or flow of night, 785, 843. Zabulonites: his dwelling, 811. Zacharia: remembrance of the Lord, or mindful of the Lord, 843. Zachaeus: justified or righteous, ibid. Zachur: mindful, 797. Zain: olive, or fornication, or this, 828. Zamri: psalm or song, 797. This Zamri: provoking, or embittering, 823. Zanoe: “he rejected,” or “this one rested,” 809. Zara: rising, or sunrise, 786. Zarda: very alienated, 838. Zare: “he rose,” 797, 843. Zava: iniquity, 823. Zavan: motion, or their fluctuation, 785. Zebedee: endowed, or “this one flowing,” 843. Zebee: victim or sacrifice, 828. Zebul: dwelling, 811. Zabulon: dwelling of strength, 789. Zechri: remembrance; this one provoking or embittering, ibid. Zemram: their song, or showing the time, 785. Zib: wolf, 811. Ziphaeans: sprouting or flowering, 815. Zocleth: drawn or prolonged, 823. Zoob: gold, 797. Zorad: alien, or descent, ibid. Zorobabel: he himself, master of confusion, 843. Zozommim: “these thoughts,” or “what is this water?” or prepared in battle-line, 800.

Saint Jerome drew very many etymologies of both Greek and Latin names from the Hebrew source; we append them here for beginners in languages. In some cases we have merely attempted to indicate the Hebrew word; in the rest, the diligent reader may, if he wishes, undertake this labour. There is no need to warn him that Jerome himself very often admits that he has proceeded by force, XXIII, 846.

Greek and Latin names derived from a Hebrew root by Saint Jerome.—Achaia: “whose brother?” or “his brother,” or “brother of the Lord,” or “my brother is the Lord,” XXIII, 851; from *acha aca*, or *acha ia*, or *achath aia*. Aeneas: answering, or poor, or misery, 846; from *anach*, “to answer, to be afflicted,” ibid. Adrias: containing evils, or place of evils, ibid. Agrippa: gathering suddenly, ibid. Alexander: lifting the distress of darkness, 855. Amphipolis: a people falling by the mouth, 846; from *am-pi-patal*, “the people rolls the mouth.” Andreas: splendour in a station, from *adar* (with *he*), “splendour.” Better from Greek Ἄνδρος, “of a man,” 845. Andronicus: splendid for the stadium, 851. Ampliatus: beaten people, ibid. Apelles: gathering them, 846; from *aphel* (with *ain*), “he was puffed up, swollen,” ibid. Apollonia: their teaching or synagogue, ibid., from *palal*, “he judged.” Forum of Appius: free or strong abundance, ibid. Aquila: suffering or bringing forth, from *ith calel* (with *coph*), “to be disturbed, divided,” ibid. Archelaus: recognising lion, 839. Areta: stupor or descent, 853. Arios pagos, or ἀρεώπαγος, Areopagus: primal solemnity, 846; from *a resith pouga*, τὸ principium remissionis vel cessationis, “the beginning of remission or cessation.” Aristarchus: mountain of superfluous manufacture, or raising a crown, 846. Aristobulus: raising a shoot by sorrow, 851. Artemis, that is Diana: raising illnesses, 846. Asia: lifting up, lofty, 851, 856, 857. Asia: taking away, or proceeding, 853. Athenians, Athens: explorers, answering, humble, scattered in time, from *anah*, “to answer,” or “to be oppressed,” 846, 855. Augustus: standing solemnly, or solemnity added, 843; from *negous*, “king, ruling, emperor.” Berenice: elegantly or choicely moved, or innocent son, [Col. 0680] compounded from Syriac and Hebrew, 847. Bithynia: beautiful daughter, little virgin, or daughter of the Lord, 851. Caesar: principal possession, 843; from *cashar*, “it succeeded well, it increased”; in Syriac, *cesara*, “prosperous success, increase.” Candaces: changed, 847. Canna, “reed,” from the Hebrew *cana*, 803. Cappadocia: redeemed by the hand of the Lord, 847. Cyrenes: heir, ibid. Claudius, Claudia: hope of tranquillity, 847, 856. Cnidus: ecstasy of mind, 847. Colony: their revelation, ibid. Colossae: voice made, 854. Cornelius: understanding circumcision, 847. Corinth: he himself rises, 856. Crescens: dark, ibid. Crete: completed calling, 857. Crispus: knowing or recognising, 847. Cyprian: sad or sorrow, ibid. Cyrenians: heirs, ibid. Dalmatia: denotes great poverty, 856. Damaris: silent head, 847. Damascus: cup of blood, ibid. Demas: silent, or earthly, or bloody, 856. Demetrius: binding very strongly, or pursuing excessively, 847. Derbe: son of generation, or speaking, ibid. Devil: flowing down, 840, 857; from *zoub*, “he flowed,” or from Arabic *zabab*, “he fluctuated, swung, moved himself in the air”; or also from *dabab*, that is, “he crept upon the earth,” in the manner of serpents. The ancients, and Jerome himself, wrote *Zabolus* in place of *Diabolus*. According to Jerome himself, *Zabdi* denotes violent flow, 823; but *Zabud* means a firebrand. Thus Devil is rightly called a circling, crawling, or flowing firebrand. According to the Greek etymology, it means “slanderer,” from the verb διαβάλλω, “to bring a slanderous accusation”; among the Hebrews he was called Satan. Dionysius: judged, or fleeing violently, from *Dan*, “he judged,” 847. Dioscuri: beautiful for covering; thus the twin Castors are called, ibid. Drusilla: of a peaceful race, ibid. Electe: ascending, 851. Elimas: unto transgression, or causing transgression, 847. Ellada: said in the Syrian language “for knowledge,” or “for ascent,” ibid. Hellenes, Greeks: “unto those ascending,” or knowledge of God, ibid. Epaphra: fruitful, or indeed seeing, 854. Ephesus: my will in it, or their end, 847. Eutyches: mad; but in Greek he is called fortunate, ibid. Evodia: laying hold of the Lord, 854. Felix: ruin of a work, 847. Festus: mouth of many, ibid. Gaius: moved; but better, valley-man, 847, 851, 853. Galatia: magnificent, translated, 847, 853. Iconium: preparation or consolation, 848. Italica: ecstasy of mind, ibid. Jason: made in a command, 851. Julius: beginning, 851. Junia: beginning, 851. Justus: sparing, or he himself lifted up, 848.

Laissa: into salvation, 848. Laodicea: tribe beloved of the Lord, or “they were in vomiting,” 857. Linus: white, or flute-player, 857. Libertines: making straw, 848. Lisanias: birth of temptation, 843; from *seloudnusah*. Luke: he himself rising, 857. Lucius: he himself raising up, 848. Libya: those coming, or entry, ibid. Lycaonia: for raising up, ibid. Lycia: weeping, ibid. Lydia: “which we cannot say,” squandered, ibid. Lysias: begotten, ibid. Macedonian: eastern, 848. Mark: lofty in command, 488, 851, 854. Medes: measuring, or measured, 848. Mesopotamia: raised in calling; better derived from Greek because it is surrounded by two rivers, ibid. Miletus: begetting, ibid. Mysia: touching, stroking, 848. Myrrh: bitter, ibid. Narcissus: ascent of joy, or lamp dividing, or gathering, 852. Neapolis: remarkable movement, 849. Nereus: lamp of the Lord, 852. Nicanor: standing lamp, 849. Nicolaus: fool of the languishing Church, ibid. Niger: ascending, ibid. Nympha: joined to their mouth, 854.

Olympas: childbirth chamber, 852.—Onesimus: beautiful, or answering, 855, 837. Paul: wonderful, 851. Pergamum: dividing their horns, 858. Persis: trying, unsewing her sides, 852. Peter: recognising, 844; from *pithroun* (with *thau*): interpretation. Again, Peter: unbinding, or unshoeing, 853; from *petra* (with *teth*): loosening, covering. Philip: mouth of a lamp, or mouth of hands, 843, 847, 854; from *pi-lapid*, “mouth of a lamp,” or *phi-laphath*, “curved, hollow mouth.” Philadelphia: saving one who clings to the Lord, 857. Philemon: wonderfully given, or mouth of their bread, ibid. Philetus: declining, or my mouth, 856. Philo (φελόνης or φενόλης): face of God, ibid. Philologus: chief in speech, or “my mouth for him in a garden,” 851. Phyton: mouth of the abyss, 849. Pilate: mouth of the hammerer, 844; from *pi-latous* (with *teth*), which has the same meaning. Pisidia: mouth of sound, 847. Pontius: declining counsel, 844, 849; from *poun*, “to be without counsel.” Pontus: bending, ibid. Portius: dividing their hardness, ibid. Prochorus: gathering fruit, ibid. Ptolemais: leading to measure, ibid. Publius: his tent, ibid. Pudens: clothed with counsel, 857. Puteolus: declining, ibid. Pyrrhus: unbinding, ibid.

Quartus: sounding superfluously, 852. Rhode: seeing or strong, 849. Rhodes: vision or descent, ibid. Rome: lofty, sublime, ibid., from Raama. Romans: lofty or thundering, ibid. Ros: head, 845, from *Rosch*.

Calamina: wave, shadow of movement, or greeting of the judge, [Col. 0681] 849. Samothrace: hearing of revelation, or of response, ibid. Sapphira: narrating, learned, or bookish, ibid., from *sepher*, “book.” Sardis: prince of beauty, 858. Sarona: singing sorrow, ibid., from *Sir-on* (with *sin*). Saulus: temptation of one looking, or fullness, 849. Sebaste: circuit or circling, 850. Scaeva: little fox crying out, 850. Secundus: lifting up, ibid. Seleucia: lifting herself, ibid. Sergius: prince of a valley, or little garden, ibid. Sicarii: drunkards, ibid. Silas: sent, 849. Silvanus: sent, 851, 853, 855. Sosipater: saving the scattered, 853. Sosthenes: saving them, or “give me joy,” 849. Spania, for Hispania: expedition or girding, 852. Stephana, Stephanus: rule, your regulation, or your watchman, 849, 853. Syntyche: speech, 854. Syracuse: wall, or rampart of sorrow, ibid. Syrtes: narrow straits, tribulations, 850. Taverns: their visions, or good vision, ibid. Tertius: joining, or attaching himself, 853. Tertullus: pleasing to dung, or to their embankment, 850. Tarsus: exploration of joy, ibid. Timon: numbering thirst, or fatness, ibid. Theophilus: bearing upward; but Jerome prefers the Greek etymology, ibid. Thessalonica: hastening to strengthen or establish a shadow, ibid., 854. Timothy: beneficent, 853. Titus: seeking, or good, ibid. Troas: serving, 857. Trophimus: unbinding chambers, ibid. Tyrannus: containing them, or strengthening them, 850. Urbanus: rejoicing in light, 853. Hymenaeus: sleeping, 856. Zeno: his movement, or moving him, or himself resting, 857.

A few matters remain to be added concerning Greek or Latin speech.

Greek.—The elegance of Attic salt and sacred discourse, XXIII, 472. The refinement and wit of Socrates, 487. Exultant Greece borrowed something from the Latins through Jerome, 453. Latin speech does not express Greek precision, 231. The fifth dialect of the Greeks is called Aeolic, 951. The breadth of the Greek language, 501. The ambiguity of the same language, ibid. Ἄγρωστις (*agrostis*): in Latin, grass, XXV, 904. Αἰῶνες (*aeons*): whence Valentinus derived his own, XXVI, 314. Ἀνεθέμην: why it is translated “I conferred” rather than “I rested content,” 332. Ἀποκάλυψις, that is, “revelation”: a name used by none of the sages of the age among the Greeks, 823. Ascodrogi: see Tascodrogi below. Ἀτυφία, or μετρώτης: philosophers call it humility, 236. Βελομαντία, or ῥαβδομαντία: a kind of divination, XXV, 206. “Divine Library”: thus Saint Jerome entitles the Sacred Books, XXIII, 683. *Cantharus*, or scarab: a dung-worm, XXV, 1297. Crypt: what it is, 575. Demons, XXV, 877, 1247, 1329. The Devil called lion, bear, and serpent, 1052. Diapsalma: what it means, 1312. Διόσπολις (*Diospolis*): an Egyptian city, and where it is situated, 289. Δῶμα (*dōma*): a roof-terrace, 399. Epilogue used in the sense of a curse, XXIII, 487. Ecstasy: what it is, XXV, 1274. Γιγαντομαχία (*Gigantomachia*): what it is, 1042. Ἰδιώτης (*idiōtēs*), that is, an ignorant person, XXVI, 526. Labyrinth: what it is; its description from Virgil, XXV, 447. Λίμνη Ἀσφαλτῖτις (*Lake Asphaltitis*), the bitumen lake, is now called the Dead Sea, 472. Λοιμός (*loimos*), that is, plague, XXV, 1314. Μεταφορικῶς: tropically, figuratively, metaphorically, XXVI, 503, 504. Μετωνυμικῶς: by metonymy, XXV, 1088. Monogamy is preferred to bigamy, XXVI, 564. Νεκρόδειπνα: meals of mourners, called *parentalia* among the Latins. Incurable opisthotonus: what it is, XXVI, 540. The name Pammachius is interpreted from πᾶς, “all,” and μαχή, “battle,” XXV, 992. *Paedagogus* is so called because he leads or guides children, XXVI, 368. Definitions of parable and enigma, XXV, 161. Parables familiar to Syrians and Palestinians, XXVI, 132. Parasangs: what they are, XXV, 986. Passaloryncitae: who they are, XXVI, 356, note. Ηεπληροφορημένον [probably ἡ πεπληροφορημένον]: what it means, 221. Periousios: what it means, 587. Peripatetics: who they are, 597. Περιοχή: “summary,” XXV, 1088. *Phantasia* is seldom or never taken in a good sense, 1323. Phylacteries, or little picture-tablets, are small slips of writing; in Greek πυκτάτιον, or little book, XXVI, 168, note. Phocaeans or Massiliots are called trilingual because they speak Greek, Latin, and Gallic, 354. Πόα (*poa*): an herb used by fullers, XXV, 685. Φυλλέα (*phyllea*): what it means, 947. The Rhône is so called from a colony of Rhodians that settled beside this river, XXVI, 354. Scenopegia is the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles, interpreted from σκηνή, “tent,” and πηγνυμι, “to fix,” XXV, 927. Στήλη denotes a statue or an inscription, 902. Scybala, that is, refuse, XXVI, 334. Cyclamen: a kind of tree, XXV, 1077. Tascodrogi: a sect of heretics, XXVI, 356, note. Tiara: a kind of cap used by Chaldeans and Persians, XXV, 508. Tristatae, that is, “threefold distillers,” 219. Tropology: a transformation of speech, 146. Ξαῖρε, that is, “hail,” XXVI, 64.

Jerome’s Latin usage.—Latin usage does not correspond to Greek idiom, XXVI, 164. Latin speech does not always unfold Greek precision; rather, at times, somewhat more diffusely and weakly, we express something other than what is written, 615. Tullius, king of orators and illuminator of the Latin tongue, is accused by the Greeks of extortion, XXIV, 935. “To worship falling down”: what it means, XXV, 507. An adulterer is one who violates holy things and corrupts chaste things, 175. The term “building” is used for small works, 509. Recognition: what it is, 459. Friend: what it is, 1219. Distresses: what we are accustomed to say when placed in distress, 1052. A year is so called because it always turns and returns into itself, 23. The eagle holds sovereignty among birds, as the lion among beasts, 793. The windings of riddles, 1290. An inkstand is named from ink, 87. Ears called gates, 1158. Jaundice: what it is, 1030. Golden rings with which women were accustomed to adorn themselves, 134, 135. *Conferre*: what it means, XXVI, 332. Confession: in how many senses it is understood, XXV, 541. Consummation: what it is and how many kinds there are, 290. “To speak heart to heart”: what it is, 836. Horn or horns for kingdom or strength, 1313, 1314. *Cubitum* and *cubitus*: the same measure, 378. What we do unwillingly is always difficult, 199. Samaria was deflowered, 216. Drunkenness of mind: what it is, 1010. The difference between a thief and a robber, 872, 873. Shoulder signifies work, 871. The letter H is said by many to be merely an aspiration, XXIV, 799. Grammarians think it should not be considered a letter, 841. Why earrings are so called, XXV, 134. *Indolorius*: painless, XXVI, 505. Injury: one who thinks of God cannot commit injury, XXV, 1245. Why the month January is so called, 277. Beasts of burden have their name from helping, XXIII, 296. A woman’s quarrel, XXVI, 416. The letter K appears superfluous in Latin, except in the word *Kalendae*, XXIII, 799. The New-Year’s gift of the Kalends, the Saturnalian purse, and the Minerva gift: what they are, XXV, 540, note. Latium was later called Lavinium, 289. Barking for slandering, XXVI, 406. Why the Dead Sea is so called, XXV, 472. *Morticinium*: what it is called, 49. Womanly quarrel, XXVI, 416. Numbers: the practice of the ancient Latins in reckoning numbers, XXV, 552, 553. What a nuptial garment is, XXVI. Oblique: what “oblique windows,” Greek τοξικαί, are, XXV, 581. Forgetfulness of truth is swift, 505. An obol is one-twentieth of a shekel or stater, 450. “All” is taken for the greater part, XXVI, 463. In what sense Jerome calls Arius a door, and Aetius and Eunomius bars, XXV, 996. A *petasatus*, a carrier of books, perhaps so named from a *petasus*, 1453. Fishing for fish and fishing for human beings, 677. Plantings of sinners: what they are, 595. Monstrosities of words which no Latin human ear has ever heard, XXVI, 323. Q, a letter which no language other than Latin possesses, XXIII, 807. Quadrans: what it is and whence it is named, XXVI, 38. The use of *quis* (“who?”), *quid* (“what?”), in Scripture, XXIII, 539–540; XXV, 1017, 1177, 1258. The queen of sins: what she is, XXV, 594, 595. The king’s side: what it is, 523. Religion: whence it is named, 1090. Extortions, of which the Greeks accuse Tullius, XXIV, 935. Roundness is the most beautiful of shapes, XXV, 23. Greeting: how it is made among Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, 64. *Saucomaria* is a vessel made from a gourd, 1148. Scandal: whence it is named, XXVI, 107. Sellers of old clothes are those who trade in worn garments, XXV, 255. The difference between carving and casting, 1304. The difference between buffoonery and foolish talk, XXVI, 520. *Scutulata* are garments woven in a net-like pattern, XXV, 255. A bold saying, 425. The value of the Italian sextarius, 48. Latins measure distance along roads by thousands of paces; Gauls by leagues; Germans by *rasti*; Persians by parasangs, 986. Filth and sin have different meanings in Scripture, XXVI, 248. The tempter who asks questions: who he is, 166. Fear is understood in a twofold sense, 537. Who are called translated persons, 318. Tumult: what it is, remarkably described, XXV, 1179, 1180. “Woe” is the last of punishments, 1050. Victory: the first victory of Catholics is to expose the secrets of heretics, 1105. The wine of the wicked: what it is, 648. A living voice is that which resounds from its author’s mouth and is uttered and distinguished with the pronunciation in which it was generated in the heart, XXVI, 386.

LUCIUS FLAVIUS DEXTER.—Saint Jerome, in the prologue to his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, teaches us what progress Dexter made under his most learned father Pacian, and how he trained his youth in humane letters, XXXI, 15. Dexter devoted himself to humane letters in such a way as diligently to apply himself to ecclesiastical history, 16. Having entered military service under Theodosius the Great, he advanced so far that he deserved to attain the prefecture of the praetorium of the Eastern Empire, ibid. He grieved greatly that pagans reproached Christians with their lack of learning, ibid. Therefore he urged Jerome to compose a Catalogue of illustrious men among Catholics, by which the detractors of Christians might be confounded, ibid. Saint Jerome’s letter on this subject. Dexter was likewise a friend and kinsman of Paulus Orosius, 19.

Greek terms excerpted from Dexter’s *Chronicle of Universal History*, or from Bivar’s commentary.—Agathoppius for Agathos Oppius, that is, “good Oppius,” XXXI, 235. The canonical [Col. 0683] epistle of the blessed apostle James is so called because it was included by the Church in the canon, that is, rule or catalogue, of Books, XXXI, 122. Chronicles, according to Cassiodorus, are images of histories and very brief records of times, 49. Eclipse of the sun, 94. Eugenius, that is, “noble,” a surname given to Saint Marcellus from the piety of the faithful, as was then customary, 235, note. Philotheus, that is, “beloved by God,” a surname of the apostle Philip, 191, 261. Theologian, that is, one speaking or preaching divine things, a surname of the blessed evangelist John, 131, 138, 232. Theophoros, that is, “God-bearer”: this had been the surname of Saint Ignatius the martyr.

On Latin speech.—*Omnimoda historia*, “universal history,” the title of the Chronicle composed by Dexter, XXXI, 30. Commentary. Prefect of the praetorium: who he is and what his office is, ibid. Praetorium: what it is, 51. Salmatas for Sarmatas, 65. Tortosa, a city of Spain, formerly called Dertosa, 273.

AUGUSTINE (Saint).—Voice properly belongs to animate beings, XXXV, 1009. Voice is sound in relation to human beings; it is affection in relation to God, XXXVIII, 1093. Voice is the material of words; words indicate voice given form, XXXIV, 257. The distinction between voice and word, XXXVIII, 1304, 1309. Voice is empty without a word, ibid. The service of voice exists for the sake of the word, 1305. Voice fails as the word grows, 1307. The whole voice is heard whole by all and whole by each individual, XXXIII, 518.

“Word” is understood in many senses, XLII, 968. A word is conceived by love, whether of creature or Creator, 967, 968. The word precedes every human work, 1073. It necessarily precedes speech and action, ibid. The word of the heart is consent, XL, 350, 352. The human word so passes to another as to remain in the heart, XXXV, 1671. On the truth and falsity of our word, XLII, 1077. When a word is true, 1072, 1078. Sound is the vehicle of the word conceived in the mind, XXXVIII, 185, 677, 1097. The word which we speak is, as it were, another mind proceeding from a mind, by which it makes itself known, XL, 183, 184. The external word is the voice of the internal word, XLII, 1071. The purpose for which words were instituted, ibid., 243. Words are necessary only for expressing the will, XXXVI, 499. Every use of words consists in signifying, 20. Misuse of words extends widely in all languages, XLII, 410. Words admonish us to seek things; they do not present them for us to know, XXXII, 1215. It is disgraceful to dwell upon words when the matter is established, 932. The meanings of words, not the words themselves, must be considered, XXXV, 2097. “Word” used for deed, XXXIV, 503, 800. To love truth in words rather than words themselves is the mark of an outstanding disposition, 100. “He never uttered a word that he wished to recall,” says Tullius of a certain man; this is more credible of one excessively foolish than of a perfectly wise man, XXXIII, 586.

Speech: its purpose, XXXII, 1193. Speech is the expression of the will, XXXVIII, 102. The distinction between speech and understanding, XL, 311. When we speak, we aim at nothing other than to bring our own mind itself into view for the mind of the hearer, 183, 184. How a child learns to speak, XXXII, 666. Speech in a metaphorical sense, XXXIV, 886. How it may be determined whether the language of Scripture is figurative, 71, 72, 74. Figurative expressions become obscure through ignorance of things, 47. What integrity of expression is, 44.

“Tongue” is understood in two ways, XLII, 296. The tongue testifies what the heart means, XXXVII, 1191. “Tongue” for the sound produced by the tongue, XXXV, 1952. “Tongue” for speech made by the tongue, XXXVI, 597. There was one original language before the tower of Babel, XXXIV, 401. The origin of the diversity of languages, XLI, 483. Proud impiety introduced the diversity of languages, and the humble piety of the Church brought it into unity, XXXVI, 636. The descent of the Holy Spirit upon unbelievers was once the greatest sign of all languages, XLI, 612. Knowledge of languages is necessary for understanding the Scriptures, XXXIV, 42. The original language should be trusted rather than its translation, XLI, 654, 455. There were as many languages as there were people dispersed from the construction of the tower into different regions, XXXVII, 2324. The division of languages, a just punishment for pride, 2160. Through this division of languages the mystery of the Scriptures remained, until its due time, among one people, ibid. Very many agree that languages were divided into seventy-two, ibid.

Grammar is called *γραμματική* in Greek and *litteratura* in Latin, XXXII, 1012, 1099. Grammar is the discipline that guards and regulates articulated speech, 894. It professes to preserve history, 1012, 1099. Whether it belongs to grammar to teach sounds and accents, 1010. The rules of grammar are zealously observed while God’s commandments are neglected, 673. Curtains hung over the thresholds of grammar schools, 670; XL, 713. A book on Grammar, written in dialogue form by Augustine when he was at Milan and about to receive baptism, 591. This book has been lost, 591. Grammar teachers wearing *paenulae*, XXXII, 672, note 1. Grammarians as judges of poets, XXXII, 1014. A preacher should not fear the criticism of grammarians, provided he instructs everyone [Col. 0684], XXXVIII, 228, 1371. The rules of grammarians should receive less attention in sermons if the people happen to understand better in barbarous speech, XXXVI, 386; XXXIX, 1776. He calls grammarians “letterlings” contemptuously, XXXIII, 443.

Letters are signs of sounds; sounds are signs of things, XLII, 1071. Teachers of the first letters, XXXII, 670. Some think letters began with the first human beings, XXXIV, 620. Mercury, inventor of letters, 49. The origin of letters, XXXII, 1011. Isis handed down letters to the Egyptians, XLI, 597, 598. What a letter is, XXXII, 1410. Vowels, semivowels, and mutes, 1385. Why letters are not common to all nations, XXXIV, 38. The great usefulness of letters, or the art of writing, XL, 872, 973. The same letter begins the name of God and that of the devil, XXXVII, 1375.

The word *nomen* (“name”) is so called as though from *notamen* (“mark”), XXXIV, 230. A name is not a name for its own sake, but for the sake of what it signifies, XXXVI, 122. Names were imposed on things according to each person’s pleasure, XXXII, 1116. Naming things is an indication of the highest wisdom, XLV, 1432. When the thing is established, one need not trouble oneself about the name, XLIII, 469. A name is of no benefit where the thing does not exist, XXXV, 2007. Various endings of nouns, XXXII, 1385 ff. Which numerical names are indeclinable (*ἄπτωτα*), and which declinable, 1408. On the pronoun, 1394. Pronouns are either definite, indefinite, or more-than-definite, ibid. On the declension of pronouns of the first, second, and third persons, 1395. On the declension of indefinite pronouns, ibid. Pronouns of quality, 1396. On the verb: its person, number, mood, and tense, 1397. On the first conjugation, 1398; the second, ibid.; the third and fourth conjugations, 1399. What a common verb is, ibid. A deponent verb, 1400. On neuter-passive and impersonal verbs, 1401. On inceptive, frequentative, and desiderative verbs, 1402. On the adverb, 1402 ff. On the preposition and its government, 1406. On the interjection, 1408. The difference between synonyms and homonyms, 1421. On paronyms, ibid.

Dialectic, in which Augustine includes syntax, XXXII, 1409. On simple words, ibid.; on combined words, ibid. What simple and combined propositions are, ibid. On the origin of the word *verbum* (“word”): why it is so called—the Stoics’ opinion, 1411. On the force of a word, 1413. What is obscure and ambiguous; the three kinds of ambiguity, 1414. Ambiguity arising from equivocal terms, 1416. On equivocal and multivocal terms according to Aristotle, 1421. On denominatives, 1422.

The authority of sacred Scripture must be sought from the original language, XLI, 455. The treatment of Scripture is a great and arduous work, XXXIV, 19. Rules for understanding Scripture, XXXVIII, 21, 30, 46, 149, 180, 198, 450, 456, 470, 556, 609; XLIII, 673. Various translations of sacred Scripture, XLI, 603. How Scripture was translated into different languages, XXXIV, 38. An ambiguity of Scripture in one language is removed by another, XXXVII, 1536. Many translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek, and countless persons into Latin, XXXIII, 43. Scripture was translated from Greek manuscripts into Latin, XLIII, 709. Very few expounders of divine Scripture write in Latin, whereas innumerable ones write in Greek, XLII, 214. The translation of the Old Scripture from Greek into Latin was made according to the Seventy translators, XXXII, 592. Why certain things occur in the Septuagint translation which are not in Hebrew manuscripts, and conversely, XLI, 604. Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint translation should both be used, 605. What obelisks and asterisks signified in Greek manuscripts, XXXIV, 590. The Latin translation of Scripture varies so greatly among different manuscripts that it can scarcely be tolerated, XXXIII, 213. Augustine wishes to be free from such great incompetence among Latin translators, 291. Scripture does not always speak literally, XXXV, 1303. Why Scripture speaks in figures, XI, 663. Figurative expressions are mixed with prophetic ones, XLI, 548; and with literal ones, 691. To take figurative expressions of Scripture literally is miserable slavery, XXXIV, 68, 69. In Scripture far more things are suggested through allegories and riddles—partly through words alone, partly also through narrated deeds, XLII, 247. How the metaphorical modes of speech of sacred Scripture are to be understood, XXXIV, 166. One who errs piously in interpreting Scripture should be corrected, 34. Many things are usefully repeated in Scripture, XXXVII, 1817. Scripture may fail to be understood because of unknown or ambiguous signs, XXXIV, 42. Scriptural ambiguity lies either in proper words or transferred words, 65. What is to be done in cases of ambiguity in the words of sacred Scripture, 43, 44, 65, 66. The same word in Scripture does not always signify the same thing, 78. In sacred Scripture everything said or done must be understood literally, figuratively, or in both ways, XXXVIII, 556. There are three kinds of expression in Scripture, XLII, 846. There are three differences among writings of any kind, 73. How knowledge of an unknown word or phrase is to be obtained, XXXIV, 45. It is a familiar feature of Scriptural language that a conjunction is used even when no preceding clause exists [Col. 0685] to which the following clause may be joined; what this signifies, XXXVI, 79, 80. How indefinite propositions in Scripture are to be understood, XXXVIII, 450. Scripture sometimes puts the container for what is contained, XXXVII, 1414. It speaks of a part as though it were the whole, XXXIII, 638; XXXVII, 1115. It uses the plural for the singular, XLI, 519. It narrates future events as past, XXXVII, 1476. It puts the future for the past and the past for the future, XL, 305; XLI, 705. The past is often used for the future, but the future rarely for the past, XXXIV, 723. What a devout reader should do in obscure passages of Scripture, 262. They must be explained from clearer passages, 79; or by recapitulation, 86. A passage of Scripture capable of bearing a double meaning must not be interpreted by a hasty assertion, 260. Nothing prevents the same Scriptural passage from being understood in different ways, 80. An uncertain passage is more safely explained through other passages of Scripture than through reason, 80. Obscure passages must be explained from other manifest and wholly unquestionable passages, XXXVIII, 264; XXXIX, 1634; XLI, 332, 333. In Scriptural difficulties the word of God must be honored, XXXVII, 1907.

Hebrew and related languages.—Hebrew letters are most ancient, XLI, 598. The Hebrew language received its name from Heber, 400. When it was invented, 522. It remained in the house of Heber, 400. Hebrew letters existed before Moses, 598. Hebrew was originally the language of all, 400, 522. It was either the first language, or formed from many languages, XXXVII, 2324. It was fitting that Moses should use the first language, ibid. It was transmitted only to God’s people, XLI, 490. Hebrew, with its letters, was preserved through succession from the Fathers, 598. It is very closely related to Punic, 488, and joined to it by a certain proximity of meaning, XXXVIII, 648. Hebrew, Punic, and Syriac are related languages, XXXV, 1520. The Hebrew, Syriac, and Egyptian names in sacred Scripture had been interpreted by Augustine’s time, XXXIV, 62. Hebrew names were translated first into Greek and then into Latin, XXXVI, 302. Among the Hebrews, it was not permitted for anyone except scribes alone to handle Hebrew letters, XLI, 365. Jewish learning, XXXVI, 888.

*Abba* and “father” are the same, XXXVI, 1012; XXXVII, 1419. Abbir Germaniciana, a city of Africa, XLIII, 211. Abel: “mourning,” XLI, 461. Abennezer: “stone of help,” 539. Abimelech: “my father’s kingdom,” XXXVI, 302, 308, 602. The change and meaning of Abraham’s name, XLI, 707. Abrahamium: the place where the bodies of the patriarchs are, XXXIV, 592, 596. What Ἀβράξας (*Abraxas*) is, XLII, 26. Absalom: “peace of the father,” XXXVI, 73, 97. Achitophel: “ruin of a brother,” 97. How Achish is rendered, 302, 305, 308. Adam: “human being,” applicable to both sexes, XLI, 460; XLV, 1583, 1585. Adam signifies the world by his own name, XXXVII, 1236. Adonai: “Lord,” XLII, 313. Egypt in Hebrew signifies darkness or tribulations, XXXVI, 1001; XXXVII, 1477, 1750. Aeinan and Aeinaim: “springs,” XLI, 457. Aethan: “strong,” XXXVII, 1120. Hagarites: “proselytes,” 1053. Alleluia: see Halleluia. Amalek: “a people licking,” 1053. Haman: “his brother,” XXXVII, 1110. Amen, that is, “true,” XLII, 313. Ammon: “son of my people,” or “son of sorrow,” XXXIV, 818. Amorites: “those who embitter,” XXXVII, 1750. Anna: “grace,” XLI, 528. Anubis, an Egyptian deity, XXXII, 750. Asaph: “synagogue,” XXXV, 1347; XXXVI, 916, 920. Assyrians: “those who direct,” XXXVI, 1021. Astaroth and Astarte: the same as Juno, XXXIV, 797. Aynan: “their sorrow,” XLII, 457. Baal, a name of Jupiter, XXXIV, 797. Babylon: “confusion,” XXXVI, 773, 774. Bala: “grown old,” XLII, 434, 435. Balaam: “reprobate and condemned,” XL, 136. Bashan: “dryness,” XXXVI, 832; and “confusion,” ibid. Benjamin: “son of the right hand,” 1022. Beersheba: “well of fullness,” or “seventh well,” XLII, 458. Cain: “possession,” XLI, 460, 461. Carthage is understood under the name Tharsis, XXXVI, 536. Cedar: that is, “darkness,” XXXVII, 1603. Ham: “hot,” XLI, 477. Canaan: that is, “humble,” XXXVII, 1394. Hittite: “cut off,” XLII, 450. Hushai: “silence,” XXXVI, 97. Kishon: “their hardness,” XXXVII, 1054. David: “strong of hand,” XXXVI, 148, 151, 302, 628. Doeg: “motion,” 601. Eden: “delights,” pleasure, or feast, XXXIV, 202. Endor: “fountain of generation,” XXXVII, 1054. Enoch: “dedication,” XLI, 460, 461. Enos: “man,” a word proper to the male alone, 460. Ephrata: “mirror,” XXXVII, 1720. Ephraim: “fruitfulness,” XXXVI, 719, 1022. Ethan: “strong,” 940. Eve: “life,” XXXIV, 212, 215; XLIV, 442. Gilead: “casting away,” or “revelation,” XXXIV, 818, 820. Galilee: “revelation,” 1216. Gebal: “a vain valley,” or “falsely humble,” XXXVII, 1053. Gath: “winepress,” XXXVI, 648. Gog: “roof,” XLI, 676. Halleluia: “praise the Lord,” XXXVII, 1938; XXXVIII, 996, 1147, 1190, 1192; XXXIX, 1632. From Heber comes the designation “Hebrews,” XLI, 598. Why the Hebrews are so called, XXXII, 636; XXXIV, 552. Whether they were named from Heber or Abraham, XLI, 481. Why the Hebrew language is so called, 400. See above. [Col. 0686] Her: Pellicius, XLII, 456. Hermon: “exalted light,” or “his anathema,” XXXVII, 1127, 1735. Jabin: “wise,” 1053. Jacob: “supplanter,” 1937. Japheth: “breadth,” XLI, 477. Idithun: “leaping over them,” XXXVI, 412, 729, 970. Idumaea: “earthly,” XXXIV, 721. Jechonias: “preparation of God,” XXXIV, 1076. Jemini: “right-handed,” XXXVI, 97. Jephthah: “opening,” XXXIV, 817, 818. Jericho: “moon,” XXXVI, 728. Jerusalem: “vision of peace,” 122, 598, 734; XXXVII, 1656, 1755, 1761; XLI, 637. Jesus: in Greek, Σωτήρ, “Savior”; in Latin, *Salvator*, XLII, 1025. Joab: “enemy,” XXXVI, 715. Jonadab: “the Lord’s willing one,” 876, 890. Joseph: “increase,” 1021; XXXVII, 1037. Joshua was formerly Auses: why his name was changed, XLII, 327. Iras: “vision of my brother,” 457. Isaac: “laughter,” XLI, 510. Ishmaelites: “obedient to themselves,” XXXVII, 1052. Israel: “seeing God,” XXXVI, 959; XXXVII, 1254, 1609, 1624. Judah: “confession,” XXXVI, 540, 835, 865; XLII, 457. Judaea: “confession,” XXXVI, 959. Laban: “whitening,” XLII, 432. Lazarus: “added,” XXXV, 1350; XXXVI, 872. Leah: “laboring,” XXXV, 1045. Lebanon: “whitening,” XXXVI, 912; XXXVII, 1370. Lot: “turning aside,” ibid., 1053. Midian: “turning aside judgment,” ibid. Maclith: “giving birth,” or “suffering,” XXXVI, 613. Magog: “from the roof,” XLI, 676. Malchus: “about to reign,” XXXV, 1931. Manasseh: “necessity,” XXXIV, 820. Massephat: “attention,” XLI, 539. Melech: “choir,” XXXVII, 1109. Merra: “bitterness,” XXXIV, 615. Moab: “from the father,” XXXVII, 1052. Moses is older than all Greek poets and philosophers, XLI, 596, 599. Naid: “commotion,” XLII, 261. Naphtali: “my expansion,” XXXVI, 835. Noema: “pleasure,” XLI, 465. Odollamite: “testimony in water,” XLI, 457. Oreb: “dryness,” XXXVII, 1053. Passover: “passage,” XXXV, 1785. Pharan: “fruitful mountain,” XXXIV, 775. Pharaoh is not the name of a person but a royal title, interpreted “dissipation,” XXXVII, 1750. Philistines: “falling through drink,” 1053. Racha: the cry of one who is indignant, XXXV, 1754; an interjection of indignation, XXXIV, 42, 43. It is said that *racha* could not be translated into another language, ibid. Rachel: “seen beginning,” XXXV, 1046; XLII, 432. Raphaim are Giants, XXXV, 749. Sabbath: “rest,” XXXVII, 1960. Salmana: “shadow of commotion,” 1054. Solomon: “peaceful,” 1668; XXXVIII, 94, 96; XLI, 541. Samaritan or Samarite: “guardian,” XXXV, 1707. Samson: “their sun,” XXXVII, 1041. *Samen* means “heavens” among the Punics, XXXIV, 797. Sarah, formerly Sarai: both names are interpreted, XLI, 507. Saul: “request” or “appearance,” XXXVI, 148, 600. The name of Saul comes from *Saul*, 916; XXXVIII, 917, 948. Seir: “hairy,” XXXIV, 774. Selmon: “shadow,” XXXVI, 826. Selom: “his dismissal,” XLII, 456. Shem: “named,” XLI, 477. Seon: “temptation of the eyes,” XXXVII, 1750; or “useless shoot,” or “burning temptation,” 1760. Seth: “resurrection,” XLI, 460, 461. Sinai: “commandment,” XXXVI, 829. Zion: “watching,” 70, 122, 598, 1006. Sisera: “exclusion of joy,” XXXVII, 1053. Sor: “narrowness” or “tribulation,” ibid. Syriac is close to Hebrew, XXXV, 260. Syria: “lofty,” XXXVI, 715. Tabor: “coming light,” XXXVII, 1127. Tamar: “bitterness,” XLII, 456; or “changing,” 457. Tharsis: “humble commandment,” XXXVI, 993, 1001. Theman: the South Wind or Africa Wind, XLI, 589. In Punic, *Tyria* means “salvation” in Latin, XXXV, 2096. Tyre derives from the Hebrew *Sor*, XXXVII, 1053. Uriah: “my light is God,” XLII, 459. Zeb: “wolf,” XXXVII, 1053. Zelpha: “gaping mouth,” XL, 435. Zychaeans: “flourishing,” XXXVI, 619.

Greek words and Hellenisms.—The Greek language holds preeminence among nations, XLI, 235. Greater credence should be given to Greek, as the language from which Scripture was translated into Latin, XXXVII, 1539. The grammatical figure by which Greek and Latin are spoken of, XXXVI, 335. Greek pronunciation whereby εἰρήνη (*peace*) is rendered in Latin as *irini*, XXXV, 2420. Greeks count by letters, 1473. Greece had nothing more illustrious than Athens, XLI, 567. No small glory comes to Athens from letters and philosophers, 561. The reputation of the Athenians in every branch of learning is everywhere renowned, ibid. The most talkative schools of philosophers arose at Athens, XLII, 454. Homer, a poet sweetly vain; reading him was bitter to Augustine as a boy, XXXII, 671. The Greek translation of the Seventy interpreters does not differ from the Hebrew, XLI, 606. Why that edition is marked by obelisks and asterisks, XXXIII, 261, 753. Augustine urges Jerome to restore it to the Latin truth, 243. Why Augustine preferred translations from Greek to those from Hebrew, 242. The dual number is used by the Greeks, XLI, 695, 696. Augustine as a boy hated Greek letters because of the difficulty of learning a foreign language, XXXII, 671. What Αβράξας (*Abraxas*) is, XLII, 26. The Academy, or Plato’s school: why it is so called, XXXII, 943. What ἀδολεσχῆσαι means, XXXIV, 565. Air is called heaven, XXXII, 865; XL, 292; XLI, 684. Whether air and ether are the same, XLI, 119. What aetiology is, XL, 68. Love-feasts (*Agapes*), 383. The difference between ἄγαν (“exceedingly”) and σφόδρα (“very”), XXXVII, 1444, 1509. The Donatists call the Circumcellions *Agonistici*, 1732. The devil is called an *agonothete*, 1859. How αἰών is customarily rendered in Latin, 1187, [Col. 0687] 1393. What αἰώνιον means, XLI, 506. What allegory is, XXXVII, 1347. *Alogia* is the name for such indulgence in feasts that one departs from the path of reason, XXXIII, 141. What ἀναβαλμοί are, XXXVI, 415; XXXVII, 1596. What analogy is, XXXVIII, 364; XLII, 69. Ἀνάστασις means “raising up”; ἐξανάστασις, “resurrection,” XXXIV, 487. The derivation and meaning of *anathema*, 510. Androgynes or hermaphrodites, 294; XLI, 486. The broad sense of the term “angels,” XXXII, 602. Angels are called *nuntii* (“messengers”) in Latin, XXXV, 1596. What an *anticategoria* is, XLIII, 510. Antiphrasis, XL, 534. Who the Antipodes are, 487. Who are called Anthropomorphites, XXXIII, 628. What ἀορασία means, XLI, 781. Ἀπάθεια (“freedom from passion”), 415. Which writings are apocryphal, XLI, 470. Ἄποιον: chaos, XLII, 195. What an *apophoretum relationis* is, XXXIII, 645. Apostles are called *missi* (“those sent”) in Latin, XXXV, 1781. If no apostle is specified, Paul is understood, XLIV, 589. Apotactites: the name by which the Apostolic heretics were designated, XLII, 32. What ἀποτελέσματα are, XXXIV, 278. Aquila translated Scripture from Hebrew into Greek, XLI, 470, 603. What Arcadian demons are, XLI, 575. Ἀρχιμάγειρος: commander of the army or of cooks, XXXIV, 582, 584. Who the Archontic heretics are, XLI, 29. Areopagus, the council-house of the Athenians, XXXVIII, 808; why it is so called, XLI, 567. Aristotle, founder of the Peripatetic school, XLI, 237. Arithmetic, XXXIV, 61. Artotyrites: why so called, XLII, 31. Ascites, ibid. Asia is the name of a province and of the third part of the earth, XXXIV, 783; “Asia” means “pride,” XXXV, 2417. What astrology is and its invention, XXXII, 1014. What *asystaton* is, XLV, 1095. Why Athens is so called, XLI, 566. What an atheist is, XXXII, 1246. Atlas: the name of an astrologer, XLI, 599, and of an African mountain, 565. Who the Atlantic philosophers are, XLI, 234. Atoms, the principles of things according to Epicurus, 230.

To be baptized: Latin usage has so adopted this word from Greek that it is not usually understood elsewhere except in the sacrament of regeneration, XLV, 837. Borborytes, a kind of Gnostic, XLII, 26.

What an ecclesiastical canon is, XLIII, 489. The canon of sacred books, XXXIV, 41. *Catacarposis*: the remains of a whole burnt offering consumed by fire, 678, 979. Who the Cataphrygians are, XXXIII, 438. A poultice made from the Eucharist, XLV, 1315. What a *catastolium* is, XLII, 375. Why the Cathari are so called, 32. Catechism, XL, 210, 219, 228. Catechumens, XXXVIII, 136; XLIII, 357. Heaven is called the chair of our teacher, XXXVIII, 1203, 1237, 1320. The Catholic name is the mark of Christ’s Church, XLII, 175. Who were called Χιλιασταί, XLI, 667; in Latin, *Millenarii*, 668. Why the surgical art is so called, XXXII, 1088. Christ: the name of a sacrament, XXXV, 2000. Christians were first so called at Antioch, XXXII, 622. *Ciceion* or *ciceia*, a kind of shrub, XXXIII, 263. The distinction between χρόνους (“times”) and καιρούς (“seasons”), 900. *Cupsones*: that is, a cave, a hollow place, from κύπτω, “I bend,” XXXVIII, 293. Why Cynic philosophers are so called, XLI, 624. What a cynocephalus is, 59, 87, 485.

Δάκτυλος: “finger,” XLII, 42. What demons are according to Apuleius, XLI, 263; according to Plato, 241. Why they are so named on account of knowledge, 273. What the ten-stringed psaltery is, XXXVIII, 79. The *Deuterosis* of the Jews: their traditions, XLII, 637, 642. The devil is called *accusator* (“accuser”) in Latin, XXXIV, 741. The devil is called *minister* (“servant”) in Latin, XXXIX, 1441. What a diapsalma is, XXXVI, 80. What a didrachma is, XXXVII, 1783. *Dogmata* are the decrees of sects, XXXV, 1326.

What *echola* is, XLIII, 639, 640. What the Church is, and its various names, 122, 123. What ecstasy is, XXXIV, 391, 464, 470; XXXVIII, 360. Greek *eleemosyna* is Latin *misericordia* (“mercy”), XXXVIII, 1043; XL, 268. Ellipsis is familiar to Greek and Hebrew speech, XXXIV, 524. What ἐναντίον means, XLI, 483. What ἔννοιαι are, 232. *Entheca*: that is, a repository of treasure, XXXIX, 1572. Ἐπιβάται, or marines, XXXIII, 977 note; XLIV, 915. The derivation of *episcopus*, XXXVIII, 580; XLI, 647. Epithalamia: songs customarily sung by scholars at weddings, XXXVI, 494, 495. The derivation of *Evangelium*, XXXVII, 1417; in Latin, “good message” or “good announcement,” XXXVIII, 266, 710; XLII, 210, 214. What the Eucharist is, XXXIV, 71; XXXV, 1723; XLII, 382, 658, 879, 881. What *eulogia bread* is, XXXIII, 100, 103; XLIII, 357. What εὐσέβεια means, XLI, 279. An exedra: the place from which a bishop spoke to the people, 770. *Exenia* for *xenia*, XXXVI, 195. What exorcism is, XXXII, 968. An ecclesiastical exorcisterium, XLIII, 578.

What the *gazophylacium* was, XXXVI, 765. Who genethliacs are, XLI, 796; XXXIV, 51. What geometry is and its invention, XXXII, 1014. The origin of the Gnostics and their name, XLII, 26. Grammar is called *γραμματική* in Greek and *litteratura* in Latin, XXXII, 1012, 1099.

What heresy is, XXXII, 999; XLIII, 469, 471. Heliopolis: “city of the sun,” XXXIV, 584. The derivation of *hero*, XLI, 299. Hesperus: the star Venus, 720. What a holocarpoma is, XXXIV, 678, 679. Homer the poet, XXXII, 671; [Col. 0688] XLI, 80. Ὁμοούσιον (“of the same substance”): although this word is not found in the Scriptures, another expression may be found to which it is rightly judged applicable, XXXIII, 1039, 1040, 1048. *Hyle*: what the Greeks understand by this word, XLII, 379, 380, 550. A hymn is a song containing praise of God, XXXVI, 914; XXXVII, 1947. What hyperbole is, XLI, 499; XLIV, 788. What hypocrisy is, XXXIV, 208. What hypogea are, XXXVIII, 267.

What ideas are, XL, 30; Plato’s ideas, XLI, 218. Idioms are the distinctive properties of a language, XXXIV, 485, 557. What an idol is, XXXVIII, 417.

Letheus: the river of forgetfulness in the underworld, XLI, 310.

What a *machaera* is, XXXVII, 1955. *Mammothrepti* (“children reared by grandmothers”), XXXVI, 246. The derivation of “martyrs,” XXXVII, 1523; Greek *martyr*, Latin *testis* (“witness”), XXXV, 1979; XXXVIII, 1297. *Martyrium*: Latin *testimonium* (“testimony”), XXXVII, 1539. Mathematicians: who they are, XXXII, 737; XXXIII, 1061; XLI, 142, 144. What *mathesis* is, XLII, 667. Melody in ecclesiastical chant, XXXII, 800. What *melos*, on which Augustine proposes to write, is, XXXIII, 369. *Metreta*: the name of a measure, XXXV, 1461. Metre: measuring or measure, XXXII, 1115. *Moechus*: “adulterer,” XXXIII, 341. What a monoceros is, XXXIV, 881. Monomachy: single combat, XXXVIII, 197. Sacred mysteries, XL, 443. *Mythicon*: Latin *fabulosum* (“fabulous”), XLI, 181. Necromancy: what kind of divination it is, 223. What new moons are, XLII, 354. The beginnings of neophytes, XL, 208. Νοϊρόν (“the intelligible”; reading uncertain), XLII, 910. What an oenophoron is, XLI, 198. Ὁμοούσιον (“of the same substance”), XLII, 707. Ophite heretics, called *Serpentini* (“Serpent-people”) in Latin, XXXIV, 217; XLIII, 589. What ὁρμή means, XLI, 628. Orphans: Latin *pupilli*, XXXV, 1829. Orthodox: those who follow the right doctrine, XXXIV, 127. Ortygometra: a kind of bird, 617. An oxymoronic statement, XLV, 1480. What παιδεία means in sacred Scripture, XXXVII, 1547. What it means to sing a παλινῳδία, XXXIII, 157, 237, 244, 290. Why Pan in Arcadia was called Lycaeus, XLI, 574. To engage in pancratium is to box, XXXVI, 679. Pantomime, XXXIV, 64; XXXVIII, 1020. What a parable is, XXXVI, 852. How it differs from a problem, 983. Paraclete is interpreted “consoler” or “advocate,” XXXV, 1828, 1868. Paradise, properly a wooded place, ibid., 482. *Paregorizare*: “to soothe,” XXXVII, 1638. *Paroecia* for diocese, XXXIII, 953, 955. Πάσσαχος: “stake,” XLII, 42. Who the Passalorynchites are, ibid. Pentapolis is Libya or Cyrene, XXXVIII, 294. The day of Pentecost, 73. What a period is, XXXIV, 94. Who perjurers are, XLI, 294. What *perizomata* are, XLIV, 564, 685, 784, 785. The Greeks call the sun *Phainon*, XXXIV, 236. *Philocalia*: “love of beauty,” XXXII, 922. What phlebotomy is, XXXVIII, 146. What phlegm is, XLI, 348. Who the frenzied are, XXXVIII, 538, 945, 1058. Incurable phthisis, ibid., 489. Natural philosophers, XL, 235. Pygmies are so called as though cubit-high, XLI, 485. Who a *pileatus* is, XXXV, 1440. Pyrites, a Persian stone that burns the hand holding it, XLI, 715. The derivation of *platea*, XXXVII, 1327. There is no pleonasm in Scripture, ibid., 1399. Why πλεονεξία (“covetousness”) is so called. Who the Πνευματομάχοι (“Spirit-fighters”) are, XLII, 59. Why poets are called riddle-makers, XXXIV, 738. Who are theological poets, XLI, 572; called wise men, 581. Polygamy, XL, 395. Presbyter: a name derived from age, XXXIV, 566. Problems, Latin *propositiones*: what they are, XXXVI, 983. Πρωτότοκα, or “firstborn,” XXXV, 758, 759. Pseudo-prophets: heretics, XXXVI, 101.

Ῥύγκος: “nose,” XLII, 42. Those whom the Greeks call Σαπρόφιλοι (“lovers of rottenness”), XXXII, 1183. Precious sarcophagi, XXXVIII, 611. What schemata are, XLII, 417; they are more commonly called figures, 1068. Schism or division, XXXVIII, 1165, 1244. Sciopods, as though “shadow-feet,” XLI, 485. Scyniphes: very small gnats; what sophistical speech is, XXXV, 58. What σπιθαμίς is, 636. What stigmata are called, ibid., 2148. Syllogism, 58; XLI, 58. What symplasia is, XXXVI, 772. What a sympsalma is, 80. The derivation of *symbolum*, XXXVIII, 1058, 1072. Symphoniacs of demons, XLIII, 748. What the Symplegades are, XLV, 1315. Synagogue is named from “congregation,” XXXV, 2089. Synaxes, or meals held at the memorials of martyrs, XXXII, 719. Various examples of synecdoche, XXXV, 578, 579.

Τελεταί: magical consecrations, XLII, 897, 900. Who the Tessarescaedecatites are, 31. The kinds of theology, XLI, 180, 192. Θεοσέβεια (“reverence for God”), XLII, 1035; XLIV, 211. Θηριακή (“theriac,” an antidote for venom), 602. Who the theurgists are, XLI, 294, 305. Theurgy: the art of invoking gods, 286. Θρησκεία (“religious worship”), 278. What a trigonus is, XXXVII, 1961. The term “tropes” is more customary than “modes,” XLII, 1068. What it means to beat a drum, XXXVI, 306, 308. *Typhus* for arrogance, XXXIII, 332. A tyrant is called an unjust king, XLI, 67.

Ὕλη in Greek, *silva* (“wood”) in Latin, XLII, 556. The difference between *ousia* and hypostasis, 917.

Zelotypy (“jealousy”): where the term properly applies, 142. What zeal is, XL, 140; XLII, 142. What tares are, 347. The difference between ζωή (“life”) and βίος (“life/livelihood”), 1004.

Augustinian Latin.—Augustine as a boy loved Latin letters [Col. 0689], not those taught by his first masters, but those taught by the persons called grammarians, XXXII, 670. The first elements, in which one learns to read, write, and count, were no less burdensome and bitter to him than Greek letters, ibid. “When I recited,” says Augustine, “I was applauded beyond many of my peers and fellow pupils,” 673. Augustine declaims against the manner of training youth in literary studies, ibid. Latin was the vernacular language in Africa in Augustine’s time, 671. Carthage and Rome, two cities productive of Latin learning, XXXIII, 436. Because of the poverty of Latin in the region of Hippo, the administration of the Gospel labors greatly, 293. Italians harassed Augustine over many word-sounds, XXXII, 1015. Why the book on Grammar, relegated to the appendix, is considered not a genuine work of Augustine, 1395, admonition. Although this Grammar sets out rules of the Latin language, whether it belongs to Augustine is not our concern; for another grammarian seems to surpass it in antiquity, and it offers no slight usefulness to beginners in Latin. We therefore excerpt what follows from this book.

All nouns end in thirteen letters: namely, the five vowels *a, e, i, o, u*; the six semivowels *l, m, n, r, s, x*; and the two mutes *c, t*. Examples of each ending are given in every gender, XXXII, 1385 ff. An epicene noun is one applicable to either sex while expressed in a single gender—for example, *lepus* (“hare”), masculine only (*hic lepus*), yet used for either sex, 1393, 1394. A common noun is one used in either gender according to the sex intended, such as *sacerdos* (“priest”), masculine or feminine (*hic* or *haec sacerdos*), 1386. Which nouns are called proper and which appellative, 1387. Neuter nouns are declined in *-um, -us, -ur, -or, -ar, -er, -os, -e, -al, -el, -en, -u, -ut,* and *-a*, 1388, 1389, 1390. The names of letters, such as *alpha*, *beta*, and so forth, are neuter; hence the saying from the Sibylline books, Τρία κάππα κάκιστα (“three very evil kappas”), interpreted of Cornelius Sulla, Cornelius Cinna, and Cornelius Lentulus, 1390. By common nouns one must understand nouns of common gender, ibid. Nouns of this class are declined in *-a, -o, -es, -is, -os, -us, -er, -ex, -eps, -unx, -ux, -ebs, -yx, -us, -il, -ul, -ur,* and *-or*, 1391, 1392. Nouns of every gender ending in *-ax, -ex, -ix, -ox, -ux, -ans, -ens, -ons, -ar, -ers, -ors, -us,* and *-es* are declined (it should be noted that these are what we now call adjectives), 1392, 1393. Some nouns have only singular or only plural number, 1394.

A pronoun is so called because it performs the function of a noun, 1394. Pronouns are either definite, indefinite, or less-than-definite, ibid. Definite pronouns denote a certain person; indefinite pronouns, someone generally; less-than-definite pronouns do not designate a person so fully that no pointing gesture is required, such as “I,” “you,” and so forth, 1394. Personal pronouns are declined, 1395; indefinite pronouns likewise, ibid. Pronouns of quality, 1396.

In verbs, the following tenses are distinguished: present, imperfect past, perfect past, pluperfect past, and future, 1397. The moods are the indicative, imperative, optative—also called subjunctive or conjunctive—and infinitive, 1397. There are three persons in the verb, both in singular and plural number, 1397. Verbs are either active, by which we signify that we do something, or neuter, by which we neither do nor suffer anything, for example *stare* (“stand”), *iacere* (“lie”), *cubare* (“recline”), and *sedere* (“sit”), 1398.

Four conjugations of verbs are assigned, 1398, 1399. A verb is common when, under a passive form, it includes both active and passive meaning, as *hortor* (“I exhort”), *iaculor* (“I throw a dart”), *consolor* (“I console”), *osculor* (“I kiss”), *tutor* (“I protect”), *scrutor* (“I examine”), and so forth, 1399, 1400. A verb is called deponent when it has active meaning under a passive form, as *opinor* (“I suppose”), *minor* (“I threaten”), *grator* (“I give thanks”), *gratulor* (“I congratulate”), and so forth, 1400. On neuter-passive and impersonal verbs, 1401. Some verbs become inceptive by changing *-o* to *-asco, -esco,* or *-isco*, as *ardeo, ardesco* (“I burn; I begin to burn”), *tepeo, tepesco* (“I am warm; I become warm”), *labo, labasco* (“I fall; I begin to fall”), *dormio, dormisco* (“I sleep; I begin to sleep”), and so forth, 1402. Likewise, some become frequentative by changing *-o* into *-ito*, such as *dicto, dictito* (“I say repeatedly”), *lego, lectito* (“I read; I read repeatedly”), *clamo, clamito* (“I cry out; I cry out repeatedly”), and so forth, ibid.

An adverb is so called because it always adheres to a verb, 1402. An adverb is a part of speech which, added to a verb, explains and completes its meaning, 1403. Adverbs derived from nouns have six endings, 1404. Prepositions governing the accusative, the ablative, or both, 1406.

Latin words and expressions.—Weaning (*ablactare*), weaning (*ablactatio*) in a spiritual sense, XXXVI, 246; XXXVII, 1713. To cut off someone’s eyes: to win their love, XXXIV, 729. Those swallowed alive and those swallowed dead: who they are, XXXVI, 761. “Abundance” is used antiphrastically of what does not exist, XXXIV, 800. “Deep calls to deep”: its meaning, XXXII, 850. An accident always indicates some change in a thing, XLII, 913. To “name” a woman to oneself (*adnominare aliquam*): to make her one’s wife, XXXIV, 624. The inward ascent to God, XXXVI, 413; XXXVII, 1629, 1639. To be sick in a spiritual sense, XXXVII, 1320; XXXVIII, 495. Why poets are called “riddle-makers” (*aenigmatistae*), XXXIV, 739. To “lighten” someone (*allevare aliquem*): to kill him, 824. Spiritual height, XXXVII, 1728. High spirit or courage (*animositas*), XLIII, 332. An antidote against every sin, XXXVIII, 1270. To be added or attached to a thing: that is, to love it, XXXIV, 495. To be attached to the people: its meaning, 594. April (*Aprilis*) as though “opening-month” (*aperilis*), XLII, 346. The fitting and the beautiful: their meaning, XXXII, 701, 703. The term “ark” is variously understood by the holy doctor, XLI, 472. “Architectonic” is the art of craftsmen working in gold, silver, or another metal, XXXVI, 654. God’s outstretched bow: that is, His threats, XXXVI, 686. The Lord’s ark: the Church, XXXIV, 127. The Silver God: who he is, XLI, 103. Not everything dry is land, XXXIV, 234. Arithmetic is not an institution of human beings, 61. Those possessed by idols: who they are, XLI, 50. How an earnest-payment (*arrha*) differs from a pledge (*pignus*), XXXVIII, 158, 858. The derivation of “art,” XLI, 128; XXXII, 1024, 1182. The liberal arts: what they are, XXXII, 1015. Vulgar art: its meaning, XXXIV, 146. Asiatic luxury, XLI, 103. To hear before God: its meaning, XXXVI, 193. The name of a father is sometimes bestowed upon a grandfather, XXXIV, 493. How *auferre* (“take away”) and *tollere* (“remove”) differ, 998. Augustine is called “a man, an example of integrity and justice,” XXXIII, 514. Paulinus calls him “this master in the faith,” XXXIII, 470. Distraction of the heart: its meaning, XXXVI, 202. Gold and silver allegorically: their meaning, XXXVIII, 331. To live blessedly: its meaning, XL, 24. Blessing (*benedictio*), that is, good speech, 320. *Beta* means one thing among the Greeks and another among the Latins, XXXIV, 54. Light-shunning moths, XLII, 363. The true good: its meaning, XXXVIII, 438. The highest good: its meaning, XXXIII, 438; XLI, 232. Everything that has an end is brief, XXXVI, 727. Among the Romans, bullae were insignia of rank, XLI, 101. Those suffering from epilepsy are called *caducarii*, XXXII, 967. How a song (*canticum*) differs from a psalm, XXXVI, 78, 813. “To take captivity captive”: its meaning, 830. *Caraenum*: boiled wine, XXXII, 1365. The goddesses Carmentes, who sing fates to those ignorant of them, XLI, 122. *Carraria*: what it means, XXXIX, 1578. *Cartigare*, XXXVI, 422. Patchwork garments (*centones*), XLI, 548. Christians were first called thus at Antioch, XXXII, 622. They were so called on account of the holy chrism, XLI, 676. City: its meaning, 447. The derivation of “clerics,” XXXVI, 824. *Cluere*, that is, to cleanse, XLI, 118. *Cluere* is equivalent to “to prevail,” XLV, 1147. How coeternal differs from coeval, XXXVIII, 666. To be “remembered by commandments,” that is, admonished, XXXIV, 706. To shorten matters for someone (*compendiare alicui*): to kill him, 824. Augustine calls the clerics to whom he writes his fellow-clerics (*conclerici*), XXXIII, 470. Concordial, 592. *Confit*, 80. The consenting gods: who they are, XLI, 130. Fellow-recruits (*contyrones*), XXXVIII, 1077. “You will hear jackdaws more easily in Africa”: a proverb, XXXIII, 436. “Tomorrow, tomorrow”: the raven’s cry by which many remained outside when the door was shut, XXXVIII, 512. To believe in God: its meaning, XXXV, 1631. Why we do not believe “in” an apostle or a human being, 1741. *Cupsones*: their meaning, XXXVIII, 293. *Curia* seems to derive from *cura*, “care,” XLI, 285. How a curious person differs from a studious one, XLII, 80. The Donatists in the city of Rome were called *Cutzupitae*, XXXIII, 196. One seeking to behead the Church, XXXVIII, 725. *Defit*, XXXIII, 833, 1076. The derivation of “offences” (*delicta*), XXXVI, 950. *Deponderare*, XXXIX, 1513. How descending properly differs from falling, XXXVI, 1598, 1631. A curse (*devotatio*) is uttered with malediction, XXXIV, 738. “Day” is understood in different ways, 231, 295. Father Day, the god to whom women who lose their child in childbirth belong, XLI, 122. To accuse someone (*differre aliquem*), XXXII, 1203. To take indignation: its meaning, 720. Dignity: its meaning, XL, 22. “Lodging-place of the saints” for a monastery, XXXII, 1340. “The Lord be with you,” XII, 1049. *Domnaedius* means “lord of the house,” XXXVI, 429. “Lord,” “poor lord” (*domnus, domne pauper*), XXXVIII, 113. *Donec* (“until”) meaning “no longer,” XI, 77. “Sleep” for death in Scripture, XXXVI, 74. “You have two”: a customary expression, 201.

Various names of the Church, XLIII, 241. A Church stenographer: who he is, 513. Elephantiasis, XXXVIII, 489. Elephantary, XLIII, 507, 528, 550. Eulogy (*elogium*) meaning reproach, XXXIX, 1571. Eloquence: its meaning, XLIII, 447. “To be” meaning “to be considered,” XXXIV, 586. Public erection: its meaning, XXXII, 717. The sons of the cast out: who they are, XXXVII, 1674. A husband who leads out his wife, XXXIII, 304.

Dog-like eloquence, XXXIII, 752. *Fulcitare*, XXXVI, 318. To bewitch (*fascinare*) meaning to envy, XXXV, 536. In Scripture leaven is used sometimes in blame and sometimes in praise, XXXVII, 1184. Confidence (*fidentia*): its meaning, XL, 21. The derivation of “faith,” XXXV, 1760. *Fiere*, XXXIII, 288. The breath of God: the soul, XXXVII, 1776. A flower signifies glory, 1728. Lending at interest: its meaning, XXXVI, 386. Formed letters: what they are called, XXXIII, 175. A sword (*framea*): its meaning, XXXVII, 1955. “Break the moon and make fortune”: a proverb, and its meaning, XL, 674. The feast of Frugalia, XLI, 51. God is rightly called our estate or property (*fundus*), XXXVIII, 651.

The genius of Carthage: what it is, XXXVIII, 419. *Glaucia proles*: its meaning, XXXIII, 79. Goetia: a kind of magic, XLI, 286. Moral beauty is intelligible beauty, XL, 19. Who is called human, XXXVIII, 940. What a dart-like prayer (*oratio jaculatoria*) is, XXXIII, 1020. “He” (*ille*) used in place of a proper name, XXXVIII, 964. Who are said to have made God bitter toward them (*inamaricasse Deum*), XXXVI, 88. “To be hardened” meaning to be made strong, XXXIV, 543. The derivation of the name infancy, XLI, 522, 730. “Weak” is understood in various ways, XXXIV, 582, 586. To signify by a gesture: its meaning, XLII, 1071. Who is called an inquiline or resident alien, XXXVI, 429; XXXVII, 1945. How an inquiline differs from an inhabitant (*incola*), XXXVIII, 1518. To defile: to pronounce defiled, XXXIV, 519. The goddess Intercidona: who she is, XLI, 188. How envy differs from emulation, XXXV, 2142. Jubilus: a sound signifying that the heart gives birth to what it cannot utter, XXXVI, 283. “Downward” (*jusum*) and “upward” (*susum*), 2036, 2060.

Joy is used to mean a feast-day, XXXIII, 115. Lares and Larvae: what they are, XLI, 265. To make a delivery or carrying-charge (*laturam facere*): its meaning, XXXIX, 1519. The poor are the carrying-men (*laturarii*) of the rich, XXXVIII, 130, 240, 406. “Law” is derived from reading (*legendo*) or choosing (*eligendo*), XXXIV, 681. Booklets: their meaning, XXXVIII, 493, 1300, 1442; XLI, 768 and following. *Litteriones*: who they are, XLII, 635. Speech is the expression of the will, XXXVIII, 102. To speak with a woman: to have sexual intercourse, XXXIV, 625. The eyes are called lights, 1858. The derivation of brothels (*lupanaria*), XLI, 578.

Masters in cloaks (*magistri penulati*): who they are, XXXII, 672. Nursing infants, XXXVII, 1235. *Mammothrepti*: who they are, XXXVI, 246. Slaves (*mancipia*) are so called because they are seized by the hand, XXXIV, 590. *Manganae*: their meaning, XXXIII, 71. *Manicare*, XXXIV, 808. *Mansuetarii*: who they are, XXXII, 1232. The derivation of “marriage,” XLII, 365. How lying differs from being deceived, XXXVIII, 157, 738. By “measure” is understood either the thing which measures or the measure by which it measures, XXXII, 380. Military speech, XXXII, 415. “The threatening day” meaning the imminent day, XXXVIII, 402. Wonder-workers: who they are, XXXV, 1501. The derivation of “small things” (*modica*), XLII, 557. Buffoons: who they are, XXXIII, 728. Who is called womanish or addicted to women (*mulierosus*), XL, 391. Mosaic painting: what it is, XLI, 485. Nest of fear, XXXVII, 1923. What *nimis* (“excessively”) ordinarily signifies, 1444, 1509. A name (*nomen*) is called, as it were, a mark of recognition (*notamen*), XXXIV, 230. The negative particle *non*, when added, does not change the category, XLII, 915. The hidden things of a son: what they are, XXXIV, 514. To show evils: to do evils, XXXIV, 502.

To console (*paregorizare*), that is, to mitigate, XXXVII, 1638. Parental rites: what they are, XXXVI, 554; XXXIX, 1601. *Pariatores*: who they are, XXXVIII, 1191. Walls in ruin (*parietinae*) are the same as ruins, XXXVII, 1298. The derivation of *parta*, *reparta*, and *comperta*, XLII, 968, 972. Who are called passive, 167. To pave, 513. The name “sin” is understood in various ways, XLIV, 599. Masters in cloaks, XXXII, 672. How inquiry (*percontatio*) differs from interrogation, XXXIV, 67. Who are called intruders or arrivistes (*perventores*), XXXV, 1101; XLII, 516. The origin of the term philosopher, 1037. How a pledge differs from an earnest-payment, XXXVIII, 158, 858. *Placor*: its meaning, XXXIV, 951, 968. The peace-cake (*placentarium pacis*), XXXVIII, 314. The derivation of “street” (*platea*), XXXVII, 1327. Portents derive from foretelling (*portendendo*), XLI, 722. Who are called precentor and succentor, XXXVII, 1109. A governorship (*praesidatus*), that is, the office of a governor, XXXII, 729. The goddess Prema: who she is, XLI, 188. A press, XXXVIII, 983. “Beginning” is understood in various ways, XXIV, 222. The derivation of prodigies, XXXV, 1524; XLI, 722. Who were called proletarians, XLI, 97. Retail dealers or hucksters (*propolarii*, *propolae*), XXXV, 1470. To whiten or beautify the face with pumice, XLIII, 706. To cleanse: to pronounce cleansed, XXXIV, 519. The difference between *quatuor* (“four”) and *quater* (“four times”), XL, 40.

How God seizes or carries off a human being, XXXII, 795. *Reburrus*, XLII, 227. How ruling differs from being ruled, XLIV, 323. The derivation of religion, XLI, 280, 281. ## MARIUS MERCATOR

That he was once a well-known man, XLXIII, 1. Yet St. Augustine cites him in a certain letter, calling him “my Mercator,” ibid. He seems to have flourished from the year 418 to 450. He wrote a *Commonitorium*, annotations, and refutations, 18. Moreover, he produced various translations of books from Greek into Latin, 26, 27.

In what sense Christ can be called Θεοφόρος (*Theophoros*, “God-bearing”), 935. ## ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE

How voice and sound differ, LI, 400. Things done without speech are also called “words” on account of their signification, 300. How wonderful, for restraining human insolence, was the justice of the divine judgment, which confused the one speech of those peoples—harmonious among themselves by signs of mutual meaning—into the diversity of seventy-two languages, so that, with concord lost amid the discordant voices of the workers, the structure of their mad undertaking might collapse, 699. From the time of Heber, the confusion of languages arose because of the building of the tower, 537. Jerome, distinguished in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin eloquence, 98.

## SALVIAN, PRIEST OF MARSEILLES

Words are nothing without things, LIII, 72. Letters engraved by God’s finger; rocky pages; a stony scroll—the people learning and [Col. 0696] God teaching, 43. At Carthage, no less than at Rome, there are institutions of various disciplines and schools for every kind of language and manner, 143. Heretics possess and follow interpolated Scriptures, 95. We alone possess the holy Scriptures in their fullness, inviolate and entire, either drinking them from the biblical fountain itself or at least drawing them from its most pure spring through the ministry of a pure translation, 95. Barbarian peoples, strangers to Roman—indeed, to human—learning, know absolutely nothing except what they hear from their teachers . . . ignorant of all literature and learning, they know the mystery of the divine law more by instruction than by reading, ibid. The priests themselves, unable to bear Roman inhumanity, migrate to the barbarians. Although they differ from those to whom they flee in custom and language, and even, so to speak, in the very stench of their bodies and clothing, they nevertheless prefer to suffer a dissimilar civilization among barbarians rather than justice run wild among Romans . . . they prefer to live free under the appearance of captivity than to be captives under the appearance of freedom, 99.
