If a cancerous wound follows, the destruction caused by cancer must necessarily follow, 185. *Exomologesis*, that is, confession of sins, 171, 185. *Malagma*, a medicament, 184. *Odea*, a kind of spectacle, 111. *Panchresta*, or soft things which draw boys more easily toward obedience, 127. Pantomimes, persons devoted to spectacles, 111. Paradise: what it is, with its description, 200. The etymology of the names Theophilus and Timothy, 173. *Thymelici*, that is, actors, 116.

Latin words and expressions.—*Affectus* is used for “wife and children.” In this period this word was customarily used to designate relatives and those whom we pursue with affection, 41. *Affectus* is used for “humanity,” 104. *Affectus* is said of animals, 80. *Afer* (“African”) means the same as “shameless,” 143. *Amor*, *amare*: their meaning, 157. *Antistare* in dignity, 197. *Antistare* in a will, 213. The Apostles were sent out without bag and even without a staff, 198. Their speech was an author of crimes rather than an advocate pleading for them, 67; Salvian is fond of nouns ending thus, such as *abdicatrix*, 201; *accusatrix*, 83; *usurpatrix*, ibid. Bagaudae: whence they were so called, 99, note. Those are called happier who are what they wish to be, 32. “To be Gaius or Seius”: a proverbial expression meaning any person whatsoever, 143. In Optatus, book III, *Cai sei* or *caia seia* was said for “a pagan man” or “a pagan woman,” 143, note; XI, 1024, note. Christians are so called from Christ, 90. What it is to believe Christ, 58, 70. Who the *curiales* and officials are, 67, 98. What is called a desert, 196. “The Lord’s house” for a church building, 127. *Excalcii*, the same as *excalceati* (“unshod”), 58. What the exile of the soul is, 204. Sardinian herbs that produce a frenzied laugh, 130. What the inexpiable evil is, 199. What “womanly endurance” means in Salvian, 146. Clouds full of God, 43. A name without its action and office is nothing, 71. Clad in a cloak, pale, and shorn to the skin: marks of any monk, 156. Purple splendour, 200. *Petaminaria*, a kind of spectacle, 116. Roman humanity, 99, 104. Roman authority, 97. The sense in which *Seius* is used, 143, note. What is called barren, 196. Untaught in the heaven of the saints, 200. A stone scroll, that is, the tables of the Law delivered to Moses, 43. Permitted pleasures, that is, honourable ones, 195.

LEO (ST.) THE GREAT, pope.—The diversity of languages which dissolved the construction of the proud tower advanced, through the Apostles, the building up of the Church, LV, 42. The seventy-two languages arose from the confusion of tongues (in Prosper, LI).

On the Greek language.—How few among the Latins knew Greek thoroughly and could produce an exact translation from Greek; likewise, how rare were Greeks who possessed Latin perfectly and could furnish an accurate translation from Latin, LIV, 568–569, Preface. Hence Leo doubts the precision of the Greek translation of his letter to Flavian, 1258, Admonition. He wishes it to be rendered into Greek by one skilled in both languages, 1080–1081. The difficulty of suitably translating into Greek works dealing with subtle matters, 1258. Many letters of Leo were translated into Greek; the authority of those translations, 569. Certain Greek letters were written and sent from the outset in both Greek and Latin to the West, and copies in both languages must be regarded as originals, 970, note. Greek-speakers at Alexandria, 1093. Some shone in the preaching of Catholic truth either in Greek or in Latin, 890. In Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, funeral rites are celebrated with singing, L, 1256.

Love-feasts (*agapae*), LVI, 451, 717. Apostates to be cut off, 556. What a *cenodochium* is, 858. *Charismata*, that is, gifts of grace, LIV, 357. What a cycle is, 601, note. *Diaconicon* for *sacrarium* (“sacristy”), LVI, 717. Which dioceses had been established in Gaul, 596–597. *Dithalassa* places: which they are, 737. Intercalary years, LIV, [Col. 0697] 601, 607, note. The “resident” (*ἐνδημοῦσον*) council: what it is, LV, 274. *Epibatae*, that is, laymen, LVI, 738. Exorcisms: their use in the Church, LIV, 439. *Idolothyta* (“things sacrificed to idols”), 1137. Metropolis, metropolitan, and metropolitan bishop, LV, 279, 497, 577, 588–589, 607, 609. *Naustologi*: who they are, LVI, 737–738. What the ancient formula *olographa manus* (“wholly written hand”) means, 119. The Roman parishes to which Manichaeans were to be denounced, LIV, 163. *Ptochia*, LVI, 858. *Xenodochia*, ibid.

On the Latin language.—Latin abounds in words, LV, 948, note. Latin translators of Greek works sometimes inserted the original Latin of passages which, in Greek manuscripts and works, had been translated from Latin into Greek and inserted there, LVI, 51. Dissertation on St Leo’s style, by Paschasius Quesnel, LVI, 413. The style of the letter to Demetrias is compared with that of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, with respect to the use of Holy Scripture, 413; with Sermon 6 on Epiphany, with respect to distinctive expressions, 414; with Sermon 4 on Lent, 415, and with many other passages, 416–417. Those wishing to assess minutely the affinity of style and the vocabulary familiar to both will readily discover that these are exactly the same, and that the whole structure of expression is the same, 418. The words found there, ibid.

What is meant by the name “annals,” LIV, 1072, note. Appeal of bishops to the Apostolic See, LV, 573, 583. “Heavenly mystery” for the Eucharist, LVI, 24. The platform of the ark: an elevated place in a church, LIV, 218. By the word *Auctoritates*, the Gallic bishops designate Apostolic Constitutions, LVI, 151 ff. What *brandea* were, LV, 536. *Brevis statutorum* is said for an abridgment or breviary, LVI, 418, 420. *Capitula* and *Breviarium* are used interchangeably, 348. Citations or summonses must be completed before trial, 981, note. Ancient Latin writers used *conventus* for a council, LV, 948, note. Canonical course for canonical hours, 536. What the dalmatic is and its use, 437, 536. Dissertation on St Leo’s style, 413 ff. Who the Elect and Elect Women were among the Manichaeans, LIV, 178. Letters of commendation, LIV, 1082; LVI, 708, 859. Intervals to be observed in ordinations, 620, 651. Ecclesiastical jurisdiction, 545. Legates *a latere*, LIV, 795, 802. Which province was called Novempopulania, LVI, 595. Saints are called patrons, 34. The office of the *proreta* on a ship, LVI, 737. Division of the provinces in Gaul under Leo, 497–498. Archives of the Apostolic See, LIV, 881, 891. *Subadjuva*, 1069. *Tinnivolentia*, for *tintinnabula* (“little bells”), L, 1240. Bridal veiling, LVI, 130. Vicar for successor, 141. Words familiar to St Leo, LVI, 413.

MAXIMUS (ST.), bishop of Turin.—The diversity of languages introduced among the builders of the tower of Babel deterred them from their work begun, LVII, 636. To the preachers of evangelical faith is given knowledge of all languages, ibid., 641.

Greek terms.—Who were called Agnoetae, LVII, 267. *Allophyli*, that is, foreigners or barbarians, 238, 266, 315, 781. Catechumens, or those to be baptized, 293, 708. Energumens, or persons possessed by a demon, 314. Heresy and heretics, 267, 331, 336, 452. Who are called neophytes, 366, 602. The Holy Spirit is called the Paraclete, 631, 641. What the Creed (*symbolum*) is, 435, note.

Latin usage.—The plough of faith, LVII, 782. What a haruspex (diviner) is, 696, note. What auspices are, 258. *Domnedius* for *dominus aedis* (“lord of the shrine”): for the subject does not sin against himself alone when he sacrifices, but also against the *domnedius*, who does not forbid it, 733. “And although the countryman stands at the altars, the detestable contamination returns to the *domnedius*,” ibid. As Muratori observes, this word belongs to the lowest Latin, ibid., note. A *Dianaticus* is one who sacrifices to Diana, the divinity of the fields, 734. What it is to break oneself into a woman, 257. A *lustrum*, a kind of superstition, 696. The Father is called the divine Voice, the Son the Word, and why, 554. To furrow through worldly vices with the spiritual ploughshare, 257. A portent: what it is to transform oneself into portents, 257. Peter’s primacy in the Church is established, 353. What rogations or litanies are, 459, Admonition. “Vessels of wrath,” an expression that is a Hebraism, 604.

VICTOR OF VITA, presbyter of Carthage.

Greek terms.—*Harpagare*, Greek ἁρπάζω, that is, “to steal what belongs to another,” is a word of the lowest Latin, LVIII, 256. The homilies of the Greeks were called *tractatus* by Latins, 185. What an Alleluia melody is, 197. What a metropolitan bishop is, 190. Catholic bishops are called Homoousians in the decree of King Huneric, 213, 238. The doctrine of *homoousia* is explained against the Arians, 219. Poisoned venom, 239. What *trochlei* are, 243.

Victor’s Latin expressions.—The Aquitani are so called from waters, 338. To lose the citadel of the brain through a fall, 246. The name “barbarian,” a term denoting only ferocity, cruelty, and terror, 255. *Bisacutum*: a kind of grain commonly allotted only to beasts of burden, 262. In the Middle Ages, *calumniare* or *calumniari* meant the same as to bring a lawsuit, 202, note. In Africa the Arian Vandals sacrilegiously appropriated shirts and breeches, together with altar-cloths, for themselves, [Col. 0698] 197. *Casmabinae* strings, 198, 243. Among medieval authors, *cannava* meant a wine-cellar, 212, note. Decayed old age, 192. The law of tenancy, 240. “Companion of good confession,” that is, companion in a good confession, 199, note. What could not the eloquence of Eusebius, or the fluency in Greek and Latin of his translator Rufinus, say? 255; not even a river of Ciceronian eloquence, ibid. To have one’s glory laudably spread abroad, 180. To offer baskets to persons ignorant of history, ibid. *Lugula*, that is, a narrow, long strip of land projecting into the sea, which Julius Caesar in book III calls *lingula*, 188, note. In Africa *magalia* were country houses, or huts of the poor and shepherds, 198. What the *millenarii* were among the Vandals, 193. “To celebrate” or “conduct” Masses in churches: an expression already accepted among Catholics, 203. Unfamiliarity with ships, 192. *Nervicae* strings, 198. *Sabana*, a word then used for linen cloths employed in baptism, 247, note. Popular discourses which the Greeks call homilies, 185. Victory for the intended end, 189.

SIDONIUS APOLLINARIS.

Greek terms.—A rehearsed recital, LVIII, 449. *Amyttides*, a kind of bowl, 730. What anadiplosis in poetry is, 606, note. The practice of withdrawal, 577. What *aplustria* are, 610, 662. Apocatastatic Mars above the centre, 608. *Archimagirus*, or superintendent of the kitchen, 484. Egyptian and Palestinian archimandrites, 612. Chief pirates, 597. Architectural harmony of walls, 592. Asyndetic Mercury above the diameter, 608. What *Atticissare* is, 508. More talkative than Athens, 597. The Attalid testament, 655. The canon of the glebe, 559. Catastrophes of ball-players, 484. *Cataplus*, or the arrival of ships in port, 556. What a *celeuma* is, 610. Who the Byzantine *chironomontes* are; who a *choraules* is, 511, 449. A water-clock marking the hours, 484, 492. What rounded colures are, 476, note. Covered porticoes, 477. The zodiacal interval, 608. The arena of Dicaearchia, 643. *Diaeta*, for a small dining-room, 477. Echoing elegiac verses, and various names of poems, 606–607. The form of an epigram, ibid. Ethical diction, ibid. Greek elegance, 448. Holographic parchments, or autographs, 627. The Hyantes maidens, that is, the Muses, 702. Water-organs, 449. Hippodrome, 476. A labyrinth of business, 480. Labyrinthine insolubility, 515. Astrology, 607. What it is to make *mechanemata* with one’s fingers, 462. Curved Saxon myoparones, 597. Onyx-coloured veneers, 621. A hanging, 448. Who a *pollinetor* is, 505. What a *pyrgus* is, 497. *Rhodanusia* for Lyons: Irenaeus calls the district around the river Rhône Ῥοδανουσία, 452, note. A writer of satire, 468. What a *schema* is, 515, 575, 607, 624. Who the rope-walkers are, 738. What *sophos* means, 465, 505, 633, 639, 659. The game of ball, 548. Ball-players contending among the revolving turns of their rolling “catastrophes,” 484. What bankers’ wrappings are, 468. What a *toreuma* is, 448.

Sidonian Latin.—“The multitude of idlers has become so great that, unless at least a very few of you rescue the pure propriety of the Latin language from the rust of commonplace barbarisms, we must soon lament its destruction and extinction,” LVIII, 486. What an abstainer is, LVII, 477. “Accent of winter,” a new meaning of the word, 511; accent of games, 548; accent of applause, 582. The blue Adda river, 452. Considered legal advocacy, 554. *Aetatula*, for childhood, 508. Friends must be used as flowers, 520. “The thresholds of the Apostles” for Rome, 454. The distinctive features of arts, 507. *As*, *ex asse*, *ad assem*, 468, 471, 498, 508, 522, 711. More talkative than Athens, 597. What the Attalid testament is, 655. To write or speak in Attic fashion, 508. Ears like those of Barrinae, or elephants, 505. A purple-clad senate, 638. Description of the dog-star’s harsh heat, 673. *Carminare*, 464, 632, 676. “Rights for the girded; privileges for the ungirded,” 537. Cleopatra’s feasts, 611. A tenant-farmer’s status, 549. *Conditorium* for tomb or monument, 547. To read in opposition, 545. The *cursoria* of Ticinum: thus he calls a public boat, 452. What *decocta* is, 477. To boil away one’s childhood, 508. The image of an utterly deformed man, 500. Milesian tales, that is, erotic and obscene tales, 566. Most exalted prosperity, 480. The wit of fatigues, 461. *Flamonia* for *Flaminia*: priestly offices, 537. *Fornicare*: “Antiquity vaulted bridges, crusted with hidden arches, for leaping all the way to the walkable embankment,” 452. To chirp like sparrows, to chatter, 575. Gallic abundance at their banquets, 448. Who the Gelasians are, 738. Gilded sedan chairs, 600. *Indoloria*, a Ciceronian word, 711. Native tenancy, 549. Sabbath luxury, 448. The gold of *legulae*, or shells, so called from their likeness to a *ligula*, which is a kind of spoon, 446, note. The tongue is called the indicator of conscience, 507. Literary letters, 521. A metal-bearing page, 604. What the Nicetian plan is, 596. The coupling of swans, 601. An Oscan translation, 591. Sooty leisure, 491. A ball game, 548. Peppery words, 607. The tolls of informers claiming fourfold penalties, 537. Letters of refusal, 626. He calls Lyons *Rhodanusia*, [Col. 0699] 452. Most rapacious *salares*, a kind of fish, 477. Who the *sandapilarii* are, 482. *Scriptianire*, 607. What clattering *sigmenta* are, 595. Chair-bearing slaves gloomier than corpse-bearers, 468. *Sophos*, 468, 505, 633, 639, 659. Ball games, 548. The consular gift-basket, 594–595. A board game, 548. Record-office clerks, 537. The game of knucklebones, 744. What bankers’ wrappings are, 468. A dining-hall: “The crowded senate goes to the dining-hall,” 459. A very practised old man, 470. Very skilfully, 627. Robe-clad repose, 494. The leisure of tunic-wearers, 537. *Tumultuatim*, for “indiscriminately”: “all the bushes, nourished by the juice of the soaking soil along the river-banks, had grown luxuriantly in confused profusion,” 453. Who corpse-bearers are, 468, 482.

GENNADIUS, presbyter of Marseilles.

Greek terms.—Pachomius wrote letters in which the alphabet is read with mystical significations, LVIII, 1064. Who the Anthropomorphites are, 1077. Who the Borborite heretics are, 993. Cenobites and Synodites, 1067. What διττοχαῖον (*dittochaeum*) is, 1068. Ἔλεγχος (*Refutation*), a book of Cyril of Alexandria, 1092. What ἐνέργεια (*energeia*, “activity/operation”) is, 999. Ἐργοδιώκτης (*ergodiōktēs*), 1079. Eucharist, 994, 997. The book *Hexaemeron*, 1068. Mathematicians, or astrologers, 1076. Ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*), that is, “of one substance,” 982; the proper meaning of this word, 1117. The parish of Barcelona, 1078. Synodites, a class of monks living in common, 1067. Thesis: Valentinus taught that Christ was incarnate “from thesis,” that is, only ostensibly, 981.

Latin usage.—*Ante mortuis*, for *antea mortuis* (“formerly dead”), LVIII, 995. Commodian wrote in unpolished language and something like verse, 1068. “To give the question of a heresy,” that is, to resolve it, 1080. Heaven and earth are called elements, 996. Jerome’s excellence in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters, 1059. Julian the Pelagian, learned in Greek and Latin, 1084. Who the new lawgivers are, 1000. *Perstare*, “to persist,” 1101. *Sed* for *scilicet* (“namely”), 994. “Three and barbarous”: expressions in Gennadius that seem disjointed, ibid.

AVITUS (ST.), bishop of Vienne.—According to Agobard, Avitus was Catholic in faith, most eloquent in speech, keenest in intellect, a most delightful interpreter of sacred literature, most learned in secular letters, and very facile in verse, LIX, 191. “Avitus,” says Ennodius, “was pre-eminent among the Gauls; learning enclosed itself in him as in a lodging of a bright house,” 192. Gregory of Tours calls him a man of great eloquence, 192.

Hebrew terms.—*Corban*, that is, “a gift,” LIX, 199. *Emmanuel* is prophetic: “God with us,” 205. *Racha* is a Hebrew word, which in Latin means “empty” and “vacant,” and in Greek is called κενός, 200.

Greek terms.—“Holy God, holy Mighty One, holy Immortal One,” Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός, ἅγιος ἰσχυρός, ἅγιος ἀθάνατος, etc.: this is the Trisagion, celebrated from ancient times in churches even of the West, LIX, 211. A written bond, 206. The difference between Χριστοτόκος (“Christ-bearer”) and Θεοτόκος (“God-bearer”), 204. The eastern world, 285. Blessings, 274. Monogram, 281. The Holy Spirit is called Paraclete, 201. A pedigree of ancient origin, 257. Eloquence of themes, 203.

Latin usage.—To be absent, 271, 277. Description of the best kind of gold, LIX, 280–281. A prodigious funeral object, 290. “Your Highness,” a title of the emperor, 284. *Fides* (“faith”) cannot be said in the plural, 311. A peacock confined in an *isicium*, 279. *Magdaliola*, a word known in the workshops of perfume-sellers, 280. *Missa*: in churches, palaces, and law-courts, a dismissal is announced when the people are released from attendance; hence this word is not derived from Hebrew, as some maintain, 199 and note. *Napa*: “I bloom in turnips,” 289. Rogations, 289. “Your Serenity,” an honorific title for emperors.

JULIANUS POMERIUS, a Maurus by birth, rhetorician of Arles and priest, at the end of the fifth century wrote three books *On the Contemplative Life*. We therefore analyse them in order that the former language of mystics may become apparent and be assessed.—What the active life is, LIX, 428; how it differs from the contemplative life, ibid. What it is to live carnally, 435. What glorification is, 427. Christ: on the imitation of Christ, 466. What it is to savour heavenly things, 429. To contemplate is the same as to see, 419. What the contemplative life is, 421–422. Who the followers of the contemplative life are, 432. The taste of the contemplative life, 429. Belief is necessary, especially for priests, 432 ff. The corruption of our nature, 477. Declamation: one method belongs to declaimers, another to teachers, 439. Woman: on conversation with women, 482–483. What the pattern of believers is, 445. In what the joy of the blessed consists, 419. What true joys and true riches are, 456. The ranks and offices of the house of the eternal King, 445. The torments of envy, 486 ff. In what sense the world should be despised, 431. Who the shepherds and sheep are, 437. Which sinners must be endured and which corrected, 443–444. To die to sin, which is never to sin again, 466. What our pilgrimage is, 427. The distinction between perfection of the contemplative life in this age and its perfection in the age to come, 423–424, 426. Possession: on possessing God, 460. What fighting and conquering mean among contemplatives, 419. [Col. 0700] What spiritual resurrection is, 466. What an obstacle earthly riches are, 457. The usefulness of fear, 489. The swelling of pride, 420. What sins arise from pride, 48. Vanity, 488. Virtue and the likeness of virtue, 473.

AURELIUS PRUDENTIUS.—Words are often joined together in manuscripts, LX, 269, note; 1054. In Prudentius, simple verbs for compound verbs, 566, n. 53. Words used in a double sense, LIX, 936, n. 188. Words having a double and contrary meaning, 182, n. 37. Verbs of the second and third conjugations used together, LIX, 730, note; 967, n. 552. Many verbs construed with the accusative in Prudentius, 894, note. Which words ancient Fathers regarded as low and vulgar, ibid. Whether the name of the writer of a letter ought formerly to have been placed before the name of the recipient, 730. Proper names were customarily written with the first letter and the last two letters, 718. Indeclinable city names in the accusative or ablative, 732, note. Poets customarily pronounce proper names with varying quantity, 730. Proper names are easily corrupted, LX, 244, note 88. Derivation of proper names, LIX, 588, note. Diversity of names after the fall of the Roman Republic, LX, 252, note. The twofold rule for names in the Middle Ages, LIX, 593. Prudentius readily uses nouns as adverbs, 787, n. 32. Names of gods in the plural out of contempt, 936, n. 189. Hebrew names: their spelling and prosody, 742. Ecclesiastical terms should not be rejected, 727, 1036, n. 347. Graeco-Latin terms, 1000, n. 1002; 1041, n. 404; LX, 82, n. 829. When quantity differs from accent in Greek-derived words, what rule they follow, LIX, 728, 739, 742. How Prudentius’ diction differs from that of Paulinus, 618. Translations of St Prudentius’ works into vernacular languages, 657. Faults of metre alleged against Prudentius, 724. Rules observed by Prudentius and other ancient Christian poets, 727 ff. Prudentius corrupted by some, wrongly corrected by others, and defended by still others. Special observations on his prosody, 736. Prudentian metres, 744 ff. On his Latin style, 748; see below.

Greek terms.—“Hide your head in the abyss,” LX, 29. *Acroma*, a festive *acroama* (“recital”), 317. *Agon*, contest, 386. *Allophylus*, LIX, 1047. *Anathema*, LIX, 1045; LX, 62. *Apotheosis*, title of a poem, LIX, 922. Archaism, or Greek imitation, in *aquai* for *aquae*, 978. Northern stars, 901. *Arthrisis*, a kind of disease, LX, 485. Atoms, LIX, 997. *Barathrum*, LX, 393. Swelling boom, LIX, 988. A milk-pressing basket, 801. Flower-baskets, LX, 356. A drinking-cup, LIX, 865. *Catamitus*, or defiled boy, LX, 123, note. *Catastae*, iron grates, 321. Prudentius’ *Cathemerinon* poems, LIX, 775. *Charisma*, 576. Green *chelydri*, tortoises, 129. Written bond, 286. Chrysoprase, LIX, 730; LX, 90, gloss. Cithara-player, LX, 220. Dark-blue pools, 85. Dark-blue nymphs, 145. Cups foaming with milk, LIX, 962. In dactylic metre, LX, 356. With a dactylic band, LIX, 799. Diadem, 964; LX, 154, 361. A dialectical word, LIX, 1020. *Dittochaeum*, a poem by Prudentius, LX, 89. Carved emblems on cups, LX, 61. The eastern quarter, 345. The eastern star, LIX, 793. An exotic sect, LX, 79. Glaucoma: “No one has seen two suns except under glaucoma,” LIX, 1018. The licence of the naked gymnasium, LX, 461. Apollinean gypsum, that is, a statue of Apollo, LIX, 961. Prudentius’ *Hamartigenia* poems, LIX, 1007. Hecatomb, LX, 521. Hendecasyllables, 424. A hero of keen excellence, 449. Glass, 566. Water-jar, LIX, 865. To sing hymns, LX, 292. Idolatries, LIX, 1041. Mastigophores, that is, whip-bearers, LX, 219. Astrology, 216, 250. A singer, LIX, 862. To sing a melody, 827. A master of mysteries, LX, 318. *Nomisma* for *numisma* (“coin”), 302. Musical instruments, LIX, 955. The instrument of the mouth, LX, 444. The instrument of words, or tongues, 514. Christian wrestling-school, 368. Wrestling-school of glory, 391. Whether *parapsis* is the same as *paropsis*, 62, note. The framework of a scaffold, 521. Prudentius’ book *Peristephanon*, LX, 275. Phalanxes of sins, 81. A common phalanx, 552. Phantom, 73. God’s formed creature, LIX, 810. Pleurisy, LX, 484. Prudentius’ poem *Psychomachia*, LX, 19. A crackling pyre, 342. Rhetorical mouth, 116. Flowering rose-laurel, LIX, 1028. Sarcophagus, 811. Monstrous sphere, LX, 488. Seal, 526. *Stemmarussum*, 512. The pedigree of Jejunus, LIX, 847. Pedigrees of the Apostles, 912. Honour accrues to a pedigree, LX, 451. The tricks of sycophants, LIX, 919. Creed, LX, 323. Harmony, 220. “He sweeps his tracks with his trailing robe,” 50. Scaly breastplate, LIX, 1042. Embossed works, 50. The course of so great a tragedy, LX, 528. Zephyr, 243.

Prudentian Latin.—Even if in Prudentius the purest style current in the age of Augustus is lacking, everything else that makes a great poet is present, LIX, 748. If anyone wishes to treat a Christian subject in verse, he can take no better model from elsewhere, 749. Since he handled the most difficult questions of theology, he necessarily had to devise many technical terms, 749. Words included in catalogues ought not always to be regarded as impure, since they may sometimes be thoroughly Latin, although rarer, 750. Macrobius himself adduces many rare words used by Virgil, 750. See what follows, 730.

Latin words and expressions.—Pig bellies, LX, 513. *Abicit*, *abjicit*, 35. To renounce a name, LIX, 941. A palm-patterned cloak, LX, 165. To abhor touching, 389. Records of the secret shore, 130. Sharpened, 394. A people born for battle-array, 218. He enslaves to love, LIX, 1036. To doubt, LX, 68, note. The adulterer neighs at her, 122. To add time to labour, LIX, 777. To grow into heated years, LX, 206. A worshipped girl, 363. *Adasico*, 337. Mature harvest, 257. An adulterous field, that is, a corrupted field, LIX, 1027. The lamp is called the rival light of day, 821. Coins are called riddles, LX, 304. Rough verdigris, 155. Covered with verdigris, 67. To surge in the heat of vices, LIX, 1031. With sin seething, 813. **DRACONTIUS, man of letters and poet.**—That in Dracontius’s time sound learning still flourished, and that a distinctive, not contemptible taste for Latinity remained, especially among poets, LX, 600. Expurgations of Dracontius’s writings, 601 and following. He is praised by St Columbanus, 603. St Ildefonsus’s judgment concerning the works of Dracontius corrected by St Eugenius, 613. Differing opinions concerning him, 615 and following. The views of Dupin, Ceillier, Goldast, Fabricius, and Barth concerning his Latinity, 668. With regard to elegance of Latin diction, Dracontius contains many things expressed purely and gracefully, but some things less polished and not fit to be proposed for imitation, 670. Those wishing to know the bounds of Latin diction ought not to be ignorant of poets such as Dracontius, since they have preserved for us many words from pure Latinity and have coined certain new expressions which should not always be rejected, ibid. After dwelling upon the works of Prudentius, it will suffice to observe concerning Dracontius: (1) that in the books *On God* he uses the adverbs *veneranter*, as does Tertullian, *moderanter*, *dominanter*, *tonanter*, *trementer* [reverently, moderately, dominantly, thunderously, tremblingly], 670; (2) that this poet is fond of the word *modestus* [modest], ibid.; (3) that he often attributes the adjective *anhelus* [panting] to fire or the sun, ibid.; (4) that Veitzius observes that Dracontius often joins two epithets or adjectives to a single substantive, 671; (5) that he rarely departs from the laws of metre, ibid.

**PAULINUS (Saint), bishop of Nola.**—Paulinus had Ausonius—an outstanding teacher in literature, renowned for poetic and rhetorical talent—as his master, LXI, 19. Paulinus confesses that he owes everything to Ausonius, ibid. Paulinus’s style shines more brightly in the homily *On Almsgiving*; his eloquence, nobility, and character were commended by St Ambrose, Idatius, Eucherius, and Jerome, 19, 20. Although Jerome considered him skilled in Greek letters, he nevertheless seems to have had only a moderate command of Greek, 21.

**ENNODIUS (MAGNUS FELIX), bishop of Ticinum.**—The most learned Sirmond speaks thus of this writer: “If his own age cast any sediment upon Ennodius, we cannot therefore fail to love the flowing fountain of intellect and eloquence in his writings, or, because verse sometimes limps in his poems, fail to embrace the soundness of thought and keen intelligence which are everywhere present”; and elsewhere: “I pass over his expressions and declamations, which are of such a kind that, although they seem the latest born of all among the Latins, they may be compared with the earliest and middle ones, and ought to be dearer, like roses that have sprung up in another season,” LXIII, 10. Ennodius says this concerning language: “Good God, into how many uses abundant language disperses itself. When it wishes, it rages like a beast, runs like a river, surges like the deep; and whatever appearance it paints with embellished images of words, it represents with the confirmation of truth,” 13. “Language is rightly believed to be the utterer of inner chambers, since by speech it calls into light the secrets of the hidden soul,” 78.

**GILDAS, called the Wise.**—We select the following few examples, from which this writer’s style and diction may be sufficiently well judged. “Meanwhile, upon the island stiff with icy cold, and, as it were, by its more distant withdrawal among lands not close to the visible sun, that true sun—not from the temporal firmament, but from the summit of heaven exceeding all times—etc.,” LXIX, 337. “They listen with ears attentively raised, not to the praises of God sweetly modulated by the tuneful voice of Christ’s recruits and by the breath of ecclesiastical melody, but rather to gallows-birds, filled with lies and foaming phlegm (things which are nothing), etc.,” 353. “You heard on that day when it would have been much worthier and much more right that you should be dragged to prison or to a penal rack than to the priesthood, etc.,” 390.

**CASSIODORUS, Roman senator and finally abbot of Vivarium.**—Knowledge of languages is praiseworthy, LXIX, 625. “If it belongs to a prudent man to know his native tongue well, what estimation can be made of that wisdom which preserves so many kinds of speech by unimpeded exercise?” ibid. Cassiodorus says of Queen Amalasuntha: “Since she enjoys such perfection in languages, she is so silent in public action that she is thought idle,” 825. An eloquent tongue heaps up every good thing, 746. He writes thus to Arator: “You did not find Roman eloquence in its own regions; and there Tullian reading made you eloquent where once the Gallic tongue resounded,” 745. **GREGORY, bishop of Tours.**—Confusion of languages, LXXI, 165. The Latin tongue unknown to the Franks, 1063. The Saxon language, thus designated in the laws of Charles the Bald, was the region of the Saxons, or Lower Britain, in the western part of Gaul, 345 note. What language the early Frankish kings properly used, 1186. Roman and Germanic speech were familiar among the sons of Louis the Pious, ibid. Besides the Latin language which they laboriously learned, they appear to have cultivated a distinctive native idiom, ibid. Thegan reports that Louis the Pious was proficient in Greek and Latin and could speak Latin as readily as his native tongue, ibid. The purity of the Ausonian tongue had been succeeded by a certain provincial and more corrupted Latin, which Sidonius called “the scale of Latin speech” and “the rust of common barbarisms,” [Col. 0714] ibid. The Franks learned Rustic Latin, later designated by the name Roman, ibid. It seems that the first Gallic kings used their native language and only much later spoke the semi-Latin or Roman language of their subjects, ibid. See what is said concerning Clovis and Pippin, 1187. Gregory candidly declares that he does not thoroughly know the rules of grammar, 161.

On the Lombard language.—The affinity of this language with Gothic and Germanic idioms demonstrates the origin of the Lombards, LXXV, 249. According to the testimony of Paul the Deacon, the Lombards were so called from *lang-baert*, which means “long beard,” ibid. The same Paul the Deacon has supplied interpretations of certain words, namely: *Wodam* or *Godan*, that is, God. *Fara*, family. *Feld*, that is, open fields. *Lama*, water. *Marpahis* or *Marhais*, groom, whence perhaps the French *maréchal*. *Scala*, bowl; *schilpor*, armour-bearer. Nearly all these words are Germanic in origin, ibid.

**GREGORY THE GREAT (St), pope.**—“In the mind of the hearer, the quality of the speech heard is the seed of ensuing thought,” LXXVI, 32. “While speech is conceived through the ear, thought is generated in the mind,” ibid. How long vowels were formerly distinguished from short ones, 526 note. Gregory does not reject confusion of barbarisms in writing, does not avoid the collision of metacism, and disdains to observe the cases in the placing and moving of propositions, LXXV, 516. Gregory does not confine the words of the heavenly oracle beneath Donatus’s rules, ibid. Remarkable mastery of every language in an unlettered boy, LXXVII, 361. Gregory complains that he lacks interpreters of Greek speech, 1099. A bishop may not teach grammar, 1172.

### Isidore, Bishop of Seville

The origin of the diversity of languages, LXXXII, 325. The patriarchs and prophets used the Hebrew language, ibid. What languages are, and why they are so called, ibid. The sacred language is threefold: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, 326. In what language God spoke at the creation of the world is uncertain, 327. Before the confusion there was one language, 328. Nations arose from languages, not languages from nations, ibid. There were seventy-two languages after the confusion, 328. All eastern peoples strike their language and words in the throat, as Hebrews and Syrians do, 327. [Col. 0717] Western peoples, however, break them with the teeth, as Italians and Spaniards do, ibid. The peoples of the middle regions, such as the Greeks, produce speech in the palate, ibid. Syriac and Chaldaic are akin to Hebrew in speech, ibid. They think the Hebrew language itself to be Chaldaic, 327. What grammar is, 81. It is called from Greek γράμμα (*grámma*), which means “letter,” ibid. Speech is called, as it were, the “reason of the mouth,” and is a connected sequence of meaningful words, ibid. Eight parts of speech are recognized, 81–82. What articulated sound is, 89. On letters, which are the first principles of the grammatical art, 74. Letters are called, as it were, *legiterae*, 75. Greek and Latin letters appear to have arisen from the Hebrews, ibid. The Hebrews received letters from the Law through Moses, and the Syrians or Chaldaeans from Abraham, ibid. Queen Isis, coming from Greece, brought letters with her into Egypt, ibid. Cadmus, son of Agenor, brought seventeen Greek letters from Phoenicia into Greece, 76. Among the Greeks numbers are represented by letters, 77. Latin letters were handed down to the Italians by the nymph Carmentis or Nicostrata, 77. Which letters are vowels and consonants, 78. Neither Greeks nor Hebrews pronounce the letter Φ, 80. The derivation, nature, and kinds of noun, 82. The derivation, nature, and kinds of pronoun, 85. Why the verb is so called, its division and forms, 86. What an adverb is, 87. On the participle, conjunction, and preposition, 88. On the interjection, 89. A syllable is called in Latin *conceptio* or *complexio*, ibid. What a syllable is and its kinds, ibid. On accents, 93, 94. Position, or punctuation, 95. On signs indicating sententiae, which were formerly innumerable in manuscripts, 90 ff. On orthography, 101. On analogy, 104. What etymology is, 105. What glosses are, 106. On barbarism, ibid. What solecism is, 107. The remaining faults of language are called acyrology, cacephaton, pleonasm, perissology, macrology, tautology, ellipsis, tapinosis, cacósynthesis, and amphiboly, 108, 109. What metaplasm is and its kinds in words, ibid. On the various schemes or figures of speech, 110 ff.

### On the Hebrew Language

Hebrew appears to be the mother of all languages, LXXXII, 75. Syriac and Chaldaic are languages akin to Hebrew, 327. The Hebrews used twenty-two alphabetical letters, 75. The etymologies of Hebrew names collected together may be found, LXXXII, 275 ff. Hebrew names of God, 259, 260.

### On the Greek Language

The Greek language is held to be more illustrious than the languages of other nations, LXXXII, 326. It is divided into five dialects, namely Common, Attic, Doric, Ionic, and Aeolic, 326, 327. On the Greek alphabet, 75, 76. We shall not give etymologies of Greek words, since Isidore has produced an excellent work on them; but we indicate certain categories pertaining to this language: (1) names of gems and stones, 564 ff.; signs of sententiae, 90; faults of speech, 108; various metaplasms, 109; schemes or various figures of speech, 110 ff.; medical terms, 185 ff.; ecclesiastical names, 291 ff.; by-names of various heretics, 298, etc.; many names of plants and trees, 609 ff., 623 ff.

### On the Latin Language

Some have said that there are four Latin languages: ancient, Latin, Roman, and mixed, 327. Ancient Latin was in use under Janus and Saturn; Latin under King Latinus, in which the Twelve Tables were written; Roman began after the expulsion of the kings; mixed Latin followed the destruction of the empire, ibid. The Latins formerly used only seventeen letters, 80. H was added for aspiration, ibid. Who added the letter K and why, 80. The Latin Q is lacking in Greek and Hebrew, ibid. X was added by Augustus; formerly it was supplied by C and S, whence it is called double, ibid. Latin borrowed two letters from Greek, namely Y and Z, 81. For exotic, new, or semi-barbarous words noted by Isidore, the reader is referred to his Glossary, LXXXIII, 1331, and to the book *On Etymologies*, LXXXII.

### Mozarabic Missal According to the Rule of St. Isidore

Let a few observations on this book suffice for the reader. First, the author suppresses the letters *ae* and substitutes *e*: *Lectio Esaye prophete* (“Reading from the prophet Isaiah”); *fraterne dilectionis* (“of brotherly love”), LXXXV, 109. T becomes C before *ia* and *ie*: *pronunciare*, *percuciet*, 109, 110. Words in the breviary are found marked with a threefold accent, something now unusual in liturgical books, which admit only the grave as a tonic accent and do not use the circumflex except in the singular sixth case of the first declension and the second case of the fourth, LXXXVI.

### Eugenius, Bishop of Toledo

Eugenius cultivated poetry that has come down to us, LXXXVII, 359. In these verses he taught us the inventors of letters:

> Moses first traced Hebrew letters;  
> The sagacious Phoenicians devised Attic letters;  
> Nicostrata produced those which we Latins write;  
> Abraham discovered Syrian letters and likewise Chaldaic;  
> [Col. 0718] Isis, by no lesser skill, brought forth Egyptian letters;  
> Gulfila—otherwise Ulfila—produced the final letters of the Getae which we see, 366.

He composed his own acrostic epitaph in eight outstanding verses, 356.

### Bede the Venerable, Anglo-Saxon Abbot and Priest

He wrote a book on orthography, XC, 123. Among the ancients initial letters are often used for names, ibid. Twenty-one letters are counted among the Latins, five of them vowels, 150, 151. Of the consonants, nine are called mutes, 151. Four are liquids, 152. What a syllable is, 152. A short and a long syllable, 152. There is also a common syllable, ibid. Which syllables are called common, 153. They are also divided into initial, medial, and final syllables, 156, 157, 158, 161. See the *Rudiments of Donatus’ Grammatical Art*, restored by Bede, XC, 613 ff.

### Greek Terms Interpreted by Bede

Δεκατῶ (*dekatô*), “I tithe,” 131. *Denariov*, whence *denarius*, ibid. Dialogue, Latin *disputatio* (“discussion”), 131. Diastole, separation, ibid. Dogmata, Latin *decreta* (“decrees”), [Col. 0719] 132. Drama, that is, a play, 131. Δύναμις (*dýnamis*), strength or power, 150. Ἑβδομάς (*hebdomás*), whence *hebdomada* (“week”), 281. *Emporia*, that is, markets, XC, 132. Ἐμπύρεον (*empýreon*), the firmament, 194 note. Ἕως σφόδρα (*héōs sphódra*), entirely, 149. Γάρος (*gáros*), what it is, 138. *Glossa*, Latin *lingua* (“tongue”), 187. What a horologium is, 304 note. Horoscope and the act of casting a horoscope, 320, 321. *Hyle*, unformed matter, 196 note. Λεπτά (*leptá*), small coins, 306. Λουτήρ (*loutḗr*), basin, 138. Μήν (*mēn*), month, 659. What *Notus* is, 248 note. Ὄλυμπος (*Ólympos*), its derivation, 245. Ὁμοίως (*homoíōs*), equally, similarly, 142. Ὥρα (*hṓra*), whence *hora* (“hour”), 279. Ὀυρανός (*ouranós*), what is called heaven, 194 note. Πανταχοῦ (*pantachoû*), everywhere, 142. Πανσέληνος (*pansélenos*), full moon, 208. Παραβολή (*parabolḗ*), proverb, 142. Πλατύ (*platý*), broad, 141. Πόλος (*pólos*), summit, 199. Πρωτοτύπιον (*prōtotýpion*), cloth, 143. Πῦρ (*pŷr*), fire, 211. Φάρος (*pháros*), what it is, 411. Φύλαξ (*phýlax*), guardian, 207. Πώγων (*pṓgōn*), beard, 244. Ῥυθμός (*rhythmós*), modulation; ῥυθμίζω (*rhythmízō*), “I modulate,” 145. *Scamma* are things placed beside high beds, 146. Schemes or figures, and the names of various schemes, 175, 176. Σκύλλω (*skýllō*), “I strip” or “I harass,” 146. Σχολάζω (*scholázō*), “I have leisure,” 150. Σιωπάω (*siōpáō*), “I am silent,” 148. *Sophia* is wisdom or knowledge, 649. Στοιχεῖον (*stoicheîon*), element, 196. Συμπάσχω (*sympáschō*), “I suffer with,” 138. *Syzygia*, conjunction of elements. Θηρίον (*thēríon*), wild beast, 148; whence *theriaca* is so called because it kills like a beast, 148. *Telonium*, in Latin a tax, 149. Θρόνος (*thrónos*), throne. ### Latin Terms Whose Meaning and Use Are Defined by Bede

The use of the prepositions *ab* and *ex*, and likewise how *ad* and *in* are employed, XC, 125. *Aeger* is said of the mind, *aegrotus* of the body, ibid. How *Aegyptus* should be divided into syllables, 126. Evils *accidunt* (“befall”), good things *contingunt* (“happen”), and either kind *eveniunt* (“comes to pass”), ibid. *Avus* is said of men, *uterus* of women, 127. Both *appetens cibum* and *appetens cibi* (“desiring food”) are said, 125. The difference between *aquatus* and *aquosus*, 127. *Armarium* contains anything; *armamentarium* weapons only, ibid. In *aspectus*, *effectus*, and *afflictus*, the C belongs to the final syllable, 126. *Balneum* is said of a bath in private houses, *balneae* of public baths and in the plural, 127. One should say *barbam hominis* (“a man’s beard”) and *barbas pecudum* (“the beards of beasts”), ibid. *Blanditiae*, *bigae*, *trigae*, and *quadrigae* are used only in the plural. Yet in our writers we find *bigam* and *quadrigam*, ibid. What *buccina* and *buccinus* signify, ibid. *Buxus* is the tree; *buxum*, the material itself, ibid. *Capo* and *capus* for a castrated cock, 128. *Carduus*, *arduus*, *fatuus*, and similar words have three syllables, ibid. The difference between *curriculus* and *curriculum*, ibid. What *delator* and *dilator* are, 130. What *deluit* and *diluit* mean, ibid. “He anointed with perfume,” *dilibuit*, not *delibuit*, ibid. What *deduco* and *diduco* mean, 131. *Decus* is honour; *decor* beauty, ibid. The difference between *dito* and *divito*, ibid. What *dimittere* and *demittere* mean, ibid. The use of the conjunction *dum*, 132. *Error* is a defect in a thing, but *erratio* a wandering from the way, 132. Bede prefers *eorundem* and *earundem*, 133. Both *egeo victum* and *egeo victu* (“I lack food”) are said, 132. What *exstruere* and *instruere* mean, ibid. *Fedus*, “shapeless,” is written with E; *foedus*, “a treaty,” with OE, 133. Both *fidens animi* and *fidens animo* (“confident in spirit”) are said, 133. What *flemina* is, ibid. *Fremor* is the murmur of humans; *fremitus*, that of beasts, ibid. Say *fidus amicus* (“a faithful friend”) and *fidelis servus* (“a loyal slave”), ibid. *Fulgeo* and *fulcio* have the same perfect, *fulsi*, 134. The difference between *fulvus* and *furvus*, 133. *Gobius* is a fish, also called *gobio*, 134. *Gaudium* chiefly belongs to the mind; *exsultatio* chiefly to words and bodily movements, ibid. Both *gluten* and *glutinum* occur, ibid. *Hilarus* and *hilaris*, ibid. *Horrendum* is sometimes used for “marvellous,” ibid. Both *impleor vini* and *impleor vino* (“I am filled with wine”) are used, 136. The use of the preposition *in*, 135. Both *incurro te* and *incurro in te* (“I rush upon you”) are used, 136; likewise *intueor te* and *intueor in te* (“I look upon you”), ibid. The difference between *invidus* and *invidiosus*, 136. Julius Modestus allows both *large* and *largiter*, 137. *Limen* and *limes*, ibid. To speak (*loqui*) belongs to a person; to speak against (*obloqui*) to a detractor; to address (*alloqui*) to one persuading or commanding; to speak out (*eloqui*) to an orator, ibid. *Lucco* and *lugeo* have the same perfect, *luxi*, 138. Both *malogranatum* and *malum granatum* are used, ibid. *Mas* is the positive; *masculus* the diminutive, ibid. We marvel at works; we admire virtues, 139. One should say *memini me facere* (“I remember myself doing”), not *memini me fecisse*, since the verb *memini* is wholly in the past tense, ibid. *Meraca*, a drink mixed with unmixed wine, ibid. *Mendum* and *menda*, ibid. The use of *nimis*, ibid. *Nequam*, “useless,” not precisely “evil,” 140. Women, not men, marry (*nubunt*), for in marrying they veil themselves, ibid. *Obriza* and *obrizum* are equally used, 140. Both *palpor* and *palpo* occur, 141. *Paveo* and *pasco* mean the same, 142. *Pauperies* is loss; *paupertas* the condition itself, ibid. *Patrium* derives from *patria*; *paternum* from *pater*, ibid. *Percussum* is struck in body; *perculsum*, in mind, 143. *Podagrosus* derives from gout (*podagra*); *podagricus*, from disease of the feet, ibid. What *pubes* signifies, ibid. *Quare* and *cur* govern either the indicative or subjunctive, 144. Bede prefers *quorundam*, like *eorundem*, with N, ibid. *Seco* makes *secturus*, not *secaturus*, 146. What *sagina* and *sagena* are, ibid. Say *stercerati agri* (“manured fields”), not *stercorati*, ibid. [Col. 0720] The use of *sub* and *super*, 145. *Terga* belongs to humans; *tergora* to quadrupeds, 149. *Vallestria* is used like *campestria*, 150. Both *vultur* and *vulturius* are used, ibid.

### Paul the Deacon, Winfrid or Warnefrid of Cividale

#### Greek Terms

*Agape*, in Latin *dilectio* (“love”). This was the name of Christian meals to which poor people were invited, XCV, 469. The famous church of Constantinople was called Ἁγία Σοφία (*Hagía Sophía*, “Holy Wisdom”), 468. Who were called *amirei*, 1045. What *angariare* means and from what it derives, 518. *Holoserica lectisternia*, 1037. Λείψανα (*leípsana*), what they are, 992. *Logothesium*, 1066. *Logotheta*, 993. The etymology of the city Thessalonica, interpreted as “place another victory,” 105. *Theotocos*, the God-bearer, the Virgin Mary, 632.

#### Terms of Medieval Latin

*Aeris* for *aureis*, XCV, 505. In Paul, the Apennine Alps are named as though after the Punic people and Hannibal, 493. *Bandum*, that is, a standard, 460. *Berbices*, that is, sheep, 619. *Calbasiae*, shirts, 1037. *Cassis*, what it is, 620. *Hisdem* for *iisdem*, 529, 544. The derivation of Italy, or Ausonia, or Latium, 496. *Molles capillorum*, that is, locks or ringlets, 659. What the morning meal eaten by Tiberius was, 1000. *Regulae* or *bractheae*, 505. The extensive Persian practice of archery, 999. The origin of the name Samnites, 495 and note. *Spatharii*, or bodyguards, 630 note. *Strator*, or superintendent of horses; French *grand écuyer*, 485, 562, 628.

#### Gothic Terms in Paul the Deacon

*Anthabet*, what it is and from what it is named, 451 note. *Bandum*, that is, a standard, 460. *Baert*, beard, 448. The derivation of *Bathaib*, 451 note. *Feld*, open fields, 458. *Feot* or *feudum*, a possession held in trust, 437. The derivation of the Gepids’ name, 399 note. *Golanda*, that is, land of the Goths, 451 note. *Lama* in Gothic, a pool, 453. *Lang*, long, 448. Hence the name Langobards was given by Venilis because of the length of their beard, ibid. *Ot* in Gothic, possession, 437. *Rhene*, a Gothic word for an animal very common in the north, 443. *Rugiland*, that is, the territory or homeland of the Rugians, 457. *Schilpor*, that is, shield-bearer; French *écuyer*, 498 note. *Scrittobini* or *scrittofini* are named from *scritten*, which in German means “to straddle” and “to leap,” 442 note and 443. The derivation of the name Veneti, 491. Vandals, or Windeli: whence they are named, 435 ff. note. *Wodam*, *Godam*, and *Gotam* have the same etymology; Wodam is thought to be Mercury, 448 note. *Wurgundasb*, what it is and why so called, 451.

### Ildephonsus, Bishop of Toledo

*Albae* is the name given to garments in which catechumens were formerly baptized, XCVI, 170. Chrism: an anointing, whence *Christus*, 162. *Creticos* for *criticos*, 92. *Ecclesia* in Greek means “assembly”; it is catholic, or καθόλου (*kath’ holou*), “according to the whole,” 138. *Exorcidiare* for *exorcizare*, 121. Hyperbatonic expression, that is, obscure and confused language, 77. *Intempesta* and *galliciana*, that is, improper time and the time at which the cock crows, 69. *Lenitudinem* for tranquillity of mind, 92. “Marriage is such a mire,” said of marriage in relation to virginity, 62. “To utter a mass of madness,” ibid. “A thing beloved by God, a thing prior among created beings,” that is, an angel, 94. Ildephonsus calls Scripture “sacred letters,” “sacred pages,” and “sacred characters,” 93. *Turnus* in the Middle Ages was used for turn or order: *non turno verborum*, that is, “not in the order of words,” 121.

### Julian, Bishop of Toledo

His style is much purer than that of the writers of his age.

#### Greek Terms

*Antikeimenon*, or a book on Scriptural passages apparently contrary to one another, by Julian, XCVI, 586. What *gastrimargia* is, 728. *Prognosticon*, or foreknowledge of the age to come, the title of a book by Julian, 456, 458. “The cave of unbelief,” 770.

#### Latin Expressions

“The compass of warlike preparation,” 500. The derivation of *infernus*, 478. “The mass of perdition,” that is, the totality of those condemned, 513. “A sorrow-stricken heart,” 456. The derivation of *mors* (“death”), 462. *Peccamen* for *peccatum*: how it differs from *crimen*, 457. Purgatorial fire, 483. What Abraham’s bosom is, 476. “The cave of unbelief,” 770. *Storici* for *historici*, an insult, 797. “By the twisting pains of wasting gout,” 455. “At a lukewarm pace,” that is, a moderate one; some read *repenti* (“sudden”), 768.

What a *breviarium* is called, XCVII, 62. *Capella*, that is, ecclesiastical service, 59. *Carpentum*, a kind of carriage in which the king was drawn in rustic fashion by yoked oxen, 27. *Consultare*, 30. *Deiciunt* for *dejiciunt*, 34. *Incolomi* for *incolumi*, ibid. ### Paulinus, Patriarch of Aquileia

Words proper to animals are applied to people speaking vain and absurd things. Thus, in Arnobius (book III), a certain foolish Cornificius is said to bleat. In Paulinus, heretics grunt with impious mouth; in Jerome, detractors bark behind one; and Ausonius himself says to a foolish speaker:

> “The barking of puppies, the neighing of horses,  
> and the bleating of goat-begotten cattle and wool-bearing flocks  
> you imitate; you might also call asses braying.”

XCIX, 176. The verb *grunnire* properly signifies muttering; in the *Usages of the Monastery of Cluny*: “Let him begin the verse again, and do this as many times as he perceives that he has grunted on account of the preceding one.” The origin of the corruption of the Latin language, 103. How the extreme barbarism of word-endings gained excessive strength in this age, ibid. Paulinus himself used phrases and words that would not be approved by the touchstone of purer Latin, 104. How one ought to speak in the language of one’s own age, ibid. Those are excessively harsh exactors who demand golden words from an iron age, ibid. How the language of Cividale departed from Roman speech and gradually became subject to what idioms, 27. Why Augustine sought a bishop thoroughly acquainted with the native language of his province, 27. The praises of grammar, 32. The difference between *grammaticus* and *grammatista*, ibid. On the spelling of the name Paulinus, 24–25.

### Paulinian Glossary

*Ablactare* for *lactare*, XCIX, 443. *Aspersi* for *abstersi*, 274. *Aldi* and *aldiones* are called freedmen in Lombard, 37. What *ambarvale* and *amburbule* are, and how they differ, 493. Many writers after Sidonius called letters or epistles *apices*, 166. Arms are so called because they hang from the shoulder (*armus*), 214 note. *Assus* or *siccus* for “alone,” “dry bread”; hence the French expression *pain sec*, 195. “To punish the ears of my humility,” 345. Interchange of the letters B and V, 426 note. *Ballare*, an Italian word meaning “to dance,” appears to derive from Greek Βαλλεῖν (*balleîn*), “to throw,” 499 note. *Balsigeri*, an unknown word in Jordanes: what it is, 516. *Beatus* and *beatitudo*, honorific titles, 20, 21. What *bibici feriendus fulminis ictu* means in Paulinus, 474. “Of a booming throat,” that is, a hoarse one, 417. *Botrium* is a Greek diminutive from *botrus*, 480. *Cachinum incrispare*, that is, to laugh, 518. *Calculi* are accounts, or tablets on which a household’s income and expenditure are entered. *Calculatores*, however, were slaves whose duty it was to write these down, 171. The derivation of the term canons, 61. “Capacious receptacles of the stomach,” 345. *Capio*, or acquisition of ownership, and how it differs from prescription, 451 note. The derivation of *castra*, 213 note. *Cataplasma*, *cataplasmare*, 345 note. *Ceriti* and *larvati*, or maniacs, 488. What a chirograph is, 271 note. What chirotony is in the election of a bishop, 485 note. What colleague and college are, 478. The derivation of *comes*, 523. *Configulare*, or to join together by potter’s work, 177. *Conflare* for to stir up or emit breath, 477. *Crudelitas* sometimes used for the Creed, 606.

David was the name by which Alcuin called Charlemagne; Angilbert, Homer; Richulf, Damoetas, 77. *Delerare* and *delirare*: their meaning and derivation, 366. *Depastus* for “well fed,” 179. *Dictator* for “writer,” 312. *Dissigans*, perhaps a new word for *dissecans*, “cutting apart,” 362. *Dulculare* for *dulcorare*, “to sweeten,” 360. The force of *efflagitare*, 437 n. *Elinguare* for “to revile,” 307. “To buy on a blind day”: what it means, 372 n. *Enorme* is that which is outside the rule or norm, 304. *Exceptare* for *excipere*, “to receive,” [Col. 0722] 400 n. *Exspectaculum* for *spectaculum*, 356. *Firmare* for *affirmare*, 363. *Foderum* and *mansionaticum*: what they are, 62. *Fuat* for *fuerit*, an ancient usage, 517. Repetition of a word intensifies speech, 233 n. *Germanitas*, *Germanus*: an honorific title, especially among bishops, 307 n. Gibraltar, or Gibilterra, is said in Arabic to be *Gabal Tarik*, “Mount Tarik,” 557. *Glovellus* for *globulus*, 426. *Graphium*, *graphiarium*: what they are, 474. *Grumi terrae*: what clods of earth are, 359. *Grunnire*, the sound of pigs: how it is used, 176. *Gurgulio* or *gurgustio*: what it is, 449 n. “To talk little throats” (*gurguliunculos fabulare*) is said of those who strive with their throats to assert absurdities, 450 n. *Herbaticum* or *herbagium*, 62. Who were called *heriles*, or *dominici*, 390. Why Spain was called Hesperia, 169–170. *Homophagia* in fasts: what it is, 195. Hypante, or the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, 493 n. *Ibifluus* for *ibi fluens*, “flowing there,” 345 n. *Inormis*, *inormiter* for *enormis*, *enormiter*, “outside the norm,” 427 n. *Intentare voces et manus*, “to threaten with voice and hand,” 373. *Jus necessarium*: what it is, 171. Languedoc is said to derive from Gothic *Landet got*, “land of the Goths,” 577. Larvae are demons, 487 n. *Lapidarii*: commonly poor grammarians, 21. *Larvati* and *cerriti*, or maniacs, 488. Lenaeus, that is, “of the winepress,” a surname of Bacchus, 480 n. In agriculture, *lira* and *lera* are the ridge of a furrow which covers seed and which farmers call a *porca*, 366. Charlemagne’s litanies in the camp, 625. Who the *liti* and *fiscalini* were, 37. *Litteriones* are moderately educated grammarians, 32. The May-field: what it was, 42. *Mandrile*, from *mandra*, “a fold” or stable in which beasts of burden were fed, 351. *Mansionaticum* and *foderum*: what they are, 62. *Massaritia mansi* is the household equipment of a holding, or the holding itself furnished with equipment; hence *massus*, *masnator*, *massarius*, *massariae*, 37. *Mascha*, or a fictitious mask: source of the Italian word *maschera*, 488. *Melos*, or a declinable song, in Paulinus, 479. *Merus* for “only,” 195. *Minutare* for “to crush into small pieces,” 422. Hubs of wheels, 425. What *morosus* means and from what it is derived, 168. *Multare aures*, “to strike the ears,” 345. *Mundanum judicium*: what it is, 330. *Mussare*, *mussitare*: that is, to murmur among one’s teeth, 179. A repeated negative does not always make an affirmation, 382 n. Widows called *nonnae*, 330. *Norma* for “rule,” 304. The derivation of *obscenus*, 393 n. *Odula*, or a little ode, 459. *Offucare* for *suffocare*, “to suffocate,” 354 n. *Optare* for “to choose” and “to adopt,” 173. *Palliare* for “to lie hidden,” 494. *Palpare*, *palpitare*, said of one who is uncertain, 365, 374. Who the *semiaxiarii* were, 480. *Sequipeda* for *pedisequus*, “attendant,” 401. *Siccus* or *solus*; *siccus panis*, “dry bread,” 195. “A cave of falsehood,” 159. *Stremma* means that which is twisted; hence a *strematicus stylus*, 375 n. *Suciva* for *sucidua poma*, “late-ripening fruit,” 517. What *sulfugare* means, 304. *Summare* for “to exhort,” 459 n. *Terminare* for “to define,” 180. *Theoriae*: what they are and why so called, 446 n. *Tincta*, *tinctum* for ink, 517. *Tristare*, “to make sad” and “to be sad,” 435 n. *Trisulcibus* for *trisulcis*, “three-furrowed,” 358 n.
