Litany, that is, supplication or petition, 1224. Logic, that is, the rational art, 947. *Nycticorax*: “night-raven,” C, 588. What an obelus-mark is, CI, 858. Why an Olympiad is so called, 1120. Who the orthodox are, 1258. What orthography is, 858. Paralipomenon, or the Book of Things Omitted, 1126. What a pandect is, 913. Pantheon: a temple dedicated in honor of all the saints, 1230. Why the Pentateuch is so called, 1125. What *Perihermeniae* is, 972. Why philosophy is so called, 952. What physics is, ibid. *Poderis*, that is, a garment reaching to the ankles, 1258. Poetry, 725. What rhetoric is, 921. *Salpix*, that is, a trumpet, 766. *Scamma*: the wrestling arena, 820. Scenopegia, C, 841. Figures of speech, CI, 858. Schism, C, 1025. What solecism is, CI, 858. What a syllable is, 855. Syllogism, 966. Why a creed or symbol is so called, 1138. Synagogue, C, 644. Synonyms, or homonyms, CI, 955. The Tetragrammaton, or holy name of God written in Hebrew with four letters, CI, 1109. What theology is, 952. *Theristrum*: a kind of bridal mantle, C, 547.

Alcuinian Latin.—*Acunumbiae Alps* for Agaunian Alps, CI, 711. Why equinoxes are so called, 1118. Why summer is so called, 1119. The source of an agnomen, 859. What friendship is, 978. Why *anima* (“soul”) is so called, 1103. Why the year is so called, 1119. *Antistes*, 1236. Why hearing is called a sense, 1105. Why autumn is so called, 1119. What a belt is, 1240, 1241. What a beard is, 976. What barbarism is, 858. Alcuin calls Bede the teacher of his age, C, 278. The dry fields of Belgium, 281. What ceremonies are, CI, 1135. Why long hair is called *caesaries*, 1106. What the skull is, ibid. The sound of bells and of timbers, 1203. Why canons are so called, 1234. Why hairs of the head and body are so called, 1106. What the head is and why so called, 1105. Castles, 1163. Waxed cloths, 1245. The source of a cognomen, 859. Who were called *comites*, C, 475, 476. Why consonant letters are so called, CI, 855. The difference between *cotidie* and *quotidie*, 915. Why locks of hair are called *crines*, 1106. Cuckoo: an assumed name, like Menalcas and Daphnis, substituted for true names according to the custom of that age, 804. How the prepositions *de*, *dis*, and *des* are to be used in compounds, C, 183. What a word is, CI, 858. What elements are, C, 519. What expression or diction is, CI, 921. What an epistle is, C, 460. Why the face is called *facies*, CI, 1106. Why feast-days are called *feriae*, 1115. What gluttony is, 1194. Why taste is so called, 1105. When the letter I takes the force of a consonant (formerly *i* and *j* were written in the same manner), 856. Who are called *imbrumati*, 1119. Why the Kalends are so called, 1118. What a *mappula* is, 1243. Why a month is so called, CI, 1117. Rank-and-file soldiers, that is, men of low station, C, 347. Why a woman is called *mulier*, C, 698. Saints’ birthdays, or the days of their departure from this world, 956. Why nature is so called, CI, 1103. *Neglegens* for *negligens*, 912. Why the Nones are so called, 1118. Why night is so called, 1116. What the back of the head is, 1105. What an *orarium* is, 1242. Why bread is called *panis*, 1267. What “perpetual” means and its derivation, C, 419. *Peteredium* is said to derive from seeking an inheritance, CI, 913. What orchards and fruit-gardens are called, 913. What verbal prepositions are, 899. What prose is, 858. Points placed to distinguish meanings are called punctuation-marks, ibid. *Rogare* means not only “to ask for” but also “to question,” C, 956. The difference between *saeculum* and *aevum*, 420. Why the Saxons are called *Saxi* or *Saxones*, CI, 815. Why *sempiternum* is so called, C, 419. Why a slave is called *servus*, 557. What *solaria* are and why so called, CI, 745. Why solstices are so called, 1118. What sophistical discourse is, 939. Why touch is so called, 1105. What tapestries and a *sagellum* are, C, 237. The several senses of “whole,” CI, 967. When U, according to ancient orthography, takes the force of consonantal V, 856. Why verses are so called, 1251. Why a man is called *vir*, C, 698. Why sight is so called, 1105.

SMARAGDUS, abbot of the monastery of St Michael of Verdun.—We shall select only a few items from him, since he merely excerpted writings of the holy Fathers already catalogued by us.

Hebrew names.—*Abba*, “father,” CII, 181. Barabbas, “son of the father,” 242. *Ben Adam*, “Son of Man,” 391. The Hebrew title of Christ’s cross, 190. Gehenna is said to derive from *ge*, “valley,” and *henna*, “gratis,” 1405, 1120. Jehovah: the Tetragrammaton, the name of God, 1125. Jeremiah, “the Lord is exalted,” 378. Malchus, “king,” 182. Noah’s four sons had wives: Puerfara, Parfia, Catafluia, and Fluia, 1120. What *Racha* is, 404. *Sicer*, whence *sicera*, that is, intoxication, 381.

[Col. 0724] Greek terms.—*Angelos*, “messenger,” 257. Apocalypse, that is, revelation, 393. The Greek particle *epi*, “upon”: it is joined to many nouns and verbs, as *epistola*, “sent upon”; *epigramma*, “writing upon”; *epitaphium*, “upon a tomb”; *episcopus*, “overseer,” 15, 1113. *Hydropsy* derives from ὕδωρ, “water,” 468. Πανοπλία, “the whole armor,” 493. Paul is said to derive from παῦλα, “cessation,” because Saul had ceased persecuting Christ’s faithful, 15. *Philargyria*, or avarice, 369. Proselytes, or newcomers, 287.

Latin words and expressions.—*Figulus*, or *frigulus*: the identity of that author is unknown, 1119. The same must be said of Victor of Capua, 1122. “By whose diligent strengthening” (*cujus confortatu sedulo*): read otherwise, *edulio*, “meal,” 14, 1113. *Latrare*, “to bark,” for “to malign”: “Let not the perversity of heretics bark,” 240. *Mavelle* for *malle*, “to prefer,” 13, 1113. *Nativa*, perhaps for *nociva*, “harmful,” ibid. Romans are interpreted as “sublime” or “thundering,” because of their power and strength, 15, 1113. St Victor of Capua: an unknown author, 1122.

AGOBARD (St), bishop of Lyons.—The apostles and evangelists said absolutely nothing contrary to the rules of grammar unless either reason or some mystical cause required it to be so said, CIV, 164. Whether rusticity of language is to be attributed to the Holy Spirit, Moses, and the prophets, 165, 166. The second person plural is used for the singular, a usage observed out of reverence in the Middle Ages, 159 and passim.

Words and expressions, Greek as well as Latin.—*Aura levatitia*: a phrase formerly used when thunder was heard and lightning flashed, 147, 154. *Carra carricata*, 158. *Cavallus* for *equus*, “horse,” 247. Agobard does not wish holy images to be called “holy,” but rather “images of saints,” and explains why, 211. *Injustitiae* in the plural, 186. “Our foolishnesses,” 187. *Joculares*: a type of entertainer subsequently called *jongleurs* in French, 249 n. The judgment of the cross, the judgment of God: what this procedure, used for deciding legal causes, was, 252 n. What Greek *latria* is, 201, 202. “The great author of Latin speech,” that is, Virgil, 201. Magonia: a fictitious and invented region of magicians, 148. *Matarus*: a kind of missile weapon, 261 n. “Memories of saints,” that is, churches dedicated under the invocation of saints, 213. *Parentes* for blood-relations and relations by marriage, 187. Painted carvings, 216. What region was called Septimania, 227. *Tempestarii* or *sortiarii*, people held to cause storms and hail, 147. Θρησκεία, that is, religion, 201, 202. What *thresceia*, *eusebeia*, *theosebeia*, and *latreia* are, and how they differ among the Greeks, ibid. *Zographia* in Greek means painting, that is, “living writing,” 216.

THEODULF, bishop of Orléans—Words and expressions. *Arabs*: “the grim Arab,” CV, 287. *Artarier* for *arctari*, “to be constrained,” 285. “Each one *boat*,” that is, exalts himself, 295. *Capitula*, *capitularia*: origin of this title, 192 n. Bacchic cups (*carchesia*), 290. *Carle* for *Carole*, 374. Why a catechumen is so called, 224. “Steel strikes steel,” 374. The name *Christicolus*, “worshipper of Christ,” 327. *Conloquio* for *colloquio*, 283. *Exedra* for the church’s *hexedra*, 210. What exorcism is, 225. *Gastrimargia*, or gluttony of the belly, 2. *Grippes* for *gryphes*, 288. *Inlitus* for *illitus*, 287. *Inriguus* for *irriguus*, ibid. *Lugdune*, as though one said *Lugdunus*, 285. *Mage* for *magis*, 314. *Moneta* for money, 297. *Navegius* for “son of Nave,” that is, Joshua, 300. *Paraenesis to the judges*: by whom this title was added, 283. The fish-bearing Rhine, 314. *Psalmicanus* for *psalmista*, “psalmist,” 285. *Rupee* for *rupeae*, ibid. Why a creed or symbol is so called, 226. Tmesis: a figure in which a compound word is divided and separated by other words, as in Virgil, *septem subjecta trioni* (“subject beneath the seven-starred constellation”). By tmesis Theodulf divided the Suevic name of Gisla’s husband in this verse: *Suaveque, Gisla, tuo feliciter utere rico*—“And, Gisla, happily enjoy your Suevic husband,” 326 n. *Unguem* for ointment, chrism, 327. Wardo for Gardo, the river flowing into the Rhône from the city of Nîmes, 285.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans.

Words and expressions.—“To be for adoration,” CVI, 354. *Agmina exsequiarum*: so a funeral procession and pomp are called, 262. *Aliud* used substantively, 300. *Cartallum*: a vessel and a measure, 123. *Celare virum* appears to stand for *zelare*, “to be jealous of a man,” 186. *Columbus* for *columba*, “dove,” 136. *Delectatur* is wrongly written; read rather *luctatur*, “struggles,” 269. Church buildings, 204. *Gravedo* for heaviness, 357. *Impiare ossa mortuorum*, “to desecrate the bones of the dead,” for “to violate,” 263. John Golden-mouth, that is, Chrysostom, 150. “You have reminded me of my extremity,” 122; “I remind your most experienced sagacity”: a manner of expression familiar in the Middle Ages, especially among monks, 124. Obscurity and corruption of words occur, 357, 358. *Ordinabiliter*, “in an orderly manner,” 185. “After how many days,” 187. Why a king is called *rex*, 287. “Arrows of words,” 338. *Scriptitasti*, that is, “you wrote stupidly,” ibid. “The missile of your composition,” 340.

AGNELLUS, abbot of St Mary at Blachernae near Ravenna.—*Ammonuit* for *admonuit*, CVI, 522. *Ardica*: the upper part by the doorway of a building, 487, 514. *Bandum*: a kind of standard, called *bannière* in French, [Col. 0725] 605. Calocerus: a proper name interpreted “good season,” 485. Whether *Cosmedin*, the name of the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary, was Latin or Greek was formerly debated, 619. What *endothis* is, 600, 602. *Glossocomum*, or bier or tomb, 515. *Graphia* for writing, 600. *Iidata me sectiret*, corrupted by the typesetters; perhaps read *ita in me saeviret*, “thus he raged against me,” 461. *Januculum* for *janiculum*, 475. *Lithostratae litterae*, that is, letters carved in stone, 606. “Anointed by your prayers” (*litus obsecrationibus vestris*), that is, anointed and covered round about, 162. *Paries* used as feminine, as “one wall,” “another wall,” 506. *Primicerius*, *secundicerius*, and so forth: ranks of notaries, 586. *Proconisa*: a tombstone, 516. Faulty punctuation; read: “I cannot otherwise make everything known to you,” 568. Who should be called a *scholasticus*, 452. *Spatha*: a two-edged kind of sword, 639. What tesserae are, 630. *Vesteraria*, a woman, for *vestiaria*, 638. *Vitales aurae*, that is, breaths or spirits of life, 493. What *zancha* is, 603.

RABANUS MAURUS, archbishop of Mainz.—The origin of diversity among languages, CIX, 284; CXI, 435. Which languages were preeminent; praise of Greek and Latin, CXI, 435, 436. Divisions of these languages, ibid. Definition, use, and praise of grammar, CVIII, 395. The living voice outweighs letters, from Jerome, CXII, 327. The authority of philosophers shows that the essential property of voice lies in the striking of air, however the stroke is made, CXI, 613. Voice is distinguished as articulated and inarticulate, literate and illiterate, ibid. Distinctions among various voices, CX, 540. What a letter is, 613; it is said to derive, as it were, from *legitera*, 615. How many Latin and how many Greek letters there are, ibid. Which are called vowels and which consonants, ibid. What a syllable is and why so called, 617. On first, or initial, syllables, 622. On medial syllables, 625. Which letters are called mutes and why, 615. Which are liquids, 616. Accent is said as though *adcantus*, “added song.” No utterance is without accent, 625. In Greek accent is called *prosodia*, ibid. On cases, 673. On the nominative, 634. On oblique cases, 642. On the pronoun, 644. On the verb and its conjugation, 646 ff. On adverbs, 657. On the participle, 661. On metrical feet, 675. Allegory properly belongs to the art of grammar, CXII, 330. On reading and correct pronunciation, CVII, 363, 364.

On the Hebrew language.—Sacred Scripture, proceeding from one perfect language, could fittingly be disseminated throughout the world; through the various languages of translators it was spread far and wide, CVII, 380. Certain things in Scripture are so obscurely expressed that they cast over us a most dense darkness, ibid. Certainly nothing ought more to be committed to memory than those kinds of words and expressions which we do not know, 385. One who wishes to become skilled in proper signs must labor, so far as languages are concerned, to know both the certain force of words and the proper manner of expressions, 386. It is probable that the language originally given to Adam remained in the household of Heber, from whom the Hebrews are named, 530. At the division of languages the Creator made nothing new, but only distributed ways and forms of speaking among the various kinds of languages, ibid.; CXI, 435. The patriarchs and prophets used the Hebrew language, ibid. It is the first among sacred languages, ibid. Some think Hebrew itself to be Chaldean because Abraham was from the Chaldeans; but they err, since we read that the three Hebrew children, one of whom was Daniel, learned a language they had not known, namely that of the Chaldeans, 436. All Eastern peoples strike language and words in the throat, as Hebrews and Syrians do, ibid. Western peoples, however, break words with their teeth, as Italians and Spaniards do, ibid. Syriac and Chaldean are linguistically near to Hebrew, agreeing with it in many respects, such as the sound of letters, ibid. Interpretation of Hebrew letters, 1183.

In the interpretation of Hebrew names Rabanus everywhere followed Jerome; therefore we refer the reader to that holy doctor’s very full index, to be consulted in its proper place.

On the Greek language.—Of the sacred languages Greek holds second place; among the languages of other nations it is clearer and more resonant, CXI, 435. It is divided into five dialects: first, Κοινή, that is, “mixed” or “common,” which all use; second, Attic or Athenian, used by all Greek authors; third, that used by Egyptians and Sicilians; fourth, Ionic; fifth, Aeolic, spoken by the Aeolians.

Greek etymologies.—The various meaning of abyss, CXI, 314, 315. Why acolytes are so called, CVII, 304. Why the Acroceraunian Mountains are so called, CXI, 363. Who are called enigmaticists, CVIII, 723. What an *agon* is, CXI, 549. What alabaster is, CVII, 1100. What relief-carving (*anaglypha*) is, CIX, 159. Who are called androgynes, CXI, 196. What anomalous forms are, 675. Why a changing-room is called an *apodyterium*, 388. Etymology of *aporia*, CIX, 961. Areopagus is interpreted “village of Mars,” and why, CXI, 382. What atoms are, 262. Why a chasm (*barathrum*) is so called, 374. What the Chimera is, 198. What a *chyrogrillus* is, 777. Why the Cyclades are so called, 366. Cyclopes, 197. Etymology of cymbals, CIX, 346, 347. Why Cynics are so called, [Col. 0726] CXI, 415. Cynocephali, 197. What a dog-fly (*cynomya*) is, 258. Why Cyprus is so called, 165. Why amber or electrum is so called, 475. *Enhydrus*, the crocodile’s enemy, 232. Why confession (*exomologesis*) is so called, CVII, 766. What ecstasy is, CXI, 1330. Etymology of *gazophylacium*, CX, 922. Geometry, CVII, 400. Gymnasium, CXI, 387. *Hippodes*: having horses’ feet, 197. Why horoscopes are so called, CX, 422. Subdeacons, CXI, 92. *Latria* and *dulia*, CVIII, 133. Why Libya is so called, CXI, 351. What litanies and supplications are, 138. Why a lamp is called *lychnus*, 605. Why Lydia and Lycaonia are so called, 344. Why Macedonia is so called, 348. Etymology of mathematics, CVII, 398, 399. *Melos* is named from roundness, CXI, 356. Etymology of Mesopotamia, 337. What it means “to commit adultery with wood and stones,” 829. *Monoceros*, that is, unicorn, CVIII, 741. What a new moon (*neomenia*) is, 783. Why natron is so called, CXI, 763. *Nycticorax*, 251. The origin and names of nymphs, 454. What Orion is, 273. Palaestra, 549. Paradise, 334. *Paraenesis*, or exhortation, CX, 236. What Pentapolis is, CXI, 341. What *phaederae* are, 612. Quiver, 151. *Philargyria*, CVIII, 887. Egyptian pyramid, 408. What a *rhomphaea* is, CIX, 902. Satyrs: what little men they are, CXI, 196. Why scarabs are so called, 256. Feast of Tabernacles, CVIII, 787, 788. Who the Sciopodes in Ethiopia are, CXI, 197. What *semeron* is and why so called, CIX, 486. What storax is, 933. Etymology of synagogue, CXI, 90. Why Tartarus is so called, 374. *Theoria*, 1228. What baths (*thermae*) are, 388. *Theristrum*, CVII, 574. What a tyrant is, CXI, 446. What xenodochia are and why so called, 397. Xerophagy, 137. Jealousy, CVIII, 619, 926, 927.

On the Latin language.—Four Latin languages are distinguished: Old, Latin, Roman, and Mixed, CXI, 436. Old is that used by the most ancient Italians under Janus and Saturn, and is unformed, as are the songs of the Salii, ibid. Latin is that spoken by the rest in Latium under Janus and the kings of Etruria; the laws of the Twelve Tables were written in this language, ibid. Roman is that used by Naevius, Plautus, Virgil, Cicero, and Horace, ibid. Mixed is that corrupted through solecisms and barbarisms under the emperors and with the irruption of barbarians, 436.

Why Africa is so called, CXI, 351. Why a friend is called *amicus*, 609, 797, 899. Why Antichrist is so called, CVIII, 1172. A boar (*aper*) is named from its wildness, CXI, 207. Why the Apennines are so called, 363. What sunny places are, 372. Why an altar (*ara*) is so called, 391. Why silver is so called, 476. What an *armarium* is, 405. Why gold is so called, 475. Why baths are called *balneae*, 388. What a belt is, CVIII, 203, 206. The typological meaning of the arm, CXII, 873, 874. *Caballus* for *equus*, “horse,” CXI, 612. Why spurs are so called, ibid. Why a singer is so called, 88. Why a carbuncle is so called, CVII, 478. Why a prison is so called, CXI, 389. Why a beaver is so called, CXI, 222. A cell is said to be named from its concealing and hiding, 390. What a citizen is, CXII, 897, 898. Why a city is so called, CXI, 375. The derivation of the name heaven, CVII, 445. What *confrages* are, CXI, 370. Why a crown is so called, 584. What a geometrical cubit is, CVIII, 517. Why a curia is so called, CXI, 387. What a dalmatic is and why so called, CVII, 307. What a *dextrariola* is, CIX, 621. Why a flood is so called, CXI, 329. Etymology of *diversorium*, 592. What an *ergasterium* and *ergastulum* are, 405. Why shrines (*fana*) are so called, CXI, 391. What a bier is, 607. Why iron is so called, 486. What the fisc is, 604. Why a hearth is so called, 605. Etymology of scissors, 610. Why the forum is so called, 544. *Framea*, 537. Bridle, 612. What a strait is, 315. The mystical meaning of fruit and tree, 512. Why a sling and slingers are so called, 541, 611. Why ropes are so called, 156. The origin of the name Gehenna, CVII, 901. Why a people (*gens*) is so called, CXI, 437. Etymology of the town Heligenstadt, CXII, 1633. What a hiatus is, CXI, 373. Origin of the name Spain, 351. The various senses of “man,” 137. The various interpretations of shoulders, CXII, 959. What an incubus is and why so called, CXI, 434. Why India is so called, 335. Why islands are so called, 353. Why a stone is called *lapis*, 462. Why laurel is so called, 511. Why a bed is so called, 706. What a lion is called, 45, 207. A hare (*lepus*) as though “light-footed” (*levipes*), 205. Why a pound-scale is called *libra*, 482. Why Libya is so called, CIX, 283; CXI, 351. What a straight line is, CVIII, 191. Why the shore is called *littus*, CXI, 372. What slipperiness is, 372. Why a grove is called *lucus*, 371. What a loincloth or girdle is, 903. What a brothel is, 353. Why the sea is called *mare*, 455. Why marble is so called, 463. Etymology of metal, CXI, 474. Why delay is called *mora*, 603. Why death is called *mors*, 194. Mouse (*mus*) from earth (*humus*), CXI, 226. Why *musio* is so called, 226. Who *nasoparvus* is, CVIII, 485. The several senses of cloud, 415; CXI, 1167. Who the messenger of death is, CXI, 734. What obstacles to prayer are, 860, 861. Why Ocean is so called, 312. Why a pot is called *olla*, 602. The various senses of *os* (“mouth,” “bone”), CXII, 1013. What oscin birds are, CXI, 255. Etymology of pedagogues, CXII, 306. Interpretation of the palm, CX, 159, 511. Why Pannonia is so called, 350. The various meanings of bread, CVIII, 80. What a pine is, CXI, 517. Plane-tree, CIX, 931. Why a harbor is so called, CXI, 372. What a cart (*reda*) is, 608. Why Mount Riphaeus is so called, 363. What a sanctuary is, 391. What satrapies and satraps are; who the satyrs, those little men, are, 196. Why Scotland is so called, 354. What a writing-case is, CXII, 1172. What painted carving is, CIX, 440. Who are properly called old men, CXI, 736. Etymology of Sicily, 357. How “without me” is to be interpreted, [Col. 0727] CVIII, 227. Why a bucket is called *situla*, CXI, 600, 601. Why *solurius* is so called, 363. What a balance is, 485. Why superstition is so called, 95. Why shoemakers are so called, 526. Why taverns are so called, 388. What *tabulatae* are, CIX, 146. Why a temple is so called, 392. The word *thalami* was introduced through an oracle, CXI, 390. Why thunder is so called and what it signifies, 277. *Vae* is a threat-making cry, CX, 560. What light-armed troops (*velites*) are, CXI, 450. Why poison is so called, 232. What *veredarii* are, CIX, 663, 664. A wether (*vervex*) is named from strength, CXI, 202. Why a viper is so called, 232. Life (*vita*) is named from vigor, CXII, 835. Origin of the name vine, CX, 474. Distinctions among various voices, CX, 510, 541.

WALAFRID STRABO, monk of Fulda, author of the *Glossa ordinaria* collected from the holy Fathers.—We examine only this writer’s other works as his own.

Various words and expressions of Walafrid interpreted.—The Hebrew names cited in the genealogy of Jesus Christ according to Matthew are interpreted, CXIV, 850 ff. *Absida*, that is, “bright,” 928. Why an *analogium* is so called, 926. Altar from *alta ara*, “high altar,” 925. Basilica, or royal hall, ibid. *Camera*, named from hollowness, 926. Bells, named from Campania, 924. What chancel-rails (*cancelli*) are and why so called, 924. Cemetery, that is, a resting-place or dormitory of the dead, 925. Crypts, 982. Etymology of church, 924. An *exedra* is a kind of apse, 925. Doors (*fores*) derive from “outside” (*foris*), 926. The angelic hymn, that is, *Gloria in excelsis*, “Glory in the highest,” 945, 951. Doors (*januae*) from Janus, 926. What suspended coffering or panelled ceilings (*lacunaria*, *laquearia*) are, 926. Churches are called martyr-shrines, ibid. Bells (*nolae*) are named from Nola, 924. Names which the Latins received from the Greeks, and the Germans (*Theodisci*) from the Latins, 927. Why gates (*portae*) are so called, 926. A pulpit, that is, something set in public, 926. What a sanctuary is, ibid. *Temptare* is written for *tentare*, “to test,” 870. German barbarism, 926. Doors (*valvae*) are named from turning, ibid.

Here we have omitted many writers: namely Ebbo, bishop of Rheims; Hartmann, monk of St Gall; Ermauric, monk of Reichenau; Erchambert, bishop of Freising; Nithard, abbot of St Richard; Amulo, bishop of Lyons; because they left extremely few writings; and Haymo himself, bishop of Halberstadt, who in his commentaries and homilies merely repeated word for word what earlier writers had said. We know of nothing new added by him either to grammatical art or to linguistic study. The same must be said of Florus, deacon of Lyons.

LUPUS, abbot of Ferrières.—*Armarium* for a library, CXIX, 464. “Honor nourishes the arts”: a saying of Cicero in the *Tusculans*, 433. *Bajulus*: this was the common name for monitors, 529. What a *brevis voluminum* and *brevis causarum* are, 435 n. Cultivation of style, 502. Lupus employs diminutive words. “In our little St Peter,” that is, in our monastery dedicated to St Peter. The orator Cotta, speaking in the middle of the Senate about the emperor Tiberius, said, “My little Tiberius,” a familiarity condemned. Matthew Paris reports that a theologian, speaking of the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, cried out so childishly: “O little Jesus, little Jesus, how greatly in this question have I confirmed and exalted your law!” The same diminutive *Jesulus* is applied to the child Jesus in the *History of Blessed Mary of the Holy Mount*. Moreover, according to Ripamonti, when a demon was ordered by St Bernard to leave a certain woman, it addressed Bernard thus: “Neither little Cyrus [St Cyrus, to whom she had already been brought] could drive me out, nor will little Bernard drive me out today,” 517, 518 n. *Exsolutim* for *indusia exsoluti*, “the undergarments of the unclothed,” 601. “Most renowned emperor,” said of Charlemagne, 433. German *glizz*, “linen cloths”; hence the *camisia glizzina* of the monks of St Gall, 532 n. *Gravate* for “laboriously,” 451. *Incolumis* for accusative plural *incolumes*, 434. *Jurative*, “by oath,” 675. What uncial letters are, 448. ## JOHN SCOT ERIGENA, monk

How he could obtain teachers of Latin and Greek, CXXII, XIX ff. It is indeed astonishing how that barbarian man, placed at the ends of the earth—who, in proportion as he was remote from intercourse with men, might be believed equally remote from the speech of another language—desired to grasp such things in intellect and translate them into another language, 15. Scotus did not know Hebrew or Syriac, 14. How he could have learned Greek letters in Ireland, ibid. From the abundance of Greek expression, prepositions are often put before words and yet add no meaning, as, for example, these three: ἀνά, καί, πρός—“again,” “and,” “to.” The same must be said of *cata*, which is translated in many renderings, 164. Although our intellect is in itself invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless it is both manifested and apprehended by certain signs, when it is made dense, as it were, into certain bodies by voices, letters, or other indications . . . when it wills, it is embodied in voices and letters, 633.

## ADO, archbishop of Vienne

With regard to the study of languages, nothing appears in Ado. See the note which wishes the Greek word *scolaces* to be interpreted by the Latin *funalia* (“torches”), from which *funera* (“funerals”) is said to derive, CXXIII, 355.

## USUARD, monk of Saint-Germain

Like Ado, he offers no elucidation of any importance for the nature and study of language. This is, however, the place to make certain observations concerning the proper names found in both catalogues of Usuard, CXXIV, 1279, 1287. We distinguish personal proper names into four principal linguistic families.

The first family concerns names belonging to Eastern languages—namely Hebrew, Syriac, Persian, Egyptian, Ethiopian, Punic, Arabic, and so forth—such as Abraham, Isaac, Moses, Elijah, Matthew, Bartholomew, John, Pachomius, etc.

The second family includes names referred to the Greek language and formed from Greek roots, such as Achilles, Agapetus, Alexander, Andrew, Basil, Chrysogonus, Cyril, Dionysius, etc.

The third family embraces names of the Latin language, or of Italians, Etruscans, or Romans, such as Agricola, Albinus, Amandus, Aquilinus, Augustine, Benedict, Domitian, Donatus, Desiderius, Honoratus, etc.

The fourth family includes names deriving from Gothic, Celtic, or Germanic origin, and especially recognizable by their roots. The Gothic roots in particular are these:

*Ald*: Aldegundis, Aldhelmus, Aldetrudis.

*Adal, Adel*: Adalbertus, Adelardus.

*Ans, Arnl, Arnf, Austr, Autb*: Anscharius, Anselmus, Arnaldus, Arnulphus, Austrudis, Autbertus, etc.

*Bald, Band, Baud*: Baldomerus, Balduinus, Bandaridus, Baudelicus, etc.

*Berr, Berc, Berl, Bern, Bert, Berth, Berw*: Berardus, Bercarius, Berlindis, Bernardus, Bernaldus, Bertinus, Bertrada, Bertha, Bertharius, Berwaldus, etc.

*Botlf, Bramb, Brand, Burch, Burg, Buth*: Botufus, Brambertus, Brandanus, Briojetta, Burchardus, Burgundus, Burgundofora, Buthelmus, etc.

*Clod, Cloth, Colm, Conrd, Cunb, Cung, Cutb, Cuthb*: Clodulfus, Clothsendis, Colmannus, Conradus, Cunibertus, Cunegundis, Cutburga, Cuthbertus, etc.

*Dod, Drog, Dunst*: Doda, Dodo, Drogo, Dunstanus, etc.

*Ead, Ebr, Edel, Edb, Edm, Egb, Egw, Elg, Emm, Engl, Engr, Erch, Erend, Erck, Ethel, Evr, Ew, Eym, Eyn*: Eadburga, Eadmerus, Ebrulfus, Edeltrudis, Edmundus, Eduardus, Egbertus, Egwinus, Einbertha, Elfegus, Eligius, Emmia, Engelbertus, Ensuitha, Erchenwaldus, Erembertus, Erendrudis, Erckembodus, Ermelindis, Ethelburga, Ethelreda, Everardus, Evurtius, Ewaldus, Ewigius, Eymerica, Eynardus, etc.

*Filb, Finn, Florb, Folq, Franc, Fraud, Fred, Frid, Fulc*: Filibertus, Findrudis, Finnianus, Florbertus, Folquinus, Franciscus, Francoveus, Fraubaldus, Fredegandus, Fredericus, Fridolinus, Frodobertus, Fulcherius, Fulco, etc.

*Gall, Gand, Gang, Geb, Gelt, Gend, Gengl, Gerdl, Gerd, Gerbr, Gerh, Gerl, Germ, Gertr, Gerv*: Gallus, Galla, Gandulfus, Gangulfus, Gebetrudis, Geldeldus, Gendulfus, Genebaudus, Genglufus, Genulfus, Geraldus, Gerardus, Gerebaldus, Gerbrandus, Gerhardus, Germanus, Gertrudis, Gervasius, etc.

*Gilb, Gild, Gisl, Glod, God, Goer, Gond, Gosw, Gotb, Grim, Grod, Grog, Gud, Guid, Guig, Guill, Gumb, Gund*: Gilbertus, Gildardus, Gildas, Gislenus, Godeslinda, Gobertus, Godardus, Godeberta, Godefridus, Godoaldus, Godscalcus, Goericus, Gondulfus, Goswinus, Gotbertus, Grimbaldus, Grodegangus, Grogbertus, Gudualdus, Guibertus, Guido, Guigo, Guillelmus, Guinbertus, Gundoifus, etc.

*Had, Hal, Harl, Henr, Hertr, Herb, Herib, Herl, Hidlf, Higb, Hild, Hub*: Herdelinus, Halfardus, Harlindis, Harwaldus, Hedwigis, Henricus, Heribertus, Herlindis, Hersuinda, Hidulfus, Hildegardis, Hildewardus, Hubertus, Humbertus, etc.

*Ida, Ideb, Ingel, Irg, Iv*: Ida, Idaberga, Ideburga, Imerus, Ingela, Iringardis, Ivo.

*Kan, Ken, Kent, Kin*: Kanutus, Keneswita, Kentigernus, Kunegundis, Kyneburga.

*Ladi, Lamb, Land, Lang, Lant, Lead, Leot, Leov, Leow, Leud, Lief, Liet, Lind, Loth, Ludg, Ludw, Luth*: Ladis, “praise”; Lambertus, Landricus, Landulfus, Langulfus, Lantfrancus, Leodegarius, Leotaldus, Leovaldus, Leudomirus, Liefardus, Lietbertus, Lindemannus, Lintrudis, Lotharius, Ludgerus, Ludovicus, Ludwinus, Lutgardis, Luthardus, etc.

*Mael, Madel, Mainl, Malb, Marclf, Mathld, Med, Menl, Meyn, Monlf*: Maclovius, Madelberth, Madelgisilus, Maingoldus, Malburga, Monegildis, Marculfus, Marnulfus, Mathildis, Medardus, Medericus, Mengoldus, Menulfus, Meynardus, Modoaldus, Monulfus.

*Nig, Niv, Nonn, Norb, Notg*: Nigundis, Nivardis, Notgerus, Nonnus, Nonna, Norbertus.

*Oda, Odg, Odil, Odo, Odol, Odul, Old, Osw, Othm*: Oda, Odalricus, Odgerus, Odilo, Odo, Odrada, Odolricus, Odulfus, Oldericus, Oswaldus, Oswinus, Othmarus, etc.

*Pegg, Pipp*: Pegga, Pippinus.

*Rad, Rag, Ray, Reg, Rel, Remb, Beyn, Rich, Rig, Rob, Rod, Rog, Rol, Rum, Rut*: Radbertus, Radbodus, Radulphus, Ragomerus, Regenfledis, Rembertus, Remundus, Reynoldus, Richardus, Rictrudis, Rigobertus, Rodulfus, Rolandus, Romualdus, etc.

*Sab, Sag, Sexb, Sigeb, Sigfr*: Sabaudus, Sagaria, Sexburga, Sigebertus, Sigefridus, Sicfridus, etc.

*Tadw, Tetb, Theod, Trutp*: Tadwinus, Tetbaldus, Theodolfus, Trutpertus, Tugdualus, etc.

*Ubald, Udal, Ug, Ulfag, Ultan*: Ubalduos, Udalricus, Ugo, Ulfagius, Ultanius, etc.

*Vastr, Ved, Vulm, Vult*: Vastradis, Vedastus, Volganus, Vulmarus, Vultanus, etc.

[Col. 0731] All names whose first letter is W belong to the Gothic language, such as Walbertus, Walfridus, Waldetrudis, Valdrada, Waso, Wereburga, Werenfridus, Wibrandis, Wichburga, Wilifridus, Willhelmus, Willibaldus, Wolfangus, Wolstanus, Wolfelmus.—Yda, Yduberga, Ythamarus.

## ABBO, monk of Saint-Germain

That writer and bad poet hands down certain exceedingly rare things in an obscurity of expression no less than in barbarous diction: let a few examples suffice, CXXXII, 748–78.

> Let us turn the plectra of the voice behind the backs of stupors;  
> Let us speak of the fragile pact by which they had been infected,  
> Of the Norman bands, unwilling to descend from the borders of France  
> To their own caves, yet desirous rather to revisit  
> You, Seine-streams, which by retaining silver for themselves  
> Might reveal cultivated fields;  
> Here Ebalus snatches a cord and vibrates an arrow  
> Which the pilot, first to do so, received into the armpit  
> Through the ship’s opening, slightly pierced by a drill.  
> Alas, they find five hundred and slaughter them with blows.  
> The excellent martial abbot Ebolus mingled with these,  
> If not too covetous, wanton, and suited to all things;  
> For he shone nobly in studies, which mistress Grammar  
> Allowed Anschericus, the bishop of the covenant, to depart, stretched out,  
> Though he ought rather to have fallen.

> Cleric, never remove the diptychs from your side;  
> Flee the little hearts of the slippery game, lest the compact  
> Coffin and the petty ruler rejoice over you;  
> Let battle be yours, where there is hierarchy, and not a sewer;  
> Let neither *enteca* nor *alogia*, but rather an apse,  
> Remain with you . . .  
> Let *gripphia* touch you, drinking-cups, and the toga often;  
> But let glauconia, the lump of crime, stand apart.  
> Then let gold-leaf, purple, *enctitiva*, and the lineage  
> Of Christ’s soldiery by no means be absent through you.  
> *Amphytappa laon* is present, and *badanola* likewise;  
> *Effipiam*, diamond, a coverlet, and likewise *propoma*.  
> The unmarried *agagula* drives the flocks, nor [is it] *ablunda*.

Odo, abbot of Cluny, is omitted, since he supplied an epitome of Saint Gregory’s *Moralia* and everywhere retained the holy doctor’s words.

## HROSWITHA

It should here be noted that we have omitted many authors—such as Widukind the monk, author of *On Saxon Affairs*; Abbot John; Gezo; Saint Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury; and others—to avoid tedious repetition. We say only a few things about the virgin Hroswitha, nun and poet of Gandersheim in Germany, A.D. 999.

Hroswitha’s Latin is worthy of a better age.—“Folly agitates,” CXXXVII, 993. What *aedepol faciendum* means, 983. “For an ass to live,” 1015. Prison squalor, 995. Simple being, that is, God, 988. *Facere* in the sense “to be ashamed,” 973. Bacchant flames, 1059. Flame-vomiting vapours, 1059. To make little account of, 980. *Gaudimonium*. (This corrupt passage is most successfully restored, 1026 note.) *Homo*, used in the feminine gender in the sense “creature,” 1045. A very tiny little woman, 1058. “By slight *famine*,” that is, by a slight sign, 1039. To sip a kiss, 987. Mary is interpreted “star of the sea,” 1015, 1069. *Matuta nifescit*, that is, dawn, 1025. *Moralis*, that is, of upright manners, 973. *Mis* for *mea*, 1016. The lesser world, that is, man, 102.
