Vassals of monasteries, 349, 351. “Holy Friday,” that is, the sixth feria of Holy Week, 348, 365.

BRUNO (St), founder of the Carthusians.

Hebrew terms interpreted. — Aaron, that is, “mountainous,” CLII, 1344. Abba, that is, “father,” CLIII, 72. Ammon: “a troubled people,” CLII, 1078. Amalek: “a licking people,” ibid. Barjona, or “son of the dove,” CLIII, 140. Chore, that is, “Calvary,” CLII, 813. Hermon: “exalted light” or “anathema,” 1345. The derivation of the name Jews, CLIII, 33. *Maranatha* in Syriac, that is, “the Lord has come,” 218. Melchizedek: “king of righteousness,” 523. Moasia: “from the father,” CLII, 1078. Pharisee, that is, “divided,” CLIII, 366. Rahab: “breadth,” CLII, 1997. Saba: “incense,” “converted,” CLII, 995. Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” 989. Simon: “obedient,” CLIII, 140. Tyre: “straitness,” CLII, 1078. Tarshish, that is, “contemplation,” 995.

Greek expressions and etymologies. — Abyss: excessive depth, CLII, 988. *Atrium* for breadth or spaciousness, 938. What unleavened bread is, CLIII, 147. *Bravium*, that is, the reward of labor, 368. *Cathedra* for government, CLII, 1210. *Catholicon*, that is, “common” or “universal,” CLIII, 476. *Chamus*: a bridle, or rather a muzzle-bridle, CLII, 762. *Charisma*: a gratuitous gift, CLIII, 192. *Clerus*, that is, election, CLII, 756. Devil: slanderer or accuser, 901. Bishop means superintendent, CLIII, 440. What ecstasy is, CLII, 752. *Idioma*, that is, what is proper or distinctive, 199. *Syptote* is a figure in which less is said and more understood, CLII, 805. What *melota* is, CLIII, 555. Mesopotamia is interpreted by St Bruno, as though from Hebrew, as “an exalted calling”; but it is derived much more correctly from Greek *Mesopotamos*, “between rivers,” on account of the situation of that region. The author followed St Jerome, CLII, 912. *Nycticorax*, that is, “night-raven,” 1163. Parables, or propositions, 847. *Plasmare*, from Greek *plasma*, that which is formed from unformed matter, 1280–1281. Who a pedagogue is, CLIII, 299. A psalm is a symphony, CLII, 648. *Rhamnus*, a kind of thorny shrub, 903. What a stadium is and whence it is named, CLIII, 171. What a female timbrel-player is, CLII, 1069.

The Latinity of St Bruno. — *Annuntiare* is said of the future, CLII, 885. The hearing of the soul is called understanding, 737. Hair for vanity, 962. Who the lame person is mystically, 707. What a council is, 642. What descending means mystically, 884. *Dicare* is the same as to devote or consecrate, 834. House for manner of life, 831. *Ecce* for “openly,” 909. What excommunication is, CLIII, 434. What a fable is, 428. Genitive for ablative, CLII, 777. Grace for face, 974. What the bed of pain means mystically, 810. Wings for swiftness, 880. To place for to humble, 946. What God’s “answering” is, 743. “Bloods” for sin, 866. Ships are called anxieties, 843. Sound for manifestation, 814. Lot for election, 756. Standing is said to mean working, 782. Crown of the head for pride, 962.

HUGH, abbot of Flavigny. — He uses improper orthography: *Aecclesia*, CLIV, 31, 34; *Oevangelista*, 208; *Catabuli fossa*, a pit where dung is heaped, 33; what a litter is, 109; *Belsarius* for Belisarius, 93, 94; *dampnatus*, 23; spinning thread, 97; *habundantissime*, 33; *hystoriarum*, 34; lamp of immortality, 139; *nancti* for *nacti*, 34; *novicii* for *novitii*, 44; “obtained as a gift,” 269; Ostrogoths, that is, eastern Goths, 7; *provincia*, 7 and 100; having assumed the burden of prelacy, 205; kings of the *Schitae* for Scythians, 81; the derivation and origin of the Saracens, 101; *sollempnizaret*, 41; the wound of *Stringii*, perhaps a fistula, 24; a digger of the earth made a monk, 206; the surname *Truditis*, given to Charles, duke of the Franks, and why, 138; garment of virginity, 139; *villare*, estates, 134.

EKKEARDUS of Aura, historian. — What it means to grant absolution to messengers, CLIV, 568. *Acta*, the ancient name of Attica, 510. Citadel of divinity, for the highest majesty of God, 497. *Caballus* for horse, 567, 573. *Catillae* for Atellan farces, 637. *Defien* of the Greeks, perhaps for *delphen*, that is, womb or begetter, 498. An earthenware or glass vessel, 588. *Exiliavit*, 1810. *Intellego*, 566. *Michi* for *mihi*, 566. *Poledrus*, that is, a foal, 567. *Pueri*, that is, servants, 814. Serapis is said to derive from *sororapis*, 510. A curved rod and a golden drinking-cup were sent by Darius to Alexander in mockery, 569, 570. *Subputare* for *supputare*, 497. “To turn one’s step,” for “to go back,” 569. *Yppotami* for hippopotami, given as monsters, 595.

GOSCELIN, monk of Canterbury. — Among the English, Goscelin is regarded as the second hagiographer after Bede, CLV, 13, preliminary observation. His Latin, for his age, is not [Col. 0738] altogether to be despised. A little maid worthy of pity, 67. The most extensive barbarism of paganism, 42. A monastic cowl, 41. *Homo* is understood of both sexes, 73. *Laterales*, that is, companions, 29. To be drowned in the sea as a martyr, 43. Saints’ relics are called pledges, 39. Queen of heaven, that is, of the world, for the Blessed Virgin Mary, 33. *Staurus*, from Greek *stauros*, for the cross, 78.

PAUL, monk of St Peter’s, Chartres. — *Absitas*, that is, uncultivated land, CLV, 197. *Actutum* for *astutum*, 188. Aganus, the name of a bishop and title of Paul’s booklet, 197. *Agmentando*, for growing or increasing, 192. What an *aripenum* of land is, 202. *Aurasia* blindness, that is, golden or deceptive blindness, 193. *Bibesia*: the vice of drinking, 192. What the *bithalapsus* of doubt is, 192. Borough or town, 200. Ardor of speaking, 189. What a *carrada* is, 211. *Cibutum*, from Greek *cibotos*, that is, a chest or box, 185. *Clerinomia*, called a clerical association, 190, 196. “In *crocotillo* time,” for a slight or short time; perhaps so called from *crocotuta*, a kind of garment for women’s use, 193. A bubbling pagan people, 187. *Episcopantes*, 192. What a *mansus* is, 215. A filthy road, 199. *Nichilum*, in accordance with the spelling of that age, 185. “It is the custom of the district,” 203. *Peredia*: greediness in eating, 192. *Plissima charity* seems to stand for “most devout charity,” 193. *Rostrum* for forum, 189. The burning Syrian wind, 188. The heavenly homeland, from Greek, 192. *Violatia* for violence, 206.

RADULFUS of Caen, associate of Duke Tancred, in the *Deeds of Tancred*. — *Allachibar*, an Arabic word, the Turks’ cry, CLV, 521. Bow-bearers, 516. *Avia* for trackless places, 497. The twofold way of the Gospel and the world, 497. *Clavengi*, a kind of armour, French *cuissarts*, 185. Tancred’s legion, made to flee in a moment, 509. Lady under the spear, 502. Farfar, the name of a river, 526. What it is to render homage, 500. “The enemy must be struck, not gnawed”: Tancred’s saying, 494. *Marchisides*, that is, Tancred, son of the marquis, 500, 502. *Mussare*, that is, to stumble or hesitate, 496. *Sandaliae*, a kind of ship, 588. *Solis* for days, ibid. *Spescassandae*, 502. Christians are fastened to spits as though to roasting-irons, 509. *Turcopoli*, that is, Turks, 496. A Turkish army, 505.

GUIBERT, abbot of St Mary of Nogent.

Hebrew. — Abel: grief, vanity, vapour, or miserable, CLVI, 79. Abimelech: “my father is king,” 156. Abraham: “exalted father,” 111. Accaron: “the grinding of sadness,” 419. (Since the author assigns the same interpretations as St Jerome, as these few instances sufficiently establish, see that holy Doctor for the rest.)

Greek words. — For these likewise consult St Jerome.

Latinity. — What it means that there are no accidents in God, CLVI, 526. *Admiravis*: a barbarous word by which city prefects are designated, 754. *Almutia*, a garment worn by the monks of St Nicasius of Reims, 1145. What an *apocalligus* patriarch is, 1152. Tree for person, 109. *Aspredo*, bread, 791. *Bacones*, bacon; *petasones*, hams, 926. *Bauda* or *banda*, that is, a fortified camp, 715. *Birrum*, commonly *pilium*, here meaning a cloak, 1187. Byzantine coins, 735. Cordovan shoes; cork toe-pieces, 858. *Capero*, that is, hood; commonly French *chaperon*, *capuchon*, 888. A castle is made up of rampart, wall, and tower, and is so called from *castrando*, “restraining,” 557. *Crepa*, a funeral urn, 1187. *Falae*, wooden towers, 792. *Freda*: see above, *crepa*, 1187. To inhabit for to rule, 173. Certain persons are mockingly called *Isengrini*, that is, wolves, 928. A customary fixed measure of wine, called in French a *ration*, 1066. *Mastigia*, the fastening of a cloak, 1168. What a *mathomarium* is, 771. *Merubidi* manner of dress, otherwise *merobidus*, that is, eager to drink wine, 484. The origin of names assigned to things, 68. What it is to practise barefoot processions, 793. *Philargyria*, love of money, 884. Scrofula or swellings, from which the king of France heals sufferers, 615, 1022. *Supplumbare*, that is, to submerge, 927. *Trudennes* (*Truando*), barbarously called *Thafur*, are those who push others aside in order that a toll may be collected, 811.

GOFFRIDUS, abbot of Vendôme and cardinal of St Prisca. — *Alodiarim*, allodial property, CLVII, 37, 56, 58. *Archilevita* is said ironically, 86. The bailey of a castle, 83. *Barbarini solidi*, or coins stamped with a barbarian image, 62. A sealed privilege, 98. To wield the keys of the Church, 99. Court, 179, note 330. To dedicate for to commend, 130. To disapprove for to condemn, 120. *Electuarium*, a medicinal plant, 171. Formal and handsome letters, 81. *Libratae*, that is, pounds, 102. To make someone a monk, 158. To revisit a Philippic, 56, 158. To plead, to litigate, 90. *Vavassores*, vassals, 194.

ANSELM (St), archbishop of Canterbury. (For Hebrew interpretations, see St Jerome, whom Anselm followed.)

Various terms, in both Latin and Greek. — What eternity is, CLVIII, 282. What love is and whence it derives, 200. Englishmen: the king of the English destined to reign among angels, CLIX, 116. Unleavened and leavened bread in the Eucharist, CLVIII, 542. What a castle is, 645. A castle is mystically called the womb of the Blessed Virgin in relation to the Son of God, 645. Dovelike simplicity, CLIX, 107. *Dissaisire*, for to dispossess, 220. “To do” and “to will” are said in six ways, CLVIII, 488. What living faith and dead faith are, 220. Hymn-singing choirs of angels, 655. What the investitures of churches are, CLVIII, 110, 124, 138, 139. What jubilee is, 657. What free will is, 489 ff. To be made learned by God’s grace, CLIX, 141. An intruded abbot is called a little wolf, 106. What evil is, CLVIII, 335 ff. “I grant my manors at farm”: what this means, CLIX, 130. The mist of lust, CLVIII, 793. To abandon the cloistered paradise, CLIX, 140. What sinning is, CLVIII, 376. What original sin is, 454. Anselm’s Church made the refuse of all, CLIX, 13. What a prebend is, 90. What procession in divine matters is, CLVIII, 297. The higher reasons, namely faith and revelation, 190. *Salsire*, for to possess, CLIX, 220. A slip of writing for a letter, 90. The supreme essence, CLVIII, 212, 221, 222. This shadowy life, 711. Truth for the author of truth, 1065. What will is, 487.

We omit the writings of EADMER, monk of Canterbury, since they furnish little for grammatical criticism and linguistic investigation.

SIGEBERT, monk of Gembloux. — In his chronicle this author copied earlier chroniclers almost word for word, citing each by name. For his orthography, see CLX, 50, in the Prolegomena. In the book *On Illustrious Men* we give certain names which are not unimportant to know from a linguistic standpoint. — Boethius, skilled in Greek and renowned for translations, 555. Cassiodorus, who laboured earnestly in linguistic study in his work *On Etymologies*. Dionysius Exiguus, distinguished in the twofold learning of Greek and Latin, who translated many works of Greeks, 553. Golphilas, inventor of Gothic letters, is given in the *New Course of Patrology* under the name Ulfilas, 549. Theoderetus: better Theodoretus, or Theodoritus as among the Greeks, 549. Embolism, or embolismic year, 553. “*Quod is est*”: perhaps it should read “*quod si est*,” 554.

The anonymous author of the *Chronicle of the Poles* appears moderately inexperienced in Latin, as will be evident from a few examples. He speaks of Poland thus: “A homeland where the air is healthful, the field fertile, the forest honey-bearing, the water full of fish, the soldiers warlike, the peasants industrious, the horses enduring, the oxen fit for ploughing, the cows rich in milk, the sheep woolly [lacuna]. Now therefore let us begin to set forth our subject in such a way that we may climb from the ray to the branch of the tree,” CLX, 844 ff. Elsewhere: “The deeds of Boleslav are more numerous and greater than can be described by us, or even recounted in bare words. For what arithmetician could calculate with a certain number his iron-clad battle-lines?” 854. Concerning the death of Boleslav, one reads the following verses, which the author calls poems:

> Let every age, every sex, every rank run forth!  
> Behold with grief the funeral of King Boleslav,  
> And lament with me the death of so great a man!
>
> [lacuna]
>
> You matrons who wore golden crowns,  
> And who had garments wholly embroidered with gold,  
> Put these off and clothe yourselves in mournful woollen garments, etc.

(Ibid., 862 ff.)

RADULPHUS TORTARIUS, monk of Fleury. — “To the fire! To the fire!”: a cry for extinguishing a blaze, CLX, 1216. *Augmentare*, 1196. Saint Benedict. Thus a woman unjustly harassed by an advocate complains at the saint’s altar in rather rustic language: “Most ancient Benedict, sluggish and lethargic one, what are you doing? Why are you sleeping? Why do you allow your servants to endure such great insults?” 1193. Beard: at that time the custom of swearing by one’s beard was prevalent, 1210. *Bordellum*, the name of a place, for which the author, out of modesty, substitutes “Evil Talent,” 1201. The boss of a shield, French *boucle*, 1197. “Isembardus having learned”: syntax requires *Isembardo*, 1196. “The flower of youth” is excellently said to clothe the cheeks, ibid. To have right and power, 1197. “Lamp of the Franks,” that is, a noble people, 1192. Single combat, or duel, approved by certain monks, 1197. The sword-point of anathema, 1201. Dew-flowing spittle: correctly said of a woman who moistens her finger while spinning in order to draw out wool, 1195. “The plough is covered with a forked thing”: it should plainly read “is guided,” 1198. “Holy wine,” French *le saint vinage*: what it is, 1208.

YVO (Blessed), bishop of Chartres. — Absence, CLXII, 31. The allod of St Peter, 171. To impose forced services contrary to lawful institutions, 190. Appeal, 486. Letters of appeal, 171. *Apices* for letters or epistles, 16. A safe ear, 314. The ban of the league; to be under ban, 120, 144. *Basileis* are called kings in Greek, as though they were the foundations of the people, 377. Who a brief-bearer is, 606. Escheated revenues, 434. To watch the heel, 16. [Col. 0740] Popular songs used to confirm an unlawful episcopal election, 86. *Carenum* wine, 286. What a house or holding is, 284. Those attached to a church, that is, vassals, 311. To annul and to shatter, 318. *Cataneus* or *captaneus* of the Church, 368. Cat-skins, 208. “Your burning words,” alternatively “harsh words,” 363. What it is not to bring the commune against a bishop, 182. Connivance for consent, 396. *Culpati* for excommunicated, 327. *Emunitas* for immunity, 143. Former bishop, 319. *Facete* for eloquently, 316. *Faucio*, perhaps for faction, 403, note. Who a *firmarius* priest is, 366. To put outside, 187, 379. The derivation of the name Franks, 611. *Guerra*, 33, 171, 308. Homage, 213. *Homagium*, the same as *hominium*, 385. Hymnody, 222. Sacred fire, a kind of disease, 389. To be incardinated, 146. To darken, 83. Investiture, 73, 384. Ban of the league: see *bannum leugae*. What a levy is, 264. Marital places, 398. *Mancha*, perhaps for stain, 299. Single combat, 96, 171. The blemish of consent, that is, a scruple, 353. What obedience is, 374. What ordeal is, among the English, 339. The name pedagogue taken in an unfavorable sense, 17. To write a palinode, 17, 301. Marriage best man, 392. What a parish is, 448. To weigh for to think, 361. Pragmatic sanction, 202. Who the lord of Puteaux is, 215. *Reculae, reiculae, resculae*, 351. Who *responsales* are, 276. To seize small possessions, 120, 134. What *sapa* is, 286. Who Sarabaites are, 389. *Scisma* and *schisma*, 407. Seneschal, or steward, 436. The standing of judgment, 414–415. What retaliation is, 146. *Tallia*, French *la taille*, an annual rent, 433. Who *tractatores* are called, 17, 300. *Vanizando*, 184. Vassals of the Church, 362.

Here we omit several authors, namely LAMBERT, bishop of Arras; the ANONYMOUS author of the *Chronicle of the Church of Dijon*; JOHN the monk, chronicler; ANSELM of Laon; Pope PASCHAL II; and others, whose examination does not sufficiently contribute to clarifying linguistic matters.

THEOGERUS, bishop of Metz. — He left a treatise *On Music*, which, like all other treatises on this subject, abounds in Greek terms, most of which we have already recorded, CLXIII, 777.

HUGH OF ST MARY, monk of Fleury. — *Amministrare* for *administrare*, CLXIII, 895. Brass, 848. *Byzantium*, a kind of coin, 908. *Caballi* for horses, 908. *Calumpnosi* for calumnious, 821. Castle, 845. Booklet, 821. Heretics dogmatize, 854. Episcopal staff, 955. Martyrs are called flowers of the Church, 832. Support: “drawing [him] by the hair from the support,” 1002. Historians, 821. A clock made by mechanical art, 848. Priestly mitre, 956. Richard the duke was called *justitiarius* because of his love of justice, 879. A species of mergus bird, 989. To read at leisure, 822. Parthians are interpreted as exiles, in the Scythian tongue, 832. A particle of the blemish of error, 826. Bronze little balls, 848. Imperial procession, French *cortège*, 965. “Who-did-nothing,” the surname of Louis, son of Carloman, 871. Sion in Hebrew, that is, “watching” or “contemplation,” 831. The shroud of our Lord Jesus Christ, 893. To tonsure, 425. The source of the surname *Tudites* of Charles, duke of the Franks, 832. *Voraciter* for *veraciter*, falsely, 924.

BRUNO (St), abbot of Asti and afterward bishop of Segni. — What sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal signify, CLXV, 908, 909. What the tongues of angels are, 908. Whom unfruitful trees designate, 838. Beelzebub in Hebrew means “god of flies,” 794. Flesh for man, 754. *Coenomia* for Greek *cynomia*, meaning “dog-fly,” 917. Not to have breeches, that is, not to have taken a wife, 931. Cast shields, 795. *Malies* through evil hands, 917. Jesus is interpreted “Saviour,” 766. Mouth for speech, 758. “Peaceful” for Solomon, which is what his name means, 923. What “feed my lambs” and “feed my sheep” signify mystically, 761. The Jewish people is called a child because of its weakness and childish understanding, 800. To each person his own language is sufficient, 908. Way: what it means mystically to be “on the way,” 824. Sound precedes word [lacuna] as soon as any kind of sound proceeds from the speaker’s mouth, it is a voice; but it is not yet a word, 754.

COSMAS of Prague, in his *Chronicle of the Bohemians*, year 1125; in this author most words are disfigured by extremely bad spelling. — Allodial estate, CLXVI, 117. *Ambo*, an elevated place in a church, 126. A wide kingdom, 162. Compulsory service imposed by decree, 125. *Archigeronta*, that is, dean, French *doyen*, 55. Beard: what it is to fly into another’s beard, 63. The derivation of the name Bohemia, 60. Money-purse, 74. To mount a horse, 67. The tithe payable to a bishop, 117. *Dominellus*, 78. To euphonize an apostrophe to oneself, 115. *Feodum*, incorrectly *pheodum*, 117. *Formaticus*, that is, cheese, 67. Who a daughter is, 114. What lemures are, 74. *Lacialius* for *latialius*, that is, “more Latin” in a somewhat better style, 55. “Mine” and “ours,” happily unknown in primitive times, 61. Travelling garments, 66. What fallow land is, 66. “Shield of victory” for “palm of victory,” 146. A bag woven from cork, 67. *Premizl*, a Gothic word, means in Latin “forethinking” or “thinking above,” 66. *Quisquis* for *quis*, 59. What witches are, 74. [Col. 0741] *Tesqua*, from Greek: deserted and wooded places, 59. The Teutonic language, 145. To shave someone, that is, to receive or send him into the clergy, 146. *Trochus*, from Greek: a circle encircled with rings, with which boys used to play, 122. What it is to fly into another’s beard, 63.

ALBERIC, canon of Aachen. — *History of the Jerusalem Expedition*. — To return to one’s native shores, CLXVI, 391. *Ammiraldus*, that is, prince; the French say *émir*, 459, 690. Balearic bow, 690. To press an assault, 683. *Barbicales* or *mangenae*, engines of war, 462. The Idumaeans, formerly called Bidumi, 700. Byzantine gold coins, 400. *Caballi* for horses, 436, 475. *Calcatibus*, incorrectly for *calcaribus*, “spurs,” 436. To continue one’s journey, 408. To make a clamor with horns, for with trumpets, 398, 460. Wicker screens to protect soldiers, 432. The enemy’s deceits, 466. Flame-spewing fires thrown into engines, 699. Impaled on spears and stakes, 475. Fire unquenchable by water, 699. Wicked report, 440. What *mangenae* are, 462. *Mortificantes* for killing, 435. The horrible-sounding growl of a bear, 439. *Nuntia*, a noun, 391. “Westward from the kingdom,” 389. Tree-trunks, that is, oak trunks, 462. *Sensavehor*, a French expression, the same as *sans avoir*, the surname of Duke Walter, 392, 400. What an upper room of a house is, 407. *Tartaron*, a kind of coin, 400. The royal way, that is, the road to Jerusalem, 440.

BALDRIC, archbishop of Dol, author of a *History of the Jerusalem Expedition*. — The Babylonian admiral, prince of the Turks, CLXVI, 1065. The arm of St George, that is, the Bosporus, 1071. Byzantine denarii, 1082. A cross fastened to garments, 1069. Disgusted teeth, 1131. To flee separately, 1127. What “to be made bishop by counsel” and “to be made bishop by office” mean, 1147. *Exoccupatior*, that is, freer from care, 1059. A hailstorm of missiles, 1080. Interlinear sentences, 1060. Restlessness, 1080. Unslumbering dispute, 1128. *Montanea*, that is, mountains, 1137. Pagan tyranny, 1066. *Patres conscripti*, as formerly in the Roman senate, 1144. What the emperor’s pyre is, 1076. Pope Urban II is called eloquent even to a half-word, 1062. “This thunder,” that is, the report of the eastern expedition, 1071. The wave-sounding sea, ibid. Verbosity is used in a favorable sense, 1057.

RUPERT (Venerable), abbot of the monastery of Deutz. (For Hebrew, consult St Jerome.) — Africa is named from Afer, CLXVII, 445. Scripture employs anticipation and post-position, 487. What arithmetic is, 1778. To look upon for to love, 1206. Bath and ephah are the same measure, of three modii, 666. *Caballus* is said to derive from *cavando*, “hollowing”; why, 282. Who chiliarchs were, CLXIX, 447. Money-changers are named from *collyba*, a trifling gift, and are a certain class of usurers, 295. What it is to keep the lawful word, 1281. The difference between transgression and sin, CLXVIII, 778. What sleeping in contemplations is, CLXIX, 112. To have one’s back turned against the temple is to despise God, CLXVII, 1454. Ellipsis gives greater force in speech, ibid. Eloquence in divine utterances, CLXIX, 242. What *encaenia* are and whence the word comes, 621. The derivation of *epistola*, CLXX, 28. What it is to empty faith, 1309. Fables are named from speaking, CLXVII, 1765. The firmament is stretched-out air, CLXVII, 219. The future tense is used for the past, 1362. The derivation of the name of the book Genesis, 201. Geometry, 1778. A *gomor* is an Attic measure containing twelve sextarii, 666. The Greek and Latin languages hold primacy over all, 364. How Scripture employs grammar, 1765. The teaching of letters is a kind of childhood of the grammatical art, 1765. What the divisions of grammar are, ibid. The Greeks falsely boast as though they had discovered tropes or figures of speech, 1765. *Hyle*, that is, matter, 203. Image is understood in various senses, 248. Jubilee means “releasing” or “remitting,” 827. *Lamia* is named from tearing, 1913. Division of languages, CLXIX, 93. Languages united in the apostles, 94. Diversity of languages necessary for the apostles, CLXX, 279. There are three sacred languages, preeminent throughout the whole world, CLXIX, 965. Why letters were invented, 1273. The inventors of letters: Moses for Hebrew, Cadmus for Greek, the nymph Carmentis for Latin, ibid. The usefulness of letters, 1288. *Mane, Thecel, Phares*: three Hebrew words explained, 1360, 1361. *Manhu*, whence manna is named, means “What is this?”, CLXIX, 665. A thousand years for all [time], CVII, 383. What a neume is, CLXX, 30. Adam assigned names after considering the natures of things; thus he called the horse *caballus* from “hollowing,” but the ass from sitting. (Accordingly, in Rupert’s view Adam would have spoken Latin, which is no small absurdity.) Various names of God, 592. Passover is understood as the moon, 1677. Our life is rightly called a pilgrimage, 544. The past for the future, 1362. Rhetoric in the Scriptures, 1766. What a *saga* is, 710. To be sanctified for abstaining from lawful things, 675. What a rush is, 675. The trumpet’s blast is called the voice of preachers, 862. What the active and contemplative lives are, CLXIX, 719.

HILDEBERT (Venerable), bishop of Le Mans. (It is enough to give a few items from this writer, to avoid repetitions.) — Delaying appeals, [Col. 0742] CLXXI, 265. The derivation of *aquilo*, the north wind, 893. Chaplaincy for diocese, 273. The antiquity of associations, 179. The difference between crown and diadem, 366. The greater and lesser creeds, 1070. A day’s journey, or journey of three days, 530. The derivation of Epiphany, 402. Water-organs, 648. Beginnings: “What begins badly ends badly,” 212. Lay investitures, 769. The pope’s red mantle, 879. *Physiologus*, Hildebert’s poem, 1218. A golden rose carried by the pope in the Palm Sunday procession, 479. What *theosebia* is, 806. What truculence is, 1024. The countenance, interpreter of the mind, 173.

MARBOD, bishop of Rennes and poet. — *Aplustris*, a certain part of a ship, 1641. *Burburea*, perhaps *purpurea*, 1735. Canonical verses, 1732. *Comeret* for *ornaret*, “would adorn,” 1618. What the definition and transference of words are, 1691. What disconnected, connected, and adjunct words are, ibid. Glass-like fortune, 1466. To be kept away by forks, 1614. What gradation of words is, 1690. The French language in Marbod’s time; verses in French transcribed by him concerning gems, 1739 ff. How Marbod describes a prostitute, 1698. What *occare* is, 1619. To return to one’s heart, 1475. “Your witticisms have no tooth,” 1180. “By leaping,” that is, by dancing or skipping, 1626. What the subjection of words is, 1690. Money is preferred to learning, 1475. Benches, or triremes, 1641. Marbod’s booklet *On Words Concerning Ornaments*, 1687. Vice-lord and vice-lordship, 1593, 1596. Viper: “By its fruit one may know what a viper is,” 1713.

HONORIUS of Autun.—Ages of the world, CLXXII, 166. What the world-soul is, 46. Honorius’s little work *The Exile and Homeland of the Soul*, 1242. What atoms are, 147. Episcopal staff, 609. Clerics’ shirts, 614. What animals called *cencocrocae* are, 124. What the watery heaven and spiritual heaven are, 146. *Galaxias* in Greek, that is, the Milky Way, 60. Honorius’s little work *The Jewel of the Soul*, 541. What a hemisphere is, 102. Artificial hours, 103. Clocks, 106. What *humutum* is, 47. Whence India takes its name, 125. Lunation, 84. What the moon’s leap is, 104. Man as a microcosm, 140, 141. Episcopal mitre, 609. Etymology of *world*, 121. What the musical phrase (*neuma*) “in a” in the chant *The Fabric of the World* is, 645. Portents, 146. Archbishop’s pallium, 611. What purgatory is, 1158. Honorius’s little work *The Ladder of Heaven*, 1229. What scrutiny is, 659. Why Sicily is called Trinacria, 132. Abbot’s rod, 615.

RADULF, abbot of Saint-Trond.—The following occur in this writer: *atrappus*, a certain vessel, CLXXIII, 39. What *aurifrigum* is, 86. A little beast, 86. A box for carrying incense, 38. A *bonarium*, a certain measure of land, 152. *Cambula*, a pastoral rod, 38. A *caminata*, a large room for guests, 155. To glitter, 37. *Corbus*, a kind of measure, 39. *Cyborium*, the same as *reba*, on which see below. *Faldones*, pitchers, 39. *Fanones*, a kind of small cloth, 38, 39. *Frisum*, that is, fringe, 38. *Firto*, a kind of weight, 86. A small image, 86. *Niquarum* for *iniquarum*, 47. *Pallium*, a kind of silk cloth, 38. *Puplicum* for *publicum*, 32. *Reba* is called the cover of a bier, 38.

LEO OF MARSICA and PETER THE DEACON, *On the Chronicle of Monte Cassino.*

Various words and expressions of late Latin.—Silken albs and albs of *matassa* [silk], CLXXIII, 795. Antiphonary, an ecclesiastical book, 800. Who standard-bearers are, 862. *Auca* for goose, 529. Bezants, a kind of coin current among Eastern peoples, 794. *Cambium*, that is, exchange, 562. Who *candidati* are, 862. What a *casalis* is, 518. A chestnut-grove, a place rich in chestnut trees, 562. *Ceraptata* for *ceroferaria*, 531. Who the *cereastaltarii* are, 862, 531. Charters, 504, 505, 518, 534. In the Middle Ages *de* is often used for the genitive, as “the fork of Valleluci,” 469; “the estates of Garigliano,” ibid., etc. Who the defenders are, 862. Who dragon-bearers are, ibid. The fourfold structure of a church, 506. *Gastaldeus*, a type of magistrate, 518. *Graphiones*, 507. *Gualdus*, from Saxon *wald*, that is, grove or forest, 562. *Lambacii*, basins, 795. Who lion-bearers and wolf-bearers are, ibid. Golden *michalati*, coins bearing the image of the Emperor Michael, 794. “To offer in this monastery” for “to this monastery,” 518. *Pantanus*, that is, a marsh, 505, 518. Passionary, an ecclesiastical book, 800. What the appurtenances of an estate are, 534, 535. *Pexlum*, that is, a crag or rock, 495, 496. What it means to write out in full, 489. Fourfold structure, 506. *Skifati*, a kind of concave coin, 794. “With the bells resounding,” 532. Who cross-bearers and grooms are, 862. Tareni, a kind of coin, 794. A stone tomb, 522.

HUGH OF SAINT-VICTOR, regular canon.—What is called an accident, CLXXVI, 55. The difference between “to gird oneself,” “to gird before,” and “to gird beneath,” CLXXVII, 781. Affinity and consanguinity, CLXXVI, 516, 518. Spiritual agriculture, CLXXVII, 201. To love and to know wisely, CLXXV, 195. Whence *antiphon* derives, CLXXVII, 412. Arithmetic, 198. Aspidochelone, an aquatic monster, 82. What an asterisk is, CLXXV, 30. What kind of animal the *bonasus* is, CLXXVII, 84. Ox and ass, that is, a dull and uncultivated man, 673. Bells, CLXXVI, 474; CLXXVII, 875. Choler: choleric persons are those whose nature is hot and dry, 1188. Episcopal gloves, CLXXVII, 406. What the belt and under-belt are, 403, 404. What the keys of heaven are, 755. What Compline is, 412, 413. Horn in the sense of strength, CLXXV, 266. What measure a cubit is, 46. What transgression and sin are, 567. The method of disputation, CLXXVI, 764. What the elements of the world are, 1184; CLXXVII, 286, 483. *Emmanuel* means “God with us,” CLXXVII, 477. Whence an epistle is so called, 421. Epithets, 134. What it means to be from God, by God, and of God, 809. Various etymologies, CLXXXVI, 787. The manifold meaning of receiving the Eucharist, CLXXVII, 824. What exorcizing and catechizing are, 138. Form for beginning a sermon, CLXXVII, 819. The moral meanings of old and new leaven, CLXXV, 794, 909. What the firmament is, CLXXVI, 200. The moral meaning of stretching a cord, CLXXV, 278. Christ-bearer, CLXXVII, 844. Griffin, a species of animal, 84. The several senses in which “to have” is used, CLXXV, 577. What hierarchy is, 931. “Today” is said in three senses, CLXXVII, 858. Whence man is so called, 119, 120. *Hydrus* and hydra, 61. What image and likeness are, CLXXV, 37. What the leucrocota is, CLXXVII, 85. What the sevenfold litany is, 268. Speech, 593, 654, 669. What “to speak with the tongue” is, CLXXXV, 537. The various senses of “morning,” CLXXVII, 947, 948. What the manticore is, 85. What mathematics is, CLXXVI, 753. What “death in the pot” means, CLXXV, 718. Nature understood in three ways, CLXXVI, 718; CLXXVII, 561. Why neophytes are so called, CLXXVI, 455. What obeli are, CLXXV, 30. Who are called godfathers, CLXXVI, 458; CLXXVII, 390. What embroidery-work is, CLXXV, 70. What it means to bear God, 524. What practical knowledge is, CLXXVII, 199, 200. What a responsory is, 454. What Rogation Days are, 817. Whence *saeculum* is so called, CLXXV, 897. Various kinds of sacrifices, CLXXVII, 991. The two schools: virtue and truth, 627. Who those sowing in the spirit and sowing in the flesh are, 795. Whence *stola* derives, CLXXV, 57. *Syntagma*, that is, composition, 30. What it means to tempt the Lord, 66. The origin of theoretical knowledge, CLXXVI, 745. Stirrings of the flesh, CLXXVII, 800. Wulfila [Ulfilas], inventor of the Gothic alphabet, 259.

PETER ABAELARD, master of the schools, later abbot of Rhuys.—Some have said *Argenteolum*, *Argentolium*, and *Argentogilum*; in French, Argenteuil, CLXXVIII, 133. “A miser in words,” 186. Abaelard’s misfortunes, 114. The covenant of marriage, 205. *Corrixarii*, 1227. Dialectical arguments, 115. Letter salutations. Heloise thus writes: “To her sole one after Christ, she his sole one in Christ,” 191; elsewhere, “To her lord in a special way, she his in a singular way,” 213. Abaelard: “Servant of the same to the bride of Christ,” 199. “I do not fear Scylla’s barking, and I laugh at the whirlpool of Charybdis,” 378. “Place of contest,” that is, school, 121. *Logos* in Greek is interpreted as “word” and “reason,” 1281. Feminine enticement, 214. “Necessity has no law,” a proverb, 717. The philosopher: “I do not wish to be such a philosopher as to kick against Paul,” 375. *Heloise’s Problems*, a work of Abaelard, 678. Abaelard the schoolman, 138. *Know Thyself*, or *Ethics*, a work of Abaelard, 634. *Yes and No*, another work of Abaelard: why he so entitled it, 1349. *Tolleret* for *toleraret* [“would take away” for “would endure”], 1279. *Vulcania* for hell, 205.

WILLIAM, monk of Malmesbury.—Styles of composition vary according to the customs of peoples. For Greeks customarily compose intricately, Romans cautiously, Gauls splendidly, and Englishmen pompously, CLXXIX, 986. Charlemagne used the vernacular language spoken by the Franks beyond the Rhine, 1022. The native language of the Franks is shared with the English, because both peoples sprang from Germany, ibid. Boethius’s books translated into English by King Alfred himself, 1083.

Expressions and words of various kinds.—What the “clothing of prison squalor” is, CLXXIX, 1356. *Aedituus* in the sense of a household servant, 1086. *Allitans*, that is, divergent, 1353. Candle for lance: William sends this answer to the king of the Franks: “I shall pour out to him a hundred thousand candles,” 1255. Historical songs from which the Malmesbury writer frequently drew the narratives he related, 1106. Charlemagne speaks the language beyond the Rhine, 1022. *Ceolae*, a kind of long ship, 962. To sound the battle-trumpet in hatred of oneself, 975. Counts held the kings of the Franks in clientship, 1023. “To take the sleep of falling asleep,” 1065. *Foedifragi* for *foederifragi* [treaty-breakers], 1074. Ditches with which cities are encircled, 1156. *Foresta* for wood, 1252. The Franks are called from the savagery of their customs, by a Greek term, 1031. Godfrey (“kingdom of God”) and Godgiva are given as derisive bynames, 1353. *Iccirco* for *idcirco* [therefore], 1162. Law: “Laws are silent amid arms,” 1082. Libitina, in which the dead man lies, 1594. Language of the Franks, 1022. Language of Normandy, 1592. *Manca* of gold, an ancient kind of coin, 789. Whence the surname Martel derives, 1214. “Monarch of the kingdom,” an expression rare among the ancients, 963. Prayer-verses, 1590. *Pausare*, to rest in the tomb, 1256. “To make days and nights perpetual,” that is, to pass through them, 1229. *Pertinacia* for *pertinentia* in the style of this period, 1264. To sketch with a brush, 987. *Providentia* in the sense of care or office, 1086. “To go to the bed of repose,” 1065. The monastery of Tewkesbury is said to be, as it were, from the Greek *Theotocosbiria*, that is, “care of the Mother of God,” 1597.

The following writers—namely Hermann, Teulf, William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, Lord Alger, and Pope Eugenius II—we pass over, since anyone seeking their examination encounters nothing but matters already repeated very frequently. So also with Hervaeus, the exegetical author, we pass over in the same sweep; for he has added nothing new in his commentaries, being wholly concerned with assigning a spiritual or allegorical sense to each word of Scripture.

BERNARD (Saint), abbot of Clairvaux and Doctor of the Church, died 1153.—What is called the Romance language, and that it was regarded as the vernacular, CLXXXIII, 14, Preface. Those who knew that language did not therefore understand Latin, ibid. It does not seem probable that Saint Bernard’s sermons were delivered in Latin, and why, ibid. What he asserts in Epistle 14 to Cardinal Peter the Deacon, CLXXXII, 119. Yet it must not be inferred from this that Saint Bernard composed his sermons in a language other than Latin, ibid. In Bernard’s time it is certain that the use of Latin among the populace was not general, although public documents are found issued in Latin, 15. Testimony of Peter the Venerable, ibid. Reasons by which it is maintained that Saint Bernard delivered his sermons only in Latin, and that the Fuliensis manuscript is a mere translation of these sermons, ibid. Fragment of a sermon of Saint Bernard in the Romance or French language, 34.

Various words and expressions of Bernard.—What *addextrare* is, CLXXXIII, 1155. What “high,” “deep,” “long,” and “broad” signify, and in what sense they must be used cautiously, CLXXXII, 754. Englishmen more dreamers than Gauls, CLXXXIII, 31, Preface. English frivolity; Gallic maturity, ibid. In what sense the soul is called bride, 1140. What a spacious soul and a narrow soul are, 919. What the soul’s skin, flesh, and bones are, 556. The soul of brute animals, CLXXXII, 239. The Arnaldists, heretics named from a certain Arnold, 437, note. “Blessedness is noon which knows no evening,” CLXXXIII, 953. Bethany, that is, “house of obedience,” CLXXXII, 939. Bethphage, “house of the mouth,” 938. The Cistercian Bible corrected, 1119. *Buricus* for ass, 412. The good: “Those who have known the good and also will it: this alone is perfect religion,” CLXXXII, 306. What the cup of demons is, CLXXXII, 85. Whence chancellors are so called, CLXXXIII, 1049. Regular canons are called *fratres* by foreigners, CLXXXII, 421. Cardinals addressed by the title “Excellency,” 119. Carthusians called saints, 108, 449. What *caesamentum* is, 147, note. “Pourable virtue,” that is, easy virtue, CLXXXIII, 147. Eating is a labor for man, though less so than hunger, 572. What it means to suffer with another, 727. Crown of poverty and misery, CLXXXIII, 148. “Tomorrow” for the future life, “today” for the present, 107. Stone knives of those circumcising, 153. *Cura* in the sense of an ecclesiastical benefice, CLXXXII, 827, note. *Dictare* for to write, 506. *Diffidare* for to declare war, 388. Duels are to be ascribed to madness, not courage, 566. Eden is interpreted “delight,” CLXXXIII, 479. *Esse* is said of a thing’s condition, 223, 273. The bride’s ecstasy is death, CLXXXIII, 1031. Epiphany, that is, manifestation, 149. To become a bishop, CLXXXII, 476. Deceitful is sense, not faith, CLXXXIII, 915. Gabriel, that is, “strength of God,” 57. *Grisca* for darkish black, 86. Coarse garments, 376. *Gullae* for *gunae*, from Greek γουναί, that is, reddish skins, 813. “Today” for the present life, CLXXXIII, 107. What homage or *hominium* is, CLXXXII, 147. “At the end” for “at last,” 146. What mitres are, 727. Israel, that is, “seeing God,” CLXXXII, 480. Jerusalem, “vision of peace,” 90. Judah, “confession,” 87. “Broad,” “long,” etc.: see “High.” *Liberum* means the same as voluntary in Bernard, 1173. *Manerius* for manner, CLXXXII, 614. Mary, that is, “Star of the Sea,” CLXXXIII, 170. Michael: “Who is like God?” 348. What is called necessary, CLXXXII, 863. Nut: “If anyone breaks a nut, he will find inside that which is more pleasant,” CLXXXIII, 158. *Palefridus*, that is, a large and distinguished horse led by the bridle, 239. Parish for diocese, 340. Pascha, passage, CLXXXIII, 281. *Passagium*, a kind of toll, 264. “We are all pilgrims”: in what sense, 183, 184. Spiced wines, CLXXXII, 911. *Placitare* for to litigate, 146. What rancor is, 340. To return to one’s homeland, CLXXXIII, 305. The title “Reverence” granted to an abbot, CLXXXII, 517. Solomon, that is, peaceful, CLXXXIII, 480. “Juice of mortality,” that is, death or the tomb, 147. Schools of theology, lofty schools, CLXXXII, 87, note. “Pious scholar” for young man, 80. The title “Serenity,” now given to the pope, 326; now to bishops, 599. The nature of Bernard’s seal, 491, 616. The title “Sublimity” given to the pontiff, 714. Temptation: the snare of temptation, against which one must beware, CLXXXIII, 165. Who a soldier of the Temple is, CLXXXII, 917. What the master of the military order of the Temple is, 135. *Tornetae*, or tournaments, playful combats, CLXXXV, 257.

ZACHARIAS, bishop of Chrysopolis.—The interpretations found in this author may be read in the writers from whom he collected them, CLXXXVI.

[Col. 0745] ROBERT PULLUS, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—What the canons’ *almutia* is, CLXXXVI, 1116. *Armilausa*, the same as *almutia*, ibid. Whence the name chancellor derives, 1110. The name chapel did not begin to be heard before the time of Gregory of Tours, 1141. *Capenum*, a house to which poor people gather to request alms, 1112. Diction: whether words should be used properly or improperly; nevertheless, authority is nowhere to be criticized, 679. “To call famine,” an expression of Scripture, 880. Expressions hostile to Catholic doctrine must be excluded from faith, 789. One must speak soberly in matters of faith, 790. What place the limbo of the Fathers is, 823. What *melote* or *melota* is, 1116. Parishes, that is, rural churches, 1111. Profane verbal novelties must be avoided, 788.

We omit GRATIAN for reasons already given concerning the others, and additionally because exceedingly little in his compilation is his own, CLXXXVII, 666.

ORDERIC VITALIS, English-born monk and historian.—Turkish princes were called admirals, CLXXXVIII, 677. Who an archiatrist is, 447, 649. Archimandrite, 268. *Carruca* for plough, 447. Key-bearer of heaven, Peter’s surname, 291. The composition of chronography, 451. Those signed with the cross, 654 and passim. *Favorabiliter*, 769. *Genicula*, that is, knots, 682. Who rank-and-file knights are, 412. A shrewd astrologer, 649. The monks’ infirmary, 665. What an *infula* is, 288. What it means to establish one’s household gods, 654. Sterlings of the pound, an English gold coin, 288. *Magistria* and *magisteria*, authority, 133. *Magistriani* for magistrates, 134. Paul *Magnilogus* for *magniloquus* [grandiloquent], 291. *Meslebren*, a Saxon word meaning “mixed bran,” 294. The Rule of Saint Benedict for *regula*, 425. Normans are so called from the English word *North*, which means “north” in Latin, and *man*, that is, man, 655. Phoebus, that is, the sun: “To shine in the Church as Phoebus,” 450. Leek: “To cut down an enemy like a tender leek,” 677. Rabbi, Hebrew for “master”: who are so called, 451. *Scira* in Saxon means province, district, or even estate; among the English it is now expressed by *shire*, 458. *Soldanus*: the Turkish king was thus called, 681. A *tricorium* near Darnetum is a certain kitchen implement, 288. Tomb, that is, sepulchre, 366, 444.

PETER THE VENERABLE, abbot of Cluny.—There are very few matters bearing on language that deserve the reader’s attention; therefore we pass over his writings. We do the same with Saint Thomas of Canterbury and Gilbert of Foliot, whose writings everywhere deal with the disputes between Lord Thomas and King Henry, CLXXXIX and CXC.

PETER LOMBARD, surnamed MASTER OF THE SENTENCES, bishop of Paris.

Hebrew words.—*Acti*, brother, CXCI, 472. *Acob* or *equeb*, heel, end, or beginning, 408. *Agag*, “he celebrated feasts with banquets,” 424. *Agal*, *Agol*, round, 454, 590. *Agaloth*, wagons and shields, 454. *Aghida*, “I shall tell,” 407. *Aral*, stag or hind, 422. *Al*, upon, for, 447. *Alam*, “he hid,” 453. *Al-mouth*, “unto death,” 464. *Almouth*, youth, 453. *Aleph*, a thousand, 482. *Aluph*, ox, 482. *Am*, people, 458. *Aouen*, vanity, iniquity, 526. *Arets*, earth, 698, 750. *Azchirah*, “I shall remember,” 459. *Balal*, “he confounded,” 681. *Bar*, son, 558. *Barac, herec*: “he blessed” or “he cursed,” 588. *Bin*, *be*, *ba*, *bi*, “giving”; thus *bacreca*, “in your city,” 681; *beleb*, “in the heart,” 447; *bimghillath*, “in the scroll,” 408. *Dabar*, word: hence *debari*, “my word”; *debaro*, “his word”; *debarai*, “my words,” 526. *Darach*, “he walked,” 447. *Dod*, beloved, 621. *Ead*, one, 472. *Ebel*, vanity, 570. *El*, strong, 422. *El*, *ele*, to, 407. *Elion*, most high, 454. *Eloim*, God, 454. *Ereb*, evening, 679. *Esch*, fire, 540. *Galal*, “he turned,” 408. *Gazal*, plunder, 570. *Hasidai*, “my saints,” 481. *Hasideo*, “his saints,” 482. *Hillanou*, “we have praised,” 436. *Jabin*, “he will understand” or “he understood,” 473. *Jaham*, “he made warm,” 494. *Jareah*, moon, 666. *Jeme*, days, plural, 680. *Jocoua*, Lord, 794. *Im*, with, 458. *Ir*, city, 681. *Isch*, man, 472. *Karitha*, “you dug” or “you prepared,” 408. *Karab*, “he approached,” 519. *Karah*, “he called upon”; *in Kera*, “we shall call upon,” 768. *Keasdeica*, “according to your mercies,” 493. *Kedosch*, holy, 454. *Kerab*, battle, 520. *Kereb*, the innermost part, middle, ibid. *Kidesch*, “he sanctified,” 454. *Kescheth*, bow, 710. *Koschet*, truth, 558. *La le*, marker of the dative case, 454. *Leb*, heart; *bleb*, “in the heart,” 447. *Lo*, with aleph, “not,” 473. *Lo*, with waw, “to him,” “him,” 464. *Magen*, shield, 794. *Manah*, “he prepared,” 562. *Machtseboth*, thoughts, 407. *Mei*, waters, 680. *Mghillath*, scroll, 408. *Min*, *me*, *ma*, preposition “from”; *mipane*, “from the face,” 558. *Mi*, “who?” among [interrogatives], 562. *Moed*, time, 703. *Meod*, much, exceedingly, 454. *Mouth*, death, 464. *Nahalath*, inheritance, 457. *Nod*, migration, movement, 527. *Nou*, “we,” “our,” 451, 457; thus *elenou*, “to us,” 407; *lanou*, “for us,” 454. *Olam*, eternity, 597. *Ozen*, ear; *osnaim*, ears, 408. *Paras*, “he spread out,” “he distributed,” 621. *Pene*, face, 558. *Raah*, “he saw,” 580. *Ram*, exalted, 424. *Reghel*, [Col. 0746] foot; *reglav*, “his feet,” 540. *Rekob*, rider, 447. *Sam*, “he placed,” 484. *Sarim*, princes, 624. *Saphar*, “he counted,” 527. *Scham*, there, 484. *Schamam*, “he was astonished,” 454. *Scharim*, singers, 623. *Schemesch*, sun, 794. *Schem*, name; *Schmaea*, “your name,” 703. *Scheol*, grave, hell, 474. *Schoschanim*, lilies, 447. *Schphathaim*, lips, 621. *Sephoroth*, number, 657. *Chaaroug*, “the stag cried aloud,” 422. *Thasoubab*, “you turned,” 558. *Thorath*, law; *Thorateca*, “your law,” 697. *Tsor*, Tyre, that is, tribulation, “very strong,” or hard stone, 448. *Ziz*, brilliance, appearance, beauty, or beasts of the field, 482. (These suffice to encourage beginners to study this language; we leave out much that we cannot bring forward here.)

Greek words.—What *aporos* is, CXCII, 32. Apostles: in Latin, “those sent” or “envoys,” CXCI, 1304. *Azyma*, unleavened; *zyma* is Greek for leaven and *a-* is privative, 1573. What the Jewish *deuterosis* is, CXCII, 328. What kind of worship *dulia* is, 242. What ecstasy is, 41. What an idol is, CXCI, 1602. What kind of worship *latria* is, CXCII, 242. Pedagogue, one who instructs childhood, 132. *Paedia*, that is, instruction, 503. What *peripsema* is, CXCI, 1569. *Schema* is more customary than “figure,” 1662. Likewise *trope* is more customary than “mode,” ibid.

Latin words.—*Brian* is a cup suited for drinking, CXCI, 1510. Carnal means the same as animal, 1554. Whence a woman is called *comata* [long-haired], 1636. What it means to confess, 1476. What the dragon—or rather the effigy of a dragon—carried in Rogation processions was, and why it was carried, 376. What *devolatio* is, CXCII, 97. Whence drunkenness derives, CXCI, 1510. What an excess of mind is, CXCII, 41. What things are to be understood, 249. What intelligible things are, CXCI, 1327. What it means to Judaize, CXCII, 109. What “to be named” means in Paul, CXCI, 1575. *Praeter* and *praeterquam* understood in the sense of “against,” CXCII, 97. What revelation is, CXCI, 1665. What sensible things are, 1327. What *uri* means in the Apostle, 1590. What a living voice can accomplish, CXCII, 145.

We omit GARNIER and GEROH alike; the former excerpted Gregory’s deeds and words, while the latter likewise followed earlier writers in expounding Scripture, CXCIII, CXCIV.

ISAAC OF STELLA, Cistercian abbot, who composed sermons redolent of Saint Bernard’s genius in a fine and polished style.—*Capabilis*, CXCIV, 1771. *Conquiniscere* for *considere*, to lower one’s head, 1726. The capital sins are called dens of demons and cradles of death, 1709. *Donabilis*, 1771. The empyrean heaven, 1701. *Galaxia* in Greek, that is, the Milky Way, 1697. In order to unite lowest, highest, and middle things, Christ chose to be stretched out, extended, and suspended upon the cross, 1729. Incorporeality, 1702. To suffer lethargy, 1695. *Minare* for *minari* [to threaten], 1726. Man is called the lesser world, 1695. The pure in heart, 1705. Cloud understood in a twofold sense: cloud of ignorance, cloud of wisdom, 1701. *Pausare* for to rest, 1704. *Ploratio* for weeping, 1730. The efficient, formal, and final principle of any thing: that is, whence it is, how it is, and why it is, 1702. *Robur* is also called the trunk of an oak tree, 1769. A pierced sack, 1705. Spleen: “To laugh and die with wanton spleen,” 1696. To theologize, 1769. Whole: “To serve the whole wholly,” 1732. What “one one; one, one in unity” means, 1707.

ECKBERT, abbot of Schönau monastery.—Cathars are so called from Greek *katharoi*, that is, “purifiers,” CXCV, 18. The Cathars in Germany are the same heretics as those called Piphles in Flanders and Texerans or Tisserands [Weavers] in France, 13. *Cathara*: “to taste of Cathara,” that is, to incline toward these heretics, 92. *Camisia* for clerics’ surplice, 130. Heretics are called lurking people and “flying leprosy,” 13. Manes, a heretic whose name is close to *mania*, 16, 17. To plant the faith, 24. To sit: “If you do not know, sit; be silent; make the little cloak run with the weft through the middle of the warp” (these heretics were almost all weavers), 54. Divine service for the divine office, 67. Princes of Tartarus, for demons, 108.

AELRED, abbot of Rievaulx, whose quite pure style affords no occasion for observation, CXCV.

RICHARD OF SAINT-VICTOR, of Paris.—What voice is, CXCVI, 976. Bodily voice and spiritual voice, 758. Whether the word of the heart differs from that of the mouth, 976. Speech is a meaningful voice established by convention, and the various kinds of voice, 1020. What inward and outward speech are, 977. At times translation should be used, at times comparison, 15.

Various words and expressions.—The mystical meanings of losing wings and tearing away wings, CXCVI, 1353, 1354. What allegory is, 200, 405. Alleluia, 845. Ambiguity of prophecies, 651. What anagogy and anagogical doctrine are, 200, 687. Whence angels are so called, 416. Whence animals are called clean and unclean, 255. To approve in the sense of to love, 8. What the inner altar is, 331. *Aser*, Hebrew for “blessed,” 77. Ass, that is, little and humble, 1063. What *azyma* are, 357. *Benjamin*, Hebrew for “son of the right hand,” 773. Mystical meaning of removing the lampstand, 717. What the daughters of songs are, 666. What collyrium is, 740. What contemplation is, 67. What are called contingent things, 893, 894. The tropological meaning of gilding, 111. What the power of being is, 896. What it means to possess the ends of the sea, 76. What the soul’s hunger is, 1200. What spiritual leaven is, 258. What Gog and Magog denote, 855. What the soul’s milk is, 497. Sickness of love, 1199. What legal observances are, 667. “Light in light,” 1344. What hidden manna is, 724. What material guidance by the hand is, 690. What the marrow of virtues is, 1033. In how many ways mystical interpretation occurs, 199. What the marriage of the Lamb is, 847. What *obtinentia* is, 937. Whence parturition is so called, 799. Pascha, that is, passage, 1060. What the *rhomphaea* is, 722. Manufacture of cloaks, 215. Whence speculative persons are so called, ibid. What tropology is, 200. What the narrow way is, 1018. Divine voices are admonitions, 744.

HILDEGARD (Saint), abbess.—Her writings add nothing new to linguistic study, except names of plants designated in the German vernacular. These may be consulted at CXCVII, 1129 and following.

ADAM THE SCOT, Premonstratensian regular canon.—The benefits of the human voice, CXCVIII, 801, 802. Analogy and antilogy of the divine and human word, 806. That the Old Testament has twenty-two books, corresponding to the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, 697. Scripture has significative things as well as words, ibid. As syllables are composed from letters, so words are composed from syllables and sentences from words; hence the usefulness of knowing letters is apparent, 91.

Various words and expressions.—*Amiton*, or alternatively the incombustible wood of paradise, CXCVIII, 681. *Creagra* in Greek, that is, a small flesh-hook, 682. “The strings of mutual exhortation do not fall silent,” 111. *Emmanuel* in Hebrew means “God with us,” 102, 390. To cast off grossness, 298. Historically, 697. Heavy and dark humanity, 298. *Iserenside*, a Saxon word and surname of King Edmund, that is, “Iron Side,” 721. Jesus, that is, Savior, 390. *Luter*, a washing vessel, 682. Diabolical phantom, 123. Solomon, that is, peaceful, 719. What *substomachare* is, 805. The twisting of iniquity, 113.

PETER COMESTOR, canon of Troyes.—Who *androgynei* or hermaphrodites are, CXCVIII, 1063. What lunar and solar years are, 1061, 1224, 1225. In what the original language remained after the Babylonian confusion, 1090. Whence Lake Asphaltitis, or the Dead Sea, is so called, 1101. *Astragalea*, a full-length garment, 1121. *Calamitus*, a species of small frog, 1150. *Concellanei*, that is, cohabitants, 1146. *Curlei*, royal birds: whence so called, 1226. *Dia* in Greek, brightness; in Latin, day, 1057. Eden means delights, 1067. *Eloim*, God or gods, because of the three persons who remain in God, 1055. *Ephimera*, a kind of fever, ibid. Who hermaphrodites are, 1063. Hermes, that is, interpreter, a surname of Mercury, 1693. *Ile* for *hyle*, that is, matter, 1055. How Josephus interprets Israel, 1121. *Machera*, that is, kitchen, or rather the cooks’ axe, from *machere*, “to kill,” 1126. *Niger* [black] is said alike in Latin and Hebrew, 1689. *Pagellae* for *paginae* [pages], 1420. *Periarchon*, that is, *On First Principles*, is a work of Origen, 1068. Whence *Phase* and Pascha derive, that is, passage, 1154. *Polymita*, from *polys*, “much,” and *micos*, “thread,” 1126. What a province is, 1550. *Rubeta*, a poisonous kind of frog, 1150. What scarabs and hornets are, 1062. Who the translators of Scripture were, 1069. Whence woman is called *virago*, 1070.

JOHN OF SALISBURY, bishop of Chartres.—He translated Dionysius’s book *On the Angelic Hierarchy* into Latin, CXCIX, 143. He admits that he was unable to render Greek elegances in Latin, and explains why, ibid. The elegances found among Greeks arising from constructions of participles and connected articles, 143. No Latin equivalent corresponds to every Greek word, 144. The Latin language is found poor in comparison with Greek, ibid. Praise of grammar from Quintilian, 856.

Words and expressions.—Ambidextrous, ambileft-handed, CXCIX, 66. “The stepmother so flatters her little darlings that she harms them,” 389. Who a cinaedus is, 404. The regions on this side of the sea, 296. To dine together, to consume together, 310. *Decessor* for predecessor, I. An unfamiliar mode of life, 761. “Trust one who has experienced it,” 386. The Gauls are said to be named from Greek *gala*, “milk,” because of their milky complexion, 613. Who the Gnathonics are, 634. Pliny elegantly touched upon gluttony, 733. *Iacynthus* means wholly a flower, or universally flourishing, 137. Κύριαι δόξαι: thus the Epicureans call their two principal maxims, 545. Letters patent, 145. *Parma*, from Greek *parme*, that is, shield, 4. *Polycraticus*, title of John of Salisbury’s work, 385. Pythagorean table, 409. Arable estates, 396. “To have one’s bladder full of wine,” 733.

We pass over POPE ALEXANDER III, whose letters and privileges have little bearing upon our subject, CC. The same must be said of ARNULF, bishop of Lisieux, CCI.

[Col. 0748] WILLIAM, bishop of Tyre.—He wrote a history of the lands beyond the sea, CC, 209.

Words and expressions.—The most ancient monuments of the letters of the Arabic language in mosaic work, CC, 215. *Beni zerra* in Arabic, that is, “sons of the armorer,” a distinguished tribe, 337. *Califa*, that is, provincial governor, 220. *Cauma* of conflagrations, 462. Dances, songs, and various public games given and approved by the emperor, 804. Mattress filled with cotton, 426. Chosen soldiery, which in French is called *troupe* or *corps d’élite*, 381. Galleys and *gati*, a type of ship used by Venetians, 541, 542. *Inpraesentiarum* is used very frequently adverbially in the Middle Ages, 342. Whence Judaea is so called, 410. Crime of injured majesty, 440. Language of the Persians and Parthians, 336. Mesopotamia, from Greek *potamos*, that is, river, 550. Monomachus, a surname of the Emperor Constantine, 219. What mosaic work is like, 215. Whence Palestine is so called, 410. Frugality is the friend of prudent men, 318. An expiatory crime, 428, 440. *Praesagire*, that is, to foresee, 343. Ladders made from hempen ropes, 347. To carry daggers beneath one’s clothing, 537. *Treuga*, a German word for suspension of hostilities, commonly called in French *trêve*, 234. Nail: “armed to the nail,” 428. Royal hangings, costly through much artistry, 803.

A continuation of William of Tyre’s history of the holy war, written in the old French idiom by an ancient author five hundred years ago, and useful for investigating the origins of that language, CC, 894 and following.

PETER, abbot of Celle, later bishop of Chartres.—Who the chancellor of the Roman Church is, CCII, 410. Head: “To waver with no dizziness of head,” 424. “Close this letter to your eyes and those of your own,” 479. Count, or king’s steward, 408. *Conversi*, what brothers they are, 407. Demon-slayer, 488. “Windows of meditation” and “bars of reading” are not felicitously found in Peter, 669. To eat too stickily, 488. Moon for the Virgin Mary: “To be satisfied with the fruits of moon and sun,” namely Mary and Christ, in the style of Scripture, 446. A poultice to be applied, 405. *Mysterium* for ministry, 476. Bread: Peter’s book *On Breads*, in which allegory is extended beyond its proper bounds, 927. Phantoms of the heart, that is, of the mind, 413. “Reason goes into exile,” 430. Epistolary salutation: Peter varies it thus: “Himself, with devotion; that little which he is and can do,” 410; “himself,” 414; “whatever he is and can do,” 418; “himself and his own,” 426. “To be zealous with zeal for the house of the God of Israel,” 424; “to reign well,” 438. Greeting, 412. Every syllable—of the written instrument of human malediction—is barbed with scorpions’ tails, destroying our latter parts, 776. Sublimity of native blood, 425. A slight suspicion, 474. “The little bell of your request,” 673.

PHILIP OF HARVENG, abbot of Good Hope.—The stratagems and expressions of lovers, CCIII, 983. Lovers’ eclipses in speaking, 334. What *anaglypha* are, 510. Apocryphal, 1300, 1301. Cadmus, bringer of letters, 1019. Who the curled-haired are, 794. The word “fortune” is unwelcome to Christian ears, 26. *Gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony, 790. Whence yoke derives, 861. Praise of the Latin language, 154. The gift of tongues granted to the apostles, 962. Speech takes place by words or signs, 946, 462. Difference between breasts and udders, 389. Whence necklaces derive, 461, 462. What a little moray eel is, 262, 263. Nicostrata gave seventeen letters to the Latins, 1021. Much is said concerning the letter O, 493. East for justice, 950. Phoenicians, inventors of letters, 1019. Who Sarabaitic monks are, 793. *Si*, a conjunction that is sometimes affirmative, 253, 471. The various senses of *usque* [until], 620.

REINER, monk of Saint Lawrence at Liège.—What the cataclysm is, CCIV, 94. Solar heat, 91. What a *craticulare* is, ibid. *Evillath*, Hebrew for “suffering,” 133. *Flower of the Desert*, Reiner’s book on the life of Saint Theobald the hermit, 69. What *mattuia levis* is, 157. *Noctanter* for “by night,” 94. Written in prose, 92. *Revirescis* for “you rise again,” 97. Angelic satiety, ibid. A lineage not common, 88. What synaloephae are, 80. *Tabellus*, a short letter, 55. To become calm, 156. *Triumphale Bulonicum*: what this title of Reiner’s book denotes, 99. Flames that burn the city, 93.

HENRY OF MARCY, abbot of Clairvaux, bishop and cardinal of Albano.—“Ala Jejunia” [possibly “fasting wings”], in the style of that age, CCIV, 266. What the Alpha and Omega of discourse are, 298. What the royal storehouse is, 220. Who archflamens and protoflamens were, 325. What the noonday demon is, 392. Defense of wards, 233. Granges, rural buildings in which grain and straw are collected, 230. A small grange, 231. What *inviscerari* is, 232. Pilgrim: *On the Pilgrim City of God*, whence the title and name of this work by Henry derive, 253, 254, 298. Zion is interpreted “watchtower,” 398.

PETRUS CANTOR, canon of Paris. — Wings of prayer, CCV, 26. *Ambisinistri* are called receivers of bribes, 84. *Aorasia*, from Greek, means blindness, 38. What *arpenna* or *arpina* is, [Col. 0749] 428. What gold fringe (*aurifrigium*) is, 450. Two-faced masses, 104. *Burdones*, a kind of bee, 156. What a *canipulus* is, 406. What *choritae* are, 134. The Key of Solomon, an apocryphal book, 470. What “to run to the anointed one” means, 417. What an *endromis* garment is, 438. Fief, 134. Who a *ganeo* is, 445. *Garciones*, that is, boys or servants, 413. *Gnato*, that is, a parasite, 441. Flattery confuses the rules of grammar, 142. What Harpies are, 208. What homage is, 436. Faith is called the hypostasis of all virtues, 268. Who a *lecator* is, 445. Who *mammotrecti* are, 472. What *marrantia* is, 427, 428. *Martrix*, in French *martre* [marten], 255. What a dry mass is, 418. What *muletrate* means, 513. What a mole is, 435. What an obelus is, 371. What *obrussa* is, 511. What the patrimony of the Crucified is, 149, 442. Who furriers are, 480. Who *permenones* are, 441. What a spear is, 480. Who a *primipilus* is, 426. What *pulmentum* is, 439. *Saburra*: the empty and useless ballast of ships, 372. Sacred fire, a disease, in Greek ἐρυσίπελας (*erysipelas*), 446. Who are called *sanguinitae*, 134. Bloodsuckers: those so called metaphorically, 94. *Sarpa* is a pruning-hook, in French *serpe*, 524. “Soon enough, if well enough,” 224. *Schacci* are gaming pieces, said to be named from climbing, 480. Seneschal, 426. *Syrma*, 480. What *trutannia* is, 444. Unicity derives from “one” (*unicus*), unity from “one” (*unus*), 429.

THOMAS OF CÎTEAUX, and JOHN ALGRINUS. — The moral meaning of the bow, CCVI, 434. “Assumption” taken in several senses, 763. “Hail,” “farewell,” and “greetings,” 143. The mystical meaning of singing, 683. Four mystical keys, 251. The origin of the word *commercium* [exchange], 23. The threefold cup, 697. The various meanings of scouts, 781, 782. The diverse senses of “flower,” 181. What the streams of grace are, 126. Who the kid is mystically, 57. The triple enemy, 80. What the idols of the flesh are, 441. Going, running, and flying, 703, 704. What the bride’s lips, tongue, and garments are, 449, 450. *Lithostratus*: the first place on a serving-dish, 373. The threefold speech of creatures, 509. What the hand of God is, 224. The bridegroom’s hand, 537. The devil’s purse, 24. The kiss of flesh, of the devil, of man, and of the beloved, 21. What spiritual feet are, 521. What the time for pruning is, 279. Who the last farthing is, 374. What the leech and its daughters are, 307. The difference between *suavium* and *basium* [two words for a kiss], 23. “Touch” used in several senses, 644. The mystical meaning of darkness, 310. What vessels of migration are, 347, 348. Who the watchmen are, 337.

PETRUS OF BLOIS. — *Amphicyrtos* is said of the moon when it approaches a full circle, CCVII, 22. To know how to behave as a maidservant, 1128. Ass: “to remain with the ass in the mire of coarser understanding,” 18. A *balatro*, a man of little worth, 49. Who barbers are, 49. Two years’ idleness, 26. — *Candidatrices*, perhaps for *cantatrices* [female singers], 49. To inform someone of his condition, 158. To become poor with the Lord, 406. The nonsense of childish derivations, 17. A day’s journey, a measure of travel, 133. *Diatomos*: the Greeks call the moon thus when it has grown to the half, 22. Lady Ambition, 185. *Dulcorarii*, sellers of liquids, 49. To follow someone immediately, 149. What it means “to be a fable,” 14. Who foresters are, 298. *Herpes estiomenus*: the swelling of a gnawing ulcer, 293. To treat uncivilly, that is, reproachfully, 8. The infernal marsh, or hell, 1134. The unending punishment of the world, 7. Logic: windy talkativeness among logicians, 26. Who the martyrs of the world are, 44. *Menoides*, that is, the new moon, 22. The native sweetness of the air, 137. Who cloud-makers or rogues are, 49. *Panselenos*, the full moon, 22. Pompous memory, 9. “A boy a hundred years old and an elementary old man,” 18. *Salarium* for wages, 92. Who pack-horses are called, note 48. Sellers of oil: hypocrites, 273. Wine: “to pour out one’s friends in wine,” 20.

MARTIN, Saint, priest of León. — An *acetabulum*, the fourth part of a hemi­mina, contains twelve drachmas, CCVII, 41. *Allegare* for *alligare* [to bind], 657. An amphora contains three urns, 41. Ass-like slowness and laziness, 234. A basilisk, that is, a little king, is a venomous animal, 34. A *batus* comprises fifty sextarii, 41. A *cadus* is the same as an amphora, ibid. A spoon is the smallest measure; it is half a drachma, 40. A *congium* measures six sextarii, 41. A *concula* is called one and a half drachmas, 40. A *conix* is a fifth part of a homer, 41. A *corus* is filled with thirty modii, ibid. A *cotula* is a hemina containing six cups, ibid. A cup weighs ten drachmas, 40. *Descipulae* for *muscipulae* [mousetraps], 672. What *deuterosis* is, 406. A hemina weighs one pound, 42. *Elnei* for *Eneni*, 417. A homer weighs the load of fifteen modii, 41. Heresy, in Greek, is called “choice,” 406. Who the Hyperboreans are, 417. *Immerobaptistae* for *hemerobaptistae*, 407. “Tongue” for “word,” 441. *Marbonaei* for *Marbothaei*, 407. What mausoleums are and whence they are named, CCIX, 21. A metreta is a measure for liquids, 41. A modius, so called from *modus* [measure], has forty-four pounds or twenty-four sextarii, 22. “Negatis” [you deny], erroneously for “asseritis” [you assert], or something similar, or “avellas” [you may remove]: conjecture uncertain, 466. *Neomenia*, that is, the new moon, 78. “Mouth” for “word,” ibid. Paradise: *hortus* [garden] in Latin, CCIX, 29. *Perterrita* for *praeterita* [past things], ibid. The past for the future, and the future for the past, 58. A *satum*, a Hebrew measure containing twenty-two sextarii, roughly a modius, 41. A sextarius, a measure of two pounds, 41. An urna is the same as a quartarius, ibid. *Usia*, in Greek, means essence or substance, 442.

[Col. 0750]

ALAN OF LILLE, surnamed the Universal Doctor. — What alteration and alterity are, CCX, 360. What *aurisia* or *avidentia* is, 585. *Calamites*, a species of frog, 173. A *carena*, a kind of ecclesiastical penance, 295. A horse is called *cornipes* [hoof-footed] or *sonipes* [sound-footed], 567. Wilderness for the world, 105. Grammar guides the tiller in the chariot of prudence, 506. The praise, nature, and usefulness of grammar, 342, 554. Grammar adapts raw material to the work, 507. The principal authors and masters of grammar, 508. What heavenly harmony is, 434. What logic is, 509. The difference between breasts and udders, 81. Mandrake, a medicinal herb, 103. *Napae*, goddesses of woods, 446. *Noys* for Greek *Nous*, that is, intellect, 478. The cloak of ignorance, 87. *Phronesis*, that is, prudence, 501. Painting is the ape of truth, 433. What knowledge of the voice is, 222. Sound is twofold, as is voice, 243. *Stilbon* is the star Mercury, 527. What a theophany is, 66. What transubstantiation is, 359. *Usia*: essence in Latin, 478. The conjunction *ut* [as, so that] is not always a mark of similarity, but is sometimes expressive of truth, 322. What a word is and whence it is named, 243. Words are the paintings of the soul, 470. What verbosity is, 164. A meaningful or articulated voice, 244.

Alan wrote the book *On the Distinctions of Theological Terms*, which beginners in linguistics may consult with great profit, CCX, 685, etc.

ABSALON, abbot of Springiersbach. — What the diapason is in music, CCXI, 122. Donatus the grammarian distinguishes the parts of speech, 180. What a foolish fruit is, 18. What ink is, 174. Insignia: those who deserve well of the emperor are marked with roses, lilies, or little moons, 228. To cut down pleasures with the knife of compunction and burn them in the fire of penance, 95. “Hand” for “power,” 181. “They exalt nature’s evil”: read “the sailors,” 18. *Per loco* used for *pro*; in “*per agmina pellicia*,” read *pro*, 174. The moral meaning of the broom, 29. Winter solstice is called Eve, while summer solstice is called the Virgin Mary: why, 21. What the little spheres of the candlestick are, 181. The moral meaning of a vessel, 218. What vocal voice and real voice are, 218.

STEPHEN, bishop of Tournai. — What annual payments of prebends are, XI, 478, note. A *biga*, *triga*, and *quadriga*: a vehicle with two, three, or four wheels, 494. *Birotus*, like *biga*, ibid. The church *capicerius*, who oversees and safeguards sacred things, formerly called in French *chevecier*, now *sacristan*, 334, note. Who are called regular clerics, 496. *Coterelli* or *ruptarii*, a most hostile kind of heretics, 371, note. What *communia* are in certain places, 337. A fief properly is not an estate, but a right in an estate, 346, note. *Ficarii Fauni*, otherwise called *incubones*: what they are, 488. Sheep: “If a sheep approaches a goat,” and, in St Bernard, “the sheep seeks wool from the goat”: an adage used in this age, signifying that a rich person borrows something from one in need, 670. What a prebend is, 478. Who semi-prebendaries are, ibid., note. A stall or *stallus*: the seat in which canons perform the hours, 475. What it means to pay *sumniatae*, 542.

ADAM, abbot of Perseigne, author of the book *Mariale*. — The Blessed Virgin Mary is called advocate, CCXI, 703. The loveliness of paradise, 745. Anchor of hope, 743. Dawn, 744. Our helper, 745. Help, ibid. Staff of the blind, 760. Dove, 750. Firm pillar, 745. Consolation, ibid. Lady of angels, ibid. Our Lady, 743. End of testaments, 762. Unbreakable lamp, 749. Moon, 745, 766. Sacred pearl, 773. Most worthy mother, 745. Mother of grace and mercy, 744. Mediatrix, 704. Deep and capacious well, 739. Mystical rose, 779. Heavenly ladder, 759. Spouse of God, 145. Star of the sea, 743. Our vine, 706, 707.

PETRUS DE RIGA OF PARIS. — We possess only a few fragments of this poet. In recapitulations of both Testaments he composed stanzas, each of which entirely omits one particular letter of the alphabet, CCXII, 32 ff.

GUNTHER, Cistercian monk. — Amphibology, which supplies the place of a single word not yet invented, CCXII, 113. Etymologies of Greek terms: Cataphrygians, Cathars, Anthropomorphites, 117. What a hypothesis is, 105. The several senses in which “speech” is used, 103. What grammatical speech is, 104. Simple and composite speech, 115. To syllogize by disputation, 105. What syntax is, ibid. What thesis is, ibid. A tetracolic division, that is, one of four members, 106. Let the reader know that this author was the first to devise a treatment of these matters in the book *On Prayer, Fasting, and Almsgiving*, because, as he himself declares at the outset, the Latin word *oratio* [prayer, speech] is also customarily used to signify these things.

HELINAND OF FROIDMONT, monk. — “Hail,” “greetings,” “farewell,” CCXII, 745. What *calathil abellula* is, 636. Hoods deeply lowered over the eyes in the dormitory, 560. Playing the cithara, organ, psaltery, and lyre, 745. The form of being, 490. *Focale* for a hearth-place, 516. *Imperatum*, that is, the shift of the Blessed Virgin Mary, 873. What it means to gnaw the bark of letters, 503. Lucifer named by antiphrasis, 486. What it means for the milk of *mammotreti* to rise, [Col. 0751] 503. *Manher* in Hebrew: what this means, 502. Negative concession; concessive negation: what they are, 665. “Occasionally,” 493. Papillate clusters, 636. To kill one’s own lice, 730. A prologue of shame in the earthly paradise, 493. *Thau* in Hebrew is interpreted “sign.” (Helinand wrote a poem *On Death* in the French language; see extracts from it, 1081 ff.)

SICARD, bishop of Cremona, author of the *Mitrale*. — What allegory, anagogy, and tropology are, CCXIII, 47. The derivation of *altare* and *ara* [altar], 18. What ascents of the heart are, 19. Apostolic tunics, like dalmatics, represent the cross before them, 60. What the *Digest* code is, 480. To whom *dulia* and *latria* are due, 16. What exedrae, cathedrae, and synhedrae are, 23. Clean breeches. In French they may be called *culote de cour* or *d’étiquette*, 486. Hebrew and Greek terms used in the mass, 96. *Hypapas*: the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, 242. What it means to Judaize, 118. What it means to make a litany, 28. Sicard derives the word *monachus* [monk] from Greek *monos*, “one,” and *chaos*, “sadness,” 66. What a novella is, 480. *Pandectae*, the same as the *Digest*, ibid. *Persina*, a kind of venomous serpent, 445. The origin of the Liutprand foot as a measure, 488. *Trabea*, an imperial and purple garment, 82.

PETER, monk of Vaux-de-Cernay. — *Bladum* for grain, CCXIII, 626. *Bucca*: to mock someone with the grimaces of a performer, 552. Borough, 593, 623. *Cabaretum*, the name of a place, 583. What *Colant* and *Colibant* are, 546. Crusaders, 564, 573. Lordship, in French *seigneurie*, 599, 650. Castle ditch, 608. The fork of divine vengeance, 545. League, 591. *Mangonelli*, a kind of war machine, 593. Who a marshal is, 622. What *patrivare* is, 545. *Pampilio* for *papilio* [butterfly], 598. A *petraria*, a war machine, 585. *Ruptarii*, a name for heretics, [Col. 0752] 553. *Schacci*, a kind of game, ibid. Seneschal, 655. *Theosebia*, that is, wisdom, 544. To fear for one’s skin, 607. Waldensians, named from a certain Waldo, 548.

INNOCENT III, Roman pontiff. — An acre, an agrarian measure, CCXV, 491. Why Jews say *Adonai* instead of *Jehovah*, 216. What appendages are, CCXIV, 156; CCXV, 936, 1335. *Canonicare*, that is, to make someone a canon, CCXIV, 200. A *carrucata*, a certain extent of land, CCXV, 491. What it means to pay *circata*, CCXIV, 156. Court or manor, 301. What horses are called *dextrarii*, 7. Women holding fiefs, 1095, note. What fief and benefice are, 156. What a hat (*galerus*) is, 880. *Gardinus* for garden, CCXV, 491. What a grange is, CCXIV, 301. What infeudation is, 209. CCXXXIII. ALPHABETICAL INDEX OF ALL MANUSCRIPTS IN WHICH THE WRITINGS OF THE HOLY FATHERS AND ECCLESIASTICAL AUTHORS ARE TO BE FOUND.

TO THE READER.

This index, neither promised nor indeed announced in the index of indexes printed on the title page, is nevertheless gladly offered to you by the editor as a supplement. It has been extracted from one of the works comprising our *Encyclopaedia*, namely the *Dictionary of Manuscripts*.

[INDEX OF MANUSCRIPTS.]
