[Col. 0835]

CCXXXIV. A GUIDING INDEX FOR EVERY READER EAGER FOR PATRISTIC LEARNING, CONCERNING THE INDIVIDUAL TENETS OF CATHOLIC DOCTRINE, WHICH EITHER SUPPLY STRENGTH AND WEAPONS FOR PRESERVING THE DEPOSIT OF THE TRUE FAITH AGAINST THE POISONED DOGMAS OF HERETICS, OR ARE OF THE GREATEST HELP IN WISELY ESTABLISHING A RIGHT WAY OF LIFE, AND FINALLY CONTRIBUTE VERY MUCH TO THE EDUCATION AND LEARNING OF NOBLE AND WELL-ENDOWED MINDS

NOTICE.

This index differs from the analytical index in that it does not bring forward every subject in the *Patrology*, but only the principal ones, and in another manner. Therefore, far from being a repetition, it will greatly assist those who lack time; and, if anything is missing for them, they will shortly find it in a more fully treated index of the same kind. Moreover, many matters omitted in the gigantic index, or treated there from a new standpoint, will very fortunately come before them.

TO THE BENEVOLENT READER.

If at some time the harsh judgment of a judge awaits a man,  
A head condemned to hardships and punishments,  
Let neither prisons tire him with the prison-mill,  
Nor let rigid mines torment him with the hand;  
Let him compile dictionaries; for why should I delay over the rest?  
This one labor contains every form of punishment.  
(Scaliger.)

Although the many things which have everywhere been said and written with distinction by the most illustrious and eminent J. P. Migne largely relieve me of the burden of writing a preface, I nevertheless see that some points remain about which I should not hesitate to forewarn the reader at the very threshold. For an account must be given of my undertaking. With God’s help, I shall do so briefly.

Before, therefore, you accuse me, excellent reader, read what follows and consider what is said and for what purpose.

First, then, to explain why I have undertaken and entered upon this mass of labor: my purpose was that you might all the more willingly, because more easily, turn over with hand by night and by day these offspring of the holy Fathers. For all these literary monuments which so many and such great teachers of the churches have left to posterity are certainly most useful and distinguished; moreover, they are such as either to furnish strength and weapons for preserving the deposit of the true faith against the poisoned dogmas of heretics, or to be of the greatest help in wisely establishing a right way of life, and finally to contribute much education and learning to noble and well-endowed minds. But amid so great a miscellany of subjects, who would not be delayed or discouraged if he resolved to investigate something, unless he proceeded, as it were, led by the hand, with some index showing the way?

Therefore, trusting that God would be favorable, I girded myself for this work, devoted my labor to it, and sweated over it, so that I might compile that index by which everyone might avail himself in questions of every kind. If, indeed, it succeeds according to my intention, students will of their own accord declare that the labor was well expended; nor is it of such small consequence that I should even briefly explain by what means I finally completed so immense a work. Let those who have dared the same know: they have sweated much and labored in vain.

Every index, moreover, is chiefly made, if I am not mistaken, to indicate, not to display or as it were represent, the very matters sought. The point is plain, I think, and self-evident. It was therefore permitted me—indeed it was proper—to keep within definite and limited bounds. Otherwise, as the well-known poet says:

> . . . There would be long tedium, long  
> detours; but I pursue the highest points of things.  
> (*Aeneid* I.345–346.)

And consequently, since the principal heads of subjects are indicated, as it were, stealthily and rapidly in summary form, you will very rarely have to disregard even the slightest indications. For very often you will find indicated in the fewest words matters which subsequently extend broadly and copiously through many pages in the text of the Fathers. To use examples, I have pointed out the source and head of the stream; you then, in its downward and sloping course, may follow its winding banks if you please, until you eventually reach its mouths and shores. Surely, I ask you, do you think that every individual item ought to have been indicated separately, and thus to the point of tedium and nausea? To what end, tell me, when at all times—and especially now—a few things will have been enough for any intelligent person?

Indeed, when any treatise on this or that subject is composed by an author, it is, I think, my office to point out the whole treatise summarily and almost incidentally to the reader; it is not my office to identify each individual chapter. You yourself will see and seek out those chapters if, prudent and watchful, you give them attention. But whatever may have fallen into this same treatise as though by accidental chance, inserted or intermingled, I have taken the utmost care not to pass over and omit, since it was my task, not yours, to search out and investigate those matters. Thus, with your leave, I would say that I wished to provide and have kept watch both for the brevity of the work and for the reader’s real benefit. Now I shall say with Propertius:

> But if strength should fail, courage at least  
> will win praise; in great matters, even to have wished is enough.

Yet I have composed and arranged this Index not so that you may be exempted from the necessity of reading the Fathers—which would most certainly shame both me and you, dear reader—but so that you might personally and, as they say, by sight itself, become acquainted with their writings, pure and unadulterated, and examine and survey them more deeply and thoroughly with your own eyes. This is also why I have deliberately set down many things in a doubtful or ambiguous form which otherwise remain in themselves altogether unquestionable and entirely unshaken.

I shall not, however, deny that I have sometimes deliberately passed over a number of matters, namely because they properly belonged to the Index of the Scriptures itself—grant me the word. But I would have you note that I have bestowed and applied particular care, indeed solicitude, upon proper names, judging that those things which acute investigators usually need should chiefly be sought there.

Moreover, I do not doubt that anyone who wants more will diligently have recourse to the particular indexes of the Fathers and writers themselves, wherever these are available. Since each of these is very richly supplied, they will certainly furnish an exceedingly abundant harvest—indeed, not merely a harvest, but a miscellany—of subjects. My purpose and intention, in noting the more general matters, was only to sample and, as it were, touch upon these. How far I have succeeded in doing this is not for me, though it is for everyone, to determine.

But lest these notices grow beyond measure, I would ask and warn you, most loving reader, that if you encounter anything omitted by me, you should not find fault with me before you have carefully consulted the entries nearest to it; there, I hope, perhaps whatever is desired in these matters will be found.

As to abbreviations—or, if you prefer, sigla—I give this one warning: for three authors, namely Augustine, Jerome, and Ambrose, because of their greater authority, and sometimes also for Tertullian, we have adopted a special naming and designation; not so for the others.

Having briefly set these things forth, candid reader, I wish you well and ask that you pray for me.

Written at Dreux, in the diocese of Chartres, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of salvation 1863.

P. Fr. VIVIER, priest of Jesus Christ.

CCXXXV. METHODICAL INDEX, ARRANGED IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER, OF THE AUTHORS AND WORKS IN THIS PATROLOGY, AND OF THE DISTINGUISHED PERSONS AND MEMORABLE MATTERS CONTAINED IN IT; NAMELY:

Comprising: first, authors, with their Lives, prolegomena, historical and literary notices, dissertations, and so forth pertaining to each; second, their works, both authentic and spurious, and likewise those attributed to them in the form of appendices; and third, matters relating to patriarchs, kings of the Old Testament, Christ, apostles, rulers, and others, as also comparable matters of the New Testament, under their names.

[METHODICAL INDEX.]

CHRISTIANS.—On the morals and laws of Christians, I, 906. How absurdly pagans boasted that the virtues of their philosophers equalled those of Christians, 923, 546.—On Christian fasts, works of penitence, and various rites, 933. On the sacred Christian assemblies, I, 948. According to Caecilius in the *Octavius*, Christians, while they fear dying after death, do not fear dying in the meantime, III, 256. Octavius first maintains that no one ought to take offense because Christians, however unlearned, discuss heavenly matters: for one must consider not the authority of the disputant, but the truth of the argument itself, 279, 409. It is clearly demonstrated that Christian morals are far holier than those of pagans, 348, 414 ff. Christians are shown not to attend spectacles and public processions, because they knew with utmost certainty that these were no less impious than cruel, 352, 536, 540. Christians abstain from things sacrificed to idols, lest anyone think either that they yield to demons or are ashamed of their religion. Yet they do not reject every color and scent of flowers; for they use flowers scattered loose and soft, and encircle their necks with garlands, but judge it superfluous and useless to crown a dead person’s head. With the same tranquility in which they live, they bury the dead, awaiting with the surest hope the crown of eternal blessedness, 355, 542.—St. Cyprian exhorts Christians to cultivate the various virtues of holy religion commended by God in the sacred Scriptures. Citations from Scripture, IV, 727.—The statements made by Caecilius concerning Christian morals are examined, VII, 882.—The virtues and qualities which ought to adorn a Christian, throughout St. Ambrose’s treatise *On Duties*, XVI, 23.—St. Augustine’s two books, On the Morals of Catholics and on the Morals of the Manichees, XXXII, 1300.

On the life and passion of St. Cyprian by Pontius.

The author recounts what Cyprian did after baptism. Continence is necessary. Cyprian’s other virtues, III, 1483.—He is quickly promoted to holy orders. He continually sets the saints before himself as examples to imitate, 1484.—Cyprian is brought to the faith by Caecilius, 1485.—Still a neophyte, he is compelled to assume the episcopate, 1486.—He shines in episcopal virtues, 1487.—Proscribed and summoned to appear before Leo, he prudently withdraws, 1487.—And this happens by the counsel of divine Providence, 1488.—When a dreadful plague is raging, by an effective address he brings his people to assist those infected by it, even pagans, III, 1489.—He is driven into exile at Curubis, 1490.—He is visited by many; refreshed by a heavenly vision, he is divinely warned concerning the martyrdom he must undergo and its postponement, 1491.—The author interprets this vision and proves that it was true, 1493.—With persecution imminent, Cyprian refuses to flee and exhorts his people to martyrdom, 1494.—He is arrested. The people keep vigil through the night before the doors, 1494.—On the following day he is led before the tribunal of the proconsul, 1495.—The sentence having been pronounced, he is condemned to death by the sword, 1496.—Proconsular acts of St. Cyprian, 1497.—The first confession of St. Cyprian before the proconsul Paternus; he refuses to betray the presbyters, 1497.—He is sent into exile at Curubis. Recalled thence by Galerius, he is arrested, 1500.—He is brought before the proconsul. His second confession, 1502.—Sentence is pronounced against him: he is ordered to be beheaded, 1503.—He is beheaded before a great crowd of people. His body, carried away by the faithful at night, is buried, 1504.—Passion of St. Cyprian, 1505.

The acts performed and writings issued by him at the close of the year 250 are listed, 113.—Cyprian sends deputies in his place. Threats of Felicissimus, [Col. 1166] 115.—The schism of Felicissimus at the beginning of 251. Novatus, one of the five schismatic presbyters. On Letter XL of St. Cyprian, 117.—Cyprian returns after the persecution has subsided and deliberates with his colleagues concerning the case of the lapsed; but before the council he writes the book *On the Lapsed*, 119.—St. Cyprian’s prudence in suppressing the schism of Novatian and confirming the episcopate of St. Cornelius, 123.—At what time the schism of Novatian broke out, 125.—At what time Novatian was ordained, 128.—The sequence of events conducted by St. Cyprian in the case of Cornelius, 131.—New efforts of Novatian. The return of the Roman confessors to the Church at Cyprian’s urging: it is shown that this occurred before the Roman council of 251, 133.—On the acts and writings of St. Cyprian in the year 252, before the persecution, 136.—Persecution is revealed to Cyprian. He exhorts the Thibaritans to the contest. At a council he restores peace to penitent lapsed persons; this council must be distinguished from another held on the Ides of May, 141.—St. Cyprian congratulates St. Cornelius on the glory of his confession. He exhorts the Carthaginian confessors in Letter LXXXI, which is shown to have been written in this persecution in the year 252, 142.—The remarkable charity of St. Cyprian during the calamity of the plague; he defends religion against Demetrian. **GOD.**—See the Index on God and what follows.

On God in general.—Letters of St. Augustine on God, CXVIII, CXX, XXXIII.—Poem of Dracontius on God, comprising three books, LX, 679.—Poem on the praises of the Lord by an unknown author, LXI, 1091.—St. Isidore’s *On God*, seventh book of the *Etymologies*, LXXXII, 259.—Blessed Rabanus Maurus, *On God* (in his work *On the Universe*), CXI, 13.—Although infinite and immeasurable, and known in his full greatness to himself alone, God cannot be seen or named by us; yet his love, if additions to the names are removed, is perceived, III, 287. What God’s name is, 440. God cannot be designated by a proper name, Novatian, 892.—On the ten names of God, Letter XXII of St. Jerome, XXV.

On God’s existence.—On God, I, 804; V, 451.—God’s existence is proved because he is known by human beings’ innermost awareness and by their very conscience, III, 422.—How Cyprian demonstrates that God exists, IV, 992.—St. Anselm’s *Proslogion*, or discourse, on God’s existence, CLVIII, 223.—On God, his affections, and the refutation of Epicurus, VII, 85, 124. On the Stoics’ view of God, 88.—Book of St. Hilary on the essence of Son and Father, X, 887.—On hypostases, Letters 15, 16, and 17 of St. Jerome, XXII.—On the essence of divinity, by St. Augustine, XLII, 1190.—St. Anselm of Canterbury’s *Monologion* on the essence of the Divinity, CLVIII, 141.

On the unity of God.—Poems of Tertullian on the one God, II, 1054.—The more eminent philosophers held almost the same view as Christians concerning one God, III, 292, 425. Another argument for one God, drawn from examples of earthly things, kingdoms, and natural objects, is examined, 437. God is one and alone, 892. If we call Christ God and the Father God, we nevertheless no more believe in two gods than in two lords or teachers, 946.—That God is one and cannot be more than one, VI, 127, 1019. Testimonies of poets and philosophers that God is one, 129, 138, 148, 1021, 1022.—On God, and on him as one, VII, 110.—Hilary’s book on the unity of Father and Son, X, 883.—Arnobius the Younger’s disputation on the triune and one God, LIII, 239.—Hincmar of Rheims, *On One and Not Threefold Deity*, CXXV, 466.

On God the Son.—The Son is equal to the Father, VII, 1085.—Candidus’s book *On Divine Generation*, VIII, 1013. Victorinus’s book *On the Generation of the Divine Word*, 1910.—The Son is consubstantial, X, 487, 497.—On the eternal generation of the Son, XI, 392, 396, 398.—Blessed Rabanus Maurus, *On the Son of God* (in his work *On the Universe*), CXI, 17.

God the Creator.—From the constitution and adornment of the world, every rational person knows that it was created by God, III, 284. He provides not only for the whole world but for each of its individual parts, 287. Poets called him the creator of all things, 292. God, the most perfect maker of all things, 886, 891.—That God the Father is the maker of the Word and of all things, and that things could in no way subsist if their causes were diverse, [Col. 1171] VIII, 405.—God creates and orders all things, XXXII, 977.—By God’s providence the world is governed and holds together, VII, 110.

Attributes of God.—On God’s divine attributes, 804.—The true God has neither beginning nor end, III, 309, 444. God is immeasurable, 444, 889; infinite, 444; omnipotent, 886; eternal, Novatian, 889; unchangeable, Novatian, 892.—On things attributed to God in Scripture, XXX, 176.—On God’s presence everywhere, Letters CLXXXVII of St. Augustine, XXXIII.—Poem of St. Paulinus enumerating various attributes of God, LXI, 440.—Book of St. Anselm of Canterbury *On the Will of God*, CLVIII, 581.—One book of Abbot Rupert *On the Will of God*, CLXX, 437. One book of the same on God’s omnipotence, 453.—Hugh of St. Victor on the power and will of God, CLXXVI, 839.—Book of the holy Alger on mercy and justice, CLXXX, 588.

Perfections of God.—If God is just, why do the wicked flourish and the upright suffer oppression? XX, 1104. Why are infants afflicted by evils? 1104.—On God’s goodness and justice in distinguishing among human beings, Letters CLXXXVI, CXC, and CLXCIX of St. Augustine, XXXIII. Treatise of St. Peter Damian on divine omnipotence in restoring corrupted nature and making undone things as though not done, CXLV, 595.

God’s benefits, gifts, and graces.—If God is said to have profited the Jews in nothing, the writers of the Jewish annals are surely most ample witnesses that the Jews forsook God before they were forsaken by him, III, 342.—That God abundantly supplies things necessary for use, VIII, 417.—Conference of Abbot Chaeremon on God’s protection, XLIX, 897.

God’s wrath.—If we maintain that certain angers, indignations, and hatreds of God are described in the sacred pages, nevertheless these must not be understood after the pattern of human vices, III, 894.—On the wrath of God, VII, 77, 92, 126, 139, 143.

God incorporeal.—Poets called God mind and spirit, III, 292. Christians are convinced that God cannot be enclosed by any temple, nor can an image of him be fashioned, 338. Although Scripture often adapts the divine face to human form, the measure of divine majesty is nevertheless not enclosed within the features of our body, Novatian, 895.—That God is without a body and has no need of sex for procreation, VI, 153.

God visible and invisible.—Letters of St. Augustine on seeing God, XCII, CLXVII, CXLVIII, XXXIII.

God as known and to be known.—How God is known by human beings, III, 440.

God is to be honoured and feared.—That God alone is to be worshipped, IV, 657.—On the fear of God, VII, 114.—Treatise of St. Zeno on fear, XI, 322.

## FIRMILIANUS, Bishop of Caesarea

—Dissertations of Fr. M. Molkenbuhr on Firmilianus, Bishop of Caesarea, III, 1357. The letter circulated under Firmilianus’s name appears to have been fabricated by a Latin writer, 1361. At any rate, St. Firmilianus did not compose it, 1365. The letter itself is reported in portions and critically examined, 1368. It is more likely that some African Donatist fabricated the spurious letter after the fourth century, or else another heretic did so, 1401. Firmilianus published no books for public circulation, 1408. On the year of St. Firmilianus’s death, in which Paul of Samosata was condemned at the celebrated Synod of Antioch, where the word *homoousion* is said also to have been rejected, 1410. These events did not occur before the year 272, 1410.

NATIONS.—Two books To the Nations, I, 559, 585, 755. How absurdly the pagans boasted that the virtues of their philosophers equalled those of Christians, 923. How absurdly the pagans alleged that certain of their laws bound them to harass Christians and make them deny [the faith], 986. Christians are calumniated by pagans, 1015, 1040, 1050, 1066, 1079. The false piety of the pagans, 1128.—Octavius demonstrates that Christians are no less falsely accused of sacrilege, incest, debauchery, and parricide than it was certain and true that precisely the same crimes, or others altogether similar and even greater, were actually committed by the pagans themselves, III, 327, 335, 493, 497, 502. Pagans cruelly expose newborn children and, before they are born, kill them by cruel abortion, 333, 488.—That the nations would be more ready to believe in Christ, IV, 689. That the nations rather than the Jews attain the kingdom of heaven, 694. With what great injustice pagans condemned Christians who were neither defended nor heard, 998.—Antonius’ poem Against the Nations, V, 261. His other work, *Dialogue between a Jew who Inquires and a Christian Who Responds to Him in Reply*, addressed to the same Honestus, 57.—Peter the Venerable’s treatise *Against the Jews*, CLXXXIX, 507.—Peter of Blois’s *Against Jewish Perfidy*, CCVII, 825.—St. Martin of León’s treatise *Against the Jews*, CCIX, 423.—Anonymous treatise against a Jew, CCXIII, 749–807.

Rejection, wickedness, perfidy, etc. of the Jews.—If it is said that God has been of no benefit to the Jews, certainly the writers of the Jewish annals are most ample witnesses that they first abandoned God before they were abandoned by him, III, 342.—That the Jews sinned grievously to God’s offense because they forsook the Lord and followed idols, IV, 679. Likewise, because they did not believe the prophets and killed them, 680. Foretold beforehand that they would neither know, understand, nor receive the Lord, 681. That the Jews would not understand the Holy Scriptures, but would have understanding in the last times after Christ had come, 682. That the Jews can understand nothing of the Scriptures unless they have first lost Christ, 683. That they would destroy Jerusalem and leave the land which they had received, ibid. That the Jews would lose the bread and cup of Christ and all his grace, while we would receive them, 693. That the nations rather than the Jews attain the kingdom of heaven, 694. That the Jews can obtain pardon for their sins only on this condition: if they wash in baptism the blood of Christ whom they killed, and, entering the Church, obey his commandments, ibid.—On Jewish unbelief, VI, 49.

THE LAPSED.—Cyprian clears himself of the suspicion of levity in the matter of the lapsed, III, 761. The lapsed must be assisted at their departure from life, though the condition of all is not the same, 779. Christians must by no means be turned away from martyrdom through indulgence toward the lapsed; those who deny peace to the lapsed contradict Holy Scripture; from the admission of adulterers to penance it follows that the lapsed too should be admitted. Whoever advises repentance while taking away hope of pardon is mocking them, 779. Councils of Carthage, held under St. Cyprian in the reign of Pope Cornelius, concerning the case of the lapsed, 849. Synodal letter of St. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, and his colleagues to Pope St. Cornelius concerning the lapsed: the African bishops explain to Cornelius that frequent divine revelations had foretold the imminent persecution and that, therefore, they had judged peace should not be delayed for those who had not ceased doing penance, 851. The crime of the *libellatici* is equal to the crime of those who deny [the faith]. To receive the lapsed with excessive leniency is the highest cruelty. Letters of confessors greatly contributed to preserving ecclesiastical discipline. Let the lapsed knock at the doors of the Church, but not break them down, Novatian, 963.—Prolegomena to an anonymous treatise addressed to Novatian the heretic, 1205. That hope of pardon must not be denied to the lapsed, ibid.—Whether St. Cyprian denied peace during the course of penance to those lapsed persons who were dying, except only those who had received certificates from martyrs, IV, 55. Whether the Council of Carthage imposed penance on those who had sacrificed for their whole lifetime, 59. On the great number of the lapsed in the persecution of Decius, 86. In what the offense of those called *libellatici* consisted, 89. Five letters of St. Cyprian concerning the lapsed, 101. St. Cyprian deliberates with his colleagues concerning the case of the lapsed, 119. At a council, St. Cyprian restores peace to penitent lapsed persons, 141. What ought to be done concerning the lapsed, 225. St. Cyprian’s letter to the clergy concerning certain presbyters who rashly granted peace to the lapsed, 250. St. Cyprian’s letter to martyrs and confessors who asked that peace be granted to the lapsed, 253. Letter of the same to the clergy concerning the lapsed, lest they depart empty-handed, 259. St. Cyprian’s letter to the clergy concerning those who hasten toward peace, 260. When certain lapsed persons, under pressure of a new persecution, had confessed Christ and consequently sought peace before setting out into exile, Caldonius asks Cyprian whether peace ought to be granted to them, [Col. 1213] 272. Cyprian replies to Caldonius that peace must not be denied to those who have merited it by genuine repentance and confession of Christ’s name, 372. Celerinus seeks peace from the Carthaginian confessors for his sisters who had lapsed at Rome, 274. By his letters Cyprian informs the Roman clergy of the seditious demand of the lapsed to be restored to peace, 282. Cyprian’s letter to the lapsed, 300. St. Cyprian’s letter concerning those overcome by tortures, 348. St. Cyprian’s letter on granting peace to the lapsed, 350. St. Cyprian’s book *On the Lapsed*, 467, 1116.

Miracles, Visions, etc.—A discussion of the abundance and richness of visions and other heavenly gifts in the earlier centuries of the Church, III, 104. This abundance and richness is established from the examples of Potamiaena no less than of Perpetua, 113; from the Life of St. Cyprian, 115; from the Acts of many martyrs, 121; concerning the visions of St. Perpetua, 122 ff.—False miracles of pagans, V, 604.—St. Ambrose’s sermon On Marvels, XVII, 675.—St. Maximus’ sermon On Marvels, LVII, 719.—St. Gregory’s two books of Miracles, LXXI, 705, 801. NOVATIANS.---The perversity of Novatian’s envoys is exposed, and therefore they are barred from communion. When they ask to be publicly heard, this is refused. Seeking everywhere to recruit allies for their schism and heresy, they are restrained, III, 699. On the letters that Cyprian wrote to confessors seduced by Novatian and Novatus, 709. What kind of men were those whom Novatian again sent as envoys to Carthage, 712. Which confessors—Maximus the presbyter, Urbanus, and Sidonius—renounced the schism and were received into the Catholic Church, 715. Cyprian praises Cornelius’ diligence, by which he promptly warned him of Novatian’s destructive schemes and the conduct of his new envoys, 725. How confessors deceived by Novatian uncovered his frauds and made them publicly known to the Church, 735. Ordained contrary to every law, he arrogates the episcopate to himself, 737. He is not deterred from schism by the great number of the Roman clergy and people, 742. When illness pressed upon him, he was sprinkled or baptized upon his bed, but was by no means sealed, 746. In time of persecution he preferred to deny that he was a presbyter rather than assist the brethren, 752. Contrary to the laws, with the clergy and very many of the people interceding, Cornelius was advanced to the presbyterate through the bishop’s favor, 752. In administering Christ’s body and blood, he compels each person to swear an oath to himself, 756. That all abandoned him, 758. Cyprian dispels for Antonianus the false opinions instilled in him by Novatian’s letters, 761. Novatian introduced Stoic doctrines into the Church, 779. On Novatian’s character as philosopher and Stoic, 779. Cyprian advises Stephen, by letters sent to the bishops of Gaul, to ensure that Marcian, bishop of Arles and adherent of Novatian, no longer boasts that he has remained unreconciled, 989. Anonymous treatise against Novatian the heretic, 1205. Saint Cyprian’s letter to Cornelius because he did not accept Novatian’s ordination, IV, 341. Saint Cyprian’s letter to Antonianus concerning Cornelius and Novatian, 347.---Three letters of Saint Pacian to Symphorianus the Novatian, XIII, 1051. Saint Pacian’s letter against the treatises of the Novatians, 1065.---Passages of Saint Jerome concerning the Novatians, Letter 42, XXII.---Saint Augustine’s letter concerning the Novatians, Letter 265, XXXIII.

OCTAVIUS, ADVENTIUS.---Saint Maximus’ homily on the feast of the holy martyrs of Turin, Octavius, Adventius, and Solutor, LVII, 427.

OCTAVIUS.---Who Octavius was, who is introduced as disputing in the work of Minucius, III, 383. D. Lumper’s Prolegomena to Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, 193. Dissertation of F. B. Alduini on *Octavius*, 199. J. Ernesti’s preface to the first Lindner edition, 219. Logical analysis of *Octavius*, 225. *Octavius* begins, 231.---Letter of L. Holstenius on the *verubae* [uncertain term] of Ephesian Diana, concerning Minucius, XXI, III, 365. Dissertation of D. Le Nourry on *Octavius*. Analysis of the book: who its author was, and who Caecilius and Octavius were, who are introduced as disputants in it, 371. On the date, style, title, subject matter, divisions, manuscripts, and editions of this book; on various observations upon it; on corrupt passages; and on what Minucius drew from others and others from him, 386. New annotations on the book of Minucius Felix: first, the arguments by which Caecilius denies God’s existence and Octavius proves it are examined, 409. On the three abominable accusations—infanticide, eating human flesh, and incest—of which Christians were accused by Caecilius and [Col. 1232] other pagans, III, 478, 484, 499. Other accusations of Caecilius, and Octavius’ answers to them, are examined, 517. Other heads of Caecilius’ most unjust accusations are considered, 536. Caecilius’ arguments, by which he attempts to prove that his gods truly exist and consequently that the religion of the Gentiles is true, are scrutinized, 550. The arguments by which Octavius shows that the gods of the Gentiles are false are considered, 555. How strong are the other arguments by which Octavius proves against Caecilius that the gods of the Gentiles are false and nonexistent, 556. How weighty is Minucius’ further argument against the gods of the Gentiles, derived from their ridiculous forms and figures and from their unworthy, shameful deeds and crimes, 573. Caecilius’ argument is examined, by which the existence of the gods of the Gentiles is proved on the ground that the Romans earned dominion over the whole world through their worship, 589. The arguments by which Caecilius supposed that the gods’ existence could be proved from miracles, oracles, auspices, auguries, dreams, and other predictions are considered, 604. Minucius’ general reply is considered, by which he demonstrates that miracles, oracles, auspices, auguries, dreams, and other extraordinary occurrences among the pagans proceeded not from the power of their gods but from the frauds and deceptions of demons, 615. On images and statues of the gods, beneath which demons, lurking there, were believed to perform certain wondrous acts and which were impiously worshipped by the pagans, 625. On a certain book which Minucius seems to have promised to write; and on certain obscure passages, some writers, and atheists mentioned by him, 645. Certain obscure passages of *Octavius* are explained, III, 645. On certain writers cited by Minucius in the *Octavius*, 649.

PRESCRIPTION.—Book on prescriptions against heretics, II, 10. Argument of this book, 11. That the apostles received from Christ himself, and the churches from the apostles, sound doctrine to be handed down to posterity, and that no doctrine is to be received from elsewhere, 31. That which was first handed down is true and divine, 41. The sure testimony of the true Church is the uninterrupted succession of bishops from the apostles, 44. Our teaching is true because it is certainly not condemned by the apostles, indeed is defended by them; any other teaching is false, as alien or unknown to the apostles, 45.

RELIGION.—Religion in general. Caecilius maintains that everything in human affairs is doubtful and uncertain, III, 242. According to him, it is regrettable that Christians, mostly uneducated and illiterate, dare to determine anything certain concerning the highest realities and divine majesty, 242. Hence he argues that no Providence governs the world, and concludes that it is better to adhere to the ancient religions, 242. In the *Octavius*, Caecilius concludes that one should not rashly pronounce on uncertain matters, 273. It is not the authority of the disputant but the truth of the argument itself that must be considered, 279.—On religion considered in general, VI, 366, and VII, 1011.

Christian Religion.—It is shown that the Christian religion is supported by the sacred writings of the Old Testament, I, 781.—That the apostles received from Christ, and the churches from the apostles, sound teaching to be handed down to posterity, and that no teaching should be received from any other source, II, 31. Why the Church’s true doctrine is one, 40. What was handed down first is true and divine, 41. The Church’s continuous succession of bishops from the apostles is a firm testimony to the true faith, 44. Our teaching is true because it is certainly not condemned by the apostles but is indeed defended by them, 45. To discover truth, one must consult the apostolic churches, and above all that blessed Church upon which the apostles poured out their entire teaching together with their blood, 48. Marks of true doctrine, 55. Jacques Pamel’s synopsis of the book addressed to a senator who had turned from Christian religion to the service of idols, 1105. According to Caecilius in the *Octavius*, the Christians’ religion is foolish: they venerate a crucified man and the very instrument of his punishment. They are said to worship an ass’s head and to adore the very nature of their own parent. They are initiated by the murder of an infant and its blood, and in shameless darkness all mingle indiscriminately, their lot uncertain, 260. Whatever they worship, they strive greatly to conceal; they have no altars, no temples, no recognizable images. Their God, like that of the Jews, is said to be one; yet, although they can neither see nor show him, they nevertheless judge him troublesome, restless, and perversely inquisitive, 263. They also assert that the whole world will be burned, and, after the resurrection of our bodies, promise the just an eternity of most blessed life and the unjust an eternity of the greatest punishments, 266. Finally Caecilius concludes that the new religion must be rejected, 273.—The arguments of pagans against the truth of the Christian religion are examined, V, 420.—On the establishment of the Christian religion, VI, 750 ff.—The arguments by which Lactantius demonstrates that the Christian religion alone is true are considered, VII, 1022, 1055. How Lactantius asserts and confirms the truth of the Christian religion from Christ’s genuine miracles, which had been foretold by our sacred writings and by other seers, 1044.—Selected decrees of Theodosius concerning religion, XIII, 521.—St. Ambrose wrote five books on the faith of Christians, XVI, 523.—St. Augustine’s four books *On Christian Doctrine*, XXIV, 15.—St. Augustine’s one book *On True Religion*, XXXIV, 121.—On certain dogmas of the Christian religion in St. Augustine’s work entitled *Eighty-Three Diverse Questions*, one book, XL, 11; one book on the eight questions of Dulcitius, 148; two books of diverse questions addressed to Simplicianus, 101. St. Augustine’s Book of Twenty-One Sentences, 725. Dialogue of Sixty-Five Questions, 733. Gennadius of Marseille’s book on ecclesiastical dogmas, LVIII, 979.—Taio’s five books of sentences, LXXX, 931–989.—St. Isidore of Seville’s three books of sentences, LXXXIII, 537–736.—Testimonies of the holy doctor from divine Scripture and the Fathers, LXXXIII, 1203–1217. St. Isidore’s work on ecclesiastical dogmas, 1227.—Regino of Prüm on ecclesiastical disciplines and the Christian religion, CXXXII, 175.—Peter Alphonsus’s dialogues, CLVII, 531.—A Jew’s disputation with a Christian, by Gilbert, Abbot of Westminster, CLIX, 342.—Robert Pullen’s eight books of sentences, CLXXXVI, 639.—Peter of Poitiers’s five books of sentences, CCXI, 783–1276.

Pagan Religion.—The arguments by which Tertullian demonstrates the falsehood of the Gentiles’ religion and of all their gods, I, 1094, 1102, 1113. On Gentile temples and sacrifices, 1138.—Every nation, and afterwards the Romans, worshipped its gods in such a manner that through their worship they attained the supreme empire over the whole world, III, 250. Roman auspices and auguries, unhappily abandoned and happily observed, 253. The impious rashness of Theodore, Diagoras, and Protagoras, who wished either entirely to abolish or at least to weaken the religion of the gods, is utterly intolerable. But, according to the defender of the gods, still less tolerable is the furtive, light-shunning race of Christians who despise the gods, 256. It is clearly shown that worship of the gods has always been foolish and impious, since the earliest mortals venerated their own kings, illustrious leaders, and inventors of arts, on account of their eminent deeds, just as if they were gods, 297, 331, 550, 555, 566. Octavius confirms this through Euhemerus, Prodicus, Persaeus, and Alexander the Great, who recount the gods’ native lands, birthdays, and tombs. He further describes the gods’ grievous ends, destinies, and funerals. Moreover, he ridicules the absurd and filthy nonsense which pagans retail about the form, figure, and deeds of their gods, 299, 558, 562, 566, 573, 577, 582, 585. By a brief survey Octavius shows how many ridiculous, obscene, and cruel rites were observed in celebrating the mysteries of certain gods, 312, 508, 511, 631, 635, 638, 642. Octavius shows that Caecilius wrongly boasts that the Romans, who gained dominion over the whole world, attained it through duly observing superstitions of this kind, 315, 589, 592, 595, 600, 602. Demons are the authors and agents of pagan religion, 615, 618, 622, 625.—They stir up the Gentiles’ hatred against Christians, III, 323.—St. Cyprian’s book on the vanity of idols, IV, 565, 1091. On Cyprian’s book on the vanity of idols, 1011, 1091. On the origin of idolatry, 1024; VI, 253 ff.—The arguments by which Arnobius demonstrates the falsehood of pagan religion, V, 499, 516, 524, 551, 564, 578, 590, 596. On Gentile temples, 609. On statues and images of the gods, 616. On Gentile sacrifices, 633, 651.—Pagan religion is proven false from the origin, life, and deeds of the gods, VI, 156, 160, 165, 184, 186, 190, 192, 201, 209, 215, 230.—On the error of those who venerate images, VIII, 407.—St. Eusebius of Vercelli’s treatise on the error of profane religions, comprising thirty chapters, XII, 981.—In *The City of God*, St. Augustine proves that pagan religion greatly harms humankind, XLI, 47, 111.—Prudentius’s two-book poem against Symmachus, LX, 111, 117.

HOLY SATURDAY.—Sermon of Saint Augustine on Holy Saturday, XLVI, 821.—Hymn of Marius, Bishop of Hydruntum, for Great Saturday, XCVI, 1345.—Homily of Blessed Rabanus Maurus on the Holy Saturday of Easter, CX, 33. SABELLIANS.—Against the Sabellians Novatian proves from Scripture that the Son is one and the Father another, III, 936. The same author answers well the text, “I and the Father are one,” which they advanced in their own favor, 938. Novatian proves that the saying “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” likewise does nothing for the Sabellians, 940.—Dialogue of Vigilius of Thapsus against Arians, Sabellians, and others, LXII, 179.

PRIEST.—That priests of the Lord must not presume to swear, as the common people are accustomed to do, or be compelled to do so, 845.—Refutation of those who deny that, in Cyprian, bishops are distinguished from presbyters by divine right, IV, 21.—On the chief duties and virtues of the priesthood, XVI, 879.—Letter on the institution of the life of clerics, XXII, 52. Of Saint Jerome. On presbyters and deacons, Saint Jerome’s Letter 146, ibid. On priestly dress, Letter 64 of Saint Jerome, XXII.—Rules given to clerics by Saint Augustine, XXXII, 1447.—Verdict of Veranus concerning the chastity of priests, LXXII, 701.—Books of Saint Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, LXXVII, 13–124. See ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINE.—Burchard’s canonical statutes concerning the office of priests, CXL, 1067.—Anselm’s *Scandal of Priests*, CLVIII, 555.—Yvo’s sermon on the significance of priestly vestments, CLXII, 519.—Hugh of Saint Mary, *On Royal Power and Priestly Dignity*, CLXIII, 939.—Instruction for a priest, CLXXXIV, 771.

PRIESTHOOD.—Saint Ambrose, *On Priestly Dignity*, XVII, 567.—How arduous and perilous is the office of presbyter and deacon: Saint Augustine’s Letter 21, XXXIII.—Agobard’s book *On the Privilege and Right of the Priesthood*, CIV, 127.—Short work of Saint Peter Damian *On the Dignity of the Priesthood*, CXLV, 491.—Honorius’s *Supreme Glory concerning the Apostle and Augustus*, CLXXII, 1257.—See ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINE.

SACRAMENTS.—Saint Cyprian did not reject sacraments administered in the Church by evil persons, IV, 35.—The sacraments of Christians are more divine and earlier than those of the Jews, XVI, 420, 438.—Various local customs in the celebration of sacraments: Letters 54 and 55 of Saint Augustine, XXXIII.—Book of Sacraments of the Roman Church by Saint Leo the Great, LV, 21.—Short work of Saint Peter Damian on the mean dress of churchmen, CXLV, 518.—Short treatise of Bonizo of Piacenza on the sacraments, CL, 857.—Anselm of Canterbury, *On the Diversity of Sacraments*, CLVIII, 547.—*The Ring*, or dialogue of a Christian and a Jew concerning the sacraments of faith, by Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, CLIX, 342.—Hugh of Saint Victor, *On the Sacraments of the Natural and Written Law*, CLXXVI, 17–172. *On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith*, 173–617.—Master Bandinus’s [Col. 1256] book *On Ecclesiastical Sacraments*, CXCII, 1089.—See LITURGY.

SACRIFICE.—Saint Cyprian’s teaching on sacrifice, IV, 71.—Treatise of Saint Zeno on the threefold kind of sacrifices, XI, 362.—Three faults of Christian offerings, XIV, 329. On the endowments of an offering, 331.—Saint Fulgentius’s book to Monimus on the offering of sacrifice, LXV, 179. See MASS.—Yvo’s short work *On the Harmony of the Old and New Sacrifice*, as its author himself entitled it, CLXII, 535.

THE WORLD.—Anonymous treatise *On the Twelve Abuses of the World*, IV, 869.—One book of Saint Ambrose, *On Flight from the World*, XIV, 567. What it is to flee the world, 578. Why we must flee from it, 581. How, although we may be held here in body, we can—and indeed ought—to flee in mind, 590. *On Contempt for the World*, Letter 145 of Saint Jerome, XXII.—Saint Augustine, *On Contempt for the World*, XL, 1215.—The same author, *On Contempt for Temporal Things*, XLVI, 971.—Paraenetic letter of Saint Eucherius, *On Contempt for the World and Secular Philosophy*, L, 711.—Rule of Saint Leander of Seville, or book *On the Instruction of Virgins and Contempt for the World*, LXXII, 871.—Short work of Saint Peter Damian, *On Contempt for the World*, CXLV, 251. *On the Fading Glory of the World and Contempt for the Age*, 807.—Poem of the monk Roger on contempt for the world, CL, 1431.—Letter of Bernard the Carthusian on flight from the world, CLIII, 883. Letter of John the Carthusian on flight from the world, 899.—Exhortation of Saint Anselm of Canterbury to contempt for temporal things and desire for eternal things, CLVIII, 677. His poem on contempt for the world, 687. Another, 687.—Hugh of Saint Victor, *On the Vanity of the World*, CLXXVI, 702.—Innocent III, *On Contempt for the World*, CCXVII, 701.
